representations.normalized:
Consider bosonic string theory on three-dimensional anti–de Sitter space AdS₃, formulated as a Wess–Zumino–Witten (WZW) sigma model with target the group manifold SU(1,1) ≃ SL(2,ℝ) (or its universal cover) at level k. The unitary irreducible representations of the affine sl(2,ℝ) current algebra include the principal continuous series and the highest/lowest-weight discrete series D±_j parameterized by a spin j > 0. A standard current-algebra (no-ghost) analysis imposes the unitarity restriction j < k/2 on physical states, but classical string motions on AdS₃ suggest the existence of physically sensible string states whose effective spin lies in the range cut off by this bound (corresponding to masses above the AdS curvature scale).

(a) Develop a treatment of the classical SU(1,1) WZW model — including the analysis of classical string trajectories on AdS₃ and a Gawędzki-style path-integral quantization — that recovers the physically expected string states with j ≥ k/2 (or otherwise reconciles unitarity with the appearance of such states above the AdS radius mass scale).

(b) In this framework, clarify the role played by the continuous-series representations of SL(2,ℝ) in the physical Hilbert space of the string.

(c) Implement explicit target-space boundary conditions at the conformal boundary of AdS₃ within the path-integral formulation, and determine whether the choice of such boundary conditions produces quantization ambiguities for the string analogous to the well-known boundary-condition ambiguities encountered when quantizing a relativistic point particle on AdS₃.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The questions raised about the SL(2,ℝ) WZW spectrum on AdS₃ were substantially resolved by Maldacena and Ooguri in "Strings in AdS₃ and the SL(2,R) WZW Model. Part 1: The Spectrum" (hep-th/0001053, 2000), which proposed and justified a Hilbert space containing both continuous-series and discrete-series representations (with the bound 1/2 < j < (k-1)/2 for discrete series) together with all spectrally-flowed images, thereby accommodating the long strings and resolving the j < k/2 puzzle. Part 2 (hep-th/0005183) showed modular invariance via the Euclidean black hole one-loop partition function, and Part 3 (hep-th/0111180) computed correlation functions. The classical and path-integral aspects, target-space boundary conditions, and role of continuous series are addressed in this body of work and subsequent literature.

representations.normalized:
Setting. Let $X$ be a Tychonoff topological space. The cellularity of $X$ is
$$c(X)=\sup\{|\mathcal A|:\mathcal A\text{ is a family of pairwise disjoint nonempty open subsets of }X\}+\aleph_0.$$

Let $\mathcal D$ denote the collection of families $\mathcal U$ of open subsets of $X$ whose union $\bigcup\mathcal U$ is dense in $X$, and let $\mathcal K\subseteq\mathcal D$ denote the subcollection consisting of those families $\mathcal U$ such that $\{U:U\in\mathcal U\}$ is an open cover of $X$.

The game $G_1(\mathcal K,\mathcal D)$ on $X$ is played in $\omega$ innings. In inning $n\in\omega$, player ONE chooses $\mathcal U_n\in\mathcal K$ and then player TWO chooses $U_n\in\mathcal U_n$. Player TWO wins if $\{U_n:n\in\omega\}\in\mathcal D$, i.e. $\bigcup_{n\in\omega}U_n$ is dense in $X$; otherwise player ONE wins.

Define the cardinal
$$\mathfrak j=\min\{\kappa:\text{for every Tychonoff space }X\text{ with }c(X)\ge\kappa,\ \text{ONE has a winning strategy in }G_1(\mathcal K,\mathcal D)\text{ on }X\}.$$

It is known that $\operatorname{cov}(\mathcal M)\le\mathfrak j\le\operatorname{non}(\mathrm{SMZ})$, where $\mathcal M$ is the ideal of meager subsets of the real line, $\operatorname{cov}(\mathcal M)$ is the least cardinality of a covering of $\mathbb R$ by meager sets, $\mathrm{SMZ}$ denotes the class of strong measure zero subsets of $\mathbb R$, and $\operatorname{non}(\mathrm{SMZ})$ is the least cardinality of a subset of $\mathbb R$ that is not strong measure zero.

Problem. Is $\mathfrak j$ provably (in ZFC) equal to one of the standard cardinal characteristics of the continuum?

Let $\mathrm{Diff}^r(\mathbb{T}^1)$ denote the group of orientation-preserving $C^r$ diffeomorphisms of the circle $\mathbb{T}^1=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$. For an irrational number $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, let $R_\alpha:\mathbb{T}^1\to\mathbb{T}^1$ denote the rigid rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha$, and define
\[
U_\alpha=\{\,f\in\mathrm{Diff}^\infty(\mathbb{T}^1):\ f\text{ is smoothly conjugate to }R_\alpha\,\}.
\]
Recall that $\alpha$ is of constant type if the partial quotients $(a_n)$ in its continued fraction expansion are bounded.

Identify a neighborhood of $0$ in the space of perturbations of $R_\alpha$ with a neighborhood in the Sobolev space $W^{4,p}(\mathbb{T}^1)$ via $f=R_\alpha+u$ with $u\in W^{4,p}(\mathbb{T}^1)$. It is known that, when $\alpha$ is of constant type, the set $U_\alpha$ is a neighborhood of $0$ in the topology of $W^{4,p}(\mathbb{T}^1)$ for every $p>1$.

Question: Does the same openness statement hold in the borderline case $p=1$? That is, when $\alpha$ is of constant type, is $U_\alpha$ a neighborhood of $0$ in the $W^{4,1}(\mathbb{T}^1)$ topology?

representations.normalized: Consider a firm that operates a multi-tier supply chain in which suppliers, manufacturers, transporters, and distributors are exposed to safety risks (e.g., workplace injuries, equipment failures, hazardous-material incidents, transportation accidents). Suppose the firm can choose to invest in a portfolio of safety interventions across its supply chain (training, audits, equipment upgrades, redesigned processes, supplier-selection criteria, monitoring technology, etc.), each with associated costs and probabilistic effects on the frequency and severity of safety incidents. Formulate a quantitative framework that takes as inputs the costs of safety interventions, the probability distributions of incidents, the direct and indirect financial consequences of incidents (medical, legal, regulatory, productivity, reputation, disruption, insurance), and the firm's discount rate and risk preferences, and that outputs the expected net present value or risk-adjusted return of the safety investment. Using such a framework, determine whether a positive "business case" can in general be established for proactively addressing safety throughout a supply chain — that is, whether there exist realistic parameter regimes (and, if so, characterize them) under which the expected discounted benefits of safety investments strictly exceed their costs. Provide either an explicit model and proof of conditions guaranteeing a positive business case, or a counterexample showing when safety investments fail this test.

Consider a construction project modeled as a sequence of phases (e.g., design, permitting, procurement, site preparation, workforce mobilization, regulatory approvals, financing). Let the project's true state of "construction readiness" be a latent binary variable R ∈ {0,1}, where R = 1 indicates that, if construction begins at the current time, the project will proceed without interruption through completion. Let X = (X_1, …, X_n) be a vector of observable, time-indexed project metrics ("candidate leading indicators") that can be measured prior to ground-breaking — for example, design completion percentage, RFI (request-for-information) closure rate, permit-approval status, supply-chain lead-time variance, contractor-bid coverage, labor availability index, weather-window forecasts, financing-disbursement timeliness, and stakeholder-alignment metrics.

Formulate and solve the following identification and decision problem:

(a) Identify a subset S ⊆ {1, …, n} of indicators and a decision rule f: ℝ^{|S|} → {start, delay} that maximizes the probability of correctly predicting R, i.e., that maximizes P(f(X_S) = start | R = 1) while controlling P(f(X_S) = start | R = 0) below a prescribed threshold α.

(b) Characterize, mathematically and quantitatively, which observable indicators X_i constitute the most informative "leading indicators" of construction readiness — that is, those with greatest predictive power for R measured a meaningful lead time τ > 0 before construction commencement — and provide ranking criteria (e.g., mutual information I(X_i; R), Granger-causal influence, or expected reduction in time-to-interruption) that minimize the probability of a premature start and maximize the probability of uninterrupted construction.

Provide both the identified set of best leading indicators and an associated decision/scoring framework.

representations.normalized:
Consider the level-$k$ Wess–Zumino–Witten model based on the non-compact group $SU(1,1)\cong SL(2,\mathbb R)$. Because the Cartan generator $J^3_0$ has a continuous, unbounded spectrum on the unitary representations (principal continuous, discrete highest/lowest weight, and their spectral-flow images), the naive characters $\chi(\tau)=\mathrm{Tr}\,q^{L_0-c/24}$ are divergent and degenerate, and one is forced to introduce a regulator by coupling a "magnetic field" $v\in\mathbb C$ to $J^3_0$, defining
$$\chi(\tau,v)\;=\;\mathrm{Tr}\Bigl(e^{2\pi i v J^3_0}\,q^{L_0-c/24}\Bigr).$$
These regulated characters carry a well-defined action of the modular group only when $v$ is transformed nontrivially, and for fixed $v\neq 0$ the resulting torus partition function fails to be modular invariant.

(a) Give an intrinsic physical interpretation of the parameter $v$: in particular, determine whether $v$ can be consistently understood as a continuous holonomy / twist of the $U(1)$ subgroup generated by $J^3$ around one of the cycles of the worldsheet torus, in analogy with the continuous twists used in parafermionic coset constructions and in the $SL(2,\mathbb R)/U(1)$ two-dimensional Euclidean black hole.

(b) Assuming such an interpretation, decide whether modular invariance of the SL(2,R) WZW partition function can be recovered by an appropriate integration (or summation) over $v$ together with a conjugate variable, and exhibit the measure and contour that achieve this, producing a modular invariant partition function with the correct spectrum of unitary representations (including spectral flow sectors).

Subsequent work by Maldacena, Ooguri and Schwimmer (hep-th/0001063) and Maldacena–Ooguri Part 2 (hep-th/0005183) computed the one-loop partition function of strings on thermal AdS_3 / Euclidean BTZ and showed that the regulator coupled to J^3_0 is naturally identified with a chemical potential / continuous holonomy of the timelike U(1)⊂SL(2,R) around the torus cycles. Modular invariance is achieved by treating this variable on the same footing as τ and integrating over it with the appropriate non-holomorphic measure, producing a modular invariant Z(τ,τ̄;u,ū) and reproducing the SL(2,R) spectrum including spectral flow. The interpretation as a continuous twist analogous to parafermionic / 2d Euclidean black hole constructions is thus confirmed.

For a topological space $X$, let $C_p(X)$ denote the space of all continuous real-valued functions on $X$ endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence (i.e., the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^X$ with the product topology). A topological space $Y$ is said to have the Reznichenko property (also called the weak Fréchet–Urysohn property) if for every subset $A \subseteq Y$ and every point $y \in \overline{A} \setminus A$, there exists a countably infinite, pairwise disjoint family $\mathcal{F}$ of finite subsets of $A$ such that for every neighborhood $U$ of $y$ in $Y$, one has $U \cap F \neq \emptyset$ for all but finitely many $F \in \mathcal{F}$.

Let $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ denote the Baire space, that is, the set of all functions from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ endowed with the product topology (where $\mathbb{N}$ carries the discrete topology).

Determine whether $C_p(\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}})$ has the Reznichenko property.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered affirmatively: it is known that $C_p(X)$ has the Reznichenko (weak Fréchet–Urysohn) property whenever $X$ is an analytic space, and the Baire space $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is analytic. This is reflected both in the compilation listing it as solved and in subsequent literature on the Pytkeev and Reznichenko properties of $C_p(X)$.

(a) Identify and rigorously characterize the set of soft skills that are causally associated with the success of project leaders across different regions and cultural environments around the globe. In particular, determine which soft skills are universally predictive of leadership success and which are culture-specific, and quantify their relative contributions to successful outcomes.

(b) Design and validate an assessment methodology (for example, a battery of instruments, simulations, behavioral interviews, situational judgment tests, or observational rubrics) that reliably measures a candidate's ability to (i) adjust to unfamiliar conditions and customs in regions different from their own, and (ii) lead a project successfully under such cross-cultural conditions. The methodology must have demonstrated reliability, construct validity, and predictive validity for project outcomes across diverse cultural contexts.

Let $AdS_3$ denote three-dimensional anti–de Sitter space, the maximally symmetric Lorentzian manifold of constant negative curvature in three dimensions. Quotients of $AdS_3$ by suitable discrete subgroups of its isometry group yield the family of three-dimensional black holes (the BTZ black holes), which have a rich causal structure including horizons and (after conformal compactification) timelike boundaries, but no asymptotically flat region.

(a) Provide a complete worldsheet formulation of string theory propagating in these three-dimensional black-hole backgrounds (i.e., on the relevant $AdS_3$ quotients, possibly times an internal compact CFT), including:
  (i) a precise definition of the worldsheet conformal field theory (e.g., as an orbifold of an $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$-WZW-type model or otherwise),
  (ii) a determination of the physical spectrum (including winding/spectral-flow sectors) free of negative-norm states,
  (iii) a modular-invariant one-loop partition function,
in a form suitable for analyzing the quantum dynamics of strings in the black-hole geometry and, in particular, addressing the black-hole evaporation problem.

(b) Formulate string theory on $AdS_3$ (and on the associated three-dimensional black holes) supported by pure non-perturbative Ramond–Ramond flux through $AdS_3$ rather than by Neveu–Schwarz–Neveu–Schwarz $H$-flux (torsion). Concretely, construct a tractable worldsheet (or equivalent) description of strings in an $AdS_3 \times \mathcal{M}$ background whose only flux through $AdS_3$ is RR, compute its spectrum, and extend the construction to the corresponding RR-supported three-dimensional black-hole backgrounds.

Substantial progress has been made on both sub-questions. The NS–NS case is well-developed: the worldsheet $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$-WZW description, no-ghost theorem, spectral-flowed spectrum, modular-invariant partition function on thermal $AdS_3$/BTZ, and a black-hole/string transition in $AdS_3$ have all been established. Nevertheless, a fully controlled quantization of strings in RR-supported $AdS_3$ black holes and a satisfactory worldsheet account of black-hole evaporation remain open.

Let $B=\{B(s,t)\}_{s,t\ge 0}$ be a two-parameter Brownian sheet taking values in $\mathbb{R}^d$; that is, $B$ is a centered Gaussian process with independent components and covariance
$$\operatorname{Cov}(B_i(s,t), B_j(u,v)) = \min(s,u)\,\min(t,v)\,\delta_{i,j}, \qquad 1\le i,j\le d.$$
For each fixed $s>0$, consider the zero set of the corresponding slice:
$$Z_s := B^{-1}\{0\} \cap (\{s\}\times(0,\infty)) = \{(s,t): t>0,\ B(s,t)=0\}.$$
Assume $d\in\{2,3\}$. Prove or disprove: there exists a single $\mathbb{P}$-null event $N$ such that, on the complement of $N$, the set $Z_s$ is finite for every $s>0$ simultaneously.

A complete solution should provide a framework or methodology, supported by quantitative or empirical evidence, showing the schedule reduction achievable and demonstrating that the proposed improvements maintain or improve performance against the safety, quality, and risk constraints.

Let $H_3^+ = SL(2,\mathbb{C})/SU(2)$ denote Euclidean three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, viewed as a target space for a WZW-type string sigma model at level $k$. Computing the worldsheet torus partition function on $H_3^+$ via a rigorous path-integral approach (with modular parameter $\tau$ of the worldsheet torus and a twist/holonomy parameter $v$) yields a one-loop expression that is not invariant under the modular group $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ acting on $\tau$.

(a) Provide a conceptual justification, or show that no such justification exists, for accepting this path-integral partition function on $H_3^+$ as a satisfactory definition of the one-loop free energy even though it fails to be modular invariant for generic finite $v$.

(b) Determine what consequences this has for the analytically continued partition function of string theory on Lorentzian $AdS_3$ (the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ or $SU(1,1)$ WZW model): namely, decide whether a modular-invariant partition function for strings on $AdS_3$ can be constructed that reduces to (or is consistent with) the $H_3^+$ path-integral result, and identify the spectrum (continuous and discrete series representations, including spectral-flow sectors) that must be included to achieve modular invariance for every finite value of $v$.

For each $s > 0$, define the slice double-point set
$$Y_d(s) := \{(t_1, t_2) \in \mathbb{R}_+^2 : t_1 \ne t_2,\ B(s,t_1) = B(s,t_2)\}.$$
Let $d \in \{4, 5\}$. Does there exist an event of probability one on which $Y_d(s)$ is a finite set for every $s > 0$ simultaneously?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as an explicit open problem in Khoshnevisan's survey on slices of Brownian sheets. A web search did not surface any subsequent paper resolving the question for $d \in \{4,5\}$; related work (Dalang and others on multiple points in critical dimensions) addresses different but related questions and does not appear to settle this slice-finiteness statement.

Devise a methodology together with a finite set of standard, well-defined quantitative metrics with the following properties:

1. Measurability: each metric is defined by an explicit data-collection procedure and computation formula that can be applied uniformly across construction projects of varying type, size, and delivery method.
2. Categorization: the metrics collectively partition Quality performance into meaningful, non-overlapping categories (for example, design quality, workmanship quality, rework, defects, conformance, and customer satisfaction).
3. Benchmarking: the metrics allow consistent comparison of Quality performance across projects, organizations, and time, including the construction of industry-wide reference distributions and percentile rankings.
4. Improvement driver: the metrics are predictive or diagnostic in the sense that targeted changes in operational practices produce measurable, statistically significant changes in metric values.

Specify the methodology, define the metrics, and demonstrate that the resulting system satisfies the four properties above.

A connected topological space X is called aspherical if its higher homotopy groups vanish, i.e. π_k(X) = 0 for all k ≥ 2 (equivalently, its universal cover is contractible). Let G be a (discrete) group, and let M and N be closed aspherical manifolds (compact, without boundary, topological manifolds) whose fundamental groups satisfy π_1(M) ≅ G ≅ π_1(N). Determine whether the following two statements always hold:

(a) M and N are homeomorphic.
(b) Every homotopy equivalence f : M → N is homotopic to a homeomorphism.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is the Borel Conjecture, one of the central open problems in geometric topology. It has been established in many special cases (e.g. by Farrell–Jones for manifolds whose fundamental groups are word-hyperbolic or CAT(0), and in low dimensions), but the general conjecture remains open as of 2026.

Let $\hat B$ denote space-time white noise on $[0,1]^2$, i.e., the formal mixed derivative of a $d$-dimensional standard Brownian sheet $B = \{B(t,x):\,(t,x)\in[0,1]^2\}$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Consider the system of nonlinear hyperbolic stochastic partial differential equations
$$\frac{\partial^2 u^i}{\partial t\,\partial x}(t,x) \;=\; b^i(u(t,x)) \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^d \sigma^{ij}(u(t,x))\,\hat B^j(t,x), \qquad 1\le i\le d,$$
on $(t,x)\in[0,1]^2$, with reasonable (e.g., vanishing on the axes) boundary conditions, where $b:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is bounded and Borel measurable and $\sigma:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ is bounded, $C^\infty$, and strongly elliptic (i.e., there exists $c>0$ such that $\sigma(y)\sigma(y)^\top\succeq c\,I_d$ for all $y\in\mathbb{R}^d$).

For the $d$-dimensional Brownian sheet $B$, suppose one has established results of the following form describing the geometry of its "slices" (the one-parameter processes $t\mapsto B(t,x_0)$ and $x\mapsto B(t_0,x)$ for fixed coordinates) and various exceptional-set theorems (for example, characterizations via potential theory or Hausdorff dimension of random sets where the slices exhibit prescribed exceptional behavior).

Question: Do these same slice and exceptional-set results extend, in the same form, to the solution $u=(u^1,\ldots,u^d)$ of the nonlinear multiplicative-noise system above?

Consider an industrial organization whose safety performance over time is modeled by a stochastic process S(t), where S(t) denotes a chosen safety metric (for example, the rate of recordable incidents per unit of exposure hours) at time t. Suppose the organization implements an intervention I at time t_0 consisting of an enhanced culture of rigorous operational discipline (also termed "performance excellence"), characterized by consistent, deliberate, and verifiable execution of established procedures, standards, and protocols throughout all levels of the organization.

Define a "sustainable step change" in safety performance to be the existence of constants Δ > 0 and T > 0 such that, after the intervention,

  E[S(t) | I applied at t_0] ≤ E[S(t) | no intervention] − Δ for all t ≥ t_0 + T,

with the inequality persisting indefinitely (i.e., the improvement does not regress to baseline over arbitrarily long time horizons).

Question: Identify general conditions under which the implementation of an enhanced culture of rigorous operational discipline is sufficient to produce a sustainable step change, in the above sense, in the safety performance metric S(t). Equivalently, formulate and prove (or disprove) a theorem giving necessary and sufficient conditions on the intervention I and on the organizational dynamics governing S(t) under which such a persistent improvement Δ exists.

Let n be a positive integer. Recall that a group G is called an n-dimensional Poincaré duality group (a PD(n)-group) if it is of type FP, satisfies H^i(G; ZG) = 0 for i ≠ n, and H^n(G; ZG) ≅ Z. A topological space X is aspherical if its higher homotopy groups π_i(X) vanish for all i ≥ 2.

Question: Is it true that, for every positive integer n, a finitely presented group G is an n-dimensional Poincaré duality group if and only if G is isomorphic to the fundamental group of some closed aspherical n-dimensional topological manifold?
representations.original:
Let n be a positive integer. Recall that a group G is called an n-dimensional Poincaré duality group (a PD(n)-group) if it is of type FP, satisfies H^i(G; ZG) = 0 for i ≠ n, and H^n(G; ZG) ≅ Z. A topological space X is aspherical if its higher homotopy groups π_i(X) vanish for all i ≥ 2.

Question: Is it true that, for every positive integer n, a finitely presented group G is an n-dimensional Poincaré duality group if and only if G is isomorphic to the fundamental group of some closed aspherical n-dimensional topological manifold?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The "only if" direction (the Wall/PD(n) realization problem) is widely regarded as open in general. It is known to hold for n = 2 (Eckmann–Linnell–Müller) and partial results exist for n = 3 (Kropholler–Thomas; further progress via geometrization). For n ≥ 4, Davis constructed PD(n) groups that are not fundamental groups of closed aspherical manifolds in some categories (e.g., groups without finite K(G,1) complexes), and the general realization question remains open and is closely tied to the Borel conjecture. The "if" direction is classical and known.

Background. For the classical orthogonal polynomial families (Jacobi, Laguerre, Hermite), Stieltjes proved that the zeros admit an electrostatic interpretation: namely, the zeros of the n-th polynomial can be realized as the equilibrium configuration of n unit positive charges confined to a fixed real interval (or the real line) which mutually repel via a logarithmic Coulomb potential and which interact with an explicit external field generated by fixed charges and/or a long-range confining potential determined by the weight function. More precisely, if w(x) = e^{-V(x)} is the weight and x_1,…,x_n are the zeros, then (x_1,…,x_n) is a critical point of the energy
   E(t_1,…,t_n) = sum_{i<j} log(1/|t_i - t_j|) + (1/2) sum_i V(t_i).

Problem. Identify and construct electrostatic models for other families of polynomials beyond the classical Jacobi, Laguerre, and Hermite cases. That is: for a given family of polynomials {P_n}_{n≥0} (for example, semiclassical orthogonal polynomials, Sobolev-type orthogonal polynomials, multiple orthogonal polynomials, exceptional orthogonal polynomials, or Heine–Stieltjes polynomials), produce a configuration space, a system of mutually interacting (logarithmic) charges, and an explicit external field Φ such that the zeros of P_n appear exactly as an equilibrium (critical point of the total energy) of this charge system. Determine for which families such a model exists, give an explicit formula for the external field Φ in terms of the data defining the family, and characterize the type of equilibrium (minimum, saddle, etc.) attained by the zeros.

Substantial progress has been made: electrostatic models have been constructed for semiclassical weights, multiple orthogonal polynomials (Hermite–Padé type II), Laguerre–Sobolev and other Sobolev-type polynomials, and quasi-orthogonal polynomials, via second-order ODE techniques. A fully general framework that covers all families of interest (including, e.g., exceptional orthogonal polynomials and arbitrary nonclassical settings) and that characterizes the nature of the equilibrium is still being actively developed, so the broad problem remains only partially solved.

Consider a large-scale construction project staffed by a craft labor workforce (e.g., electricians, welders, pipefitters, carpenters, ironworkers). Suppose the demographic composition of available craft labor undergoes major shifts, characterized by parameters such as age distribution (including a wave of retirements producing a so-called demographic "cliff"), experience level distribution, gender composition, ethnic composition, and entry rates of new apprentices. Define the following project-level performance metrics as functions of the workforce demographic state over the life of a project:

1. Labor availability: the fraction of required craft positions that can be filled at each phase.
2. Productivity: output per craft labor hour, possibly measured against a baseline benchmark.
3. Safety: incident rates per worker-hour (e.g., OSHA recordables, lost-time injuries).
4. Project cost: total realized cost relative to budgeted cost, including overruns due to schedule slip, rework, and wage premia.

Quantify, ideally through a predictive model calibrated to empirical data, how each of these four metrics responds to major shifts in craft labor demographics. Specifically:
(a) Identify the functional relationships (or statistical estimates thereof) between demographic-shift variables and each of the four performance metrics.
(b) Determine whether there exists a critical demographic regime — a "craft labor cliff" — beyond which one or more of these performance metrics degrades sharply (i.e., a threshold or phase-transition-like effect).
(c) Provide estimates of the magnitude of impact for representative shift scenarios.

Consider a large-scale construction project staffed by a craft labor workforce (e.g., electricians, welders, pipefitters, carpenters, ironworkers). Suppose the demographic composition of available craft labor undergoes major shifts, characterized by parameters such as age distribution (including a wave of retirements producing a so-called demographic "cliff"), experience level distribution, gender composition, ethnic composition, and entry rates of new apprentices. Define the following project-level performance metrics as functions of the workforce demographic state over the life of a project:

1. Labor availability: the fraction of required craft positions that can be filled at each phase.
2. Productivity: output per craft labor hour, possibly measured against a baseline benchmark.
3. Safety: incident rates per worker-hour (e.g., OSHA recordables, lost-time injuries).
4. Project cost: total realized cost relative to budgeted cost, including overruns due to schedule slip, rework, and wage premia.

Quantify, ideally through a predictive model calibrated to empirical data, how each of these four metrics responds to major shifts in craft labor demographics. Specifically:
(a) Identify the functional relationships (or statistical estimates thereof) between demographic-shift variables and each of the four performance metrics.
(b) Determine whether there exists a critical demographic regime — a "craft labor cliff" — beyond which one or more of these performance metrics degrades sharply (i.e., a threshold or phase-transition-like effect).
(c) Provide estimates of the magnitude of impact for representative shift scenarios.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is a broad applied/industry research prompt rather than a precise mathematical conjecture, and no definitive resolution exists. Industry bodies (e.g., the Construction Industry Institute, Associated General Contractors of America) and academic studies continue to investigate craft labor shortages, aging workforce effects, and productivity/safety impacts, but no closed-form or universally accepted quantitative answer has been established. The problem remains an active area of empirical investigation.

Background. For many classical families of polynomials $\{p_n\}$ whose zeros lie on the real line (e.g., Jacobi, Laguerre, Hermite, and more generally orthogonal polynomials with respect to a weight on $\mathbb{R}$), there is a well-known electrostatic interpretation: the $n$ zeros $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $p_n$ are the equilibrium configuration of $n$ unit positive point charges confined to an interval (or the real line), interacting through a logarithmic (two-dimensional Coulomb) potential $-\sum_{i<j}\log|x_i-x_j|$, in the presence of an external field $Q(x)$ determined by the weight (often with additional fixed charges at the endpoints). Equivalently, $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ minimizes the energy functional
$$E(t_1,\dots,t_n)=-\sum_{i<j}\log|t_i-t_j|+\sum_{i=1}^n Q(t_i)$$
over the prescribed real interval.

Problem. Suppose $\{p_n\}$ is a family of polynomials (for instance, polynomials orthogonal with respect to a varying or complex-valued weight, Sobolev-orthogonal polynomials, or solutions of a second-order linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients) whose zeros are not all real but include genuinely complex zeros $z_1,\dots,z_n\in\mathbb{C}$. Determine the appropriate electrostatic model for these complex zeros. Specifically:

(a) Identify the charges to be placed at the zeros (their signs, magnitudes, and whether additional fixed "external" charges or "partner" charges in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{z_1,\dots,z_n\}$ must be introduced).

(b) Identify the ambient set $S\subset\mathbb{C}$ on which the movable charges are constrained to lie (e.g., a system of analytic arcs, a level set of a potential, or the full complex plane).

(c) Identify the extremal principle (energy functional, min-max saddle-point condition, or critical-point/equilibrium condition) such that $(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ is exactly its critical configuration.

The goal is to produce a model that, in the limit where all zeros become real, reduces to the classical real-line electrostatic equilibrium description.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question of giving an electrostatic interpretation of complex zeros of polynomials has seen significant partial progress since it was posed. General critical-point ("equilibrium with partner charges") interpretations have been developed for broad classes of semiclassical and Sobolev-type orthogonal polynomials, and electrostatic models for zeros of Laguerre–Sobolev and perturbed Laguerre polynomials, as well as discrete orthogonal polynomials, have been obtained. However, a unified extremal (energy-minimization) electrostatic model covering all relevant families with complex zeros — in particular for Type I multiple orthogonal polynomials — is still cited as an open direction.

Specifically, propose a formal framework (mathematical, decision-theoretic, stochastic, or otherwise quantitative) for planning and executing complex projects—particularly in unfamiliar or highly uncertain environments—such that the framework: (i) yields quantifiable predictions of project outcomes (e.g., schedule, cost, scope, risk) with calibrated uncertainty; (ii) provides a step-change improvement in predictability over heuristic, expertise-driven approaches; (iii) is robust to novel settings where historical analogs are limited; and (iv) admits empirical validation criteria by which its predictive accuracy can be tested against observed project results. Fix real parameters $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>-1$ and set
$$w(x)=|x|^{\gamma}(1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta},\qquad x\in[-1,1].$$
For each positive integer $n$, let $p_{2n}$ be the monic polynomial of degree $2n$ (unique up to normalization) determined by the Angelesco-type multiple orthogonality conditions
$$\int_{-1}^{0} p_{2n}(x)\,x^{k}\,w(x)\,dx \;=\; \int_{0}^{1} p_{2n}(x)\,x^{k}\,w(x)\,dx \;=\; 0,\qquad k=0,1,\dots,n-1.$$
It is known that under these conditions $p_{2n}$ has exactly $n$ simple zeros $\{x_1^{-},\dots,x_n^{-}\}$ in $(-1,0)$ and exactly $n$ simple zeros $\{x_1^{+},\dots,x_n^{+}\}$ in $(0,1)$.

Consider the following electrostatic model. Place unit movable positive charges at $n$ points $t_1,\dots,t_n$ in an interval $I$, subject to:
 (i) mutual logarithmic repulsion $\sum_{i<j}\log\frac{1}{|t_i-t_j|}$;
 (ii) an external field generated by fixed charges of magnitude $\alpha/2$ at $1$, $\beta/2$ at $-1$, and $\gamma/2$ at $0$ (each contributing a logarithmic potential);
 (iii) an external field generated by $n$ fixed charges, each of weight $1/2$, placed at the zeros of $p_{2n}$ lying in the interval other than $I$.

Question: Is it true that for every $n\ge 1$ and all admissible $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>-1$, the configuration $\{x_1^{+},\dots,x_n^{+}\}$ minimizes (equivalently, is a critical point of) the total energy of the above model on $I=(0,1)$, and simultaneously the configuration $\{x_1^{-},\dots,x_n^{-}\}$ minimizes the corresponding energy on $I=(-1,0)$?

The problem was posed as open in 2005. Subsequent work (e.g., Martínez-Finkelshtein and collaborators, 2022) has developed electrostatic-partner frameworks and electrostatic interpretations for type II Hermite–Padé/Angelesco multiple orthogonal polynomials, but the search did not produce a clear, explicit confirmation that the specific Angelesco–Jacobi model on $[-1,0]\cup[0,1]$ with the precise charge assignment ($\alpha/2,\beta/2,\gamma/2$ and weight $1/2$ for opposite-interval zeros) has been rigorously established in full generality. The current status appears to be at least partially addressed but not conclusively resolved by accessible sources.

Consider a capital project delivery cycle, modeled as the end-to-end process by which large capital projects (e.g., construction, energy, or infrastructure projects) are planned, designed, executed, and commissioned. Let the "typical project organizational structure" denote the standard hierarchy of roles, decision rights, communication channels, contracting arrangements, and governance processes used to deliver such projects. Suppose that new and rapidly evolving technologies (for example, advanced digital tools, automation, data-driven analytics, and other next-generation innovations) become continuously available during the project lifecycle.

Identify and characterize the specific structural changes and the degree of organizational adaptability that a typical capital project's organizational structure must possess in order to:
(i) systematically absorb and benefit from new, rapidly changing technologies and next-generation innovations as they emerge, and
(ii) achieve a step change (i.e., a discontinuous, order-of-magnitude improvement rather than incremental gains) in productivity across the capital project delivery cycle.

Provide a framework that specifies the required organizational dimensions to be modified (e.g., decision rights, contracting models, team composition, governance, information flows), the metrics by which adaptability and productivity gains are measured, and the conditions under which the proposed changes guarantee the targeted step change in productivity.

Consider a capital construction project in which a sequence of deliverables must arrive at the job site before associated field work can proceed. The relevant deliverable categories are: (i) regulatory permits, (ii) completion of front-end engineering design (FEED), (iii) detailed engineering documents, (iv) piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs), (v) special engineering studies, (vi) procured items, (vii) tagged equipment, (viii) bulk materials, and (ix) specialty items. For each deliverable category k, let A_k denote its anticipated (baseline-planned) arrival date at the site and let R_k denote its realized arrival date; define the lateness as L_k = max(R_k − A_k, 0).

Develop a quantitative model that maps the vector of lateness values (L_1, …, L_9) — together with project-context covariates such as project size, contracting strategy, craft labor availability, and concurrent activity density — to four project outcome metrics:
• Safety performance (e.g., recordable incident rate per 200,000 work-hours),
• Quality performance (e.g., rework cost as a percentage of installed cost),
• Cost performance (cost growth relative to the approved control budget), and
• Schedule performance (schedule growth relative to the approved control schedule).

Specifically:
(a) Define a precise notion of "real cost" of a late deliverable that captures direct, indirect, and ripple-effect costs (e.g., crew standby, out-of-sequence work, rework, acceleration, overtime, productivity loss, and claims).
(b) Establish quantitative cause–effect relationships, with uncertainty bounds, between each L_k and each of the four outcome metrics, including any interaction effects among categories.
(c) Identify which deliverable categories have the largest marginal impact on each outcome and characterize threshold behavior (i.e., values of L_k beyond which outcomes deteriorate nonlinearly).

Provide either a closed-form analytical model, a validated statistical/econometric model, or a simulation-based framework, supported by empirical project data, that answers (a)–(c).

Consider a population of construction or industrial project teams that, during the execution of projects, may experience "near miss" events: incidents that did not result in injury, illness, or damage, but had the potential to do so. Suppose each team can implement a near-miss reporting system, which is a structured protocol for (i) recording near-miss events together with contextual data (time, location, task, contributing factors), (ii) classifying events according to a fixed taxonomy of hazard categories and root causes, (iii) aggregating the resulting data over time, and (iv) feeding insights back into safety training, procedures, and engineering controls.

Formalize and answer the following:

1. Define a quantitative framework that models the relationship between near-miss reporting activity and realized safety performance. Specifically, let N_t denote the rate of reported near misses per worker-hour in period t, let A_t denote the rate of recordable accidents per worker-hour in period t, and let L_t denote a vector of latent "safety gap" indicators (e.g., procedural noncompliance, training deficits, equipment hazards). Propose a statistical or dynamical model relating (N_t, L_t) to A_{t+1} that captures the leading-indicator role of near-miss data.

2. Given the model in (1), describe an estimation and inference procedure for identifying which latent gaps L_t most strongly predict subsequent accidents, using only near-miss report data and accident outcomes.

3. Design a reporting and feedback protocol (specifying what information must be collected, how reports are classified, how feedback is delivered to teams, and how the protocol updates over time) that, under the model in (1), is shown to reduce the expected accident rate E[A_{t+1}] over a finite planning horizon. Provide conditions under which the reduction is statistically significant.

4. Identify and analyze potential biases in near-miss reporting (e.g., underreporting, selection bias, observer effects) and propose mathematical corrections that yield consistent estimators of the true underlying near-miss rate and its relationship to accident risk.

Define an 'interface' as any point of required coordination, information exchange, or hand-off between two such teams, partners, or workforce groups, and measure the quality of an interface by attributes such as latency of information transfer, rate of rework caused by miscommunication, schedule slippage attributable to the interface, and associated cost overruns. Identify and characterize the practices, techniques, and processes—organizational, contractual, procedural, and technological—that most effectively improve the quality of these interfaces. In particular, determine which interventions (for example, integrated project delivery frameworks, common data environments, structured interface registers, cross-cultural training, co-location strategies, or governance protocols) yield statistically significant improvements in interface performance, and establish under what project conditions each intervention is most effective.

Let $W$ be a positive-definite matrix-valued weight function of size $N\times N$ on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, and let $\{P_n(x)\}_{n\ge 0}$ be the associated sequence of monic matrix orthogonal polynomials, namely $N\times N$ matrix polynomials satisfying
$$\int_I P_n(x)\,W(x)\,P_m(x)^*\,dx = \delta_{nm}\,H_n,\qquad H_n>0.$$
Assume that $\{P_n\}$ satisfies a second-order matrix differential equation of hypergeometric type
$$P_n''(x)\,A_2(x)+P_n'(x)\,A_1(x)+P_n(x)\,A_0(x)=\Lambda_n\,P_n(x),$$
where $A_2,A_1,A_0$ are fixed matrix polynomials of degrees at most $2,1,0$ respectively, and $\Lambda_n$ is an $N\times N$ matrix (a "matrix eigenvalue"), in analogy with the scalar classical (Hermite, Laguerre, Jacobi) case.

The zeros of $P_n$ are defined as those points $x\in\mathbb{C}$ for which $\det P_n(x)=0$.

Problem: Develop an electrostatic interpretation of these zeros. That is, exhibit an external field (depending on $W$) and an interaction law (analogous to the logarithmic repulsion between equal point charges in the scalar case) such that the zeros of $\det P_n(x)$, together with appropriate multiplicities or weights, are characterized as the equilibrium configuration of a finite system of charges in that field.

Consider a project modeled as a finite collection of activities A = {a_1, ..., a_n}, each activity a_i consuming a vector of resources r_i = (r_{i,1}, ..., r_{i,m}) ∈ R^m_{≥0} (e.g., materials, labor-hours, energy, time, capital) and producing a planned output o_i. Let the planned (or value-adding) resource consumption for activity a_i be p_i ∈ R^m_{≥0}, where p_{i,k} ≤ r_{i,k} for every resource k. Define the unintended waste of the project to be the vector W = Σ_{i=1}^n (r_i − p_i), or, given a unit-cost vector c ∈ R^m_{≥0}, the scalar waste w = c · W = Σ_{i,k} c_k (r_{i,k} − p_{i,k}).

The problem is to develop a rigorous, operational methodology that:
(1) specifies a procedure to identify, for each activity a_i, the value-adding baseline p_i (i.e., the minimum resource consumption required to produce o_i under stated process constraints);
(2) quantifies the resulting waste vector W and scalar waste w from observable project data, including a statistical estimator for W with explicit confidence bounds when r_i and p_i are subject to measurement uncertainty;
(3) provides a decomposition of w into interpretable categories (such as overproduction, waiting, transportation, over-processing, inventory, motion, defects) so that Σ of the category contributions equals w; and
(4) is consistent under aggregation, meaning that the methodology applied to any partition of A into sub-projects yields category sums that aggregate to the project-level values.

Construct such a methodology, prove its consistency under (4), and characterize conditions under which the estimator in (2) is unbiased and minimum-variance among a stated class.

Consider an organization that simultaneously oversees a finite collection of projects $P = \{p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n\}$, called a project portfolio. Each project $p_i$ is characterized by attributes such as cost, schedule, scope, risk, expected benefit, and resource requirements, and the organization seeks to allocate limited resources across $P$ over time so as to maximize aggregate value while controlling aggregate risk and maintaining strategic alignment.

Identify and justify the set of practices, techniques, technologies, and processes that are most effective for managing such a portfolio of projects. Specifically:

(a) Propose a quantitative framework (including measurable metrics and key performance indicators) for evaluating the performance of a portfolio management methodology, covering at minimum: project selection, prioritization, resource allocation, risk balancing, monitoring, and termination decisions.

(b) Within this framework, determine which combinations of decision-support techniques (e.g., scoring models, mathematical-programming-based selection, real-options valuation, Monte Carlo risk simulation, balanced scorecards, stage-gate processes, agile portfolio methods, AI/analytics tools) yield demonstrably superior portfolio outcomes, and characterize the conditions (industry, portfolio size, uncertainty level, organizational maturity) under which each combination is optimal.

(c) Provide criteria, supported by empirical or theoretical evidence, for declaring one set of portfolio-management practices ``most effective'' relative to another.

A closed smooth manifold $M$ is called aspherical if its universal cover is contractible (equivalently, $\pi_k(M)=0$ for all $k\ge 2$). A Riemannian metric $g$ on $M$ has positive scalar curvature if its scalar curvature function $\operatorname{Scal}_g$ is everywhere strictly positive.

Question: Does there exist a closed aspherical smooth manifold $M$ that admits a Riemannian metric of positive scalar curvature? Equivalently, prove or disprove the following conjecture: every closed aspherical smooth manifold fails to admit any Riemannian metric of positive scalar curvature.

Question: Does there exist a closed aspherical smooth manifold $M$ that admits a Riemannian metric of positive scalar curvature? Equivalently, prove or disprove the following conjecture: every closed aspherical smooth manifold fails to admit any Riemannian metric of positive scalar curvature.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture (often attributed to Gromov–Lawson) that no closed aspherical manifold admits a metric of positive scalar curvature is known to hold in dimensions ≤ 5 (dimension 3 by Gromov–Lawson and Perelman; dimensions 4 and 5 by recent work using generalized soap bubbles / μ-bubbles, e.g. Chodosh–Li and Gromov). It remains open in dimensions ≥ 6.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote a fixed class of finite positive Borel measures with compact support in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ (for instance, measures whose support is contained in a prescribed system of analytic arcs, possibly with prescribed total masses on each connected component). For a measure $\mu$ in $\mathcal{A}$, define its logarithmic energy with external field $\varphi$ (a fixed real-analytic function on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}\mu$) by
$$ E_\varphi(\mu) = \iint \log\frac{1}{|z-t|}\,d\mu(z)\,d\mu(t) + 2\int \varphi(z)\,d\mu(z). $$
Following the standard notion, call $\mu \in \mathcal{A}$ a continuous critical measure (with respect to $\varphi$ and the class $\mathcal{A}$) if for every smooth compactly supported vector field $h:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ that preserves the class $\mathcal{A}$ (i.e. the push-forwards $(\mathrm{id}+\varepsilon h)_*\mu$ lie in $\mathcal{A}$ to first order in $\varepsilon$), the first variation
$$ \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0} E_\varphi\bigl((\mathrm{id}+\varepsilon h)_*\mu\bigr) = 0. $$
Equivalently (under mild regularity), $\mu$ is a continuous critical measure if the function
$$ R(z) := \left(\int \frac{d\mu(t)}{z-t} + \varphi'(z)\right)^2 $$
extends as a single-valued analytic function on $\mathbb{C}$ minus a finite set.

The collection of all such continuous critical measures in $\mathcal{A}$ (for a fixed $\varphi$) forms a multi-parameter family, parametrized by the periods of the associated quadratic differential $R(z)\,dz^2$ on the relevant Riemann surface.

Problem: Provide a feasible (explicit and effective) description of this multi-parametric family of continuous critical measures — for example, a parametrization of the family by an explicit set of moduli (such as a complete set of period or homological parameters of $R(z)\,dz^2$) together with effective conditions characterizing which parameter values correspond to genuine positive measures in $\mathcal{A}$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Critical measures and their connection with quadratic differentials have been developed substantially since 2006 (work of Martínez-Finkelshtein, Rakhmanov, and collaborators, e.g. the 2009 paper on critical measures and Stieltjes polynomials, and subsequent work on electrostatic partners through 2022). These works give structural results (representation by quadratic differentials, period parametrizations in specific genera) but no general feasible description of the full multi-parametric family has been provided; the problem appears to remain open in its general form.

Consider a capital construction project modeled as a finite collection of activities executed over a bounded time horizon, each consuming material, energy, water, labor, and transportation resources, and producing measurable environmental outputs (e.g., greenhouse-gas emissions, waste streams, water discharge, noise, ecological disturbance). Define a "sustainability-focused construction practice" as any operational policy applied during the execution (construction) phase that alters resource consumption or environmental output without compromising scope, schedule, cost, safety, or quality constraints. Define a "sustainability metric" as a quantifiable indicator (with explicit units, measurement protocol, and baseline) used to evaluate the environmental, social, or economic performance of such a practice.

Problem: Identify and characterize the set of construction-phase sustainability practices that are most effective in improving overall project sustainability performance, and determine an associated set of metrics that:
(a) admit a well-defined measurement methodology during the construction phase;
(b) are sensitive to the adoption of the practices in (a);
(c) permit consistent comparison across projects of differing type, scale, and location; and
(d) can be aggregated into a defensible overall sustainability score for the construction phase.

Provide criteria for "effectiveness" (e.g., measurable reduction in a given environmental output per unit of work-in-place, normalized to baseline), a procedure for selecting and validating practices and metrics, and conditions under which the recommended practice–metric pairs remain robust across project contexts.

Define a "sustainability-focused construction practice" as any operational policy applied during the execution (construction) phase that alters resource consumption or environmental output without compromising scope, schedule, cost, safety, or quality constraints. Define a "sustainability metric" as a quantifiable indicator (with explicit units, measurement protocol, and baseline) used to evaluate the environmental, social, or economic performance of such a practice.

Problem: Identify and characterize the set of construction-phase sustainability practices that are most effective in improving overall project sustainability performance, and determine an associated set of metrics that:
(a) admit a well-defined measurement methodology during the construction phase;
(b) are sensitive to the adoption of the practices in (a);
(c) permit consistent comparison across projects of differing type, scale, and location; and
(d) can be aggregated into a defensible overall sustainability score for the construction phase.

Provide criteria for "effectiveness" (e.g., measurable reduction in a given environmental output per unit of work-in-place, normalized to baseline), a procedure for selecting and validating practices and metrics, and conditions under which the recommended practice–metric pairs remain robust across project contexts.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The question is an open-ended industry research prompt rather than a formal mathematical conjecture. No definitive resolution exists; sustainability practices and metrics for construction (e.g., LEED, Envision, ISO 21931, GHG Protocol Scope 3 Category 2) are actively developed but no consensus "most effective" set has been established. Status is therefore unknown/ongoing.

Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $n>1$, be a bounded domain with smooth connected boundary $S$. Let $L$ and $M$ be second-order, selfadjoint, strictly positive elliptic operators on $D$ with real-valued coefficients, equipped with the Dirichlet boundary condition. Let $a, b \in C^\infty(\overline{D})$ be strictly positive functions on $\overline{D}$. Suppose real-valued functions $u, v$ satisfy
\[
Lu + a(x)\, v = 0 \quad \text{in } D, \qquad -b(x)\, u + Mv = 0 \quad \text{in } D, \qquad u = v = 0 \quad \text{on } S.
\]
Must $u \equiv v \equiv 0$ in $D$? If not, exhibit a counterexample satisfying all the stated hypotheses.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

A 2025 note by Ramm ("A Uniqueness Result for a Coupled System of Elliptic PDEs", Annals of Mathematics and Physics) establishes the uniqueness conclusion u = v = 0 in the case where a and b are positive constants. The general case with variable positive smooth coefficients a(x), b(x) does not appear to be settled in the literature, so the problem as originally stated is only partially resolved.

Consider a capital project supply chain modeled as a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E) whose nodes V represent suppliers, fabricators, distributors, contractors, and an end-user (the owner of a capital project), and whose edges E represent material/equipment transfers. Each item flowing through G is either authentic or counterfeit; counterfeit items are constructed to imitate authentic ones and may enter at any node. The owner may impose, at any subset of nodes and edges, a collection of verification, qualification, traceability, and auditing controls drawn from a control set C (e.g., supplier prequalification, factory inspection, serialization/tagging, chain-of-custody documentation, sampling and destructive/non-destructive testing, blockchain-based provenance records, third-party certification verification, receiving inspection, and anomaly detection). Each control c ∈ C has a deployment cost, an associated detection probability for counterfeit items at the node/edge where it is applied, and a false-positive rate.

Problem: Determine the necessary, prudent, and most effective set of processes and practices — formalized as a deployment policy that assigns controls from C to nodes and edges of G — that ensures counterfeit construction materials and equipment do not enter the supply chain reaching the end-user. Specifically:
(a) Identify a minimal set of mandatory ("necessary") controls without which counterfeits cannot be reliably excluded.
(b) Characterize "prudent" augmentations of this minimal set that provide defense in depth against adversarial suppliers.
(c) Among all policies meeting (a)–(b), determine the one(s) that maximize the probability of detecting or preventing counterfeit entry subject to a bounded total deployment cost, and describe the resulting processes and practices.

Consider a project modeled as a tuple P = (T, D, R, S, U), where T is a finite set of tasks, D ⊆ T × T is a precedence relation (a directed acyclic graph) representing dependencies between tasks, R is a finite set of resources together with assignment functions specifying which resources each task requires, S = {s_t}_{t∈T} is a collection of stakeholders and interfaces associated with each task, and U encodes uncertainty in the form of probability distributions over task durations, costs, and outcomes. A complexity measure for projects is a function C that assigns to each such project P a nonnegative real number C(P) and satisfies natural axioms such as: (i) monotonicity under refinement (adding tasks or dependencies does not decrease complexity), (ii) invariance under relabeling of tasks and resources, (iii) sensitivity to structural features of D (e.g., depth, branching, cycles in undirected projection), and (iv) sensitivity to the entropy of U.

Problem.
(a) Propose and rigorously define such a complexity measure C(P) that incorporates structural, resource, stakeholder, and uncertainty components, and prove that C satisfies a stated list of axioms.
(b) Given a decision framework in which a project manager must choose among discrete decisions d ∈ Δ (e.g., choice of contract type, level of contingency reserve, monitoring frequency, governance structure), formulate and justify a decision rule d*(P) = f(C(P), P) that prescribes decisions as a function of the measured complexity, and prove (under stated stochastic assumptions on U) that this rule optimizes a specified expected utility or risk-adjusted objective compared to complexity-independent rules.

Let $\mathbb{H}$ denote the algebra of quaternions, and consider the right $\mathbb{H}$-module $\mathbb{H}^2$ as a hypercomplex Euclidean space. A left hyperplane in $\mathbb{H}^2$ is an affine subset of the form $\{z \in \mathbb{H}^2 : a_1 z_1 + a_2 z_2 = b\}$ for some $a_1, a_2, b \in \mathbb{H}$ with $(a_1, a_2) \neq (0,0)$, where multiplication is on the left. A set $E \subset \mathbb{H}^2$ is called linearly convex if for every $z \in \mathbb{H}^2 \setminus E$ there exists a left hyperplane $l$ with $z \in l \subset \mathbb{H}^2 \setminus E$.

Does there exist a compact linearly convex set $E \subset \mathbb{H}^2$ such that, for some integer $m$ with $4 \leq m \leq 6$, all cohomology groups of $E$ coincide with the corresponding cohomology groups of the sphere $S^m$?

Let $n>1$ and let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain. For a nonzero function $f\in L^2(D)$ (extended by zero to $\mathbb{R}^n$), let
\[
F(z)\;=\;\int_{D} f(x)\,e^{-i\,z\cdot x}\,dx,\qquad z\in\mathbb{C}^n,
\]
so that $F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ is an entire function of exponential type (the Fourier–Laplace transform of $f$).

Fix two nonempty subsets $L_1,L_2\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ (thought of as the two "directions" of evaluation and shift, as in the associated Problem 3.1). Fix an arbitrary positive integer $M$.

Question: Do there exist points $p_1,p_2,\dots,p_M\in L_2$ such that the $M$ functions
\[
z\longmapsto F(z+p_m),\qquad z\in L_1,\quad m=1,2,\dots,M,
\]
are linearly independent as functions on $L_1$? Equivalently, can one choose $p_1,\dots,p_M\in L_2$ so that, for any complex coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_M$, the identity
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{M} c_m\,F(z+p_m)\;=\;0\qquad\text{for all }z\in L_1
\]
forces $c_1=c_2=\dots=c_M=0$?

Consider a project modeled as a finite set of tasks T = {t_1, ..., t_n} with precedence constraints encoded as a directed acyclic graph G = (T, E). A planning effort is quantified by a nonnegative real number p ∈ [0, P_max], interpreted as the total resource (time, cost, or labor) invested in planning before execution begins. Suppose that the probability of successful project execution is a nondecreasing function S: [0, P_max] → [0, 1], where S(p) denotes the probability of project success when planning effort p has been expended, and suppose that a project is deemed "successful" if it completes all tasks within prescribed budget and deadline constraints with probability at least a fixed threshold α ∈ (0, 1).

Determine, in terms of S and α, the minimum planning effort
   p*(α) = inf { p ∈ [0, P_max] : S(p) ≥ α },
and characterize the structural properties of S (for example, concavity, smoothness, or diminishing-returns behavior) under reasonable stochastic models of task execution that ensure p*(α) is finite, strictly positive, and continuously dependent on α. Equivalently, find the minimum amount of planning effort p required so that the project can be executed successfully with probability at least α.

representations.normalized:
Work in the hypercomplex Euclidean space H^n, where H denotes the algebra of quaternions and n > 1. A left hyperplane in H^n is an affine subset of the form {z ∈ H^n : a_1 z_1 + ... + a_n z_n = b} for some fixed a_1, ..., a_n, b ∈ H with (a_1, ..., a_n) ≠ 0, where the coefficients act on the left. A hypercomplex line is an affine subset of the form {z_0 + t v : t ∈ H} for fixed z_0, v ∈ H^n with v ≠ 0.

A subset E ⊂ H^n is called H-convex if, for every hypercomplex line γ, the intersection γ ∩ E is acyclic (i.e., has the reduced singular homology of a point).

A domain D ⊂ H^n is called locally linearly convex if, for every boundary point z ∈ ∂D, there exist a left hyperplane l with z ∈ l and an open neighborhood U(z) of z such that D ∩ l ∩ U(z) = ∅.

Question: Let D ⊂ H^n (n > 1) be a bounded locally linearly convex domain with smooth boundary. Must D necessarily be H-convex, and must D be homeomorphic to the closed 4n-dimensional Euclidean ball in R^{4n}?

Let a facility (or a system or piece of equipment within a facility) have a life cycle of T years, during which it incurs time-indexed costs comprising initial capital cost C_0, operating costs O(t), maintenance costs M(t), energy costs E(t), repair/replacement costs R(t), and end-of-life disposal cost D, all discounted at rate r. The (present-value) life cycle cost is

    LCC = C_0 + \int_0^T \frac{O(t)+M(t)+E(t)+R(t)}{(1+r)^t}\,dt + \frac{D}{(1+r)^T}.

"Commissioning" denotes a structured quality-assurance process applied at design, installation, and/or operational stages that adjusts the cost streams: it introduces an additional up-front cost K_c and modifies the subsequent cost functions to O_c(t), M_c(t), E_c(t), R_c(t), and lifetime T_c, yielding LCC_c.

Develop a quantitative model that expresses the savings

    \Delta(\text{LCC}) = LCC - LCC_c

as an explicit, measurable function of commissioning-related parameters (such as scope, timing, and intensity of commissioning activities, building type, system type, climate zone, and operational profile). Specifically:

(a) Define a parametrized class of cost-modification functions induced by commissioning and prove (or empirically estimate, with stated confidence intervals) the resulting change in each cost component.

(b) Derive a closed-form or algorithmic expression for \Delta(\text{LCC}) and for the payback time \tau, defined as the smallest \tau>0 such that the cumulative discounted savings up to time \tau equal K_c.

(c) Identify the conditions on the parameters under which \Delta(\text{LCC}) > 0, and quantify the sensitivity of \Delta(\text{LCC}) to each parameter.

Provide the model and a validated quantification.

Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space whose norm is of class $C^{1,1}$ away from the origin (i.e., $X$ admits an equivalent norm whose square is $C^{1,1}$). Let $A\colon X\to X$ be a bounded linear operator with bounded inverse, $A,A^{-1}\in L(X)$, whose spectrum lies strictly inside the open unit disk (so that $A$ is a linear strict contraction in some equivalent norm). Let $\mathcal{X}\colon U\to X$ be a $C^{1,1}$ map defined on a neighborhood $U$ of $0\in X$, satisfying $\mathcal{X}(0)=0$ and $D\mathcal{X}(0)=0$, and set
$$T(x)=Ax+\mathcal{X}(x),\qquad x\in U.$$
Then $T$ is a $C^{1,1}$ strict contraction germ at $0$.

Question: Is it always the case that $T$ is locally $C^1$-linearizable at $0$? Equivalently, does there exist a neighborhood $V\subset U$ of $0$ and a $C^1$ map $R\colon V\to X$ of the form $R(x)=x+\varphi(x)$ with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $D\varphi(0)=0$ such that $R$ is a local $C^1$-diffeomorphism near $0$ and
$$R\circ T\circ R^{-1}=A$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood of the origin — without imposing any non-resonance or spectral-gap condition on the spectrum of $A$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether every $C^{1,1}$ strict contraction germ in an infinite-dimensional Banach space is $C^1$-linearizable without non-resonance assumptions appears to remain open in general. Known positive results (Rodrigues–Solà-Morales 2004, ELE Rayskin and others) all require non-resonance/spectral-gap hypotheses. Counterexamples in infinite dimensions have been constructed, but they rely on an infinite-dimensional Jordan block structure, and whether this feature is necessary — equivalently, whether non-resonance is genuinely required — is reported as an open problem.

representations.normalized:
Consider a project that, at an initial authorization time $t_0$, has planned outcomes consisting of a target cost $C^*$, a target completion schedule $S^*$ (e.g., a target end date or set of milestone dates), and a target performance vector $P^* \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (a vector of technical performance metrics). The project is executed over a time interval $[t_0, T]$ where $T$ is the (random) completion time. At each intermediate time $t \in [t_0, T]$, decision-makers possess an information set $\mathcal{F}_t$ (a filtration) containing all data observed up to time $t$ (e.g., expenditures, progress reports, earned value indicators, risk register updates, external indicators). Based on $\mathcal{F}_t$, they produce forecasts $\hat{C}_t$, $\hat{S}_t$, $\hat{P}_t$ of the eventual realized outcomes $C$, $S$, $P$ observed at completion.

Define the forecast error processes $e^C_t = \hat{C}_t - C$, $e^S_t = \hat{S}_t - S$, $e^P_t = \hat{P}_t - P$. Say that the forecasting procedure is unbiased if $\mathbb{E}[e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = 0$ for $X \in \{C, S, P\}$ and for all $t$, optimistic if $\mathbb{E}[e^C_t] < 0$, $\mathbb{E}[e^S_t] < 0$, or $\mathbb{E}[e^P_t] > 0$ in the favorable direction, and cautious in the opposite sense.

Problem. Develop a forecasting methodology that takes as input the information set $\mathcal{F}_t$ and produces forecasts $(\hat{C}_t, \hat{S}_t, \hat{P}_t)$ such that:
(a) the expected total forecast loss $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{t_0}^{T} L(e^C_t, e^S_t, e^P_t)\, dt\right]$ is minimized for a specified loss function $L:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ (for instance, weighted squared error);
(b) the procedure is calibrated, meaning $\mathbb{E}[e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = 0$ for each outcome $X$ and each $t$, thereby guarding against systematic optimism or pessimism;

Specifically, characterize procedures—e.g., using reference-class forecasting, Bayesian updating, machine-learning regressors, or earned-value-management updates—that simultaneously achieve (a), (b), and (c) under realistic data-availability assumptions, and quantify the achievable rate at which the conditional variances $\mathrm{Var}(e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t)$ contract as $t \to T$.

Consider a project that, at an initial authorization time $t_0$, has planned outcomes consisting of a target cost $C^*$, a target completion schedule $S^*$ (e.g., a target end date or set of milestone dates), and a target performance vector $P^* \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (a vector of technical performance metrics). The project is executed over a time interval $[t_0, T]$ where $T$ is the (random) completion time. At each intermediate time $t \in [t_0, T]$, decision-makers possess an information set $\mathcal{F}_t$ (a filtration) containing all data observed up to time $t$ (e.g., expenditures, progress reports, earned value indicators, risk register updates, external indicators). Based on $\mathcal{F}_t$, they produce forecasts $\hat{C}_t$, $\hat{S}_t$, $\hat{P}_t$ of the eventual realized outcomes $C$, $S$, $P$ observed at completion.

Define the forecast error processes $e^C_t = \hat{C}_t - C$, $e^S_t = \hat{S}_t - S$, $e^P_t = \hat{P}_t - P$. Say that the forecasting procedure is unbiased if $\mathbb{E}[e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = 0$ for $X \in \{C, S, P\}$ and for all $t$, optimistic if $\mathbb{E}[e^C_t] < 0$, $\mathbb{E}[e^S_t] < 0$, or $\mathbb{E}[e^P_t] > 0$ in the favorable direction, and cautious in the opposite sense.

Problem. Develop a forecasting methodology that takes as input the information set $\mathcal{F}_t$ and produces forecasts $(\hat{C}_t, \hat{S}_t, \hat{P}_t)$ such that:
(a) the expected total forecast loss $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{t_0}^{T} L(e^C_t, e^S_t, e^P_t)\, dt\right]$ is minimized for a specified loss function $L:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ (for instance, weighted squared error);
(b) the procedure is calibrated, meaning $\mathbb{E}[e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = 0$ for each outcome $X$ and each $t$, thereby guarding against systematic optimism or pessimism;
(c) the methodology supplies calibrated probabilistic intervals: predicted intervals $I^X_t(\alpha) \subset \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^k$) such that $\Pr(X \in I^X_t(\alpha)) = 1 - \alpha$ for any chosen confidence level $\alpha \in (0,1)$.

Specifically, characterize procedures—e.g., using reference-class forecasting, Bayesian updating, machine-learning regressors, or earned-value-management updates—that simultaneously achieve (a), (b), and (c) under realistic data-availability assumptions, and quantify the achievable rate at which the conditional variances $\mathrm{Var}(e^X_t \mid \mathcal{F}_t)$ contract as $t \to T$.

There is an extensive ongoing literature (reference-class forecasting, earned value management, Bayesian project forecasting, machine-learning cost/schedule estimation) but no single accepted solution; systematic optimism bias in large projects remains a well-documented unresolved phenomenon.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A : X 	o X$ be a bounded linear operator whose spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is hyperbolic, i.e. $\sigma(A) \cap \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| = 1\} = \emptyset$. Consider a $C^1$ map $T : X 	o X$ of the form
$$T(x) = A x + f(x),$$
where $f : X 	o X$ is $C^1$, $f(0) = 0$, $Df(0) = 0$, and $f$ together with $Df$ is bounded on $X$ (or, equivalently, one considers a local diffeomorphism near $0$ with $T(0)=0$, $DT(0)=A$).

The map $T$ is said to be $C^1$ linearizable (near $0$) if there exists a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $H$ defined on a neighborhood of $0$ in $X$ with $H(0)=0$ such that
$$H \circ T = A \circ H$$
on a neighborhood of $0$.

Assume the following spectral non-resonance condition on the spectrum $\sigma(A) = \sigma_s \cup \sigma_u$ (the splitting into stable part $\sigma_s \subset \{|z|<1\}$ and unstable part $\sigma_u \subset \{|z|>1\}$): there exist constants $a, b, A_u, B_u$ with
$$0 < a \le |\lambda| \le b < 1 \quad 	ext{for all } \lambda \in \sigma_s, \qquad 1 < A_u \le |\mu| \le B_u \quad 	ext{for all } \mu \in \sigma_u,$$
and the non-resonance gap
$$b < a^2, \qquad A_u > B_u^{1/2}$$
holds (this is the standard spectral non-resonance condition (∗) used to obtain $C^1$ linearization).

It is known that there exist $C^1$ maps $T$ on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces, with hyperbolic linear part $A$, for which no $C^1$ linearization exists; all such known counterexamples use a linear part $A$ that contains an infinite-dimensional Jordan block (i.e., $A$ is not diagonalizable on any spectral subspace).

Questions:

(a) Is the presence of an infinite-dimensional Jordan-block structure in $A$ necessary for the failure of $C^1$ linearization? Equivalently, does there exist a counterexample $(A, f)$ to $C^1$ linearization on some Banach space (or Hilbert space) $X$ in which $A$ is selfadjoint (in the Hilbert space case) or, more generally, normal?

(b) If no such counterexample exists when $A$ is selfadjoint (respectively, normal), can the spectral non-resonance condition above be weakened in those cases, i.e. can one establish $C^1$ linearization for selfadjoint (or normal) hyperbolic $A$ under a weaker spectral gap condition than $b < a^2$ and $A_u > B_u^{1/2}$?

representations.normalized:
The classical Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation $u_t = u_{xxx} + 6 u u_x$ for a single bosonic field $u(x,t)$ admits supersymmetric extensions in which one introduces additional fermionic (Grassmann-odd) fields, and the resulting system is Hamiltonian with respect to some (possibly graded) Poisson bracket on the space of fields. Recall that a Poisson bracket $\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}$ on a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded algebra of functionals is called even if $|\{F,G\}| = |F|+|G| \pmod 2$, and odd if $|\{F,G\}| = |F|+|G|+1 \pmod 2$. An odd Poisson bracket (antibracket) satisfies graded skew-symmetry and a graded Jacobi identity with a shift in parity.

There exists an $N=2$ supersymmetric extension of the KdV equation that is Hamiltonian with respect to an odd Poisson structure, but in which the time-evolution equations for the bosonic fields involve only the bosonic fields themselves (the fermionic fields do not appear in the right-hand sides of the bosonic evolution equations).

Problem: Construct an integrable supersymmetric extension of the KdV equation, equipped with an odd Poisson (Hamiltonian) structure, such that the system is integrable (admits an infinite hierarchy of commuting conserved quantities or a Lax / bi-Hamiltonian formulation) and such that the time-evolution equations for the bosonic fields depend nontrivially on the fermionic fields. Equivalently, find an "odd" integrable supersymmetric extension of KdV in which the bosonic sector is genuinely coupled to the fermionic sector through the dynamics.

representations.normalized: Consider the construction industry as a workforce system in which a substantial fraction of experienced employees are approaching retirement, while the remaining workforce consists of mid-career personnel and newly hired entrants. Each near-retirement employee possesses a body of tacit and explicit knowledge (technical know-how, safety practices, project management experience, client and supplier relationships, problem-solving heuristics, and undocumented procedures) accumulated over decades of practice. Design and analyze a framework — combining organizational processes, mentoring structures, documentation methods, training programs, and supporting technological tools (such as knowledge repositories, expert systems, video capture, or AI-based assistants) — that enables the effective, efficient, and verifiable transfer of this knowledge from employees nearing retirement to those who remain on the job and to new entrants. The framework should specify: (i) how to elicit and represent both tacit and explicit knowledge from departing experts; (ii) how to identify which knowledge is most critical to preserve; (iii) how to deliver and embed this knowledge in receivers so that operational performance, safety, and productivity are maintained or improved; and (iv) quantitative metrics by which the success of the transfer can be measured.

representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $T:X\to X$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with $T(0)=0$, written as
$$T(x) = Ax + f(x),$$
where $A=DT(0)\in\mathcal{L}(X)$ is a hyperbolic bounded linear operator (its spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is disjoint from the unit circle) and $f:X\to X$ is a $C^1$ map satisfying the higher-order condition
$$\|f(x)\| = O(\|x\|^{1+\eta}),\qquad \|Df(x)\| = O(\|x\|^{\eta})\quad\text{as } x\to 0,$$
for some fixed $\eta>0$. One says that $T$ is $C^1$-linearizable near $0$ if there exist neighborhoods $U,V$ of $0$ in $X$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $H:U\to V$ with $H(0)=0$, $DH(0)=I$, such that
$$H\circ T = A\circ H\quad\text{on } U.$$

Classical sufficient conditions for $C^1$ linearization impose spectral gap and non-resonance restrictions on $\sigma(A)$ (for instance, separation of the contracting and expanding parts into narrow bands, and avoidance of finitely many resonance relations). The problem is the following.

Determine the sharp limits to which the spectral assumptions on $A$ guaranteeing $C^1$ linearization can be relaxed when the nonlinearity $f$ is of order $1+\eta$ with $\eta>0$. Concretely, for each $\eta>0$, construct examples of pairs $(A,f)$ on a Banach space $X$ satisfying the above order-$(1+\eta)$ condition, with $A$ hyperbolic but violating proposed weakened spectral conditions, such that $T=A+f$ admits no $C^1$ linearization near $0$. The aim is to identify, as a function of $\eta$, the precise spectral conditions on $A$ that are both necessary and sufficient for $C^1$ linearization in this class.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The literature on $C^1$ (and $C^{1,\beta}$) linearization for hyperbolic diffeomorphisms of Banach spaces (e.g. ElBialy; Rodrigues–Solà-Morales; and later works on $C^{1,1}$ hyperbolic diffeomorphisms) provides successively weakened spectral band/gap conditions sufficient for linearization, and classical Hartman-type examples show that some spectral restriction beyond hyperbolicity is needed. However, no published work appears to give matching counterexamples that pin down the optimal spectral conditions for nonlinearities of order $1+\eta$ for general $\eta>0$; the question of sharp counterexamples in this regime is still posed as an open problem in the area.
