Let $\mathbb{H} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Im}(z) > 0\}$ denote the upper half-plane. For a parameter $\kappa \geq 0$, the chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa$ in $\mathbb{H}$ from $0$ to $\infty$ is the random curve $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to\overline{\mathbb{H}}$ whose Loewner driving function is $\sqrt{\kappa}\,B_t$, where $(B_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is a standard real Brownian motion; equivalently $\gamma$ is generated by the conformal maps $g_t:\mathbb{H}\setminus K_t\to\mathbb{H}$ satisfying $\partial_t g_t(z) = 2/(g_t(z) - \sqrt{\kappa}B_t)$ with $g_0(z)=z$.

Fix $\kappa < 8$ and let $\gamma$ denote the trace of $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa$ in $\mathbb{H}$. Provide necessary conditions, sufficient conditions, or a characterization, expressed in terms of geometric or potential-theoretic properties of a deterministic compact set $K \subset \overline{\mathbb{H}}$, that determine whether
$$\mathbb{P}\!\left(\gamma \cap K \neq \emptyset\right) > 0.$$
The case $K \subset \mathbb{R}$ is of particular interest (note that for $\kappa \leq 4$ the curve $\gamma$ almost surely does not intersect $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, while for $4<\kappa<8$ the intersection with $\mathbb{R}$ is a nontrivial random fractal).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial partial results are known but no complete necessary-and-sufficient characterization has been established. Beffara determined the almost-sure Hausdorff dimension of the SLE trace (1+κ/8 for κ≤8); Alberts–Sheffield (2008) proved that the intersection of SLE_κ (4<κ<8) with ℝ has Hausdorff dimension 2−8/κ and gave two-interval estimates; Alberts–Binder–Viklund and others have studied dimension spectra and multifractal boundary spectra for SLE_κ(ρ). These yield sharp dimension thresholds (sufficient/necessary conditions in terms of Hausdorff dimension or appropriate capacities), but a precise capacity-type characterization of hittable compact sets for general K ⊂ H or K ⊂ ℝ remains open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classification of compact manifolds admitting Einstein metrics is a long-standing open problem in Riemannian geometry. Even in dimension 4, no full topological obstruction/classification is known: only partial obstructions (e.g., Hitchin–Thorpe inequality, LeBrun's Seiberg–Witten obstructions) and constructions (Kähler–Einstein, homogeneous, Sasaki–Einstein) are available. In higher dimensions the problem is essentially wide open, as discussed in Besse's monograph "Einstein Manifolds" and subsequent surveys.

Let $M^{2n}$ be a smooth, connected, closed (compact without boundary) manifold of real dimension $2n$ with $n>2$. An almost complex structure on $M^{2n}$ is a smooth bundle endomorphism $J : TM \to TM$ of the tangent bundle satisfying $J^2 = -\mathrm{Id}$. Such a $J$ is said to be integrable if it is induced by an underlying complex-analytic structure on $M^{2n}$; equivalently, by the Newlander–Nirenberg theorem, if its Nijenhuis tensor
$$N_J(X,Y) = [X,Y] + J[JX,Y] + J[X,JY] - [JX,JY]$$
vanishes identically for all smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $M^{2n}$.

Prove or disprove: every smooth closed manifold $M^{2n}$ with $n>2$ that admits some almost complex structure also admits an integrable complex structure (not necessarily homotopic to the given one).

The general question of whether every closed almost complex manifold of real dimension $2n$ with $n>2$ admits an integrable complex structure is widely regarded as open. Even the most famous test case, the 6-sphere $S^6$, remains unresolved as of recent surveys. While Gromov–Landweber-type results handle the open (non-compact) case, no comparable criterion exists for compact manifolds.

Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective algebraic manifold, and let $V \to X$ be a complex vector bundle (in the topological sense). Recall that the integral cohomology $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Z})$ maps into $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{C})$, which carries the Hodge decomposition $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{C})=\bigoplus_{p+q=2k} H^{p,q}(X)$; an integral class is said to be of Hodge type $(k,k)$ if its image in $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{C})$ lies in $H^{k,k}(X)$. Let $K^{\mathrm{top}}(X)$ denote the topological complex K-theory of $X$, generated by isomorphism classes of complex vector bundles modulo $[E\oplus F]=[E]+[F]$, and let $K^{\mathrm{hol}}(X)$ denote the analogous Grothendieck group generated by holomorphic vector bundles on $X$, with natural map $K^{\mathrm{hol}}(X)\to K^{\mathrm{top}}(X)$.

Suppose that for every $k\ge 1$ the $k$-th Chern class $c_k(V)\in H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Z})$ is of Hodge type $(k,k)$. Determine whether there must exist holomorphic vector bundles $W_1, W_2$ on $X$ such that $[V]+[W_1]=[W_2]$ in $K^{\mathrm{top}}(X)$; equivalently, whether the class $[V]\in K^{\mathrm{top}}(X)$ lies in the image of $K^{\mathrm{hol}}(X)\to K^{\mathrm{top}}(X)$.

The question is a well-known problem connecting the Hodge conjecture to K-theory: whether every topological complex vector bundle whose Chern classes are Hodge classes is, stably in K-theory, holomorphic. It is closely tied to the (rational/integral) Hodge conjecture and to results showing that Chern classes of coherent sheaves on Kähler manifolds need not be combinations of analytic cycle classes. No general resolution appears in the literature; the problem is generally regarded as open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem appears to be open. The closely related Smarandache concatenation sequence 1, 121, 12321, ... (OEIS A173426) has been computationally examined: only two probable primes are known (the 20-digit term and a 17350-digit probable prime), with no further primes found for n up to 60000, and only heuristic arguments (attributed to D. Broadhurst) suggest infinitely many primes. No proof of either finiteness or infinitude is known for the analogous "descend then ascend" mirror variant. No rigorous resolution of the primality question for the mirror sequence was located.

Define a sequence of subsets $A_0 \supseteq A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$ of the positive integers as follows. Set $A_0 = \mathbb{N} = \{1,2,3,\dots\}$, written in increasing order. For each $k \ge 1$, obtain $A_k$ from $A_{k-1}$ by deleting every $2^k$-th term in the increasing enumeration of $A_{k-1}$; that is, at stage $k=1$ delete every 2nd remaining number, at stage $k=2$ delete every 4th remaining number, at stage $k=3$ delete every 8th remaining number, and so on. Let $S = \bigcap_{k\ge 0} A_k$ be the resulting "binary sieve" sequence of surviving integers.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:
(a) $S$ contains infinitely many prime numbers.
(b) $S$ contains infinitely many composite numbers.

(a) Does $S_n$ contain infinitely many prime numbers?

Background and definitions.

For a square complex matrix $A$, let $\sigma(A)$ denote its spectrum. Assume throughout that $A$ has at least one real eigenvalue, and write $l(A)$ for the smallest real eigenvalue of $A$. For a nonzero complex number $z$, let $\arg(z) \in (-\pi,\pi]$ denote its principal argument.

A matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is called a $\tau$-matrix if every principal submatrix $B$ of $A$ (including $A$ itself) has a real eigenvalue and its smallest real eigenvalue $l(B)$ satisfies $l(B) \le l(C)$ for every principal submatrix $C$ of $B$ (i.e., the smallest real eigenvalue is monotone non-decreasing under taking principal submatrices). A matrix $A$ is called a GKK matrix if all principal minors of $A$ are positive and $A$ is weakly sign-symmetric, meaning $a_{ij} a_{ji} \ge 0$ for all $i,j$. A GKK $\tau$-matrix is a matrix that is simultaneously a GKK matrix and a $\tau$-matrix.

For positive integers $n,k$ and $t \in (0,1)$, let $A_{n,k,t}$ denote the matrix class consisting of $n \times n$ matrices defined by certain $k$- and $t$-parametrized constructions arising in the study of the above classes (the same family $A_{n,k,t}$ used to study stability of GKK and $\tau$-matrices).

The spectral angle inequality. For an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with $l(A)$ defined, consider the inequality
$$|\arg(\lambda - l(A))| \le \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{n}, \qquad \text{for every } \lambda \in \sigma(A). \tag{$\ast$}$$

Problem. For each of the following four classes $\mathcal{C}$ of matrices, let $\mathcal{C}_n$ denote the subclass consisting of those members of $\mathcal{C}$ whose order is at most $n$. Determine the largest integer $n$ such that every matrix $A \in \mathcal{C}_n$ satisfies $(\ast)$:

(i) $\mathcal{C} = \{A_{n,k,t} : n,k \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0},\ t \in (0,1)\}$;
(ii) $\mathcal{C}$ = the class of GKK $\tau$-matrices;
(iii) $\mathcal{C}$ = the class of GKK matrices;
(iv) $\mathcal{C}$ = the class of $\tau$-matrices.

Let $(u_i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a strictly increasing sequence of integers with $u_i > 1$ for all $i$. Define a sieve on the positive integers $1,2,3,\dots$ as follows. At step $i=1,2,3,\dots$, consider the current sequence of remaining integers (with step $0$ being the full sequence of positive integers). Partition the remaining integers, starting from the first one not yet processed, into consecutive blocks of length $u_i$; in each such block, keep the first $u_i - 1$ entries and delete the $u_i$-th entry. After performing this step for every $i\geq 1$, let $R = (r_1 < r_2 < \cdots)$ denote the sequence of integers that are never deleted.

Establish a precise relationship between the generator sequence $(u_i)$ and the resulting surviving sequence $R$. In particular, derive formulas, recursions, asymptotic density estimates, or analytic/combinatorial identities that express properties of $R$ (such as its counting function, asymptotic density, or generating function) in terms of the sequence $(u_i)$.

(Note: the classical case $u_i = $ the $i$-th surviving integer greater than $1$ recovers a self-referential sieve in the spirit of the lucky-number sieve; here $(u_i)$ is an arbitrary prescribed strictly increasing sequence.)

Question: Are there infinitely many positive integers $n$ that are themselves prime and are also pseudo-primes of the third kind? Equivalently, do there exist infinitely many primes $p$ whose decimal digits can be nontrivially permuted to produce a prime?

Let f(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 be a monic polynomial of degree n ≥ 2 with complex coefficients and n pairwise distinct zeros ζ_1, ..., ζ_n ∈ C (the zeros may be real or complex). The classical Weierstrass (Durand–Kerner) simultaneous iteration is the map W: U → C^n defined on the open set U = { z = (z_1, ..., z_n) ∈ C^n : z_i ≠ z_j for i ≠ j } by

  W(z)_i = z_i − f(z_i) / ∏_{j ≠ i} (z_i − z_j),  i = 1, ..., n.

Starting from z^{(0)} ∈ U, set z^{(k+1)} = W(z^{(k)}) whenever z^{(k)} ∈ U. Say that the iteration converges (to the zeros of f) from z^{(0)} if z^{(k)} ∈ U for all k and there is a permutation σ of {1, ..., n} such that z^{(k)}_i → ζ_{σ(i)} as k → ∞ for every i.

(a) For n = 2, determine the set E_2 ⊂ C^2 of starting points z^{(0)} ∈ U from which the Weierstrass iteration fails to converge to (ζ_1, ζ_2) (in some order), and prove that E_2 has Lebesgue measure zero in C^2 ≅ R^4.

(b) For arbitrary n ≥ 2 and arbitrary monic f of degree n with simple zeros, decide whether the set E_n ⊂ C^n of starting points in U from which the Weierstrass iteration fails to converge to the zeros of f has Lebesgue measure zero in C^n ≅ R^{2n}; equivalently, decide whether the Weierstrass iteration is globally convergent outside a set of measure zero in the starting space.

Let $p(z) = z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \cdots + a_0 \in \mathbb{C}[z]$ be a monic polynomial of degree $n \geq 2$ with pairwise distinct roots. The Weierstrass (Durand–Kerner) iteration is the map $W_p \colon \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^n$ defined componentwise, for an approximation vector $z = (z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with pairwise distinct entries, by
$$ W_p(z)_i \;=\; z_i \;-\; \frac{p(z_i)}{\prod_{j \neq i} (z_i - z_j)}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n. $$
Starting from an initial vector $z^{(0)} \in \mathbb{C}^n$, the iteration generates the sequence $z^{(k+1)} = W_p(z^{(k)})$. It is classically known that certain "critical" starting vectors (for instance, configurations whose entries are equally spaced on a circle centred at a root, or vectors mapped by $W_p$ outside its domain of definition) cause the iteration to fail to converge to the multiset of roots of $p$.

Question: Do there exist initial vectors $z^{(0)} \in \mathbb{C}^n$, beyond such already-identified critical starting configurations, for which the full sequence $\{z^{(k)}\}_{k \geq 0}$ produced by the Weierstrass iteration fails to converge to the root vector of $p$? Equivalently, is there a polynomial $p$ for which the set of non-converging initial vectors is strictly larger than the previously known exceptional set?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Recent work by Reinke, Schleicher and Stoll ("The Weierstrass root finder is not generally convergent", arXiv:2004.04777, 2020) and the subsequent paper on the Durand–Kerner version proves that for every degree $d \geq 3$ there are open sets of polynomials with open sets of initial vectors whose Weierstrass orbits converge to attracting periodic cycles different from the roots, and that almost every polynomial of degree $\geq 3$ admits orbits diverging to infinity. This affirmatively answers the question: there are non-converging starting vectors beyond the previously known critical ones, forming open sets of positive measure.

Let p(z) be a monic polynomial of degree n ≥ 2 with n simple complex roots. The Weierstrass (Durand–Kerner) iteration for simultaneously approximating all roots is given, for an n-tuple z^{(k)} = (z_1^{(k)}, …, z_n^{(k)}), by

  W_i(z^{(k)}) = p(z_i^{(k)}) / ∏_{j ≠ i} (z_i^{(k)} − z_j^{(k)}),
  z_i^{(k+1)} = z_i^{(k)} − W_i(z^{(k)}),    i = 1, …, n.

For a real acceleration parameter ω > 0, define the SOR-like modification of the Weierstrass method by

  z_i^{(k+1)} = z_i^{(k)} − ω · W_i(z^{(k)}),    i = 1, …, n.

It is known that ω = 1 is locally optimal in the sense that the linearization at a root cluster is minimized there. The problem is: determine, for this SOR-like Weierstrass iteration, the globally optimal value of the acceleration parameter ω that yields the fastest convergence (rather than only the local optimality statement ω = 1).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of determining the minimum number of points (equivalently, of fixed-radius balls) needed to cover a given planar or spatial region is a classical geometric covering question. While many particular instances (covering a disk by smaller disks, covering a square, etc.) have been studied with partial results and bounds, there is no general closed-form answer for arbitrary planar figures or three-dimensional bodies; it remains an active area in computational and discrete geometry, with exact optimal values known only for special cases.

Let p(z) be a complex polynomial of degree n ≥ 2 with n pairwise distinct zeros ζ_1, …, ζ_n ∈ ℂ. The simultaneous Euler–Chebyshev iteration is the map T : U ⊂ ℂ^n → ℂ^n defined componentwise, for a vector x = (x_1, …, x_n) of pairwise distinct approximations to the zeros, by

  T_i(x) = x_i − (p(x_i)/p'(x_i)) · ( 1 + (1/2) · A_i(x) + (1/2) · A_i(x)^2 ),

where
  A_i(x) = (p(x_i)/p'(x_i)) · Σ_{j ≠ i} 1/(x_i − x_j),

and the iterates are x^{(k+1)} = T(x^{(k)}), starting from x^{(0)} ∈ ℂ^n with all components pairwise distinct and away from the critical set of T.

Problem. Prove or disprove the following statement, and in the affirmative case give an explicit description of the exceptional set:

  For every n ≥ 2, the simultaneous Euler–Chebyshev iteration is globally convergent — in the sense that the sequence x^{(k)} converges to a permutation of (ζ_1, …, ζ_n) — for all initial vectors x^{(0)} ∈ ℂ^n outside a subset E ⊂ ℂ^n of (2n-dimensional Lebesgue) measure zero. Identify and characterize the exceptional set E for arbitrary degree n.

  T_i(x) = x_i − (p(x_i)/p'(x_i)) · ( 1 + (1/2) · A_i(x) + (1/2) · A_i(x)^2 ),

where

Let $G$ be a compact (Hausdorff topological) group and let $M$ be a von Neumann algebra. Suppose $\sigma\colon G\to \mathrm{Aut}(M)$ is an action of $G$ on $M$ by $*$-automorphisms which is ergodic, in the sense that the fixed-point algebra
$$M^{\sigma}=\{x\in M : \sigma_g(x)=x \text{ for all } g\in G\}$$
equals $\mathbb{C}\,1$. (Continuity of $g\mapsto \sigma_g(x)$ in the appropriate topology is assumed, e.g.\ $\sigma$ is pointwise $\sigma$-weakly continuous.)

Must $M$ be a finite von Neumann algebra, i.e.\ must $M$ admit a faithful normal tracial state (equivalently, must the unique $G$-invariant normal state on $M$ be a trace)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question was answered affirmatively by Høegh-Krohn, Landstad and Størmer: if a compact group acts ergodically on a unital C*-algebra (in particular on a von Neumann algebra), the unique invariant state is a trace, so the von Neumann algebra is finite (and in fact injective). This is a classical, well-cited finiteness theorem, with later extensions to compact quantum groups.

The sequence sf(n) = ∏_{k=1}^n k! is the superfactorial sequence (OEIS A000178), and the question concerns primality of sf(n)+1. The corresponding superfactorial-plus-one primes are tabulated by prime hunters; only finitely many small values have been verified prime and there is no known proof that infinitely many (or only finitely many) such primes exist. Heuristics based on the prime number theorem suggest infinitely many should occur, but this is unproved, so the problem appears open.

A generalized Smarandache palindrome (GSP) is a positive integer whose decimal representation can be partitioned into a concatenation of nonempty blocks of digits B_1 B_2 ... B_k (each B_i being the decimal representation of a positive integer, with no requirement that B_i have no leading zeros internally beyond the usual representation of positive integers) such that one of the following symmetry patterns holds:

- (even case) k = 2n and the block sequence has the form B_1, B_2, ..., B_n, B_n, ..., B_2, B_1;
- (odd case) k = 2n-1 and the block sequence has the form B_1, B_2, ..., B_{n-1}, B_n, B_{n-1}, ..., B_2, B_1.

In other words, the ordered list of blocks reads the same forwards and backwards. (Ordinary digit-palindromes are the special case where each block has length 1.)

Question: Do there exist infinitely many prime numbers that are generalized Smarandache palindromes?

representations.normalized:
Work in ZFC. Recall the Foreman–Magidor notion of mutual stationarity: given a sequence ⟨κ_n : n < ω⟩ of regular uncountable cardinals and a sequence ⟨T_n : n < ω⟩ with T_n ⊆ κ_n, the sequence ⟨T_n⟩ is mutually stationary if for every algebra (structure with countably many finitary functions) on a set containing sup_n κ_n there exists an elementary substructure N of size ℵ_0 such that sup(N ∩ κ_n) ∈ T_n for every n < ω.

Specialize to κ_n = ℵ_n (so n ≥ 1). For each set A ⊆ ω with 0 ∉ A, define a stationary "cofinality pattern" by
   T_n^A = { α < ℵ_n : cof(α) = ℵ_0 }    if n ∈ A,
   T_n^A = { α < ℵ_n : cof(α) = ℵ_{n−1} }  if n ∉ A (and n ≥ 2),
and ignore n = 0,1 as needed. Say that S_A is stationary to mean that the sequence ⟨T_n^A : 2 ≤ n < ω⟩ is mutually stationary in the above sense.

Restrict attention to those A ⊆ ω that contain infinitely many "successor pairs" (i.e., infinitely many n with both n ∈ A and n+1 ∈ A) and also omit infinitely many successor pairs (i.e., infinitely many n with both n ∉ A and n+1 ∉ A).

Question. Is the following true? If there exists even a single such set A ⊆ ω for which S_A is stationary, then there exists an inner model containing a strong cardinal.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The conjecture is stated as an unverified conjectural lower bound (with only a sketched, unchecked proof) in Welch's 2005 commentary on open problems in mutual stationarity. Subsequent literature on mutual stationarity at the ℵ_n (e.g., Koepke–Welch, and later work by Adolf, Ben-Neria, and others) discusses related consistency strength bounds, but no published source confirms the specific lower bound of an inner model with a strong cardinal from stationarity of S_A for a single such A. The status appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
Consider the generalized Lamé differential equation
$$A(z)\,p''(z) + 2B(z)\,p'(z) + C(z)\,p(z) = 0,$$
where $A(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{N}(z-a_j)$ with pairwise distinct complex numbers $a_1,\dots,a_N$, and $B(z)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $N-1$ written as
$$\frac{B(z)}{A(z)} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\rho_j}{z-a_j}, \qquad \rho_j\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}.$$
For a given integer $n\ge 0$, a Van Vleck polynomial is a polynomial $C(z)$ of degree at most $N-2$ such that the equation above admits a (Heine–Stieltjes) polynomial solution $p(z)$ of degree exactly $n$. Heine claimed that, in the generic case, the number of distinct Van Vleck polynomials producing a polynomial solution of degree $n$ equals
$$\sigma(n,N) := \binom{n+N-2}{n}.$$

(a) Provide a complete modern proof of Heine's count: under suitable genericity assumptions on the parameters $(a_j,\rho_j)$, the number of distinct Van Vleck polynomials $C(z)$ for which the generalized Lamé equation has a polynomial solution of degree exactly $n$ is exactly $\sigma(n,N)$.

(b) Characterize all exceptional configurations of the parameters $(a_1,\dots,a_N;\rho_1,\dots,\rho_N)$ for which the number of distinct Van Vleck polynomials producing a degree-$n$ polynomial solution is strictly less than $\sigma(n,N)$.

There has been substantial modern work on Heine–Stieltjes and Van Vleck polynomials (asymptotics, interlacing, zero distribution, complex parameter regimes, BCS/Bethe ansatz connections), and several authors have given modern arguments establishing Heine's generic count in particular settings. Let $Y$ be a Banach space (over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$). For a Banach space $Z$, denote by $B_Z$ its closed unit ball, by $S_Z$ its unit sphere, and by $Z^*$ its topological dual. For a bounded linear operator $T:Z\to Z$, the numerical range of $T$ is
$$V(T)=\{x^*(Tx): x\in S_Z,\ x^*\in S_{Z^*},\ x^*(x)=1\},$$
its numerical radius is $v(T)=\sup\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in V(T)\}$, and the numerical index of $Z$ is
$$n(Z)=\inf\{v(T): T\in L(Z),\ \|T\|=1\}.$$
A predual of $Y$ is a Banach space $X$ such that $X^*$ is isometrically isomorphic to $Y$.

Assume that $Y$ is a dual Banach space. Must there always exist a predual $X$ of $Y$ such that
$$n(X)=n(Y)\,?$$

Let $\mu_0,\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m$ be positive Borel measures on the real line with finite moments of all orders, and consider the Sobolev inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_S \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{m} \int_{\mathbb{R}} f^{(k)}(x)\,g^{(k)}(x)\,d\mu_k(x),$$
defined on the space of polynomials. For each non-negative integer $n$, let $P_n$ denote the unique monic polynomial of degree $n$ satisfying $\langle P_n,q\rangle_S = 0$ for every polynomial $q$ of degree strictly less than $n$ (i.e., the monic Sobolev orthogonal polynomial of degree $n$).

In analogy with the Fokas–Its–Kitaev characterization of standard orthogonal polynomials on the real line — where the monic orthogonal polynomial of degree $n$ associated with a weight $w$ appears as the $(1,1)$-entry of the unique $2\times 2$ matrix-valued function $Y(z)$ that is analytic in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$, has prescribed jump $Y_+(x)=Y_-(x)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & w(x)\\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and behaves like $Y(z)=(I+O(1/z))\,\mathrm{diag}(z^n,z^{-n})$ as $z\to\infty$ — does there exist a matrix-valued Riemann–Hilbert problem (with explicit jump contour, jump matrices, and asymptotic normalization determined by the data $(\mu_0,\dots,\mu_m)$) whose unique solution encodes the monic Sobolev orthogonal polynomials $P_n$ in a designated entry?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For Sobolev inner products of the discrete/coherent-pair type and several specific Sobolev settings, matrix Riemann–Hilbert characterizations have been derived (e.g., by reformulating scalar Sobolev orthogonality as matrix orthogonality on the real line, after work of Fokas–Its–Kitaev and subsequent extensions by Cassatella-Contra, Mañas, Branquinho and others). However, a fully general matrix Riemann–Hilbert characterization for arbitrary continuous Sobolev inner products with several derivatives does not appear to be established in a uniform way, and the question is best described as partially answered rather than completely resolved.

Let $X$ be a Banach space (over the real or complex field). The numerical index of $X$ is defined as
$$n(X) = \inf\{v(T) : T \in L(X),\ \|T\| = 1\},$$
where $L(X)$ denotes the space of bounded linear operators on $X$ and the numerical radius of $T \in L(X)$ is
$$v(T) = \sup\{|x^*(Tx)| : x \in X,\ x^* \in X^*,\ \|x\| = \|x^*\| = x^*(x) = 1\}.$$
A predual of a Banach space $Y$ is a Banach space $X$ such that $X^*$ is isometrically isomorphic to $Y$. We say $Y$ has a unique predual (up to isometric isomorphism) if any two preduals of $Y$ are isometrically isomorphic.

Question: Suppose $Y$ is a dual Banach space that admits a unique predual $X$ (up to isometric isomorphism). Must $n(Y) = n(X)$?

Question: Suppose $Y$ is a dual Banach space that admits a unique predual $X$ (up to isometric isomorphism). Must $n(Y) = n(X)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem appears to remain open in general. Partial results are known: for L-embedded spaces (in particular preduals of von Neumann algebras and JBW*-triples) and for C*-algebras the numerical index coincides with that of the dual. However, the analogous equality fails for successive preduals — there exist examples where X** is a C*-algebra with n(X) = 1 but n(X*) = 1/2 — so the general unique-predual question is not subsumed by these positive results.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$ be positive Borel measures on the real line (with all finite moments and infinite support) and consider the Sobolev inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_S \;=\; \int f(x)g(x)\,d\mu_0(x) \;+\; \int f'(x)g'(x)\,d\mu_1(x).$$
For each integer $n\ge 1$ let $Q_n$ be the monic polynomial of degree $n$ that is orthogonal with respect to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_S$. The sequence $\{Q_n\}$ is called balanced when, asymptotically, both terms in $\langle Q_n,Q_n\rangle_S$ contribute on the same scale (i.e. neither the $\mu_0$-part nor the $\mu_1$-part dominates as $n\to\infty$).

In a restricted (e.g. coherent-pair / classical-weight) setting it is known that the balanced monic Sobolev orthogonal polynomials $Q_n$ behave asymptotically like the standard monic orthogonal polynomials with respect to a single "combined" measure $\nu$ canonically constructed from the pair $(\mu_0,\mu_1)$; for instance, ratios $Q_n(z)/P_n(z;\nu)$ converge locally uniformly outside the support of $\nu$ to $1$, and analogous relative-asymptotic and zero-distribution statements hold.

Problem. Determine whether this equivalence between balanced monic Sobolev orthogonal polynomials and standard orthogonal polynomials for a combined measure persists in a substantially broader class of pairs $(\mu_0,\mu_1)$ — beyond the coherent-pair / classical-weight framework — and, if so, identify the appropriate construction of the combined measure and the precise sense (relative outer asymptotics, $n$-th root asymptotics, weak zero asymptotics, etc.) in which the equivalence holds.

Let X be a real or complex Banach space, with closed unit ball B_X and topological dual X*. The numerical radius of a bounded linear operator T: X → X is defined by
  v(T) = sup{ |x*(T x)| : x ∈ B_X, x* ∈ B_{X*}, x*(x) = 1 },
and the numerical index of X is
  n(X) = inf{ v(T) : T ∈ L(X), ‖T‖ = 1 }.
Assume that n(X) = 1; equivalently, v(T) = ‖T‖ for every bounded linear operator T on X.

Let ext(B_X) denote the set of extreme points of B_X and ext(B_{X*}) the set of extreme points of B_{X*}.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space with closed unit ball $B_X$ and unit sphere $S_X$. A nonempty convex subset $F \subseteq S_X$ is called a maximal convex subset of $S_X$ if it is maximal (with respect to inclusion) among the convex subsets of $S_X$. The space $X$ is called a CL-space if
$$B_X = \operatorname{aconv}(F)$$
for every maximal convex subset $F$ of $S_X$, where $\operatorname{aconv}(F)$ denotes the absolutely convex hull of $F$ (the convex hull of $F \cup (-F)$). The space $X$ is called an almost-CL-space if
$$B_X = \overline{\operatorname{aconv}(F)}$$
for every maximal convex subset $F$ of $S_X$, i.e., the closed absolutely convex hull of every maximal convex subset of $S_X$ equals $B_X$.

Every CL-space is an almost-CL-space. Determine whether there exists a real almost-CL-space that is not a CL-space.

$$x p_n(x) = a_{n+1} p_{n+1}(x) + b_n p_n(x) + a_n p_{n-1}(x), \qquad n \ge 0,$$
with recurrence coefficients $\{a_n, b_n\}$. Define the (differential) entropy of $p_n$ with respect to the orthogonality measure by
$$E_n(\mu) := -\int_I p_n(x)^2 \log igl(p_n(x)^2 igr)\, d\mu(x).$$

For measures supported on a bounded interval there exists a numerically stable algorithm that computes $E_n(\mu)$ taking as input only the recurrence coefficients $\{a_k, b_k\}_{k=0}^{n}$.

Problem: Devise a numerically stable algorithm that, given only the recurrence coefficients $\{a_k, b_k\}$ associated with a measure $\mu$ on an unbounded interval $I$, computes the entropy $E_n(\mu)$ for each $n$. The problem of characterizing Banach spaces admitting an equivalent renorming with numerical index 1 is widely regarded as open. Partial results are known: every separable Banach space containing an isomorphic copy of c_0 can be renormed to be lush (hence to have numerical index 1), and for Asplund spaces lushness is equivalent to numerical index 1. Let $w$ be a non-negative weight function on a compact set $E\subset\mathbb{R}$ (with $w>0$ a.e. on $E$ and sufficiently regular, e.g., satisfying the Szegő/Erdős-class conditions on $[-1,1]$), and let $\{p_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be the sequence of polynomials orthonormal with respect to $w(x)\,dx$ on $E$. For each $n$, let
$$\nu_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{x_{j,n}}$$
denote the normalized zero-counting measure of $p_n$, and let $\mu_n$ denote the probability measure $|p_n(x)|^2 w(x)\,dx$ on $E$. Define the mutual logarithmic energy
$$I(\nu_n,\mu_n)=\iint \log\frac{1}{|x-y|}\,d\nu_n(x)\,d\mu_n(y).$$
It is known that, for the classical setting, an asymptotic expansion of the form
$$I(\nu_n,\mu_n)=A\log n+\tfrac12\cdot\frac{\log n}{n}+o\!\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)$$
(or the analogous "universal" second-order term with constant $1/2$) appears, derived via an entropy identity relating $I(\nu_n,\mu_n)$ to the logarithmic energy of $\nu_n$ and the entropy of $\mu_n$.

Provide a conceptual explanation of this universal second-order term. In particular:
(i) Determine whether the constant $1/2$ appearing in the second term equals the logarithmic capacity of the support of the orthogonality measure, or identify what quantity it represents.
(ii) Give a direct proof of the second-order asymptotic that does not pass through the entropy identity.
(iii) Determine the largest natural class of weights $w$ for which the same second-order asymptotic remains valid.

Let $G\subset\mathbb{C}$ be a bounded simply connected domain whose boundary $\Gamma=\partial G$ is a piecewise analytic Jordan curve without cusps (i.e. a finite union of analytic arcs meeting at corners with interior angles in $(0,2\pi)$, none of which equals $0$ or $2\pi$). Let $\Omega:=\overline{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\overline{G}$ be the exterior domain, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to\{w:|w|>1\}$ be the conformal map normalized by $\Phi(\infty)=\infty$ and $\Phi'(\infty)>0$, so that $\mathrm{cap}(\Gamma)=1/\Phi'(\infty)$ is the logarithmic capacity of $\Gamma$.

Let $\{p_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be the sequence of Bergman orthogonal polynomials of $G$, i.e. the polynomials $p_n(z)=\lambda_n z^n+\cdots$ with $\lambda_n>0$ that are orthonormal with respect to the area measure on $G$:
$$\int_G p_n(z)\,\overline{p_m(z)}\,dA(z)=\delta_{n,m}.$$

Prove or disprove the following two strong asymptotic formulas:

1. (Leading coefficient asymptotics)
$$\lambda_n=\sqrt{\frac{n+1}{\pi}}\,\mathrm{cap}(\Gamma)^{-(n+1)}\bigl(1+O(1/n)\bigr),\qquad n\to\infty.$$

2. (Exterior asymptotics) Uniformly for $z\in\Omega$,
$$p_n(z)=\sqrt{\frac{n+1}{\pi}}\,\Phi'(z)\,\Phi(z)^{n}\bigl(1+O(1/n)\bigr),\qquad n\to\infty.$$

For piecewise analytic Jordan curves without cusps, strong asymptotics for the leading coefficients $\lambda_n$ and for $p_n$ outside $G$ have been established, with an error term of order $O(1/n)$ shown to be best possible in the leading-coefficient asymptotics (Miña-Díaz and collaborators, Constr. Approx. 2013; Numer. Algorithms 2015). Let $X$ be a real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|$ and topological dual $X^*$. For a bounded linear operator $T: X \to X$, define its numerical radius by
$$v(T) := \sup\{|x^*(T x)| : x \in X,\ x^* \in X^*,\ \|x\| = \|x^*\| = x^*(x) = 1\}.$$
The numerical index of $X$ is the constant
$$n(X) := \inf\{v(T) : T \in \mathcal{L}(X),\ \|T\| = 1\} \in [0,1].$$
Equivalently, $n(X)$ is the greatest constant $k \geq 0$ such that $k\|T\| \leq v(T)$ for every bounded linear operator $T$ on $X$.

Find a characterization of those real Banach spaces $X$ satisfying $n(X) = 0$ that is expressed purely in terms of the geometry of $X$ (its norm, unit ball, or related geometric structures), without referring to bounded linear operators, their norms, or their numerical ranges.

Let $T^d=\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_d)\in\mathbb{R}^d: x_i\ge 0,\ x_1+\cdots+x_d\le 1\}$ be the standard simplex in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and set $x_{d+1}:=1-x_1-\cdots-x_d$. For a multi-index $\kappa=(\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_{d+1})$ with $\kappa_i\ge 0$, consider the Jacobi-type weight on the simplex
$$W_\kappa^T(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{d+1} x_i^{\kappa_i-1/2},\qquad x\in T^d.$$
Let $\{P_n\}$ be the orthogonal polynomial expansion in $L^2(T^d, W_\kappa^T)$. There is an associated generalized translation operator $\tau_y^T$ defined spectrally by
$$\tau_y^T f(x)=\sum_{n\ge 0}\frac{P_n(x,y;W_\kappa^T)\;\hat f_n}{\|P_n\|^2},$$
where $P_n(x,y;W_\kappa^T)$ are the reproducing kernels of the orthogonal polynomial subspaces. In the analogous case of the unit ball $B^d$ with weight $W_\kappa^B(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}|x_i|^{2\kappa_i}(1-\|x\|^2)^{\kappa_{d+1}-1/2}$, the corresponding translation operator is known to admit an explicit integral representation that is compatible with the Dunkl intertwining operator $V_\kappa$.

Problem: Find an explicit integral representation for $\tau_y^T f(x)$ on $T^d$ that is positive (or otherwise bounded on appropriate function spaces), is compatible with the intertwining operator for the Dunkl operators associated to $W_\kappa^T$, and reduces, under the standard quadratic map $B^d\to T^d$, to the known integral formula for the generalized translation operator on the ball.

Let $\ell_1$ denote the Banach space of absolutely summable complex sequences $b=(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots)$, and let $\sigma:\ell_1\to\ell_1$ denote the left shift $\sigma(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots)=(b_1,b_2,b_3,\ldots)$. Fix a bounded sequence $t=(t_0,t_1,t_2,\ldots)$ of complex numbers with $t_0=1$, and define the bilinear pairing $b\cdot t=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}b_n t_n$ (which converges absolutely since $b\in\ell_1$ and $t$ is bounded). Set
$$H_t=\{b\in\ell_1 : (\sigma^l b)\cdot t = 0 \text{ for all } l=0,1,2,\ldots\}.$$
Consider the generating function $R(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t_n z^n$, holomorphic in the open unit disk $|z|<1$. For each root $\rho$ of $R$ inside the open unit disk, let $m=m(\rho)\ge 1$ be its multiplicity, and for each integer $j$ with $0\le j\le m-1$ consider the sequence
$$b^{(\rho,j)}=(\nu^{j}\rho^{\nu})_{\nu=0}^{\infty}\in\ell_1.$$
Let $H_t^{(e)}$ be the closure in $\ell_1$ of the set of all finite linear combinations of the sequences $b^{(\rho,j)}$, taken over all roots $\rho$ of $R$ in $|z|<1$ and all $0\le j\le m(\rho)-1$.

Prove or disprove: For every such $t$, one has $H_t^{(e)}=H_t$.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $L(X)$ denote the Banach algebra of bounded linear operators on $X$. An operator $T \in L(X)$ is called a multiplier if every extreme point $p$ of the dual unit ball of $X$ is an eigenvector of the adjoint $T^*$, i.e., $T^*p = a_T(p)\, p$ for some scalar $a_T(p)$. The centralizer of $X$, denoted $Z(X)$, is defined as
$$Z(X) = \{T \in L(X) : T \text{ and } S \text{ are multipliers for some } S \in L(X) \text{ with } a_S = i a_T \text{ in the complex case}\},$$
or equivalently, in the real case, $Z(X)$ is the set of multipliers $T$ for which the corresponding function $a_T$ is real-valued on the extreme points of the dual unit ball; $Z(X)$ is a closed unital subalgebra of $L(X)$ which is isometrically isomorphic, as a real Banach algebra, to $C_{\mathbb{R}}(K)$ for some compact Hausdorff space $K$.

Determine the set of all possible values of $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} Z(X)$ as $X$ ranges over all $5$-dimensional real Banach spaces.

Fix an integer $k \geq 1$. Call $\{\lambda_n\}$ an interval-filling sequence of order $k$ if every $x \in [0, kL_0]$ admits an expansion
$$x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n \lambda_n, \qquad \varepsilon_n \in \{0, 1, \ldots, k\}.$$
Call $\{\lambda_n\}$ smooth if there exists an integer $T \geq 1$ with $\lambda_{n+T} \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\lambda_n$ for every $n \geq 1$.

A function $F : [0, kL_0] \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to be additive with respect to $\{\lambda_n\}$ if there exist functions $f_n : \{0,1,\ldots,k\} \to \mathbb{C}$ with $f_n(0) = 0$ such that, for every $x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n \lambda_n \in [0, kL_0]$ with $\varepsilon_n \in \{0,1,\ldots,k\}$,
$$F(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n(\varepsilon_n),$$

Call $\{\lambda_n\}$ smooth if there exists an integer $T \geq 1$ with $\lambda_{n+T} \leq \tfrac{1}{2}\lambda_n$ for every $n \geq 1$.

A function $F : [0, kL_0] \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to be additive with respect to $\{\lambda_n\}$ if there exist functions $f_n : \{0,1,\ldots,k\} \to \mathbb{C}$ with $f_n(0) = 0$ such that, for every $x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n \lambda_n \in [0, kL_0]$ with $\varepsilon_n \in \{0,1,\ldots,k\}$,
$$F(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n(\varepsilon_n),$$
the value being independent of which valid expansion is chosen.

Assume $\{\lambda_n\}$ is a smooth interval-filling sequence of order $k$, and let $F : [0, kL_0] \to \mathbb{C}$ be continuous and additive with respect to $\{\lambda_n\}$. Suppose $F$ is differentiable at at least one point of $[0, kL_0]$. Must there exist a constant $c \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $F(x) = cx$ for all $x \in [0, kL_0]$?

$$d(X,Y)=\inf\{\|T\|\,\|T^{-1}\|: T:X\to Y\text{ is a linear isomorphism}\}.$$
For a real Banach space $X$, the numerical radius of a bounded linear operator $T:X\to X$ is
$$v(T)=\sup\{|x^{*}(Tx)|:x\in X,\;x^{*}\in X^{*},\;\|x\|=\|x^{*}\|=x^{*}(x)=1\},$$
and the numerical index of $X$ is
$$n(X)=\inf\{v(T):T\in\mathcal{L}(X),\;\|T\|=1\}.$$
Let $\mathcal{M}_m\subset\mathcal{N}_m$ be the subset consisting of (isometry classes of) those $m$-dimensional real normed spaces $X$ with numerical index $n(X)=1$.

Determine the diameter
$$\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{M}_m)=\sup\{d(X,Y):X,Y\in\mathcal{M}_m\}$$
as a function of $m$, and decide whether $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{M}_m)$ is asymptotically comparable to $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{N}_m)$ as $m\to\infty$ (which is known to be of order $m$).

Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ be the open unit disk, equipped with normalized area measure $dA$. For $1 < p < \infty$, let $A^p = A^p(\mathbb{D})$ denote the Bergman space of analytic functions $f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C}$ with $\|f\|_{A^p}^p = \int_\mathbb{D} |f(z)|^p\, dA(z) < \infty$. Let $P : L^2(\mathbb{D}) \to A^2$ denote the orthogonal Bergman projection, defined by $(Pg)(z) = \int_\mathbb{D} \frac{g(w)}{(1-z\bar w)^2}\, dA(w)$, which extends naturally to a class of distributional symbols.

For a symbol $a$ (taken to be in $L^1(\mathbb{D})$, $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{D})$, or a suitable space of distributions on $\mathbb{D}$), define formally the Toeplitz operator $T_a f = P(a f)$ on analytic polynomials $f$.

For a non-negative integer $m$ and a radial weight $\nu$ on $\mathbb{D}$ comparable to $(1-|z|)^{2m}$ near $\partial \mathbb{D}$, define the weighted negative-order Sobolev space $W^{-m,\infty}_\nu(\mathbb{D})$ as the space of distributions $a$ that can be represented as
$$ a = \sum_{|\alpha| \le m} \partial^\alpha b_\alpha, \qquad \text{with each } b_\alpha \in L^\infty(\mathbb{D}, \nu),$$
i.e., $\nu^{1/2} b_\alpha \in L^\infty(\mathbb{D})$, and equip it with the natural quotient norm.

(a) Find a condition on the symbol $a$ that is both necessary and sufficient for $T_a$ to extend to a bounded linear operator $A^p \to A^p$, in the three settings $a \in L^1(\mathbb{D})$, $a \in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{D})$, and $a$ a distribution, for $1 < p < \infty$ (or at least for the Hilbert case $p = 2$).

(b) In particular, for $a \in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{D})$ (or even $a \in L^1(\mathbb{D})$), determine whether the condition $a \in W^{-m,\infty}_\nu(\mathbb{D})$ for some $m$ — known to be sufficient — is also necessary for the boundedness of $T_a : A^p \to A^p$, $1 < p < \infty$, at least when $p = 2$.

Denote by $\mathcal{P}(^kX;X)$ the Banach space of such polynomials endowed with the norm $\|P\|=\sup\{\|P(x)\|:\|x\|\le 1\}$. The numerical radius of $P\in\mathcal{P}(^kX;X)$ is
$$v(P)=\sup\bigl\{|x^*(P(x))|:x\in X,\ x^*\in X^*,\ \|x\|=\|x^*\|=x^*(x)=1\bigr\}.$$
The polynomial numerical index of order $k$ of $X$ is
$$n^{(k)}(X)=\inf\{v(P):P\in\mathcal{P}(^kX;X),\ \|P\|=1\}.$$
Compute explicitly the values $n^{(k)}(H)$ for every $k\ge 2$, where $H$ is an infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and the values $n^{(k)}(\ell_1)$ for every $k\ge 2$, where $\ell_1$ is the complex Banach space of absolutely summable sequences.

Let $\mathbb{D}$ denote the open unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$, and let $A^p = A^p(\mathbb{D})$ ($1 < p < \infty$) be the Bergman space of analytic functions on $\mathbb{D}$ that are $p$-integrable with respect to area measure. Let $P:L^p(\mathbb{D}) \to A^p$ be the Bergman projection. For a bounded measurable function $a$ on $\mathbb{D}$, the Toeplitz operator $T_a$ is defined on $A^p$ by $T_a f = P(a f)$. For an $N \times N$ matrix-valued symbol $a = (a_{ij})$ with entries in $L^\infty(\mathbb{D})$, $T_a$ acts coordinatewise on $(A^p)^N$.

Consider the symbol algebra $C(\overline{\mathbb{D}}) + H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$, consisting of sums of continuous functions on $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ and bounded analytic functions on $\mathbb{D}$, and its $N \times N$ matrix-valued analogue $M_N(C(\overline{\mathbb{D}}) + H^\infty(\mathbb{D}))$. Also consider the Zhu class $L^\infty(\mathbb{D}) \cap \mathrm{VMO}_\partial(\mathbb{D})$ of bounded functions of vanishing mean oscillation (with respect to the Bergman metric), and its matrix-valued analogue.

Problems:
(a) For $p = 2$ (and more generally $1 < p < \infty$), find an explicit index formula for Fredholm block Toeplitz operators $T_a$ on $(A^p)^N$ whose matrix-valued symbols $a$ lie in $M_N(C(\overline{\mathbb{D}}) + H^\infty(\mathbb{D}))$, expressing $\mathrm{ind}(T_a)$ in terms of the symbol $a$.

(b) Find an analogous index formula for Fredholm block Toeplitz operators $T_a$ on $(A^p)^N$ whose matrix-valued symbols belong to $M_N(L^\infty(\mathbb{D}) \cap \mathrm{VMO}_\partial(\mathbb{D}))$.

For a graph $H$, the domination number $\gamma(H)$ is the minimum size of a set $D \subseteq V(H)$ such that every vertex in $V(H)\setminus D$ has a neighbor in $D$.

Let $\mathbb{D}$ denote the open unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$ with normalized area measure $dA$. For $1 \le p < \infty$, let $L^p = L^p(\mathbb{D}, dA)$ and let the Bergman space $A^p \subset L^p$ be the closed subspace of holomorphic functions in $L^p$. Let $P : L^2 \to A^2$ be the orthogonal Bergman projection, given by
$$ (Pf)(z) = \int_{\mathbb{D}} \frac{f(w)}{(1-z\bar w)^2}\, dA(w), $$
which extends to a bounded operator on $L^p$ for $1 < p < \infty$.

For a measurable symbol $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$, define the Hankel operator with symbol $f$ formally by
$$ H_f g = (I - P)(fg), $$
acting on suitable holomorphic functions $g$.

Problem. Give a complete characterization of those symbols $f$ for which the Hankel operator $H_f$ is (i) bounded on $L^1(\mathbb{D}, dA)$ (in an appropriate sense, e.g. as an operator from $A^1$ to $L^1/A^1$ or to a suitable companion space), and (ii) compact in the same setting. The characterization should be sufficient to develop a Fredholm theory for Toeplitz operators $T_f = P M_f$ on the Bergman space $A^1$.

For a graph $G$, let $P_n$ denote the path on $n$ vertices, and let $G \square P_n$ denote the Cartesian product of $G$ with $P_n$ (the graph on vertex set $V(G) \times V(P_n)$ in which $(u,i)$ and $(v,j)$ are adjacent iff either $u=v$ and $ij \in E(P_n)$, or $i=j$ and $uv \in E(G)$). A graph parameter is a function $A$ assigning to each finite graph an element of some fixed set (e.g.\ an integer, like the domination number $\gamma$).

Say that $A(G \square P_n)$ admits a closed form (as a function of $n$, with $G$ fixed) if there exist finitely many polynomials $p_0,\dots,p_{k-1}$ in $n$ and an integer $n_0$ such that $A(G \square P_n) = p_{n \bmod k}(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$ (i.e.\ $A(G \square P_n)$ is eventually quasi-polynomial in $n$), where the polynomials and $n_0$ are allowed to depend on $G$.

Problem: Exhibit an "interesting" formal language (logic) $L$ for expressing graph parameters and graph properties, with the following property: whenever a graph parameter or graph property $A$ (such as the domination number) is expressible in $L$, then for every fixed finite graph $G$, the value $A(G \square P_n)$ admits a closed form in $n$ in the above sense. The language $L$ should be rich enough to express natural parameters such as the domination number.

Let $P_n$ denote the path graph on $n$ vertices, and let $P_m \square P_n$ denote the Cartesian product (the $m \times n$ grid graph), whose vertex set is $\{1,\dots,m\} \times \{1,\dots,n\}$ with edges between vertices that differ by 1 in exactly one coordinate. A fractional dominating function on a graph $G = (V,E)$ is a function $f : V \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ such that for every vertex $v \in V$, $f(v) + \sum_{u \sim v} f(u) \ge 1$, where the sum is over the neighbors of $v$. The fractional domination number $\gamma_f(G)$ is the infimum of $\sum_{v \in V} f(v)$ over all fractional dominating functions $f$.

Question: For each fixed positive integer $m$, does there exist a closed-form expression (as a function of $n$) for $\gamma_f(P_m \square P_n)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question appears to remain open in general. Closed-form expressions are known for small values of $m$ (notably $m = 2$, by Hare and Stewart, with connections to Fibonacci numbers), and various near-sharp upper and lower bounds have been established for grid graphs, but no closed-form formula is known for arbitrary fixed $m$ as a function of $n$.

For a (real or complex) Banach space $X$, let $\mathcal{P}(^kX;X)$ denote the Banach space of continuous $k$-homogeneous polynomials $P:X\to X$ endowed with the norm $\|P\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le 1}\|P(x)\|$. The numerical radius of $P\in\mathcal{P}(^kX;X)$ is
$$v(P)=\sup\{|x^*(P(x))|:x\in X,\ x^*\in X^*,\ \|x\|=\|x^*\|=x^*(x)=1\},$$
and the polynomial numerical index of order $k$ of $X$ is
$$n^{(k)}(X)=\inf\{v(P):P\in\mathcal{P}(^kX;X),\ \|P\|=1\}.$$
For a positive $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$ and a Banach space $X$, let $L_1(\mu,X)$ and $L_\infty(\mu,X)$ denote the usual Bochner spaces of $X$-valued integrable, respectively essentially bounded, measurable functions.

Fix an integer $k>2$. Determine whether there is any general relationship (e.g., an equality, or two-sided inequalities valid for every $X$ and every $\mu$) between $n^{(k)}(L_1(\mu,X))$ and $n^{(k)}(X)$, and analogously between $n^{(k)}(L_\infty(\mu,X))$ and $n^{(k)}(X)$.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk and, for $\nu>-1$, let $dA_\nu(z)=(\nu+1)(1-|z|^2)^\nu\,dA(z)/\pi$ denote the standard weighted area measure on $\mathbb{D}$. For an integer $m\ge 0$, define the weighted Sobolev-type space $W^{-m,\infty}_\nu$ as the space of distributions on $\mathbb{D}$ that admit a representation
$$a=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}(-1)^{|\alpha|}D^{\alpha}b_\alpha,$$
where each $b_\alpha\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{D})$ satisfies $b_\alpha(z)(1-|z|^2)^{-|\alpha|}\in L^\infty(\mathbb{D},dA_\nu)$, and $D^\alpha$ denotes a (real) partial derivative of order $|\alpha|$ in distributional sense.

For the normalized reproducing kernel of the weighted Bergman space $A^2_\nu(\mathbb{D})$,
$$k_z(w)=\frac{(1-|z|^2)^{(\nu+2)/2}}{(1-\bar z w)^{\nu+2}},\qquad z,w\in\mathbb{D},$$
the Berezin transform of $a\in W^{-m,\infty}_\nu$ is defined (via duality) by
$$\tilde a(z)=\langle a,\,|k_z|^2\rangle,\qquad z\in\mathbb{D}.$$

Suppose $a\in W^{-m,\infty}_\nu$ admits a representation as above in which, for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le m$, the function $z\mapsto b_\alpha(z)(1-|z|^2)^{-|\alpha|}$ is continuous on $\mathbb{D}$.

Question: Must the Berezin transform $\tilde a$ then be continuous on $\mathbb{D}$?

Let G be a finite simple graph. For graphs H₁ and H₂, the Cartesian product H₁ □ H₂ is the graph with vertex set V(H₁) × V(H₂) in which (u₁, u₂) is adjacent to (v₁, v₂) if and only if either u₁ = v₁ and u₂v₂ ∈ E(H₂), or u₂ = v₂ and u₁v₁ ∈ E(H₁). A dominating set of a graph H is a subset D ⊆ V(H) such that every vertex not in D has at least one neighbor in D, and the domination number γ(H) is the minimum cardinality of a dominating set of H.

It is known that, for any fixed graph G, when F(n) = Pₙ is the path on n vertices, the function n ↦ γ(G □ F(n)) admits a closed-form expression (eventually a fixed linear function of n with a periodic correction). This extends to the families F(n) = Cₙ (cycles) and to F(n) = the complete t-ary tree of depth n. Closed forms are also obtainable for certain doubly-indexed families, for example F(n) = the rooted tree consisting of m subtrees each isomorphic to Pₙ.

Problem: Characterize, as broadly as possible, the parameterized families of finite graphs {F(n)}_{n≥1} with the following property: for every finite graph G, the domination number γ(G □ F(n)), viewed as a function of n, admits a closed-form expression (in the sense above). Provide a structural description, or general sufficient conditions on the way F(n) is built up as n grows, that guarantee the existence of such a closed form, and identify natural construction operations on families that preserve this property.

For a real number $r \ge 1$, let $AP_r(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$ denote the Besicovitch-type space of almost periodic functions defined as follows. A trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $P(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k e^{i\lambda_k t}$ with $a_k\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\lambda_k\in\mathbb{R}$. On the linear space of trigonometric polynomials consider the seminorm
$$\|f\|_{r} \;=\; \left(\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}|f(t)|^{r}\,dt\right)^{1/r}.$$
Define $AP_r(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$ to be the completion of the space of trigonometric polynomials with respect to $\|\cdot\|_r$.

It is known that:
(i) for $r=1$, the elements of $AP_1$ may be realized as honest pointwise-defined functions $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$;
(ii) for $r=2$, the space $AP_2$ coincides with the Besicovitch space $B^2$, whose elements are equivalence classes of measurable functions modulo functions with vanishing quadratic mean.

Determine the precise nature of the elements of $AP_r(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$ for intermediate exponents $1<r<2$: can each element be canonically represented by an actual function $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$, must it be regarded as an equivalence class of measurable functions modulo a suitable null subspace, or is some other description required?

Let X be a Banach space over the real field, and let L(X) denote the Banach algebra of bounded linear operators on X with the operator norm. For T ∈ L(X), the numerical radius of T is defined by
  v(T) = sup{ |x*(T x)| : x ∈ X, x* ∈ X*, ‖x‖ = ‖x*‖ = x*(x) = 1 }.
The skew-Hermitian part (Lie algebra) of L(X) is
  Z(X) = { T ∈ L(X) : v(T) = 0 },
and on the quotient space L(X)/Z(X) one considers the quotient norm ‖[T]‖ = inf{ ‖T + S‖ : S ∈ Z(X) }. The second numerical index of X is defined as
  n^{(2)}(X) = inf{ v(T) : T ∈ L(X), ‖[T]‖ = 1 },
equivalently, the largest constant k ≥ 0 such that k · ‖[T]‖ ≤ v(T) for every T ∈ L(X). One always has 0 ≤ n^{(2)}(X) ≤ 1, and for the one-dimensional space ℝ one trivially has n^{(2)}(ℝ) = 1.

Question: Does there exist a real Banach space X, with X ≠ ℝ (i.e. of dimension at least 2), such that n^{(2)}(X) = 1?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered in the affirmative. A subsequent work introducing and studying the second numerical index proves that every real Hilbert space has second numerical index equal to 1, providing a family of real Banach spaces other than ℝ with n^{(2)}(X) = 1.

Propose a theoretical framework, an experimental program, or a combination of both capable of resolving the following cluster of open questions in elementary-particle physics and quantum theory:

1. Does a "Dirac ether" — a relativistically invariant fluid-like vacuum medium of the type proposed by Dirac — exist as a physical entity?
2. Can Dirac's 1951 reformulation of electron theory (a nonlinear, ether-based extension of the Dirac equation) eliminate the ultraviolet/self-energy infinities of the electron and produce a single consistent description that unifies the quantum-mechanical and the classical-electrodynamical pictures of the electron?
3. What dynamical mechanism, if any, underlies the empirical Koide relation for the charged-lepton masses,
   (m_e + m_μ + m_τ) / (√m_e + √m_μ + √m_τ)² = 2/3 ?
4. Do neutrinos have nonzero rest mass, and if so what are the absolute masses and the mass hierarchy?
5. Do composite-substructure models of quarks and leptons (preon or rishon models) yield predictions that surpass those of conventional quantum chromodynamics (QCD)?
6. Is there a derivation from first principles of the physical mechanism responsible for quark confinement in QCD?
7. Is there a precise mathematical correspondence between QCD and a "quantum fluid dynamics" describing the QCD vacuum or hadronic interior as a quantum fluid?
8. Can isolated free quarks or rishons exist as asymptotic states, and can they be produced and detected?
9. Do the properties of quarks, rishons, and neutrinos admit consistent reformulations in terms of (a) quaternionic quantum mechanics, (b) multivalued logics, or (c) Gross–Pitaevskii–type nonlinear Schrödinger condensate descriptions?
10. How does the gravitational interaction affect the effective electric charge of quarks?
11. Under what (if any) physical processes can the electric charge or rest mass of a quark be altered, or be converted directly into energy?
12. Is there a consistent quantum field theory in which anti-hydrogen arises automatically, and are there detectable signatures of cosmic anti-hydrogen?
13. Can a "ring" (extended, toroidal) model of the electron be made compatible with relativistic quantum theory?
14. Could a population of "hidden" neutrinos be present within ordinary matter (e.g., the human body) and be experimentally detected?

The problem is to give, for as many of items (1)–(14) as possible, either a definitive theoretical resolution, a feasible experimental test, or a rigorous demonstration of inconsistency.

No comprehensive resolution of the full list exists.

Setting. Consider a strictly proper rational transfer function G(z) of a discrete-time single-input single-output (SISO) linear system. A positive realization of G(z) of order N is a triple (A, b, c) with A ∈ R^{N×N}, b ∈ R^{N×1}, c ∈ R^{1×N} whose entries are all nonnegative, such that G(z) = c (zI − A)^{-1} b. The minimal positive realization order N*(G) is the smallest N for which such a nonnegative triple exists; it can be strictly larger than the McMillan degree of G(z).

Two general lines of attack have been proposed:
(i) the invariant-cone (polyhedral cone) approach, in which one seeks a proper polyhedral cone K ⊂ R^N invariant under A and compatible with b and c, with minimality of N tied to the minimum number of extreme rays of such a K; and
(ii) the positive-matrix factorization approach, in which one studies factorizations H = U V of an associated nonnegative Hankel-type matrix H into nonnegative factors U, V, with N*(G) related to the nonnegative rank of H.

Problem. Provide a mathematical framework that yields effective necessary and sufficient criteria for the minimal order N*(G) of a positive realization of an arbitrary strictly proper rational SISO transfer function G(z). In particular:

(a) Determine whether the invariant-cone approach can be extended to give necessary and sufficient conditions for N*(G) beyond the third-order case (currently the only general order for which such conditions, expressed via invariant polyhedral cones, are known).

(b) Alternatively, decide whether a nonnegative factorization formulation (factorization of an associated nonnegative matrix into nonnegative factors) provides the correct general instrument, and if so, derive from it computable necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing N*(G) for transfer functions of arbitrary order.

The general minimality problem for positive realizations of SISO rational transfer functions remains open. Necessary and sufficient conditions are known only in restricted settings — e.g., third-order transfer functions with distinct positive real poles, and certain classes with nonnegative or negative real poles or specific pole/residue structures. Recent works (e.g., on transfer functions with two distinct poles, 2022) continue to address special cases, indicating no general criterion has been established via either the invariant-cone method or nonnegative factorization.

The base-10 case is the well-known Smarandache–Wellin-style "consecutive concatenation" sequence (OEIS A007908). No prime term is known: extensive searches have ruled out primes for n up to at least the hundreds of thousands, but no proof exists that the sequence contains no primes or only finitely many. representations.normalized:
Consider continuous-time linear time-invariant systems of the form
  x'(t) = A x(t) + B u(t),  y(t) = C x(t) + D u(t),
where A ∈ ℝ^{n×n}, B ∈ ℝ^{n×m}, C ∈ ℝ^{p×n}, D ∈ ℝ^{p×m}. Such a quadruple (A, B, C, D) is called a positive realization if A is a Metzler matrix (i.e., its off-diagonal entries are nonnegative) and B, C, D have all entries nonnegative; equivalently, every nonnegative input u(·) and nonnegative initial state x(0) produces a nonnegative state trajectory x(·) and nonnegative output y(·). Given a proper rational transfer function H(s) (or, equivalently, an impulse response) that admits at least one positive realization, define the minimal positive realization dimension n⁺(H) to be the smallest integer n ≥ 0 for which there exists a positive realization (A, B, C, D) of H with state dimension n.

Problem: Develop a complete minimality theory for positive realizations of continuous-time systems. Specifically:
  (a) Provide a characterization of n⁺(H) in terms of the data of H (e.g., its Markov parameters, Hankel matrix factorizations over the nonnegative orthant, or geometric/cone-theoretic invariants), accounting for the fact that A must be Metzler rather than entrywise nonnegative as in the discrete-time case.
  (b) Provide necessary and sufficient conditions on a given positive realization (A, B, C, D) under which it is minimal, i.e., no positive realization of the same transfer function has strictly smaller state dimension.

Van der Waerden's theorem states that for every finite coloring of the positive integers $\mathbb{N}^{*}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$, at least one color class contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. Consider now partitions of $\mathbb{N}^{*}$ into infinitely many nonempty classes $\mathbb{N}^{*}=\bigsqcup_{i\in\mathbb{N}} A_i$ (with no restriction on the classes other than that they form a partition).

(a) Does there exist an integer $\ell>3$ such that, for every partition of $\mathbb{N}^{*}$ into infinitely many classes, at least one class $A_i$ contains an arithmetic progression of length $\ell$?

(b) If such integers $\ell$ exist, determine the largest one — i.e., find
$$\ell^{*}=\sup\{\ell\in\mathbb{N}: \text{every partition of }\mathbb{N}^{*}\text{ into infinitely many classes has some class containing an AP of length }\ell\}.$$
In particular, decide whether $\ell^{*}$ is finite or infinite.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

A direct construction shows that one can partition $\mathbb{N}^{*}$ into infinitely many classes none of which contains any 3-term arithmetic progression (e.g., place each integer in its own singleton class), so the naive form of the question is trivial. The intended non-trivial formulation (with some implicit regularity constraint on the classes) does not appear to have a definitive resolution in the literature, and no widely cited solution could be located. The status is therefore taken to be unknown.

A single-input single-output linear time-invariant discrete-time system is called positive if its state, input and output remain in the nonnegative orthant for all nonnegative inputs and nonnegative initial states. A positive realization of a rational transfer function $H(z)$ is a quadruple $(A,b,c,d)$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n}$, $c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{1\times n}$, $d\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ satisfying $H(z)=d+c(zI-A)^{-1}b$. Such a positive realization is called minimal if its state-space dimension $n$ is the smallest possible among all positive realizations of $H(z)$ (note that this minimal positive dimension may strictly exceed the McMillan degree of $H$).

Fix a rational transfer function $H(z)$ that admits at least one minimal positive realization, and let $n$ denote the minimal positive dimension. Characterize the set of all minimal positive realizations of $H(z)$: describe explicitly the group, semigroup, or family of admissible transformations $(A,b,c,d)\mapsto(\tilde A,\tilde b,\tilde c,\tilde d)$ that takes any minimal positive realization to any other, and determine the structure (e.g., connectedness, orbit decomposition) of this set in $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{1\times n}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$.

Let k and s be integers with k > 3 and 1 < s < k. Consider representations of an integer N in the form
    N = (p_1 + p_2 + ... + p_{k-s}) - (q_1 + q_2 + ... + q_s),
where p_1, ..., p_{k-s} and q_1, ..., q_s are prime numbers.

(a) Prove or disprove the following: if k is odd, then every odd integer N can be represented in the above form, and if k is even, then every even integer N can be represented in the above form, where the primes p_i are allowed to repeat among themselves and the primes q_j are required to be distinct from one another (and distinct from the p_i, in the sense intended for "other primes").

(b) Determine whether the statement in (a) remains true under the stronger requirement that all k primes p_1, ..., p_{k-s}, q_1, ..., q_s are pairwise distinct.

(c) For each admissible target integer N (odd if k is odd, even if k is even), determine the number of representations of N in the form above (with the distinctness conditions as in (a) and as in (b)).

$$G(z) = C(zI_n - A)^{-1}B + D$$

Develop a constructive procedure that, given such a positive realization $(A,B,C,D)$ of dimension $n$ and a tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$, produces another positive realization $(\tilde A, \tilde B, \tilde C, \tilde D)$ of dimension $\tilde n < n$ (with all entries of $\tilde A, \tilde B, \tilde C, \tilde D$ nonnegative) such that the corresponding transfer function $\tilde G(z) = \tilde C(zI_{\tilde n} - \tilde A)^{-1}\tilde B + \tilde D$ approximates $G(z)$ in a prescribed system norm, e.g.
$$\|G - \tilde G\|_{\mathcal H_\infty} \le \varepsilon \quad\text{or}\quad \|G - \tilde G\|_{\mathcal H_2} \le \varepsilon.$$

Equivalently: characterize, for a given positive system, the smallest dimension $\tilde n$ achievable by a positive approximant within tolerance $\varepsilon$, and provide an algorithm that attains it while preserving nonnegativity of all matrices.

Let $d\geq 1$ and let $V:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ be a complex-valued potential belonging to $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$, where $p\geq 1$ if $d=1$, $p>1$ if $d=2$, and $p\geq d/2$ if $d\geq 3$. Define the Schrödinger operator $H = -\Delta + V$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ (as a closed operator obtained, e.g., as an m-sectorial extension via the form sum or via relative boundedness). Let $\sigma_d(H)$ denote the discrete spectrum of $H$ (the isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity), and counted with their algebraic multiplicities. For $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$, let $\mathrm{dist}(\lambda,[0,\infty))$ denote the Euclidean distance from $\lambda$ to the nonnegative real half-line.

For real-valued potentials, the classical Lieb–Thirring inequality asserts that
$$\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma_d(H)} |\lambda|^{p-d/2} \leq C(p,d)\,\|V\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)}^p,$$
with a constant $C(p,d)$ depending only on $p$ and $d$.

Question: Does there exist a constant $C(p,d)$, depending only on $p$ and $d$, such that for every complex-valued $V\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ in the above range, the eigenvalues of $H=-\Delta+V$ satisfy
$$\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma_d(H)} \frac{\mathrm{dist}(\lambda,[0,\infty))^{p}}{|\lambda|^{d/2}} \leq C(p,d)\,\|V\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)}^p\;?$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjectured inequality has been disproved. Bögli and Štampach constructed counterexamples in the one-dimensional case (J. Spectr. Theory 11 (2021), 1391–1413), and the construction has subsequently been extended to all dimensions $d\geq 2$ in recent work (e.g., arXiv:2510.02192), showing that the proposed Lieb–Thirring-type inequality for complex-valued potentials fails in general. Weakened versions (with worse exponents or extra factors) are known to hold.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classification of all integer solutions to x³ + y³ + z³ = 1 (and more generally A x³ + B y³ + C z³ = D and its n-variable analogues) is widely regarded as open. While infinitely many solutions to x³ + y³ + z³ = 1 are known via several polynomial parametric families (e.g., Mahler's family (9t⁴)³ + (1 − 9t³)³ + (3t − 9t⁴)³ = 1 and others catalogued by Rowland), it is not known whether every integer solution lies in finitely many such families. The general question of describing or counting integer solutions to ternary cubic forms A x³ + B y³ + C z³ = D, and the higher-variable generalizations, remains an active and largely unresolved problem in Diophantine number theory.

Let $B_r(0) \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be the open ball of radius $r$ centered at the origin, and fix exponents $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $p > 1$. Consider the singular semilinear elliptic boundary value problem
$$
-\Delta u + \frac{1}{u^{\alpha}} = \lambda\, u^{p} \quad \text{in } B_r(0), \qquad u > 0 \text{ in } B_r(0), \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial B_r(0),
$$
where $\lambda > 0$ is a real parameter, and solutions are understood in a suitable weak sense allowing the singular absorption term $1/u^\alpha$.

Restrict attention to radial positive solutions $u = u(|x|)$. Suppose it is known that there exist values $0 < \lambda_* < \lambda_{**} < \infty$ such that:

1. For $\lambda \in (\lambda_*, \lambda_{**})$ the problem admits exactly two radial positive solution branches, a "lower" branch and an "upper" branch (ordered, e.g., by their $L^\infty$-norm or by energy).
2. For $\lambda > \lambda_{**}$ only the upper radial branch persists, while the lower radial branch ceases to exist.

Determine, with rigorous justification, the mechanism by which the lower radial positive solution branch terminates precisely at $\lambda = \lambda_{**}$. $$
where $\lambda > 0$ is a real parameter, and solutions are understood in a suitable weak sense allowing the singular absorption term $1/u^\alpha$.

Restrict attention to radial positive solutions $u = u(|x|)$. Suppose it is known that there exist values $0 < \lambda_* < \lambda_{**} < \infty$ such that:

1. For $\lambda \in (\lambda_*, \lambda_{**})$ the problem admits exactly two radial positive solution branches, a "lower" branch and an "upper" branch (ordered, e.g., by their $L^\infty$-norm or by energy).
2. For $\lambda > \lambda_{**}$ only the upper radial branch persists, while the lower radial branch ceases to exist.

Consider the following collection of idealized celestial-mechanics and classical-mechanics thought experiments, and provide rigorous answers (with proofs or quantitative analyses) to each.

1. (Relativistic speed limit.) Within the framework of special relativity, suppose a massive particle is already travelling at speed 0.99 c in an inertial frame, where c is the speed of light in vacuum. Show whether it is possible, by application of any finite sequence of accelerations, to make its speed in that frame exceed c. Treat also the case of a photon: can a photon be further accelerated to a speed exceeding c?

2. (Bridge between planets.) Two spherical planets of given masses M₁, M₂ and radii R₁, R₂ orbit their common centre of mass on a Keplerian orbit. Determine necessary conditions (in terms of the orbital parameters, tidal forces, material tensile strength, and the rotational states of the planets) for a rigid mechanical bridge connecting fixed surface points on the two bodies to remain in static equilibrium, or prove that no such bridge can exist.

3. (Split planet.) A spherical, self-gravitating planet of uniform density ρ and radius R is instantaneously cut into two equal hemispheres separated by a small gap. Assuming only Newtonian self-gravity and rigid hemispheres, describe the subsequent dynamical evolution: do the hemispheres reunite, oscillate, or separate, and on what time scale?

4. (Mutual visibility of Earth and Moon.) Model the Earth–Moon system as two rigid spheres in synchronous-locked or freely rotating motion. Explain rigorously why, for an observer fixed on the surface of one body at a point from which the other body is visible, the other body always appears "above" the local horizon, and characterize precisely the set of surface points where this holds.

5. (Tunnel through the Earth.) Model the Earth as a sphere of radius R with spherically symmetric mass distribution (consider both the uniform-density case and a realistic radial density profile).
   (a) An object of mass m is dropped from rest at one end of a straight tunnel passing through the centre. Neglecting friction and air resistance, determine whether the object comes to rest at the centre or executes periodic oscillation; compute the period in the uniform-density case.
   (b) Repeat (a) for a straight tunnel that is a chord not passing through the centre.
   (c) Analyze the behaviour of an incompressible fluid filling such a tunnel.
   (d) Taking the Earth's rotation into account, compute the Coriolis deflection experienced by an object falling through a polar tunnel and through an equatorial tunnel, and discuss the stability of an elevator constrained to the tunnel axis.

Provide complete derivations for each part.

$$N > \frac{2(1+\alpha)(1+\beta)}{(1-\alpha)(1-\beta)},$$
and let $\lambda > 0$ be a parameter. Consider the singular semilinear elliptic boundary value problem
$$-\Delta u + u^{\alpha} = \lambda\, u^{\beta} \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
seeking nonnegative weak solutions $u$ that are positive in $\Omega$ and whose normal derivative $\partial u/\partial n$ exists on $\partial\Omega$ in the appropriate sense.

Suppose $w_\lambda$ is a positive solution of this problem (constructed for suitable $\lambda$) satisfying the property that $\partial w_\lambda/\partial n$ does not vanish identically on $\partial\Omega$ (i.e. $\partial w_\lambda/\partial n \not\equiv 0$).

Question: Must such a solution $w_\lambda$ necessarily satisfy the sign condition
$$\frac{\partial w_\lambda}{\partial n} \le 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega\,?$$

Formulate a unified mathematical theory of large-scale geophysical processes on Earth that meets the following requirements:

1. Provide a system of Newtonian dynamical equations (a coupled system of PDEs/ODEs on a rotating, deformable spheroidal body) governing the joint evolution of:
   (a) the Earth's solid interior dynamics (mantle convection, core flows, elastic-plastic deformation),
   (b) the rotational motion of the Earth, including the free Eulerian/Chandler polar wobble of its instantaneous rotation axis relative to the body-fixed principal axes,
   (c) Coriolis and centrifugal forces in the rotating frame,
   (d) thermal forcing by solar radiation and internal heat sources,
   (e) atmospheric and oceanic climatic variables coupled to the solid Earth,
   (f) seismic events (earthquakes) as part of the dynamics rather than as external inputs.

2. Within this framework, derive a quantitative mechanism that explains the observed persistence, amplitude, and period (~433 days) of the Chandler wobble despite dissipation, and exhibit the explicit coupling between the interior Newtonian dynamics and the polar wobble.

3. Investigate whether macroscopic ordered/coherent phenomena in the Earth's interior admit a description analogous to superconductivity (e.g., effective London-type or Ginzburg–Landau-type equations for some collective geophysical field), and determine whether such an analogy yields an electromagnetic stabilization mechanism for the Earth's rotation or wobble.

4. Provide a general-relativistic reformulation of the above Newtonian system: write a covariant set of field equations on a curved spacetime (sourced by the Earth's stress–energy tensor including elastic, fluid, thermal and electromagnetic contributions) whose post-Newtonian limit reproduces the Newtonian theory of (1)–(3), and identify any genuinely relativistic corrections relevant to polar motion, geodynamics, or seismic phenomena.

Either exhibit such a theory with explicit governing equations and demonstrate consistency with observed geophysical data (Chandler wobble, climatic variability, seismicity statistics), or prove that no such unified system can simultaneously satisfy the listed requirements.

$$
with parameters $\lambda > 0$ and $0 < \beta < 1$, where $\chi_{\{u>0\}}$ denotes the characteristic function of the positivity set of $u$.

For $\varepsilon > 0$, regularize the singular nonlinearity and consider the smooth approximating problem
$$
-\Delta u_\varepsilon = f_\varepsilon(u_\varepsilon) \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u_\varepsilon = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,
$$
where $f_\varepsilon$ is a suitable smooth approximation of $\lambda\,\chi_{\{s>0\}} - s^{-\beta}\chi_{\{s>0\}}$, chosen so that the associated energy functional $J_\varepsilon$ on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ admits both a global minimizer $u_\varepsilon \geq 0$ and a second nonnegative critical point $v_\varepsilon \geq 0$ obtained via the Mountain Pass Theorem, with $u_\varepsilon \not\equiv v_\varepsilon$.

Suppose that, as $\varepsilon \to 0$, one has $u_\varepsilon \to u$ and $v_\varepsilon \to v$ in an appropriate sense, where $u \geq 0$ and $v \geq 0$ are two distinct nonnegative limit functions, each a solution of the original singular problem in a suitable weak sense.

Question: Must the limit $u$ obtained from the global minimizers $u_\varepsilon$ satisfy $u(x) > 0$ for all $x \in \Omega$?

Within the framework of general relativity and special relativity, provide rigorous answers to the following thought-experiment questions:

(i) Consider a rigid plane disk rotating with constant angular velocity about its center, observed from an inertial frame in Minkowski spacetime. Taking into account length contraction of circumferential elements but not of radial elements (the Ehrenfest setup), determine the intrinsic geometry experienced by co-rotating observers on the disk: is the induced spatial metric flat (Euclidean), Minkowskian, or a non-flat Riemannian metric of nonzero Gaussian curvature? Give an explicit form of the spatial metric and its curvature.

(ii) Consider a system in free fall that is simultaneously rotating (for example, a freely falling laboratory spinning about an axis through its center of mass). Does Einstein's equivalence principle apply in the usual local sense to such a rotating freely falling frame? Identify precisely which tidal/Coriolis/centrifugal effects can or cannot be eliminated by passing to a freely falling rotating frame, and state in what sense (if any) the equivalence principle holds.

(iii) (Airplane-and-elevator thought experiment.) An airplane moves with constant horizontal velocity relative to the ground in a uniform gravitational field. Inside the airplane an "elevator" cabin is in free fall. Determine the trajectories, as seen by (a) a ground-based observer, (b) an observer at rest in the airplane, and (c) an observer inside the freely falling cabin, of: an object released from rest within the cabin, and a projectile launched horizontally within the cabin. Show consistency of the three descriptions via the appropriate coordinate transformations.

(iv) In the Einstein field equations G_{μν} = 8πG T_{μν}, the stress–energy tensor T_{μν} of a relativistic fluid or radiation field depends on its temperature (e.g., through energy density and pressure of a thermal distribution). Determine quantitatively whether and how the temperature of matter/radiation filling a region of space affects the spacetime curvature and the metric, and identify whether "temperature" enters the metric in any way beyond its contribution to T_{μν}.
