representations.normalized: Recall that a topological space $X$ has countable tightness if, whenever $A\subseteq X$ and $x\in\overline{A}$, there is a countable subset $B\subseteq A$ with $x\in\overline{B}$. A subset $Y\subseteq X$ is countably compact if every infinite subset of $Y$ has an accumulation point in $Y$ (equivalently, every countable open cover of $Y$ has a finite subcover, in the Hausdorff setting). The Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA) is the statement that for every proper forcing notion $\mathbb{P}$ and every collection $\{D_\alpha:\alpha<\omega_1\}$ of dense subsets of $\mathbb{P}$, there is a filter on $\mathbb{P}$ meeting each $D_\alpha$.\n\nDetermine whether it is consistent with ZFC that, in every topological space of countable tightness, every countably compact subset is closed. In particular, decide whether the Proper Forcing Axiom implies this statement.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Alan Dow proved that PFA implies countably compact subsets are closed in regular spaces of hereditary countable π-character, which gives a partial positive answer in a restricted class. The general question for arbitrary countably tight spaces does not appear to have been fully resolved; the question remains an active topic in set-theoretic topology, with results known under PFA(S)[S] and related axioms but no published full solution.

Call a topological space α-realcompact if every countably complete ultrafilter of closed sets in the space is fixed (equivalently, every maximal family of closed sets with the countable intersection property has nonempty intersection). A space is hereditarily α-realcompact if each of its subspaces is α-realcompact. Recall that a topological space X is sequential if a set A ⊆ X is closed whenever it is sequentially closed (i.e., whenever it contains the limit of every convergent sequence from A), and the character of X is the supremum over x ∈ X of the minimum cardinality of a neighborhood base at x.

Question: Is every compact Hausdorff sequential space of character ω₁ hereditarily α-realcompact? More generally, is every compact Hausdorff sequential space of cardinality ω₁ hereditarily α-realcompact?

A discrete-time linear time-invariant system with p inputs and q outputs is described by a transfer matrix H(z), an q×p matrix of rational functions of z that are strictly proper (i.e. each entry tends to 0 as z → ∞). A positive realization of H(z) of dimension n is a quadruple (A, B, C, D) with A ∈ R^{n×n}, B ∈ R^{n×p}, C ∈ R^{q×n}, D ∈ R^{q×p} whose entries are all nonnegative, such that

  H(z) = D + C (zI − A)^{-1} B.

The dimension n is called the order of the realization. A positive realization is called minimal if no positive realization of H(z) has strictly smaller order. Denote by n_+(H) the minimal order of a positive realization of H(z), when one exists.

Problem. Develop necessary and sufficient conditions, together with constructive procedures, that determine n_+(H) for an arbitrary q×p strictly proper rational transfer matrix H(z) admitting a positive realization, in the genuinely multi-input multi-output setting (p > 1 or q > 1). In particular:

(a) Characterize n_+(H) in terms of intrinsic data of H(z) (e.g. its poles, residue structure, factorizations, or associated cone-invariance data), going beyond the known lower and upper bounds.

(b) Provide an algorithm that, given H(z) admitting a positive realization, computes a positive realization (A, B, C, D) whose order equals n_+(H).

A complete solution is known to be elusive because the MIMO minimality problem does not reduce in a direct way to the single-input single-output case (where H(z) is scalar), in contrast with the corresponding existence problem.

Recent surveys and research on minimal positive realizations indicate that, even in the SISO case, no general procedure is known to determine the minimum state dimension of a positive realization, and only lower/upper bounds are available. The MIMO extension is recognized as significantly harder and remains open, with ongoing work providing only partial results (e.g., bounds, special transfer-function classes, Markov-realization variants).

Let $H(z)$ be a rational transfer function with non-negative impulse response (so that it admits positive realizations). A positive realization of $H(z)$ of dimension $N$ is a quadruple $(A,b,c,d)$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$, $c^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$, $d\in\mathbb{R}$ such that all entries of $A$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are non-negative and
$$H(z)=c^{T}(zI-A)^{-1}b+d.$$
Let $N_{\min}(H)$ denote the smallest integer $N$ for which such a positive realization exists, and let $\mathcal{M}(H)$ denote the set of all positive realizations of $H(z)$ of dimension exactly $N_{\min}(H)$, considered up to permutation similarity (i.e., $(A,b,c,d)\sim(PAP^{T},Pb,Pc,d)$ for any permutation matrix $P$).

Describe the structure of $\mathcal{M}(H)$. In particular, determine whether $\mathcal{M}(H)$ is always connected (in a suitable natural topology, e.g., as a subset of Euclidean space modulo permutation equivalence), and more generally describe how any two minimal positive realizations of $H(z)$ can be transformed into one another.

representations.normalized:
Consider zero-surface-tension Saffman–Taylor (Laplacian) growth of a viscous fluid in a two-dimensional Hele–Shaw channel of finite width with periodic boundary conditions in the transverse direction. The interface separating the displaced fluid from the inviscid one is described, via a conformal map from a reference half-plane to the fluid domain, by a meromorphic function whose singularities are simple poles. Under the zero-surface-tension dynamics, each pole obeys a system of ODEs (the standard pole-decomposition equations for Laplacian growth in a channel), and the number of poles inside the analyticity domain is conserved.

It is known that the limit of vanishingly small surface tension does not coincide with the zero-surface-tension dynamics built from a finite collection of poles: to reproduce the small-surface-tension behavior using pole solutions one must continually supply new poles arriving from infinity ("remote poles") that subsequently migrate toward the interface. Two mechanisms have been proposed for the permanent source of these remote poles:

(A) external stochastic noise acting on the interface, which generates new poles at large distance at all times; or

(B) an infinite reservoir of poles present already in the initial condition, which one-by-one approach the interface as time evolves.

Question: In the channel Laplacian-growth setting, determine which of mechanisms (A) or (B) correctly reproduces the small-surface-tension limit of the dynamics. Equivalently, decide whether an appropriately chosen deterministic initial condition with infinitely many poles can reproduce all features of the vanishing-surface-tension limit (such as the dependence of characteristic interface velocities and finger-formation statistics on the channel width), or whether external noise is necessary.

representations.normalized:
Consider two-dimensional Laplacian growth in a channel (the zero-surface-tension Saffman–Taylor problem in a Hele–Shaw cell of finite width with periodic or no-flux lateral boundary conditions). The moving interface separating the inviscid fluid (or burnt region, in the equivalent flame-front formulation) from the viscous fluid is described by a time-dependent conformal map z = f(w,t) from the exterior (or interior) of the unit disk in an auxiliary w-plane onto the physical domain occupied by the displaced fluid. The map is taken in the meromorphic "pole" ansatz

  f(w,t) = w + V(t) + Σ_{k=1}^{N} α_k(t) · log(w − w_k(t)),

where N is a fixed positive integer and {α_k(t), w_k(t)} are the (complex) strengths and locations of a finite number of logarithmic singularities ("poles"). Substituting this ansatz into the zero-surface-tension Laplacian-growth equation yields a finite-dimensional dynamical system for the parameters (α_k(t), w_k(t)).

An initial pole configuration {α_k(0), w_k(0)}_{k=1}^{N} is said to be "allowed" if the resulting solution remains conformal for all t > 0, i.e. the interface develops no finite-time singularity (no cusp formation and no pole crossing the unit circle in finite time); otherwise the configuration is called singular.

Problem. Determine the exact necessary and sufficient conditions on the initial data {α_k(0), w_k(0)}_{k=1}^{N} that characterize the set of allowed configurations (those whose evolution under the pole dynamics never reaches a finite-time singularity).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Available literature on pole dynamics in zero-surface-tension Laplacian growth (Mineev-Weinstein, Dawson, and collaborators) gives sufficient conditions ensuring non-singular evolution (e.g. restricting pole strengths and excluding certain pole configurations) and shows that generic non-singular initial data produce an asymptotic half-width finger, but no complete necessary-and-sufficient characterization of the set of allowed initial pole configurations appears to have been established; the problem is generally treated as open in subsequent work.

Consider the Saffman–Taylor problem of a viscous finger advancing in a Hele-Shaw channel of unit width in the absence of surface tension. The interface admits an exact family of pole solutions, parameterized by a finite collection of complex pole locations together with their (complex) strengths α_i. For such a configuration define the real parameter
   α = Σ_i α_i ∈ ℝ,
and recall that the corresponding asymptotic finger has thickness 1 − α/2; thus physically meaningful finger widths between 0 and 1 correspond to α ∈ (0, 2), with α = 1 yielding the half-channel-width finger.

Call an initial pole configuration "allowed" if its dynamical evolution under the zero-surface-tension Saffman–Taylor pole equations remains regular for all positive times (does not develop a finite-time singularity of the pole system before the finger forms), and call it "singular" otherwise.

For each α ∈ (0, 2), let ρ(α) denote the fraction (relative measure, with respect to a natural parameterization of all pole configurations whose strengths sum to α) of allowed initial pole configurations among all possible initial pole configurations with that prescribed value of α.

Problem.
(a) Determine the function ρ : (0, 2) → [0, 1].
(b) Decide whether ρ(α) is peaked (or otherwise distinguished) at α = 1, in such a way that the half-channel-width finger emerges as the most probable asymptotic outcome of a generic admissible initial pole configuration.

Web search reveals an extensive literature on Saffman–Taylor finger selection (Combescot–Hakim–Pomeau, Tanveer, Magdaleno–Casademunt, and rigorous work on kinetic-undercooling selection) and on pole dynamics in zero-surface-tension Laplacian growth, but none of the located sources address the specific question of the measure-theoretic distribution ρ(α) of allowed versus singular initial pole configurations as a function of the total pole-strength parameter α, nor establish that this distribution selects the half-width finger as most probable. Consider the two-dimensional Saffman–Taylor problem of Hele-Shaw channel flow with zero surface tension. The channel has width 1, and a less viscous fluid displaces a more viscous fluid satisfying Darcy's law, so that the interface evolves by Laplacian growth (the normal velocity of the interface equals the normal derivative of a harmonic pressure field, with constant pressure on the interface). Using a conformal map from the exterior of the unit disk to the fluid domain, the dynamics admit a pole-decomposition formulation: the conformal map has the form of a sum of logarithmic poles whose positions in the complex plane evolve according to an autonomous system of ODEs. New poles may be continually introduced into the configuration during the evolution.

Adopt the following regularization rule (without invoking surface tension): at every time, exclude any pole configuration (whether initial or newly introduced) that would lead to a finite-time singularity (a cusp on the moving interface). With this rule in force, and allowing continual introduction of new admissible poles:

Provide a rigorous mathematical proof that the asymptotic state (as t → ∞) of this dynamics is, in the privileged or "most probable" sense (e.g., almost surely under a reasonable measure on admissible pole insertions, or as the unique attractor of the regularized dynamics), a single Saffman–Taylor finger occupying exactly one half of the channel width. Equivalently, prove that the relative finger width λ(t) converges to 1/2 under the pole-dynamics formulation with the above non-surface-tension regularization.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Several works (Mineev-Weinstein, PRL 1998; subsequent Laplacian Growth papers) claim that pole dynamics with regularization (no surface tension) selects a single 1/2-width finger asymptotically and present arguments toward an "exact result." However, this claim was contested by a published Comment (PRL 81, 5950), and the rigor and generality of the proof remain debated. No universally accepted strict proof appears in the literature, so the precise question of a fully rigorous proof of half-width selection in this pole formulation is best classified as unknown/partially addressed.

Consider the Sivashinsky-type flame-front evolution equation governing the propagation of an outward-expanding cylindrical premixed flame front in two dimensions. Let the flame front be parameterized in polar form, and let its mean radial velocity (relative to the unburnt gas) be denoted V(t). Assume the dynamics are deterministic: no explicit stochastic external forcing is added to the equation, and the only perturbations present are those introduced by inevitable round-off and discretization errors in a numerical simulation.

Numerical evidence indicates that during all accessible computation times the mean flame-front velocity V(t) continuously increases, with no observable approach to a constant limit. The question is to determine the long-time behaviour of V(t) as t → ∞: does V(t) saturate to a finite limit (so that lim sup V(t) < ∞), or does V(t) grow without bound (i.e., accelerate indefinitely)? Provide a rigorous answer based solely on the deterministic flame-front motion equation in the cylindrical geometry.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent literature on the Sivashinsky equation for outward (cylindrical/spherical) expanding flames continues to discuss self-similar acceleration and possible saturation regimes, but the question of whether the deterministic cylindrical Sivashinsky dynamics (without external noise) exhibit eventual velocity saturation or unbounded acceleration is still treated as unresolved; numerical simulations show ongoing acceleration with no observed saturation, and analytical proofs in either direction have not appeared.

Consider the Sivashinsky equation governing the dynamics of an outward-propagating (cylindrical/radial) premixed flame front in two dimensions. Let the front be described by a single-valued function whose evolution is given by the (Michelson–)Sivashinsky equation supplemented with an additive Gaussian white-noise forcing term of amplitude ε > 0:

  ∂_t Φ = (1/2)(∂_x Φ)^2 + ν ∂_x^2 Φ + I[Φ] + ε η(x,t),

where I[Φ] denotes the singular (Landau–Darrieus) linear integral operator with symbol |k|, the geometry is cylindrical (radially outward propagating front of growing radius R(t)), and η is zero-mean Gaussian white noise with unit variance.

Perform numerical simulations of this system and answer the following:

(a) Does the mean propagation velocity V(t) of the cylindrical flame front, computed in the presence of explicit Gaussian noise of amplitude ε, exhibit a finite saturation point — i.e., a time t_sat(ε) (or equivalently a radius R_sat(ε)) at which V transitions from systematic growth/acceleration to an approximately steady (saturated) behaviour?

(b) If such a saturation point exists, determine how its location t_sat(ε) (or R_sat(ε)) and the saturated velocity V_sat(ε) depend on the noise amplitude ε. In particular, characterize the scaling/behaviour of these quantities as ε → 0, and determine whether the extrapolation ε → 0 yields a well-defined limiting saturation behaviour distinct from that produced by intrinsic numerical roundoff noise alone.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The analogous question for planar and outward-propagating (cylindrical) Sivashinsky fronts with explicit Gaussian forcing has been investigated numerically and analytically: scaling laws for velocity/acceleration versus system size and noise amplitude have been obtained, and in radial geometry external noise is reported as crucial and capable of producing accelerated fronts via the appearance of new poles. While saturation phenomena and noise-amplitude dependence have been documented for related setups (planar, channel, and outward-propagating cases), a complete, quantitative characterization of the saturation point as a function of ε with controlled ε → 0 extrapolation in the cylindrical geometry does not appear to be fully settled.

Consider the radiative alpha-capture reaction $^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\mathrm{O}$, whose cross section near the helium-burning Gamow peak energy $E_{\mathrm{c.m.}} \approx 300$ keV controls the carbon-to-oxygen ratio produced during stellar helium burning. Define the astrophysical S-factor by
$$S(E) = E\,\sigma(E)\,\exp(2\pi\eta(E)),$$
where $\sigma(E)$ is the c.m. cross section and $\eta(E) = Z_\alpha Z_C e^2/(\hbar v)$ is the Sommerfeld parameter. Decompose the ground-state capture cross section into its dominant electric-dipole (p-wave, E1) and electric-quadrupole (d-wave, E2) multipole components, yielding partial S-factors $S_{E1}(E)$ and $S_{E2}(E)$.

Determine the numerical values of $S_{E1}(300\text{ keV})$ and $S_{E2}(300\text{ keV})$ to a total accuracy of approximately $10\%$ or better, using direct experimental input (rather than relying solely on extrapolations from higher-energy capture data and from R-matrix analyses incorporating the $\beta$-delayed $\alpha$-emission spectrum of $^{16}\mathrm{N}$), in such a way that small-$S_{E1}(300)$ solutions (e.g., values in the range $10$–$20$ keV·b) can be definitively excluded or confirmed.

Recent analyses (including a 2024 multilevel R-matrix study incorporating prospective $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'\alpha)^{12}\mathrm{C}$ data) continue to extrapolate $S_{E1}(300)$ and $S_{E2}(300)$ with uncertainties substantially larger than 10%, and published values from different methods still disagree (e.g., $S_{E1}(300)\sim 80$–$100$ keV·b and $S_{E2}(300)\sim 40$–$70$ keV·b with sizable error bars). No direct sub-Gamow-peak measurement has yet achieved the 10% goal, so the problem remains open.

Consider the body of experimental measurements obtained in high-energy heavy-ion collisions concerning (i) quarkonium production yields (e.g., J/ψ, ψ(2S), Υ states and their suppression or enhancement patterns relative to proton–proton or proton–nucleus baselines), and (ii) electromagnetic probes (direct photons and dilepton invariant-mass spectra in the low, intermediate, and high mass regions). Let a "conventional baseline explanation" denote any combination of (a) measured or extrapolated proton–proton and proton–nucleus reference cross sections with their quoted uncertainties, (b) cold nuclear matter effects (nuclear parton distribution modifications, initial-state energy loss, nuclear absorption, Cronin-like broadening), and (c) standard hadronic-phase contributions (resonance decays, hadronic rescattering, in-medium hadron production) treated within accepted modeling uncertainties. Define "new physics in heavy-ion collisions" to mean phenomena that cannot be accommodated by any such conventional baseline explanation — in particular, signatures requiring deconfined partonic matter, chiral symmetry restoration, or thermal radiation from a quark-gluon plasma.

Question: Do the currently available experimental data on quarkonium production and on electromagnetic probes in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, taken together, establish the existence of new physics in the above sense beyond reasonable doubt, in the precise sense that no conventional baseline explanation (within stated experimental and theoretical uncertainties of the references and cold/hot hadronic effects) is compatible with the observed yields, spectra, and centrality/system-size dependences?

Setup and definitions.

(1) A cubic graph is a graph in which every vertex has degree 3. A graph G is essentially 4-edge-connected if G is connected and every edge cut of size at most 3 isolates a single vertex (equivalently, G has no edge cut of size ≤ 3 separating two components each containing at least one edge).

(2) For a graph H, let δ(H) denote its minimum degree and let V_2(H) denote the set of vertices of H of degree exactly 2.

(3) A closed trail in a graph is a closed walk that uses no edge more than once. A closed trail T in a graph G is called dominating if every edge of G has at least one endpoint on T.

Question. Let G be an essentially 4-edge-connected cubic graph and let H be a subgraph of G with δ(H) = 2 and |V_2(H)| = 4. Write V_2(H) = {x, y, w, z}. Form a new graph H* by adding to H two new edges e_1 = xy and e_2 = wz (so that the four degree-2 vertices of H are paired off by these two new edges).

Must H* necessarily contain a dominating closed trail that uses both of the added edges e_1 and e_2?

The statement is a known reformulation related to the Dominating Circuit Conjecture (equivalent to Ash–Jackson, Fleischner, Thomassen-type conjectures). It is widely cited as an open conjecture; recent works on essentially 4-edge-connected cubic graphs treat it as still unresolved, with no proof or counterexample reported.

Consider J/ψ production in proton–proton, proton–nucleus, and nucleus–nucleus collisions at center-of-mass energies ranging from fixed-target SPS energies (√s_NN ≈ 17–29 GeV) up to RHIC energies (√s_NN = 200 GeV). The inclusive J/ψ yield in these reactions receives contributions from direct production and from feed-down decays of higher charmonium states, in particular ψ′ → J/ψ + X and χ_c → J/ψ + γ. In a Glauber-type model the J/ψ yield in p–A and A–A collisions, relative to the binary-scaled pp yield, is modified by (i) initial-state nuclear modifications of the parton distribution functions (nuclear shadowing/antishadowing), (ii) effective final-state absorption of the pre-resonant or formed charmonium state on cold nuclear matter, parametrized by an effective absorption cross section σ_abs, and (iii) the differing absorption cross sections of the feed-down components.

(a) Determine, within a self-consistent treatment that incorporates all three effects above, the dependence of the effective σ_abs(√s_NN) on the collision energy across the SPS-to-RHIC range.

(b) Using this energy-dependent σ_abs together with the appropriate nuclear PDFs and feed-down decomposition, construct the "cold nuclear matter" baseline for the J/ψ nuclear modification factor R_AA in heavy-ion collisions at SPS and RHIC energies, and quantify whether, and at what level of significance, the J/ψ suppression observed in heavy-ion collisions exceeds this baseline (i.e. is genuinely "anomalous").

Subsequent analyses (e.g., Lourenço–Vogt–Wöhri, JHEP 2009; Phys. Rev. C 76, 064906) have parametrized a decreasing effective σ_abs with increasing √s_NN using p–A data from 200 to 920 GeV beam energies and RHIC d-Au data at 200 GeV, providing improved cold-nuclear-matter baselines. Nevertheless, residual uncertainties from nuclear PDFs, the production mechanism, and the feed-down decomposition remain, so a fully consensus baseline establishing or refuting "anomalous" J/ψ suppression at SPS and RHIC energies has not been definitively settled.

Let G be an essentially 4-edge-connected cubic graph (a 3-regular graph G such that for every edge cut F with |F| ≤ 3, at least one side of G − F consists of a single vertex). Let H be a subgraph of G with minimum degree δ(H) = 2, and let V_2(H) denote the set of vertices of degree 2 in H. Assume |V_2(H)| = 4.

A dominating closed trail in a graph is a closed trail T such that every edge has at least one endpoint on T. The graph H is called V_2(H)-dominated if, for every choice of two new edges e_1, e_2 each joining two vertices of V_2(H) so that H + e_1 + e_2 has minimum degree at least 3, the graph H + e_1 + e_2 contains a dominating closed trail.

Call H strongly V_2(H)-dominated if both:
(i) H is V_2(H)-dominated, and
(ii) for any single new edge e = uv with {u, v} ⊆ V_2(H), the graph H + e admits a dominating closed trail that contains the edge e.

Prove or disprove: every such subgraph H (subgraph of an essentially 4-edge-connected cubic graph, with δ(H) = 2 and |V_2(H)| = 4) is strongly V_2(H)-dominated.

In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions of indium nuclei on indium nuclei at a beam energy of 158 GeV per nucleon, dimuon pairs are produced. After subtracting (i) the expected Drell–Yan contribution computed from perturbative QCD with standard parton distributions, and (ii) the contribution from correlated semi-muonic decays of pairs of charmed hadrons (D and anti-D mesons), a residual prompt excess of dimuons is observed in the intermediate-mass region 1 GeV < M_{μμ} < 3 GeV, where the excess pairs originate from the primary interaction vertex rather than from displaced decay vertices.

(a) Identify the physical production mechanism that accounts for this prompt intermediate-mass dimuon excess.

(b) Under the hypothesis that the excess is thermal electromagnetic radiation emitted from the hot, dense medium produced in the collision, determine whether the radiation originates predominantly from a hadronic (confined) phase, from a deconfined partonic phase (quark–gluon plasma), or from a combination of both, and quantify the relative contributions as a function of dimuon invariant mass and transverse momentum.

Subsequent NA60 analyses and theoretical interpretations indicate the prompt intermediate-mass excess is consistent with thermal radiation: below 1 GeV it is dominated by in-medium π+π− → ρ → μ+μ− annihilation with a strongly broadened ρ spectral function, while above 1 GeV the lack of significant radial flow and the spectral shape suggest a dominantly partonic (deconfined) emission source, consistent with parton–hadron duality. representations.normalized:
Consider high-energy hadronic collisions producing prompt muon pairs (dimuons) in the intermediate invariant-mass region 1 GeV/c² < M_{μμ} < 2.5 GeV/c². In this region the observed prompt dimuon yield in heavy-ion (nucleus–nucleus) collisions is expected to contain:

(i) a Drell–Yan contribution (q q̄ → γ* → μ⁺μ⁻, including possible higher-order partonic corrections and contributions involving additional partons from the colliding hadrons),
(ii) correlated semileptonic decays of D D̄ pairs (open charm),
(iii) a putative "thermal" component originating from a hot, possibly partonic, medium produced in the collision.

The Drell–Yan cross section at such low dimuon masses is not reliably calculable from perturbative QCD because higher-order effects are large, and nuclear effects (e.g., extra-parton interactions in pA and AA) may enhance it relative to a pp extrapolation.

Problem. Determine whether measurements of prompt dimuon production in proton–nucleus (pA) collisions, used as a non-thermal baseline, can be made precise and theoretically controlled enough to fix the non-thermal prompt dimuon yield (Drell–Yan plus correlated open-charm decays, including possible nuclear-enhancement effects) in the intermediate-mass region 1 GeV/c² < M_{μμ} < 2.5 GeV/c² with sufficient accuracy that an excess in nucleus–nucleus collisions over this pA-based baseline constitutes unambiguous evidence for genuine thermal dimuon production.

Equivalently: Is it possible, using only pA data together with current or foreseeable theoretical inputs, to subtract the non-thermal prompt dimuon contribution in AA collisions in the intermediate-mass region to a precision that isolates a thermal signal?

Consider proton–nucleus (p–A) collisions at CERN-SPS fixed-target energies (proton beam momentum of order 400–450 GeV/c) and the production of muon pairs (dimuons) in the intermediate-mass region (roughly 1.5 GeV/c² < M_{μμ} < 2.5 GeV/c², between the φ and the J/ψ resonances). The dimuon mass and transverse-momentum spectra in this region are conventionally described as a superposition of two "expected" sources: (i) the Drell–Yan process, and (ii) correlated semileptonic decays of open-charm pairs (D D̄ → μ⁺μ⁻ + X), normalized by an open-charm production cross section σ_{cc̄}.

Direct measurements of charm production (from D-meson and single-lepton observables across multiple experiments) yield a value of σ_{cc̄}(p–A) that is approximately a factor of two smaller than the open-charm yield needed to reproduce the intermediate-mass dimuon spectra measured in p–A collisions when only Drell–Yan and open-charm semileptonic decays are included as sources.

Problem: Determine the correct open-charm baseline for the interpretation of intermediate-mass dimuon spectra in p–A collisions. Equivalently, identify and quantify the physical mechanism(s) responsible for the discrepancy between (a) the open-charm cross section σ_{cc̄} inferred from direct charm measurements and (b) the effective open-charm normalization required to describe the intermediate-mass dimuon data, and decide whether the excess in the intermediate-mass dimuon yield in p–A collisions is due to enhanced open-charm production or to an additional prompt dimuon source (such as thermal/partonic radiation or other non-charm contributions).

Subsequent measurements by NA60 using a vertex pixel tracker separated prompt dimuons from open-charm decay dimuons in the intermediate-mass region. representations.normalized:
Consider the production of φ(1020) mesons in high-energy nuclear collisions. In proton–nucleus (p–A) collisions, ordinary "cold nuclear matter" effects (e.g., nuclear shadowing/anti-shadowing of parton distributions, initial-state multiple scattering, and final-state hadronic absorption) are known to modify φ-meson production relative to elementary proton–proton (p–p) baselines; in particular, the ratio σ(φ)/σ(ω) is observed to grow with the mass number A.

Define the φ nuclear modification factor in nucleus–nucleus (A–A) collisions at center-of-mass energy √s_NN as
  R_{AA}^{φ}(p_T, y; √s_NN) = (1/⟨N_coll⟩) · (d²N_{AA}^{φ}/dp_T dy) / (d²N_{pp}^{φ}/dp_T dy),
and the analogous factor R_{pA}^{φ} for p–A collisions. Let the "expected" φ yield in A–A collisions from a smooth extrapolation of p–A data be the value of R_{AA}^{φ} obtained by composing/scaling the measured R_{pA}^{φ} (e.g., via a Glauber-based folding of cold nuclear matter effects from each colliding nucleus). Define the "anomalous" φ enhancement as
  Δ^{φ}_{anom}(p_T, y; √s_NN) = R_{AA}^{φ,measured} − R_{AA}^{φ,from p-A extrapolation}.

Problem: Quantify Δ^{φ}_{anom} as a function of collision energy √s_NN, centrality (⟨N_coll⟩ or ⟨N_part⟩), transverse momentum p_T, and rapidity y. In particular, determine whether, after a complete and consistent extrapolation of p–A observations (including A-dependence of σ(φ)/σ(ω), shadowing, and absorption) to the A–A geometry, any statistically significant enhancement of φ production in A–A collisions remains, and characterize its magnitude and kinematic dependence.

Reviews of φ-meson production in heavy-ion collisions and dedicated p–Pb measurements (e.g., at the LHC by ALICE) have substantially clarified cold nuclear matter effects, but a definitive, quantitative subtraction of p–A baselines yielding a universally agreed residual "anomalous" φ enhancement across energies, centralities, and kinematics has not been established. In proton–nucleus collisions at moderate energies, the dilepton invariant-mass spectrum in the low-mass region (roughly below 1.1 GeV/c²) is conventionally described by a "hadronic cocktail" of contributions from light-meson Dalitz decays and the direct dileptonic decays of the vector mesons ρ, ω, and φ, with their vacuum masses, widths, and branching ratios as measured in elementary (e.g. e+e−) reactions. In the KEK-PS E325 experiment, e+e− invariant-mass spectra produced in 12 GeV proton–copper collisions were measured and a significant excess on the low-mass side of the ω and φ peaks was reported, which the experiment interprets as in-medium modifications (mass shifts and/or broadening) of the ρ, ω, and φ mesons inside ordinary nuclear matter at normal density ρ₀.

Formulate and address the following question: assuming the standard vacuum-based "elementary-collision baseline" for ρ, ω, and φ production and decay into dileptons, identify a consistent theoretical and phenomenological framework that simultaneously
(i) reproduces dilepton spectra in elementary p+p (and p+d) reactions with vacuum vector-meson properties,
(ii) accounts quantitatively for the low-mass excess and the βγ (velocity) and target-mass (C vs. Cu) dependences observed by E325 in 12 GeV p+A collisions, and
(iii) is compatible with results from other experiments probing in-medium vector mesons (e.g. CLAS/g7, CBELSA/TAPS, HADES) which have not confirmed comparable mass shifts at normal nuclear density.

Specifically, determine whether the E325 excess can be explained without invoking a density-dependent shift of the pole masses of ρ, ω, φ — for instance by collisional broadening, coupled-channel effects, final-state interactions, or modifications of production amplitudes inside the nucleus — or whether a genuine in-medium pole-mass modification at normal nuclear density is required.

Consider exclusive quasi-elastic electron-induced single-proton knockout reactions $A(e,e'p)B$, in which a high-energy electron scatters off a nucleus $A$ with four-momentum transfer $q^\mu=(\omega,\mathbf{q})$ and $Q^2=-q^\mu q_\mu$, ejecting a proton while leaving the residual nucleus $B$ in a definite (typically valence) bound state $\alpha$. Within a one-body current picture, the cross section is proportional to the squared overlap between the initial state of $A$ and the final state $|B,\alpha\rangle\otimes|p\rangle$. The normalization of this overlap defines the spectroscopic factor $S_\alpha\in[0,1]$, which many-body nuclear structure calculations (including short-range and long-range correlations) typically predict to lie near $S_\alpha^{\text{th}}\approx 0.7$–$0.9$ for valence orbitals of stable nuclei.

Experimental extractions of $S_\alpha$ from such $(e,e'p)$ data require a reaction model that accounts for: (i) final-state interactions between the outgoing proton and the residual nucleus (usually treated through a complex optical potential in a distorted-wave framework), (ii) ambiguities in the off-shell electromagnetic single-nucleon current operator (different prescriptions such as $CC1$, $CC2$, $CC3$), and (iii) relativistic kinematic and dynamical effects in the bound-state wave function, the current, and the distorted outgoing wave.

Empirically, analyses of low-$Q^2$ exclusive $(e,e'p)$ data (with $Q^2$ well below $1\,\text{GeV}^2$) yield strongly quenched valence-shell spectroscopic factors $S_\alpha^{\text{exp}}\approx 0.6$–$0.7$ of the independent-particle-shell-model value, whereas analyses performed at $Q^2\gtrsim 1\,\text{GeV}^2$ yield $S_\alpha^{\text{exp}}$ close to unity using analogous reaction frameworks.

Problem. Construct a single, internally consistent reaction-theoretical framework for $A(e,e'p)B$ that simultaneously incorporates final-state interactions, off-shell single-nucleon current ambiguities, and relativistic effects, in which the extracted valence-shell spectroscopic factors $S_\alpha$ become independent of $Q^2$ across the kinematic range from a few hundred $\text{MeV}^2$ up to several $\text{GeV}^2$, and either reconcile the resulting $Q^2$-independent values with the predictions of modern nuclear many-body theory or identify, within that consistent framework, the specific physical ingredient whose omission produces the observed apparent $Q^2$ dependence. In particular, account for the difference between low-$Q^2$ quenched values and high-$Q^2$ near-unity values without invoking uncontrolled model dependence of the reaction mechanism.

Consider exclusive quasi-elastic electron–nucleus scattering of the form A(e,e'p)B, in which an electron of four-momentum transfer squared Q² knocks a single proton out of a nuclear target while leaving the residual nucleus in a well-defined state. Let n̂ denote the unit vector normal to the scattering plane (the plane spanned by the incident and scattered electron momenta and the ejected proton momentum), and let P_N be the component of the ejected proton's recoil polarization along n̂, induced even with an unpolarized electron beam and an unpolarized target. Under the standard reaction-mechanism description (one-photon exchange, distorted-wave impulse approximation with final-state interactions modeled by an optical potential or Glauber-type rescattering), P_N is generated entirely by final-state interactions (FSI) between the outgoing proton and the residual nuclear system: in the absence of FSI one has P_N = 0.

(a) Determine the dependence of P_N on Q² for representative target nuclei (e.g., ¹²C, ¹⁶O, ⁴⁰Ca) in the kinematic regime accessible at modern electron-scattering facilities (Q² up to several GeV²), as a function of missing momentum and outgoing-proton kinematics.

(b) Decide whether the measured Q²-dependence of P_N can be used to isolate the energy dependence of FSI cleanly enough to (i) extract a model-independent nuclear transparency, and (ii) provide an unambiguous signal of color transparency — i.e., the predicted onset, at sufficiently large Q², of a suppression of FSI due to the propagation of a small-size, color-neutral configuration of the struck proton through the nuclear medium — while disentangling such effects from competing reaction-mechanism uncertainties (relativistic effects, two-body currents, spinor distortion, off-shell ambiguities, choice of optical potential).

representations.normalized:
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ be a finite set (the subtraction set). The (impartial) subtraction game $\mathrm{Sub}(S)$ is played on nonnegative integers: from position $n$, a player may move to $n-s$ for any $s\in S$ with $n\ge s$; a player unable to move loses. The Sprague–Grundy (nim-)value $\mathcal{G}(n)$ is the smallest nonnegative integer not in $\{\mathcal{G}(n-s):s\in S,\ s\le n\}$. It is classical that the sequence $(\mathcal{G}(n))_{n\ge 0}$ is eventually periodic.

Address the following questions.

(a) Period from the subtraction set. Determine in general how the finite subtraction set $S$ controls the length and structure of the eventual period of $(\mathcal{G}(n))$.

(b) Three-element sets. Give a complete analysis of $\mathrm{Sub}(S)$ for every three-element subtraction set $S=\{a,b,c\}$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$: describe the period length, preperiod, and the pattern of nim-values.

(c) Growth of period. Decide whether the period length of $\mathrm{Sub}(S)$, as a function of $\max S$ (or of the bit-length of $S$), can grow superpolynomially, or whether it is always bounded by a polynomial.

(d) Pure periodicity. Characterize the finite subtraction sets $S$ for which $(\mathcal{G}(n))_{n\ge 0}$ is purely periodic (i.e., has preperiod $0$).

(e) Partizan analogue. For partizan subtraction games, where Left has subtraction set $S_L$ and Right has subtraction set $S_R$, develop the analogous theory: prove an appropriate periodicity result for the sequence of game values and describe how $(S_L,S_R)$ controls the period length, structure, and purity.

(f) Infinite and aperiodic variants. For infinite subtraction sets $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, determine conditions under which $(\mathcal{G}(n))$ is eventually periodic, and study the period length and purity. Also treat division/subtraction variants whose nim-sequences may be aperiodic, characterizing when aperiodicity occurs.

Consider the quasi-elastic electron-scattering reactions A(e⃗,e′p⃗)B on nuclear targets A (e.g., A = 4He, 16O), in which a longitudinally polarized electron knocks out a proton whose recoil polarization components Px′ (transverse) and Pz′ (longitudinal, along momentum transfer) are measured. Define the polarization-transfer ratio R(A) = Px′/Pz′ and the super-ratio

  S(A) = [Px′/Pz′]_A / [Px′/Pz′]_{1H},

i.e., the ratio measured on the nucleus normalized to that for elastic e p scattering on a free proton (1H(e,e′p)). For a free proton, R is proportional to the ratio of the proton electric to magnetic Sachs form factors GE^p/GM^p; for a bound proton, conventional reaction effects (meson-exchange currents (MEC), isobar/Δ configurations, and final-state interactions (FSI)) plus possible medium-induced changes of the bound nucleon's electromagnetic form factors all contribute.

Problem. (a) Determine whether nucleons bound inside a nucleus possess electromagnetic form factors that differ from their free-space values, in a manner observable through polarization-transfer observables in A(e⃗,e′p⃗)B reactions. (b) Provide a theoretical and experimental framework that unambiguously separates such genuine in-medium form-factor modifications from the conventional contributions of meson-exchange currents, isobar configurations, and final-state interactions in the components of the induced (transferred) recoil polarization. (c) In particular, decide whether high-precision measurements of the super-ratio S(A) extended beyond A = 4He to nuclei such as A = 16O can distinguish genuine medium modifications from reaction-model ambiguities, and identify the specific kinematic regimes and observables in which this separation is achievable.

An octal game is a two-player impartial combinatorial heap game specified by a finite "octal code" $d_0 \cdot d_1 d_2 d_3 \cdots d_k$, where each digit $d_i \in \{0,1,\dots,7\}$ encodes which moves are legal when removing exactly $i$ tokens from a single heap. Writing $d_i = b_0 + 2 b_1 + 4 b_2$ in binary, removing $i$ tokens from a heap is allowed and may (i) leave the heap empty if $b_0 = 1$, (ii) leave the heap as one nonempty heap if $b_1 = 1$, or (iii) split the heap into two nonempty heaps if $b_2 = 1$. Players alternate; the player unable to move loses (normal play). The Sprague–Grundy (nim) value $G(n)$ of a single heap of size $n$ is defined recursively as the mex of the Grundy values of all positions reachable in one move (using XOR for split positions). A finite octal game is one with only finitely many nonzero digits.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every finite octal game, the sequence $(G(n))_{n\ge 0}$ is ultimately periodic.

(b) For each of the still-unresolved octal codes with at most four digits (notably including the game $\cdot 007$, i.e. Treblecross), determine whether $(G(n))$ is ultimately periodic, and if so compute its period and preperiod. In particular, determine whether the Grundy value $2048$ ever occurs in the nim-sequence of Treblecross.

(c) For those octal games already proved ultimately periodic, give a structural explanation for the observed periods (for example, why $\cdot 16$ has period $149459$, why $\cdot 56$ has period $144$, etc.).

(d) Determine the computational complexity of deciding outcomes of (multi-heap) octal games, of partizan octal games, and of related poset-based heap games.

Guy's conjecture that every finite octal game has an ultimately periodic nim-sequence remains open. Of the 79 nontrivial octal games with at most 3 digits, only 14 are settled; vast computations by Flammenkamp and others (including for Treblecross $\cdot 007$) have not revealed periodicity. Recent progress includes Gangolli–Plambeck-type resolutions of individual codes (e.g. $\cdot 16$, $\cdot 56$, $\cdot 127$, $\cdot 376$), but the general conjecture, the Treblecross question, and the complexity questions are unresolved.

representations.normalized:
Consider the exclusive electron-induced proton knockout reaction on an oxygen-16 target, $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'p)$, in which an incident electron scatters and is detected in coincidence with an ejected proton, leaving a residual nucleus. Denote by $p_m$ the missing momentum and by $E_m$ the missing energy reconstructed from the kinematics of the detected electron and proton. In the standard distorted-wave impulse approximation (DWIA) "single-particle" picture, the cross section factorizes into a kinematic factor, the off-shell electron-proton cross section, and a distorted single-particle spectral function describing the removed proton.

Experimental observations in the regime of high missing energy include: (i) the longitudinal/transverse-separated cross section exhibits an enhanced transverse component that cannot be reproduced by DWIA one-nucleon knockout from bound shell-model orbitals; (ii) for missing momenta $p_m \gtrsim 200\ \mathrm{MeV}/c$ the differential cross section becomes nearly independent of $p_m$; and (iii) coincidence measurements of two outgoing nucleons, $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pp)$ and $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pn)$, account for roughly half of the inclusive-in-final-state $(e,e'p)$ strength in this region.

Problem. Identify and quantitatively characterize the reaction mechanisms responsible for the enhanced transverse strength and the flat, nearly momentum-independent high-$p_m$ cross section observed in $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'p)$ at high $E_m$. In particular, determine the relative contributions of:
(a) short-range central and tensor nucleon–nucleon correlations in the initial-state wave function,
(b) meson-exchange currents (two-body electromagnetic currents),
(c) intermediate $\Delta$-isobar and other resonance currents,
(d) final-state interactions and rescattering of the knocked-out nucleon,
and establish, as functions of $p_m$ and $E_m$, the kinematic boundary beyond which the single-particle DWIA description of one-nucleon knockout ceases to be valid.

Subsequent theoretical work (e.g., the Pavia and Ghent groups) has identified tensor correlations as the dominant source of pn knockout strength and meson-exchange/isobar currents as the principal source of transverse strength at deep missing energies, with refined two-nucleon knockout calculations reproducing much of the (e,e'pn) data. Background. A heap game is specified by a code string in the form $d_0 \cdot d_1 d_2 d_3 \cdots$, where each digit $d_k$ is a nonnegative integer written in hexadecimal (so $0 \le d_k \le 15$). From a single heap of $n$ tokens, a player may move by choosing some $k \ge 1$ such that $d_k > 0$, then removing $k$ tokens from the heap and splitting the remainder into $j$ nonempty heaps, where $j \in \{0,1,2,3\}$ is allowed if and only if the bit corresponding to $2^j$ is set in $d_k$ (the digit $d_0$ governs analogous moves that do not remove tokens). The player unable to move loses (normal play). The Sprague–Grundy (nim-)value $\mathcal{G}(n)$ of a heap of size $n$ is defined recursively as the minimum excludant of the multiset of Grundy values of positions reachable in one move, where the Grundy value of a disjoint union of heaps is the bitwise XOR of their Grundy values.

A code is called periodic if there exist $p \ge 1$ and $n_0$ such that $\mathcal{G}(n+p) = \mathcal{G}(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$, and arithmetically periodic with period $p$ and saltus $s$ if $\mathcal{G}(n+p) = \mathcal{G}(n) + s$ for all $n \ge n_0$.

Problem. For each hexadecimal code whose Sprague–Grundy sequence is currently not known to be ultimately periodic or arithmetically periodic — in particular for the code $\cdot 9$ — determine whether the Sprague–Grundy sequence $\{\mathcal{G}(n)\}_{n \ge 0}$ is ultimately periodic or arithmetically periodic, and if so exhibit an explicit preperiod, period, and (where applicable) saltus; otherwise establish a precise alternative regularity (for instance ruler-type regularity) characterising the sequence.

The Sprague–Grundy sequences of hexadecimal heap games such as ·9 and others remain not fully analyzed. Howse–Nowakowski and later Grossman–Nowakowski work has identified many periodic, arithmetic-periodic, and ruler-regular cases, but several hexadecimal codes (including ·9) still lack a complete classification, and it is known that not all hexadecimal games are periodic or arithmetic-periodic.

representations.normalized:
Consider exclusive electron-induced two-nucleon knockout reactions of the form A(e,e'NN) on a nuclear target A, in which an incoming electron scatters to a detected final electron while two outgoing nucleons N (either pp or pn) are detected in triple coincidence with the scattered electron, leaving the residual (A−2) nucleus in a specified discrete final state. The cross section receives contributions from (i) nucleon–nucleon short-range and tensor correlations in the initial-state nuclear wave function, (ii) two-body meson-exchange currents (MEC), (iii) intermediate isobar (e.g., Δ) excitation currents, and (iv) final-state interactions (FSI) between the outgoing nucleons and the residual system. Even in the absence of FSI, the triple-coincidence cross section does not factorize as a product of an elementary electron–nucleon-pair cross section times the two-hole spectral density of the target, so correlation information cannot be read off directly from the measured cross section.

Problem: Determine the kinematic conditions (e.g., choices of momentum transfer q, energy transfer ω, missing momentum, missing energy, relative and center-of-mass momentum of the outgoing pair, super-parallel vs. other kinematics) and final-state selections (channel pp vs. pn, choice of discrete final state of the residual nucleus, angular configurations of the detected nucleons) under which the exclusive A(e,e'NN) cross section is maximally sensitive to ground-state nucleon–nucleon correlations and minimally contaminated by meson-exchange, isobar, and other two-body current mechanisms. Identify observables (cross sections, ratios, or polarization/asymmetry observables) for which the correlation contribution dominates over the competing two-body current contributions.

representations.normalized:
N-heap Wythoff Game. Fix an integer N ≥ 3. A position is an N-tuple (a_1, a_2, …, a_N) of non-negative integers, regarded as the sizes of N heaps of tokens. A legal move consists of either:
(i) removing a positive number of tokens from exactly one heap, or
(ii) removing positive numbers of tokens from two or more heaps in such a way that the resulting multiset of removed amounts forms a P-position (losing position for the player to move) of the corresponding lower-dimensional Wythoff game on those heaps (Fraenkel's generalization: the simultaneous decrements must form a losing position of the (k)-heap Wythoff game when tokens are taken from k ≥ 2 heaps).
A player unable to move loses. The P-positions are the losing positions for the player about to move.

For each fixed choice of values a_1, …, a_{N-2} of the first N − 2 heaps, sort the P-positions (a_1, …, a_{N-2}, x, y) with x ≤ y by their (N−1)st coordinate, and denote the n-th such P-position by (a_1, …, a_{N-2}, A_n^{N-1}, A_n^{N}).

Let φ = (1 + √5)/2 denote the golden ratio, and for a finite set S ⊂ ℤ_{≥0} let mex(S) be the least non-negative integer not in S.

Prove or disprove the following two conjectures:

Conjecture 1 (mex + shift). For all sufficiently large n, A_n^{N-1} equals mex of a certain explicit set built from previously computed P-positions, together with an additive shift, while A_n^{N} = A_n^{N-1} + n.

Conjecture 2 (golden-ratio asymptotics). There exists an integer constant α (depending on a_1,…,a_{N-2}) and a bounded integer-valued error ε_n ∈ {−1, 0, 1} such that, for all sufficiently large n,
   A_n^{N-1} = ⌊ n φ ⌋ + ε_n + α,    A_n^{N} = A_n^{N-1} + n.

Sun and Zeilberger (Annals of Combinatorics, 2004) and follow-up work proved sufficient conditions and verified the conjectures for the 3-heap case with the smallest heap up to 10 tokens, but a full proof for arbitrary N ≥ 3 has not been obtained.

Consider the exclusive electron-induced two-proton knockout reaction $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pp)^{14}\mathrm{C}$, in which an incoming electron scatters from an $^{16}\mathrm{O}$ target and two protons are detected in coincidence with the scattered electron, leaving the residual nucleus $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ in a specific discrete final state (ground state or low-lying excited states). For kinematics that favor sensitivity to short-range correlations (small center-of-mass momentum of the pp pair, moderate energy and momentum transfer, with the pair predominantly in a relative ${}^1S_0$ state), the state-resolved differential cross section depends on (i) the two-nucleon overlap (spectroscopic) amplitudes for the transition, (ii) the central short-range correlation function $g(r)$ used to defect the relative pair wave function, (iii) tensor and other induced correlations, and (iv) two-body currents including meson-exchange and intermediate $\Delta$-isobar contributions.

Question: Can exclusive cross-section measurements of $^{16}\mathrm{O}(e,e'pp)^{14}\mathrm{C}$ to selected final states—especially those transitions dominated by knockout of a relative ${}^1S_0$ proton pair—be performed with sufficient precision in correlation-favored kinematics to:

(a) discriminate among competing models of the central nucleon-nucleon short-range correlation function $g(r)$ through their distinct predictions for these state-resolved cross sections; and

(b) thereby place quantitative constraints on the off-shell behavior of the nucleon-nucleon potential?

Specifically, determine whether achievable experimental precision and theoretical control (including treatment of final-state interactions, two-body currents, and competing reaction mechanisms) allow the state-resolved cross sections to uniquely fix $g(r)$ to within a tolerance that translates into a meaningful constraint on the off-shell $NN$ interaction.

Subsequent measurements and analyses (e.g., MAMI/Mainz high-resolution data and microscopic calculations including central SRC and Δ excitations) have demonstrated that the $^{16}$O(e,e′pp)$^{14}$C ground-state transition is indeed dominated by knockout of $^1S_0$ pp pairs and carries clear SRC signatures, with parameter-free calculations reproducing data. representations.normalized:
Consider the following combinatorial games and resolve the questions stated for each.

(1) End-Nim. Several heaps of beans are arranged in a row. On a move, a player removes any positive number of beans from either the leftmost or the rightmost heap (a heap that becomes empty disappears, possibly exposing a new end-heap). The last player to move wins (normal play). Determine the exact Sprague–Grundy values of all positions in End-Nim.

(2) End-Wythoff (impartial and partizan). With heaps in a row, a player may either (a) remove any positive number of beans from the leftmost or rightmost heap, or (b) remove the same positive number of beans from both end heaps simultaneously. Analyze the impartial version (compute Sprague–Grundy values or P-positions) and the partizan version (compute its game-theoretic values in the sense of Conway).

(3) Generalized end-heap Wythoff variant. Generalize End-Wythoff by allowing combined moves taken simultaneously from the two end heaps under more general rules (the natural Fraenkel-style generalization of Wythoff to end-heaps). Determine the P-positions and/or Grundy values.

(4) Hub-and-Spoke Nim. The heaps are placed at the vertices of a star graph: one central "hub" heap and several "spoke" heaps. A move consists of removing beans according to a prescribed rule involving the hub and the spokes. Analyze the game; in particular determine its P-positions and Grundy function. Also analyze the natural forest generalization in which beans may only be removed from a leaf of an underlying forest of heaps.

(5) Red-Blue Cherries. Consider the following combinatorial games and resolve the questions stated for each.

(1) End-Nim. Several heaps of beans are arranged in a row. On a move, a player removes any positive number of beans from either the leftmost or the rightmost heap (a heap that becomes empty disappears, possibly exposing a new end-heap). The last player to move wins (normal play). Determine the exact Sprague–Grundy values of all positions in End-Nim.

(2) End-Wythoff (impartial and partizan). With heaps in a row, a player may either (a) remove any positive number of beans from the leftmost or rightmost heap, or (b) remove the same positive number of beans from both end heaps simultaneously. Analyze the impartial version (compute Sprague–Grundy values or P-positions) and the partizan version (compute its game-theoretic values in the sense of Conway).

(3) Generalized end-heap Wythoff variant. Generalize End-Wythoff by allowing combined moves taken simultaneously from the two end heaps under more general rules (the natural Fraenkel-style generalization of Wythoff to end-heaps). Determine the P-positions and/or Grundy values.

(4) Hub-and-Spoke Nim. The heaps are placed at the vertices of a star graph: one central "hub" heap and several "spoke" heaps. A move consists of removing beans according to a prescribed rule involving the hub and the spokes. Analyze the game; in particular determine its P-positions and Grundy function. Also analyze the natural forest generalization in which beans may only be removed from a leaf of an underlying forest of heaps.

(5) Red-Blue Cherries. In a partizan game played on a structure of "cherries" colored red and blue (Left moves on blue, Right on red, with the standard cherries move-rule), decide whether every Red-Blue Cherries position has an integer game value, and more generally characterize the class of positions for which the game value is (or fails to be) an integer.

Consider the exclusive electron-induced two-nucleon knockout reaction $A(e,e'pn)B$ on a nuclear target, in which an incident electron scatters off a nucleus, transferring four-momentum $(\omega,\mathbf{q})$ via a virtual photon, and a proton-neutron pair is detected in coincidence with the scattered electron in the final state, leaving a residual nucleus $B$ in a discrete or low-lying state. The cross section receives contributions from:

(i) one-body currents acting on a correlated proton-neutron pair described by the two-hole spectral density $S_{pn}(\mathbf{p}_1,\mathbf{p}_2;E)$, in which short-range and tensor nucleon-nucleon correlations in the initial state allow the pair to absorb the virtual photon; and

(ii) two-body currents, including meson-exchange currents and isobar ($\Delta$) currents, which can excite a proton-neutron pair directly.

In the so-called superparallel kinematics, in which both ejected nucleons are detected along the direction of the momentum transfer $\mathbf{q}$ (one parallel and one antiparallel), theoretical calculations predict a substantial enhancement of the $(e,e'pn)$ cross section relative to the $(e,e'pp)$ cross section.

Problem. Devise an experimental and/or theoretical procedure (for example, a choice of kinematics, observables, or polarization degrees of freedom, together with a determination of the proton-neutron two-hole spectral density of sufficient accuracy) that allows one to separate quantitatively the contribution of ground-state tensor correlations from the contribution of two-body meson-exchange and isobar currents to the exclusive $(e,e'pn)$ cross section, so that the predicted enhancement in superparallel kinematics can be unambiguously attributed to its two physical origins.

Kotzig's Nim is the following impartial combinatorial game. Fix a finite set M of positive integers (the move set) and a positive integer n (the circle length). The board consists of n vertices arranged on a directed cycle Z/nZ. A token starts at vertex 0; vertex 0 is marked "used". Players alternate moves. On each turn a player chooses some m ∈ M and advances the token m steps clockwise around the cycle; the move is legal only if the destination vertex has not previously been used. After a legal move, the destination vertex is marked used. Under normal play, a player unable to move loses; under misère play, a player unable to move wins.

Resolve the following:

(a) (Periodicity.) Prove or disprove: for every finite move set M ⊂ Z_{>0}, the outcome (Previous-player or Next-player win) of normal-play Kotzig's Nim on the cycle of length n is eventually periodic in n, i.e. there exist integers n_0 ≥ 1 and p ≥ 1 such that for all n ≥ n_0 the outcome on length n equals the outcome on length n+p.

(b) (Misère version.) Determine the outcome classes (and, more generally, the structural theory) of misère Kotzig's Nim for arbitrary finite move sets M; in particular decide whether eventual periodicity in n also holds in the misère convention.

(c) (Specific move sets.) Resolve the outcome sequences and the existence/period of eventual periodicity for the move sets M = {1,4} and M = {3,5}, in both normal and misère play.

Recent work by S. Arun ("Geography, Kotzig's Nim, and Variants", RSI 2023, published in Theoretical Computer Science 2024) makes progress on these questions: it places Kotzig's Nim in the framework of Geography, partially resolves a Tan–Ward conjecture, and provides results for misère play including a "diamond" winning strategy when the move set is {a, a+1} on composite-length cycles, plus results for {2,3}. Consider exclusive electron-induced two-nucleon knockout reactions on a nuclear target, in which an incoming electron with four-momentum k scatters to a final electron with four-momentum k', exchanging a virtual photon of four-momentum q = k - k', and two outgoing nucleons (either a pp pair or a pn pair) are detected in coincidence while the residual (A-2)-nucleus is left in a specific discrete final state f. The differential cross section for such an (e,e'NN) reaction can be decomposed in terms of hadronic response functions that depend on bilinear combinations of the transition amplitudes M_{fi} between the initial nuclear ground state and the chosen residual state, mediated by (i) one-body currents acting on correlated nucleon pairs arising from short-range and tensor correlations in the nuclear wave function, and (ii) explicit two-body meson-exchange and isobar currents (including pion exchange and intermediate Δ excitation). In addition to unpolarized cross sections, one may consider polarization observables, defined as follows: the recoil polarization P = (P_L, P_T, P_N) of one of the ejected nucleons (longitudinal, transverse in the scattering plane, and normal to it) measured with unpolarized beam and target, and the polarization-transfer coefficients P'_i obtained with a longitudinally polarized electron beam. Each such observable is a specific bilinear function of the amplitudes M_{fi}.

Question: Do the recoil-polarization observables of one outgoing nucleon in (e,e'pp) and (e,e'pn) reactions, taken together with the experimental resolution of individual residual-nucleus final states f, supply sufficiently many independent bilinear functionals of the amplitudes M_{fi} to (a) cleanly decompose the cross section into contributions originating from nucleon-nucleon correlations versus contributions from two-body currents (including Δ-isobar excitation), and (b) achieve a complete determination of all independent complex scattering amplitudes M_{fi} (up to an overall phase) for the chosen final state?

Consider the following two-player combinatorial game, called Put-or-Take-a-Square. The state of the game is a nonnegative integer n (a heap of n stones). Players alternate turns. From a position n > 0, the player to move must make one of the following legal moves:
 (i) remove a positive perfect square number k² ≤ n of stones, moving to position n − k²; or
 (ii) if n is even and n > 0, add one stone, moving to position n + 1.
A player who cannot move (the position n = 0) loses under normal play convention.

Classify each position n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} as:
 • a P-position if the previous player wins (the player to move loses under optimal play and the game terminates),
 • an N-position if the next player wins (the player to move has a winning strategy), or
 • an O-position if optimal play from n leads to an infinite (drawn) game (neither player has a winning strategy because each can force the game to continue indefinitely).

For each N ≥ 1, let p(N), n(N), and o(N) be the number of integers in {1, 2, …, N} that are P-, N-, and O-positions respectively.

Determine the asymptotic behavior of the proportions p(N)/N, n(N)/N, and o(N)/N as N → ∞. In particular, determine whether each limit exists and, if so, compute its value.

Consider an A-nucleon quantum mechanical Hamiltonian of the form
H = sum_{i=1}^{A} T_i + sum_{i<j} V_{ij} + sum_{i<j<k} W_{ijk},
where T_i is the kinetic energy of nucleon i, V_{ij} is a two-nucleon potential (possibly nonlocal, i.e. an integral operator with kernel V(r,r') rather than a multiplication operator V(r) delta(r-r')), and W_{ijk} is an explicit three-nucleon force. Two two-nucleon potentials V and V' are called phase-equivalent if they produce identical NN scattering phase shifts and identical deuteron binding for all energies; such potentials may nevertheless differ off the energy shell and yield different predictions for A >= 3 systems.

It is known that for A = 3, 4 the low-energy binding energies depend on only a small number of effective parameters, so that any discrepancy between a two-nucleon-only prediction and experiment can be repaired either by (i) adding a three-nucleon force W_{ijk} fitted to the binding energies, or (ii) replacing V_{ij} by a phase-equivalent nonlocal two-nucleon potential V'_{ij} with different off-shell behavior. Thus binding energies alone cannot distinguish genuine three-nucleon forces from nonlocal two-nucleon off-shell effects.

Problem. Identify a set of continuum observables in the four-nucleon system (for instance, positions and widths of the low-lying resonances and thresholds in the 4N continuum, and elastic and reaction cross sections in n+³H, p+³He, d+d channels) and prove or disprove the following:

(a) There exist observables O_1, ..., O_k among these continuum quantities such that, for any two Hamiltonians H and H' that reproduce all NN scattering data, the deuteron, and the experimental ³H and ⁴He binding energies, requiring O_j(H) = O_j(H') for j = 1,...,k forces the three-nucleon-force parts of H and H' to be related to the nonlocal off-shell parts of V_{ij} and V'_{ij} in a uniquely determined way (i.e. the ambiguity between "explicit 3N force" and "nonlocal 2N off-shell content" is removed by these observables).

(b) Quantify the minimal k and exhibit explicit observables achieving (a), or prove that no finite set of such continuum observables suffices.

Gale's Nim is the following impartial combinatorial game. There are four heaps of tokens. On a turn, a player removes any positive number of tokens from a single heap (as in ordinary Nim). The game ends as soon as three of the four heaps have been emptied, leaving one heap remaining; under normal play convention, the player unable to move (equivalently, the player who would have to make the third heap vanish in a position with no legal move available within that restriction) loses.

(a) Determine the P-positions (previous-player wins) of Gale's Nim in the case of four heaps whose sizes are pairwise distinct and each strictly greater than 2. That is, give a complete characterization of the losing positions (a, b, c, d) with 2 < a < b < c < d.

(b) More generally, consider the variant played with h heaps in which play terminates as soon as k of the heaps have been emptied (so Gale's Nim is the case h = 4, k = 3). Determine the P-positions of this h-heap, k-vanishing variant.

Background and setup. A two-nucleon (NN) interaction is a (possibly nonlocal) operator V acting on the relative-motion wave function of two nucleons, designed to reproduce NN scattering phase shifts up to a chosen laboratory energy and the deuteron observables (binding energy, asymptotic normalization, D-state probability constraints, etc.). A class of phenomenological nonlocal NN interactions (the INOY and Doleschall-type potentials) is constructed in coordinate space with a short-range nonlocal part and a long-range one-pion-exchange tail, with the property that, when used alone (without any explicit three-nucleon force), they reproduce the experimental triton binding energy E(³H) ≈ 8.482 MeV in addition to the two-nucleon data.

When such an NN interaction V is used in an ab initio bound-state calculation for the four-nucleon system (the α particle, ⁴He), define:
 • E_α(V) = the binding energy of ⁴He computed from the nonrelativistic four-body Schrödinger equation with V as the only nuclear interaction,
 • r_p(V) = the point-proton root-mean-square radius of the ⁴He ground state computed with V.

The experimental values are E_α^exp ≈ 28.30 MeV and r_p^exp ≈ 1.46 fm (the precise reference value being the one extracted from electron-scattering charge-radius data after standard corrections).

Observed failure. Existing INOY/Doleschall-type interactions V₀ satisfy
 E_α(V₀) − E_α^exp ≈ +0.8 MeV (overbinding by about 800 keV),
 r_p(V₀) ≈ 0.9 · r_p^exp (about 10% too small),
indicating that they are too "soft" at short distances.

Problem. Construct a nonlocal two-nucleon interaction V (of the same general INOY/Doleschall coordinate-space, nonlocal-short-range plus one-pion-exchange-tail form, with no explicit three-nucleon force) such that simultaneously:
 (i) V reproduces the standard two-nucleon scattering observables (phase shifts and mixing parameters in all relevant partial waves up to lab energies of order 350 MeV) and the deuteron properties to the same accuracy as existing INOY/Doleschall models;
 (ii) V reproduces the experimental triton binding energy E(³H) without invoking any three-nucleon force;
 (iii) V reproduces the α-particle binding energy: E_α(V) = E_α^exp within the accepted experimental and few-body computational uncertainty;
 (iv) V reproduces the point-proton root-mean-square radius of ⁴He: r_p(V) = r_p^exp within the same tolerance.

A natural strategy is to increase the short-range repulsion between nucleons in the nonlocal part of V. The question is whether such a modification can be carried out while preserving (i) and (ii), and, if so, to exhibit it explicitly; otherwise, to demonstrate an obstruction.

Searches indicate that Doleschall-type nonlocal NN interactions (INOY) continue to reproduce the triton binding energy without a 3NF but still fail to simultaneously reproduce the α-particle binding energy and proton rms radius; no published phenomenological nonlocal NN potential is known that solves all four constraints at once. Euclid's Nim is the two-player combinatorial game whose positions are pairs (a,b) of positive integers; a move from (a,b) with a≤b consists of replacing b by b−ka for some positive integer k with b−ka≥0 (some conventions require >0), and the player unable to move loses. Its theory (P-positions, game values) is classically understood via the continued fraction expansion of b/a.

Consider the following two extensions:

(1) Three-integer Euclid. Positions are triples (a,b,c) of positive integers. A move consists of subtracting from one of the integers a positive integer multiple of another, provided the result remains positive (or, in a variant, subtracting from the largest a positive multiple of the smallest). Determine the P-positions and, more generally, the Sprague–Grundy values of all positions in these three-integer variants.

(2) Partizan Euclid. Positions are pairs (a,b) of positive integers, but Left and Right have asymmetric move-sets derived from the Euclidean algorithm (for instance, Left subtracts a positive multiple of the smaller from the larger giving certain prescribed remainders, while Right has the complementary moves). Determine, in the sense of combinatorial game theory, the game-theoretic values of all Partizan Euclid positions, or at least determine their atomic weights (the all-small/infinitesimal valuation used to compare loopfree games near 0).

Provide a complete solution: closed-form or algorithmic descriptions of values, P-positions, or atomic weights, in each of these settings.

Collins and Lengyel (Discrete Mathematics, 2008) introduced the game of 3-Euclid and solved special cases; further variants were treated by other authors (e.g., a 2012 paper analyzing two variations of 3-Euclid). McKay and Nowakowski analyzed Outcomes of Partizan Euclid (Integers, 2012), determining outcome classes but not full values. No source found that fully determines all game values or atomic weights for Partizan Euclid or general 3-Euclid positions, so the broader problem remains open.

representations.normalized:
Consider the four-nucleon scattering problem for a neutron incident on a triton (3H) at zero and very low energy. The dynamics are governed by a nucleon-nucleon (NN) interaction supplemented by a three-nucleon force (3NF). A representative realistic model is the Argonne v18 (AV18) NN potential combined with the Urbana IX (UIX) three-nucleon force; this combination is tuned to reproduce the experimental triton binding energy (~8.48 MeV).

For the n+3H system at zero energy, two key low-energy observables are:
(i) the zero-energy total cross section σ(0), and
(ii) the spin-dependent coherent scattering lengths a_c (and the singlet a_s and triplet a_t scattering lengths from which a_c is constructed).

Empirically, while AV18+UIX yields a zero-energy cross section in fair agreement with experiment, the coherent (and spin-projected) scattering lengths for n+3H remain in tension with measured values. Nonlocal NN interaction models (such as INOY-type interactions) tend to improve the description of low-energy n+3H data, particularly near the elastic-cross-section minimum at center-of-mass energy E_cm ≈ 0.4 MeV.

Identify and characterize the missing or incompletely modeled interaction ingredients in the nuclear Hamiltonian that are responsible for the residual discrepancies between theoretical predictions (based on AV18+UIX or similar local NN+3NF Hamiltonians that reproduce the triton binding energy) and experimental low-energy n+3H scattering observables — in particular the coherent scattering lengths — while simultaneously preserving agreement with the zero-energy cross section and the triton binding energy. The task is to determine which interaction effects (e.g., specific components of the three-nucleon force, nonlocalities in the NN interaction, charge-symmetry-breaking terms, four-nucleon forces, or other dynamical ingredients) must be added or modified so that the full set of low-energy n+3H observables is described consistently.

Schuhstring is a take-away game played on a finite collection of strings of beads (each string consisting of a fixed positive number of beads). On each turn a player chooses one string and removes a positive number of beads from its end, subject to a fixed global maximum deduction Y (the same upper bound on the number of beads removed in a single move applies to every move and every string). A move that removes the last remaining bead(s) of a string is said to "terminate" that string. The game ends under the usual normal/misère convention of the underlying take-away rule.

A "simultaneous termination" of order k in a Schuhstring position refers to a single move (in optimal play, within a position arising from some legal Schuhstring game) after which exactly k strings end up terminated at the same moment, in the precise sense used for Schuhstrings: k distinct strings reach length 0 on the same move under the analysis of the game. It is known that there exist Schuhstring games (with suitable choice of Y and initial string lengths) admitting a simultaneous termination of three strings.

Question: Determine whether, for every positive integer k, there exists a Schuhstring game (with some choice of the maximum deduction Y and initial string lengths) admitting a simultaneous termination of order at least k. Equivalently, can the number of strings that terminate simultaneously in a Schuhstring game be arbitrarily large?

The problem appears in a list of unsolved problems in combinatorial games. Consider the four-nucleon scattering problem of a neutron incident on a triton (³H) in the elastic channel. The ⁴H compound system possesses two narrow, nearly spin-degenerate negative-parity resonances at low energy, producing a peak in the n+³H elastic cross section at center-of-mass energy E_cm ≈ 3 MeV. Solve the four-body scattering problem (e.g., via Faddeev–Yakubovsky, AGS, or hyperspherical-harmonics methods) using a realistic nuclear Hamiltonian H = T + Σ V_{NN} + Σ V_{3N}, where V_{NN} is a realistic two-nucleon interaction (such as AV18, CD-Bonn, Nijmegen, or a nonlocal interaction with one-pion-exchange tail like INOY) and V_{3N} is a three-nucleon force (such as Urbana IX).

Empirically, every such realistic interaction yields an elastic n+³H cross section near the resonance peak (E_cm ≈ 3 MeV) that lies more than 10% below the measured value. The following partial remedies are known to be ineffective for resolving this deficit: (i) modifying off-shell behavior of V_{NN}; (ii) including standard three-nucleon forces of the Urbana/Tucson–Melbourne type; (iii) replacing local two-nucleon forces by phenomenologically nonlocal ones. Since the deficit lies in the negative-parity resonance region, where NN P-waves contribute on a par with S-waves, the missing physics must reside in components of the nuclear interaction that act in odd-parity (predominantly P-wave) NN channels.

Problem. Identify the component(s) of the nucleon–nucleon and/or many-nucleon interaction whose inclusion or modification—consistent with current constraints from 2N and 3N data—simultaneously reproduces the measured n+³H elastic cross section at the resonance peak near E_cm ≈ 3 MeV (within experimental uncertainty) and the positions and widths of the negative-parity ⁴H resonances, without spoiling the successful description of low-energy n+³H observables (e.g., the doublet and quartet scattering lengths) and of A=3 binding energies.

Consider the following two-player combinatorial game, called DUDE (unbounded Dudeney). A position consists of a finite multiset of nonnegative integer heap sizes together with a "forbidden move size" m (with m = 0 meaning no restriction, used for the starting position). On each turn, the player to move chooses a heap and removes a positive number t of tokens from it, subject to the single restriction t ≠ m (the opponent's previous move size). After the move, the forbidden size for the opponent becomes t. The player unable to move (all heaps empty) loses; play is under the normal convention. Equivalently, DUDE is Nim in which a player may not remove exactly as many tokens as the opponent just removed, with no upper bound on the size of a single removal.

For a position G, let 𝒢(G) denote its Sprague–Grundy (nim) value, defined recursively by 𝒢(G) = mex{𝒢(G') : G' a legal option from G}, where mex denotes the minimum excludant.
