Consider the following two-player combinatorial game, called DUDE (unbounded Dudeney). A position consists of a finite multiset of nonnegative integer heap sizes together with a "forbidden move size" m (with m = 0 meaning no restriction, used for the starting position). On each turn, the player to move chooses a heap and removes a positive number t of tokens from it, subject to the single restriction t ≠ m (the opponent's previous move size). After the move, the forbidden size for the opponent becomes t. The player unable to move (all heaps empty) loses; play is under the normal convention. Problem: Determine the Sprague–Grundy (nim) values of all positions of DUDE. In particular, give an explicit, easily described formula or pattern for 𝒢([h₁, h₂, …, h_k; m]) in terms of the heap sizes h₁ ≤ h₂ ≤ … ≤ h_k and the forbidden value m, or otherwise explain the structural reason such a simple description should not exist.

The problem is listed among unsolved problems in combinatorial games. While the P-positions of DUDE have been described, the nim-values are reported as not showing any easily described pattern, and no full Sprague–Grundy analysis appears in the literature. No solution was found in available sources.

representations.normalized:
Consider the standard framework of low-energy nuclear physics in which two nucleons (proton p and neutron n) interact via a charge-dependent nucleon-nucleon (NN) potential decomposed into partial waves, supplemented when needed by a three-nucleon force (3NF). A widely used realistic potential of this kind (e.g. of the AV18 type) is fit primarily to proton-proton (pp) and neutron-proton (np) scattering data plus the deuteron, with charge-symmetry/charge-independence breaking used to infer neutron-neutron (nn) partial waves. Because no direct free nn scattering experiments exist, the nn P-wave components are not directly constrained by data; meanwhile pp P-waves at low energy are masked by the Coulomb repulsion.

Investigate the following questions:

(a) Are the NN P-wave interactions in current realistic NN potentials — in particular the nn ¹P₁, ³P₀, ³P₁, ³P₂ components and their charge dependence relative to pp and np — incorrectly constrained, in the sense that the present treatment of charge dependence in P-waves is insufficient to reproduce P-wave-sensitive observables in light nuclei?

(b) Does there exist a physically acceptable modification of the nn P-wave potential (i.e. a modification consistent with all directly measured NN data, with charge-symmetry-breaking expectations, and with deuteron and few-body bound-state properties) that simultaneously
 (i) brings calculations of the n + ³H elastic cross section in the resonance region into agreement with measurement,
 (ii) accounts for the systematic, approximately linear growth with neutron excess of the discrepancy between computed and measured helium-isotope binding energies that persists after inclusion of standard 3NFs, and
 (iii) is compatible with (or helps resolve) the nucleon-deuteron vector analyzing-power (Aᵧ) puzzle?

Quantitatively, determine whether a change of order 20% in the nn P-wave potential strength needed to reproduce the n + ³H resonance cross section with an AV18-type interaction is admissible as genuine charge dependence in the P-waves (noting that only of order 6–8% modification of NN P-waves is typically associated with the Aᵧ puzzle), or whether such a large modification must instead be attributed to missing many-nucleon dynamics.

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions. A finite impartial combinatorial game is played by two players who alternate moves; the player unable to move loses (normal play). The Sprague–Grundy value G(P) of a position P is defined recursively by G(P)=mex{G(P′):P→P′}, where mex denotes the minimum excludant of a set of nonnegative integers. A position P is a P-position iff G(P)=0.

Adding a pass. Given an impartial game Γ, the "Γ with a (single) pass" is the variant in which each player has, in addition to the legal moves of Γ, the option to "pass" (make no change to the position) at most once during the entire play; a pass may not be played from a terminal position, and once either player has used the pass, the pass option is removed from the game for both players. More generally, "Γ with k passes" denotes the variant in which the pass option may be used a total of k times (over both players combined).

Specific games.
(1) Nim: positions are tuples (a₁,…,aₙ) of nonnegative integers; a move reduces some aᵢ to a strictly smaller nonnegative integer.
(2) Chocolate-Bar game with parameter s: a position consists of a rectangular bar broken according to standard chocolate-bar rules (a known impartial game), parameterized by an integer s ≥ 1.
(3) Octal games: an impartial heap game specified by an octal code d₀.d₁d₂d₃…, where the digit dₖ encodes which of the moves "remove k tokens leaving 0, 1, or 2 nonempty heaps" are legal. The G-sequence of an octal game is the sequence (G(0),G(1),G(2),…) of Grundy values of single heaps; an octal game is said to be (arithmetically) regular if its G-sequence is eventually periodic.
(4) Oslo version of a game: the variant in which exactly one designated heap (or component) is restricted in a prescribed Oslo-style manner; see standard usage.

Problems to solve.
(a) Nim with a pass. Determine the P-positions, and more generally the Sprague–Grundy values, of n-pile Nim with a single pass move, for all n ≥ 3.
(b) Chocolate Bar with a pass. Solve (determine the P-positions of) the Chocolate-Bar game with a single pass for all even values of the parameter s.
(c) Octal games with a pass. For each octal game whose G-sequence (without a pass) is eventually periodic, determine which forms of regularity (eventual periodicity, arithmetic periodicity, etc.) can or must occur in the G-sequence of the game with a single pass added, and classify the possible behaviors.
(d) Multiple passes. Extend the analyses in (a)–(c) to the case in which more than one pass move is allowed during a single play, and describe how the Sprague–Grundy theory changes as the number k of available passes increases.
(e) Oslo versions. For each of the games above, analyze the structural properties (P-positions, Grundy values, regularity of G-sequences) of the corresponding Oslo version, with and without pass moves.

Adding a pass to classical Nim is widely cited as an open problem; David Gale famously offered a prize for solving three-pile Nim with a pass, and recent works (e.g., on Wythoff's game with a pass, and restricted Nim with a pass in Integers 23 (2023)) only address restricted variants. Consider the nucleon resonance commonly labeled S11(1535): a spin-1/2, negative-parity, isospin-1/2 baryon resonance with mass near 1535 MeV that couples strongly to the ηN channel and dominates η-meson production off single nucleons by hadronic and electromagnetic probes near threshold.

Two competing structural hypotheses are to be distinguished:
(i) a compact three-quark state, as in standard constituent quark models;
(ii) a dynamically generated meson–baryon (in particular ηN, KΛ, KΣ) quasi-bound state — a "molecular" state — produced by coupled-channel hadronic interactions.

Following Weinberg's compositeness criterion, the residue and energy dependence of the elastic scattering amplitude T_{ηN→ηN}(E) near the resonance pole encode the probability that the physical state is dominated by the ηN two-hadron component: a purely molecular ηN state implies specific low-energy parameters (scattering length a_{ηN}, effective range r_{ηN}, and a characteristic shape of T_{ηN→ηN}) that differ sharply from those of a compact state weakly coupled to the ηN continuum.

The problem is the following.

(A) Determine, in a model-independent way using Weinberg's compositeness argument, the precise quantitative criterion on the elastic ηN amplitude (and equivalently on the pair (a_{ηN}, r_{ηN})) that distinguishes an ηN molecular interpretation of S11(1535) from a compact three-quark interpretation.

(B) Since direct elastic ηN scattering is not experimentally accessible (no η beams or targets), derive constraints on the elastic ηN amplitude — in particular on a_{ηN} and r_{ηN} — from available non-diagonal hadronic and photon-induced reactions producing ηN final states (e.g. πN → ηN, γN → ηN, NN → NNη, γd → ηX, η-production on nuclei), using analyticity, unitarity, and final-state interaction arguments.

(C) Apply these constraints to decide whether the S11(1535) is best described as a compact quark-model baryon, a dynamically generated state, or specifically an ηN molecular state.

representations.normalized:
Consider the following combinatorial game framework. A "Muller twist" game is a two-player game in which, after each move, the player who has just moved imposes a restriction on the next move of the opponent; once the opponent has moved, the restriction is forgotten. Specialize as follows.

Blocking Nim with k blocks on n heaps: There are n heaps of tokens of sizes (h_1,...,h_n) with n ≥ 2. Players alternate; on each turn a player first declares at most k "blocked" positions (each consisting of a heap index together with a forbidden new size strictly less than the current size of that heap), and then the opponent must make an ordinary Nim move (choose one heap and reduce its size to any strictly smaller nonnegative integer) which does not result in any of the blocked positions. The player unable to move loses (normal play).

(a) Determine the set of P-positions (previous-player winning positions) and a winning strategy for Blocking Nim with one block (k=1) on exactly two heaps (n=2).
(b) Do the same for Blocking Nim with one block on exactly three heaps (n=3).
(c) Do the same for Blocking Nim with one block on n heaps for every n > 3, and more generally for k blocks on n heaps.

Complementary subtraction games: Let S ⊆ ℤ_{≥1} be a subtraction set. The complementary subtraction game on a single heap with subtraction set S is played by alternately removing a number of tokens from S; the player unable to move loses. Determine the Sprague–Grundy function (or at least the P-positions) of the complementary subtraction game when S is each of the following:
  (i) the set of Fibonacci numbers {1,2,3,5,8,13,...};
  (ii) a "modular" set {n : n ≡ r (mod m)} for prescribed integers m ≥ 2 and r;
  (iii) a Wythoff-type set, namely S = {⌊nφ⌋ : n ≥ 1} where φ = (1+√5)/2, and analogously S = {⌈nφ⌉ : n ≥ 1}.

Consider the light-baryon spectrum of QCD, with particular focus on the low-lying nucleon resonances: the Roper resonance N(1440) with quantum numbers P11, the P11(1710), and the negative-parity S11(1535). In the original nonrelativistic constituent quark model, the lowest positive-parity radial excitation of the nucleon is predicted to lie above the lowest negative-parity excitation, in conflict with the observed ordering in which the Roper N(1440) lies below the S11(1535). Two distinct theoretical pictures have been proposed to resolve this discrepancy:

(A) A "dynamically generated" picture in which the Roper N(1440) is not a genuine three-quark state but arises as a meson–baryon quasi-bound state generated by coupled-channel hadronic dynamics, and in which the first genuine radial three-quark excitation of the nucleon is identified instead with P11(1710).

(B) A "modified quark–quark interaction" picture in which the Roper N(1440) remains a genuine three-quark state, but a flavor-dependent (e.g. Goldstone-boson-exchange-type) quark–quark interaction is introduced into the constituent quark model so as to reorder the radial and orbital excitations and place the P11 nucleon excitation below the S11.

Determine whether there is a precise mathematical/dynamical relationship between pictures (A) and (B): for instance, whether one can be derived as an effective limit or rearrangement of the other, whether they make distinguishable predictions for observables (such as electromagnetic transition form factors, decay couplings, or large-N_c scaling), or whether they are genuinely inequivalent descriptions of the same spectrum. In the analysis, address also the scenario in which chiral coupled-channel dynamics generates S11(1535) itself as a dynamically generated (e.g. KΣ–ηN) state, and explain how each picture must be modified to accommodate this, including the assignment of the lowest genuine three-quark negative-parity nucleon excitation in that case.

(B) A "modified quark–quark interaction" picture in which the Roper N(1440) remains a genuine three-quark state, but a flavor-dependent (e.g. Goldstone-boson-exchange-type) quark–quark interaction is introduced into the constituent quark model so as to reorder the radial and orbital excitations and place the P11 nucleon excitation below the S11.

Determine whether there is a precise mathematical/dynamical relationship between pictures (A) and (B): for instance, whether one can be derived as an effective limit or rearrangement of the other, whether they make distinguishable predictions for observables (such as electromagnetic transition form factors, decay couplings, or large-N_c scaling), or whether they are genuinely inequivalent descriptions of the same spectrum. In the analysis, address also the scenario in which chiral coupled-channel dynamics generates S11(1535) itself as a dynamically generated (e.g. KΣ–ηN) state, and explain how each picture must be modified to accommodate this, including the assignment of the lowest genuine three-quark negative-parity nucleon excitation in that case.

The nature of the Roper resonance — genuine three-quark state versus dynamically generated meson–baryon structure — and its relation to flavor-dependent quark-interaction models and to a possibly dynamically generated S11(1535) remains an active debate. Recent lattice QCD, Dyson–Schwinger/Faddeev, and coupled-channel studies (e.g. 2017–2026) give differing answers, and a survey from 2026 explicitly describes the Roper as "still controversial 60 years later." No unified reconciliation of the two pictures has been established.

Background. An impartial combinatorial game under misère convention is one in which the last player to move loses. For a finite set A of impartial games, the misère quotient Q(A) is the commutative monoid obtained from the free commutative monoid on positions reachable from A by quotienting by the indistinguishability congruence (G ≡ H iff for every position X, G+X and H+X have the same misère outcome). An octal game is specified by a code 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 …, where each digit d_k ∈ {0,1,…,7} (binary expansion encoding which of "leave a heap unchanged," "remove the heap entirely," and "split the heap" are allowed when removing k tokens). A quaternary game is the analogous notion with digits in {0,1,2,3}. Dawson's Kayles is the octal game 0.07.

Let Q_n(0.07) denote the partial misère quotient generated by Dawson's Kayles positions of heap size at most n. It is known that Q_33(0.07) is finite of order 638.

Problems.
(a) Decide whether Q_34(0.07) is finite or infinite, and more generally whether the full misère quotient of Dawson's Kayles is infinite.
(b) Given a finite set A of impartial games, give a finite presentation procedure and a decision algorithm that determines whether Q(A) is infinite.
(c) Formulate a precise definition of "algebraic periodicity" of misère quotient sequences for octal and quaternary games, and give an algorithm to detect such periodicity. Use it to give complete misère analyses of those octal games conjecturally exhibiting algebraic periodicity in misère play.

representations.normalized:
Consider the nucleon resonance S11(1535), a spin-1/2, isospin-1/2, negative-parity baryon resonance lying close to and strongly coupled to the eta-nucleon (ηN) channel. Two competing pictures of its internal structure are:

(i) a loosely bound ηN (and KΛ, KΣ) hadronic "molecule," generated dynamically as a quasi-bound state of meson–baryon channels by coupled-channel hadronic interactions; and

(ii) a compact three-quark (or genuine quark-model) excited baryon state of small spatial extent.

In the single-nucleon sector the two pictures can be tuned to reproduce essentially the same ηN scattering amplitude near threshold and the same pole position, so they are difficult to distinguish from πN → ηN and γN → ηN data alone. However, in environments containing additional baryons the two pictures are expected to behave differently: a loosely bound molecule should be substantially modified (e.g., Pauli blocking of its nucleon component, dispersive effects on its meson component, level rearrangement) when embedded in a few-nucleon system, whereas a compact quark state should be comparatively inert and behave more like a point-like resonance whose properties are dressed only by standard nuclear medium effects.

Problem. Develop a systematic theoretical framework for the η-deuteron (ηd) and η-helium-3 (η³He) systems that:

(a) treats the η meson, the nucleons, and the S11(1535) resonance as explicit degrees of freedom, and incorporates both structural hypotheses (i) and (ii) for S11(1535) on an equal footing within the same few-body scattering formalism (e.g., Faddeev/Faddeev–Yakubovsky or AGS-type equations with a coupled ηN–πN–S11 subsystem);

(b) yields predictions for low-energy ηd and η³He observables — including the complex η-nucleus scattering lengths, near-threshold elastic and inelastic cross sections, possible quasi-bound or virtual η-mesic states, and the energy dependence of the production amplitudes near threshold — as functions of which hypothesis (i) or (ii) is adopted for S11(1535);

(c) identifies observables in ηd and η³He for which the molecule and compact-quark interpretations give quantitatively or qualitatively distinguishable predictions, thereby providing experimentally accessible tests of the nature of S11(1535).

Construct such a framework and determine whether the resulting differences between the two interpretations are large enough, given current and foreseeable experimental precision, to discriminate between them.

Consider the following two impartial combinatorial games played on positions (n, k) with integers n ≥ k ≥ 1.

MEM: From the position (n, k), a legal move is to any position (n − i, i) with k ≤ i ≤ n − i (equivalently k ≤ i and the resulting first coordinate is at least i).

MNEM: From the position (n, k), a legal move is to any position (n + i, i) for 1 ≤ i < k, together with the MEM moves (so the second coordinate is required to be strictly less than the previous one, and one may increase the first coordinate by i while setting the second coordinate to i for any 1 ≤ i < k).

The last player to move wins. Define the nim-value (Sprague–Grundy value) G(n, k) of a position in the usual recursive way: G(n, k) = mex{ G(n′, k′) : (n′, k′) is a legal successor of (n, k) }, where positions with no legal moves have nim-value 0, and mex denotes the minimum excludant of a set of nonnegative integers (which is ∞ if the set of values reached includes ∞ in such a way that no finite value is missing — equivalently, a position has finite nim-value iff this recursion terminates with a finite value).

Establish or refute each of the following:

(a) Every position (n, k) of MNEM has finite nim-value.

(b) In both MEM and MNEM, whenever k² ≥ n one has G(n, k) = ⌊n / k⌋.

Fix a real (or rational) parameter α ≥ 1. The α-Fibonacci Nim on a single heap is the impartial game in which a position consists of a heap of n tokens together with a bound b ≥ 1 on the next move; a legal move removes any number k of tokens with 1 ≤ k ≤ min(n, αb), after which the bound becomes k (so the opponent then faces the position (n−k, k)). The first move from a heap of n is unrestricted (b = ∞), and the player unable to move loses. For α = 2 a classical theorem (Whinihan/Zeckendorf) determines the P-positions in terms of Fibonacci representations.

The multiheap version is played on k heaps of sizes n₁, …, n_k with a common bound b; a move chooses one heap and removes 1 ≤ m ≤ min(n_i, αb) tokens from it, after which the bound becomes m. For the case α = 2 and k = 2 heaps there is a known characterization of the P-positions.

Problem. For values α ≠ 2 and for numbers of heaps k ≥ 2 (and in particular for α = 2 with k ≥ 3), determine the P-positions, and more generally compute the Sprague–Grundy values, of multiheap α-Fibonacci Nim.

Consider the production reaction A + B → η + X, where η denotes the eta meson and X denotes a nuclear final state, measured near the η-X production threshold. Let q denote the relative η-X momentum in the final state, and let f_η(q) be the η-X elastic scattering amplitude with low-energy expansion

   q cot δ(q) = 1/a + (1/2) r_0 q^2 + O(q^4),

where a is the (in general complex) η-X scattering length and r_0 is the effective range. The Watson–Migdal prescription approximates the production amplitude as M(q) ≈ M_0 · f_η(q), giving a direct proportionality between the energy dependence of the production cross section and that of elastic η-X scattering only when |a| is much larger than |r_0|.

Develop a quantitative and reliable method to extract the η-X scattering parameters (scattering length a, effective range r_0, and analogous complex low-energy parameters) from measured η-production data subject to the following complications simultaneously:

   (i) The final-state η-X interaction must be included beyond the leading scattering-length approximation, accounting for effective-range corrections when |a| and |r_0| are comparable.
   (ii) Inelastic channels (e.g., πN, ππN openings coupled to ηN, or breakup channels for nuclear targets) are open at the relevant energies, so that no closed-form Watson–Migdal-type final-state interaction factor is known.
   (iii) The production operator (the "short-distance" part M_0) may itself depend on q and must be disentangled from the final-state interaction in a controlled, model-independent way.

The problem is to construct such an extraction scheme and to quantify rigorously the theoretical uncertainty it incurs on a and r_0.

Consider the following two self-referential subtraction games played on finite multisets of nonempty heaps of tokens.

SUSEN. A position is a finite multiset of positive integers (the heap sizes). On each turn the player to move chooses one heap and removes from it a positive number of tokens equal to one of the current nonzero heap sizes of the position (the subtraction set is the multiset of current heap sizes itself). A heap that is reduced to 0 is removed. The player who cannot move loses (normal play convention). For example, from (2,3) the legal moves are: subtract 2 from the heap of size 2 (giving (3)), subtract 3 from the heap of size 3 (giving (2)), or subtract 2 from the heap of size 3 (giving (2,1)); subtracting 3 from the heap of size 2 is illegal, and there is no move using "2" applied to itself producing (2,2)-style results other than as listed.

ALBUS. A position is again a finite multiset of positive heap sizes. The legal subtractions from a chosen heap are determined self-referentially by the current multiset of heap sizes according to the ALBUS rule (the variant of self-referential subtraction in which the allowed subtraction from any heap equals one of the other heap sizes, rather than the heap's own size). Normal-play convention applies.

Problem.
(a) Determine the set of P-positions (previous-player-winning positions) of SUSEN for positions with n heaps for every n ≥ 4. (The cases n ≤ 3 are known; in particular a triple (a,b,c) is a P-position of SUSEN under an explicit known characterization.)
(b) Determine the set of P-positions of ALBUS for positions with exactly two heaps.

Consider the following two self-referential subtraction games played on finite multisets of nonempty heaps of tokens.

SUSEN. A position is a finite multiset of positive integers (the heap sizes). On each turn the player to move chooses one heap and removes from it a positive number of tokens equal to one of the current nonzero heap sizes of the position (the subtraction set is the multiset of current heap sizes itself). A heap that is reduced to 0 is removed. The player who cannot move loses (normal play convention). For example, from (2,3) the legal moves are: subtract 2 from the heap of size 2 (giving (3)), subtract 3 from the heap of size 3 (giving (2)), or subtract 2 from the heap of size 3 (giving (2,1)); subtracting 3 from the heap of size 2 is illegal, and there is no move using "2" applied to itself producing (2,2)-style results other than as listed.

ALBUS. A position is again a finite multiset of positive heap sizes. The legal subtractions from a chosen heap are determined self-referentially by the current multiset of heap sizes according to the ALBUS rule (the variant of self-referential subtraction in which the allowed subtraction from any heap equals one of the other heap sizes, rather than the heap's own size). Normal-play convention applies.

Problem.
(a) Determine the set of P-positions (previous-player-winning positions) of SUSEN for positions with n heaps for every n ≥ 4. (The cases n ≤ 3 are known; in particular a triple (a,b,c) is a P-position of SUSEN under an explicit known characterization.)
(b) Determine the set of P-positions of ALBUS for positions with exactly two heaps.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

SUSEN and ALBUS are self-referential subtraction games introduced by Larsson and Nowakowski. Available sources list these problems in the open-problem compendium on combinatorial games; no published resolution of SUSEN for n ≥ 4 heaps or of two-heap ALBUS was found in the search.

Consider an eta meson interacting with a nucleus, characterized at low energies by a complex s-wave scattering length a = Re(a) + i Im(a). The near-threshold structure of the eta-nucleus amplitude may contain a pole; depending on the sign of Re(a), this pole corresponds either to a true bound state (negative Re(a) in the standard convention) or to a virtual (unbound) state. Observables for elastic eta-nucleus scattering at center-of-mass energies above the eta-nucleus threshold are sensitive to |Re(a)| and |Im(a)| but, because they depend only on |a|^2-like combinations near threshold, are insensitive to the sign of Re(a). The sign of Im(a) is fixed by unitarity.

Devise an experimentally realizable program of measurements that uniquely determines the sign of Re(a) for a given eta-nucleus system, thereby classifying the near-threshold pole as a bound state or a virtual state. Specifically:

(a) Identify what observables of the eta-nucleus amplitude must be measured above threshold to fix the magnitudes |Re(a)| and |Im(a)| with high accuracy.

(b) Identify a set of inelastic hadronic channels which couple strongly to the eta-nucleus channel and whose amplitudes, analytically continued below the eta-nucleus threshold, retain measurable sensitivity to the eta-nucleus scattering length, and explain how the energy dependence of these inelastic observables across the eta threshold (cusp/threshold behavior) can be used to extract the sign of Re(a).

(c) Provide an analytic framework (e.g., a coupled-channel or Flatté-type parametrization) showing rigorously that the combined above-threshold and below-threshold data determine the sign of Re(a) uniquely, and quantify the experimental precision required to distinguish a bound state from a virtual state for light nuclear targets (such as 3He and 4He) where existing theoretical predictions disagree on whether a bound state exists.

In the combinatorial game theory of Go, consider the Jiang–Rui position (a specific finely-balanced endgame configuration on the 19×19 Go board involving multiple interacting kos and capturable groups, in which after move 85 Black has just taken the ko at the intersection L6).

(a) Determine the exact temperature, in the sense of Combinatorial Game Theory (the critical cooling value at which the canonical form of the position becomes infinitesimal), of the local game at the intersection N4 in this position immediately after Black's ko capture at L6.

(b) Develop a single unified framework that subsumes (or, alternatively, exhibit precise mathematical differences between) the following two theories used to evaluate Go positions:
 (i) Atomic weight theory, the all-small / *-based valuation theory assigning to each position an "atomic weight" (an integer-valued infinitesimal-order invariant) measuring its strength in sums of all-small games; and
 (ii) Nakamura's theory of liberties, which assigns numerical liberty counts to groups of stones in capturing races (semeai) and predicts the winner of a race based on differences of these counts.

(c) Extend Nakamura's liberty theory so that it correctly handles the additional complications that arise when one or more simple kos — either internal kos (kos located inside the eye-space of one of the racing groups) or external kos (kos located outside but affecting the race) — are present in a capturing race, producing quantitative liberty-count formulas whose predictions agree with the exact combinatorial-game-theoretic value of the race.

representations.normalized: Consider the low-energy elastic scattering of an η-meson on a ³He nucleus, characterized by a complex scattering length a(η³He) = Re a + i Im a. Near threshold the η-nucleon system couples strongly to the πN channel, and on naive grounds one would expect that this strong coupling, propagated through πNN intermediate states inside the nucleus, would force Im a(η³He) to be of order at least 1 fm. Empirical analyses of near-threshold η³He production data, however, are compatible with Im a(η³He) ≈ 0.\n\nAssess the following proposed resolution: the antisymmetrization of the two-nucleon final state in the dominant inelastic intermediate channel ηNN → πNN forces the πNN system into quantum numbers that are largely forbidden by the Pauli principle near threshold, so that this otherwise prominent inelastic channel is strongly suppressed in η-deuteron and (to a lesser extent) η-³He systems. Show, within a coupled-channel few-body framework for the η-³He system, that Pauli blocking of the πNN intermediate state suppresses Im a(η³He) sufficiently to render it consistent with zero, and quantify the residual contribution from channels not affected by this blocking.

Woodpush is a two-player combinatorial game played on a finite one-dimensional strip of squares. Each square is either empty or occupied by a Left (black) or Right (white) piece. On a turn, a player either retreats one of their own pieces by one square toward their own end of the board, or pushes one of their own pieces one square toward the opponent's end; in a push, any contiguous string of pieces immediately in front of the moving piece is shoved along with it, and any pieces pushed off the board are removed from play. A player who cannot move loses. The superko rule forbids any move that would recreate a previously seen global position; if all legal moves of the player to move would violate superko, the position is declared a draw.

Top-down thermography (the standard thermographic construction adapted to loopy games with ko-like repetition constraints) has been used to compute the values and temperatures of all three-piece Woodpush positions.

Problem: Extend the thermographic analysis of Woodpush from three-piece positions to positions containing four or more pieces. In particular:

(a) Develop a systematic top-down thermographic procedure that computes the value (or thermograph) of an arbitrary multi-piece Woodpush position under the superko rule.

(b) Characterize, for each n ≥ 4, which n-piece Woodpush positions are draws by superko (i.e., become drawn because every legal continuation would repeat a global position), and give a structural description of such drawn positions.

Consider the strong interaction between an η meson and a light nucleus. For a near-threshold production reaction X → Y η on a target with final-state nucleus Y, one can extract an η–Y "final-state-interaction (FSI) amplitude" from the measured total cross section by dividing out the appropriate phase-space and primary-production factors, thereby isolating the energy dependence due to η–Y rescattering. Empirically, when this FSI amplitude is plotted as a function of the η center-of-mass momentum (or excess energy Q) for the η–d system (extracted, e.g., from pn → dη) and for the η–³He system (extracted, e.g., from dp → ³He η), the two curves exhibit a strikingly similar energy dependence near threshold, including a rapid rise consistent with a large η-nucleus scattering length.

Regarding ³He as a three-nucleon bound state with a significant deuteron-like (np) substructure plus a spectator proton, formulate and decide the following question:

Is the energy dependence of the η–³He interaction near threshold predominantly governed by the interaction of the η meson with the deuteron (np) substructure inside ³He? More precisely, does there exist a quantitative model in which the η–³He near-threshold scattering amplitude factorizes (up to a slowly varying spectator factor) through an η–d subamplitude in such a way that the observed coincidence of energy dependences of the η–d and η–³He FSI amplitudes is reproduced, and is this mechanism in fact the dominant one?

In combinatorial game theory, a position in a two-player game (with the normal play convention) has a Nim-value (Nimber) *k if it is equivalent, under disjunctive sum, to the single-pile Nim position of size k. Consider chess restricted to pawn endings on an m×n board (no other pieces, with the usual chess pawn moves and captures, treated as a combinatorial game).

(a) Prove that for every nonnegative integer k there exists a pawn ending (on some sufficiently large rectangular board) whose game-theoretic value is *k.

(b) Develop the theory of "Impartial Chess", the variant in which both players may move pieces of either color (so the game is impartial). Determine its game-theoretic values and analyze winning strategies.

(c) For Infinite Chess (chess played on the infinite board Z×Z with the standard pieces) and for 3-dimensional Chess (an analogue of chess played on a three-dimensional board), determine larger transfinite ordinal game values (in the sense of Conway's surreal/ordinal game theory for loopy or long games) than are currently known to be realizable.

Entrepreneurial Chess (ECHESS) is the following two-player combinatorial game played on the quarter-infinite board {(x,y) : x,y ≥ 0} with integer coordinates. A position consists of a White king and a White rook, together with a Black king. The players (White and Black) move alternately, with the usual chess move rules for kings and rooks adapted to the quarter-infinite board (no captures put one's own king in check; kings may not occupy adjacent squares; the rook moves any number of squares orthogonally). In addition, on Black's turn, instead of making an ordinary chess move Black may "cash out": this terminates the play, removes the board, and the value of the resulting terminal position is the integer x + y, where (x,y) are the coordinates of Black's king at the time of cashing out. Sums of ECHESS positions (played on independent boards) form combinatorial games in the sense of Conway's surreal-number / temperature theory, and one may assign to ECHESS the temperature-theoretic quantity known as its boiling point (the supremum of the temperatures arising in the thermographs of ECHESS positions).

(a) Provide an improved analysis of the king-and-rook versus king subgame of Entrepreneurial Chess on the quarter-infinite board.

(b) Determine whether the boiling point of Entrepreneurial Chess equals 55/8, confirming or refuting this conjectured value.

Let $G_E^p(q^2), G_M^p(q^2), G_E^n(q^2), G_M^n(q^2)$ denote the Sachs electric and magnetic form factors of the proton and neutron, viewed as functions of the squared four-momentum transfer $q^2$ carried by a virtual photon coupling to the nucleon. In the space-like region $q^2 = -Q^2 < 0$, accessible through elastic electron–nucleon scattering, these form factors are real-valued functions of $Q^2$. In the time-like region $q^2 > 0$, accessible through annihilation processes such as $e^+ e^- \leftrightarrow N\bar{N}$ above threshold $q^2 \geq 4 M_N^2$, the form factors become complex-valued analytic functions, related to the space-like values by analytic continuation and constrained by causality, analyticity, and unitarity (with imaginary parts arising from on-shell intermediate hadronic states).

Construct, or determine whether there exists, a single theoretical model (parametrization) of the four nucleon Sachs form factors $G_{E,M}^{p,n}(q^2)$ that simultaneously reproduces, within experimental uncertainties, the full body of measured data in both the space-like region (proton and neutron, electric and magnetic) and the time-like region (modulus and, where available, phase or ratio $|G_E/G_M|$ of proton and neutron form factors), respecting the standard analyticity and asymptotic constraints (including perturbative QCD scaling at large $|q^2|$ and the correct normalizations $G_E^p(0)=1$, $G_M^p(0)=\mu_p$, $G_E^n(0)=0$, $G_M^n(0)=\mu_n$).

representations.normalized:
Consider the following impartial combinatorial game played on an $n \times n$ chessboard, called Nonattacking Queens. A position consists of a finite set of queens placed on distinct squares of the board such that no two queens attack each other (i.e., no two share a row, column, or diagonal). Players alternate moves; on each turn the current player must place a new queen on an empty square so that, together with all queens already on the board, the resulting configuration is still nonattacking. A player who cannot move loses (normal play convention).

For such an impartial game, the Sprague–Grundy (nim) value of a position $P$ is defined recursively by
$$\mathcal{G}(P) = \operatorname{mex}\{\mathcal{G}(P') : P' \text{ is a position reachable from } P \text{ in one move}\},$$
where $\operatorname{mex}(S)$ denotes the least nonnegative integer not in $S$. Let $g(n)$ denote the nim-value of the empty $n \times n$ board.

The values $g(n)$ are known for $1 \le n \le 10$. Determine $g(n)$ for $n \ge 11$, or more generally describe the nim-values of the Nonattacking Queens game on boards of size larger than $10$.

Background and setup. For elastic electron–nucleon scattering, the nucleon electromagnetic structure is encoded in two form factors per nucleon: the Sachs electric form factor G_E(Q^2) and the Sachs magnetic form factor G_M(Q^2), where Q^2 is the negative of the squared four-momentum transfer. Historically, Rosenbluth-separation measurements on the proton suggested the dipole-scaling behavior

  G_E^p(Q^2) ≈ G_M^p(Q^2)/μ_p ≈ G_D(Q^2),   G_D(Q^2) = (1 + Q^2[GeV^2]/0.71)^{-2},

with μ_p the proton magnetic moment. Polarization-transfer measurements of elastic e–p scattering instead yield a ratio μ_p G_E^p(Q^2)/G_M^p(Q^2) that decreases significantly (approximately linearly) with increasing Q^2 over the few-GeV^2 range, in clear disagreement with the dipole-scaling assumption.

Light nuclei such as the deuteron (^2H) and helium-3 (^3He) are commonly described theoretically by combining a nuclear wave function (from a nucleon–nucleon interaction model, possibly supplemented by two- and three-body currents and relativistic corrections) with the single-nucleon electromagnetic form factors G_E^{p,n}(Q^2), G_M^{p,n}(Q^2) entering through the one-body electromagnetic current operator. Elastic electron scattering observables of these nuclei (e.g. the deuteron form factors A(Q^2), B(Q^2), and tensor polarization T_{20}(Q^2); the ^3He charge and magnetic form factors F_C(Q^2), F_M(Q^2)) thus depend explicitly on the nucleon form factors used as input.

Problem. Determine, quantitatively and qualitatively, the consequences for theoretical predictions of elastic electromagnetic observables of light nuclei — in particular the deuteron and ^3He — when the proton form factors used as nucleon-level inputs are taken consistent with the polarization-transfer behavior (μ_p G_E^p/G_M^p decreasing with Q^2) rather than with the older dipole-scaling assumption G_E^p ≈ G_M^p/μ_p ≈ G_D. Specifically:

(a) Identify and compute the modifications induced in the predicted deuteron observables A(Q^2), B(Q^2), and T_{20}(Q^2), and in the ^3He elastic charge and magnetic form factors F_C(Q^2) and F_M(Q^2), over the momentum-transfer range where the polarization data deviate appreciably from dipole scaling.

(b) Assess how such input changes affect the extraction of the neutron electromagnetic form factors G_E^n(Q^2) and G_M^n(Q^2) from quasi-elastic or elastic electron scattering on deuteron and ^3He targets, where nuclear corrections are required because no free-neutron target exists.

(c) Determine to what extent the resulting discrepancies (if any) between theory and data on light nuclei can be absorbed into meson-exchange currents, relativistic corrections, or modifications of nucleon structure in the nuclear medium, versus indicating genuine new physics in the nuclear electromagnetic current.

The Game of the Amazons is a two-player, perfect-information, no-chance combinatorial game played on a rectangular board. In the n×n version, each player controls a set of amazons (queens) of one color. Players alternate moves, starting with White. A move consists of two parts: (i) move one of your own amazons in a straight line (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally) any number of empty squares, in the manner of a chess queen, not passing through or landing on any amazon or burned square; (ii) from its new square, the amazon "shoots an arrow" in the same queen-like fashion to an empty square along an unobstructed line; the chosen target square is then permanently burned (becoming an obstacle that cannot be entered or passed through by amazons or arrows). The player who cannot make a legal move on their turn loses.

For the 6×6 board, the standard starting position places White amazons at b6, c1, d6, e1 and Black amazons at b1, c6, d1, e6 (i.e., on the 6×6 board, the amazons are placed symmetrically as in the canonical setup, with White to move first), and no squares are initially burned.

Determine, with proof, the game-theoretic outcome (first-player win or second-player win) of the 6×6 Game of the Amazons under optimal play from this initial position.

Let F(q^2) denote a hadron (in particular nucleon) electromagnetic form factor, regarded as an analytic function of the four-momentum transfer squared q^2 in the complex plane, with the space-like region corresponding to q^2 < 0 and the time-like region to q^2 > 0. The Phragmén–Lindelöf theorem, applied to such an analytic function, asserts that, provided F is bounded along suitable rays, its limiting values in the space-like and time-like asymptotic directions coincide:

   lim_{q^2 → -∞} F_{SL}(q^2) = lim_{q^2 → +∞} F_{TL}(q^2).

Perturbative QCD also predicts a definite asymptotic scaling behavior (for example, a Dirac form factor falling as 1/Q^4 up to logarithms, with the Pauli form factor suppressed by an additional 1/Q^2).

Problem. Determine the momentum-transfer scale Q^2 = |q^2| at which the electromagnetic form factors of hadrons, and of the nucleon in particular, actually enter their asymptotic regime, i.e. the scale above which both
  (a) the QCD-inspired asymptotic scaling predictions, and
  (b) the Phragmén–Lindelöf equality of the space-like and time-like limits
become quantitatively valid for the measured space-like and time-like form factors.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent literature (dispersion-theoretical analyses, vector-meson-dominance fits, and time-like measurements such as those probing oscillating features of the nucleon form factors) continues to investigate the onset of asymptotic behavior and the Phragmén–Lindelöf equality between space-like and time-like limits. Phutball (Philosopher's Football) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a grid with one distinguished black stone (the "ball") and white stones (the "men"). On each turn a player either (a) places a white man on an empty grid point, or (b) executes a sequence of "jumps": the ball leaps over a contiguous nonempty line of white men (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally) to the empty point immediately beyond them, and those jumped-over men are removed; multiple jumps may be chained in a single move. The two players try to bring the ball to (or past) opposite goal lines.

A position in a loopy combinatorial game is called a stopper if it has no infinite alternating play. A wild cycle is a cycle of positions in the move graph that does not correspond to mere repetition agreed upon by both players. A P-position is one from which the Previous player (the one who just moved) has a winning strategy under optimal play.

The following variants are considered:
(i) "PHLAG Phutball": Phutball played on an n×n board where the ball is restricted to lie on points with both coordinates even (eliminating tackling).
(ii) "Directional Phutball": Phutball in which each player is allowed to jump the ball only in a fixed prescribed direction.

Resolve the following:
(1) Do there exist natural positions in Phutball-like games which are stoppers but which contain a wild cycle?
(2) In standard Phutball, do noncollusive drawn positions or P-positions exist?
(3) Provide an analysis of PHLAG Phutball boards.
(4) Give a complete analysis of Directional Phutball on the 2×n board.

In elastic electron–proton scattering $e^- p \to e^- p$, the proton's electromagnetic structure is characterized by the Sachs electric and magnetic form factors $G_E^p(Q^2)$ and $G_M^p(Q^2)$, where $Q^2$ is the squared four-momentum transfer. Under the standard assumption that the reaction proceeds dominantly by one-photon exchange, two experimental methods to extract these form factors are:

(i) the Rosenbluth (longitudinal–transverse) separation, in which the reduced unpolarized differential cross section is written as
$$\sigma_R(Q^2,\varepsilon) \;=\; \tau\, G_M^p(Q^2)^2 \;+\; \varepsilon\, G_E^p(Q^2)^2,$$
with $\tau = Q^2/(4 M_p^2)$ and $\varepsilon$ the virtual-photon longitudinal polarization parameter, and the two form factors are extracted from the linear dependence on $\varepsilon$ at fixed $Q^2$;

(ii) the polarization-transfer method, in which a longitudinally polarized electron beam scatters from an unpolarized proton target and the ratio of the transferred recoil-proton transverse and longitudinal polarization components determines the ratio
$$\frac{G_E^p(Q^2)}{G_M^p(Q^2)} \;\propto\; -\frac{P_t}{P_l}\,\sqrt{\frac{\tau(1+\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}}.$$

At momentum transfers $Q^2$ of a few GeV$^2$ and above, these two methods yield significantly different results for $G_E^p/G_M^p$.

Beyond one-photon exchange, the next correction is the two-photon exchange (TPE) amplitude, suppressed nominally by one power of the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ but with potentially enhanced kinematic dependence.

Question: Is the inclusion of two-photon exchange contributions in elastic electron–proton scattering quantitatively responsible for the observed discrepancy between $G_E^p/G_M^p$ extracted by the Rosenbluth method and that extracted by the polarization-transfer method?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Theoretical calculations and phenomenological analyses have established that hadronic two-photon exchange corrections, kinematically enhanced in the Rosenbluth method but suppressed in the polarization-transfer method, can largely account for the discrepancy in $G_E^p/G_M^p$ extractions. Three dedicated experiments comparing $e^+p$ and $e^-p$ elastic scattering (VEPP-3, CLAS, OLYMPUS), as well as recent positron-beam Super-Rosenbluth measurements, have confirmed the existence of a small TPE effect of the expected order. However, the precision and kinematic reach remain insufficient to definitively confirm the theoretical treatments or to show that TPE quantitatively closes the discrepancy at all $Q^2$. The question is therefore partially resolved.

Hex is a two-player game played on a rhombic board of n×n hexagonal cells. The two players, called First and Second, alternately place stones of their own color on empty cells, with First moving first. Each player is assigned two opposite sides of the rhombus; First's goal is to form a connected chain of his stones joining his two assigned sides, and Second's goal is to do the same for his sides. It is known that with optimal play First has a winning strategy.

Answer the following two questions for every positive integer n:

(1) Determine the smallest integer s(n) such that First has a strategy guaranteeing a win in which, at the end of the game, his winning chain (a path of First's stones connecting his two sides) consists of exactly s(n) stones — i.e. find the minimum possible length of a guaranteed winning chain.

(2) Determine the smallest integer m(n) such that First has a strategy guaranteeing that the game ends (with First having won) within m(n) total moves by First.

Give exact values, or sharp upper and lower bounds, for s(n) and m(n) as functions of n.

The catalogue of observables sensitive to two-photon exchange is well established theoretically: nonlinearity of the Rosenbluth plot, the e^+ p / e^- p cross-section ratio (charge-odd), normal single-spin asymmetries (T-odd), deviations of the polarization-transfer ratio P_T/P_L from the Born value, and forward–backward asymmetries in time-like e^+e^- ↔ p\bar p. Dedicated experiments (VEPP-3 Novosibirsk, CLAS at JLab, OLYMPUS at DESY, and BESIII in the time-like region) have measured several of these and confirm the qualitative picture, with BESIII recently reporting a significant angular asymmetry attributed to 2γ exchange. However, the quantitative resolution of the Rosenbluth-vs-polarization form-factor discrepancy and a complete extraction of 2γ amplitudes remain active research, so the broader physics program is only partially solved.

Fox and Geese is a two-player combinatorial game played on an n×n (or n×m) square board with one Fox and four (or more) Geese placed on dark squares. The Geese move one square diagonally forward (toward the Fox's home side); the Fox moves one square diagonally in any direction. The Geese win if they trap the Fox so that it cannot move; the Fox wins if it reaches the Geese's home row (or otherwise escapes past the Geese). Define a position's span to be the difference between the maximum and minimum rank (row index measured in the Geese's direction of advance) of the Geese.

Formalize and resolve each of the following assertions:

(a) (Large-board escape.) Determine, for sufficiently large n, the precise set of starting positions on the n×n board from which the Fox can guarantee escape against k Geese, and prove the resulting characterization.

(b) (Critical rank.) Determine the critical rank r(n,k) such that, with k Geese all at rank ≥ r on an n×n board, the Geese win against any Fox starting position of lower rank, and prove the value of r(n,k).

(c) (Retreat rule, Welton.) Suppose the Fox's backward moves are extended so that the Fox may slide backward like a bishop along a diagonal by any number of squares from a prescribed set S ⊂ ℤ_{>0}. Compare the cases S = {1,2} and S = {1,3} (the latter preserving parity): decide which of the two gives the Fox a greater winning advantage, and more generally determine the outcome class as a function of S.

(d) (Board widths and goose counts.) Determine the outcome (Fox-win, Geese-win, or draw, with optimal play) for the standard initial position on an n×m board with g Geese, as a function of (n,m,g). In particular, prove the following explicit conjectures:
  (i) For every sufficiently large n, the standard n×4 position is [Fox-win / Geese-win — give the precise outcome].
  (ii) For every sufficiently large n, the standard n×6 position is [the precise outcome].
  (iii) Under the Ceylonese rule (in which a Goose may also move sideways), determine the outcome for all sufficiently large n.

Provide complete proofs of each assertion (or determination), thereby giving a uniform solution to the Fox-and-Geese problems above.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question remains experimentally open. Polarization-transfer measurements at Jefferson Lab (GEp-II and GEp-III) extended the ratio $\mu_p G_{E_p}/G_{M_p}$ up to $Q^2 \approx 8.5\ \text{GeV}^2$ and observed continued decrease but no zero crossing within the measured range; some data suggest possible flattening. New Hall C measurements (SBS GEp-V) aim to extend coverage further (up to roughly $Q^2 \approx 12\ \text{GeV}^2$) to determine whether $G_{E_p}$ actually crosses zero. As of recent reports, no zero has been definitively observed and the matter is not settled.

Hare and Hounds is a combinatorial game played on a rectangular board of width 3 and length L. Three hounds start in one short edge of the board and the hare starts in the opposite short edge. The hounds move one at a time, each step being a diagonal or straight forward or sideways move (never backward), while the hare moves one step in any of the available directions (forward, sideways, or backward). The hounds win if they trap the hare so it cannot move; the hare wins if it escapes past the line of hounds. Standard combinatorial game theory associates to every position a game value (with concepts of temperature, "heat", and atomic weight in the sense of Conway's theory of partizan games).

Consider, for each n ≥ 1, the natural family of Hare and Hounds positions on a (6n+5) × 3 board obtained by taking the standard starting configuration (three hounds on the bottom row, hare on the top row).

(a) Determine whether the sequence of these positions (indexed by n, or by the natural increasing-length families of positions that arise from them) becomes increasingly hot as n → ∞, i.e. whether the temperature of the position is unbounded.

(b) Determine whether the same family has arbitrarily large negative atomic weight as n → ∞.

(c) Prove or disprove the conjecture that gives an explicit closed-form combinatorial game value for the starting position on the (6n+5) × 3 board for every n ≥ 1.

Consider the electromagnetic form factors of the nucleon (proton and neutron), defined through the matrix element of the electromagnetic current between nucleon states and parametrized by the Sachs electric and magnetic form factors G_E(q^2) and G_M(q^2). In the space-like region (q^2 < 0) these are real functions of q^2, while in the time-like region (q^2 > 0, accessible through reactions such as e^+ e^- → N \bar N or \bar p p → e^+ e^-) they are complex analytic functions and acquire a relative phase.

(a) Devise an experimental and theoretical procedure based on time-like measurements in e^+ e^- annihilation and/or proton–antiproton reactions that separately determines |G_E^p|, |G_M^p|, |G_E^n|, |G_M^n| as functions of q^2, rather than only effective combinations.

(b) Show that the single-spin polarization observable A_y (the analyzing power normal to the scattering plane) and the double-spin observable A_xz are proportional, respectively, to Im(G_E G_M^*) and Re(G_E G_M^*) in the time-like region, and use these observables to determine the relative phase between G_E(q^2) and G_M(q^2) as a complex function of q^2 above threshold.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent measurements at BaBar, BESIII, and CMD-3 have achieved separation of |G_E| and |G_M| for the proton in the time-like region via the proton helicity angular distribution, and the ratio |G_E/G_M| has been extracted at several q^2 values. Relative phase measurements between G_E and G_M for baryons in the time-like region have also been reported recently. However, individual separation of the neutron G_E and G_M and a full mapping of the relative phase remain incomplete, so the program is partially solved.

representations.normalized:
Domineering is a two-player combinatorial game played on a subset of the square lattice (typically an $m \times n$ rectangular board). Players alternate moves: Left places a $1\times 2$ vertical domino covering two adjacent unoccupied cells, while Right places a $2\times 1$ horizontal domino covering two adjacent unoccupied cells. A player who cannot move loses. Each Domineering position has a value in the universe of combinatorial games (in the sense of Conway), with associated invariants such as canonical form, temperature, and infinitesimal part.

Address the following open questions about Domineering:

1. (Rectangular boards) Determine the exact game-theoretic value of the $2 \times n$ board for even $n$ (currently known only up to an "ish" infinitesimal), and resolve the remaining open game values of $3 \times n$ and $4 \times n$ rectangular boards.

2. (Hot positions) Characterize all hot Domineering positions up to infinitesimal shift; i.e., describe completely the set of positions whose canonical form has positive temperature, modulo infinitesimal differences.

3. (Temperatures) Exhibit a Domineering position whose temperature does not appear in the currently known list of Domineering temperatures, or prove that no new temperatures occur.

4. (Tromineering) Tromineering is the variant of Domineering played with $1\times 3$ vertical (Left) and $3\times 1$ horizontal (Right) trominoes. Extend the partial analysis of Tromineering on $m \times n$ rectangular boards: determine winners and game values for further families of boards.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial progress has been made via endgame databases (Uiterwijk–Barton, 2015) covering single-component positions up to 15 squares, along with new structural theorems (Bridge Destroying Theorem) and results on infinitesimals and dyadic rational values. Variants such as Triomineering and Tridomineering have partial winner classifications for small m. However, the exact value of the $2\times n$ board for even $n$, complete characterization of hot positions modulo infinitesimals, the question of new temperatures, and a full Tromineering analysis remain open.

representations.normalized:
Consider elastic electron–proton scattering, $e^- p \to e^- p$, parametrized by the squared four-momentum transfer $Q^2 = -q^2 > 0$. In the one-photon-exchange (Born) approximation, the unpolarized cross section is the Rosenbluth formula
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\right)_{\text{Mott}}\frac{1}{\varepsilon(1+\tau)}\Big[\tau\, G_M^2(Q^2) + \varepsilon\, G_E^2(Q^2)\Big],$$
where $\tau = Q^2/(4M_p^2)$, $\varepsilon$ is the virtual-photon longitudinal polarization, and $G_E, G_M$ are the proton electric and magnetic Sachs form factors. The ratio $G_E/G_M$ can be measured (i) via a Rosenbluth (longitudinal–transverse) separation of the reduced cross section, or (ii) via polarization-transfer experiments that measure the ratio of recoil-proton transverse to longitudinal polarizations.

At large $Q^2$ the electric contribution to the unpolarized cross section is kinematically suppressed relative to the magnetic one, and the experimentally applied radiative corrections (real and virtual photon emission, vacuum polarization, soft and hard two-photon exchange, lepton–proton bremsstrahlung interference, etc.) reach magnitudes of order $30$–$40\%$. In standard practice, radiative corrections are not applied to the polarization-transfer extraction under the assumption that they cancel in the polarization ratio, even though no complete calculation of all such contributions and their mutual interferences has been performed.

Problem. Develop a complete and quantitatively controlled calculation of the radiative corrections to elastic $ep$ scattering — including all contributions and their interference terms, and tracking separately their effects on the electric and magnetic pieces of the reduced cross section as well as on the polarization observables — such that:
(a) the Rosenbluth extraction of $G_E/G_M$ and the polarization-transfer extraction of $G_E/G_M$ become consistent at large $Q^2$;
(b) the non-cancellation of radiative effects in the polarization ratio is quantified;
(c) the residual theoretical uncertainty is small compared to the experimental precision of current and planned measurements.
Either construct such a calculation, or prove obstructions to its existence within QED plus a controlled hadronic model.

The discrepancy between Rosenbluth and polarization-transfer extractions of the proton form factor ratio at large Q^2 is widely attributed to two-photon-exchange and related higher-order radiative corrections, but as of 2024 a complete calculation including all interference terms is not available. Recent dedicated experiments (OLYMPUS at DESY, CLAS12, VEPP-3) confirm a small TPE effect at moderate Q^2 but do not validate theoretical treatments at large Q^2, and the proposed TPEX experiment aims to extend the kinematic range. Theory and experiment in this area remain active, and the question is regarded as open.

NoGo is a partizan combinatorial game played on a (subset of a) grid graph by two players, Left (Black) and Right (White), who alternately place a stone of their own color on an empty vertex. A move is legal only if, after the placement, every maximal monochromatic connected group of stones still has at least one adjacent empty vertex (a "liberty"). A player who cannot make a legal move loses (normal play convention).

For a partizan game G, its (combinatorial-game-theoretic) value lies in the universe of surreal-number / switch / loopfree game values. Given a class C of positions, define the nim-dimension of C to be the supremum, over all positions P in C, of the Grundy-like complexity measure obtained as follows: the smallest integer d such that every position in C has a canonical value expressible using nimbers (stars) of dimension at most d (equivalently, the largest n for which a position whose value involves *n arises in C); if no such finite bound exists the nim-dimension is infinite.

Questions:
(a) Determine the nim-dimension of NoGo played on one-dimensional boards (i.e. on path graphs P_n, for all n ≥ 1).
(b) Determine the nim-dimension of NoGo played on two-dimensional rectangular boards (i.e. on grid graphs P_m □ P_n, for all m, n ≥ 1).
(c) Decide whether there exists a finite bound B such that for every position arising on a two-dimensional rectangular NoGo board, the canonical game value, when written as a dyadic rational (or sum involving dyadic rationals and infinitesimals), uses only fractions whose denominators are at most B.

Let $G_E^N(q^2)$ and $G_M^N(q^2)$ denote the Sachs electric and magnetic electromagnetic form factors of a nucleon $N$ (proton or neutron), considered as analytic functions of the squared four-momentum transfer $q^2$. For space-like momentum transfer ($q^2 < 0$), these form factors are measured in elastic electron–nucleon scattering. For time-like momentum transfer ($q^2 \ge 4 m_N^2$, where $m_N$ is the nucleon mass), they are accessed through reactions such as $e^+ e^- \leftrightarrow N \bar N$. Empirical data indicate that, when compared at $|q^2|$ values of comparable magnitude, the moduli $|G^N(q^2)|$ in the time-like region are systematically larger than the corresponding values in the space-like region.

Determine whether this systematic enhancement of the time-like nucleon electromagnetic form factors relative to their space-like counterparts can be explained by the existence of a narrow resonance in the nucleon–antinucleon ($N\bar N$) system located just below the $N\bar N$ production threshold $q^2 = 4 m_N^2$. Specifically: does such a narrow subthreshold $N\bar N$ resonance exist, and if so, does it quantitatively account for the observed space-like/time-like asymmetry of $G_E^N$ and $G_M^N$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent literature (through 2024–2025) on nucleon electromagnetic form factors continues to discuss the enhancement of time-like form factors over space-like ones and proposes a possible narrow $N\bar N$ subthreshold resonance as one explanation, alongside competing accounts based on final-state $N\bar N$ interactions (e.g., chiral EFT distorted-wave Born approximation) and extended vector-meson-dominance models with oscillatory structures. No definitive experimental confirmation of such a narrow subthreshold resonance has been established, and dispersion-theoretical analyses still list this as an open question requiring dedicated threshold-region measurements.

Dots-and-Boxes is the well-known impartial-style game played on an m×n array of dots: two players alternately draw a horizontal or vertical unit edge between adjacent dots; if a move completes the fourth side of a unit square ("box"), the moving player captures that box and must move again. In the normal scoring version, the player capturing more boxes wins. Several national variants modify the rules:

• Swedish Dots-and-Boxes: the player capturing a box is not required to move again (capturing does not grant a bonus turn); play continues with the alternation rule.
• Faroese Dots-and-Boxes: a variant in which moves that close boxes are governed by Faroese-specific rules described in the combinatorial-games literature ("staples" version).
• Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes: a further variant of the rules of Swedish/Faroese type.
• Misère convention: the player capturing fewer boxes (or under suitable misère convention, the player making the last move) wins.

Consider the 1×n narrow-board case of each variant (so the dots lie on a 2×(n+1) grid).

Establish the following:

(a) (Faroese 1×n conjecture.) Prove that in 1×n Faroese Dots-and-Boxes, a winning first move (when one exists) is a vertical edge that splits the strip into two shorter strips, with the split position determined by the conjectured rule.

(b) (Icelandic 1×n parity conjecture.) Prove that in 1×n Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes with n odd, the first player loses by exactly one box under optimal play.

(c) (Misère Swedish periodicity.) Prove that the outcome sequence of misère 1×n Swedish Dots-and-Boxes is eventually periodic in n.

(d) (Impartial Icelandic theory.) Develop a complete theory (Sprague–Grundy values and a closed-form solution) for the impartial version of 1×n Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes.
representations.original:
Dots-and-Boxes is the well-known impartial-style game played on an m×n array of dots: two players alternately draw a horizontal or vertical unit edge between adjacent dots; if a move completes the fourth side of a unit square ("box"), the moving player captures that box and must move again. In the normal scoring version, the player capturing more boxes wins. Several national variants modify the rules:

• Swedish Dots-and-Boxes: the player capturing a box is not required to move again (capturing does not grant a bonus turn); play continues with the alternation rule.
• Faroese Dots-and-Boxes: a variant in which moves that close boxes are governed by Faroese-specific rules described in the combinatorial-games literature ("staples" version).
• Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes: a further variant of the rules of Swedish/Faroese type.
• Misère convention: the player capturing fewer boxes (or under suitable misère convention, the player making the last move) wins.

Consider the 1×n narrow-board case of each variant (so the dots lie on a 2×(n+1) grid).

Establish the following:

(a) (Faroese 1×n conjecture.) Prove that in 1×n Faroese Dots-and-Boxes, a winning first move (when one exists) is a vertical edge that splits the strip into two shorter strips, with the split position determined by the conjectured rule.

(b) (Icelandic 1×n parity conjecture.) Prove that in 1×n Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes with n odd, the first player loses by exactly one box under optimal play.

(c) (Misère Swedish periodicity.) Prove that the outcome sequence of misère 1×n Swedish Dots-and-Boxes is eventually periodic in n.

(d) (Impartial Icelandic theory.) Develop a complete theory (Sprague–Grundy values and a closed-form solution) for the impartial version of 1×n Icelandic Dots-and-Boxes.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

These narrow-board Dots-and-Boxes conjectures (Faroese, Icelandic, misère Swedish periodicity, and a complete impartial Icelandic theory) appear in the unsolved-problems compilation in Games of No Chance 5 (2017) and are stated there as open conjectures, verified only for small n. No subsequent resolution was located.

Let $E$ be a (real) Banach space with continuous dual $E^*$, and let $C \subset E$ be a bounded closed convex subset. Let $x_0 \in C$ be an extreme point of $C$ (i.e., $x_0$ cannot be written as $\tfrac12(u+v)$ with $u,v \in C$ and $u \neq v$). Fix $y^* \in E^*$ and $\varepsilon > 0$.

Question: Does there necessarily exist a constant $M \geq 0$ such that, for all $u, v \in C$,
$$ M\,\|u + v - 2x_0\| \;\geq\; \langle v - x_0,\, y^*\rangle - \varepsilon \,?$$

If the answer is not always affirmative, characterize precisely those triples $(C, x_0)$ for which the above implication holds for every $y^* \in E^*$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been resolved. Without loss of generality assume $x_0 = 0$. The required constant $M$ exists for every $y^* \in E^*$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ if and only if $0$ is an extreme point of the weak-$*$ closure of $J(C)$ in $E^{**}$, where $J:E\hookrightarrow E^{**}$ is the canonical embedding. Thus the property need not hold for an arbitrary extreme point of $C$; it holds exactly under this stronger extremality condition.

Sprouts is a two-player combinatorial game played on a sheet of paper, defined as follows. The game starts with a fixed number n ≥ 1 of spots (dots) drawn on the plane. Players alternate moves. A move consists of: (i) drawing a new curve that either connects two distinct existing spots or forms a loop from one spot back to itself, such that the curve does not cross itself, does not cross any previously drawn curve, and does not pass through any other spot; and (ii) placing a new spot somewhere on the interior of the newly drawn curve. Each spot is allowed to have at most three curve-ends incident to it (so a spot already incident to three curve-ends is "dead" and cannot be used again). Under the normal play convention, the player who cannot move loses; under the misère convention, the player who cannot move wins.

For each n ≥ 1 and for each of the two conventions (normal and misère), determine which player has a winning strategy in the n-spot game of Sprouts, and more generally determine the Sprague–Grundy / game-theoretic value of the corresponding starting position. Equivalently, extend the known analysis of normal-play and misère-play Sprouts to as many starting spot counts n as possible, and ideally establish a general theorem describing the outcome (and Grundy value) of n-spot Sprouts as a function of n in each convention.

Let $E$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional Banach space with topological dual $E^*$. Denote by $\mathrm{PC}(E)$ the class of proper convex functions $f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, and for $f\in\mathrm{PC}(E)$ let $f^*:E^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be its Fenchel conjugate, defined by $f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in E}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle - f(x)\}$.

A pair $(f,g)$ with $f,g\in\mathrm{PC}(E)$ is said to satisfy Fenchel duality if there exists $z^*\in E^*$ such that
$$f^*(-z^*)+g^*(z^*)=(f+g)^*(0).$$
The pair $(f,g)$ is called totally Fenchel unstable if it satisfies Fenchel duality and, whenever $y^*,z^*\in E^*$ satisfy
$$f^*(y^*)+g^*(z^*)=(f+g)^*(y^*+z^*),$$
one necessarily has $y^*+z^*=0$.

Question: Does there exist a nonzero finite-dimensional Banach space $E$ and proper convex functions $f,g\in\mathrm{PC}(E)$ such that the pair $(f,g)$ is totally Fenchel unstable?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem has been resolved negatively: in any nonzero finite-dimensional Banach space, no pair of proper convex functions can be totally Fenchel unstable. This was established by Boţ and Löhne in "On totally Fenchel unstable functions in finite dimensional spaces" (Mathematical Programming, 2010).

Sylver Coinage is a two-player game defined as follows. Two players alternate naming positive integers, subject to the rule that no player may name an integer that is a nonnegative-integer linear combination of previously named integers. The player who is forced to name 1 loses. Equivalently, at any point the set S of integers named so far generates a numerical sub-semigroup of the positive integers; a legal move is any positive integer not in the semigroup generated by S together with 1, and a player loses if forced to play 1.

Provide a general analysis of this game. Specifically:
(a) Determine, for as broad a class of opening positions as possible, which positions are P-positions (previous-player wins) and which are N-positions (next-player wins).
(b) In particular, for each prime p ≥ 5, decide whether the move "p" (i.e., the position {p} after the first player names p) is a winning or losing move for the first player, and identify an explicit winning strategy whenever one exists.
(c) More generally, classify the P-positions among finite sets {a_1, ..., a_k} of pairwise coprime positive integers greater than 1.

Give complete proofs of any claimed classifications and strategies.

Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space, and let $S,T:X\to X$ be commuting self-maps (i.e., $S\circ T = T\circ S$). Suppose there exists a constant $c$ with $0\le c<1$ such that for all $x,y\in X$,
$$d(Sx,Ty)\le c\cdot\operatorname{diam}\{x,y,Sx,Ty\},$$
where $\operatorname{diam}A=\sup\{d(u,v):u,v\in A\}$ for $A\subseteq X$.

Determine whether, under these hypotheses, $S$ and $T$ must have a unique common fixed point. More precisely, identify the range of values of $c\in[0,1)$ for which the conclusion holds for every such pair $(S,T)$, and for the remaining values exhibit a counterexample.

Von Neumann's Game is the following two-player combinatorial game played on a finite directed graph G with a distinguished token-bearing vertex. A position consists of a finite directed graph together with a token placed on some vertex. Players alternate moves; a move consists of sliding the token along a directed edge from its current vertex to a successor vertex, after which the originating vertex (and all edges incident to it) is deleted. A player unable to move loses. When the underlying graph is a directed forest (a disjoint union of out-trees), the game has been completely analyzed: there are known closed-form formulas/criteria characterizing the P-positions and N-positions, as well as the game-theoretic values.

Problem: Extend this analysis to the class of finite directed acyclic graphs. Specifically, determine the outcome class (first-player win or second-player win) and, more strongly, the Sprague–Grundy value of an arbitrary position (D, v), where D is a finite directed acyclic graph and v is a vertex of D carrying the token, in terms of structural invariants of D. Provide either a polynomial-time algorithm or an explicit combinatorial formula that generalizes the known directed-forest analysis.

Blue–Red Hackenbush is played on a finite graph with a distinguished set of "ground" vertices, in which every edge is colored either blue (Left) or red (Right). On their turn, Left deletes a blue edge and Right deletes a red edge; after the deletion, all edges no longer connected to the ground are also removed. Under the normal-play convention, the player unable to move loses. Two variants are defined as follows.

(a) Inverting Hackenbush: played exactly as Blue–Red Hackenbush, except that immediately after a player removes an edge (together with the edges that drop off), every remaining edge in the position has its color swapped (blue ↔ red).

(b) Reversing Hackenbush: played exactly as Blue–Red Hackenbush, except that immediately after a player removes an edge (together with the edges that drop off), the moving player may (or, in the strict variant, must) reverse the colors of some specified set of remaining edges (for instance, all edges on a designated path or in a designated component).

Develop a theory of these two games. In particular:

1. Determine the game-theoretic value (in the sense of Conway's surreal-number theory of partizan games) of an arbitrary blue–red stalk (a path with one end on the ground) under each of these rule sets, giving a closed-form description analogous to the Hackenbush sign-expansion (sign-expansion) value for ordinary Blue–Red Hackenbush.

2. Establish, or disprove, a "Colon Principle" or analogous reduction theorem for trees under each variant.

3. Decide whether each variant admits a polynomial-time algorithm for evaluating positions on trees, and locate the complexity of evaluating general (graph) positions.

4. Characterize which surreal numbers arise as values of finite positions in each variant.

Let $\mathbb{R}^{1,1}$ denote the two-dimensional Minkowski space-time, i.e., $\mathbb{R}^2$ equipped with the (indefinite) bilinear form of signature $(1,1)$. For two points $A=(t_A,x_A)$ and $B=(t_B,x_B)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{1,1}$, define their temporal distance by
$$\tau(A,B)=\sqrt{\,(t_A-t_B)^2-(x_A-x_B)^2\,}\qquad\text{when }(t_A-t_B)^2\ge (x_A-x_B)^2,$$
and leave $\tau(A,B)$ undefined (or set to $0$) otherwise; thus $\tau(A,B)=1$ means $A$ and $B$ are time-like separated with unit Minkowski proper-time interval.

Define the temporal chromatic number $\chi_\tau(\mathbb{R}^{1,1})$ to be the smallest cardinality of a set of colors that admits a coloring $c:\mathbb{R}^{1,1}\to C$ such that whenever $\tau(A,B)=1$, one has $c(A)\ne c(B)$.

Determine the value of $\chi_\tau(\mathbb{R}^{1,1})$. In particular, decide whether $\chi_\tau(\mathbb{R}^{1,1})$ is finite.

Beanstalk is the following two-player combinatorial game. A position is a positive integer n. From a position n, the unique legal moves are:
- if n is even, move to n/2;
- if n is odd, move to either 3n+1 or 3n-1.
Players alternate moves, and the player who moves to the position 1 wins.

For each position n, define its remoteness in the usual game-theoretic sense: a position from which the player to move can win is called an N-position, and one from which every move leads to an N-position (or has no moves) is a P-position; the remoteness of an N-position is one more than the minimum remoteness of its winning-move successors, while the remoteness of a P-position is one more than the maximum remoteness of its successors. A position whose remoteness is infinite (i.e., neither player can force the game to terminate at 1) is called an O-position.

Question: Does the game of Beanstalk admit any O-positions? Equivalently, does there exist a positive integer starting position from which, under optimal play, the game never terminates?
