Let a, d, n be positive integers with a ≥ d ≥ 3. The Erdős–Szekeres Sequence Game is played by two players who alternately extend a sequence of distinct real numbers x_1, x_2, …, x_n (with Player I moving first). A player loses (in normal play) as soon as the move they make creates either an increasing subsequence of length a+1 or a decreasing subsequence of length d+1 within the sequence constructed so far; in misère play, the player who is forced to create such a subsequence wins. By the Erdős–Szekeres theorem, the game must end after at most a·d + 1 moves. Let N denote "first-player win" and P denote "second-player win".

(a) Prove or disprove: for all a ≥ d ≥ 3 and all sufficiently large n, the Erdős–Szekeres Sequence Game is an N-position under both normal and misère play.

(b) Prove or disprove the analogous statement when the players are allowed to choose entries from the rational numbers (rather than from a prescribed finite set), under normal play.

(c) Analyze the variant of the game in which the two players alternately name pairs (i, π_i), thereby building a partial permutation π, with the same losing condition based on monotone subsequences. Determine the outcome class (N or P) as a function of a, d, n under both normal and misère conventions.

$$Q(x-y) = (x_0 - y_0)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{d}(x_i - y_i)^2.$$

Determine the chromatic number $\chi(G)$, that is, the smallest cardinal $k$ such that there exists a map $c:\mathbb{R}^{1,d}\to\{1,\dots,k\}$ with $c(x)\neq c(y)$ whenever $Q(x-y)=1$. A thicket is a finite directed graph in which a nonempty subset of the vertices is designated as roots and every arc lies on a directed path leading to some root. In the two-player combinatorial game Thinning Thickets, each arc of the thicket is colored blue, red, or green. Players Left and Right alternate moves; on a move, Left removes a blue or green arc, Right removes a red or green arc, and after removing an arc one also deletes every arc that is no longer on a directed path to a root. The first player unable to move loses (normal play convention). The Grundy value (and partizan game value) of all-green positions and various restricted positions has been determined for so-called "very thin trees" — thickets whose underlying undirected graph is a tree in which every non-root vertex has out-degree 1 and the structure is restricted to be a single path-like "cordon" (tall, thin, singly rooted, with limited attachment vertices).

Problem: Extend this analysis of Thinning Thickets from very thin trees (cordons) to arbitrary finite rooted trees. Specifically, determine the Sprague–Grundy values (in the impartial all-green case) and, more generally, the game values, of Thinning Thickets positions whose underlying directed graph is an arbitrary rooted tree with arcs directed toward the root.

Chomp is the following two-player game. A position is an order ideal (lower set) of a poset P; equivalently, in the rectangular case, it is the set of remaining squares of an m×n grid that has the shape of a Young diagram (anchored at a fixed corner, the "poisoned" cell). On each turn a player chooses a remaining cell x and removes every cell y with y ≥ x (in the product partial order). The player who is forced to take the poisoned corner cell loses. The game extends naturally to higher-dimensional boxes and, replacing finite dimensions by ordinals, to transfinite boxes (with the usual convention that moves create a position which is still a down-set, and play must terminate by well-foundedness of the ordinal product under the standard ordering).

Address each of the following questions for Chomp:

(a) Infinite three-dimensional Chomp. Determine the outcome class and, if possible, an explicit winning strategy for Chomp played on the box ω × ω × ω.

(b) Uniqueness of the winning move in 3×n Chomp. For every integer n ≥ 1, the position 3×n is known to be a first-player win. Give a deterministic (non strategy-stealing) proof that the winning first move from the 3×n rectangle is unique.

(c) Nim-value of ω×4. Compute the Sprague–Grundy value (nim-value) of the transfinite Chomp position ω × 4.

(d) Transfinite stratification conjecture. Prove or disprove the following conjecture: for transfinite Chomp positions, the dominant ordinal term of the Sprague–Grundy value is determined by the dominant ordinal term of the position's "size"; more precisely, for any finite Chomp position A and any ordinal h, the Grundy value G(A + (1^{d−1} × h)) has the same leading ordinal term as h.

Define the temporal distance $\tau(A,B)=\sqrt{D(A,B)}$ when $D(A,B)\ge 0$, and the spatial distance $\rho(A,B)=\sqrt{-D(A,B)}$ when $D(A,B)\le 0$. Define the temporal chromatic number $\chi_\tau(\mathbb{R}^{m,n})$ as the smallest number of colors needed to color all points of $\mathbb{R}^{m,n}$ so that no two points $A,B$ with $\tau(A,B)=1$ receive the same color, and analogously define the spatial chromatic number $\chi_\rho(\mathbb{R}^{m,n})$ with the relation $\rho(A,B)=1$. Let $n \ge k \ge 1$ be integers, and let $P_{n,k}$ denote the poset of all nonempty subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ of size at most $k$, ordered by inclusion. The $(n;k)$ Subset Take-Away game is played on $P_{n,k}$ as follows. Two players alternate turns; on each turn the current player names an element $S \in P_{n,k}$ that has not previously been named and does not contain (as a subset) any previously named element. A player who cannot move loses. Equivalently, naming $S$ removes from the poset every $T$ with $T \supseteq S$, and play continues on the remaining poset until empty.

For each pair $(n,k)$, determine which player has a winning strategy in $(n;k)$ Subset Take-Away. In particular, give a complete characterization of the pairs $(n;k)$ for which the second player wins, taking into account that the simple proposed criteria (such as "the second player wins exactly when $k$ divides $n$", or "the second player always wins when $k=n$") are known to fail (for example, the first player wins $(7;7)$ by playing the top set, while the second player wins $(7;3)$ even though $3 \nmid 7$).

The original broad conjectures of Gale and Neyman about $(n;k)$ Subset Take-Away (Chomp on a hypercube) were disproved by Brouwer and Christensen, who found counterexamples such as the first player winning $(7;7)$ and the second player winning $(7;3)$ despite $3 \nmid 7$. No complete characterization of the winner for general $(n;k)$ appears to be known, and the problem is still listed as unsolved in current surveys of combinatorial games.

Let $D = (V, E)$ be a finite directed graph. In the k-Annihilation game on $D$, a position is a placement of tokens on distinct vertices of $V$. Two players alternate moves; a move consists of selecting one token and sliding it along a directed edge from its current vertex $u$ to a vertex $v$ with $(u,v) \in E$. If the destination $v$ is already occupied by another token (and $u \neq v$), then both tokens involved are removed (annihilated). If a player cannot move, that player loses (normal convention). The parameter $k \geq 1$ specifies that each player must, on a single turn, perform exactly $k$ such moves (consecutively, with one or more tokens). The decision problem k-Annihilation asks, given a digraph $D$ and an initial placement of tokens, whether the player to move has a winning strategy.

For $k = 1$, a polynomial-time algorithm to determine the winner (and to compute a winning strategy) is known. Determine whether, for every fixed integer $k > 1$, there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that decides k-Annihilation.

The six Painlevé equations P_I, P_II, P_III, P_IV, P_V, P_VI are a distinguished list of second-order nonlinear ordinary differential equations of the form w'' = F(z, w, w'), where F is rational in w and w' and locally analytic in z, characterized by the Painlevé property that all movable singularities of their solutions are poles. Their generic solutions, the Painlevé transcendents, define nonlinear special functions. Each Painlevé equation admits an isomonodromic Lax pair: solutions correspond to monodromy-preserving deformations of an associated linear system, and the Cauchy problem can be linearized through a Riemann–Hilbert problem on a contour in the complex plane with prescribed jump matrices determined by Stokes data. Each Painlevé equation also has integrable discrete analogues (the discrete Painlevé equations), which are integrable difference/q-difference equations whose continuum limits recover the Painlevé equations.

Problem: Design a reliable, easy-to-use numerical method (and supporting software) for computing solutions of the Painlevé equations that improves on generic adaptive Runge–Kutta-type ODE integrators by exploiting the integrable structure of these equations. Specifically:

(a) Develop and analyze a numerical scheme based on the isomonodromy formulation that computes a Painlevé transcendent at a point z by numerically solving the associated Riemann–Hilbert problem with prescribed Stokes/monodromy data, providing rigorous error bounds, robust handling of the movable poles, and uniform accuracy across the complex plane (including near critical points and along Stokes rays).

(b) Determine whether using an integrable discretization (a discrete Painlevé equation that has the given continuous Painlevé equation as a continuum limit) as the underlying time-stepping scheme yields provable advantages—such as preservation of geometric/integrable structure, improved stability near poles, or better long-range accuracy—over standard non-structure-preserving ODE solvers, and either construct such an integrable-discretization-based solver with quantitative comparison to Runge–Kutta methods, or rule out asymptotic advantages.

Toppling Dominoes is the partizan combinatorial game played on a finite row (string) of dominoes, each colored Left (bL), Right (bR), or neutral (g). On their turn, Left chooses any domino of color bL or g and topples it either to the left or to the right; toppling removes the chosen domino together with every domino on the chosen side of it. Right plays analogously with bR or g dominoes. The first player unable to move loses. Each position has a well-defined game value in the universe of short partizan games.

Timber is the impartial game played on a finite row of vertical sticks; on a move a player chooses a stick and topples it left or right, removing that stick and all sticks on the chosen side. Partizan Timber is the partizan refinement in which each stick is colored Left, Right, or neutral, and a player may topple only sticks of their own color or neutral sticks.

A position (string) is called a palindrome if it reads identically from left to right and from right to left.

Answer the following:

(a) Prove or disprove: if G is a palindrome in Toppling Dominoes, then no other Toppling Dominoes position has the same game value as G (i.e., palindromic positions realize their values uniquely).

(b) Provide a systematic method to compute the game values of arbitrary positions in Timber and in Partizan Timber.

(c) In Partizan Timber, determine whether there exist short partizan game values that do not occur as the value of any position; characterize the set of values which are (or are not) realized.

Consider the following two-player variants of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle.

Setup. There are three pegs and a finite collection of disks of distinct sizes. A legal position is any distribution of the disks among the three pegs in which, on each peg, the disks are stacked in strictly decreasing size from bottom to top. A move consists of transferring the topmost disk of one peg onto another peg, subject to the constraint that the moved disk may not be placed on top of a strictly smaller disk. Two players alternate moves, starting from a prescribed initial legal position and aiming at a prescribed legal terminal position.

(A) Scoring two-player Tower of Hanoi. Fix a real-valued scoring rule that assigns a payoff to each terminal play (for instance, sums of weights of disks moved, parity-based scores, or move-count differentials). With optimal play under this scoring rule, declare a position a first-player win, second-player win, or draw in the usual minimax sense. Question: exhibit a scoring rule for the two-player Tower of Hanoi under which the second player wins from the standard starting position (all disks on one peg, to be transferred to another fixed peg), or prove that no such scoring rule exists.

(B) Hanoi Stick-Up. In this variant, the disks are initially distributed as a given collection of stacks (in legal decreasing order on each peg), and on each turn a player makes a legal Tower of Hanoi move; a player unable to move loses under the normal convention, or wins under the misère convention. Determine, for every initial configuration with seven or more stacks, the normal-play and misère outcome classes (N- or P-positions) of Hanoi Stick-Up, thereby extending the known classification beyond configurations with at most six stacks.

Beggar-My-Neighbor is a deterministic two-player card game played with a standard 52-card deck. The deck is split into two face-down hands held by the two players. The players alternate turns: on each turn the current player turns the top card of their hand face up onto a central pile. If the card played is a non-penalty card (2 through 10), the turn passes to the opponent. If the card played is a "penalty" card — a Jack, Queen, King, or Ace — the opponent must then play, respectively, 1, 2, 3, or 4 cards from the top of their hand onto the central pile; if during this payment they play another penalty card, the obligation switches and the original player must pay. If the payment is completed without a new penalty card appearing, the player who laid the most recent penalty card takes the entire central pile, placing it face down at the bottom of their hand, and then begins a new trick by playing the next card. A player who runs out of cards loses; otherwise the game continues.

Decide whether there exists an initial distribution of the 52-card deck into the two hands such that the resulting play never terminates (equivalently, produces a draw or enters an infinite cycle).

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

In February–March 2024, Brayden Casella (with collaborators) exhibited an explicit initial deal of the full 52-card deck that produces a non-terminating game of Beggar-My-Neighbor, identifying a cycle of 62 tricks reached by 30 distinct starting hands. Let r be a positive integer and let F_q denote the finite field with q = 3^r elements, viewed as an abelian group under addition (equivalently, as the vector space F_3^r). A subset A ⊆ F_q is called progression-free (or a cap set) if it contains no three-term arithmetic progression, i.e., no three distinct elements x, y, z ∈ A with x + z = 2y (equivalently, since the characteristic is 3, no three distinct elements summing to 0). Denote by f(r) the maximum size of a progression-free subset of F_q.

It is known that f(r) ≤ 2·3^r / r (Meshulam) and that f(r) ≥ (2.217...)^r (Edel).

Address the following:
(a) Improve Meshulam's bound by showing that every progression-free subset A ⊆ F_q satisfies |A| = o(3^r / r).
(b) Determine whether there exists an absolute constant c < 3 such that f(r) ≤ c^r for all sufficiently large r.
(c) More generally, determine the asymptotic growth rate of f(r) as r → ∞.

In combinatorial game theory, a switch is a short game of the form {x | y} with x > y, where x and y are numbers. Consider the special class of switch games of the forms

  G_1 = { a-k | a+k | c }  (written compactly as "a k b | c", interpreted as the switch with Left option a+k, Right option a-k, against a constant c on one side), and

  G_2 = { a | b-k | b+k }  (written compactly as "a | b k c"),

where a, b, c, k are real (or rational) numbers given as input. A position G is a disjunctive sum G = G^{(1)} + G^{(2)} + ... + G^{(n)} of finitely many such switch components. Two players, Left and Right, alternately move (with one of them designated to move first), and each move replaces one summand by one of its options; the player who cannot move loses (normal play convention).

Problem: Determine the computational complexity of deciding, given such a disjunctive sum G of switches of the above two forms and a designated player to move, which player wins under optimal play. Specifically, decide whether this problem admits a polynomial-time algorithm in the input size, or whether it is NP-hard.

In the theory of combinatorial games (in the sense of Conway), a game G is built recursively from sets of left and right options, with loopy games allowed to have cycles in their game graphs. Thermography assigns to each game G a thermograph encoding the temperature and mean value of G under cooling by a parameter t, and overheating is the operator that, given a base game, integrates a game over a range of temperatures. The operator ∗ sends a game G to its star-companion ∗G, which is known to annihilate all infinitesimals.

Solve the following four problems:

(a) Provide a rigorous formal definition of the heuristic strategy known as sentestrat (a sente-based strategy for playing sums of hot games) and prove that it achieves optimal play in an appropriate precise sense; in particular, give a complete formal proof that sentestrat works.

(b) Give an explicit algorithm for top-down thermography that, given the game tree of a (possibly loopy) game G, computes its thermograph, and prove its correctness and analyze its complexity.

(c) Develop the machinery to compute, and characterize explicitly, the dogmatic thermographs of double kos (loopy positions of double-ko type arising in Go).

(d) Develop a temperature theory (cooling, heating, thermographs, temperature, mean value) that applies uniformly to all loopy games.

(e) Identify and prove a natural set of necessary and sufficient conditions on a map φ from a class of combinatorial games to itself under which φ is the unique homomorphism (with respect to disjunctive sum) that annihilates every infinitesimal game; in particular, characterize when the map G ↦ ∗G is the unique such homomorphism.

representations.normalized:
In combinatorial game theory, a loopy game is a (possibly infinite) game graph in which positions may recur, allowing draws or infinite play. A stopper is a loopy game with no infinite alternating run. The standard theory of canonical (simplest) form for loopfree games (via reversibility and domination) extends to certain classes of loopy games (e.g. stoppers, plumtrees), but is known to fail in general — for instance, the loopy game CAROUSEL has no canonical form under the existing definitions. A position in a loopy game is said to contain a wild cycle if it has a cycle that is essential to play and cannot be eliminated by the usual simplification rules. The atomic weight of an infinitesimal game g is, when defined, an integer-valued "uppitiness" measure aw(g) satisfying the usual atomic-weight calculus (e.g. aw(g+h)=aw(g)+aw(h) when both sides are defined, and aw(*)=0); for general infinitesimal stoppers it is not known when this invariant exists.

Tasks:
(a) Define a notion of "simplest form" for finite loopy games — i.e. a canonical representative inside each equivalence class under game equality — that is well-defined for every finite loopy game, and in particular produces a canonical form for CAROUSEL.
(b) Give a procedure that, in a playable loopy game such as Phutball, detects the presence of a wild cycle arising naturally in actual play (as opposed to one constructed artificially).
(c) Characterize precisely those infinitesimal stoppers g for which a well-defined atomic weight aw(g) exists, and provide an algorithm that, given such an infinitesimal stopper, computes aw(g).

In combinatorial game theory, a (short, loopfree) two-player game G has, by the Sprague–Grundy theory, a value associated with each impartial position; nimbers are denoted ∗k for nonnegative integers k, where ∗0 = 0 and ∗k is the value of a single Nim-heap of size k. A "natural" combinatorial game is given by a fixed ruleset (e.g. Domineering, Konane, Hackenbush, Go, etc.) whose positions generate values in the universe of combinatorial games.

For a given ruleset G, define the nim-dimension of G to be the smallest nonnegative integer n such that whenever a position of G has value ∗k, one has k < 2^n (and ∞ if no such n exists).

(a) Characterize, among natural combinatorial games, those rulesets that admit a position of value ∗2 (i.e., describe the "habitat of ∗2").

(b) More generally, for each natural ruleset G, determine its nim-dimension n(G), i.e., the smallest exponent n such that every nimber value ∗k attained by a position of G satisfies k < 2^n.

Berlekamp's question on the "habitat of ∗2" remains an open guiding problem in combinatorial game theory. Partial progress is known: ∗2 positions have been found in various games (e.g. Domineering, with difficulty), and Carlos dos Santos showed Konane has infinite nim-dimension by exhibiting positions of value ∗k for every k. Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and let $Q \subset \mathbb{F}_p^*$ denote the set of nonzero quadratic residues modulo $p$. Consider subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ with the property that $a - a' \in Q$ for every pair of distinct $a, a' \in A$ (equivalently, $A$ is a clique in the Paley graph on $\mathbb{F}_p$, whose vertex set is $\mathbb{F}_p$ and whose edges join $x, y$ with $x - y \in Q$). Let $\omega(p)$ denote the maximum size of such a set $A$.

Known lower bounds give $\omega(p) \geq (1/2 + o(1)) \log_2 p$ in general, and $\omega(p) \geq c \, \log p \, \log\log\log p$ for infinitely many primes $p$. The only generally known upper bound is the elementary estimate $\omega(p) < \sqrt{p}$.

Problem: Determine improved upper bounds on $\omega(p)$. In particular, prove or disprove that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ one has $\omega(p) < p^{\varepsilon}$ for all sufficiently large primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and more generally describe the true asymptotic order of $\omega(p)$.

One may also pose the analogous questions with the difference set replaced by the sumset (i.e., $A + A \subseteq Q$, or $A + A = Q$, or $|(A+A) \triangle H|$ small), and with $Q$ replaced by an arbitrary proper multiplicative subgroup $H$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^*$: estimate the largest $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q$ with $A - A \subseteq H \cup \{0\}$.

The trivial bound $\omega(p) < \sqrt{p}$ was improved by Hanson and Petridis (2019/2021) using Stepanov's method to $\omega(p) \leq \sqrt{(p-1)/2} + 1$ (i.e. roughly $\sqrt{p/2}$). Further refinements and extensions to Paley graphs of prime-power order and to cyclotomic graphs have appeared since (e.g. Yip and collaborators, 2023–2025), and SOS lower-bound results (2023) suggest the polynomial-method approach has limitations. However, the conjectured polylogarithmic / $p^\varepsilon$ upper bound remains open.

In combinatorial game theory, a (short) game is defined recursively as an ordered pair G = {G^L | G^R} of finite sets of previously constructed games called the Left and Right options of G; the unique game born on day 0 is 0 = { | }, and a game is born by day n if all of its options are born by day n−1. Equality and the partial order ≤ on games are defined by Conway's recursion: G ≥ H iff no Right option of G is ≤ H and no Left option of H is ≥ G. For each n ≥ 0, the set L_n of (canonical forms of) games born by day n is a finite distributive lattice under ≤. A game G is all-small if every position reachable from G has at least one Left option and at least one Right option (or is 0); let L^0_n denote the lattice of all-small games born by day n. A game is option-closed if it equals every game obtained by replacing any subset of its options by their canonical forms (one standard formalization).

Address the following:

(a) Improve the known asymptotic upper and lower bounds on |L_n|, the number of distinct games born by day n.

(b) Describe the structure of L_3 explicitly: give its order dimension, its maximum longitude (length of a longest chain), and a combinatorial description of its covering relations.

(c) Determine the exact structure and parameters (size, dimension, longitude, planarity) of L_4.

(d) For a finite set S of games, let L(S) denote the lattice generated by S under the game ordering. Characterize those S for which L(S) is distributive, and determine whether there exists S such that L(S) is modular but not distributive.

(e) Determine whether the elements of the all-small lattice L^0_n possess an intrinsic "handedness" (a canonical Z/2-symmetry distinguishing Left-favored from Right-favored elements), and describe it.

(b) Describe the structure of L_3 explicitly: give its order dimension, its maximum longitude (length of a longest chain), and a combinatorial description of its covering relations.

(g) Count the number of option-closed games born by day n.

(h) Exhibit and classify natural infinite families of combinatorial games whose birthday lattices are planar.

In combinatorial game theory, a (short) game is built recursively from sets of Left and Right options: G = { G^L | G^R }. Under disjunctive sum, the class of short partizan games forms a partially ordered abelian group, with G = H iff G + K and H + K have the same outcome for every game K. More generally, given a submonoid (or subgroup) K of the universe of games (for instance, the monoid generated by a specified rule set or "universe" such as all-small games, dicotic games, scoring games, misère games of a particular class, etc.), one defines K-equivalence by G ≡_K H iff G + X has the same outcome as H + X for every X ∈ K. Each K-equivalence class has a notion of "simplest" representative, where simplicity is measured by the formal birthday (recursive depth of construction) and the size/complexity of the game tree.

Problem: Develop a general method (algorithm or constructive procedure) that, given a monoid or group K of combinatorial games together with a game G, produces the simplest representative of the K-equivalence class of G. The method should apply uniformly across choices of K (rather than being tailored to a single specific universe), and should, in principle, allow one to compute canonical simplest forms modulo any reasonable monoid of games.

representations.normalized:
In combinatorial game theory, a partizan game is a finite game tree in which, at each position, the two players (Left and Right) may have different sets of available moves. The disjunctive sum (or union) G + H of two games G and H is the game in which, on each turn, the player to move chooses one of the component games and makes a legal move there; play ends when no moves remain in any component. Under the misère convention, the player who makes the last move loses.

Two games G and H are misère-equivalent (G ≡ H) if for every game X, the outcome (under optimal play) of G + X equals the outcome of H + X. While the disjunctive theory of partizan games under the normal-play convention is well developed (yielding the surreal-number-valued theory of Conway), the corresponding theory under the misère convention is far less understood, since many simplifications (dominated and reversible options, additive inverses, canonical forms) that hold under normal play fail in misère play.

Problem: Develop a comprehensive structural theory of disjunctive sums (unions) of partizan games under the misère-play convention. In particular, give a workable notion of canonical form, identify natural equivalence classes and their algebraic structure (e.g. the monoid of partizan games modulo misère equivalence), and provide tools for computing outcomes of disjunctive sums of partizan misère games analogous to those available in the normal-play partizan theory.

A subset $A$ of a group $G$ is called product-free if the equation $xy=z$ has no solutions with $x,y,z\in A$. For each $n\ge 2$, let $A_n$ denote the alternating group on $n$ letters, and let $\mathrm{pf}(A_n)$ denote the maximum size of a product-free subset of $A_n$. Prove or disprove the following conjecture of Green:
$$\mathrm{pf}(A_n)=o(|A_n|)\quad\text{as }n\to\infty,$$
i.e., for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $N$ such that for all $n\ge N$, every product-free subset $A\subseteq A_n$ satisfies $|A|<\varepsilon\,|A_n|$. More quantitatively, determine the correct order of magnitude of $\mathrm{pf}(A_n)/|A_n|$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Green's conjecture that the largest product-free subset of $A_n$ has density $o(1)$ was established by Gowers (via his theory of quasirandom groups), giving density at most $n^{-1/3}$. Eberhard improved this to $O(n^{-1/2}\log^{7/2}n)$, and a 2022/2024 work of Keevash, Lifshitz and Minzer determined the maximum density up to constants as $\Theta(n^{-1/2})$, settling the qualitative conjecture and pinning down the order of magnitude.

In classical combinatorial game theory, a two-player game between Left and Right is analyzed under a fixed convention (most commonly normal play, where the player unable to move loses, or misère play, where the player unable to move wins). Under normal play of impartial games, the Sprague–Grundy theory provides a complete additive structure, and partizan normal-play games admit Conway's theory of surreal numbers and game values. Each finite game position falls into one of four outcome classes under optimal play:
- N (Next player to move wins),
- P (Previous player wins, i.e. the player who just moved),
- L (Left wins regardless of who moves first),
- R (Right wins regardless of who moves first).

In the standard normal-play and misère-play conventions, the outcome class is determined by the win/loss rule applied to terminal positions, and the four classes arise as derived information.

Problem. Identify a class of two-player combinatorial games in which the four outcomes N, P, L, R are taken as primitive winning conditions (rather than as consequences of a normal- or misère-play terminal rule) and develop a useful general theory for such games. In particular, determine whether there exists a natural disjunctive-sum structure, an equivalence relation refining outcome equality, and a value theory (analogous to Sprague–Grundy values or Conway game values) on this class, with proofs of additivity, simplification, and comparison theorems. If no such general theory exists, demonstrate obstructions to its development.

Let $t\geq 1$ be an integer and $N\geq 1$. Consider subsets $A\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,N\}$ with the property that for every pair of integers $(m,n)$ with $1\leq m,n\leq t$, the equation
$$mx+ny=(m+n)z$$
has no non-trivial solution with $x,y,z\in A$ (a solution is trivial when $x=y=z$).

Let $F_t(N)$ denote the maximum possible size of such a set $A$. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $F_t(N)$ as $N\to\infty$. In particular, close the gap between the known bounds
$$N\exp(-C(t)\sqrt{\log N})\ \leq\ F_t(N)\ \leq\ r_3(N),$$
where $C(t)>0$ is a constant depending only on $t$, the lower bound is obtained from a modification of Behrend's construction, and $r_3(N)$ denotes the largest size of a subset of $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$ containing no non-trivial three-term arithmetic progression.

representations.normalized:
Background. Let Γ be a finite set of impartial combinatorial game positions, closed under taking options, considered under misère-play convention (the player unable to move wins). Let F(Γ) be the free commutative monoid on Γ. Two positions x,y are said to be misère-equivalent in Γ, written x ≡ y, if for every position z built from Γ, the misère outcome of x+z equals the misère outcome of y+z. The quotient monoid Q(Γ) = F(Γ)/≡ is called the misère quotient of Γ, and it comes with a distinguished subset P ⊂ Q(Γ) consisting of images of positions whose misère outcome is a previous-player win. A position has period n if it has order n in Q(Γ). A quotient map φ : Q(Γ) → Q(Γ′) (for Γ ⊂ Γ′) is called faithful if x ≡_{Γ′} y implies x ≡_Γ y for all x,y ∈ F(Γ); equivalently, φ is injective on the natural images.

Resolve each of the following structural questions about impartial misère quotients:

(1) Is every quotient map between impartial misère quotients faithful?

(2) For any nontrivial submonoid S ⊂ Q(Γ) arising from a sub-ruleset, must S ∩ P be nonempty?

(3) Extend the classification of impartial misère quotients (e.g., by order, or by associated combinatorial structure) beyond what is currently known.

(4) Exhibit an impartial misère quotient containing an element of period 5 (and likewise of period 8), or prove that no such quotient exists.

(5) Determine the smallest impartial misère quotient (by order) that contains an element of period 4; period 3; period 6.

These structural questions about impartial misère quotients (faithfulness of quotient maps, nonempty intersection of submonoids with the P-set, classification extensions, and existence/smallest examples of quotients with elements of specified periods) are listed as open problems in the misère-quotient literature (Plambeck–Siegel and Siegel's surveys). Let $s \geq 3$ be a fixed integer. Call a strictly increasing sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \dots\}$ of non-negative integers $s$-locally AP-free if for every $i \geq 0$ the consecutive block $(a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}, \dots, a_{i+s})$ contains no three-term arithmetic progression (i.e., no three indices $i+1 \leq j_1 < j_2 < j_3 \leq i+s$ with $a_{j_1} + a_{j_3} = 2 a_{j_2}$).

For such a sequence $A$, let
$$\overline{d}(A) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{|A \cap [0,N]|}{N+1}, \qquad \underline{d}(A) = \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{|A \cap [0,N]|}{N+1}.$$

Determine
$$D(s) := \sup\{\overline{d}(A) : A \text{ is } s\text{-locally AP-free}\}.$$

It is known that if $n(s)$ denotes the smallest positive integer $N$ such that $[1,N]$ contains an $s$-element subset free of three-term arithmetic progressions, then every $s$-locally AP-free sequence $A$ satisfies $\overline{d}(A) \leq s/n(s)$, and there exist $s$-locally AP-free sequences with $\underline{d}(A) \geq s/(2 n(s))$. For example, for $s = 4$ one has $D(4) \geq 2/3$ (achieved by integers congruent to $0$ or $1$ modulo $3$), and for $s = 8$ one has $D(8) \geq 4/9$ (achieved by integers congruent to $0,1,3$, or $4$ modulo $9$). Find the exact value of $D(s)$ for all $s \geq 3$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is a problem of Freiman from a collection of open problems in additive combinatorics. Only the bounds $s/(2 n(s)) \le D(s) \le s/n(s)$ (with $n(s)$ the smallest $N$ such that $[1,N]$ contains an $s$-element AP-3-free subset) appear to be known, and no exact formula for $D(s)$ has been established. The problem is generally regarded as open.

representations.normalized:
In combinatorial game theory under misère convention, a partizan game G has a conjugate (or negative) denoted by overline{G}, obtained by swapping the roles of the two players (Left and Right) in every position of G. A *universe* U is a class of partizan games closed under disjunctive sum, options, and conjugation. Two games G and H are equivalent modulo U, written G ≡ H (mod U), if G + X has the same outcome as H + X for every X ∈ U. The *dicotic universe* D consists of all partizan games in which every position either has both Left and Right options or is the zero game.

Answer the following three questions about inverses in partizan misère universes:

(a) Characterize exactly which games G ∈ D satisfy G + overline{G} ≡ 0 (mod D); that is, give a necessary and sufficient condition on G for its conjugate to be its inverse in the dicotic misère universe.

(b) For a universe U that is closed under conjugation and disjunctive sum, determine whether the implication "G + H ≡ 0 (mod U) implies H = overline{G}" must hold; i.e., is every inverse of G necessarily its conjugate?

(c) Classify the universes U (within the partizan misère setting) for which no nonconjugate inverses exist — i.e., for which G + H ≡ 0 (mod U) forces H = overline{G}.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

A 2020 paper (Fisher, Nowakowski, Santos) characterizes the invertible elements of the misère dicotic universe D, resolving question (a). A 2024 work titled "Invertibility in the misère multiverse" (Davies & Yadav) further develops invertibility theory across universes, showing every universe has the conjugate property and characterizing invertible elements universe by universe, providing substantial progress on (b) and (c). Some aspects (full classification of universes with no nonconjugate inverses) remain active research.

representations.normalized:
Background. A scoring game is a finite two-player combinatorial game in which every position has options for Left and Right and every terminal position is assigned a real-valued score (positive favoring Left, negative favoring Right). For a scoring game G, let G^c denote its conjugate (swap the roles of Left and Right and negate the score). The disjunctive sum G+H is defined recursively, with terminal scores added. A universe U of scoring games is a class closed under taking options, conjugation, and disjunctive sum. The class N of (Conway) normal-play games (no score, last-player-to-move wins, terminal score 0 with the loser convention) sits inside the scoring world via the standard embedding sending a normal-play game G to its scoring version with all terminal scores 0. One says N order-embeds in U if there is an injection ι: N → U preserving the partial order ≤ (G ≤ H iff Left does at least as well in H as in G under every disjunctive context), conjugation, and disjunctive sum. Call a scoring game G guaranteed if for every position, the Left-stop is at least the Right-stop (equivalently, scores cannot decrease for the player to move under optimal stopping play); let GS denote the universe of guaranteed scoring games.

Problem.
(a) Prove or disprove: GS is the largest conjugation-closed and disjunctive-sum-closed universe of scoring games into which the universe N of normal-play games order-embeds. Equivalently, show that every universe U of scoring games (closed under options, conjugation, and disjunctive sum) into which N order-embeds satisfies U ⊆ GS, or exhibit a strictly larger such universe.

(b) Solve the combinatorial game BRUSHES: determine its complete game-theoretic value (in the appropriate scoring universe) and provide an explicit strategy / closed-form evaluation for arbitrary positions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The guaranteed scoring games framework was introduced and developed by Larsson, Nowakowski, and Santos (arXiv:1505.07905; Electronic J. Combinatorics 2016) and related papers around 2017. Their results establish that normal-play games order-embed into GS and characterize GS as a maximal-type universe, but the precise maximality question and the explicit solution of the game BRUSHES are listed as open problems in the unsolved-problems compendium for combinatorial games, and no published solution was found.

representations.normalized:
In the game of Nim, a position consists of a finite multiset of nonnegative integers (the pile sizes); two players alternate turns, on each turn choosing one pile of positive size and removing any positive number of tokens from it; the player unable to move (i.e., facing all piles empty) loses. A position is a P-position if the Previous player (the one who just moved) has a winning strategy, equivalently if the bitwise XOR (nim-sum) of the pile sizes equals 0. Define the "size" of a Nim position to be the total number of tokens, i.e., the sum of all pile sizes.

(a) Find a closed-form formula, as a function of n, for the number of Nim P-positions of size exactly 2n (counted as multisets of pile sizes, with empty piles ignored).

(b) More generally, develop a method to compute, for an arbitrary impartial combinatorial game equipped with a notion of "size" of a position, the number of P-positions of any given size.

Call a finite set E of homogeneous linear equations in integer variables partition regular if, for every positive integer r and every r-coloring of the positive integers, the system E has a non-trivial monochromatic solution (one in which not all variables are equal). For positive integers N and r, let f_E(N;r) denote the minimum, over all r-colorings of {1,2,...,N}, of the number of non-trivial monochromatic solutions of E with all coordinates in {1,2,...,N}.

Take r = 2 and let E consist of the single equation x + y = 2z (so monochromatic solutions correspond to monochromatic 3-term arithmetic progressions, including those with x = y = z when counted as trivial, which are excluded). Determine the limiting constant
   c = lim_{N → ∞} f_E(N;2) / N^2,
or equivalently determine the asymptotic value of f_E(N;2) up to a factor 1 + o(1).

It is known that this constant satisfies the bounds 1/21.67... ≤ c ≤ 117/2192 = 1/18.735..., while a uniformly random 2-coloring achieves 1/16. The problem asks for the exact value of c (in particular, whether c = 117/2192).

The exact asymptotic constant for the minimum number of monochromatic 3-term APs in a 2-coloring of [1,N] remains open. Recent work (e.g., arXiv:2301.00336, 2023) has improved the lower bound and connected the problem to a continuous analogue on [0,1], proving the Parrilo–Robertson–Saracino conjectured coloring is optimal among certain restricted (anti-symmetric, ≤12 block) colorings, but the gap between the lower bound (~1/21.67) and the upper bound 117/2192 has not been closed.

Consider impartial combinatorial games encoded as "lattice games" in the following sense. Fix a pointed rational cone Q ⊆ Z^d (the set of positions), a finite set Γ ⊂ Z^d \ {0} of move vectors, and a "misère" set of forbidden ending positions (or, under normal play, the origin is the unique terminal position). From a position p ∈ Q, a player may move to p − γ provided γ ∈ Γ and p − γ ∈ Q (and p − γ is not forbidden). Players alternate; a player unable to move loses. P-positions are previous-player wins; N-positions are next-player wins.

A lattice game is called square-free if its defining data satisfy the square-free condition generalizing octal games (no move vector has a component greater than 1 in the relevant encoding, so that subtraction of moves does not produce repeated coordinates).

Problem: Determine whether, for every square-free lattice game (and more generally for lattice-point rulesets defined as above), there exists an algorithm that, given any N-position p, computes a winning move from p in time polynomial in the bit-size of p.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For square-free lattice games under normal play, Guo and Miller established that the rational-strategy and affine-stratification conjectures hold and gave an algorithm to compute winning positions; given a rational strategy, a polynomial-time algorithm decides P/N status and produces a winning move. However, the broader rational-strategy conjecture for general lattice games was disproved by Fink (lattice games support universal computation; a 3-dimensional example has non-rational winning-position generating function), so efficient algorithms cannot exist for all lattice-point rulesets. The square-free case is essentially resolved positively, while the general lattice-game case is resolved negatively.

Background. Let G be a short combinatorial (two-player, perfect-information, no-chance) game. For a position P of G, write P for its game-tree value modulo equivalence by Conway's theory. An impartial position has a Sprague–Grundy (nim-) value, a single nonnegative integer. For partizan games, one considers the "atomic weight" or, more generally, the structure of *-values that arise: the nim-dimension of a game G is defined as the smallest nonnegative integer d such that every sum of positions of G is equivalent (in the sense of game equality) to a partizan game value plus a nim-heap whose size lies in the additive group generated by some finite collection of nim-values of dimension ≤ d; equivalently, it measures the minimal k such that the set of nim-values appearing among positions of G can be described as the set of XOR-sums of integers from a base set of "dimension" k (so a game whose nim-values are exactly the set of nonnegative integers has nim-dimension 1, while a game whose nim-values realize the full structure of Z_2^k requires dimension k).

Problem.
(a) Determine the nim-dimension of natural combinatorial games. In particular, prove or disprove the conjecture that the game DOMINEERING (played on a rectangular grid, where Left places vertical 1×2 dominoes and Right places horizontal 1×2 dominoes, last mover wins) has nim-dimension equal to 1.
(b) Prove or disprove the conjecture that the game AMAZONS (played on a 10×10 board with four amazons per side, where on each turn a player moves one of her amazons like a chess queen and then shoots an arrow, like a queen move, from its new square, blocking that square thereafter; last mover wins) has nim-dimension equal to 2.
(c) More generally, describe the range of possible nim-dimensions across natural partizan combinatorial games, exhibiting games of each finite nim-dimension (or showing this fails).

representations.normalized:
In the theory of impartial and loopfree combinatorial games (in the sense of Conway's On Numbers and Games / Winning Ways), recall the following notions:

- The atomic weight (or "uptitude") of an all-small game G is a value, usually an integer, that measures G in units of the infinitesimal up (↑). It is computed by a recursive rule analogous to the mex/Grundy calculation, but the rule is subject to a finite list of "exceptional" positions ("eccentric" cases) in which the naive atomic-weight calculus must be corrected.
- A class C of games is said to have nim-dimension at most d if every Grundy value (nim-value) occurring among positions of games in C is bounded above by 2^d − 1, i.e. all nim-values lie in a fixed finite range. C has bounded nim-dimension if such a finite d exists.

Question: Is it true that for every class of games of bounded nim-dimension, the atomic-weight calculation has only finitely many exceptional positions? Equivalently, prove or disprove: bounded nim-dimension implies that, beyond a finite set of exceptional cases, the atomic weights of positions in the class are determined by the standard (non-eccentric) atomic-weight calculus.

representations.normalized:
In combinatorial game theory, a (short) partizan game is built recursively from finitely many Left and Right options, and the collection of game values forms a partially ordered abelian group under disjunctive sum. A ruleset R is said to be a universal partizan ruleset if every short partizan game value occurs as the value of some position of R. Generalized Konane is known to be such a universal partizan ruleset.

(a) Exhibit other universal partizan rulesets, i.e. natural combinatorial rulesets, distinct from Generalized Konane, such that every short partizan game value arises as the value of some position.

(b) Develop general techniques (applicable to a wide class of rulesets) that, given a particular ruleset R, allow one to prove that certain game values cannot occur as the value of any position of R.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (a) has seen substantial recent progress: beyond Generalized Konane, Turning Tiles and additional rulesets have been proven universal partizan rulesets (e.g., arXiv:2201.06069 and arXiv:2301.05497, the latter also providing a universal dicotic partizan ruleset). Part (b), concerning general techniques for ruling out game values in a given ruleset, does not appear to have a general solution and remains open in that broader sense.

For a positive integer $N$, let $r_3(N)$ denote the largest cardinality of a subset of $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$ that contains no nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression (i.e., no triple $(a,b,c)$ with $a+c=2b$ and $a\ne b$). For a finite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, let $2A=\{a+a':a,a'\in A\}$ denote its sumset.

Define
$$f(n) \;=\; \min\bigl\{\,|2A|\;:\; A\subseteq \mathbb{Z},\ |A|=n,\ A \text{ contains no three-term arithmetic progression}\bigr\}.$$

It is known that $f(n)/n\to\infty$ and that $f(n)/n \ge \tfrac12 (n/r_3(n))^{1/4}$. On the other hand, choosing $N$ with $r_3(N)=n$ yields an $n$-element progression-free set $A\subseteq[1,N]$ with $|2A|/n < 2N/n = 2N/r_3(N)$; in particular the Behrend-type constructions give $|2A|/n = O(e^{c\sqrt{\log n}})$ for an absolute constant $c>0$.

Determine the true order of growth of $f(n)/n$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular, decide whether $f(n)/n$ can be bounded above by a polynomial in $\log n$, and close the gap between the lower bound $\tfrac12 (n/r_3(n))^{1/4}$ and the Behrend-type upper bound $O(e^{c\sqrt{\log n}})$.

No source found establishing the exact growth of the minimum sumset size for $n$-element progression-free subsets of $\mathbb{Z}$. The known bounds remain Ruzsa's $\tfrac12(n/r_3(n))^{1/4}$ from below and the Behrend-construction bound $e^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ from above; the problem appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
In the theory of combinatorial games under the normal-play convention, recall the following. A short combinatorial game G has a well-defined temperature t(G), obtained from the thermograph of G: starting from G, one forms the cooled game G_t by subtracting a tax t from every nonterminal move, and t(G) is the least t ≥ −1 for which G_t becomes infinitesimally close to a number. For a ruleset R (a class of positions closed under play), the boiling point of R is defined as

   bp(R) = sup { t(G) : G is a position of R }.

DOMINEERING is the two-player combinatorial game played on a subset of the square lattice, in which Left places vertical 1×2 dominoes and Right places horizontal 1×2 dominoes on empty cells; the first player unable to move loses.

(a) Determine bp(DOMINEERING). In particular, decide whether bp(DOMINEERING) = 2.

(b) More generally, develop feasible methods (algorithmic or theoretical) that yield strong upper bounds on the temperatures t(G) of positions G of a given ruleset such as Domineering.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Berlekamp's conjecture that the boiling point of Domineering equals 2 remains open. Recent computational work (endgame databases, 2015; and follow-up papers in 2019 and 2026) provides strong supporting evidence — exactly one known position attaining temperature 2 and none exceeding it — but no formal proof. Research on feasible methods for upper bounds on temperatures (e.g., via confusion intervals) is ongoing.

For a finite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$, let $2A := A+A = \{a+b : a,b\in A\}$ denote its sumset, and let $r_3(N)$ denote the largest size of a subset of $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$ containing no three-term arithmetic progression.

Define
$$ f(n) := \min\{\,|2A| : A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z},\ |A|=n,\ \text{no three points of } A \text{ are collinear}\,\}. $$

It is known that
$$ f(n) \ge \tfrac{1}{2}\, n\, \bigl(n/r_3(n)\bigr)^{1/4}, $$
and that there exist arbitrarily large $n$ and corresponding $n$-element collinear-triple-free sets $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ with
$$ |2A| \le n\,\exp\!\bigl(C\sqrt{\ln n}\bigr) $$
for some absolute constant $C>0$.

Determine the true order of magnitude of $f(n)$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular, close the gap between the above lower and upper bounds.

Consider three-player impartial combinatorial games played from a position that is a disjunctive sum of Nim heaps. Players move in a fixed cyclic order, and on each turn a player removes any positive number of tokens from a single heap. A player who cannot move loses. Adopt the following "podium" preference system: each player's first priority is to win (be the last to make a move that puts an opponent in a no-move position in their favor); if a player cannot win, the player's second priority is to determine which of the other two players wins, according to a specified preference. More generally, fix for each player a strict preference order over the three possible outcomes "I win", "player A wins", "player B wins", and assume each player plays optimally with respect to that preference.

(a) Determine the outcome (under perfect play) of every position in misère three-player Nim, where the player who makes the last move loses, in the remaining open case in which a player who cannot personally win is indifferent or has a nontrivial preference between making either of the other two players the winner.

(b) Carry out the analogous analysis for misère three-player Nim under each of the other possible preference systems among the three players.

(c) Develop a theory of disjunctive sums for such cooperative/preference-based multiplayer games: give a recursive construction of game values, a comparison procedure between game forms, and a notion of canonical form (a unique simplest representative in each equivalence class under equality of games).

Recent work (Krawec, Cincotti, Suetsugu, and others) has analyzed three-player Nim under specific preference systems such as the podium rule and i-misère play, and has begun developing canonical-form theory for multiplayer impartial games. However, several preference cases for misère three-player Nim remain unresolved, and a complete theory of recursive construction, comparison, and canonical forms for cooperative/preference-based multiplayer sums is still being developed.

$$f(n,K) := \sup\left\{ \frac{|nA|}{|A|} : A \subset \mathbb{Z} \text{ finite, } |2A| < K|A| \right\}.$$
The Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequalities yield the bound $f(n,K) \leq K^n$. Determine the true asymptotic growth rate of $f(n,K)$ as $n \to \infty$ (for fixed $K > 1$): improve the upper bound on $f(n,K)$, or construct examples showing this bound is essentially tight.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question on the precise growth rate of f(n,K) = sup |nA|/|A| under the doubling assumption |2A| < K|A| is a known open problem in additive combinatorics. The Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality gives f(n,K) ≤ K^n, and refining this remains an active area, with no published proof of a sharp asymptotic resolution found in the search.

Let $m,n$ be positive integers with $m \le n$, and let $K \ge 1$ and $\delta \in (0,1]$ be real parameters. Let $A, B$ be finite subsets of integers with $|A| = m$ and $|B| = n$, and let $G \subseteq A \times B$ be a "graph" of admissible pairs with $|G| \ge \delta\, m n$. Define the restricted sumset
$$A \stackrel{G}{+} B \;=\; \{\, a + b : (a,b) \in G \,\}.$$
Suppose that $|A \stackrel{G}{+} B| \le K m$.

Question: Must there exist subsets $A' \subseteq A$ and $B' \subseteq B$ with
$$|A'| \ge c\, m, \qquad |B'| \ge c\, n, \qquad |A' + B'| \le C\, m,$$
where $A' + B' = \{a+b : a \in A', b \in B'\}$ is the full (unrestricted) sumset, and where the positive constants $c$ and $C$ depend only on $\delta$ and $K$ (and not on $m$ or $n$)?

The case $m = n$ is the classical Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem. For each fixed ratio $\lambda > 1$ with $n \le \lambda m$, the assertion is known with constants depending additionally on $\lambda$. The problem is to obtain such a structural conclusion uniformly for arbitrary $m \le n$.

An asymmetric/unbalanced Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem has been established (e.g., the "asymmetric Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem" of Green–Tao and related works), which yields proportional subsets A' ⊆ A, B' ⊆ B with polynomial control on |A'+B'| under additive-energy-type hypotheses, including unbalanced regimes |A| ≠ |B|. Thus the problem is partially resolved by the asymmetric BSG machinery, with the strongest form as literally stated remaining sensitive to the precise conclusion sought.

Let $A$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ with $|A|=n$, and let $G \subseteq A\times A$. Define the partial sumset and partial difference set along $G$ by
$$A\stackrel{G}{+}A := \{a'+a'' : (a',a'')\in G\}, \qquad A\stackrel{G}{-}A := \{a'-a'' : (a',a'')\in G\}.$$
The problem is to obtain an upper bound on $|A\stackrel{G}{-}A|$ in terms of $|A\stackrel{G}{+}A|$ and $n$, and to characterize the finite sets $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ (together with the choice of $G$) for which $|A\stackrel{G}{-}A|$ attains the maximum possible value.

It is known that:
(i) if $|A\stackrel{G}{+}A|=1$, then $|A\stackrel{G}{-}A|\le n$, with equality only when $A$ is symmetric (i.e. $A=c-A$ for some $c\in\mathbb{Z}$);
(ii) if $|A\stackrel{G}{+}A|=2$, then $|A\stackrel{G}{-}A|\le 2n-1$, with equality only when $A$ is an arithmetic progression.

Provide the analogous sharp bound and extremal characterization for general values of $|A\stackrel{G}{+}A|$.

For a prime $p$, let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the field with $p$ elements. Call a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ a sumset if there exists $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ with $S = A + A := \{a_1 + a_2 : a_1, a_2 \in A\}$. Define
$$M(p) := \max\{|S| : S \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p,\ S \neq A+A \text{ for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p\}.$$
It is known that there exist absolute constants $c, C > 0$ such that, for all sufficiently large primes $p$,
$$p - C\, p^{2/3}(\log p)^{1/3} \;<\; M(p) \;<\; p - c\, p^{1/2}(\log p)^{1/2}.$$
Determine the correct order of $p - M(p)$ as $p \to \infty$; in particular, close the gap between these lower and upper bounds.

Let $p$ be a prime and consider the affine plane $\mathbb{F}_p \times \mathbb{F}_p$ over the finite field with $p$ elements. For a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p \times \mathbb{F}_p$, define the number of unit-distance pairs in $A$ by
$$U(A) := \#\{((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)) \in A \times A : (x_1-x_2)^2 + (y_1-y_2)^2 = 1\}.$$
Determine the maximum order of magnitude of $U(A)$ over all subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p \times \mathbb{F}_p$ with $|A| = p$. More precisely, find the smallest exponent $\alpha$ (and matching constructions) such that
$$\max_{|A|=p} U(A) = \Theta(p^{\alpha})$$
as $p \to \infty$ through primes. The trivial construction $A = \{(x,0) : x \in \mathbb{F}_p\}$ gives $U(A) = 2p$, while a simple incidence/covering argument yields $U(A) = O(p^{3/2})$; the question is whether either bound is tight.

For an integer $r\geq 1$ and a finite set $A\subset \mathbb{Z}^r$, write $A-A=\{a-a': a,a'\in A\}$ for its difference set. Say that $A$ is $r$-dimensional if it is not contained in any affine hyperplane of dimension strictly less than $r$ (equivalently, the affine hull of $A$ has dimension $r$).

It is known that for every $r$-dimensional finite set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}^r$,
$$|A-A|\;\geq\;(r+1)\,|A|-\tfrac{1}{2}r(r+1),$$
and this bound is sharp for $r\in\{1,2\}$. For $r=3$ the sharp bound is
$$|A-A|\;\geq\;4.5\,|A|-9.$$

Problem. Determine, as a function of $|A|$ and $r$, the smallest possible value of $|A-A|$ over all $r$-dimensional finite sets $A\subset\mathbb{Z}^r$. In particular, prove or disprove the conjecture that for every $r\geq 4$ there exists a constant $C_r$ (depending only on $r$) such that for every $r$-dimensional finite $A\subset\mathbb{Z}^r$,
$$|A-A|\;\geq\;\Bigl(2r-2+\tfrac{1}{r-1}\Bigr)\,|A|-C_r.$$
(Constructions are known showing that, if true, this inequality is asymptotically best possible.)

Let $\delta\in(0,1)$ be fixed. For a prime $p$, a multiplicative subgroup $H\le \mathbb{F}_p^{*}$ with $|H|>p^{\delta}$, and an integer $k\ge 1$, define
$$kH := \underbrace{H+H+\cdots+H}_{k\text{ summands}} = \{h_1+h_2+\cdots+h_k : h_i\in H\}.$$
Determine the smallest integer $k=k(\delta)\ge 1$ such that for every prime $p$ and every multiplicative subgroup $H\le \mathbb{F}_p^{*}$ with $|H|>p^{\delta}$ one has $kH=\mathbb{F}_p$. In particular, determine the optimal order of growth of $k(\delta)$ as $\delta\to 0^{+}$. It is known that $k(\delta)$ can be taken with $\log k\le C/\delta$ for some absolute constant $C$, and that $k\le C^{4/\delta}$ suffices; can these bounds be improved?

$$S(H,a) := \sum_{x \in H} e^{2\pi i a x / p}.$$
Determine the threshold on the size $|H|$ (as a function of $p$) which is necessary and sufficient to guarantee that
$$S(H,a) = o(|H|) \quad \text{as } p \to \infty,$$
uniformly in $a \in \mathbb{F}_p^*$. In particular, find the smallest function $f(p)$ such that whenever $|H| \geq f(p)$ the above bound holds for every $a \in \mathbb{F}_p^*$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial progress exists but the optimal threshold is not known. Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin established nontrivial cancellation for subgroups of size $|H| \geq p^\varepsilon$ for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, and subsequent work (Shkredov, Shakan, Shteinikov, and others) has refined the bounds to subgroups of size somewhat smaller than $p^{1/4}$ with explicit savings. However, pushing down to subgroups of size $(\log p)^C$ — conjecturally the right threshold — remains open. Hence the problem is partially solved.

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions. For finite sets $A,B$ with $|A|=|B|=N$, let $G_0\subseteq A\times B$ be a bipartite graph. We say $G_0$ is "sparsely $c(\varepsilon,\delta)$-quasirandom" (with density $p=|G_0|/N^2$) if it satisfies a standard discrepancy/codegree condition relative to the constant $p$, namely that for every $U\subseteq A$, $V\subseteq B$, $|e_{G_0}(U,V)-p|U||V||\le c(\varepsilon,\delta)\,pN^2$, together with the corresponding $C_4$-count (or two-blow-up) bound. For $G\subseteq G_0$ with $|G|\ge\delta|G_0|$, call a pair $(X,Y)\subseteq A\times B$ "$\varepsilon$-regular relative to $G_0$" if for all $X'\subseteq X$, $Y'\subseteq Y$ with $|X'|\ge\varepsilon|X|$, $|Y'|\ge\varepsilon|Y|$, one has $\bigl||G\cap(X'\times Y')|/|G_0\cap(X'\times Y')|-|G|/|G_0|\bigr|<\varepsilon$.

The following bipartite-graph statement is known: there exist functions $c(\varepsilon,\delta)$ and $C(\varepsilon,\delta)$ such that for any sparsely $c(\varepsilon,\delta)$-quasirandom $G_0$ and any $G\subseteq G_0$ with $|G|\ge\delta|G_0|$, there are equitable partitions $A=A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_s$ and $B=B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_t$ with $s,t\le C(\varepsilon,\delta)$ such that at least $(1-\varepsilon)st$ of the pairs $(i,j)$ satisfy: $G$ restricted to $A_i\times B_j$ is $\varepsilon$-regular relative to $G_0$.

Problem. Establish a $k$-uniform hypergraph analogue of this lemma. Concretely, for every $k\ge 3$, formulate and prove a regularity lemma which, given a suitably pseudorandom (in an appropriate hypergraph quasirandomness sense, e.g.\ in terms of vanishing octahedral/Gowers-type norms) sparse $k$-uniform hypergraph $H_0$ on vertex set $V$, and a subhypergraph $H\subseteq H_0$ of positive relative density, produces an equitable polyad-decomposition of $V^{(k-1)}$ of bounded complexity such that, relative to $H_0$, all but an $\varepsilon$-fraction of the polyads are $\varepsilon$-regular for $H$, with quantitative bounds independent of $|V|$.

A relative hypergraph regularity/counting framework for subsets of sparse pseudorandom hypergraphs was developed and applied to give a new, simpler proof that the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. In particular, Conlon, Fox and Zhao (2013, "A relative Szemerédi theorem", arXiv:1305.5440) proved a relative Szemerédi theorem assuming only a linear-forms condition on the majorant, by means of a relative hypergraph regularity/counting approach, which yields a simplified proof of the Green–Tao theorem; related sparse hypergraph regularity/counting lemmas were also obtained by Conlon–Fox–Zhao and by Schacht/Tao and collaborators. This essentially resolves the question affirmatively.

For a prime $p$, let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the field with $p$ elements. For a polynomial $P(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ and a subset $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p$, write
$$P(A,A) := \{P(a',a'')\bmod p : a',a''\in A\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p.$$

Say that $P\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ has the expansion property if for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2]$ there exists $\delta=\delta(\varepsilon)>0$ and $p_0=p_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for every prime $p>p_0$ and every $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p$ with $|A|\le p^{\varepsilon}$, one has
$$|P(A,A)| \;\ge\; |A|^{1+\delta}.$$

It is known that $P(x,y)=x(x+y)$ and $P(x,y)=x^2+y$ both have this expansion property.

Problem: Classify all polynomials $P(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ that have the expansion property defined above.

The problem of classifying two-variable integer polynomials with the stated expansion property over prime fields remains open. For a subset $A$ of the integers, let $\ell(A)$ denote the maximum length of an arithmetic progression contained in $A$ (with $\ell(A)=\infty$ if arbitrarily long progressions are contained in $A$). For a real number $\delta\in[0,1)$ and an integer $N\ge 1$, define
$$F(\delta,N)\;:=\;\min\bigl\{\,\ell(A+A)\;:\;A\subseteq[1,N],\ |A|\ge N^{1-\delta}\,\bigr\},$$
where $A+A=\{a+a':a,a'\in A\}$. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $F(\delta,N)$ as $N\to\infty$ with $\delta\in(0,1)$ fixed. In particular, close the gap between the known lower bound, which is of the form $(\log N)^{2/\delta+O(1)}$, and the known upper bound of the form $\exp\!\bigl(C(\log N)^{2/3-o(1)}\bigr)$ for some absolute constant $C>0$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of pinning down the maximum guaranteed length of an arithmetic progression in $A+A$ for dense $A\subseteq[1,N]$ remains open. Bourgain established a lower bound of roughly $\exp(c(\log N)^{1/3})$ in the regime $|A|\gg N/(\log N)^{O(1)}$, later improved by Green and by Croot–Ruzsa–Schoen, while constructions give upper bounds of the form $\exp(C(\log N)^{2/3})$. For a finite group $G$, define a three-term arithmetic progression in $G$ to be a triple of the form $(a,\,ad,\,ad^2)$ with $a,d\in G$ and $d\neq 1$. Let $r_3(G)$ denote the largest cardinality of a subset $S\subseteq G$ that contains no three-term arithmetic progression. Address the following questions.

(a) Exhibit an infinite family $\{G_n\}_{n\ge1}$ of finite non-abelian groups together with explicit functions $f(G_n)\le r_3(G_n)\le F(G_n)$ such that $F(G_n)/f(G_n)$ is bounded above by an absolute constant independent of $n$.

(b) Determine whether there exists an absolute constant $K>0$ and an infinite family of finite non-abelian groups $\{G_n\}$ with $|G_n|\to\infty$ such that
$$r_3(G_n) \;>\; \frac{|G_n|}{(\log |G_n|)^K}.$$

(c) (Gowers-type question.) Fix $\theta\in(0,1]$. Decide whether there exist infinitely many primes $p$ such that, taking $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$, for every triple of subsets $A,B,C\subseteq G$ satisfying $\min\{|A|,|B|,|C|\}>\theta|G|$ the Cartesian product $A\times B\times C$ contains a triple of the form $(a,\,da,\,d^2a)$ for some $a,d\in G$. (Equivalently, asking whether there exist $a\in A$, $b\in B$, $c\in C$ with $c=ba^{-1}b$.)

(d) Given $K>0$, decide whether there exist infinitely many finite groups $G$ such that every subset $A\subseteq G$ with $|A|\ge|G|/(\log|G|)^K$ contains elements $a,b,c\in A$ satisfying $c=ba^{-1}b$; and decide whether there exist infinitely many finite groups $G$ admitting subsets $A\subseteq G$ with $|A|>|G|/(\log|G|)^K$ in which no such triple $(a,b,c)$ exists.

The mixing/Gowers-style question in part (c) for $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(p)$ and related quasirandom or finite simple groups has been resolved: results of Tao (for $\mathrm{SL}_d(\mathbb{F}_q)$) and Peluse (for all non-abelian finite simple groups), together with subsequent work on mixing of three-term progressions in quasirandom groups, establish the desired mixing for triples $(x,xg,xg^2)$. However, the quantitative questions on $r_3(G)$ for infinite families of non-abelian groups (parts (a), (b), and the log-power versions in (d)) do not appear to have been settled in the literature found, so the overall problem is best classified as partially solved.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $\mathbb{F}_p = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. For any function $f : \mathbb{F}_p \to \mathbb{C}$, define its Fourier transform by
$$\widehat{f}(z) := \sum_{u \in \mathbb{F}_p} f(u)\, e^{2\pi i u z / p}, \qquad z \in \mathbb{F}_p.$$
Fix $\varepsilon \in (0,1]$ and constants $A, B > 0$. Decide whether the following statement holds for all sufficiently large primes $p$:

Suppose $f, g : \mathbb{F}_p \to [0,1]$ satisfy
$$\widehat{f}(0) = \widehat{g}(0) > \frac{p}{(\log p)^A}$$
and
$$\max_{z \in \mathbb{F}_p} \bigl|\widehat{f}(z) - \widehat{g}(z)\bigr| < p \exp\!\bigl(-\sqrt{\log p}\bigr).$$
Then for every function $h : \mathbb{F}_p \to [0,1]$ with $h(u) \le f(u)$ for all $u \in \mathbb{F}_p$ and $\widehat{h}(0) \ge \varepsilon\, \widehat{f}(0)$, there exists a function $h' : \mathbb{F}_p \to [0,1]$ such that $h'(u) \le g(u)$ for all $u \in \mathbb{F}_p$ and
$$\max_{z \in \mathbb{F}_p} \bigl|\widehat{h'}(z) - \widehat{h}(z)\bigr| < \frac{p}{(\log p)^B}.$$

(In the hypothesis, $\exp(-\sqrt{\log p})$ may be replaced by any function that decays to $0$ faster than every negative power of $\log p$.)

Let $\mathbb{F}_3 = \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ and consider the elementary abelian group $\mathbb{F}_3^r$ for an integer $r \geq 1$. A subset $A$ of an additively written abelian group $G$ is called sum-free if there are no elements $x,y,z \in A$ with $x+y=z$. A sum-free subset $A \subseteq G$ is called induced if there exists a non-zero subgroup $H \leq G$ such that $A$ is the full preimage under the canonical homomorphism $G \to G/H$ of a sum-free subset of $G/H$; equivalently, $A$ is a union of cosets of some non-zero subgroup of $G$ (i.e., $A$ is periodic). A sum-free subset that is not contained in any induced sum-free subset is called primitive.

Prove or disprove the following conjecture: for every integer $r \geq 1$, if $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_3^r$ is a sum-free subset with
$$|A| > \frac{3^{r-1}+1}{2},$$
then $A$ is contained in an induced sum-free subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^r$.

Equivalently, determine whether the maximum size of a primitive (not contained in any induced) sum-free subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^r$ equals $(3^{r-1}+1)/2$.

For finite sets $A,B\subset\mathbb{Z}$, define the representation function
$$\rho_{A,B}(n):=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B : a+b=n\},\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
Arrange the nonzero values of $\rho_{A,B}$ in non-increasing order $r_1\ge r_2\ge r_3\ge\cdots$ (the "column heights"), so that $\sum_k r_k=|A||B|$. This sequence visualizes a Ferrers diagram with $|A||B|$ boxes whose $k$th column has height $r_k$; equivalently, the $t$th row from the bottom has length
$$N_t:=\#\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:\rho_{A,B}(n)\ge t\}.$$

It can be shown that the column heights satisfy
$$r_k^{\,2}\le r_k+r_{k+1}+r_{k+2}+\cdots \qquad (k\ge 1),\qquad(*)$$
and from this (or from Pollard's theorem) one obtains
$$N_1+N_2+\cdots+N_t\ge t\bigl(|A|+|B|-t\bigr)\qquad\text{for every } 1\le t\le \min\{|A|,|B|\}.$$

Problem. Identify general structural properties of the function $\rho_{A,B}$ (equivalently, of the sequence $(r_k)_{k\ge 1}$, or of the partition of $|A||B|$ it determines) that hold for all finite sets $A,B\subset\mathbb{Z}$ and that are not consequences of the inequality $(*)$. In particular, find further inequalities or constraints satisfied by $(r_k)$, beyond $(*)$ and its consequences, that characterize which non-increasing sequences of positive integers summing to $|A||B|$ can arise as the spectrum of $\rho_{A,B}$ for some pair $(A,B)$ of finite integer sets.

Let $r \geq 1$ be an integer, and let $z_1, \dots, z_r$ be complex numbers on the unit circle (so $|z_1| = \cdots = |z_r| = 1$). Let $p_1, \dots, p_r$ be nonnegative real weights satisfying the normalization
$$p_1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_r = r.$$
Prove or disprove the following assertion: for every such choice of points $\{z_j\}$ and weights $\{p_j\}$, there exists a complex number $z$ with $|z|=1$ such that
$$\prod_{j=1}^{r} |z - z_j|^{\,p_j} \;\geq\; 2.$$
(The constant $2$ on the right-hand side is best possible, as seen by taking $r=1$, $p_1=1$, and any $z_1$ on the unit circle.) Equivalently, show that the Chebyshev-type extremal quantity
$$\sup_{|z|=1} \prod_{j=1}^{r} |z - z_j|^{p_j}$$
is at least $2$ for all admissible configurations $(z_j, p_j)$.

Consider a stochastic network modeled as a directed (or undirected) graph G = (V, E) in which each node v ∈ V is an information source or sink (or relay) and each edge e ∈ E is a noisy communication channel described by a conditional probability transition kernel p_e(y|x) between input and output alphabets. A set of source processes {X_s : s ∈ S} with prescribed joint distribution is to be transmitted to a set of sinks, where each sink t ∈ T demands a specified subset of the sources. A coding scheme assigns, at each node and each time step, a (possibly random) function of past observations to be transmitted on outgoing edges; decoders at sinks produce estimates of demanded sources. The capacity region of the network is the closure of all rate tuples for which arbitrarily small probability of error is achievable.

Develop a general theory of information flow in such stochastic networks. Concretely, give a single-letter (or otherwise computable) characterization of the capacity region of an arbitrary multi-source, multi-sink stochastic network with noisy channels, statistically dependent sources, and arbitrary demand structure, identifying the fundamental limits on simultaneously achievable communication rates and the optimal coding strategies (including the role of network coding, cooperation, feedback, and source–channel separation) that attain them.

Formulate a comprehensive mathematical theory of computational complexity. Concretely, propose a unified framework that:

1. Defines a general notion of a computational problem and a model of computation (e.g., Turing machines, Boolean circuits, arithmetic circuits, communication protocols, query/decision trees, quantum circuits, distributed/parallel models), together with associated resource measures (time, space, circuit size and depth, communication, randomness, queries, energy, nonuniformity, etc.).

2. Specifies complexity classes as sets of problems solvable within prescribed bounds on these resources, and defines reductions and completeness in a model-independent way.

3. Provides general principles or axioms (in the spirit of Blum's axioms or abstract complexity) from which the main known separations, hierarchies (time, space, nondeterministic), simulations, and trade-offs follow uniformly, and which permit proofs of unconditional lower bounds for explicit problems.

4. Yields, as theorems within the framework, resolutions of the central open separation questions: P vs NP, NP vs coNP, P vs PSPACE, NL vs P, BPP vs P, BQP vs classical classes, and the existence of one-way functions.

5. Explains and unifies the known barriers (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization) to proving such separations, and identifies which proof techniques can or cannot circumvent them.

The problem is: construct such a theory, prove its internal consistency and explanatory power, and use it to settle at least one of the major separation problems listed above, or prove that no such theory satisfying the stated criteria can exist.

Computation, on the other hand, is typically modeled by a Boolean circuit, Turing machine, or algorithm that maps inputs to outputs, with fundamental limits described in terms of time, space, or circuit-size complexity.

Formulate and establish (or refute) a precise duality principle between computation and communication. That is, exhibit an explicit correspondence under which: (i) every communication problem (a triple consisting of a source distribution, a channel, and a fidelity criterion) is associated with a dual computation problem (a function class, model of computation, and a resource measure), and conversely; (ii) optimal achievable rates / capacity-type quantities on the communication side correspond to optimal resource bounds (e.g. circuit size, depth, time, space) on the computation side, in a way that converts direct (achievability) theorems on one side into converse (lower bound) theorems on the other, and vice versa; and (iii) the correspondence is functorial in the sense that composition of channels corresponds to composition of computational reductions.

Either construct such a duality and prove the corresponding equivalence of fundamental limits, or prove that no such duality can exist by exhibiting an obstruction.

For an infinite binary sequence ω ∈ {0,1}^ℕ, say that ω is Martin-Löf random with respect to the uniform (fair-coin) measure if there is a constant c such that K(ω↾n) ≥ n − c for all n, where ω↾n denotes the first n bits of ω. Recall that the Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable X with distribution p is H(X) = −Σ_x p(x) log p(x), and that for computable distributions p on {0,1}^n one has the identity E_p[K(X)] = H(X) + O(log n).

Develop a comprehensive theory describing the ultimate impact of algorithmic (Kolmogorov) complexity on classical probability theory, and articulate its precise relationship to Shannon information theory. Concretely:

(a) Identify the largest natural class C of probability statements (e.g. almost-sure laws such as the strong law of large numbers, the law of the iterated logarithm, ergodic theorems, martingale convergence theorems) for which the classical "almost surely" can be replaced by "for every Martin-Löf random sequence" in a uniform effective manner, and characterize the obstruction for statements outside C.

(b) Determine the exact quantitative correspondence between Kolmogorov complexity K and Shannon entropy H beyond the known O(log n) coincidence on computable sources: in particular, give a meaningful interpretation of K-based quantities (algorithmic mutual information I(x:y) = K(x) + K(y) − K(x,y), algorithmic sufficient statistics, the algorithmic minimal sufficient statistic) as limits or refinements of their Shannon counterparts, valid for individual objects rather than ensembles.

(c) Decide whether there is a single unified framework subsuming both classical probability theory and algorithmic information theory in which entropy, complexity, randomness, and typicality are aspects of one underlying invariant.

Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer network modeled as a dynamic graph G=(V,E) whose vertices are autonomous peers, each holding a local collection of data objects annotated with sets of keywords. Peers communicate only by sending messages along edges of G; no peer has global knowledge of V, E, or of the data held by other peers. A keyword query is a finite set Q of keywords issued at some peer v∈V, and a result for Q is any data object (held at some peer) whose keyword annotation contains every keyword in Q. A search mechanism is a distributed protocol that, given a query Q at v, returns a set R(Q,v) of results to v.

Call a search mechanism comprehensive if, for every query Q and every issuing peer v, R(Q,v) equals the set of all results for Q present anywhere in the network at query time. Call the mechanism efficient if the total number of messages exchanged, the per-peer processing cost, and the per-peer auxiliary storage are each bounded by a function that grows strictly sub-linearly (e.g., polylogarithmically) in |V| and in the total number of data objects, uniformly over queries and network states. Flooding (broadcasting the query to every reachable peer) is excluded as it is not efficient under this definition.

Question: Does there exist a distributed search mechanism for keyword queries on such a peer-to-peer network that is simultaneously comprehensive and efficient in the above sense, or can it be proved that no such mechanism exists?
