Consider a peer-to-peer system consisting of a dynamic set of N autonomous nodes, where each node n stores a local collection D_n of text documents and peers may join, leave, or fail at any time. The union D = ⋃_n D_n forms a global document collection. A user issues a keyword query q = (t_1, …, t_k) at some node and expects a ranked list of the top documents from D under a ranking function R(d, q) that depends on global corpus statistics. Specifically, for each term t, let df(t) = |{d ∈ D : t ∈ d}| (the global document frequency) and |D| (the global collection size); typical ranking functions (e.g., TF–IDF or BM25 variants) require values such as idf(t) = log(|D|/df(t)) together with local term frequencies.

Design a fully distributed protocol that, in the presence of node churn and failures, allows every node to obtain, for any query term t, an estimate d̂f(t) of df(t) and an estimate |D̂| of |D| such that:
(a) (Robustness) The protocol continues to provide such estimates with bounded relative error ε with high probability even when an adversarially chosen fraction of nodes fail or depart between updates.
(b) (Efficiency) The expected per-node communication, storage, and computation costs grow sublinearly (ideally polylogarithmically) in N and in |D|.
(c) (Distribution) There is no central coordinator; every node executes the same protocol using only local state and messages exchanged with a bounded number of neighbours.

Provide such a protocol, together with a proof of its accuracy, robustness, and resource bounds, or establish impossibility results showing the optimal achievable trade-offs among (a), (b), and (c).

Consider a distributed data-sharing network modeled as a set of N nodes, each holding a local document collection, where N can be very large (e.g., 10^6 or more). Each document d has, for each query q drawn from some query space Q, a real-valued relevance score s(d,q). A ranked-search protocol is an algorithm that, given a query q issued at one node, returns the k documents in the entire network with the highest scores s(d,q), for a user-specified parameter k much smaller than the total number of relevant documents.

Design a ranked-search protocol for this setting that simultaneously achieves the following properties as N grows:

1. Correctness: with high probability the returned set equals (or has bounded approximation ratio to) the true global top-k by score s(·,q).
2. Scalability: the per-node communication, computation, and storage cost grows sublinearly (ideally polylogarithmically) in N, and the total network traffic per query is asymptotically smaller than the cost of retrieving the full result set.
3. Top-k exploitation: the protocol must take essential advantage of the bound k, so that its cost depends on k and decreases substantially when k is small compared to retrieving all matching documents.
4. Robustness: the protocol should remain effective under node churn, heterogeneous node capacities, and skewed score and document distributions across nodes.

Provide such a protocol and prove matching upper and lower bounds on its communication complexity as a function of N, k, and the score distribution, or prove that no protocol can simultaneously achieve all four properties.

For a predicate φ defining a subset S_φ = { t ∈ ⋃_{p∈P} R_p : φ(t) holds } of tuples distributed across the network, suppose there exist distributed protocols that, without centralizing the data and tolerating churn and partial failures, compute the aggregate COUNT(S_φ) = |S_φ| approximately or exactly with bounded message, bandwidth, and round complexity.

The problem is to determine whether such peer-to-peer protocols for COUNT can be generalized to compute the following aggregates over S_φ on a designated numeric attribute a:
  (i) SUM(S_φ) = Σ_{t ∈ S_φ} t.a,
  (ii) MAX(S_φ) = max_{t ∈ S_φ} t.a,
  (iii) MEDIAN(S_φ) = the order statistic of rank ⌈|S_φ|/2⌉ of the multiset { t.a : t ∈ S_φ }.

Specifically, design distributed algorithms that evaluate SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN over a fully decentralized peer-to-peer network, establish their correctness (exact or with provable approximation guarantees), and analyze their communication, computation, and round complexity in the presence of dynamic membership, replication, and possible faulty or adversarial peers.

Consider a peer-to-peer data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes, each storing a local collection of data items. A search technique is a distributed protocol by which any node may issue a query and receive matching data items (or pointers to them) held by other nodes. Three qualitative properties of such a protocol are of interest:

1. Peer autonomy: the degree to which each node may independently decide which data it stores, which other nodes it connects to, when it joins or leaves, and how it routes or answers queries, without being forced into a globally imposed structure.
2. Search efficiency: small expected message complexity, low latency, and high recall/precision of queries, measured as a function of the number of nodes N and the data distribution.
3. Robustness: the protocol continues to deliver correct query answers under high churn (frequent joins/leaves), node failures, and adversarial behavior.

Existing classes of techniques exhibit apparent tradeoffs: structured overlays (e.g., distributed hash tables) achieve high efficiency and robustness but constrain autonomy by dictating data placement and topology; unstructured flooding/random-walk overlays preserve autonomy and robustness but scale poorly; hybrid and hierarchical schemes mitigate but do not eliminate these tensions.

Problem. Design a peer-to-peer search protocol, together with a formal model of autonomy, efficiency, and robustness, that provably improves on the current Pareto frontier of these three properties. Specifically, exhibit a protocol whose performance triple (autonomy, efficiency, robustness) strictly dominates that achievable by any structured-overlay or unstructured-overlay scheme in the same model, or prove that no such protocol exists by establishing a three-way lower-bound tradeoff.

Consider a peer-to-peer search system modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes that may join, leave, or fail at arbitrary times. Each node independently decides which other nodes to connect to, what queries to forward, and what local resources to share; the degree of "autonomy" of the design is a parameter measuring how freely each node may make these decisions without coordination from a central authority or fixed protocol-imposed constraints. The "robustness" of the system is a parameter measuring the stability of its search service — for example, the probability that queries are answered correctly within a bounded number of hops — under adversarial schedules of node failures and departures.

Question: Does there exist a peer-to-peer search mechanism, together with a formal model of the above kind, in which the autonomy parameter and the robustness parameter can be tuned independently? More precisely, is it possible to design a search mechanism whose autonomy level can be increased or decreased by the system designer while a chosen robustness guarantee continues to hold, and conversely whose robustness can be strengthened without forcing a reduction in node autonomy?

Define peer autonomy as the degree of control a peer has over (i) which documents it stores locally, (ii) which queries it forwards or answers, and (iii) which neighbors it maintains in the overlay. Define efficiency as the expected cost (in messages, latency, or bandwidth) for successfully locating and retrieving a document. Existing designs typically fix a single point on the autonomy–efficiency tradeoff for the whole deployment: structured systems (e.g., distributed hash tables) achieve high efficiency at the cost of dictating document placement and routing, while unstructured systems preserve autonomy but incur higher search cost.

Problem. Design a single peer-to-peer protocol with an explicit tunable parameter (or family of parameters) θ, ranging continuously between a high-autonomy regime and a high-efficiency regime, such that:

1. Each document d (or each user/use case) in the system may independently select its own value θ(d), specifying the storage placement constraints, replication policy, and search strategy used for that document.
2. The system simultaneously supports documents with different choices of θ(d) within the same overlay, without partitioning the peers into separate subsystems.
3. For each choice of θ, prove quantitative bounds on (a) the autonomy granted to peers regarding documents tagged with θ, and (b) the expected search and storage cost, showing that varying θ smoothly interpolates between the autonomy and efficiency extremes.

Either construct such a protocol with provable interpolation guarantees, or prove that no protocol satisfying (1)–(3) can exist subject to a stated formal model of autonomy and efficiency.

Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer system modeled as a dynamic network of nodes, where each node stores a subset of data items and communicates only with a bounded number of neighbors. A partial-search algorithm is a distributed protocol that, given a query for a data item, terminates after locating some (not necessarily all) copies of the item in the network. Associated with such an algorithm are two measures: a resource cost C (e.g., total number of messages exchanged, bandwidth consumed, or nodes visited) and a quality-of-service metric Q (e.g., probability of locating a copy, search latency, or fraction of available copies discovered). For a given workload and network model, a (C, Q) pair is called Pareto-optimal if no algorithm achieves strictly better cost without degrading Q, and vice versa.

Question: Does there exist a general (universal) decentralized partial-search technique that, for every reasonable choice of quality-of-service metric Q and every workload/network instance from a broad class, achieves with high probability a (cost, QoS) tradeoff that is Pareto-optimal?

Either exhibit such a general technique together with a proof of its optimality, or prove that no such universal technique exists.

Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes that interact according to a protocol P. The protocol P specifies, for each node, (i) how it responds to incoming messages (response rules), (ii) how it forwards or routes queries and data (routing rules), and (iii) how it allocates local resources such as bandwidth, storage, and CPU to handle requests (resource allocation rules). A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a strategy executed by a bounded coalition A of adversarial nodes (with |A| small relative to the total population) whose goal is to cause a disproportionate degradation of service availability for honest participants — formally, to drive some measurable performance metric (e.g., query success rate, average response latency, or fraction of reachable honest peers) below a chosen threshold while expending only o(1) of the resources required from the attacker compared to the damage inflicted on the system.

Say that a protocol feature is "loosely constrained" if it permits a node, upon receiving a single message of size s, to be obligated (by the protocol rules) to generate responses, forwarded traffic, or resource commitments whose total cost is ω(s), or if it permits an adversary to trigger arbitrarily many such actions without supplying a commensurate proof of work, identity, or prior interaction.

Problem. Design a P2P data-sharing protocol P satisfying the following properties simultaneously:

(1) Correctness/efficiency in the honest setting: with all nodes following P, the system supports data lookup, storage, and retrieval with polylogarithmic per-operation cost in the number of nodes.

(2) DoS resistance: for every adversarial coalition A of size at most a constant fraction ε of the network and every strategy A may follow within the syntactic rules of P, the ratio (damage inflicted on honest peers) / (resources expended by A) is bounded by a constant, where damage and resources are measured in a uniform cost model covering bandwidth, computation, and memory.

(3) No loosely constrained features: every response rule, routing rule, and resource-allocation rule of P must be tightly constrained in the sense above — i.e., the work induced on any honest node by a single adversarial message of size s is O(s), up to amortization by verifiable proofs.

Provide such a protocol together with a proof of its DoS resistance, or prove that no protocol can satisfy (1)–(3) simultaneously under standard cryptographic assumptions.

Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) overlay network: a distributed system in which autonomous nodes (peers) communicate directly with one another over an underlying packet-switched network (such as the Internet) to share data, route lookups, and forward messages, without relying on a fixed centralized server. A P2P protocol specifies (i) how peers join and leave the overlay, (ii) how they discover and maintain connections to other peers, (iii) how queries, requests, and responses are forwarded, and (iv) how data is published, located, and retrieved.

For such a protocol, define the following adversarial notions:

1. An amplification mechanism is any protocol feature that allows an attacker who sends a request of size s (in bytes, or in number of packets) and consumes effort e (CPU, bandwidth, or state) to cause one or more honest peers, or the protocol as a whole, to generate aggregate traffic of size S ≫ s or effort E ≫ e directed at a target chosen by the attacker. The amplification factor is the ratio S/s (or E/e). A protocol is said to introduce a new amplification mechanism (relative to the bare underlying network) if there exists an attacker strategy whose amplification factor, when measured against a chosen victim (which may be a peer, a non-participant host, or a network link), is strictly larger than what the same attacker could achieve by direct use of the underlying network.

2. A back-door communication channel is any protocol-induced capability that enables an attacker to relay, indirect, or coordinate messages among compromised or colluding nodes (or to reach a victim) in a way that is not available, or is significantly harder to achieve, using the underlying network alone. This includes using overlay routing, caches, or forwarding rules to obscure the origin of attack traffic, to synchronize distributed attackers, or to bypass network-level filtering.

A denial-of-service (DoS) attack against a target T is any attacker strategy that renders T (a peer, a host outside the overlay, or a network resource) unable to provide its normal service to legitimate users for a sustained period.

Problem. Design a P2P protocol Π satisfying the following properties simultaneously, or prove that no such protocol exists:

(a) Functionality: Π supports the standard primitives of a data-sharing P2P system, namely peer join/leave, peer discovery, key-based lookup, and data publication/retrieval, with performance (latency, lookup cost, maintenance overhead) within a constant factor of known efficient overlays.

(b) No new amplification: There exists a constant c ≥ 1 such that for every polynomial-time adversary controlling any constant fraction of peers and any chosen victim T, the amplification factor obtainable via Π (in bandwidth and in computational effort) is at most c. In particular, Π must not enable amplification factors that grow with the size of the overlay.

(c) No back-door channels: For every polynomial-time adversary, any covert relaying, indirection, or coordination capability obtainable through Π can be simulated, up to polynomial overhead, by an adversary with only direct access to the underlying network; equivalently, Π provides no protocol-level capability that materially assists an attacker in scaling or coordinating a DoS attack beyond what is possible at the network layer.

(d) Robustness: Properties (b) and (c) must hold under realistic adversarial conditions, including Sybil identities, churn, and partial compromise of peers.

Either exhibit a concrete protocol Π meeting (a)–(d) together with a rigorous proof of (b)–(d), or establish an impossibility result showing that any protocol satisfying (a) must violate (b), (c), or (d).

Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) distributed system consisting of a large, dynamic set of autonomous nodes that join and leave the network without central coordination. Nodes communicate by message passing over an overlay network in which secure, complete pairwise connectivity among all participants is not available, individual nodes may exhibit fail-stop behavior (halting unexpectedly) or Byzantine behavior (deviating arbitrarily and possibly maliciously from the prescribed protocol), and message overhead and protocol complexity directly impact system performance.

Classical fault-tolerance techniques developed for fail-stop and Byzantine-failure models in tightly coupled distributed systems (such as state-machine replication via Byzantine agreement, quorum-based replication, and cryptographic group protocols) typically assume reliable channels, bounded participant sets, and authenticated all-to-all communication, and they incur high message and computational overhead.

Problem: Design protocols, or prove impossibility results, for adapting fail-stop and Byzantine-failure fault-tolerance techniques to the P2P setting described above so that the resulting mechanisms are simultaneously:
(i) acceptable in performance, i.e., the message complexity, latency, and computational cost scale to large dynamic populations of peers; and
(ii) acceptable in security, i.e., they tolerate a non-trivial fraction of Byzantine peers in the absence of secure complete pairwise connectivity.

Specifically, exhibit a Byzantine-tolerant P2P protocol that provides guarantees analogous to classical Byzantine agreement or replicated state machines while meeting (i) and (ii), or establish lower bounds showing such guarantees are unattainable in the P2P model.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer, and let $\Omega_n$ denote the set of $n \times n$ doubly stochastic matrices, i.e., matrices $A = (a_{ij})$ with nonnegative real entries such that every row sum and every column sum equals $1$. For a matrix $A \in \Omega_n$, define its permanent by
$$\operatorname{per}(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $J_n$ denote the $n \times n$ matrix all of whose entries equal $1/n$.

It is known that for every $A \in \Omega_n$,
$$\operatorname{per}(A) \geq \frac{n!}{n^n},$$
with equality if and only if $A = J_n$.

Produce a proof of this inequality (and of the equality case) that proceeds entirely by techniques of constrained optimization. Specifically, view $\operatorname{per}$ as the objective function on the convex polytope $\Omega_n$ (a multilinear form in the rows and columns), and derive the bound using only constrained-optimization tools such as Lagrange multipliers and first-, second-, or higher-order necessary/sufficient optimality conditions at critical points of $\operatorname{per}$ on $\Omega_n$, without appealing to algebraic identities, hyperbolic polynomial theory, geometric programming duality, or other non-optimization machinery.

The Van der Waerden inequality itself is a theorem (Egorychev 1981, Falikman 1981), with subsequent simplifications by Gyires, Bapat, and others, and a geometric-programming approach by Gurvits. However, the specific request for a proof relying purely on higher-order constrained-optimality conditions for the multilinear objective on the doubly stochastic polytope does not appear to have a clearly documented affirmative answer in the literature; existing "optimization" proofs (geometric programming, hyperbolic polynomials) use additional algebraic structure beyond optimality conditions. Status of this precise question is unclear from the search.

Consider a distributed peer-to-peer data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic network of nodes (peers), where at any given time only an unpredictable subset of nodes is online. Each file f in the system is stored at some collection of nodes, and a user requesting f succeeds if and only if at least one node currently online holds a retrievable copy (or sufficient encoded fragments) of f. Each document $d \in \mathcal{D}$ has an associated cryptographic-style signature $\sigma(d)$ drawn from a signature space $\Sigma$, but peers may return spurious, corrupted, mislabeled, or adversarially substituted documents in response to $q$.

When a user issues query $q$ and receives a multiset $R(q) \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ of returned documents from the network, design and analyze a mechanism that determines which elements of $R(q)$ belong to $A(q)$. Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer file-sharing network in which there is no trusted central authority. Each participating node may publish files and may cast votes attesting to the authenticity (i.e., the correctness of content and provenance) of files offered by other nodes. The collective authenticity judgment for a file is to be derived from the votes cast by the nodes.

Design a voting-based authenticity protocol for this setting that simultaneously achieves the following three security properties, under realistic adversarial assumptions in which a bounded fraction of nodes may be malicious and may collude:

1. Vote unforgeability: an adversary cannot inject votes that were not actually cast by legitimate, distinct participating nodes, nor duplicate, replay, or alter genuine votes.

2. Node non-spoofing (Sybil resistance): an adversary cannot create or impersonate an unbounded number of pseudonymous nodes in order to amplify its voting weight or impersonate honest participants.

3. File non-spoofing: an adversary cannot cause a file with different content to be accepted under the identifier or name of a genuine file, i.e., the file-to-identifier binding used in voting must be tamper-evident.

The problem is to specify identity, naming, and vote-aggregation mechanisms (and to prove their security) such that all three properties hold while still allowing the distributed set of participants to collectively determine file authenticity without relying on a trusted third party.

Consider a peer-to-peer data-sharing system modeled as a dynamic distributed network in which a set of autonomous peers store data objects and respond to queries from other peers. Each peer may act as a publisher, a requester, or a forwarder. Define the following desiderata for such a system:

(1) Anonymity: there exists a precise indistinguishability-style guarantee (for example, publisher anonymity, requester anonymity, and/or unlinkability between requesters and the content they retrieve) that holds against a global passive adversary, or at least against an adversary that controls a constant fraction of peers and observes all network traffic adjacent to those peers.

(2) Efficiency: queries are resolved using poly-logarithmic (in the number of peers and objects) communication, latency, and per-peer storage and bandwidth overhead.

(3) Decentralization: no peer or fixed set of peers is required to participate in every query or to hold global state; all operations are symmetric across peers up to local resources.

(4) Peer discovery and content location: any peer can, starting from limited local knowledge, discover other participating peers and successfully locate any content that is published in the system, with high probability.

Question: Does there exist a protocol for such a peer-to-peer data-sharing system that simultaneously satisfies properties (1), (2), (3), and (4), or is there an inherent trade-off (provable lower bound) showing that some pair among anonymity, efficiency, decentralization, and discoverability cannot be jointly achieved?

Consider a peer-to-peer network: a distributed system consisting of a dynamic collection of nodes (peers) that jointly store a set of documents, with each document replicated on some subset of nodes (its "servers"). Users issue queries naming a document, and the system must locate and retrieve a copy. We say that the system provides:

(i) Server anonymity: for any document D in the system, no participant (other than a server of D itself) and no external observer can determine, with non-negligible advantage over random guessing, which nodes store D, even given the ability to issue queries and observe network traffic.

(ii) Efficient search: any document present in the system can be located by a query whose total communication and computation cost is bounded by a polylogarithmic function (or, more weakly, a sublinear function) of the number of nodes N, ruling out flooding/broadcast-style search whose cost is Ω(N).

Design a peer-to-peer protocol (specifying the routing/indexing structure, the placement of documents, and the search procedure) that simultaneously achieves (i) and (ii), or prove that no such protocol exists under a specified adversary model.

Consider a peer-to-peer network modeled as a graph G=(V,E) whose nodes are participants and whose edges represent communication links. An anonymity protocol on G is a randomized routing scheme in which a message originating at a source s in V is forwarded to a destination d in V through a sequence of intermediate proxy nodes, with the goal that no observer can determine the identity of the sender (sender anonymity), the receiver (receiver anonymity), or the linkage between them (relationship anonymity). Formalize an adversary model in which a subset C of the proxy nodes is actively malicious and colluding: the adversary controls the nodes in C, can observe all traffic passing through them, can drop, delay, replay, or inject messages, and can share all observations among the nodes in C. Quantify anonymity by a measure such as the entropy of the posterior distribution that the adversary assigns to the identity of the sender (or to the sender–receiver pair) given its observations, or by the probability that the adversary correctly identifies the sender.

(a) Give tight upper and lower bounds, as a function of |C|/|V|, of the network topology, and of the protocol parameters (e.g., path length, mixing strategy, cover-traffic rate), on the anonymity provided by representative anonymity protocols for peer-to-peer systems (such as Crowds-style probabilistic forwarding, onion-routing/Tor-like layered encryption, and DC-net-based broadcast schemes) under the above active colluding-proxy adversary.

(b) Determine whether there exists a protocol that, under such active colluding adversaries controlling a constant fraction of proxy nodes, preserves a non-trivial level of sender, receiver, and relationship anonymity (e.g., adversary success probability bounded away from 1 by a constant, or anonymity-set size growing with |V|), and exhibit such a protocol or prove its impossibility.

Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) data-sharing system in which a collection of autonomous peers store, replicate, and exchange documents without a central server. Each document has an owner who wishes to enforce access rights (e.g., read, write, redistribute) over copies of the document held by other peers. Two architectural approaches are available:

(a) Network-level enforcement: the P2P overlay itself (its routing, storage, and replication protocols) is responsible for ensuring that only authorized peers can obtain or operate on a document.

(b) Endpoint enforcement: documents are protected cryptographically (e.g., encrypted or wrapped with policy-bound keys), and access control is enforced only at the endpoints that consume the document, with the network treated as untrusted transport and storage.

Formulate a precise model that specifies:
1. A trust model for peers (honest, honest-but-curious, Byzantine, or colluding adversaries) and for the underlying overlay.
2. A key-management model (who generates, distributes, revokes, and stores cryptographic keys; whether a public-key infrastructure, threshold scheme, or purely peer-managed keys are used).
3. A precise definition of "enforcing access rights," including persistence of rights against copying, revocation, and offline use.

Under this model, determine necessary and sufficient assumptions on trust and key management under which each of approaches (a) and (b) can correctly enforce the specified access-control policy, and characterize the regimes (if any) in which one approach is strictly preferable to the other, or in which a hybrid scheme is required.

Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer data-sharing system, modeled as a dynamic network of autonomous nodes that can publish, replicate, and retrieve digital objects without relying on a central trusted authority. Assume each digital object carries a set of usage policies (e.g., restrictions on copying, redistribution, modification, time-limited access, and payment obligations) specified by its rights holder. Design and analyze a concrete protocol (or family of protocols) that equips such a peer-to-peer system with mechanisms for intellectual-property management and digital-rights management, satisfying at least the following requirements:

1. Policy binding: every replicated copy of an object remains cryptographically bound to its usage policy.
2. Enforcement: participating peers can verify and enforce the declared policies before granting access, with provable security guarantees against a defined adversary model (e.g., a constant fraction of colluding malicious peers).
3. Decentralization: no single trusted third party is required for routine policy verification, key distribution, or access control.
4. Accountability: violations (unauthorized copying or redistribution) can be detected and attributed with non-trivial probability.
5. Scalability: protocol overhead (communication, storage, cryptographic operations per access) grows at most polylogarithmically in the number of peers and objects.

Determine whether a protocol meeting all five requirements simultaneously is feasible. If feasible, exhibit such a protocol and prove its correctness, security, and scalability bounds; if not, prove an impossibility result identifying which subset of the requirements can and cannot be jointly satisfied in the stated model.

Design a shared context protocol for wireless distributed communities of mobile devices and services with the following requirements:

1. (Scope) The protocol must operate with near-ubiquitous scope, rather than being confined to a single local transport mechanism or a service-discovery layer (such as Bluetooth's service discovery).

2. (Dimensions) The protocol must expose a fixed, well-understood collection of context dimensions (e.g., identity, location, capability, availability, trust, time, environment) through which mobile devices and fixed or mobile services can mutually interpret one another's state and intent.

3. (Permeation) The architecture must allow context information to permeate every layer of both device software and the surrounding service infrastructure, so that context is not encapsulated as a narrowly local mechanism but is accessible and consistent at all layers of implementation.

4. (Interaction model) Specify how mobile devices and services interact through these context dimensions: the messages exchanged, the consistency guarantees on shared context across heterogeneous wireless transports, and the way services discover, negotiate, and adapt to context.

The problem is to give an architecture and protocol specification meeting (1)–(4), together with a justification that it generalizes existing local context handling (such as service-discovery-layer approaches) while preserving interoperability across wireless transports and service infrastructures.

Consider a distributed community modeled as a dynamic set of participants P(t) interacting over a peer-to-peer (non-centralized) communication network, together with a shared context state S(t) (e.g., shared documents, conventions, histories, or knowledge artifacts) that evolves over time. Design a membership-management protocol/framework that simultaneously satisfies all of the following requirements:

1. Awareness. Every current participant p ∈ P(t) can discover the existence of the community and obtain a verifiable view of the other current participants, despite the absence of a central directory.

2. Join and leave. There are well-defined mechanisms by which a new participant may join P(t) and by which an existing participant may leave, such that the resulting transitions are consistent across the views held by other participants under realistic network conditions (asynchrony, partitions, churn).

3. Contribution expectations. The protocol specifies, communicates, and (where appropriate) enforces the ways in which participants are expected to contribute to the community, so that each member has an unambiguous understanding of their role.

4. Privacy. Participants retain control over personal data and over data they generate within the community; the mechanisms used for awareness, join/leave, and contribution must not require disclosing information beyond what each participant explicitly authorizes.

5. Onboarding into shared context. When a participant joins at time t, there is a procedure that introduces them to a faithful and sufficient representation of S(t), enabling them to interact meaningfully with existing members.

Formulate such a protocol, give a precise model in which the five requirements can be stated, and either exhibit a construction satisfying all five simultaneously or prove an impossibility result delineating the achievable trade-offs.

1. Every interaction of types (i)–(iv), whether mediated by the shared context or initiated outside it, can be incorporated into a single coherent shared context maintained by the community.
2. From the standpoint of any individual participant, the infrastructure is transparent: the participant need not be aware of the particular device or device capabilities used by other participants, of the geographic location of any participant or resource, or of the underlying structural representation of the information being exchanged.
3. The infrastructure supports different communication styles appropriate to the purpose of each interaction (collaborative, informational, or social).

Specify the components, abstractions, and guarantees of such an infrastructure, and justify that the three requirements above hold.

Consider a peer-to-peer distributed network in which each participating community shares a common "context," modeled as a tuple of values along a finite set of dimensions D = {d_1, ..., d_n}. The state of the context evolves over time as participants modify values along these dimensions, producing a stream of context-change events. Maintaining a complete log of every context change across the network is infeasible due to serialization and archival overhead.

Develop a formal framework for selective context history preservation. Specifically:

(a) Define what it means for a subset S ⊆ D of dimensions to be "archivable" by a community C, and propose a precise notion of "utility" U(H, Q) of a stored history H with respect to a class Q of queries or reconstructions that members of C may wish to perform later.

(b) Define a snapshot policy as a function π that, given the current context state and the recent change stream, decides at each change event whether to record a snapshot of a chosen subset S ⊆ D. Formulate the problem of finding a policy π that maximizes expected utility E[U(H_π, Q)] subject to a bound B on expected storage/communication overhead per unit time.

(c) Identify conditions on the change process (e.g., as a stochastic process on the dimension values) and on Q under which an optimal or approximately optimal policy exists, and characterize how the optimal policy depends on the community C, the dimension subset S, and the trigger dimensions whose changes initiate snapshots.

(d) Show that different communities, given different query classes Q and overhead budgets B, may rationally adopt different policies, and provide a method for each community to select its own (S, π) pair without global coordination while preserving sufficient cross-community utility.

Consider a distributed community of computational participants that maintains a shared "context" — a body of information (e.g., location, preferences, sensor data, presence, identity attributes) collected from and distributed among the participants. Design a formal framework for such a shared context that cleanly separates and simultaneously supports the following three concerns, and prove that the framework satisfies precise guarantees in each:

1. Basic security: specify the cryptographic mechanisms and protocols (encryption schemes, authentication, key management) that keep context information confidential against an adversary with a stated capability (e.g., a Dolev–Yao or computationally bounded eavesdropper), and prove standard confidentiality/integrity guarantees.

2. Privacy: specify a policy language and enforcement mechanism that determines, for each item of context information and each potential recipient, whether sharing is permitted according to the originating user's stated preferences; prove that any release of information by the system is consistent with these policies (a noninterference- or policy-compliance-style theorem).

3. Trust: specify system properties and supporting protocols (e.g., attestation, provenance, reputation, verifiable computation) that allow a user to justifiably believe (a) that their stated privacy preferences are being honored by other participants and the infrastructure, and (b) that the context information they receive from others is correct; formalize this as a soundness/accuracy guarantee under a stated adversary model.

The problem asks: produce such a framework in which the three concerns are treated as independent, composable layers, give precise definitions of the security, privacy-compliance, and trust/correctness properties, and exhibit concrete mechanisms together with theorems establishing each property within a single distributed-community model.

Consider a dynamic distributed community modeled as a time-varying set of autonomous nodes that may join, leave, or become temporarily unreachable, and that exchange shared context information (state describing the participants and their interactions). Assume there is no centralized or globally well-known transaction manager available, and no a priori designated coordinator can be guaranteed to be reachable.

Design and analyze a framework for replication and consistency of the shared context information in such a community. Specifically:

1. Specify a set of mechanisms, communication protocols, and data formats by which nodes exchange shared context information.
2. Provide a decision procedure that determines, for each item of shared information, whether it should be replicated, how it should be replicated (e.g., full copy, partial copy, encoded fragments), and where (on which subset of nodes) replicas should reside, as a function of the current community membership, connectivity, and access patterns.
3. Prove that the resulting scheme simultaneously achieves:
   (a) improved availability and persistence of shared information relative to a non-replicated baseline,
   (b) a well-defined and tractable consistency guarantee (to be specified by the solution, e.g., eventual consistency, causal consistency, or a stronger criterion) that does not rely on the existence of centralized or well-known transaction managers, and
   (c) bounded resource overhead (communication, storage, and reconciliation cost) under realistic models of node churn and intermittent connectivity.

The problem is to exhibit such a framework together with the protocols, decision rules, and formal guarantees, or to prove impossibility results that delineate which combinations of availability, persistence, and consistency are achievable in this transaction-manager-free dynamic setting.

Consider a distributed community modeled as a tuple (A, I, C_t) where A is a set of autonomous agents (individuals), I is a set of permissible interactions among subsets of A, and C_t is a shared context at time t — formalized as a structured collection of facts, norms, protocols, and resources that all agents in A reference when interacting. The context evolves over discrete time steps as a sequence (C_t)_{t \ge 0}. Three classes of update events are distinguished:

(i) External updates: changes that originate outside C_t (for example, from the environment or from agent behavior that is not currently expressible within C_t) and that must be reflected back into C_{t+1}.
(ii) Individual updates: changes to C_t initiated by a single agent a ∈ A.
(iii) Interaction-driven updates: changes to C_t that arise either from a single interaction i ∈ I, or as a self-adaptation derived from an observed sequence of interactions (i_1, i_2, …, i_k).

Design a formal framework, together with update operators U_ext, U_ind, U_int, and U_seq acting on the space of contexts, that:

(a) specifies how external changes are detected and "drawn back" into the context (i.e., gives a procedure C_{t+1} = U_ext(C_t, e) for an external event e that guarantees consistency of C_{t+1} with both the prior context and the observed event);
(b) specifies how individual and interaction-level updates compose with one another while preserving a chosen notion of community-level consistency;
(c) specifies how self-adaptations derived from sequences of interactions are integrated, with provable convergence or stability properties as t → ∞.

State and justify what properties (consistency, monotonicity, convergence, fairness across agents) such a framework should satisfy, and exhibit a concrete instantiation that realizes them.

Let $\{X(t):t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ be a centered Gaussian stochastic process with stationary increments, almost surely continuous sample paths, and variance function $\sigma_X^2(t)=\mathrm{Var}(X(t))$. Fix a constant output rate $c>0$ such that the associated fluid queue is stable, and let $\{Q(t):t\geq 0\}$ denote the stationary buffer content (workload) process defined by

Fix a service rate $c>0$ such that $\mathbb{E} X(t) - ct \to -\infty$ as $t\to\infty$ (so that the queue is stable), and define the stationary buffer content
$$Q \;\stackrel{d}{=}\; \sup_{s \ge 0}\bigl(X(s) - cs\bigr).$$
Assume that the system starts empty at time $0$, so the transient buffer content at time $t>0$ satisfies
$$Q^{tr}(t) \;\stackrel{d}{=}\; \sup_{s \in [0,t]}\bigl(X(s) - cs\bigr).$$
For a fixed threshold $u>0$, define
$$\gamma(u,t) \;:=\; \mathbb{P}(Q > u) \;-\; \mathbb{P}(Q^{tr}(t) > u).$$
Determine the exact asymptotic behavior of $\gamma(u,t)$ as $t \to \infty$, with $u$ held fixed; that is, find an explicit function $f(u,t)$ such that $\gamma(u,t) \sim f(u,t)$ as $t \to \infty$.

Let $\{X(t)\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a centered Gaussian process with stationary increments, $X(0)=0$, and continuous sample paths, and let $c>0$ be a constant drift such that the net input process $X(t)-ct$ has negative drift. Define the stationary Gaussian fluid queue workload
$$Q(t)=\sup_{s\le t}\bigl(X(t)-X(s)-c(t-s)\bigr),\qquad t\in\mathbb{R},$$
and the corresponding transient workload starting empty at time $0$,
$$Q^{tr}(t)=\sup_{0\le s\le t}\bigl(X(t)-X(s)-c(t-s)\bigr),\qquad t\ge 0.$$
Assume the stationary distribution of $Q$ exists. For $u>0$ and $t\ge 0$ set
$$\gamma(u,t)=\mathbb{P}(Q>u)-\mathbb{P}(Q^{tr}(t)>u),$$
and define the relaxation-to-stationarity metrics
$$D_1(t)=\sup_{u>0}\gamma(u,t),\qquad D_2(t)=\int_0^\infty \gamma(u,t)\,du.$$
Let
$$K=\inf\{s\ge 0:Q(s)=0\}-\sup\{s\le 0:Q(s)=0\}$$
denote the length of the ongoing busy period at time $0$ in the stationary regime.

Determine the exact asymptotics, as $t\to\infty$, of each of the three quantities $D_1(t)$, $D_2(t)$, and $\mathbb{P}(K>t)$; that is, find explicit functions $f_1,f_2,f_3$ such that $D_1(t)\sim f_1(t)$, $D_2(t)\sim f_2(t)$, and $\mathbb{P}(K>t)\sim f_3(t)$ as $t\to\infty$.

Let $\eta=\{\eta(t):t\ge 0\}$ be a centered Gaussian process with stationary increments, almost surely continuous sample paths, $\eta(0)=0$, and variance function $\sigma_\eta^2(t)=\mathrm{Var}(\eta(t))$. For $T>0$, define
$$H_\eta(T) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\,\exp\!\Big(\max_{t\in[0,T]}\big(\sqrt{2}\,\eta(t)-\sigma_\eta^2(t)\big)\Big),$$
and assume the limit
$$H_\eta \;=\; \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{H_\eta(T)}{T}$$
exists in $(0,\infty)$; this number is called the generalized Pickands constant associated with $\eta$.

The classical Pickands constant $\mathcal{H}_\alpha$ corresponds to the case $\eta(t)=B_\alpha(t)$, a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $\alpha/2\in(0,1]$, in which case $\sigma_\eta^2(t)=t^\alpha$. For general admissible $\eta$, only crude bounds on $H_\eta$ are known, and explicit values are available only in isolated cases (e.g.\ $\mathcal{H}_1=1$, $\mathcal{H}_2=1/\sqrt{\pi}$).

Problem: Find new equivalent characterizations or representations of the generalized Pickands constant $H_\eta$ (for instance, as expectations not involving a limit, variational formulas, or expressions in terms of auxiliary stochastic processes) that yield sharper quantitative estimates—upper bounds, lower bounds, or asymptotic expansions—for $H_\eta$ than those currently available.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The folklore identity $\mathcal{H}_\alpha = 1/\Gamma(1/\alpha)$ (with $\alpha = 2H$) was disproved by A. J. Harper (Bernoulli, 2017; arXiv:1404.5505) for all sufficiently small $\alpha$, where he showed $\mathcal{H}_\alpha \ge (1.1527)^{1/\alpha}/\Gamma(1/\alpha)$. This corresponds to $H$ close to $0$, outside the range $H \in [1/2,1)$ for standard fractional Brownian motion. For the actual Hurst range $H \in [1/2,1)$ (equivalently $\alpha \in [1,2)$) the conjecture has not been confirmed nor refuted; simulation evidence is often cited as suggesting it is not exact, but no rigorous resolution in this range appears in the literature.

It is known that the limit
   H_η = lim_{T → ∞} H_η(T)/T
exists in (0, ∞); this is the generalized Pickands constant associated with η.

The problem is to construct a provably reliable and computationally efficient simulation (Monte Carlo) algorithm that produces consistent estimates of H_η with quantifiable error (bias and variance) for the whole class of admissible Gaussian processes η described above. The algorithm should avoid the instability of naive Monte Carlo schemes based directly on the ratio H_η(T)/T (whose variance blows up as T grows, while bias decreases), and should come with rigorous error bounds and a clear prescription for choosing its tuning parameters.

Let $(X,Y)$ be a random pair taking values in $\mathbb{R}^d \times \{1,2,\dots,M\}$ with joint distribution $P$, where $X$ is the feature vector and $Y$ is the class label. Given an i.i.d. training sample $\mathcal{D}_n = \{(X_1,Y_1),\dots,(X_n,Y_n)\}$ drawn from $P$, and an integer $k \ge 1$, the $k$-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) decision rule classifies a query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ by majority vote among the labels $Y_{(1)}(x),\dots,Y_{(k)}(x)$ of the $k$ training points whose features $X_i$ are closest to $x$ under the Euclidean metric (ties broken in a fixed way). Let
$$P_e[\text{k-NN}](n) \;=\; \Pr\!\big(g_{n,k}(X) \neq Y\big)$$
denote the probability of error of the k-NN rule (where $g_{n,k}$ is the classifier built from $\mathcal{D}_n$), and let
$$P_e^* \;=\; \inf_{g} \Pr(g(X) \neq Y)$$
denote the Bayes error (the infimum over all measurable classifiers $g:\mathbb{R}^d \to \{1,\dots,M\}$).

(a) Determine the rate at which $P_e[\text{k-NN}](n) - P_e^*$ tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$ (with $k=k(n)$ chosen suitably, e.g.\ $k(n)\to\infty$ and $k(n)/n \to 0$), in terms of natural assumptions on the underlying distribution $P$ (smoothness/Lipschitz conditions on the regression function $\eta(x) = \Pr(Y=1\mid X=x)$, margin conditions, and dimension $d$).

(b) Provide non-asymptotic (finite-sample) bounds on $P_e[\text{k-NN}](n) - P_e^*$ as a function of $n$, $k$, and the distributional parameters.

Substantial progress has been made on this classical question. Under margin (Tsybakov-type) and smoothness assumptions on the regression function, both asymptotic rates such as $O(k^{-(1+\alpha)/2}) + O((k/n)^{(\alpha+1)/d})$ and finite-sample/minimax-optimal bounds (e.g.\ $O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$ with local choice of $k$) have been established by Chaudhuri–Dasgupta, Samworth, Gadat–Klein–Marteau, Döring–Györfi–Walk and others. General consistency ($P_e[\text{k-NN}]\to P_e^*$ when $k\to\infty,\ k/n\to 0$) is classical (Stone, 1977). Sharp rates without distributional assumptions or under minimal assumptions remain an active research area, so the question is partially solved.

The question of how to choose the neighborhood size $k$ in $k$-NN classification optimally and in a fully data-driven way remains an active research area. Cross-validation is standard practice but is known to suffer from multiple minimizers of the estimated misclassification rate, and the theoretically optimal $k$ depends on unknown quantities (dimension, smoothness, class-conditional densities, sample proportions). Various proposals (Bayesian, smoothed CV, adaptive $k$) exist, but no universally accepted optimal data-driven rule has been established.

This is the second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture (1923). Hensley and Richards (1973) showed it is incompatible with the prime k-tuples conjecture, so it is widely believed to be false, although no explicit counterexample is known. Udrescu (1975) proved it for sufficiently large x, y (without effective bounds). A 2021 arXiv preprint by Visser claims an unconditional proof using effective bounds, but this is not generally accepted given the tension with the k-tuples conjecture, and the problem is still typically regarded as open.

Let $(X,Y)$ be a random pair taking values in $\mathbb{R}^d \times \{1,\dots,c\}$ with unknown joint distribution, and let $\mathcal{D}_n = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be an i.i.d. sample from this distribution. For a query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a fixed integer $k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, let $x_{(1)}(x),\dots,x_{(k)}(x)$ denote the $k$ nearest neighbors of $x$ in $\mathcal{D}_n$ under a chosen metric $\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with corresponding labels $y_{(1)}(x),\dots,y_{(k)}(x)$ and distances $d_i(x) = \rho(x, x_{(i)}(x))$. A weighted $k$-nearest-neighbor rule assigns nonnegative weights $w_1(x),\dots,w_k(x)$ (possibly depending on $x$, on the distances $d_i(x)$, or on the index $i$) and classifies $x$ as
$$\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_{j \in \{1,\dots,c\}} \sum_{i=1}^{k} w_i(x)\,\mathbf{1}\{y_{(i)}(x) = j\}.$$
The uniform rule corresponds to $w_i(x) \equiv 1/k$.

Address the following: Is the uniform weighting $w_i \equiv 1/k$ optimal for minimizing the classification risk $P(\hat{Y}(X) \neq Y)$, or does there exist a weighting scheme $\{w_i(x)\}$ that strictly improves on it? In the latter case, give a principled prescription for choosing the weights $w_i(x)$ — as a function of the index $i$, the neighbor distances $d_i(x)$, the sample size $n$, the dimension $d$, the number of classes $c$, and properties of the underlying distribution — and characterize the optimality criterion (e.g., minimizing asymptotic or finite-sample misclassification probability, or excess risk over the Bayes rule) that the prescription satisfies.

Let $2 = p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ denote the sequence of all prime numbers in increasing order, and for each positive integer $n$ set $d_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$ (the $n$th prime gap). Answer the following two questions about the sequence $(d_n)_{n \ge 1}$:

(a) Do there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ for which $d_n = d_{n+1}$, i.e., two consecutive prime gaps coincide?

(b) Are there infinitely many positive integers $n$ for which three consecutive prime gaps form a strictly monotone run, in the sense that $d_n < d_{n+1} < d_{n+2}$? Equivalently (and more weakly), do there exist infinitely many $n$ for which either $d_n < d_{n+1} < d_{n+2}$ or $d_n > d_{n+1} > d_{n+2}$ holds?

Part (b) on strictly monotone runs of three (and in fact arbitrarily many) consecutive prime gaps was resolved by Banks, Freiberg, and Turnage-Butterbaugh (2015), who used the Maynard–Tao machinery to prove that for every m ≥ 1 there are infinitely many n with d_n < d_{n+1} < ⋯ < d_{n+m}, and similarly for decreasing runs. Consider an instance-based (lazy) learning rule that classifies a query point x ∈ ℝ^n by comparing it to a stored set of labeled training instances {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N using a parameterized distance of the form

   d_w(x, x') = ( Σ_{j=1}^n w_j · ρ(x_j, x'_j) )^{1/2},

where w = (w_1, …, w_n) is a vector of nonnegative feature weights and ρ is a per-feature dissimilarity (e.g. squared difference for numeric features, 0/1 mismatch for symbolic features). The prediction at x is obtained from the labels of the nearest stored instances under d_w (e.g. by k-nearest-neighbor voting).

Address the following:

(a) Determine whether the uniform choice w_1 = w_2 = … = w_n (equal weighting of all measured features/attributes) is, in general, an appropriate choice for such a learning rule, in the sense of minimizing expected generalization error over arbitrary learning problems.

(b) If equal weighting is not appropriate, provide a principled, general method for selecting the weight vector w from the training data (and any available prior information about feature relevance), and justify the choice by characterizing the class of problems on which the method yields provably good predictive performance.

Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ denote the sequence of prime numbers in increasing order, and for each positive integer $n$ define the prime gap $d_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$. Establish the following two assertions:

(a) Show that
$$\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{d_n}{\log n} = 0,$$
i.e. that the ratio of consecutive prime gaps to the average gap size $\log n$ has infimum limit zero.

(b) Show the twin prime conjecture: there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $d_n = 2$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (a) was solved by Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım in 2005, who proved that liminf d_n/log n = 0. Subsequent work by Zhang (2013), Maynard (2013), and the Polymath8 project proved that liminf d_n is finite (currently known to be at most 246), but the twin prime conjecture (part b), that d_n = 2 infinitely often, remains open.

Consider instance-based (memory-based) learning, in which a training set $S = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ is stored, and predictions at a query point $x \in \mathcal{X}$ are made from the labels of the $k$ training instances $x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_k}$ minimizing $d(x, x_i)$ for some distance function $d : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. The performance of such a learner (e.g., its generalization error on an unknown data distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$) depends critically on the choice of $d$.

Problem. Provide a principled, general theory for selecting the distance metric $d$ used to determine nearest neighbors in instance-based learning. Specifically:

(a) Identify properties of the data distribution $\mathcal{D}$, the feature space $\mathcal{X}$ (which may mix numeric, ordinal, nominal, and structured attributes), and the target $\mathcal{Y}$ that determine when a given distance $d$ (for example, weighted Minkowski $d_p(x,x') = \big(\sum_j w_j |x_j - x'_j|^p\big)^{1/p}$, Mahalanobis $d_A(x,x') = \sqrt{(x-x')^\top A (x-x')}$ with $A \succeq 0$, value-difference metrics for nominal attributes, or learned metrics) is optimal or near-optimal for $k$-nearest-neighbor prediction.

(b) Give an algorithm that, from the training sample $S$ alone, selects or constructs a distance $d$ whose resulting $k$-NN rule attains generalization error close to $\inf_{d \in \mathcal{F}} \mathrm{err}_{\mathcal{D}}(k\text{-NN}_d)$ over a specified family $\mathcal{F}$ of admissible distances, with finite-sample guarantees.

The question of how to choose the distance metric in nearest-neighbor / instance-based learning is a longstanding open research direction. Many partial answers exist (Mahalanobis metric learning, LMNN, neighborhood components analysis, value-difference metric, deep metric learning, etc.), but no general theory prescribes the optimal metric for arbitrary data, and the problem is still treated as open in the literature on instance-based learning.

Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ denote the sequence of prime numbers, and let $d_k = p_{k+1} - p_k$ denote the $k$-th prime gap.

Prove or disprove: for every pair of positive constants $c_1$ and $c_2$, there exists $n_0 = n_0(c_1, c_2)$ such that for every integer $n > n_0$ one can find an index $k$ and an integer $r$ with
$$k < n, \qquad r > c_2 \log n,$$
and
$$d_{k+i} > c_1 \quad \text{for all } 0 \le i \le r.$$

That is, must every sufficiently large $n$ admit a block of more than $c_2 \log n$ consecutive prime gaps (with starting index below $n$) each exceeding $c_1$, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ may be prescribed arbitrarily in advance?

A sieve-method (Brun) argument establishes that for every $c_1$ there exists some $c_2 = c_2(c_1) > 0$ for which such long runs of large gaps exist, but the stronger statement that $c_2$ may be chosen arbitrarily (independent of $c_1$) does not appear to be settled in the literature surveyed. Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a feature space and let $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \ldots, c\}$ be a finite set of class labels. Suppose we are given a training sample $S = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ drawn from an unknown joint distribution $P$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, where the distribution $P$ may exhibit:

(a) class overlap, meaning that there exist regions $R \subseteq \mathcal{X}$ with $P(Y = j \mid X \in R) > 0$ for more than one class $j$; and

(b) label noise, meaning that each observed label $y_i$ may differ from the true latent class $\tilde y_i$ with some unknown probability.

The standard nearest-neighbor decision rule classifies a query $x \in \mathcal{X}$ by assigning it the label of its nearest training point under a chosen metric $\rho$ on $\mathcal{X}$, namely $\hat{y}(x) = y_{i^*}$ where $i^* \in \arg\min_i \rho(x, x_i)$.

Design a modification of the nearest-neighbor decision rule (allowing, for example, weighting schemes, editing or condensing of $S$, locally adaptive metrics, $k$-NN extensions, reject options, or other geometric devices) that is provably robust to class overlap and label noise in the following sense: as $n \to \infty$, the expected misclassification probability of the modified rule converges to (or stays close to) the Bayes-optimal risk of $P$, even when a positive fraction of labels in $S$ are corrupted and the class-conditional supports overlap. Specify the rule, identify the assumptions on $P$, the noise model, and the metric under which the robustness guarantee holds, and quantify the convergence rate.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The conjectured bound $\sum_{p_k<x}(p_{k+1}-p_k)^2 \ll x\log x$ and the existence of the corresponding normalized limit remain open unconditionally. Selberg (assuming the Riemann Hypothesis) and later authors using pair-correlation type assumptions have obtained partial results on second moments of primes in short intervals (e.g. Heath-Brown, Goldston–Montgomery, Montgomery–Soundararajan), which would imply the conjectured order of magnitude conditionally, but no unconditional proof of the $x\log x$ bound, nor a proof of existence of the limit, is known.

Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a feature space and let $T = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $x_i \in \mathcal{X}$ and $y_i$ a class label be a labeled training set. For a metric $\rho : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, the (1-)nearest-neighbor decision rule is the classifier
$$ f_{T,\rho}(x) \;=\; y_{i^*(x)}, \qquad i^*(x) \in \arg\min_{1 \leq i \leq n} \rho(x, x_i). $$
For any vector $s = (s_1, \dots, s_d) \in (0,\infty)^d$ of positive scale factors, let $D_s : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ denote the diagonal scaling $D_s(x) = (s_1 x_1, \dots, s_d x_d)$, and write $D_s(T) = \{(D_s(x_i), y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$.

Construct, in a fully data-driven way, a decision rule $g_T : \mathbb{R}^d \to \{\text{labels}\}$ depending only on the training set $T$, such that for every training set $T$, every query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and every $s \in (0,\infty)^d$,
$$ g_{D_s(T)}(D_s(x)) \;=\; g_T(x), $$
while $g_T$ retains the nearest-neighbor character (i.e., $g_T(x) = y_{i^*(x)}$ for some training index $i^*(x)$ chosen according to a notion of proximity that is intrinsically determined by $T$). In other words, design a nearest-neighbor classifier whose output is invariant under arbitrary coordinatewise rescalings of the measurements, and specify the proximity / metric construction that achieves this invariance.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Numerous approaches address scale sensitivity of nearest-neighbor classifiers, including feature standardization, Mahalanobis-distance learning, large-margin nearest-neighbor metric learning, and adaptive/dynamic feature-scaling schemes. Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space and let $P = \{p_1, \ldots, p_n\} \subset X$ be a finite set of $n$ points, given in advance and available for preprocessing. For a positive integer $k$, the $k$-nearest-neighbor problem asks, given a query point $q \in X$, to return a subset $N_k(q) \subseteq P$ of size $k$ such that for every $p \in N_k(q)$ and every $p' \in P \setminus N_k(q)$, $d(q,p) \le d(q,p')$.

Design a data structure that, after preprocessing $P$, answers $k$-nearest-neighbor queries efficiently. Specifically, identify schemes that achieve sublinear query time (ideally polylogarithmic in $n$) using only polynomial space and preprocessing, while remaining effective in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces $X = \mathbb{R}^d$ as well as in general metric spaces. Characterize the best achievable trade-offs among space, preprocessing time, and query time for both exact and $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate nearest-neighbor search, and determine whether the "curse of dimensionality" — the apparent impossibility of obtaining query time sublinear in $n$ with space polynomial in $n$ and $d$ for exact nearest neighbors when $d$ is large — can be overcome.

Let $S = \{(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \{1, \dots, k\}$ be a finite labeled training set with all $x_i$ distinct. The nearest-neighbor decision rule $f_S : \mathbb{R}^d \to \{1, \dots, k\}$ is defined (up to ties on a measure-zero set) by
$$f_S(x) = y_{i^*(x)}, \qquad i^*(x) \in \arg\min_{1 \le i \le n} \|x - x_i\|_2.$$
A feedforward neural network is a directed acyclic computational graph whose nodes (neurons) compute, on inputs $z \in \mathbb{R}^m$, an output of the form $\sigma(w^\top z + b)$ for some weights $w \in \mathbb{R}^m$, bias $b \in \mathbb{R}$, and a fixed activation function $\sigma$ (e.g. threshold, ReLU, or sigmoid). The size of the network is the total number of neurons (or, equivalently, one may also count layers, weights, and bit-precision of parameters).

Problem. Determine the smallest feedforward neural network (in terms of number of neurons, depth, and number of parameters) such that, for every finite labeled set $S$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, there exist parameter values making the network compute $f_S$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (except possibly on the measure-zero tie set). More precisely, characterize the minimum size, depth, and weight complexity—as functions of $n$, $d$, and $k$—of a neural network architecture that exactly realizes the nearest-neighbor classifier of any such training set.

Let $\{X, Y\} = \{(x_i, y_i) : 1 \le i \le n\}$ be a training set of $n$ labeled patterns, where each $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and each $y_i$ is a class label drawn from a finite set. For a subset $S \subseteq \{X, Y\}$, define the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_S$ which assigns to a query point $q \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the label of the closest point in $S$ under the Euclidean metric (ties broken by some fixed rule). A subset $C \subseteq \{X, Y\}$ is said to be training-set-consistent if $\mathrm{NN}_C(x_i) = y_i$ for every $i = 1, \ldots, n$.

Hart's Condensed Nearest Neighbor (CNN) rule produces such a consistent subset $C$ by the following procedure: initialize $C$ with one arbitrary labeled pattern; then repeatedly scan the remaining points of $\{X, Y\}$, and for each point $(x_i, y_i)$ for which $\mathrm{NN}_C(x_i) \neq y_i$, add $(x_i, y_i)$ to $C$. Repeat the scanning process until an entire pass through the training set produces no additions to $C$. The output $C$ depends on the order of scanning, but in all cases the naive brute-force implementation of this rule runs in time $O(d n^3)$.

Determine the best possible worst-case time complexity, as a function of $n$ and $d$, for computing a subset $C$ produced by Hart's CNN rule. In particular, by how much can the $O(d n^3)$ bound of the brute-force algorithm be improved?

The general problem of determining the minimum largest element of an $n$-set with distinct subset sums (equivalently, the maximum size of such a set bounded by $N$) remains open. Conway and Guy (1967) gave a construction with largest element $\le 2^{n-2}$, and Bohman (1996, 1998) proved the Conway-Guy sets have distinct subset sums and improved the constant to about $0.22002\cdot 2^n$. Thus existence of $k+2$ such integers $\le 2^k$ is known (and more), but Erdős' asymptotic conjecture that the largest element must be $\ge c\cdot 2^n/\sqrt n$ is still open. The specific question of $k+3$ integers $\le 2^k$ is subsumed by the known constructions for large $k$.

Let $T = \{(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$ be a labeled training set, where $\mathcal{C}$ is a finite set of class labels. For a subset $S \subseteq T$, the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_S : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathcal{C}$ assigns to each point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the label of the element of $S$ closest to $x$ in Euclidean distance (with ties broken by a fixed rule). The subset $S$ is said to be training-set-consistent with respect to $T$ if $\mathrm{NN}_S(x_i) = y_i$ for every $(x_i, y_i) \in T$.

Define the following two-stage reduction procedure on $T$:

1. (Condensed Nearest Neighbor, CNN) Initialize $S \subseteq T$ by Hart's procedure: start with one arbitrarily chosen element of $T$ placed in $S$, then iterate through the remaining points of $T$ (in a fixed order), adding to $S$ any point that is currently misclassified by $\mathrm{NN}_S$; repeat passes over $T$ until no more points are added.

2. (Reduced Nearest Neighbor, RNN, post-processing) Given the output $S$ of step 1, iterate through the points of $S$ (in a fixed order) and remove any point whose removal leaves a subset that is still training-set-consistent with $T$; continue until no further removal is possible. Let $S^\ast \subseteq S$ denote the resulting set.

Determine the computational complexity, as a function of $n$ and $d$, of computing $S^\ast$ from the input $T$.

For a subset $S \subseteq T$, the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_S : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathcal{C}$ assigns to each point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the label of the element of $S$ closest to $x$ in Euclidean distance (with ties broken by a fixed rule). The subset $S$ is said to be training-set-consistent with respect to $T$ if $\mathrm{NN}_S(x_i) = y_i$ for every $(x_i, y_i) \in T$.

Define the following two-stage reduction procedure on $T$:

1. (Condensed Nearest Neighbor, CNN) Initialize $S \subseteq T$ by Hart's procedure: start with one arbitrarily chosen element of $T$ placed in $S$, then iterate through the remaining points of $T$ (in a fixed order), adding to $S$ any point that is currently misclassified by $\mathrm{NN}_S$; repeat passes over $T$ until no more points are added.

2. (Reduced Nearest Neighbor, RNN, post-processing) Given the output $S$ of step 1, iterate through the points of $S$ (in a fixed order) and remove any point whose removal leaves a subset that is still training-set-consistent with $T$; continue until no further removal is possible. Let $S^\ast \subseteq S$ denote the resulting set.

Determine the computational complexity, as a function of $n$ and $d$, of computing $S^\ast$ from the input $T$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Surveys of nearest-neighbor condensation techniques describe RNN as roughly twice as costly as CNN in practice, but no formal tight complexity bound for computing the RNN-reduced consistent subset after CNN post-processing was located in the search. The precise computational complexity appears to remain unresolved in the literature reviewed.

A finite set A of positive integers is called a Sidon set (equivalently, a B_2 set) if all pairwise sums a_i + a_j with a_i, a_j ∈ A (allowing i = j) are distinct. For a positive integer n, define f(n) to be the maximum cardinality of a Sidon set A ⊆ {1, 2, …, n}.

It is classically known that f(n) = (1 + o(1))√n, and more precisely that
   √n − O(n^{1/4}) ≤ f(n) ≤ √n + O(n^{1/4}).

Problem. Determine the sharp asymptotic behavior of f(n) beyond the leading term √n. In particular, prove or disprove that for every ε > 0,
   f(n) = √n + O(n^{ε}),
and more generally identify the true order of the error term f(n) − √n.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of sharp asymptotics of f(n) for Sidon sets in {1,...,n} is a long-standing open problem of Erdős–Turán–Sidon. The best known bounds remain √n − O(n^{1/4}) ≤ f(n) ≤ √n + O(n^{1/4}), with only minor improvements to the constant (e.g., Balogh–Füredi–Roy giving f(n) ≤ √n + 0.998 n^{1/4}). The Erdős conjecture f(n) = √n + O(n^ε) remains unresolved, as recorded on the Erdős Problems catalogue (problem 329).

Setup. Let $S = \{(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$ be a labeled training set, where $\mathcal{C}$ is a finite set of class labels. For a query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a subset $T \subseteq S$, the nearest neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_T(x)$ assigns to $x$ the label of the point in $T$ whose feature vector is closest (in Euclidean distance) to $x$.

A subset $T \subseteq S$ is called consistent with $S$ if $\mathrm{NN}_T(x_i) = y_i$ for every $(x_i, y_i) \in S$. The selective nearest neighbor (SNN) rule produces a minimum-cardinality subset $T^* \subseteq S$ such that, for every $(x_i, y_i) \in S$, the nearest point of $T^*$ to $x_i$ has label $y_i$ and is at least as close to $x_i$ as the nearest neighbor of $x_i$ in $S \setminus \{x_i\}$ (so that selecting $T^*$ preserves the original $1$-NN classification on every training point).

Assume the points $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ are drawn i.i.d. from some reasonable probability distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (e.g., absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on a bounded region, with the labels generated by some measurable rule).

Problem. Prove (or disprove) a rigorous average-case complexity bound of the form
$$\mathbb{E}[\,t_{\mathrm{SNN}}(S)\,] \;=\; O(d\,n^{3}),$$
where $t_{\mathrm{SNN}}(S)$ denotes the running time of a specified algorithm that computes the SNN subset $T^*$ from $S$, and the expectation is taken over the random draw of $S$. More generally, establish theoretical average-case running-time bounds for algorithms implementing the SNN rule.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Erdős, via a probabilistic (random) construction, established the existence of an infinite sequence of positive integers that is an asymptotic additive basis of order 2 such that the representation function $g(n)$ satisfies $c_1 \log n \le g(n) \le c_2 \log n$ for all sufficiently large $n$. This bound is much stronger than $n^{\varepsilon}$, so the original Sidon question is answered affirmatively. The sharper question of whether $g(n)/\log n$ must tend to a limit, and related refinements, remain studied.

Let P be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane (or, more generally, in R^d for some d ≥ 2), and let c : P → {0, 1} be a 2-coloring of P (the two "classes"). A subset S ⊆ P is called training-set consistent (or a consistent subset) if, for every point p ∈ P, every nearest neighbor of p in S (with respect to Euclidean distance) has the same color as p. Equivalently, the nearest-neighbor classifier built from the labeled set (S, c|_S) correctly classifies every point of P.

The minimum consistent subset problem (MCS) asks, given (P, c), to determine a consistent subset S ⊆ P of smallest possible cardinality. It is known that for three or more color classes the corresponding decision problem ("is there a consistent subset of size at most k?") is NP-complete.

Problem: Determine the computational complexity of the minimum consistent subset problem in the two-class case. Specifically, decide whether the decision version of MCS restricted to instances with exactly two colors is NP-complete, polynomial-time solvable, or of some intermediate complexity.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The two-class case was settled by Khodamoradi, Krishnamurti, and Roy (WALCOM 2018, "Consistent Subset Problem with Two Labels"), who proved that the minimum consistent subset problem is NP-complete already for two-colored point sets in R^d for every d ≥ 2, via a reduction from planar rectilinear monotone 3-SAT. Subsequent work (e.g., Biniaz–Cabello–Maheshwari–Smid, Algorithmica 2021) cites this as the resolution of the open two-class case left by Wilfong (1991).

representations.normalized:
Let $S = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite set of $n$ points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space (think of $d$ as large, possibly comparable to $n$). Define the following two proximity graphs on the vertex set $S$:

1. The Gabriel graph $G(S)$: an unordered pair $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge if and only if the closed Euclidean ball whose diameter is the segment $\overline{x_i x_j}$ (i.e. the ball of radius $\|x_i - x_j\|/2$ centered at the midpoint $(x_i+x_j)/2$) contains no other point of $S$ in its interior. Equivalently, $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge iff for every $x_k \in S \setminus \{x_i, x_j\}$,
$$\|x_i - x_j\|^2 \le \|x_i - x_k\|^2 + \|x_j - x_k\|^2.$$

2. The rectangular-influence graph $R(S)$: an unordered pair $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge if and only if the open axis-aligned hyperrectangle (in the coordinate system in which $x_i$ and $x_j$ are taken as a pair of opposite corners) determined by $x_i$ and $x_j$ contains no other point of $S$. Equivalently, $\{x_i, x_j\}$ is an edge iff there is no $x_k \in S\setminus\{x_i,x_j\}$ with each coordinate of $x_k$ strictly between the corresponding coordinates of $x_i$ and $x_j$.

A straightforward brute-force algorithm computes either graph in $O(d\,n^3)$ worst-case time by checking, for each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ candidate edges, the defining condition against all remaining $n-2$ points (each check costing $O(d)$ time).

Question: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that, given any input $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ of $n$ points, computes the Gabriel graph $G(S)$ in worst-case time $o(d\,n^3)$? Likewise, does there exist such an algorithm computing the rectangular-influence graph $R(S)$ in worst-case time $o(d\,n^3)$?

$$\sigma(A) = \inf_{n \ge 1} \frac{|A \cap \{1,2,\dots,n\}|}{n}.$$
For two such sets $A, B$ (each containing $0$), let $A+B = \{a+b : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$ denote their sumset.

A set $B$ of nonnegative integers (containing $0$) is called a Khintchine essential component if for every set $A$ with $0 < \sigma(A) < 1$ one has $\sigma(A+B) > \sigma(A)$.

Question: Does there exist a Khintchine essential component $B$ with the following property? For every function $f:(0,1) \to (0,\infty)$ (i.e., $f(\alpha) > 0$ for all $0 < \alpha < 1$), there exists some set $A$ with $\sigma(A) = \alpha$ for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$ such that
$$\sigma(A+B) < \alpha + f(\alpha).$$
Equivalently: does there exist an essential component $B$ for which no positive function $f$ on $(0,1)$ uniformly witnesses a density increment $\sigma(A+B) \ge \sigma(A) + f(\sigma(A))$ for all $A$ with $\sigma(A) \in (0,1)$?

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $S=\{(x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\}\subset X\times\{1,\dots,c\}$ be a labeled training set. Fix an integer $k\ge 1$ and define the $k$-nearest-neighbor graph $G_k(S)$ on $S$ in which each $x_i$ is connected to its $k$ nearest neighbors in $S\setminus\{x_i\}$ under $d$. For a query point $q\in X$, let $N_k(q)\subseteq S$ denote the set of exact $k$ graph neighbors of $q$ (the $k$ points of $S$ closest to $q$), and let $\hat h_k(q)$ be the classifier that assigns to $q$ the plurality label among $N_k(q)$. Let $\mathcal D$ be an unknown distribution on $X\times\{1,\dots,c\}$ from which $S$ and test points are drawn i.i.d., and let $\mathrm{err}(\hat h_k)=\Pr_{(q,y)\sim\mathcal D}[\hat h_k(q)\ne y]$ denote its classification error.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm $\mathcal A$ which, given $S$, $k$ and a query point $q$, returns a set $\widetilde N_k(q)\subseteq S$ of size $k$ (a possibly approximate set of graph neighbors) using strictly sub-linear time in $n$ per query, and induces a classifier $\tilde h_k$ via plurality vote on $\widetilde N_k(q)$, such that for every distribution $\mathcal D$ and every $n$,
$$\mathrm{err}(\tilde h_k)\le \mathrm{err}(\hat h_k)+\varepsilon(n),$$
with $\varepsilon(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ (or, more strongly, $\varepsilon(n)=0$)? Characterize the conditions on $(X,d)$, on $\mathcal D$, and on the approximation rule used by $\mathcal A$ under which the approximate neighbor computation provably does not adversely affect classification error.

Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a finite set of points in general position. Recall the following proximity graphs on $S$:

- The Gabriel graph $\mathrm{GG}(S)$: vertices $p,q \in S$ are joined by an edge iff the closed disk with diameter $pq$ contains no point of $S \setminus \{p,q\}$.
- The relative-neighborhood graph $\mathrm{RNG}(S)$: $p,q$ are joined iff the lune $\{x : \|x-p\| < \|p-q\|\} \cap \{x : \|x-q\| < \|p-q\|\}$ contains no point of $S \setminus \{p,q\}$.
- The rectangular-influence graph: $p,q$ are joined iff the axis-aligned rectangle having $p$ and $q$ as opposite corners contains no point of $S \setminus \{p,q\}$.

Design data structures and algorithms that maintain each of these three graphs under the operations of inserting a point into $S$ and deleting a point from $S$, with provably efficient (sub-linear amortized or polylogarithmic) update times per operation, while supporting the queries on graph adjacencies needed for rotation-based and related error-estimation procedures used in instance-based learning. Establish the best possible update-time bounds and matching lower bounds.
