Setting. In instance-based (nearest-neighbor type) classification, a training set $T = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ is used directly at prediction time: a query $x \in \mathcal{X}$ is classified using the labels of its nearest neighbors in $T$ under a metric $d$ on $\mathcal{X}$. A condensing algorithm is a procedure $\mathcal{A}$ that outputs a subset (or, more generally, a set of prototypes) $S = \mathcal{A}(T)$ with $|S| \ll |T|$, intended to be used in place of $T$ for nearest-neighbor classification.

Call a labeled training set homogeneous if the class-conditional distributions are well separated and class regions form compact connected clusters with low overlap; call it non-homogeneous otherwise (e.g., classes with overlapping supports, multimodal class regions, varying local density, or high boundary complexity).

For a condensing algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ and a data distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, define its performance to consist of (i) the reduction ratio $|S|/|T|$ and (ii) the generalization accuracy of the nearest-neighbor classifier built on $S = \mathcal{A}(T)$, measured against $\mathcal{D}$.

Problem. Does there exist a single condensing algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that simultaneously achieves high reduction ratio and high generalization accuracy in both the homogeneous and the non-homogeneous regimes, rather than performing well only in one of the two regimes? Equivalently, exhibit such an algorithm together with theoretical or empirical guarantees over both regimes, or prove that no condensing algorithm can be uniformly competitive across both regimes.

Let $N$ be a prime number. Let $H_2^+(N)$ denote the set of normalized weight-2 holomorphic newforms $f$ for the congruence subgroup $\Gamma_0(N)$ whose completed $L$-function $\Lambda(f,s)$ satisfies a functional equation with sign $+1$ (i.e., even functional equation). For each $f \in H_2^+(N)$, let $L(f,s)$ denote its Hecke $L$-function, normalized so that the center of the critical strip is $s=1$ (equivalently, after the shift $s \mapsto s+1/2$, the central value is $L(f,1)$).

It is known that, as $N \to \infty$ through primes, at least $50\%$ of the values $\{L(f,1) : f \in H_2^+(N)\}$ exceed $(\log N)^{-2}$; in particular, at least $50\%$ of these central values are nonzero.

Problem: Prove that, as $N \to \infty$ through primes, strictly more than $50\%$ of the central values $L(f,1)$, for $f \in H_2^+(N)$, are nonzero. That is, show that
$$\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\#\{f \in H_2^+(N) : L(f,1) \neq 0\}}{\#H_2^+(N)} > \frac{1}{2}.$$

Problem: Prove that, as $N \to \infty$ through primes, strictly more than $50\%$ of the central values $L(f,1)$, for $f \in H_2^+(N)$, are nonzero. That is, show that
$$\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\#\{f \in H_2^+(N) : L(f,1) \neq 0\}}{\#H_2^+(N)} > \frac{1}{2}.$$

The 50% non-vanishing result of Iwaniec–Sarnak (Israel J. Math., 2000) remains the benchmark. They showed that breaking the 50% barrier (with central values not too small) would rule out Landau–Siegel zeros, which is why the problem is regarded as very hard. Subsequent works (e.g., on prime power level by Balkanova–Frolenkov and others, and various one-level density investigations) have not surpassed 50% in this family. No proof of strict exceedance of 50% for weight-2 even newforms of prime level appears in the literature.

Let $k$ be a number field and let $V$ be a smooth projective variety over $k$. Let $L$ be an ample line bundle on $V$ equipped with an adelic metric, giving rise to a height function $h_L : V(k) \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$. The associated height zeta function is the Dirichlet-type series
$$Z(V,L;s) \;=\; \sum_{x \in V(k)} h_L(x)^{-s},$$
which converges in some right half-plane whenever $V(k)$ is not too dense. For toric varieties and certain homogeneous spaces, $Z(V,L;s)$ is known to admit a meromorphic continuation with controlled poles, encoding precise asymptotics for the number of rational points of bounded height. However, for general (non-homogeneous) projective varieties $V$, the height zeta function $Z(V,L;s)$ is not expected to have good analytic properties (e.g. meromorphic continuation, functional equation, or a controlled set of poles) comparable to those of classical Hasse–Weil–Serre $L$-functions.

Problem: Construct a class of generating series associated with the pair $(V,L)$ over $k$, different from the naive height zeta function $Z(V,L;s)$, with the following properties:
(a) the series genuinely counts (or weights) the rational points $V(k)$, in a way that recovers meaningful arithmetic information such as asymptotics for points of bounded height;
(b) the series possesses good analytic behavior, including meromorphic continuation to a large region of $\mathbb{C}$, a precise description of its poles, and ideally a functional equation, holding for a class of varieties $V$ broader than toric or homogeneous ones.

This is a programmatic open question in the style of Manin's program on rational points. Refined conjectures (Batyrev–Manin, Peyre, Batyrev–Tschinkel) describe expected leading asymptotics, and height zeta functions have been analyzed for toric varieties, equivariant compactifications of algebraic groups, and certain fibrations. However, no general satisfactory class of "good" generating series for arbitrary non-homogeneous projective varieties is known, and the problem remains open.

The asymptotic growth rate of the Schur numbers remains unresolved. Only finitely many values are known (through S(5)=160, established in 2017 via SAT computation), and current bounds give roughly 3·(3^n−1)/2 ≤ f(n) ≤ O(n!), with no proof of an exponential upper bound nor of the existence of the limit f(n)^{1/n}. Recent literature on Schur and generalized Schur numbers continues to treat both conjectures as open.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ with algebraic closure $\bar k$. Let $X$ be a smooth irreducible curve over $k$, and let $\pi\colon \mathcal{A}\to X$ be an abelian scheme. Denote by $\mathcal{A}(X)$ the group of sections of $\pi$, and let $\Gamma\subseteq \mathcal{A}(X)$ be a finitely generated subgroup. Assume that no nonzero element of $\Gamma$ factors through an abelian subscheme of $\mathcal{A}\to X$ whose fibers are of relative dimension one (equivalently, $\Gamma$ has no nonzero element lying in a one-dimensional abelian subscheme of $\mathcal{A}$ over $X$).

For each geometric point $P\in X(\bar k)$, let $\Gamma_P\subseteq \mathcal{A}_P(\bar k)$ denote the image of $\Gamma$ under the specialization map $\sigma_P\colon \mathcal{A}(X)\to \mathcal{A}_P(\bar k)$ at $P$, and write $\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)$ for the rank of $\Gamma_P$ as a finitely generated abelian group. By Silverman's specialization theorem one has $\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)\ge \mathrm{rank}(\Gamma)$ for all but finitely many $P$.

Prove or disprove: there are only finitely many points $P\in X(\bar k)$ for which
$$\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)=\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma).$$
Equivalently, for all but finitely many $P\in X(\bar k)$ one has $\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma_P)>\mathrm{rank}(\Gamma)$.

For a finite set $S$ of rational primes, a nonzero rational number is called an $S$-unit if every prime appearing (with nonzero exponent) in its factorization belongs to $S$. Define
$$X(S) = \{ x \in \mathbb{Q} : x \text{ and } 1-x \text{ are both } S\text{-units}\},$$
and let
$$N(s) = \max_{|S|=s} |X(S)|,$$
where the maximum is taken over all finite sets $S$ of rational primes of cardinality $s$.

Determine whether there exists a lower bound for $N(s)$ that grows faster than every polynomial in $s$; that is, does there exist a function $f(s)$ with $f(s)/s^k \to \infty$ as $s \to \infty$ for every fixed $k \ge 1$, such that $N(s) \ge f(s)$ for all sufficiently large $s$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Erdős, Stewart and Tijdeman (Compositio Math. 66 (1988), 37–56) proved that there exist arbitrarily large sets $S$ of $s$ primes for which the $S$-unit equation $x+y=1$ has at least $\exp((4+o(1))(s/\log s)^{1/2})$ solutions, which grows faster than every polynomial in $s$. This gives an affirmative answer to the question. Konyagin–Soundararajan and Evertse–Moree–Stewart–Tijdeman later refined and generalized such bounds.

A covering system of congruences is a finite collection of residue classes $a_i \pmod{n_i}$ for $i=1,\dots,k$, with integer moduli $n_i\ge 2$, such that every integer $m$ satisfies $m\equiv a_i \pmod{n_i}$ for at least one $i$. The covering system is called distinct if $n_1<n_2<\dots<n_k$.

Question: Does there exist, for every positive integer $c$, a distinct covering system of congruences $a_i \pmod{n_i}$ ($i=1,\dots,k$) whose moduli all satisfy $n_i>c$? Equivalently, can the least modulus of a distinct covering system be made arbitrarily large?

Question: Does there exist, for every positive integer $c$, a distinct covering system of congruences $a_i \pmod{n_i}$ ($i=1,\dots,k$) whose moduli all satisfy $n_i>c$? Equivalently, can the least modulus of a distinct covering system be made arbitrarily large?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Resolved negatively by Robert Hough (Annals of Math., 2015), who proved that the minimum modulus of any distinct covering system is at most $10^{16}$. Hence such a system does not exist for all sufficiently large $c$. The bound has since been improved to 616{,}000 by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba.

representations.normalized:
Consider a multiserver job queueing system with a fixed number n of identical servers and First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process and are partitioned into finitely many classes indexed by i = 1, 2, …, K. A class-i job arrives with probability p_i (independently of the past), simultaneously requires exactly n_i of the n servers (1 ≤ n_i ≤ n), and, once it begins service, holds those n_i servers for a service duration S_i. Under FCFS, the head-of-line job waits until n_i servers are simultaneously available, at which point it occupies n_i servers for its entire service duration; jobs behind it in the queue cannot leapfrog ahead. Assume the system is stable. The response time T of a job is the elapsed time from its arrival until its service completion.

Specialize to the case in which every job, regardless of class, has the same service-time distribution S_i = S ~ Exp(μ) (independent across jobs). For each fixed n ≥ 3, determine the mean response time E[T] in closed form (as a function of n, the server-need distribution {(n_i, p_i)}, the arrival rate λ, and μ).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Exact closed-form expressions for the mean response time of FCFS multiserver job systems with n ≥ 3 servers remain unknown, even when all job classes share a common exponential service-time distribution. Recent work (Hong–Wang 2021 on sharp waiting-time bounds; Grosof–Scully–Harchol-Balter–Scheller-Wolf 2022 on heavy-traffic optimal scheduling; the finite-skip method; and 2025 lower bounds by Wang–Grosof) provides bounds, asymptotic results in heavy traffic, and stability characterizations, but no exact analysis for general n > 2 has appeared. The problem is consistently described as open in the recent literature.

representations.normalized:
Consider a continuous-time multiserver-job queueing model defined as follows. There are k servers and J classes of jobs. Class-j jobs arrive according to independent Poisson processes with rates λ_j (j = 1, ..., J), each class-j job requires simultaneous use of exactly s_j ∈ {1, ..., k} servers for the entire duration of its service, and class-j service times are i.i.d. samples from a distribution F_j with mean 1/μ_j. Jobs are served in first-come-first-served (FCFS) order: the head-of-line job waits until s_j servers become simultaneously available, and jobs may pass one another only when blocked by capacity. A job in service cannot be preempted, and idle servers cannot work on waiting jobs that need more servers than currently available.

Define the system to be stable if the number-in-system process is positive recurrent. Determine, in closed form, the exact stability region — that is, the set of arrival-rate vectors (λ_1, ..., λ_J) for which the system is stable — as a function of (k, {s_j}, {F_j}, {μ_j}), in the general setting of arbitrarily many classes J ≥ 2 with possibly distinct server requirements s_j and possibly non-exponential service-time distributions F_j.

(Known special cases include: (i) all classes share a common exponential service-time distribution but may have different server requirements; (ii) J = 2 classes with class-dependent exponential service-time distributions. The problem asks for the characterization in the remaining general cases.)

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (a) concerns whether a logarithmic density exists for sets defined by congruence exclusions; the classical Davenport–Erdős theorem establishes the existence of logarithmic density for sets of multiples, and analogous results have been obtained in related settings, but the general congruence-exclusion form stated here does not appear to have a definitive published resolution. Part (b), asking whether every positive-density sequence contains three distinct terms with lcm$(a_i,a_j)=a_r$, was explicitly noted as open by Erdős and is closely related to quasi-primitive-sequence questions still discussed in current literature; no resolution was located.

Recent surveys and research papers on multiserver job queueing models (since approximately 2020) emphasize that performance analysis is tractable mainly in two extreme regimes: the infinite-buffer FCFS model (where only limited stability and asymptotic results exist) and the zero-buffer dropping model (which is analytically tractable). For a positive integer $n$, say that $n$ has a pair of close divisors if there exist divisors $d_1, d_2$ of $n$ with $d_1 < d_2 < 2 d_1$. Let
$$A = \{ n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : n \text{ has divisors } d_1 < d_2 \text{ with } d_2 < 2 d_1 \}.$$
Prove or disprove that $A$ has natural density $1$; equivalently, determine whether
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N} \#\{ n \le N : \exists\, d_1, d_2 \mid n,\ d_1 < d_2 < 2 d_1 \} = 1.$$

Solved affirmatively by H. Maier and G. Tenenbaum, "On the set of divisors of an integer," Inventiones Mathematicae (1984). They proved Erdős's conjecture that almost every integer has two divisors d₁ < d₂ with d₂ < 2 d₁, so the density equals 1.

representations.normalized:
Consider a queueing system with a fixed number $n$ of identical servers. Jobs arrive over time according to some stochastic arrival process. Each job $j$ has an inherent (sequential) size $X_j$ that is unknown at the time of arrival; the sizes $X_j$ are i.i.d. samples from a known distribution $F$ that is not exponential (and in particular need not be memoryless). All jobs share a common speedup function $s:\{1,2,\dots,n\}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ which is concave and sublinear (i.e., $s(k+1)-s(k)$ is non-increasing in $k$ and $s(k)<k\,s(1)$ for $k\ge 2$). If at a given instant a job is allocated $k$ servers, then it processes its remaining inherent work at rate $s(k)$. Allocations may be changed continuously over time, subject to the constraint that the total number of servers allocated to active jobs is at most $n$ (and jobs may be served in parallel, preempted, and reallocated at no cost). The response time of a job is the time between its arrival and its completion.

Determine the server-allocation policy (a mapping from the system state, namely the set of jobs in the system and their ages, to an allocation of the $n$ servers among them) that minimizes the mean response time in steady state.

Recent works (2024–2026) have advanced the theory of optimal scheduling for parallelizable jobs with concave speedup functions, including the Consistent Derivative Ratio rule and SmartFill / General Water-Filling algorithms for known sizes, and ServerFilling-Gittins for unknown sizes in related multiserver-job models. However, none of these works appears to give a definitive solution for the specific setting of unknown inherent sizes drawn from a general (non-exponential) distribution with a common concave sublinear speedup on a fixed number of servers. The status thus appears unresolved in full generality.

representations.normalized:
Let S = { x^2 + y^2 : x, y ∈ ℤ_{≥0} } ⊆ ℤ_{≥0} denote the set of nonnegative integers expressible as a sum of two squares of integers. For an integer n ≥ 1, let g(n) denote the smallest positive integer g such that the open interval (n, n + g) contains at least one element of S.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every constant C > 0, there exists n_0(C) such that for every n ≥ n_0(C), the interval (n, n + C·n^{1/4}) contains an element of S. Equivalently, is it true that g(n) = o(n^{1/4}) as n → ∞?

(b) Prove or disprove the stronger statement: for every ε > 0, there exists n_0(ε) such that for every n ≥ n_0(ε), the interval (n, n + n^ε) contains an element of S. Equivalently, is g(n) = O(n^ε) for every ε > 0?

(b) Prove or disprove the stronger statement: for every ε > 0, there exists n_0(ε) such that for every n ≥ n_0(ε), the interval (n, n + n^ε) contains an element of S. Equivalently, is g(n) = O(n^ε) for every ε > 0?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (a), in the form g(n) = O(n^{1/4}), was established by Bambah and Chowla (1947), who proved that for α > 2√2 and all sufficiently large n the interval [n, n + α n^{1/4}) contains a sum of two squares; explicit improvements have been given by Uchiyama, Shiu, and Jameson. The o(n^{1/4}) refinement and especially the stronger conjecture (b) (gaps of size O(n^ε) for every ε > 0) remain open; current best lower bounds on the largest gap up to X are of order log X (Dietmann–Elsholtz, and improvements c. 2019).

representations.normalized:
Consider a parallel scheduling system with $k$ identical servers (cores) and a stream of jobs arriving over time. Each job $j$ has an inherent size $x_j > 0$, which is fully known to the scheduler at the moment of its arrival. All jobs share a common speedup function $s : [0,k] \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, which is nondecreasing, concave, satisfies $s(0)=0$, and specifies the instantaneous service rate of a job when $a \in [0,k]$ servers are allocated to it. At each time $t$, a scheduler must choose a (possibly time-varying) allocation $(a_j(t))_j$ of the $k$ servers among the jobs currently in the system, where $a_j(t) \ge 0$ and $\sum_j a_j(t) \le k$. A job $j$ that arrives at time $r_j$ departs at the first time $c_j$ such that $\int_{r_j}^{c_j} s(a_j(t))\, \mathrm{d}t = x_j$, and its response time is $T_j = c_j - r_j$.

Determine the allocation policy (possibly preemptive, with full knowledge of remaining sizes and elapsed system state) that minimizes the long-run mean response time $\mathbb{E}[T]$ for jobs arriving according to a Poisson process with arbitrary size distribution, under a common concave speedup function $s$. Specifically, characterize the optimal policy and prove its optimality.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general problem (Poisson arrivals, arbitrary size distribution, general concave speedup) appears largely open. Partial results are known: heSRPT (Berg, Dorsman, Harchol-Balter) gives an optimal allocation minimizing mean slowdown/response time in the all-jobs-present-at-time-0 setting under a common speedup curve, and EQUI is optimal under common speedup with exponential sizes. Recent work (2025) characterizes optimal policies under general concave speedup via a Consistent Derivative Ratio rule, but optimal scheduling for general size distributions with arrivals remains incompletely resolved.

representations.normalized:
Setup. Consider a system with $n$ identical servers and $m$ jobs, all present at time $0$. Each job has an inherent (sequential) size $X_i>0$. There is a common speedup function $s:\{1,2,\dots,n\}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with $s(1)=1$ that is the same for every job: if a job is currently allocated $k$ servers, its remaining size decreases at rate $s(k)$. A scheduling policy is a (possibly time-varying) assignment of nonnegative integers $k_1(t),\dots,k_m(t)$ to the alive jobs at each time $t\ge 0$, subject to $\sum_i k_i(t)\le n$. Let $T_i$ denote the completion time of job $i$ under a given policy. Define the mean response time $\overline{T}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m T_i$ and the mean slowdown $\overline{S}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m T_i/X_i$.

Known special cases. When $s(k)=k^p$ for some $p\in(0,1]$, and when $s$ is a "threshold" speedup of the form $s(k)=k$ for $k\le k^\ast$ and $s(k)=s(k^\ast)$ for $k\ge k^\ast$, optimal allocation policies minimizing $\overline{T}$ (and $\overline{S}$) are known explicitly.

Problem. For an arbitrary speedup function $s$ that is neither a power law $s(k)=k^p$ nor a threshold function of the above form, determine the policy that allocates the $n$ servers to the $m$ jobs over time so as to minimize the mean response time $\overline{T}$, and separately the policy minimizing the mean slowdown $\overline{S}$, given that all jobs are present at time $0$.

An arithmetic function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ is called additive if $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$ for every pair of coprime positive integers $a,b$. Suppose there exists a constant $c_1>0$ such that
$$|f(n+1)-f(n)|<c_1\quad\text{for all }n\ge 1.$$
Prove or disprove: there exist constants $c_2\in\mathbb{R}$ and $c_3>0$ such that
$$f(n)=c_2\log n+g(n),\qquad |g(n)|<c_3\text{ for all }n\ge 1.$$

$$|f(n+1)-f(n)|<c_1\quad\text{for all }n\ge 1.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This conjecture of Erdős on additive functions with bounded consecutive differences was resolved affirmatively. Erdős himself had proved the conclusion under the stronger hypotheses that f(n+1) ≥ f(n) for all n, or f(n+1)-f(n) → 0. E. Wirsing (and independently I. Kátai) later established the result under the bounded-differences hypothesis, and indeed under the weaker averaged assumption that (1/X)Σ_{n≤X}|f(n+1)-f(n)| → 0.

Consider a single-server-pool system with $k$ identical servers (or processors). Jobs arrive over time according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, and each arriving job $j$ has an i.i.d. size (work requirement) $X_j$ drawn from a known distribution. Each job has a threshold-based speedup function: there is a parameter $s_j \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ such that if $a$ servers are allocated to job $j$ at some instant, the instantaneous service rate of job $j$ is $\min(a, s_j)$ (i.e., the job experiences linear speedup up to $s_j$ servers and no additional speedup beyond that). Let $0 = a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers tending to infinity such that $a_{i+1}/a_i \to 1$ as $i \to \infty$. The points $\{a_i\}$ determine a subdivision $\mathcal{A}$ of $[0,\infty)$ into the intervals $I_i = [a_{i-1}, a_i)$. For a real number $x \geq 0$, let $\rho_{\mathcal{A}}(x) \in [0,1)$ be defined by $\rho_{\mathcal{A}}(x) = (x - a_{i-1})/(a_i - a_{i-1})$ when $x \in I_i$ (the "fractional part" of $x$ with respect to the subdivision $\mathcal{A}$). A sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge1}$ of nonnegative reals is said to be uniformly distributed modulo the subdivision $\mathcal{A}$ if the sequence $(\rho_{\mathcal{A}}(x_n))_{n\ge1}$ is uniformly distributed in $[0,1)$ in the classical sense, i.e. for every $0 \le c < d \le 1$,
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N} \#\{1 \le n \le N : \rho_{\mathcal{A}}(x_n) \in [c,d)\} = d-c.$$
Question: Is it true that for every such sequence $(a_i)$, and for Lebesgue-almost every real number $\alpha$, the sequence $(n\alpha)_{n\ge 1}$ is uniformly distributed modulo the subdivision determined by $(a_i)$?

Consider a queueing system with $k$ servers and $J$ distinct job types arriving over time according to independent stochastic arrival processes. Each job type $j \in \{1,\dots,J\}$ is characterized by:

(i) an inherent size distribution $S_j$ (the amount of inherent work a job of type $j$ requires when run on a single server), and

(ii) a speedup function $s_j : \{1,2,\dots,k\} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, where $s_j(a)$ is the instantaneous service rate received by a type-$j$ job when allocated $a$ servers (typically $s_j$ is non-decreasing and sublinear, i.e., concave with $s_j(1)=1$).

A scheduling policy dynamically allocates, at every time $t$, the $k$ servers among the jobs currently in the system, with the constraint that the total number of servers allocated does not exceed $k$ and each job receives an integer number of servers. A job of type $j$ assigned $a$ servers completes service after receiving cumulative work equal to its inherent size at rate $s_j(a)$.

Problem: Determine an allocation policy that minimizes the long-run mean response time (mean sojourn time) of jobs in this system, valid for general $J$, general inherent-size distributions $\{S_j\}$, and general (concave) speedup functions $\{s_j\}$. Either characterize an optimal policy explicitly or establish provable approximation/asymptotic optimality guarantees in terms of $(k, J, \{S_j\}, \{s_j\})$ and the arrival rates.

Consider a queueing system with $n$ identical servers. Jobs arrive over time according to a stochastic arrival process (for concreteness, take a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$). Each arriving job is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose vertices are tasks and whose directed edges encode precedence constraints: a task may begin processing only after all of its predecessor tasks have completed. Each task has a (random) service requirement drawn from a known distribution, and at most one task may be processed on a server at a time; a server processes at most one task at a time, and tasks are non-preemptive (or, equivalently, preemptive — both variants are of interest). The DAG structure and task sizes of each job are revealed upon arrival.

A scheduling policy must, at every moment, decide (a) which of the currently present jobs to work on and (b) which eligible tasks (those whose predecessors have completed) of each chosen job to assign to which of the $n$ servers. Let $T$ denote the response time of a job (the time from its arrival until the completion of its final task), and let $\mathbb{E}[T]$ denote the long-run mean response time over all jobs.

Problem. Determine the scheduling policy that minimizes $\mathbb{E}[T]$, and characterize the resulting optimal value as a function of $n$, the arrival rate, and the joint distribution of DAG structure and task sizes.

Consider a queueing model in which jobs arrive over time according to a stochastic arrival process (for example, a Poisson process with rate λ) and are served by a system of identical servers (say k ≥ 2 servers, each of unit speed). Each arriving job J is described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G_J = (V_J, E_J), where each vertex v ∈ V_J represents a task with an associated random service requirement S_v drawn from a known distribution, and each directed edge (u, v) ∈ E_J expresses a precedence constraint: task v may not begin execution until task u has been completed. Tasks of the same job may be executed in parallel on distinct servers, subject to the precedence constraints. A job is regarded as complete only when all of its tasks have completed.

Fix an allocation (scheduling) policy π that, at every decision epoch, assigns ready tasks (those whose predecessors are all done) to available servers based only on the current system state, the DAG structures of jobs in the system, and information about task service distributions. Let T_J denote the response time of job J under policy π, i.e., the time elapsed between J's arrival and the completion of its last task. Define the mean job response time of policy π as
   E[T^π] = lim_{n→∞} (1/n) Σ_{J=1}^{n} E[T_J],
assuming the system is stable under π.

Problem: Develop a method to compute or characterize E[T^π] as a function of the arrival rate, the distribution over job DAG structures, the task service time distributions, the number of servers k, and the policy π. In particular, derive a closed-form expression, tight bounds, or an asymptotically exact analysis (e.g., heavy-traffic or large-k limits) for E[T^π] for natural families of allocation policies acting on DAG-structured jobs.

A family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ of distinct subsets is called union-free if there do not exist three distinct sets $A,B,C\in\mathcal{F}$ with $A\cup B=C$. Let $f(n)$ denote the maximum possible size of a union-free family of subsets of $[n]$.

Determine $f(n)$, or at least its asymptotic behavior. In particular, decide whether
$$f(n)\le (1+o(1))\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$$
holds as $n\to\infty$, and determine the optimal constant and lower-order terms.

Determine $f(n)$, or at least its asymptotic behavior. In particular, decide whether

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Kleitman established the asymptotic upper bound $f(n)\le (1+o(1))\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, confirming the conjectured asymptotic order. Improvements to lower-order terms and related variants (a-union-free, partition-free) have been studied by Frankl and others, but the exact maximum size and the precise asymptotics (error term/constants) are not fully determined.

representations.normalized:
Consider the limited fork-join queueing model defined as follows. There are $n$ parallel server stations, each with its own FIFO queue and a single server with unit service rate (service times are i.i.d. from some distribution, e.g. exponential). Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\Lambda(n)$. Upon arrival, each job splits into $k = k(n) \le n$ tasks, which are dispatched to $k$ distinct stations chosen uniformly at random; a job is considered complete only when all of its $k$ tasks have finished service. Assume the per-server load $\rho = \Lambda(n)\, k(n)/n$ is held in $(0,1)$.

We say the system exhibits asymptotic independence (in the regime $n \to \infty$) if, for any fixed integer $m$, the joint stationary distribution of the workloads at any $m$ of the $n$ queues converges to the product of $m$ copies of the stationary workload distribution of a single M/G/1 queue with load $\rho$. More generally, one may ask for joint independence of $k(n)$ queues (with $k(n)$ growing with $n$).

It is known that asymptotic independence of any $k(n)$ queues holds whenever $k(n) = o(n^{1/4})$.

Problem. Determine the largest growth rate of $k(n)$ (as a function of $n$) for which asymptotic independence of the queues continues to hold in this limited fork-join model. In particular, does asymptotic independence persist for $k(n)$ growing faster than $n^{1/4}$, and what is the sharp threshold?

representations.normalized:
Consider finite or infinite words over the alphabet {1,2,3,4}. For a finite word w, let its Parikh vector (symbol-count vector) be (n_1(w), n_2(w), n_3(w), n_4(w)), where n_i(w) is the number of occurrences of the symbol i in w. Two finite words u and v are called abelian-equivalent (or "identical" up to reordering) if they have the same Parikh vector. An abelian square is a non-empty word of the form uv where u and v are abelian-equivalent (in particular |u|=|v|).

Question: Does there exist an infinite sequence x_1 x_2 x_3 … with each x_i ∈ {1,2,3,4} such that no factor of the form x_{j+1}…x_{j+2k} (k ≥ 1) is an abelian square, i.e., such that no two consecutive blocks of equal length occurring in the sequence have the same symbol-count vector?

Consider the following limited fork–join queueing model. There are N identical first-come-first-served servers, each with its own infinite-capacity queue and unit service rate. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λN (so that the per-server arrival rate is λ < 1). Each arriving job consists of exactly k ≤ N tasks. The task service times are i.i.d. exponential with mean 1 (or, in a second variant, i.i.d. from a general distribution G with finite mean). A job is considered complete only when all k of its tasks have finished service; its response time is the time from arrival until the last of its k tasks completes.

In the standard limited fork–join model the k tasks of each arriving job are dispatched to k servers chosen uniformly at random (without replacement) from the N servers. Consider instead the following two dispatch policies:

(a) Join-the-k-Shortest-Queues (JSQ-k): upon arrival, the job sends its k tasks to the k servers whose queues currently contain the fewest tasks (ties broken arbitrarily).

(b) Join-the-k-Least-Work (JLW-k): upon arrival, the job sends its k tasks to the k servers with the smallest remaining workload (sum of remaining service requirements of all tasks currently at that server).

Determine, in closed form or via a tractable analytical expression, the mean job response time E[T] in steady state under each of policies (a) and (b), as a function of N, k, λ, and the service-time distribution.

Let $H$ be a (real or complex) Hilbert space, and let $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_n \in H$ be vectors with $\|Z_i\| \geq 1$ for every $i$. For each choice of signs $\varepsilon = (\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n) \in \{-1, +1\}^n$, form the signed sum $S_\varepsilon = \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i Z_i$. For a fixed vector $v \in H$, let $N(v)$ denote the number of sign sequences $\varepsilon \in \{-1,+1\}^n$ such that $S_\varepsilon$ lies in the open unit ball $\{x \in H : \|x - v\| < 1\}$.

Prove or disprove: for every such collection $(Z_i)$ and every $v$,
$$N(v) \;\leq\; \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor},$$
matching the sharp bound from the classical Littlewood–Offord inequality for real numbers of absolute value at least $1$. (Equivalently, the question asks whether the Erdős sharpening of the Littlewood–Offord inequality continues to hold when the scalars are replaced by complex numbers, or more generally by vectors of norm at least $1$ in an arbitrary Hilbert space.)

Consider a distributed service system consisting of $k \ge 2$ identical server stations. Consider an M/G/1 queue: jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ to a single server, and each job has an i.i.d. size drawn from a distribution $S$ with finite mean, so that the load is $\rho = \lambda \mathbb{E}[S] < 1$. The scheduler may preempt jobs at any time but does not know the exact remaining size of a job; instead, for a job that has so far received service (age) $a$, the scheduler knows the conditional distribution of its remaining size given that it has been served for $a$ time units. A scheduling policy is a rule, based only on each job's age, deciding which job to serve at each instant. Let $\mathbb{E}[T^\pi]$ denote the steady-state mean response time (sojourn time) under policy $\pi$, and let $\mathrm{Gittins}$ denote the Gittins index policy, which is known to minimize $\mathbb{E}[T^\pi]$ in this setting.

Define the policy M-SERPT (monotonic shortest expected remaining processing time), which assigns to each job of age $a$ the rank
$$r(a) = \sup_{b \ge a} \, \mathbb{E}[S - a \mid S > a, \text{ remaining work after age } a \text{ is observed up to age } b],$$
or more simply a monotonized version of the expected-remaining-size function, and at all times serves the job of smallest rank. It is known that
$$\mathbb{E}[T^{\text{M-SERPT}}] \le 5 \, \mathbb{E}[T^{\text{Gittins}}]$$
for every job size distribution $S$ and every load $\rho < 1$.

(a) Can the constant $5$ in the above inequality be replaced by a smaller universal constant (and what is the optimal constant)?

(b) Does there exist another scheduling policy $\pi$, whose rank function is "simple" in the sense of being substantially less complex to compute than the Gittins index, such that $\mathbb{E}[T^\pi] \le C \, \mathbb{E}[T^{\text{Gittins}}]$ holds for a universal constant $C$, ideally with $C$ smaller than $5$?

Consider an M/G/k queue: jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ to a system with $k$ identical servers (each of unit speed), and job sizes (service requirements) are i.i.d. samples from a general distribution $S$ with finite mean, so that the system load is $\rho = \lambda \mathbb{E}[S]/k < 1$. Job sizes are not known to the scheduler a priori; instead, for each job in the system, the scheduler observes only the amount of service the job has received so far (its attained service / age).

For a job of age $a$, define its Gittins rank as
$$ \mathrm{rank}(a) \;=\; \inf_{\Delta > 0} \frac{\mathbb{E}[\min(S-a, \Delta) \mid S > a]}{\mathbb{P}(S - a \le \Delta \mid S > a)}, $$
i.e. the smallest possible ratio of expected additional service to probability of completion within an additional service quantum. The Gittins-$k$ policy is the preemptive scheduling rule that, at every moment, serves the (up to) $k$ jobs in the system whose current Gittins ranks are smallest, one on each server.

Question: Is the Gittins-$k$ policy optimal for minimizing the mean response time (expected sojourn time) in the M/G/k queue with unknown job sizes for all loads $\rho \in (0,1)$, and not merely in the heavy-traffic limit $\rho \to 1$?

Consider a single-server queue serving jobs that arrive over time. Each arriving job $j$ has a known size (service requirement) $s_j > 0$ and a known deadline $d_j$ (a time by which its service must be completed). At any moment, given the current set of queued jobs (with their remaining sizes and deadlines) and the current time, call a set of jobs "feasible" if there exists a schedule that completes every job in the set by its deadline; otherwise it is "infeasible." A job that cannot be completed by its deadline under any continuation is called "hopeless."

Define the Drop-The-Larger-Hopeless (DTLH) admission/scheduling policy as follows. The server serves jobs in First-Come-First-Served order. Whenever a new job arrives such that admitting it would render the queue infeasible, DTLH compares the new job's size with the sizes of currently queued jobs: if some queued job has size strictly larger than the new arrival's size and dropping that larger job restores feasibility, then DTLH drops such a larger queued job and admits the new (smaller) one; otherwise DTLH drops the new arrival. Jobs that are not dropped must be completed by their deadlines; dropped jobs count as deadline misses.

Let $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{DTLH}}(\omega)$ denote the number (or long-run rate) of dropped jobs under DTLH on an arrival instance $\omega$, and let $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\omega)$ denote the corresponding minimum over all online (non-clairvoyant beyond knowing each job's size and deadline upon arrival) policies, or equivalently over all admissible causal policies in the chosen stochastic or adversarial model.

Problem: Determine the worst-case (or, in a specified stochastic arrival model, the typical) ratio or additive gap between $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{DTLH}}$ and $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{OPT}}$. In particular, find tight bounds on
$$\sup_{\omega}\,  rac{\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{DTLH}}(\omega)}{\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\omega)},$$
and characterize how close DTLH is to optimal for minimizing the number (or rate) of deadline misses.

Consider a single-server queue serving jobs that arrive over time. Each arriving job $j$ has a known size (service requirement) $s_j > 0$ and a known deadline $d_j$ (a time by which its service must be completed). At any moment, given the current set of queued jobs (with their remaining sizes and deadlines) and the current time, call a set of jobs "feasible" if there exists a schedule that completes every job in the set by its deadline; otherwise it is "infeasible." A job that cannot be completed by its deadline under any continuation is called "hopeless."

Define the Drop-The-Larger-Hopeless (DTLH) admission/scheduling policy as follows. The server serves jobs in First-Come-First-Served order. Whenever a new job arrives such that admitting it would render the queue infeasible, DTLH compares the new job's size with the sizes of currently queued jobs: if some queued job has size strictly larger than the new arrival's size and dropping that larger job restores feasibility, then DTLH drops such a larger queued job and admits the new (smaller) one; otherwise DTLH drops the new arrival. Jobs that are not dropped must be completed by their deadlines; dropped jobs count as deadline misses.

Let $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{DTLH}}(\omega)$ denote the number (or long-run rate) of dropped jobs under DTLH on an arrival instance $\omega$, and let $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\omega)$ denote the corresponding minimum over all online (non-clairvoyant beyond knowing each job's size and deadline upon arrival) policies, or equivalently over all admissible causal policies in the chosen stochastic or adversarial model.

Problem: Determine the worst-case (or, in a specified stochastic arrival model, the typical) ratio or additive gap between $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{DTLH}}$ and $\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{OPT}}$. In particular, find tight bounds on
$$\sup_{\omega}\,  rac{\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{DTLH}}(\omega)}{\mathrm{Miss}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\omega)},$$
and characterize how close DTLH is to optimal for minimizing the number (or rate) of deadline misses.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No published results were located that quantify the optimality gap of the Drop-The-Larger-Hopeless policy for minimizing deadline misses; the question is posed as an explicit open problem in the queueing-theory open-problems literature and no resolution appears in subsequent literature.

Part (b): Altman (1963/1972) proved that every n points in convex position determine at least ⌊n/2⌋ distinct distances, with equality attained by regular polygons (for odd n); so g(n) = ⌊n/2⌋ is established. Thus the convex-position part is solved while the general planar question is only partially solved.

Let n ≥ 1 be an integer. Consider any configuration of 2n+1 points in n-dimensional Euclidean space R^n. Must there always exist three points among them that determine an angle strictly greater than π/2?

Equivalently, is the maximum cardinality of a subset of R^n in which every angle determined by three distinct points is strictly less than π/2 (an "acute set") at most 2n?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture was disproved by Erdős and Füredi (1983), who used a probabilistic construction to produce acute sets in R^n of size greater than c·(1.2)^n, which exceeds 2n for n large. Thus 2n+1 points do not in general force an angle > π/2. Subsequent work (Gerencsér–Harangi, Harangi, and others) improved the constructions, with acute sets of size 2^(n−1)+1 and further exponentially optimal sizes.

Consider the M/M/k queueing system with server setup times, defined as follows. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λ to a system with k identical servers, each of which serves jobs at exponential rate μ; let ρ = λ/(kμ) < 1 denote the load. Each server can be in one of three states: BUSY (currently serving a job), OFF, or SETUP. A server in the OFF state cannot serve jobs; when a job needs a server and an OFF server is available, that server enters the SETUP state, during which it incurs an Exp(α) setup delay before it can begin serving. Whenever a server completes a job and no jobs are waiting, it immediately transitions to OFF. Jobs waiting in a FCFS queue are assigned to servers as soon as any server becomes BUSY-ready.

Let E[T(k)] denote the mean response time (sojourn time) of a job in this system, and let E[T_{M/M/k}] denote the corresponding mean response time in the standard M/M/k system (no setup) with the same λ, μ, k.

Problem: Derive a simple closed-form approximation, as an explicit function of k (and of the other parameters λ, μ, α, ρ), for E[T(k)] in the M/M/k/Setup system that accurately captures how the additional response-time penalty E[T(k)] − E[T_{M/M/k}] due to setup behaves and diminishes as k grows large.

Recent work (Williams, Harchol-Balter and collaborators, 2023–2024 PhD thesis and SIGMETRICS/ACM publications, plus a 2025 arXiv preprint) has produced closed-form multiplicatively-tight lower and upper bounds and a highly accurate approximation for mean waiting time in many-server systems with setup times (mainly deterministic setup, and with offered load R = kρ assumed reasonably large). Consider finite sets of points in the Euclidean plane.

(a) An ordinary line of a finite point set P is a line passing through exactly two points of P. Let G_n denote the minimum, over all sets P of n points in the plane that are not all collinear, of the number of ordinary lines determined by P. Determine the exact value of G_n for all sufficiently large n; in particular, decide whether G_n = n − 1 holds for all n ≥ n_0.

(b) Show that, except possibly when the configuration is close to collinear (i.e. except for finitely many "near‑collinear" extremal configurations), every sufficiently large set of n noncollinear points in the plane contains three points forming a triangle each of whose three sides is an ordinary line (a line of P containing exactly two points of P).

(c) An ordinary circle of a finite point set P is a circle passing through exactly three points of P (with lines considered as degenerate circles excluded). Let C_n denote the minimum, over all sets P of n points in the plane that do not all lie on a single circle (and are not all collinear), of the number of circles passing through at least three points of P. Determine C_n exactly for all sufficiently large n.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The Dirac–Motzkin conjecture in (a) was resolved by Green and Tao (2013), who determined the exact minimum number of ordinary lines for all sufficiently large n, confirming the n/2 (n even) and roughly 3n/4 (n odd) bounds and characterizing the extremal configurations. The "ordinary triangle" question (b) is closely related and addressed within the Green–Tao framework. The ordinary-circles problem (c) was treated by Elliott (1967) with successive improvements (Bálintová–Bálint, Zhang) and ultimately resolved asymptotically by Lin–Makhul–Mojarrad–Schicho–Swanepoel–de Zeeuw, who determined the exact minimum number of ordinary circles for all sufficiently large n. Thus the original Erdős questions are essentially solved for large n, while small-n cases may remain open.

representations.normalized:
Consider an M/G/k queueing system with setup times defined as follows. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λ to a system with k identical parallel servers. Job service requirements are i.i.d. samples from a general distribution G with finite mean 1/μ (not necessarily exponential). Each server is in one of three states: BUSY (serving a job), OFF (powered down), or SETUP (powering up). When a server completes a job and finds no waiting jobs, it immediately switches to the OFF state. When a job arrives and finds at least one server in the OFF state (and no idle BUSY-eligible server), one OFF server is switched to SETUP; after an i.i.d. setup time drawn from a given distribution S, that server becomes available and begins serving a waiting job (if any remain). Assume ρ = λ/(kμ) < 1 for stability.

Provide an exact analysis of this M/G/k queue with setup times: in particular, derive the stationary distribution of the number of jobs in the system, or equivalently the mean response time E[T], as a function of λ, k, the service-time distribution G, and the setup-time distribution S.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The M/G/k queue with setup times remains a wide open problem. Existing analyses cover M/M/k with exponential setup times (closed-form decomposition results) and recent work on M/M/k with deterministic setup times (bounds rather than exact analysis), but no exact analysis of the fully general M/G/k with general setup times has appeared.

Let $S_0 \ge 0$ be a nonnegative random variable, and let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. strictly positive random variables, independent of $S_0$. Define the renewal process $S_n = S_0 + X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ for $n \ge 0$. For each $t \ge 0$, let
\[ N_t = \inf\{n \ge 0 : S_n > t\}, \qquad A_t = t - S_{N_t - 1}, \qquad B_t = S_{N_t} - t, \]
\[ D_t = X_{N_t} = A_t + B_t, \qquad U_t = A_t / D_t, \]
called respectively the age, residual life, total life and relative age at time $t$. Assume the renewal process is null recurrent in the sense that $\mathbb{E}[X_1] = \infty$.

Question: Does $U_t$ converge in distribution to a Uniform$[0,1]$ random variable as $t \to \infty$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been resolved negatively in general. Work on the ratio of current age to total life for null recurrent renewal processes shows that when the inter-arrival distribution is regularly varying with index $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $A_t/D_t$ converges in distribution to a nondegenerate limit (a generalized arcsine / Beta-type law, e.g. $U^{1/\alpha}$ with $U$ Uniform$[0,1]$ in one parameterization) rather than to Uniform$[0,1]$. Hence the Uniform$[0,1]$ limit characteristic of the positive-recurrent case does not extend to the null-recurrent case.

$$A(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \min_{1 \leq i < j < k \leq n} \operatorname{area}(\triangle x_i x_j x_k),$$
the minimum area among all triangles determined by triples of the $n$ points. Let
$$H(n) = \max_{x_1, \dots, x_n \in D} A(x_1, \dots, x_n).$$
Determine the correct asymptotic behavior of $H(n)$ as $n \to \infty$; that is, find matching upper and lower bounds of the same order of magnitude for $H(n)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Heilbronn triangle problem remains open. The best known lower bound is of order $(\log n)/n^2$ (Komlós–Pintz–Szemerédi, 1982). The upper bound was $n^{-8/7-1/2000}$ by Cohen–Pohoata–Zakharov (2023), improved to $n^{-7/6+o(1)}$ in subsequent work. A substantial gap between the bounds remains, so the correct asymptotic value is not determined.

Let $(X_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of independent, identically distributed, strictly positive random variables with common distribution $F$ on $(0,\infty)$. Set $S_0 = 0$ and $S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ for $n \ge 1$, and define the renewal counting process
$$N_t = \sup\{n \ge 0 : S_n \le t\}, \qquad t \ge 0.$$
Define the total life at time $t$ by
$$D_t = X_{N_t + 1} = A_t + B_t,$$
where $A_t = t - S_{N_t}$ is the age and $B_t = S_{N_t+1} - t$ is the residual life.

Assume that $F$ is null recurrent in the sense that $E[X_1] = \infty$ (so that $D_t \to \infty$ in distribution as $t \to \infty$).

Question: Does there exist a non-decreasing function $\varphi : (0,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ and a non-degenerate random variable $D_\varphi$ such that
$$\frac{D_t}{\varphi(t)} \xrightarrow{\;d\;} D_\varphi \qquad \text{as } t \to \infty\,?$$
In particular, can one take $\varphi(t) = E[\min(X_1, t)]$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general question appears to remain open. A partial answer is known in the regularly-varying regime: when the inter-arrival distribution is regularly varying with index $\alpha \in (0,1)$, scaling-limit results for the age, residual life and total life have been established (e.g., Blanchet–Glynn–Thorisson and subsequent work on the limiting ratio of current age to total life for null-recurrent renewal processes). representations.normalized: Does there exist a partition of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ into four sets $\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \varphi_3, \varphi_4$ such that for each $i \in \{1,2,3,4\}$, no two points $x, y \in \varphi_i$ satisfy $\|x - y\| = 1$? Equivalently, is the chromatic number of the unit-distance graph on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (the graph whose vertices are the points of the plane and whose edges connect pairs of points at Euclidean distance exactly $1$) at most $4$?
representations.original: Does there exist a partition of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ into four sets $\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \varphi_3, \varphi_4$ such that for each $i \in \{1,2,3,4\}$, no two points $x, y \in \varphi_i$ satisfy $\|x - y\| = 1$? Equivalently, is the chromatic number of the unit-distance graph on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (the graph whose vertices are the points of the plane and whose edges connect pairs of points at Euclidean distance exactly $1$) at most $4$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

In 2018, Aubrey de Grey exhibited a finite unit-distance graph in the plane that is not 4-colorable, proving that the chromatic number of the plane is at least 5. Hence a partition of the plane into four sets, none containing two points at distance 1, does not exist. The exact chromatic number is still only known to lie in {5, 6, 7}, but the question of whether 4 colors suffice is resolved negatively.

Let $S_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent random variables with $X_1, X_2, \dots$ i.i.d. and strictly positive, and set $S_n = S_0 + X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ for $n \ge 0$. Assume the renewal process $\{S_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is null-recurrent, i.e., $\mathbb{E}[X_1] = \infty$. For $t \ge 0$, let
\[
N_t = \inf\{n \ge 0 : S_n > t\}, \qquad A_t = t - S_{N_t - 1}, \qquad B_t = S_{N_t} - t, \qquad D_t = A_t + B_t = X_{N_t},
\]
denote, respectively, the age, the residual lifetime, and the total length of the current renewal interval at time $t$. Define the relative age
\[
U_t = \frac{A_t}{D_t} \in [0,1].
\]
Suppose there exists a positive measurable function $\varphi:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ and a random variable $D_\varphi$ such that
\[
\frac{D_t}{\varphi(t)} \xrightarrow{d} D_\varphi \quad\text{and}\quad U_t \xrightarrow{d} U \quad\text{as } t \to \infty,
\]
where $U$ is uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$.

Question: Does it then follow that the pair $\bigl(D_t/\varphi(t),\, U_t\bigr)$ converges jointly in distribution as $t \to \infty$ to a pair $(D_\varphi, U)$ in which $D_\varphi$ and $U$ are independent?

Subsequent work (Blanchet, Glynn, and Thorisson, around 2015–2020) established the marginal limit $A_t/D_t \Rightarrow U^{1/\alpha}$ when the inter-arrival distribution is regularly varying with index $\alpha\in(0,1)$, which resolves a closely related marginal problem. Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ that is neither discrete (not supported on a countable set) nor spread out (no convolution power $\mu^{*n}$ has a nontrivial absolutely continuous component with respect to Lebesgue measure). Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be i.i.d. random variables with common distribution $\mu$, and define the random walks
$$S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n X_k, \qquad S'_n = x + \sum_{k=1}^n X_k', \quad n \ge 0,$$
where $(X_k')_{k\ge 1}$ is an independent copy with the same distribution $\mu$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Say that $S$ and $S'$ admit an exact coupling if there exists a probability space carrying processes $(\tilde S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ and $(\tilde S'_n)_{n\ge 0}$ with the same laws as $S$ and $S'$ respectively, and an almost surely finite random time $T$ such that $\tilde S_n = \tilde S'_n$ for all $n \ge T$.

Characterize the set of starting offsets $x \in \mathbb{R}$ for which $S$ and $S'$ admit an exact coupling.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A 2017 preprint (arXiv:1706.06968, "Exact Coupling of Random Walks on Polish Groups") explicitly states that it solves Thorisson's problem and provides the characterization: the random walk started at 0 admits a successful exact coupling with the version started at x if and only if there exists $n \ge 1$ with $\mu^{*n} \wedge \mu^{*n}(x + \cdot) \ne 0$ (i.e., the n-fold convolutions have a common component after shifting by x). The paper also gives convergence rates depending on the order of x.

Let f(z) = z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + … + a_0 be a monic polynomial of degree n with complex coefficients, and let E_f = { z ∈ ℂ : |f(z)| ≤ 1 } be its filled lemniscate. Cartan's lemma asserts that E_f can be covered by at most n closed disks the sum of whose radii is at most 2e. Investigate the following three questions:

(a) (Sharp Cartan covering constant.) Can the constant 2e in Cartan's covering be replaced by 2? That is, does there exist, for every monic polynomial f of degree n, a covering of E_f by at most n closed disks whose radii sum to at most 2?

(b) (Sharp derivative bound on a connected lemniscate.) Suppose in addition that E_f is connected. Is it true that
        max_{z ∈ E_f} |f′(z)| < n^2/2 ?

(c) (Bounded number of large components.) For every c > 0, does there exist a constant A(c) independent of n such that the set E_f has at most A(c) connected components of diameter greater than 1 + c?

Determine the answers to (a), (b), and (c), proving the stated bounds or producing counterexamples.

(b) (Sharp derivative bound on a connected lemniscate.) Suppose in addition that E_f is connected. Is it true that
        max_{z ∈ E_f} |f′(z)| < n^2/2 ?

(c) (Bounded number of large components.) For every c > 0, does there exist a constant A(c) independent of n such that the set E_f has at most A(c) connected components of diameter greater than 1 + c?

Determine the answers to (a), (b), and (c), proving the stated bounds or producing counterexamples.

However, the three specific questions (sharp Cartan covering constant 2, the n²/2 derivative bound on connected lemniscates, and uniform bound A(c) on components of diameter > 1+c) do not appear to be fully resolved in the published literature.

Let $G$ be a locally compact second countable Abelian group with Haar measure $\lambda$, acting measurably on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ by shifts $\{\theta_t : t \in G\}$. Let $\xi$ be a random measure on $G$ defined on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, and let $X$ be a random element taking values in a measurable $G$-space, so that $(X, \xi)$ carries a natural shift action $\theta_t(X, \xi)$.

Assume $\xi$ is diffuse (i.e.\ $\xi(\{t\}) = 0$ almost surely for every $t \in G$).

A measurable map $\pi$ from the state space of $(X, \xi)$ to $G$ is called a preserving allocation if it produces shifts $T = \pi(X, \xi)$ that preserve the joint distribution in the appropriate balanced sense (the shift $\theta_{-T}$ moves the origin to a point of $\xi$-mass selected in a translation-equivariant way).

Consider the condition
$$\theta_{-T}(X, \xi) \stackrel{d}{=} (X, \xi) \qquad \text{for every shift } T = \pi(X, \xi) \text{ induced by a preserving allocation.} \tag{$\ast$}$$

The pair $(X, \xi)$ is called mass-stationary if, for every relatively compact Borel set $C \subset G$,
$$(\theta_{-V_C}(X, \xi),\, V_C + U_C) \stackrel{d}{=} ((X, \xi),\, U_C),$$
where $U_C$ is uniformly distributed on $C$ independently of $(X, \xi)$ and $V_C$ is sampled from $\xi(\cdot \cap (U_C + C)) / \xi(U_C + C)$ on the event $\{\xi(U_C + C) \in (0, \infty)\}$.

It is known that, when one adjoins a stationary random field $Y$ on $G$ independent of $(X, \xi)$, mass-stationarity of $(X, \xi)$ is equivalent to condition $(\ast)$ holding for $((X, Y), \xi)$.

Question: If $\xi$ is diffuse, is mass-stationarity of $(X, \xi)$ already equivalent to condition $(\ast)$ for $(X, \xi)$ itself, without the auxiliary independent stationary field $Y$?

Let $G$ be a locally compact second countable topological group with Haar measure $\lambda$, and let $(X,\xi)$ be a pair consisting of a random element $X$ and a random measure $\xi$ on $G$ defined on a probability space. A kernel $Q(X,\xi)(s,\cdot)$ from $G$ to $G$ (depending measurably on $(X,\xi)$) is called an invariant preserving $G\times G$ kernel for $(X,\xi)$ if it is bounded and satisfies the appropriate $G$-invariance and $\xi$-preserving properties (so that integrating $Q$ against $\xi$ produces an invariant balance with respect to the group action).

Recall the following characterization of mass-stationarity: the pair $(X,\xi)$ is mass-stationary if and only if the identity
$$\mathbb{E}\!\int\!\!\int f(\theta_s X,\theta_s \xi,-s)\,Q(X,\xi)(0,ds)\,\xi(d\cdot) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\int\!\!\int f(X,\xi,s)\,Q(X,\xi)(\cdot,ds)\,\xi(d\cdot) \qquad (\ast)$$
holds for every bounded measurable function $f$ and every bounded invariant preserving $G\times G$ kernel $Q(X,\xi)$.

Recall the following characterization of mass-stationarity: the pair $(X,\xi)$ is mass-stationary if and only if the identity

holds for every bounded measurable function $f$ and every bounded invariant preserving $G\times G$ kernel $Q(X,\xi)$.

A kernel $Q(X,\xi)$ is called Markovian if $Q(X,\xi)(s,G)=1$ for every $s\in G$ (almost surely).

Question: Does the above characterization of mass-stationarity remain valid if the class of test kernels in $(\ast)$ is restricted to those invariant preserving $G\times G$ kernels $Q(X,\xi)$ that are Markovian?

Let $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a non-constant entire function, and let $M(r) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|$ denote its maximum modulus. It is known that there exists a continuous path $\Gamma$ in the complex plane tending to infinity (i.e., an unbounded continuous curve) such that, as $z\to\infty$ along $\Gamma$, $|f(z)|\to\infty$ faster than every power of $|z|$ (that is, $|f(z)|/|z|^n \to \infty$ along $\Gamma$ for every positive integer $n$).

Address the following two questions:

(a) For each $r>0$, let $\ell(r)$ denote the length of the portion of $\Gamma$ contained in the disk $\{|z|\le r\}$. Can $\Gamma$ be chosen so that $\ell(r)$ admits an upper bound expressed as a function of $M(r)$ only (a bound that is uniform over all such entire functions $f$)?

(b) Does there exist, for every non-constant entire function $f$, a path $\Gamma$ tending to infinity along which $|f(z)|$ grows faster than a prescribed function of $M(|z|)$, for instance such that $|f(z)|\ge M(|z|)^{c}$ along $\Gamma$ for some absolute constant $c>0$ (and $|z|$ large enough)?

Consider the two-species Ricker competition system on the positive quadrant $\mathbb{R}_+^2$:
$$x_{n+1} = x_n\, e^{K - x_n - a y_n}, \qquad y_{n+1} = y_n\, e^{L - y_n - b x_n},$$
where $K, L > 0$ are the carrying capacities and $a, b \in (0,1)$ are the competition parameters. Assume the coexistence fixed point
$$(x^*, y^*) = \left( \frac{aL - K}{ab - 1},\ \frac{bK - L}{ab - 1} \right)$$
lies in the open positive quadrant, and that the parameters satisfy the local stability inequality
$$4(ab - 1) + 2(1 - a)L + 2(1 - b)K \;\le\; (aL - K)(bK - L) \;<\; (1 - a)L + (1 - b)K.$$
Prove or disprove: for every quadruple $(K, L, a, b)$ satisfying these conditions, the coexistence fixed point $(x^*, y^*)$ is globally asymptotically stable in the open positive quadrant; that is, every orbit starting in $\mathbb{R}_+^2$ with $x_0, y_0 > 0$ converges to $(x^*, y^*)$.

$$\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{n_k}{k} = \infty.$$

$$M(r) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|$$
and the maximum term
$$m(r) = \max_{k\ge 0} |a_k|\, r^{n_k}.$$
Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses one necessarily has

A strong law of large numbers for the number of real roots of Kac random polynomials with i.i.d. coefficients having zero mean, unit variance, and bounded (2+ε)-th moment (which covers ±1 Bernoulli coefficients) was recently established: almost surely $N_n([-1,1])/\log n \to 1/\pi$, hence the total real-root count satisfies $R_n/((2/\pi)\log n)\to 1$ a.s. Let $\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots$ be independent random variables each taking the values $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, and for each positive integer $n$ set
$$P_n(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \varepsilon_k z^k.$$
Define $M_n = \max_{|z|=1} |P_n(z)|$ and $m_n = \min_{|z|=1} |P_n(z)|$.

(a) Prove or disprove that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that, with probability one,
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M_n}{\sqrt{n \log n}} = C.$$

(b) As a weaker statement, prove or disprove that there exist absolute constants $0 < c_1 \le c_2 < \infty$ such that, for every $n$, with probability tending to $1$ as $n \to \infty$,
$$c_1 \sqrt{n \log n} \le M_n \le c_2 \sqrt{n \log n}.$$

(c) Prove or disprove that the proportion of sign sequences $(\varepsilon_0, \ldots, \varepsilon_n) \in \{-1, +1\}^{n+1}$ for which the corresponding polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \varepsilon_k z^k$ has $\min_{|z|=1} \left|\sum_{k=0}^{n} \varepsilon_k z^k\right| < 1$ equals $2^{n+1} - o(2^{n+1})$, i.e. holds for all but $o(2^{n+1})$ choices of signs.

The two-sided high-probability bound $M_n \asymp \sqrt{n\log n}$ goes back to Salem–Zygmund, and Halász established the almost-sure asymptotic $M_n / \sqrt{n \log n} \to 1$, settling parts (a) and (b). Overall the problems are essentially resolved, though they are still referenced as classical Erdős problems.

Let $A : \mathbb{R}^d 	o \mathbb{R}^d$ be an (unknown) map modeling the interaction rule of a network of $d$ genes, and let $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be an (unknown) initial state representing the gene-expression levels at time $0$. Define the discrete-time trajectory by $x_{n+1} = A(x_n)$ for $n \geq 0$, and assume that the limit
$$x_f \;=\; \lim_{n 	o \infty} A^n(x_0)$$
exists in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (so that $x_f$ is a fixed point of $A$ on the orbit closure of $x_0$ and represents an experimentally observed attractor state).

Suppose that the only data available about the system are either:
(i) the attractor state $x_f$ alone, or
(ii) $x_f$ together with the values $x_{n}$ at a small finite collection of intermediate times $n \in S \subset \mathbb{N}$.

Because many distinct pairs $(A, x_0)$ can produce the same $x_f$ (and even the same partial orbit data), the map $A$ cannot be uniquely reconstructed from such observations. The problem is to identify and characterize mathematical invariants of $A$ that are nevertheless determined by the data:

1. Determine which properties of $A$ (for example, structural features such as the support pattern of its Jacobian at $x_f$, its local linearization spectrum, its monotonicity class, Lipschitz constants, fixed-point index, the topology or combinatorics of its basin of attraction, or other suitably defined invariants) are uniquely determined by $x_f$ alone.

2. Determine which additional properties of $A$ become uniquely determined when $x_f$ is augmented with partial intermediate-state observations $\{x_n : n \in S\}$.

3. Define, where necessary, new invariants of $A$ and of $x_f$ that make precise the correspondence between observable features of the attractor (or partial trajectory) and recoverable structural properties of the underlying interaction rule, and prove rigorous identifiability theorems linking the two.

Two related questions in probability theory.

(A) Random covering of the circle. Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of real numbers with $a_n \ge 0$, $a_n \to 0$, and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n = \infty$. On the unit circle $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ of total length $1$, place independent random arcs $I_n$, where $I_n$ has length $a_n$ and its center (or left endpoint) is chosen uniformly at random on $\mathbb{T}$, the choices for distinct $n$ being independent. Give a necessary and sufficient condition, in terms of the sequence $(a_n)$, for the event
$$\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} I_n = \mathbb{T}$$
to have probability $1$ (i.e., every point of the circle is almost surely covered by some arc).

(B) Random power series on the unit circle. Let $(b_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a sequence of complex numbers with $b_n \to 0$ and $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |b_n|^2 = \infty$. Let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be independent random signs, each taking values $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$. Consider the random power series
$$f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n b_n z^n.$$
Decide whether, for almost every realization of the signs $(\varepsilon_n)$, there exists at least one point $z$ with $|z| = 1$ at which the series $\sum_n \varepsilon_n b_n z^n$ converges.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Both questions appear to be solved. The covering problem was answered by L. A. Shepp (1972, "Covering the circle with random arcs", Israel J. Math. 11, 328–345): the circle is almost surely covered iff $\sum_{n\ge 1} n^{-2}\exp(a_1+\cdots+a_n) = \infty$. The random power series question, posed in the form whether $\sum|b_n|^2=\infty$ and $b_n\to 0$ force almost surely a point of convergence on $|z|=1$, has been settled affirmatively (and strengthened to Hausdorff dimension $1$ for the convergence set) in recent work (arXiv:2509.02729, "Convergent points for random power series on the unit circle", 2025).

  dx_i/dt = F_i(x_1, ..., x_N) - γ_i x_i,   i = 1, ..., N,

where γ_i > 0 are degradation rates and the interaction term F_i is built from single-gene nonlinear responses; specifically, assume there exist sign labels s_{ij} ∈ {+1, -1, 0} (stimulation, inhibition, no interaction) and constants h > 0, x_{j0} > 0 such that

representations.normalized:
A Grothendieck topos is a category equivalent to the category of sheaves on some small site. Given Grothendieck toposes E and F, a geometric morphism f : E → F is an adjoint pair f* ⊣ f_* with f* : F → E left exact. Such a morphism is called connected if f* is fully faithful, and surjective if f* is faithful; equivalently, the connected surjective geometric morphisms with domain E correspond (up to equivalence) to idempotent left exact comonads on E, and the codomain F is recovered as the category of coalgebras for the comonad. Two such quotients are identified when the corresponding comonads on E are isomorphic.

Question: Does there exist a Grothendieck topos E such that the collection (taken up to equivalence) of connected surjective geometric morphisms with domain E — equivalently, the collection of idempotent left exact comonads on E — fails to be small, i.e., forms a proper class rather than a set?

Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a Grothendieck topos. Recall that a subtopos of $\mathcal{E}$ (an equivalence class of geometric inclusions into $\mathcal{E}$) is classified internally by a Lawvere–Tierney topology, i.e. by a left-exact idempotent monad $j : \Omega \to \Omega$ on the subobject classifier; equivalently, the poset of subtoposes of $\mathcal{E}$ is in bijection with the internal poset of Lawvere–Tierney topologies in $\mathcal{E}$.

Dually, by a quotient of $\mathcal{E}$ one means (an equivalence class of) a connected surjective geometric morphism $\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{F}$ out of $\mathcal{E}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is a Grothendieck topos, "connected" meaning the inverse image is fully faithful and "surjective" meaning the inverse image is faithful.

Question: Do the connected surjective quotients of an arbitrary Grothendieck topos $\mathcal{E}$ admit an internal parameterization analogous to that of subtoposes? That is, does there exist an internally definable object (or internal structure) in $\mathcal{E}$ whose global elements (or appropriate internal points) are in natural bijection with the quotients of $\mathcal{E}$?

Recent work by Ryuya Hora (2023, "Internal Parameterization of Hyperconnected Quotients", arXiv:2302.06851) introduces a "local state classifier" giving an internal parameterization of the hyperconnected quotients of a topos, resolving the Boolean/hyperconnected case. A follow-up (arXiv:2407.17105, 2024) shows the general problem of "smallness" of quotients fails: the presheaf topos on the countably infinitely generated free monoid has a proper class of quotient toposes, so a fully analogous internal parameterization of all connected surjective quotients is not possible in general. Thus the problem is partially solved: positive in the hyperconnected case, negative in full generality.

Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an elementary topos. The collection $\mathrm{Sub}(\mathcal{E})$ of (equivalence classes of) subtoposes of $\mathcal{E}$, ordered by inclusion, forms a co-Heyting algebra: it carries a join $\vee$, a meet $\wedge$, a top element $\mathcal{E}$, a bottom element (the degenerate subtopos), and a co-implication (subtraction) $\smallsetminus$ left adjoint to $\vee$. On any co-Heyting algebra one defines the boundary operator
$$\partial S \;=\; S \wedge (\top \smallsetminus S),$$
which is the co-Heyting analogue of "$S \wedge \neg S$" and which satisfies the Leibniz rule $\partial(S\wedge T) = (\partial S \wedge T) \vee (S \wedge \partial T)$. One also has the double-negation core operator $S \mapsto \neg\neg S$, where $\neg S = \top \smallsetminus S$ in the co-Heyting sense (equivalently, on each subtopos one can take the associated double-negation subtopos).

By the theory of classifying toposes, when $\mathcal{E}$ is the classifying topos of a geometric theory $\mathbb{T}$, the subtoposes of $\mathcal{E}$ correspond bijectively to the "quotient" (positive) geometric extensions of $\mathbb{T}$ modulo syntactic equivalence; equivalently, each subtopos $S \hookrightarrow \mathcal{E}$ determines, in every Grothendieck topos $\mathcal{F}$, a class $\mathrm{Mod}_S(\mathcal{F}) \subseteq \mathrm{Mod}_{\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{F})$ of $\mathbb{T}$-models, namely those models that factor through $S$.

Problem. Give an explicit description, both
(a) semantically — as an operation on the corresponding classes of $\mathbb{T}$-models $\mathrm{Mod}_S(\mathcal{F})$ for varying $\mathcal{F}$ — and
(b) syntactically — as an operation on the geometric quotient theories of $\mathbb{T}$ —
of the two operators $S \mapsto \partial S$ (the co-Heyting boundary) and $S \mapsto \neg\neg S$ (the double-negation core) on the co-Heyting algebra of subtoposes of $\mathcal{E}$.

Let $\mathbf{F}$ denote the category of finite non-empty sets and all functions between them, and let $\mathcal{E} = \mathbf{Set}^{\mathbf{F}^{op}}$ be the topos of presheaves on $\mathbf{F}$ (the "Boolean algebra classifier", equivalently the topos of symmetric simplicial sets).

A level of a topos $\mathcal{E}$ is an essential subtopos: a geometric inclusion $i\colon \mathcal{F}\hookrightarrow \mathcal{E}$ whose inverse image $i^*$ has a left adjoint $i_!$ (in addition to the right adjoint $i_*$). The levels of $\mathcal{E}$ form a poset under inclusion. For the topos $\mathcal{E}$ above, the levels are indexed by $\{-\infty\}\cup\mathbb{N}$, where level $n\in\mathbb{N}$ corresponds (via the truncation/skeleton functors) to presheaves determined by their values on sets of cardinality at most $n+1$, and $-\infty$ is the smallest level.

For two levels $K$ and $L$ in this poset, write $K\ll L$ ("$K$ is way below $L$") if for every directed family of levels whose join is $\ge L$, some member of the family is already $\ge K$. Equivalently (under the chain conditions that hold here), the "Aufhebung" $\mathrm{Auf}(K)$ of a level $K$ is the smallest level $L$ such that every level strictly above $K$ contains $L$; the way-below relation is determined by the function $K\mapsto \mathrm{Auf}(K)$.

Problem: Describe, in combinatorial or number-theoretic terms, the way-below relation between levels of $\mathcal{E}$, i.e., compute $\mathrm{Auf}(l)$ as a function of $l\in\{-\infty,0,1,2,3,\dots\}$.

Recall that a continuous t-norm is a binary operation $*\colon [0,1]	imes[0,1]	o[0,1]$ that is commutative, associative, continuous, has $1$ as identity, and is non-decreasing in each argument. A fuzzy metric space (in the sense of George and Veeramani) is a triple $(X,M,*)$ where $X$ is a non-empty set, $*$ is a continuous t-norm, and $M\colon X	imes X	imes(0,\infty)	o[0,1]$ satisfies, for all $x,y,z\in X$ and $t,s>0$:
(i) $M(x,y,t)>0$;
(ii) $M(x,y,t)=1$ if and only if $x=y$;
(iii) $M(x,y,t)=M(y,x,t)$;
(iv) $M(x,y,t)*M(y,z,s)\le M(x,z,t+s)$;

Let K be a fixed commutative rig (a commutative semiring with 0 and 1). A K-rig is a commutative K-algebra in the category of rigs, and let FPRig_K denote the category of finitely presented K-rigs. Consider the opposite category as a category of affine schemes, and define a Grothendieck topology on it as follows: a morphism A → B in FPRig_K is declared to be a covering precisely when there exists an averaging process from B onto A, that is, a retraction of A-modules r : B → A (so that B → A → B... — more precisely, A → B has a left inverse in the category of A-modules). Let E denote the resulting sheaf topos on (FPRig_K)^{op} with this "averaging" topology.

Recall that in a topos with a chosen ring object R of line type, an object M is called micro-linear if it perceives every finite limit diagram of small infinitesimal objects (Weil-prolongations) that R perceives as a limit; micro-linear objects form a class closed under finite limits, exponentiation, and étale descent, and they play the role of well-adapted manifolds in synthetic differential geometry.

Problem: Determine the precise relationship, in the topos E above, between the class of micro-linear objects and the class of objects represented by, or built from, averaging-type coverings A → B. In particular:
(a) Is every representable sheaf in E micro-linear with respect to the canonical ring object?
(b) Conversely, is every micro-linear object in E obtainable, up to suitable colimit completion, from averaging coverings of finitely presented K-rigs?
(c) Characterize the averaging coverings intrinsically in terms of the infinitesimal/micro-linear structure of E.

Background. Let C be a small category equipped with a Grothendieck topology J. Recall that J is determined by specifying, for each object B of C, a collection of covering sieves (or covering families {A_i → B}_i) satisfying the usual stability, transitivity, and identity axioms. In some natural settings, a covering family {f : A → B} on a category of models of an algebraic theory T can be characterized by an "averaging" condition: there exists an operation that, using extra structure on A (or on B) coming from a theory T' weaker than T (i.e., T' has fewer operations/axioms and every T-model is canonically a T'-model), allows one to define a retraction or section-like map that exhibits f as a cover.

A concrete instance of this construction occurs for the category of finitely presented K-rigs (commutative semirings with unit over a commutative rig K), where a Grothendieck topology can be defined by declaring f : A → B to be covering when there is an averaging operation with respect to the underlying K-module (or K-semimodule) structure, which is a strictly weaker structure than that of a K-rig.

Problem. Exhibit, or prove the nonexistence of, further examples of the following kind: a small category C of finitely presented models of some algebraic (or essentially algebraic) theory T, together with a strictly weaker theory T' such that every T-model is canonically a T'-model, for which the assignment

   {f : A → B in C} is covering  ⟺  f admits an averaging with respect to the T'-structure

(in the precise sense generalizing the K-rig case) defines a nontrivial Grothendieck topology on C, distinct from the finitely presented K-rig example.

In particular, determine whether such "averaging-with-respect-to-weaker-structure" topologies arise beyond the K-rig setting, and characterize the pairs (T, T') for which this construction yields a Grothendieck topology.
