Background and definitions.

(a) A fuzzy metric space, in the sense of George and Veeramani, is a triple (X, M, *) where X is a non-empty set, * is a continuous t-norm on [0,1], and M: X × X × (0, ∞) → [0,1] is a function satisfying, for all x, y, z ∈ X and t, s > 0:
  (i) M(x, y, t) > 0;
  (ii) M(x, y, t) = 1 if and only if x = y;
  (iii) M(x, y, t) = M(y, x, t);
  (iv) M(x, y, t) * M(y, z, s) ≤ M(x, z, t + s);
  (v) t ↦ M(x, y, t) is continuous from (0, ∞) to [0,1].
The space (X, M, *) is compact if the topology induced by M on X is compact.

(b) A fuzzy metric-measure space is a quadruple (X, M, *, μ) where (X, M, *) is a compact fuzzy metric space and μ is a Borel probability measure on X.

(c) Recall the classical analogues that should be mimicked:
  • Kantorovich (Wasserstein) metric. For a compact metric space (X, d) and probability measures μ, ν on X, dK(μ, ν) = inf_{π} ∫_{X×X} d(x, y) dπ(x, y), where the infimum is taken over all couplings π of μ and ν.
  • Gromov's λ-metric (or □λ-metric). Given a probability space (X, B, μ) and bounded measurable functions r, s: X × X → R, one defines □λ(r, s) as the infimum over measurable subsets A ⊂ X with μ(A) ≥ 1 − λ of sup_{x,y ∈ A} |r(x, y) − s(x, y)|; this extends to a metric on isomorphism classes of metric-measure spaces by taking the infimum over couplings of the two measures.

Problem. Construct fuzzy counterparts of the Kantorovich metric and of Gromov's λ-metric in the setting of compact fuzzy metric-measure spaces, namely:

1. Define, for a fixed compact fuzzy metric space (X, M, *), a fuzzy metric M_K on the set P(X) of Borel probability measures on X that plays the role of the Kantorovich metric, in the sense that for each t > 0 the value M_K(μ, ν, t) ∈ [0,1] reflects the optimal-transport cost between μ and ν computed against the fuzzy distance M, and verify that (P(X), M_K, *) is itself a fuzzy metric space.

2. Define a fuzzy analogue M_λ of Gromov's λ-metric on the collection of isomorphism classes of compact fuzzy metric-measure spaces (X, M, *, μ), establish that it satisfies the fuzzy metric axioms (up to isomorphism), and relate the induced topology to natural notions of convergence of fuzzy metric-measure spaces.

In both cases, the constructions should reduce, in the special case where the fuzzy metric M arises from an ordinary metric d (e.g. via M(x, y, t) = t/(t + d(x, y))), to the classical Kantorovich metric and to Gromov's λ-metric on metric-measure spaces, respectively.

Background and setup. In synthetic / functional-analytic approaches to differential geometry, one often considers an inclusion $A \subseteq B$ of (commutative) algebras (or, dually, a map of geometric objects) and asks for the existence of an "averaging" operator: an $A$-linear retraction $\mu : B \to A$ that exhibits $B$ as covered by $A$ in a way compatible with infinitesimal structure (microlinearity). Such a pair $(A \subseteq B, \mu)$ is called a covering admitting averaging. A standard example is provided when $A$ is an algebra of test functions / smooth functions and $B$ is the algebra obtained by extending $A$ by distributions, with the averaging produced by integration against a chosen distribution (such as a fixed measure or a Dirac-type functional).

Problem. Develop an analogue of this averaging-based covering construction in which the basic objects are
- $C^{\infty}(M)$, the algebra of smooth real-valued functions on a smooth manifold $M$, and
- $\mathcal{E}'(M)$, the space of distributions of compact support on $M$ (the topological dual of $C^{\infty}(M)$),
viewed together as data for a single geometric / topos-theoretic structure. Concretely:

(a) Define an appropriate notion of inclusion $A \subseteq B$ involving $C^{\infty}(M)$ and $\mathcal{E}'(M)$ (for instance, by enlarging $C^{\infty}(M)$ by a class of operations built from compactly supported distributions), together with an averaging operator $\mu : B \to A$ that makes this inclusion a covering in the sense above.

(b) Show that the resulting coverings satisfy the microlinearity / infinitesimal-compatibility properties required of an averaging covering, so that the construction yields a well-behaved site (or topos) modelling smooth geometry with distributions of compact support.

(c) Establish a representation or comparison theorem relating this construction to the classical averaging-covering constructions phrased in terms of smooth functions and measures (or other dualities), exhibiting the $C^{\infty}$/$\mathcal{E}'$ version as a genuine analogue.

Does such a construction exist, and what are its properties?

An F-norm on a real or complex vector space $X$ is a function $\|\cdot\|:X\to[0,\infty)$ such that: (i) $\|x\|=0$ iff $x=0$; (ii) $\|\alpha x\|\le\|x\|$ for every scalar $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le 1$; (iii) $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$; and (iv) $\|\alpha_n x\|\to 0$ whenever scalars $\alpha_n\to 0$, and $\|\alpha x_n\|\to 0$ whenever $\|x_n\|\to 0$. An F-space is a vector space equipped with an F-norm whose induced translation-invariant metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ is complete. Two F-norms on $X$ are called equivalent if they induce the same topology.

Let $K$ be a commutative ring in which the natural numbers are invertible, and consider the category of commutative $K$-algebras. Call an inclusion of $K$-algebras $A \subseteq B$ a covering "admitting averaging" if there exists a $K$-linear retraction (averaging operator) $p : B \to A$ which is $A$-linear and satisfies $p|_A = \mathrm{id}_A$; a typical example is provided by a finite group $G$ acting on $B$ with fixed subalgebra $A$, the averaging being $b \mapsto |G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G} g\cdot b$. Such covering families, when extended in the natural stable way (using that the coproduct of $A$-algebras is functorial on the weaker structure), generate a Grothendieck topology $J_{\mathrm{av}}$ on (the opposite of) the category of commutative $K$-algebras, and the associated topos of sheaves enjoys certain properties analogous to those of microlinear objects in synthetic differential geometry.

Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a topos. Call an object $D \in \mathcal{E}$ an ATOM if the exponential endofunctor $(-)^D : \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{E}$ has a right adjoint, denoted $(-)^{1/D}$; equivalently, $D$ is internally tiny. For any finite collection $\{D_1, \dots, D_n\}$ of ATOMs, one can form the full subcategory of objects that are simultaneously $D_i$-discrete (i.e., the unit of each adjunction $(-)^{D_i} \dashv (-)^{1/D_i}$ is an isomorphism on them); this subcategory is itself a topos — a "lower topos" — and the adjunctions $(-)^{D_i} \dashv (-)^{1/D_i}$ are enriched over it.

Problem. Given a topos $\mathcal{E}$, can the class of all ATOMs of $\mathcal{E}$ be parameterized in a suitable categorical/internal manner (for instance by an object or indexed family in $\mathcal{E}$ or in a related topos)? Furthermore, can one construct a single "lower topos" $\mathcal{E}_0 \hookrightarrow \mathcal{E}$ — analogous to the finite case — over which the family of all adjunctions $\{(-)^D \dashv (-)^{1/D} : D \text{ an ATOM}\}$ is simultaneously enriched?

Let X be an F-space, that is, a complete metrizable topological vector space whose topology is induced by a translation-invariant metric. Let (Ω, Σ) be a measurable space, and let μ : Σ → X be a countably additive vector measure that is nonatomic, meaning that for every E ∈ Σ with μ(E) ≠ 0 there exists F ∈ Σ with F ⊂ E such that μ(F) ≠ 0 and μ(E \ F) ≠ 0.

For a bounded Σ-measurable scalar-valued function x : Ω → 𝕂 (where 𝕂 is the scalar field), one may consider Σ-simple functions x_n converging uniformly to x and form the elements ∫_Ω x_n dμ ∈ X defined in the usual way for simple functions. The integral ∫_Ω x(t) dμ(t) is said to exist if such approximating sums converge in X to a limit independent of the chosen approximating sequence.

Question: Must the integral ∫_Ω x(t) dμ(t) exist for every bounded Σ-measurable scalar-valued function x, whenever μ is a nonatomic countably additive X-valued measure on a σ-field Σ with values in an F-space X?

For Banach-space-valued countably additive measures, the Bartle–Dunford–Schwartz theorem yields a control measure and integration of bounded measurable scalar functions is standard. In the non-locally-convex F-space setting, the existence of control measures and the integration theory are subtle (works of Turpin, Kalton, and others address related issues such as galbs and integrability), but no source found directly confirms or refutes the existence of the integral for every bounded measurable scalar function against an arbitrary nonatomic X-valued countably additive measure when X is a general F-space. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

Definitions. An F-space is a complete metrizable topological vector space whose topology is given by a translation-invariant metric (not necessarily locally convex). For a bounded subset B of an F-space X and ε>0, let N(ε,B) denote the smallest cardinality of an ε-net for B (in the invariant metric), and define the diametral approximative dimension of X as the collection of all sequences (t_n) of positive reals such that for every neighborhood U of 0 there is a neighborhood V of 0 with t_n · δ_n(V,U) → 0, where δ_n(V,U) is the n-th Kolmogorov diameter of V with respect to U. Call an F-space X nuclear (in the sense of diametral approximative dimension) if its diametral approximative dimension contains every sequence (t_n) of positive reals tending to infinity, equivalently if it satisfies the Kolmogorov diameter characterization of nuclearity adapted to F-spaces.

A series ∑ x_n in X is said to converge unconditionally if ∑ x_{π(n)} converges in X for every permutation π of ℕ. It is said to converge absolutely if for every continuous F-seminorm (equivalently, for the invariant metric d) one has ∑ d(x_n, 0) < ∞.

Question. Let X be a nuclear F-space in the above sense. Is it true that every unconditionally convergent series in X is absolutely convergent?

For non-locally-convex nuclear F-spaces defined via diametral approximative dimension, no resolution was located in the search; the question appears to remain unresolved in the literature accessible online.

Recall the following definitions. A topological vector space $X$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ is called an F-space if its topology is induced by a complete translation-invariant metric. A subset $U$ of $X$ is called $p$-convex (for some $0 < p \le 1$) if for all $x, y \in U$ and all scalars $\alpha, \beta \ge 0$ with $\alpha^p + \beta^p = 1$ one has $\alpha x + \beta y \in U$. The space $X$ is called locally pseudo-convex if it has a base of neighborhoods of $0$ each of which is $p$-convex for some $p \in (0,1]$ (the value of $p$ may depend on the neighborhood). It is locally convex if it has a base of convex (i.e. $1$-convex) neighborhoods of $0$. A locally pseudo-convex space $X$ is called nuclear if for every continuous $p$-homogeneous seminorm $q$ on $X$ there exists a continuous $r$-homogeneous seminorm $\tilde q \ge q$ (with $0 < p, r \le 1$) such that the canonical map between the associated local quasi-Banach spaces is nuclear in the appropriate $p$-normed sense.

Question: Does there exist a nuclear F-space that is locally pseudo-convex but not locally convex?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved
The problem was resolved in the negative shortly after being posed: J.-P. Ligaud proved that every nuclear locally pseudo-convex space is locally convex, so no such F-space exists.

An F-space is a topological vector space whose topology is induced by a complete translation-invariant metric (equivalently, by an F-norm). Such a space is not assumed to be locally convex. A notion of nuclearity can be defined for general (not necessarily locally convex) F-spaces, for instance via the existence, for every neighborhood U of 0, of another neighborhood V of 0 such that the canonical map between the associated quotient/completion spaces is a nuclear operator in an appropriate metric-linear sense.

Question: Does every nuclear F-space E admit a nontrivial continuous linear functional, i.e., a continuous linear map f : E → ℝ (or ℂ) with f ≢ 0?

Equivalently: is it impossible for a nuclear F-space to have trivial topological dual {0}?

Standard references treat nuclear spaces in the locally convex setting (where the Hahn–Banach theorem trivially yields nontrivial continuous linear functionals), while there exist non-locally-convex F-spaces (such as L^p for 0 < p < 1) whose continuous dual is trivial. No clear published source was found confirming whether the question for nuclear F-spaces in the non-locally-convex sense has been settled.

Let $(X,\tau)$ be an F-space, that is, a topological vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$) whose topology is induced by a complete translation-invariant metric (local convexity is not assumed). A subset $B\subset X$ is bounded if for every neighborhood $U$ of $0$ there exists $t>0$ with $B\subset tU$. Call $X$ a Montel space if every bounded closed subset of $X$ is compact.

A nuclear F-space is defined as follows. For an F-seminorm (or, equivalently, a sequence of F-seminorms generating the topology) $\|\cdot\|$ on $X$, a continuous linear operator $T:X\to Y$ between F-spaces is nuclear if it admits a representation
$$T(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda_n\, f_n(x)\, y_n,$$
where $(f_n)$ is an equicontinuous sequence in the dual of $X$, $(y_n)$ is a bounded sequence in $Y$, and $(\lambda_n)\in\ell^1$. The F-space $X$ is called nuclear if for every continuous F-seminorm $p$ on $X$ there exists a continuous F-seminorm $q\ge p$ such that the canonical map $X_q\to X_p$ between the associated quotient/completion spaces is nuclear.

Question: Is every nuclear F-space a Montel space?

Let $\mathbb{Z}^k$ denote the $k$-dimensional integer lattice. A self-avoiding walk of length $n$ starting at the origin is a sequence $\omega = (\omega_0, \omega_1, \ldots, \omega_n)$ with $\omega_0 = 0$, $\|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1 = 1$ for $0 \le i < n$, and $\omega_i \ne \omega_j$ whenever $i \ne j$. Let $f(n,k)$ denote the number of such self-avoiding walks of $n$ steps in $\mathbb{Z}^k$.

It is known (by submultiplicativity) that the connective constant
$$C_k \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty} f(n,k)^{1/n}$$
exists and is finite for every $k \ge 2$.

(a) Obtain sharper asymptotic estimates for $f(n,k)$ beyond the existence of $C_k$. In particular, establish, for $k=2$ and $k=3$, an asymptotic formula of the form
$$f(n,k) \;\sim\; A_k \, C_k^{\,n}\, n^{\gamma_k - 1} \qquad (n\to\infty)$$
for suitable constants $A_k > 0$ and $\gamma_k$, or otherwise give rigorous sharper upper and lower bounds on $f(n,k)$.

(b) For a self-avoiding walk of length $n$ chosen uniformly at random from the $f(n,k)$ such walks, determine the asymptotic behaviour of the expected squared end-to-end distance
$$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\omega_n\|^2\bigr]$$
and, more generally, the limiting distribution of $\omega_n$ after suitable rescaling, especially in dimensions $k=2$ and $k=3$.

Let $f(n,k)$ denote the number of such self-avoiding walks of $n$ steps in $\mathbb{Z}^k$.

It is known (by submultiplicativity) that the connective constant
$$C_k \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty} f(n,k)^{1/n}$$
exists and is finite for every $k \ge 2$.

(a) Obtain sharper asymptotic estimates for $f(n,k)$ beyond the existence of $C_k$. In particular, establish, for $k=2$ and $k=3$, an asymptotic formula of the form
$$f(n,k) \;\sim\; A_k \, C_k^{\,n}\, n^{\gamma_k - 1} \qquad (n\to\infty)$$
for suitable constants $A_k > 0$ and $\gamma_k$, or otherwise give rigorous sharper upper and lower bounds on $f(n,k)$.

(b) For a self-avoiding walk of length $n$ chosen uniformly at random from the $f(n,k)$ such walks, determine the asymptotic behaviour of the expected squared end-to-end distance
$$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\omega_n\|^2\bigr]$$
and, more generally, the limiting distribution of $\omega_n$ after suitable rescaling, especially in dimensions $k=2$ and $k=3$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For dimensions $k \ge 5$, Hara and Slade (1992) used the lace expansion to prove that the number of self-avoiding walks satisfies $f(n,k) \sim A_k C_k^n$ (with $\gamma=1$) and that the end-to-end distance scales diffusively, with a Gaussian scaling limit. For $k=2$ and $k=3$, the problem remains essentially open: no power-law correction $n^{\gamma-1}$ has been rigorously established, and even showing that the mean-square displacement grows at least as fast as simple random walk and strictly slower than ballistically is open. The connective constant itself is known exactly only on the hexagonal lattice (Duminil-Copin–Smirnov, 2010), not on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ or $\mathbb{Z}^3$. Conjectured values are $\gamma_2 = 43/32$, $\nu_2 = 3/4$ (with a conjectural SLE$_{8/3}$ scaling limit) and $\nu_3 \approx 0.588$.

Let $X$ be an $F$-space, i.e., a topological vector space whose topology is induced by a complete translation-invariant metric. A subset $U \subseteq X$ is called starlike (with respect to $0$) if for every $x \in U$ and every $t \in [0,1]$ one has $tx \in U$; the point $0$ is an internal point of $U$ if for every $x \in X$ there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $tx \in U$ for all $t \in [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$. For a bounded subset $K \subseteq X$, an open starlike neighborhood $U$ of $0$ with $0$ as an internal point, and an integer $n \geq 0$, define the $n$-th diametral approximative quantity
$$\delta_n(K,U) \;=\; \inf\Big\{\, t > 0 \;:\; \text{there exists a linear subspace } L \subseteq X \text{ with } \dim L \leq n \text{ such that } K \subseteq L + tU \,\Big\}.$$
Suppose that $K$ is a bounded subset of $X$ such that for every open starlike set $U \subseteq X$ containing $0$ as an internal point, one has $\delta_n(K,U) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Must $K$ be relatively compact?

An F-space is a topological vector space $X$ over $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$) whose topology is induced by a complete translation-invariant metric. A continuous linear functional on $X$ is a continuous linear map $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$); call $f$ nontrivial if $f\not\equiv 0$. Recall:
- $X$ is locally bounded if it has a bounded neighborhood of $0$ (equivalently, its topology is given by a $p$-norm for some $0<p\le 1$).
- $X$ is nuclear if for every continuous $F$-seminorm $p$ on $X$ there is a continuous $F$-seminorm $q\ge p$ such that the canonical map between the associated local spaces is nuclear.
- An unbounded norm on $X$ is a (not necessarily continuous) norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $X$ such that $\|\cdot\|$ is unbounded on every neighborhood of $0$; one says $X$ has no unbounded norms if no such norm exists.

Question. Does every infinite-dimensional F-space $X$ contain a closed infinite-dimensional linear subspace $Y\subset X$ on which there exists a nontrivial continuous linear functional? Does the same conclusion hold under each of the additional hypotheses that $X$ is locally bounded, or that $X$ is nuclear, or that $X$ has no unbounded norms?

Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be an F-space, i.e., a topological vector space over the scalar field $\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$ whose topology is induced by a complete translation-invariant metric, with associated F-norm $\|\cdot\|:X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $\|x\|=0\iff x=0$, $\|\lambda x\|\le\|x\|$ for $|\lambda|\le 1$, and $\lim_{\lambda\to 0}\|\lambda x\|=0$ for every $x\in X$. A continuous F-norm $p$ on $X$ (i.e., a continuous function with the same properties as above) is called unbounded if $\sup_{x\in X}p(x)=\infty$. Say that $X$ has no unbounded norm if every continuous F-norm on $X$ is bounded.

Let $s$ denote the F-space of all scalar sequences $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ equipped with the topology of coordinatewise convergence, which is metrizable by the complete F-norm
$$\|(x_n)\|_s=\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}\frac{|x_n|}{1+|x_n|}.$$

Question: Must every F-space $X$ with no unbounded norm contain a closed linear subspace topologically isomorphic to $s$?

$$m_{p,d} \;=\; \inf\bigl\{\,|f|_{W^{1/p,p}(S^1)}^p \;:\; f\in W^{1/p,p}(S^1;S^1),\ \deg f = d\,\bigr\}.$$
(Here the degree is well defined for maps in $W^{1/p,p}(S^1;S^1)$.)

(a) Is it true that
$$m_{p,d} \;=\; |d|\,m_{p,1}\qquad\text{for every } d\in\mathbb{Z}?$$

(b) For each $d\in\mathbb{Z}$, is the infimum defining $m_{p,d}$ attained by some map $f\in W^{1/p,p}(S^1;S^1)$ of degree $d$?

For $\alpha \in (0,1)$, let $\mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu)$ denote the space of $C^{1+\alpha}$ diffeomorphisms of $M$ preserving $\mu$, endowed with the $C^{1+\alpha}$ topology. For a diffeomorphism $f \in \mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu)$ and a point $x \in M$ where the Oseledets theorem applies, denote by $\chi_1(f,x) \geq \cdots \geq \chi_{\dim M}(f,x)$ its Lyapunov exponents. $$H = \{ f \in \mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu) : \mu(\{x \in M : \chi_i(f,x) \neq 0 \text{ for all } i\}) > 0 \}.$$
Is $H$ dense in $\mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu)$?

For $f\in\mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu)$ and $\mu$-almost every $x\in M$, the Oseledets theorem assigns Lyapunov exponents $\lambda_1(f,x)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{\dim M}(f,x)$. Let
$$H=\{\,g\in\mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu) : \mu(\{x\in M : \lambda_i(g,x)\neq 0\text{ for some }i\})>0\,\}$$
be the set of volume-preserving $C^{1+\alpha}$ diffeomorphisms with nonzero Lyapunov exponents on a set of positive $\mu$-measure. A subset of a topological space is called residual in an open set $U$ if it contains a countable intersection of open dense subsets of $U$.

Suppose $f\in\mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu)$ has nonzero Lyapunov exponents at $\mu$-almost every point. Must there exist an open neighbourhood $U\subset\mathrm{Diff}^{1+\alpha}(M,\mu)$ of $f$ such that $H\cap U$ is residual in $U$?

Let $M$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold and let $f\colon M\to M$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism preserving a smooth (volume) measure $\mu$. Assume that $f$ is partially hyperbolic: there is a $Df$-invariant continuous splitting $TM = E^s\oplus E^c\oplus E^u$ and constants such that $Df$ uniformly contracts $E^s$, uniformly expands $E^u$, and the rates on $E^c$ lie strictly between those on $E^s$ and $E^u$. The strong stable and strong unstable foliations $W^s$ and $W^u$ tangent to $E^s$ and $E^u$ exist. The diffeomorphism $f$ is called accessible if any two points of $M$ can be joined by a piecewise smooth path made of finitely many arcs each contained in a single leaf of $W^s$ or $W^u$, and is called essentially accessible if every measurable set that is a union of accessibility classes has $\mu$-measure $0$ or $1$.

For $\mu$-a.e. $x\in M$ the Lyapunov exponents of $f$ along $E^c(x)$ are defined as the limits
$$\chi^c_i(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\|Df^n(x)v_i\|$$
for vectors $v_i$ in a suitable filtration of $E^c(x)$; these are the central Lyapunov exponents. Assume that on a set $A\subset M$ with $\mu(A)>0$, all central Lyapunov exponents are nonzero, and moreover at $\mu$-almost every point of $A$ some central exponents are strictly positive and some are strictly negative.

(a) Under these hypotheses, must $\mu$ be ergodic for $f$?

(b) Must $f$ be stably ergodic, i.e., must every $C^2$-small $C^2$ volume-preserving perturbation of $f$ also be ergodic?

Let $S^2$ denote the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$, equipped with its standard area measure. For a map $f \in H^1(S^2; S^2)$ (i.e. $f \in H^1(S^2; \mathbb{R}^3)$ with $|f(x)|=1$ a.e.), its (Brouwer) degree $\deg f \in \mathbb{Z}$ is well-defined, and for each integer $d$ define the homotopy class
$$E_d = \{ f \in H^1(S^2; S^2) : \deg f = d \}.$$
For two integers $d_1, d_2$ define the asymmetric homotopy-class distance
$$\mathrm{Dist}_{H^1}(E_{d_1}, E_{d_2}) = \sup_{f \in E_{d_1}} \inf_{g \in E_{d_2}} \|\nabla(f - g)\|_{L^2(S^2)}.$$
Decide whether the identity
$$\mathrm{Dist}_{H^1}(E_{d_1}, E_{d_2})^2 = 8\pi |d_1 - d_2|$$
holds for every pair of integers $d_1, d_2$.

The Katok map is a celebrated example of a C^∞ area-preserving diffeomorphism of the 2-torus T² (or, in a variant, of the 2-sphere with a suitable smooth area form), obtained by a smooth slow-down of a linear hyperbolic automorphism near a fixed point. It preserves Lebesgue (area) measure m, is ergodic with respect to m, and has nonzero Lyapunov exponents at m-almost every point.

Fix α ∈ (0,1) and consider Diff^{1+α}_m(M), the space of C^{1+α} diffeomorphisms of the underlying surface M preserving the smooth area form m, equipped with the C^{1+α} topology. Say that a diffeomorphism f ∈ Diff^{1+α}_m(M) "has nonzero Lyapunov exponents on a set of positive measure" if the set of points x ∈ M at which all Lyapunov exponents of f are nonzero has positive m-measure.

Question: Does there exist an open neighbourhood U ⊂ Diff^{1+α}_m(M) of the Katok map such that the set
   { f ∈ U : f has nonzero Lyapunov exponents on a set of positive m-measure }
is a residual subset of U (i.e. contains a dense G_δ subset of U)?

Let $M$ be a smooth compact Riemannian manifold and let $f: M \to M$ be a $C^{1+\alpha}$ diffeomorphism. A non-empty open set $U \subset M$ with $\overline{f(U)} \subset U$ is called a trapping region, and the corresponding topological attractor is
$$\Lambda \;=\; \bigcap_{n\ge 0} f^n(U).$$
A Milnor attractor is a compact invariant set $A \subset M$ such that its basin
$$B(A) \;=\; \{x \in M : \omega_f(x) \subset A\}$$
has positive Lebesgue measure, and no proper compact invariant subset of $A$ has the same property up to a null set.

An $f$-invariant Borel probability measure $\mu$ supported on $\Lambda$ is said to be a non-uniformly hyperbolic SRB measure if (i) all Lyapunov exponents of $\mu$ are nonzero (some positive and some negative on a set of full $\mu$-measure when $\dim M \ge 2$, allowing mixed signs), and (ii) the conditional measures of $\mu$ on local unstable manifolds are absolutely continuous with respect to the induced Lebesgue measure on those manifolds.

Problem. Identify general geometric and dynamical conditions on the pair $(f,U)$ — and hence on the topological attractor $\Lambda$ — under which there exists a non-uniformly hyperbolic SRB measure $\mu$ supported on $\Lambda$, and such that the support (or some appropriate minimal "observed" invariant subset) of $\mu$ is a Milnor attractor $A \subset \Lambda$. In particular, give verifiable sufficient conditions on $f|_U$ that allow one to construct such an SRB measure on $\Lambda$ by pushing forward and averaging Lebesgue measure on $U$ along the orbits of $f$.

A nonempty open set $U \subset M$ with $\overline{f(U)} \subset U$ is called a trapping region; the associated attractor is $\Lambda = \bigcap_{n \ge 0} f^n(U)$. Let $m$ denote the normalized Lebesgue (volume) measure on $M$, and define the sequence of averaged pushforward measures
$$\mu_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f^k_* m.$$
For a point $x \in M$ the Lyapunov exponents are the numbers

Let $M$ be a smooth compact Riemannian manifold and let $f : M \to M$ be a $C^{1+\alpha}$ diffeomorphism. A nonempty open set $U \subset M$ is called a trapping region for $f$ if $\overline{f(U)} \subset U$. Denote by $m$ the normalized Lebesgue (Riemannian volume) measure on $M$, and for each $n \ge 1$ consider the empirical averages
$$\mu_n \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f_*^k m\big|_U .$$
For $x \in M$ and $0 \neq v \in T_x M$ define the upper Lyapunov exponent
$$\chi_+(x,v) \;=\; \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}\log \|D_x f^n(v)\|.$$
Say that the pair $(f,U)$ satisfies condition (H) if $\chi_+(x,v) \neq 0$ for Lebesgue-almost every $x \in U$ and every nonzero $v \in T_x M$.

An invariant Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $M$ is called a physical measure for $f$ if the set of points $x \in M$ for which $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_{f^k(x)} \to \mu$ in the weak-$*$ topology has positive Lebesgue measure. The measure $\mu$ is called hyperbolic if all its Lyapunov exponents are nonzero almost everywhere, and it is an SRB (Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen) measure if it has at least one positive Lyapunov exponent almost everywhere and its conditional measures on local unstable manifolds are absolutely continuous with respect to the Riemannian volume on those manifolds.

Problem. Find natural additional hypotheses on $(f,U)$, beyond condition (H), under which every weak-$*$ accumulation point of the sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ is (a) a hyperbolic invariant measure, and (b) an SRB measure for $f$.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary, fix $p \in [1,\infty)$, and for a measurable function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda>0$ set
$$E_\lambda(u) := \Big\{(x,y)\in \Omega\times\Omega : x\neq y,\ \frac{|u(x)-u(y)|}{|x-y|^{1+N/p}} > \lambda \Big\},$$
and define the "tail-measure" functional
$$\Phi_{\lambda,p}(u) := \lambda^{p-1}\,\big|E_\lambda(u)\big|,$$
where $|\cdot|$ denotes the $2N$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on $\Omega\times\Omega$. Let $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ denote the usual Sobolev space (for $p>1$) and $BV(\Omega)$ the space of functions of bounded variation, with $\|\nabla u\|_{\mathcal{M}}$ the total variation of the measure $\nabla u$. Define, for $p>1$,
$$\Psi(u) := \begin{cases} c_p\,\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p, & u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega),\\ +\infty, & u\notin W^{1,p}(\Omega),\end{cases}$$
and for $p=1$,
$$\Psi(u) := \begin{cases} c_1\,\|\nabla u\|_{\mathcal{M}}, & u\in BV(\Omega),\\ +\infty, & u\notin BV(\Omega).\end{cases}$$

Question. Do there exist positive constants $c_p$ (for $p>1$) and $c_1$ (for $p=1$), depending only on $N$ and $p$, such that the family of functionals $\lambda\,\Phi_{\lambda,p}$ on $L^p(\Omega)$ $\Gamma$-converges as $\lambda\to\infty$ to $\Psi$?

A Borel probability measure $\mu$ supported on $\Lambda$ is called a $u$-measure if its conditional measures along local strongly unstable manifolds (tangent to $E^u$) are absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on those manifolds.

(1) $\Lambda$ is partially hyperbolic;

(3) every weak-$*$ accumulation point of the sequence $(\mu_n)$ is a $u$-measure.

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ (for instance $\Omega = \mathbb{T}^3$ or $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^3$),
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu \Delta u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\]
for a divergence-free velocity field $u:\Omega\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p$, with $\nu>0$ and prescribed smooth initial data $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$. Since global-in-time regularity of strong solutions is not known, several families of regularized modifications have been proposed which do admit globally regular solutions:

(i) Hyperdissipative models: replace $-\nu\Delta u$ by $\nu(-\Delta)^{\alpha} u$ with $\alpha$ large enough (e.g. the bi-Laplacian $\alpha=2$, or higher-order elliptic dissipation).

(ii) Filtered (alpha-type) models: replace the advecting velocity $u$ in the nonlinearity by a smoothed field $\bar u = F_\alpha u$, where $F_\alpha$ is a Fourier multiplier of order $\le 0$ with parameter $\alpha>0$ (e.g. Leray-$\alpha$, Navier–Stokes-$\alpha$, or Bardina-type filters), so the system becomes $\partial_t u + (\bar u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0$ (or a variant respecting energy balance).

(iii) Nonlinear regularizations: add nonlinear dissipative terms (e.g. of $p$-Laplacian or Smagorinsky type, $-\nabla\cdot(|Du|^{p-2}Du)$) that enforce a priori bounds sufficient for regularity.

(iv) Galerkin truncations: project the equation onto a finite-dimensional subspace $P_N L^2_\sigma(\Omega)$ spanned by eigenfunctions of the Stokes operator, yielding a finite-dimensional ODE that preserves the energy balance.

Each of these modifications is, in some appropriate sense, formally consistent with the Navier–Stokes equations in the limit of the regularization parameter tending to its singular value (high-frequency cutoff removed, $\alpha\to 0$, $N\to\infty$, etc.).

Problem. Determine to what extent the choice among the families (i)–(iv) (and within each family, the choice of order/filter/parameter) affects predictions of macroscopic fluid behavior. Specifically:

(a) Identify a principled criterion (mathematical and/or physical) selecting one regularization as the "correct" closure for Navier–Stokes turbulence, or prove that no such canonical choice exists.

(b) For each family, determine whether statistical observables (long-time averages, energy spectrum, structure functions, invariant measures) of solutions of the regularized system converge, as the regularization is removed, to those of weak solutions of the unmodified Navier–Stokes equations, and whether the limit is independent of the family chosen.

(c) Exhibit, or rule out, examples of initial data and observables for which different regularizations from the list above produce different macroscopic limits.

Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (or on the torus $\mathbb{T}^3$) with viscosity $\nu>0$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
with smooth, divergence-free, finite-energy initial data $u_0$. Let $\omega = \nabla\times u$ denote the vorticity, and on the set $\{|\omega|>0\}$ define the vorticity direction
$$\xi(x,t) = \frac{\omega(x,t)}{|\omega(x,t)|}.$$
For Leray–Hopf weak solutions, the following bounds are known to hold for all time:
(i) $\omega \in L^2(0,T;L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$ (the energy/enstrophy dissipation bound), and
(ii) the averaged geometric bound
$$\nu \int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\omega(x,t)|\,|\nabla \xi(x,t)|^2\, dx\, dt < \infty.$$
On the other hand, classical regularity criteria guarantee global smoothness if one assumes the stronger conditions
(a) $\omega \in L^4(0,T;L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$, or

Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (or on the torus $\mathbb{T}^3$) with viscosity $\nu>0$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
with smooth, divergence-free, finite-energy initial data $u_0$. Let $\omega = \nabla\times u$ denote the vorticity, and on the set $\{|\omega|>0\}$ define the vorticity direction
$$\xi(x,t) = \frac{\omega(x,t)}{|\omega(x,t)|}.$$
For Leray–Hopf weak solutions, the following bounds are known to hold for all time:
(i) $\omega \in L^2(0,T;L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$ (the energy/enstrophy dissipation bound), and
(ii) the averaged geometric bound
$$\nu \int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\omega(x,t)|\,|\nabla \xi(x,t)|^2\, dx\, dt < \infty.$$
On the other hand, classical regularity criteria guarantee global smoothness if one assumes the stronger conditions
(a) $\omega \in L^4(0,T;L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$, or
(b) the direction field $\xi$ is essentially Lipschitz (e.g. $|\nabla \xi|$ is bounded, possibly only in regions of high vorticity).

Problem: Close the gap between the universally available controls (i)–(ii) and the regularity-implying conditions (a)–(b). Specifically, determine whether the bounds (i) and (ii), possibly combined with additional natural a priori estimates available for Leray–Hopf solutions, are sufficient to imply global regularity of three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes flows; or alternatively, produce intermediate geometric/integrability criteria—weaker than (a) and (b) but verifiable from (i)–(ii)—that imply smoothness.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The global regularity of three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations remains a Clay Millennium Prize open problem. The specific gap between the available enstrophy and geometric (vorticity-direction) bounds and the known regularity criteria (Constantin–Fefferman type direction conditions, Serrin/Prodi-type integrability) has not been closed; recent work continues to refine such criteria but does not bridge the gap.

Setup. Let $G$ be a graph with vertex set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and edge set $E$. A tensegrity framework realizing $G$ in the plane is a configuration $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in(\mathbb{R}^2)^n$ together with the straight-line edges $\overline{p_ip_j}$ for $\{i,j\}\in E$. A self-stress on $(G,p)$ is an assignment $w:E\to\mathbb{R}$ such that for every vertex $i$,
$$\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}(p_j-p_i)=0.$$
The set of self-stresses forms a real vector space $W(G,p)$, called the self-stress fiber at $p$. Fix the graph $G$ and consider the configuration space $\mathcal{C}(G)=(\mathbb{R}^2)^n$ minus the locus where the dimension of $W(G,p)$ jumps; on its open part $B_d(G)$ where $\dim W(G,p)=d$, declare two configurations $p,q$ equivalent if there is a linear isomorphism $W(G,p)\to W(G,q)$ that preserves the sign of every edge weight (sign-preserving equivalence of fibers). A stratum is a maximal connected component of $B_d(G)$ consisting of configurations all of which are mutually equivalent in this sense.

Problem. For $n=10$ labeled points in the plane, describe every possible type of stratum that can arise in this stratification, ranging over all graphs $G$ on $10$ vertices.

Let $\zeta(s)$ denote the Riemann zeta function, defined for $\Re(s) > 1$ by $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ and extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a single simple pole at $s = 1$. For a real number $\sigma$, define the Lindelöf $\mu$-function by
$$\mu(\sigma) = \inf\{\, c \ge 0 : \zeta(\sigma + it) \ll (|t|+4)^{c} \text{ as } |t| \to \infty \,\},$$
so that $\mu(\sigma)$ is the infimum of all $c \ge 0$ such that $|\zeta(\sigma + it)| \le C_c (|t|+4)^{c}$ for some constant $C_c > 0$ and all real $t$.

Prove or disprove the following statement (the Lindelöf Hypothesis): for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2} + it\right) \ll_{\varepsilon} (|t|+4)^{\varepsilon},$$
or equivalently $\mu\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0$.

Let q > 1 be an integer and let χ be a primitive Dirichlet character modulo q, i.e., a completely multiplicative function χ : ℤ → ℂ with χ(n) = 0 whenever gcd(n, q) > 1, χ(n+q) = χ(n), and such that χ is not induced from any character modulo a proper divisor of q. Define the Dirichlet L-function for Re(s) > 1 by

    L(s, χ) = ∑_{n=1}^∞ χ(n) n^{-s},

and extend L(s, χ) to a meromorphic (in fact entire, since χ is non-principal) function of s ∈ ℂ via analytic continuation. The functional equation relates L(s, χ) to L(1−s, χ̄) and produces so-called trivial zeros at certain non-positive integers (s = 0, −2, −4, … if χ(−1) = 1, and s = −1, −3, −5, … if χ(−1) = −1). All other zeros are called non-trivial zeros; they lie in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1.

Problem: Prove or disprove that for every integer q > 1 and every primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo q, every non-trivial zero ρ = β + iγ of L(s, χ) satisfies β = 1/2.

representations.normalized:
Let q be a prime power and n a positive integer with gcd(n,q)=1. A cyclic code C of length n over the finite field F_q is an ideal in F_q[x]/(x^n-1), generated by a divisor g(x) of x^n-1; equivalently, C is specified by its set of zeros (the "defining set") among the n-th roots of unity in an extension of F_q. The minimum distance d(C) of C is the smallest Hamming weight of a nonzero codeword in C.

Two classical families:
(1) BCH codes. Fix a primitive n-th root of unity α in an extension of F_q, a "designed distance" δ with 2 ≤ δ ≤ n, and an integer b ≥ 0. The BCH code BCH_q(n,δ,b) is the cyclic code over F_q whose defining set contains {α^{b}, α^{b+1}, …, α^{b+δ-2}}; that is, its generator polynomial is the least-degree monic divisor of x^n−1 over F_q having these elements as zeros. The BCH bound gives d(BCH_q(n,δ,b)) ≥ δ, but the exact value of d is in general not known.
(2) Quadratic residue (QR) codes. Let p be an odd prime such that q is a quadratic residue mod p, and let Q ⊂ (Z/pZ)^* be the set of nonzero quadratic residues mod p. Let β be a primitive p-th root of unity in an extension of F_q. The (binary or q-ary) quadratic residue codes of length p are the cyclic codes over F_q with generator polynomials ∏_{i∈Q}(x−β^i) and ∏_{i∈Q∪{0}}(x−β^i), together with their counterparts using the set of nonresidues. The exact minimum distances of these codes are known in only finitely many cases.

Problem. Determine, in closed form or by an effective rule, the exact minimum distance d(C) of every BCH code BCH_q(n,δ,b) and of every quadratic residue code of prime length p over F_q, in the infinite families of parameters for which this exact value is currently unknown.

Determining the exact minimum distance of BCH codes and quadratic residue codes is widely regarded as a hard open problem. Let $p$ be an odd prime such that $2$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$, and let $\mathbb{F}_2$ denote the binary field. Let $Q \subset \mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ be the set of nonzero quadratic residues modulo $p$, and let $\alpha$ be a primitive $p$-th root of unity in some extension field of $\mathbb{F}_2$. The (binary) quadratic residue code of length $p$ is the cyclic code $\mathcal{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^p$ whose generator polynomial is
$$g(x) = \prod_{i \in Q} (x - \alpha^i) \in \mathbb{F}_2[x].$$
Such codes have minimum distance $d$ satisfying $d^2 \geq p$ (the square-root bound) and the designed error-correcting capability $t = \lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor$.

Problem: Construct an explicit decoding algorithm that, given any received word $r = c + e \in \mathbb{F}_2^p$ where $c \in \mathcal{Q}$ and $e$ has Hamming weight at most $t$, recovers the error vector $e$ (and hence the codeword $c$). The algorithm should work for general primes $p$ in the above family, achieving the full error-correcting capability of the code up to half the minimum distance.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Since the late 1980s, many algebraic decoding algorithms have been developed for binary quadratic residue (QR) codes, including methods based on the Berlekamp–Massey algorithm, lookup tables, syndrome-weight decoding, and difference-of-syndromes techniques. These algorithms successfully decode binary QR codes up to half the minimum distance for code lengths up to roughly 113 (with explicit algorithms published for lengths 41, 47, 71, 73, 79, 89, 97, 113). However, decoding long binary QR codes and non-binary QR codes in full generality remains an active research problem.

For a designed distance $\delta$ with $2\le \delta\le n$, the narrow-sense primitive binary BCH code $\mathrm{BCH}(n,\delta)$ of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is defined as the cyclic code whose generator polynomial is the least common multiple of the minimal polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_2$ of $\alpha,\alpha^{2},\ldots,\alpha^{\delta-1}$, where $\alpha$ is a primitive element of $\mathbb{F}_{2^{m}}$. For odd designed distances $\delta$ that are not attained as Bose distances (so-called "non-narrow-sense gap" cases), determining whether $d(\mathrm{BCH}(n,\delta))=\delta$ or $d(\mathrm{BCH}(n,\delta))=\delta+2$ is of interest.

Let $q$ be a prime power and let $n$ be a positive integer with $\gcd(n,q)=1$. A linear code $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ is called cyclic if it is invariant under the cyclic shift $(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{n-1}) \mapsto (c_{n-1},c_0,\dots,c_{n-2})$. Equivalently, via the identification $\mathbb{F}_q^n \cong \mathbb{F}_q[x]/(x^n-1)$, $C$ is an ideal in this quotient ring. The (Hamming) weight $\operatorname{wt}(c)$ of a codeword $c \in C$ is the number of nonzero coordinates, and the minimum distance is $d(C) = \min\{\operatorname{wt}(c) : c \in C,\ c \neq 0\}$. Let $M(C) \subseteq C$ denote the set of minimum-weight codewords of $C$, i.e., those with $\operatorname{wt}(c) = d(C)$.

It is known that binary Reed–Muller codes (which form a class of cyclic-extended codes) have the property that they are generated as $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector spaces by their minimum-weight codewords.

Problem: Characterize, beyond the Reed–Muller family, all cyclic codes $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with the property that $C = \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_q} M(C)$, i.e., $C$ is generated by its minimum-weight codewords.

Let $q$ be a prime power and $m\ge 1$ an integer. For an integer $r$ with $0\le r\le m(q-1)$, the generalized Reed–Muller code $\mathrm{GRM}_q(r,m)$ of order $r$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is the $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear code consisting of the evaluation vectors $(f(x))_{x\in\mathbb{F}_q^m}$ of all polynomials $f\in\mathbb{F}_q[X_1,\dots,X_m]$ of total degree at most $r$ in which each variable appears with degree at most $q-1$. The minimum distance of $\mathrm{GRM}_q(r,m)$ is known, and the set of minimum-weight codewords has been characterized by classical arguments (Delsarte–Goethals–MacWilliams and subsequent work).

A "Newton-identity method" approach proceeds as follows. Identify a codeword $c\in\mathrm{GRM}_q(r,m)$ with its associated polynomial $f$, and let $Z(f)\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^m$ be the zero set of $f$. Using Newton's identities relating the power sums $p_k=\sum_{x\in Z(f)} x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_m^{a_m}$ (over appropriate monomials) to the elementary symmetric functions of the coordinates of points in $Z(f)$, together with the constraints imposed on these power sums by the degree restriction on $f$, one derives algebraic identities forcing the structure of $Z(f)$ when $|Z(f)|$ is maximal (equivalently, when $\mathrm{wt}(c)$ equals the minimum distance). This method has been shown to recover the description of the minimum-weight codewords of $\mathrm{GRM}_q(r,m)$ for certain orders $r$.

Question: Can the Newton-identity method be extended to recover the complete description of the set of minimum-weight codewords of $\mathrm{GRM}_q(r,m)$ for every order $r$ with $1\le r\le m(q-1)-1$? More modestly, does there exist such an extension yielding a proof of the classification of minimum-weight codewords of $\mathrm{GRM}_q(r,m)$ strictly shorter than the classical proofs?

For integers r, s with 0 ≤ r < s ≤ n-1, define the binary cyclic code C_{r,s} of length n to be the binary cyclic code whose dual has as zeros exactly the conjugates of α^r and α^s, where α is a primitive n-th root of unity in F_{2^m}; equivalently, C_{r,s} is the binary cyclic code of length n whose defining set is the union of the 2-cyclotomic cosets of r and s modulo n. For a pair of integers $1 \le i < j \le 2^m-2$ such that $\alpha^i$ and $\alpha^j$ lie in distinct 2-cyclotomic cosets modulo $2^m-1$, consider the binary cyclic code $\mathcal{C}_{i,j}$ of length $n = 2^m-1$ defined as the cyclic code whose generator polynomial is $M_i(x) M_j(x)$; equivalently, $\mathcal{C}_{i,j}$ has the two zeros $\alpha^i$ and $\alpha^j$ (together with their conjugates). Such a code is called a binary cyclic code with two zeros.

(b) has minimum distance at least $5$.

In particular, describe new infinite families of such pairs $(i,j)$ (for $m$ ranging over infinitely many values) that yield codes satisfying (a) or (b), and that are not equivalent to previously known constructions.

For an integer $\ell$ coprime to $n$, define the binary cyclic code $C_{1,\ell}$ of length $n$ as the cyclic code whose zeros include $\alpha$ and $\alpha^{\ell}$; equivalently, $C_{1,\ell}$ is the binary code of length $n$ consisting of all vectors $(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n}$ such that
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} c_i\, \alpha^{i} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} c_i\, \alpha^{\ell i} = 0.$$
Take $\ell = 2^{t} + 3$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: the code $C_{1,\ell}$ has minimum distance $5$, and its weight enumerator is identical to that of the binary $2$-error-correcting BCH code of length $n = 2^{m}-1$ (i.e., the code $C_{1,3}$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The statement (often called the Welch conjecture on binary cyclic codes $C_{1,2^t+3}$ of length $2^{2t+1}-1$) is listed among the long-standing open problems on cyclic codes, and recent surveys and papers on minimum distances of related BCH-like and cyclic codes continue to refer to such weight-distribution questions as unsettled. No published proof or counterexample establishing minimum distance 5 and the BCH weight enumerator in full generality could be located.

A binary cyclic code of length n = 2^m − 1 is called primitive: it is an ideal in the ring F_2[x]/(x^n − 1), and can be specified by its set of zeros, namely a union of 2-cyclotomic cosets modulo n, where each zero is a power α^i of a fixed primitive n-th root of unity α in F_{2^m}. The minimum distance of the code is the smallest Hamming weight of a nonzero codeword.

Problem: Give a complete classification of all primitive binary cyclic codes of length n = 2^m − 1 (for all m ≥ 2) whose minimum distance equals exactly 3. Equivalently, determine all unions S of 2-cyclotomic cosets modulo 2^m − 1 such that the cyclic code with zero set {α^i : i ∈ S} has minimum distance precisely 3, in a closed-form / explicit description covering every m.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

A complete classification of primitive binary cyclic codes with minimum distance 3 is not known. Partial results exist (notably by Charpin, Tietäväinen, and Zinoviev, "On binary cyclic codes with minimum distance three", Problems of Information Transmission 33 (1997)), connecting the problem to questions about exponential sums and APN-like properties, but no full description has been published. Recent works (e.g., new constructions and bounds on cyclic codes through 2024–2025) continue to address related parameters without giving a complete classification.

Let $m\ge 3$ and let $\alpha$ be a primitive element of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$, so that $n=2^m-1$. For integers $i,k\ge 0$, consider the binary cyclic code $C(i,k)$ of length $n$ whose zeros are the conjugates of $\alpha^{2^i+2^k}$ (i.e. the cyclic code whose defining set is the union of the 2-cyclotomic cosets modulo $n$ containing $2^i+2^k$). Equivalently, the dual of $C(i,k)$ is a subcode of the second-order Reed–Muller code $\mathrm{RM}(2,m)$.

(a) Determine the weight enumerator $W_{C(i,k)}(x,y)=\sum_{c\in C(i,k)} x^{n-\mathrm{wt}(c)} y^{\mathrm{wt}(c)}$ of $C(i,k)$ for all admissible pairs $(i,k)$ as a function of $m,i,k$.

(b) In particular, classify all triples $(m,i,k)$ such that the cyclic code with zeros $\alpha,\alpha^{2^i+2^k}$ (together with $\alpha^3$ when appropriate, giving a code of designed minimum distance comparable to the 3-error-correcting primitive narrow-sense binary BCH code of length $n$) has the same weight enumerator as that 3-error-correcting BCH code, and compute the weight enumerator explicitly.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Partial results are known: Kasami (1971) and Bracken–Helleseth (2009) identified families of 3-error-correcting cyclic codes with zero sets {1, 2^ℓ+1, 2^{3ℓ}+1} and {1, 2^ℓ+1, 2^{2ℓ}+1} (gcd(ℓ,m)=1) that share the weight distribution of the 3-error-correcting BCH code, verified for small m. Subsequent work (e.g. on triple-error-correcting cyclic codes from Gold and Kasami–Welch APN functions) has determined further weight distributions of specific subfamilies. However, a complete determination of the weight enumerators of all cyclic codes with zeros of the form α^{2^i+2^k}, and a full characterization of those sharing the 3-error-correcting BCH weight enumerator, remains open in general.

Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and let $L=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ be an $n$-tuple of distinct elements of an extension field $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$, and let $g(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{q^m}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $t$ with $g(\alpha_i)\neq 0$ for every $i$. The associated Goppa code is
$$\Gamma(L,g)=\Big\{(c_1,\dots,c_n)\in\mathbb{F}_q^n : \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{c_i}{x-\alpha_i}\equiv 0 \pmod{g(x)}\Big\}.$$
Let $G$ be a generator matrix of $\Gamma(L,g)$, and let $P$ be an $n\times n$ permutation matrix (and possibly $S$ an invertible $k\times k$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$), so that the published matrix is $G'=SGP$. Given only $G'$ (and the parameters $q,n,t$), provide a polynomial-time algorithm that recovers, up to the natural equivalences, the underlying Goppa structure — namely a tuple $L'$ and polynomial $g'$ such that $G'$ is a generator matrix of a code permutation-equivalent to $\Gamma(L',g')$ — or prove that no such algorithm exists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of recovering the Goppa structure from a permuted (and scrambled) generator matrix remains open and underlies the security of McEliece-type cryptosystems. Known results provide only partial progress: distinguishers exist for high-rate Goppa codes and for special parameter choices, and recent work shows efficient key recovery when a constant fraction (e.g., a quarter) of the secret key is leaked. No polynomial-time algorithm is known for the general case, and binary Goppa codes continue to resist structural attacks, supporting the NIST-standardized Classic McEliece scheme.

Let q be a prime power, and let L = (α_1, …, α_n) be a tuple of pairwise distinct elements of an extension field F_{q^m}, and let g(x) ∈ F_{q^m}[x] be a polynomial (the Goppa polynomial) such that g(α_i) ≠ 0 for all i. The classical Goppa code Γ(L, g) is the F_q-linear code

  Γ(L, g) = { (c_1, …, c_n) ∈ F_q^n : ∑_{i=1}^{n} c_i / (x − α_i) ≡ 0 (mod g(x)) }.

The (permutation) automorphism group Aut(Γ(L, g)) is the group of permutations σ ∈ S_n such that (c_{σ(1)}, …, c_{σ(n)}) ∈ Γ(L, g) for every codeword (c_1, …, c_n) ∈ Γ(L, g); more generally, one may consider the monomial or semilinear automorphism group.

Problem: Give an explicit description of the automorphism group Aut(Γ(L, g)) for arbitrary classical Goppa codes Γ(L, g), in terms of the data L and g.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The automorphism groups of Goppa codes have been determined in several special cases (e.g., classical Goppa codes associated with the Hermitian and Deligne–Lusztig curves; codes with non-trivial dihedral or alternating automorphism groups have been constructed). Sufficient conditions are known under which the automorphism group of a geometric Goppa code coincides with that of the underlying curve. However, a general explicit description of Aut(Γ(L,g)) for arbitrary classical Goppa codes does not appear in the literature, so the problem remains only partially solved.

Let q be a prime power, m a positive integer, and let F = GF(q^m) be the finite field with q^m elements. Let L = (α_1, …, α_n) be a tuple of distinct elements of F (the support) and let g(x) ∈ F[x] be a polynomial (the Goppa polynomial) such that g(α_i) ≠ 0 for all i. The classical Goppa code Γ(L, g) is the GF(q)-linear code of length n consisting of all vectors (c_1, …, c_n) ∈ GF(q)^n satisfying

    Σ_{i=1}^{n} c_i / (x − α_i) ≡ 0  (mod g(x))

in F[x]/(g(x)). The extended Goppa code is obtained from Γ(L, g) by appending an overall parity-check coordinate.

A linear code C ⊆ GF(q)^N is called cyclic if it is invariant under the cyclic shift (c_1, c_2, …, c_N) ↦ (c_N, c_1, …, c_{N−1}) (after a suitable ordering of the coordinates).

Problem: Give a complete characterization of those triples (q, L, g) for which the classical Goppa code Γ(L, g) is (equivalent to) a cyclic code, and, separately, of those triples for which the extended classical Goppa code is (equivalent to) a cyclic code.

The problem of fully characterizing which classical Goppa codes (extended or not) are cyclic remains open. Numerous works (Berlekamp–Moreno, Tzeng–Zimmermann, Berger, and more recent papers including a 2024 preprint on generator polynomials of cyclic expurgated or extended Goppa codes) provide sufficient conditions and new families of cyclic (extended) Goppa codes, but no complete characterization has been established.

Let $q = 2^m$ with $m \geq 3$, and let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be the finite field with $q$ elements. The binary Melas code $M(2,m)$ of length $n = q - 1$ is the cyclic code over $\mathbb{F}_2$ whose dual is generated (as a cyclic code) by the parity-check matrix whose columns are the pairs $(\alpha^i, \alpha^{-i})$, where $\alpha$ is a primitive element of $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $i = 0,1,\dots,n-1$; equivalently, $M(2,m)$ is the binary cyclic code of length $2^m - 1$ whose defining set consists of the cyclotomic cosets of $1$ and $-1$ modulo $2^m - 1$, i.e. its zeros are $\alpha$ and $\alpha^{-1}$. The weight enumerator of $M(2,m)$ is the polynomial
$$W_{M(2,m)}(X,Y) = \sum_{c \in M(2,m)} X^{n - \mathrm{wt}(c)} Y^{\mathrm{wt}(c)} = \sum_{w=0}^{n} A_w\, X^{n-w} Y^w,$$
where $A_w$ is the number of codewords of Hamming weight $w$. For a nontrivial additive character $\psi$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$, the Kloosterman sum is
$$K(a) = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{F}_q^{*}} \psi\!\left(x + a x^{-1}\right), \qquad a \in \mathbb{F}_q^{*}.$$
It is known that the weights in the dual of $M(2,m)$ are expressible in terms of values of $K(a)$, but the precise distribution of these values, and hence the full weight distribution of $M(2,m)$, is not known in closed form.

Problem: Determine explicitly the complete weight enumerator $W_{M(2,m)}(X,Y)$, i.e. give a closed-form expression for the coefficients $A_w$ for every $m \geq 3$ and every $0 \leq w \leq 2^m - 1$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Available literature indicates that the weight distribution of the Melas code (equivalently, the distribution of binary Kloosterman sum values) remains an active object of study, with only partial results — such as divisibility characterizations (e.g., Kloosterman sums divisible by 3), moment computations, and asymptotic Sato–Tate type distribution results — but no closed-form complete weight enumerator. No source found indicates a full resolution.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \ge 2$) be a bounded domain, and let
\[
0 < \lambda_1(\Omega) < \lambda_2(\Omega) \le \lambda_3(\Omega) \le \cdots
\]
denote the eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) of the Dirichlet Laplacian on $\Omega$, i.e. the values $\lambda$ for which there exists a nonzero $u \in H^1_0(\Omega)$ with $-\Delta u = \lambda u$ in $\Omega$ and $u = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

For a real parameter $\nu \ge 0$, let $J_\nu$ denote the Bessel function of the first kind of order $\nu$, and let $j_{\nu,k}$ denote its $k$-th positive zero. Set $p = (n-2)/2$. It is known that, when $\Omega = B \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is the Euclidean unit ball, the first eigenvalue equals $j_{p,1}^2$, while $\lambda_2(B) = \cdots = \lambda_{n+1}(B) = j_{p+1,1}^2$, so that
\[
\frac{\lambda_2(B) + \lambda_3(B) + \cdots + \lambda_{n+1}(B)}{\lambda_1(B)} = \frac{n\, j_{p+1,1}^2}{j_{p,1}^2}.
\]

Prove or disprove: for every bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
\frac{\lambda_2(\Omega) + \lambda_3(\Omega) + \cdots + \lambda_{n+1}(\Omega)}{\lambda_1(\Omega)} \;\le\; \frac{n\, j_{p+1,1}^2}{j_{p,1}^2}.
\]
In particular, for $n = 2$, decide whether
\[
\frac{\lambda_2(\Omega) + \lambda_3(\Omega)}{\lambda_1(\Omega)} \;\le\; \frac{2\, j_{1,1}^2}{j_{0,1}^2} \;\approx\; 5.077
\]
holds for every bounded planar domain $\Omega$, with equality (in the limit) only for the disk.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ ($n\ge 2$) be a bounded domain, and let
$$0<\lambda_1(\Omega)\le \lambda_2(\Omega)\le \lambda_3(\Omega)\le\cdots$$
denote the eigenvalues (counted with multiplicities) of the Dirichlet Laplacian $-\Delta$ on $\Omega$, i.e. of the problem
$$-\Delta u=\lambda u\text{ in }\Omega,\qquad u=0\text{ on }\partial\Omega.$$
For an integer $m\ge 0$ and positive integer $k$, let $j_{m,k}$ denote the $k$-th positive zero of the Bessel function $J_m$. For a ball $B\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, the Dirichlet eigenvalues are known explicitly in terms of zeros of Bessel functions $J_{p+\ell}$ with $p=(n-2)/2$, and one has in particular that $\lambda_1(B)$ corresponds to $j_{p,1}^2/R^2$ (where $R$ is the radius), while the next eigenvalue cluster involves $j_{p+1,1}^2/R^2$, and the subsequent cluster involves $j_{p+2,1}^2/R^2$.

On a ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the first eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ is simple, the next cluster $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_{n+1}$ consists of $n$ equal eigenvalues, and the following cluster $\lambda_{n+2},\dots,\lambda_{n(n+3)/2}$ consists of $\tfrac{(n-1)(n+2)}{2}$ equal eigenvalues. In particular, for a disk in $\mathbb{R}^2$ ($n=2$, $p=0$),
$$\frac{\lambda_4(B)+\lambda_5(B)}{\lambda_1(B)}=\frac{2\,j_{2,1}^2}{j_{0,1}^2}\approx 9.121.$$

Prove or disprove the following conjectured isoperimetric inequalities for arbitrary bounded domains $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$:

(a) In dimension $n=2$,
$$\frac{\lambda_4(\Omega)+\lambda_5(\Omega)}{\lambda_1(\Omega)}\le \frac{2\,j_{2,1}^2}{j_{0,1}^2}.$$

(b) In general dimension $n\ge 2$, writing $p=(n-2)/2$,
$$\frac{\lambda_{n+2}(\Omega)+\lambda_{n+3}(\Omega)+\cdots+\lambda_{n(n+3)/2}(\Omega)}{\lambda_1(\Omega)}\le \frac{(n-1)(n+2)}{2}\cdot\frac{j_{p+2,1}^2}{j_{p,1}^2},$$
with equality if and only if $\Omega$ is a ball.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The conjecture that the disk minimizes $\lambda_3$ among planar domains of fixed area (and that the $n$-ball minimizes $\lambda_{n+1}$ among $n$-dimensional domains of fixed volume) appears to remain open. For $\lambda_1$ the Faber-Krahn inequality is classical, and for $\lambda_2$ the Krahn-Szegő theorem gives two equal balls as the minimizer. For $\lambda_3$ only existence of an optimal domain (and connectedness in dimensions 2 and 3) is known; the conjecture that the optimizer is a single ball is unresolved.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a smooth bounded domain, and let
$$0=\mu_0<\mu_1\le\mu_2\le\cdots$$
denote the Neumann eigenvalues of the Laplacian on $\Omega$, i.e. the values $\mu$ for which there exists a nontrivial function $v$ satisfying $-\Delta v=\mu v$ in $\Omega$ and $\partial v/\partial n=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. Write $|\Omega|$ for the Lebesgue measure of $\Omega$, let $C_n=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$ denote the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $p_{\nu,1}$ denote the first positive zero of the derivative of $t^{1-\nu}J_\nu(t)$, where $J_\nu$ is the Bessel function of the first kind of order $\nu$.

Prove or disprove the following sharp isoperimetric inequality:
$$|\Omega|^{-2/n}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_1}+\frac{1}{\mu_2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{\mu_n}\right)\ \ge\ \frac{n}{C_n^{2/n}\,p_{n/2,1}^{\,2}},$$
with equality (in the limiting sense) when $\Omega$ is a ball. In particular, in dimension $n=2$, prove or disprove that for every smooth bounded planar domain of area $A$,
$$\frac{1}{A}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_1}+\frac{1}{\mu_2}\right)\ \ge\ \frac{2}{\pi\,p_{1,1}^{\,2}}.$$

Let $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the unit sphere. A spherical cap of angular radius $r \in (0,\pi)$ centered at $x \in S^2$ is the set $C(x,r) = \{ y \in S^2 : d(x,y) \le r \}$, where $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes geodesic (great-circle) distance on $S^2$.

For each integer $n \ge 2$, define
$$\rho(n) = \inf\Big\{ r > 0 : \text{there exist } x_1,\dots,x_n \in S^2 \text{ with } S^2 = \bigcup_{i=1}^{n} C(x_i, r) \Big\}.$$

Equivalently, $\rho(n) = \min_{x_1,\dots,x_n \in S^2} \max_{y \in S^2} \min_{1 \le i \le n} d(x_i, y)$.

Determine $\rho(n)$ for every integer $n \ge 2$, and exhibit configurations $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\} \subset S^2$ achieving this minimum (i.e., describe the optimal placements of $n$ points on the sphere so that the maximum distance from any point of $S^2$ to its nearest chosen point is as small as possible).

$$\Delta^2 w = \Gamma\, w \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad w = 0,\ \ \frac{\partial w}{\partial \nu} = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega,$$

$$|\Omega|^{4/n}\, \Gamma_1(\Omega) \ \geq \ |B|^{4/n}\, \Gamma_1(B),$$
with equality if and only if $\Omega$ is a ball.

(a) Determine the exact value of $\tau_0$.
(b) Exhibit a convex universal cover $T^* \in \mathcal{T}$ with $\operatorname{area}(T^*) = \tau_0$.
(c) Characterize all convex universal covers attaining the minimum area $\tau_0$.

$$\Delta^2 v = -\Lambda \Delta v \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad v = 0 \text{ and } \frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
and let $\Lambda_1(\Omega)$ denote its lowest eigenvalue (equivalently, the smallest $\Lambda$ for which a nontrivial $v \in H_0^2(\Omega)$ exists). Let $B \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a ball, and let $|\cdot|$ denote $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Prove or disprove that
$$|\Omega|^{2/n}\, \Lambda_1(\Omega) \;\geq\; |B|^{2/n}\, \Lambda_1(B),$$
with equality if and only if $\Omega$ is a ball (up to a set of measure zero).

The Faber-Krahn-type inequality for the first buckling eigenvalue (the Pólya–Szegő buckling conjecture, ca. 1950) remains open in general dimension. Partial results exist (e.g., Ashbaugh–Bucur and others establish that the ball is at least a local minimizer and prove related bounds), but the full conjecture for arbitrary bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\geq 2$, has not been established.

representations.normalized:
A packing of congruent (unit) circles in the Euclidean plane is a family of closed disks of radius 1 with pairwise disjoint interiors. Such a packing is called rigid (or stable) if every disk in the packing is touched by at least three other disks of the packing, and the contact points on the boundary of each disk are arranged so that no two consecutive contact points (in cyclic order around the disk) are separated by an arc of length greater than or equal to a semicircle. Under this condition, no single disk can be translated without overlapping another disk of the packing.

The (lower) density of a packing P is defined as
  d(P) = liminf_{R→∞} area(P ∩ B(0,R)) / area(B(0,R)),
where B(0,R) denotes the disk of radius R centered at the origin.

Determine
  inf { d(P) : P is a rigid packing of congruent circles in the plane },
and decide whether this infimum is attained.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

K. Böröczky (1964) constructed stable (rigid) packings of congruent circles in the plane whose density is arbitrarily close to 0; consequently the infimum of densities of rigid congruent-circle packings in the plane equals 0, and this infimum is not attained. This result is standard and is recorded in surveys on packing and covering (e.g., Fejes Tóth's handbook chapter and the MathWorld entry on rigid circle packing).

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain. Consider the Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalue problem
$$-\Delta u = \lambda u \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u=0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
whose eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are $0<\lambda_1(\Omega)\le \lambda_2(\Omega)\le \lambda_3(\Omega)\le \cdots$. Consider also the buckling (clamped-plate) eigenvalue problem
$$\Delta^{2} v = -\Lambda\,\Delta v \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad v = \frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu}=0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
whose smallest eigenvalue is denoted $\Lambda_1(\Omega)$.

Decide whether the inequality
$$\Lambda_1(\Omega) \;\ge\; \frac{1}{n}\bigl(\lambda_2(\Omega) + \lambda_3(\Omega) + \cdots + \lambda_{n+1}(\Omega)\bigr)$$
holds for every bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.

representations.normalized:
Consider arrangements of congruent (closed) circular discs of equal radius in the Euclidean plane.

A family F of such discs is called a k-fold packing if every point of the plane lies in the interior of at most k members of F. The density of F (defined as the limit, as R → ∞, of the ratio between the total area of the parts of the discs lying inside the disc of radius R centered at the origin, and the area πR² of that disc) exists for suitably regular families; the k-fold packing density d_k is defined as the supremum of these densities over all k-fold packings of congruent circles in the plane.

A family F of such discs is called a k-fold covering if every point of the plane belongs to at least k members of F. The k-fold covering density D_k is defined as the infimum of the densities of all k-fold coverings of the plane by congruent circles.

(For k = 1 it is classically known that d_1 = π/√12 and D_1 = 2π/√27.)

Problem: For each integer k ≥ 2, determine the exact values of d_k and D_k.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general problem of determining exact k-fold packing and covering densities of congruent circles in the plane is still open for arbitrary k ≥ 2. Substantial partial results exist: in the lattice setting, the densest k-fold lattice packing and thinnest k-fold lattice covering densities have been determined for several values of k (work of Blundon, Heppes, Yakovlev, Temesváry, Horváth, Sriamorn, and others), and bounds for the non-lattice case are known. Restricted versions (e.g., two-fold covering under congruent Voronoi polygon conditions) have been resolved, but the unrestricted extremal densities d_k and D_k for all k > 1 are not known.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ ($n\ge 2$) be a bounded domain with sufficiently smooth boundary, and let $|\Omega|$ denote its $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

Define $\lambda_1(\Omega)$ as the first eigenvalue of the Dirichlet Laplacian on $\Omega$, i.e. the smallest $\lambda$ such that there exists a nontrivial $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ with
$$-\Delta u=\lambda u\text{ in }\Omega,\qquad u=0\text{ on }\partial\Omega.$$

Define $\Lambda_1(\Omega)$ as the first buckling eigenvalue of $\Omega$, i.e. the smallest $\Lambda$ such that there exists a nontrivial $u\in H_0^2(\Omega)$ with
$$\Delta^2 u=-\Lambda\Delta u\text{ in }\Omega,\qquad u=\partial_\nu u=0\text{ on }\partial\Omega.$$

Let $p=(n-2)/2$, and for $\nu\ge 0$ let $j_{\nu,1}$ denote the first positive zero of the Bessel function $J_\nu$. Let $C_n=\omega_n^{-2/n}\,j_{p,1}^{\,2}$ be the scale-invariant value of $|\Omega|^{2/n}\lambda_1(\Omega)$ when $\Omega$ is an $n$-ball, where $\omega_n$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Question: Does the inequality
$$|\Omega|^{4/n}\,\lambda_1(\Omega)\,\Lambda_1(\Omega)\;\ge\;C_n^{4/n}\,j_{p,1}^{\,2}\,j_{p+1,1}^{\,2}$$
hold for every bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, with equality when $\Omega$ is an $n$-ball?

representations.normalized:
Consider coverings of the unit sphere $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ by $N$ congruent closed spherical caps of angular radius $r$. For fixed $N$, an extremal covering is one that minimizes $r$; equivalently it attains the smallest angular radius such that the caps still cover $S^2$. Associated with any such covering is its covering graph: vertices are the intersection points of the boundary circles (arcs) of the caps, and edges are the arcs of boundary circles joining consecutive vertices. An intersection point is called an $I$-point of order $k$ if exactly $k$ boundary arcs of caps meet at that point.

Prove or disprove: in every extremal covering of $S^2$ by $N$ congruent spherical caps (for every $N$), the covering graph contains no $I$-point of order $4$; that is, no vertex of the covering graph has four incident boundary arcs.

A packing of congruent closed balls in three-dimensional Euclidean space is a collection of solid balls of equal radius with pairwise disjoint interiors. The (upper) density of such a packing is

  δ = limsup_{R→∞} V(R) / ((4/3)π R^3),

where V(R) is the total volume of the parts of the balls contained in the ball of radius R centered at the origin. A packing is called rigid (or stable) if no finite subset of its spheres can be continuously moved (keeping all spheres congruent and pairwise non-overlapping) while all other spheres remain fixed; equivalently, every sphere is held in place by its contacts with neighbors so that no local motion of finitely many spheres is possible.

Problem: Determine the infimum of the densities δ over all rigid packings of congruent spheres in three-dimensional Euclidean space, and exhibit a packing (or sequence of packings) attaining this infimum.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of determining the minimum density of a rigid (mechanically stable / strictly jammed) packing of congruent spheres in 3-space appears to remain open. The lowest known density of a strictly jammed periodic congruent-sphere packing is the "tunneled fcc" crystal of Torquato and Stillinger with density π√2/9 ≈ 0.4936, but it has not been proven that no rigid packing has lower density, and infinite families of low-density strictly jammed crystals are known. No proof of optimality has been published.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain with sufficiently smooth boundary. Consider two fourth-order eigenvalue problems on $\Omega$:

(a) The clamped plate problem
$$\Delta^2 u = \Gamma\, u \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
with eigenvalues $0 < \Gamma_1 \le \Gamma_2 \le \Gamma_3 \le \cdots$.

(b) The buckling problem
$$\Delta^2 u = -\Lambda\, \Delta u \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
with eigenvalues $0 < \Lambda_1 \le \Lambda_2 \le \Lambda_3 \le \cdots$.

Among all bounded domains $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ (with fixed volume, say), determine:

1. Whether the ball maximizes the first nontrivial ratios $\Gamma_2/\Gamma_1$ and $\Lambda_2/\Lambda_1$, i.e. prove or disprove that
$$\frac{\Gamma_2(\Omega)}{\Gamma_1(\Omega)} \le \frac{\Gamma_2(B)}{\Gamma_1(B)}, \qquad \frac{\Lambda_2(\Omega)}{\Lambda_1(\Omega)} \le \frac{\Lambda_2(B)}{\Lambda_1(B)},$$
where $B$ is a ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

2. More generally, find sharp upper bounds (and identify the extremal domains) for the ratios
$$\frac{\Gamma_{m+1}}{\Gamma_m}, \qquad \frac{\Lambda_{m+1}}{\Lambda_m}, \qquad \frac{\Gamma_2 + \Gamma_3}{\Gamma_1}, \qquad \frac{\Lambda_2 + \Lambda_3}{\Lambda_1}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture (originally raised by Grünbaum and L. Fejes Tóth) that four points suffice to pierce any family of pairwise intersecting disks in the plane has been established. Stachó (1981) and Danzer (1986) gave (non-constructive) proofs that four points always suffice. More recently, Har-Peled, Kaplan, Mulzer, Roditty, Seiferth, Sharir, Sharir, and Yang, as well as Carmi, Katz, and Morin, provided simpler and constructive (linear-time) proofs of the four-point bound. Hence the answer is yes: four points always suffice.

$$W_k \;=\; \frac{(2\pi)^2 \, k^{2/n}}{(\omega_n V)^{2/n}},$$
where $\omega_n$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$, denote the leading Weyl asymptotic value. Is it true that
$$\mu_k \;<\; W_k \;<\; \lambda_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge 1?$$

Pólya's conjectures are known for tiling domains (Pólya, 1961). Filonov, Levitin, Polterovich, and Sobolev (Inventiones, 2023; arXiv:2203.07696) proved the Dirichlet form of Pólya's conjecture for Euclidean balls in all dimensions and for planar disks and sectors; extensions to annuli appeared in 2025/2026 (arXiv:2505.21737), and to cylinders in 2025 (arXiv:2511.17050). Two polyhedra P and Q in Euclidean 3-space are said to be equivalent by dissection (scissors-congruent) if P can be partitioned into finitely many polyhedral pieces that can be reassembled (via rigid motions) to form Q. To each polyhedron P one associates its Dehn invariant

  D(P) = Σ_e ℓ(e) ⊗ θ(e) ∈ ℝ ⊗_ℤ (ℝ/πℚ),

where the sum runs over the edges e of P, ℓ(e) is the length of e, and θ(e) is the dihedral angle of P along e. Dehn proved that if P and Q are equivalent by dissection, then vol(P) = vol(Q) and D(P) = D(Q).

Problem: Determine whether the converse holds. That is, given two polyhedra P and Q of equal volume satisfying D(P) = D(Q), must P and Q be equivalent by dissection? Equivalently, must every polyhedron whose Dehn invariant vanishes (i.e. for which the only remaining edge contributions have dihedral angles that are rational multiples of π) be dissection-equivalent to a cube of the same volume?

The problem was solved by J.-P. Sydler in 1965: he proved that two polyhedra in Euclidean 3-space are scissors-congruent if and only if they have the same volume and the same Dehn invariant. A simplified proof was given by Dupont and Sah in 1990 using group homology.

This is Tarski's circle-squaring problem, posed in 1925. It was solved affirmatively by Miklós Laczkovich in 1990, who showed that the disk and a square of equal area are equidecomposable into finitely many (non-measurable) pieces, in fact using only translations. A constructive (Borel) solution was later given by Grabowski, Máthé and Pikhurko (2016/2017), and a fully Borel solution by Marks and Unger.

Let $G$ be a simple graph. The energy of $G$ is $E(G)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\lambda_i|$, where $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of $G$. A connected graph on $n$ vertices with $m$ edges is called $r$-cyclic if $m=n+r-1$ (equivalently, its cyclomatic number is $r$).

For positive integers $r$ and $n$ with $n\ge 6r+4$, set $p=\lfloor r/2\rfloor$ and $q=\lceil r/2\rceil$. Let $C_6^{(1)},\dots,C_6^{(r)}$ be $r$ vertex-disjoint copies of the 6-cycle, and let $P_{n-6r}$ be a path on $n-6r$ vertices with endpoints $u$ and $v$. Define the graph $P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}$ to be obtained from the disjoint union of $P_{n-6r}$ and the $r$ copies of $C_6$ by adding $r$ edges: from $u$ to exactly one vertex of each of $p$ of the 6-cycles, and from $v$ to exactly one vertex of each of the remaining $q$ 6-cycles (one edge per attached cycle). Note that $P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}$ is a connected $r$-cyclic graph on $n$ vertices.

Prove or disprove: for every connected $r$-cyclic graph $G$ on $n$ vertices,
$$E(G)\le E\bigl(P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}\bigr),$$
with equality if and only if $G\cong P_n^{p\times 6;\, q\times 6}$.

The conjecture appears to remain open in general. It was formulated via AutoGraphiX experiments as a general $r$-cyclic extension of the maximum-energy conjectures for unicyclic, bicyclic, tricyclic and tetracyclic graphs. An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) are graded by rank from -1 to n, in which every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly one face of each rank, which is strongly flag-connected, and which satisfies the diamond condition: whenever F < G are faces with ranks differing by 2, there are exactly two faces strictly between F and G. Provide a general construction that recovers P as a coset geometry of Γ from this generator data alone, giving necessary and sufficient conditions (on the generators and on intersections of certain subgroups) under which an abstractly given group with such a generating set arises as the automorphism group of a k-orbit polytope reconstructable from those generators.
