Background. An abstract n-polytope is a ranked partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) have ranks in {-1,0,...,n} with unique minimum and maximum, in which every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly one face of each rank, which is strongly flag-connected, and which satisfies the diamond condition: whenever F < G with rank(G) = rank(F)+2, there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G. The facets are the faces of rank n-1. A maniplex of rank n is an edge-n-colored connected graph in which, for each pair of distinct colors i,j with |i-j| > 1, every connected component of the subgraph spanned by edges of colors i and j is a 4-cycle; abstract polytopes correspond to maniplexes satisfying the (strong) path-intersection property. A polytope (or maniplex) Q is a cover of P if there is a rank- and adjacency-preserving surjection of flags from Q to P. A polytope is called regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on flags, and chiral if it has two orbits of flags under automorphisms with adjacent flags lying in different orbits.

A known "quotient criterion" in the regular and chiral settings states that, under suitable assumptions on the facets, a regular (respectively chiral) cover of a regular (respectively chiral) polytope is itself polytopal, i.e. satisfies the intersection property.

Problem. Formulate and prove a purely combinatorial criterion, applicable to arbitrary abstract polytopes or maniplexes (not assumed to be regular or chiral), which serves the same role as the quotient criterion: namely, given a cover Q -> P of polytopes (or maniplexes), provide combinatorial conditions under which the polytopality (intersection property) of P, together with hypotheses on the facets, guarantees polytopality of Q.

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions:

An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set P with a strictly monotone rank function having range {-1, 0, ..., n}, with a unique minimum face F_{-1} and unique maximum face F_n, such that every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly n+2 faces, P is strongly flag-connected, and the diamond condition holds: whenever F < G with rank(G) − rank(F) = 2, there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G. For each i ∈ {0, 1, ..., n−1} and each flag Φ of P there is a unique flag Φ^i differing from Φ only in its rank-i face.

A maniplex of rank n is a combinatorial generalization of a polytope: it is an n-edge-colored connected graph whose vertices represent flags and whose i-colored edges represent the i-adjacency, satisfying the same local conditions as the flag graph of a polytope, but without requiring the existence of an underlying poset. Every abstract polytope gives rise to a maniplex via its flag graph, but not every maniplex arises this way.

A rooted polytope (resp. rooted maniplex) is a pair (P, Φ) where P is an abstract polytope (resp. maniplex) and Φ is a distinguished base flag of P. For each i, let r_i denote the involution that sends a flag to its i-adjacent flag. The monodromy group Mon(P) is the group generated by r_0, ..., r_{n−1} acting on the flags of P.

Given two rooted polytopes (P_1, Φ_1) and (P_2, Φ_2) of the same rank n, their mix (P_1 ◇ P_2, (Φ_1, Φ_2)) is the rooted maniplex defined as follows. Consider the subgroup of Mon(P_1) × Mon(P_2) generated by the diagonal elements (r_i^{P_1}, r_i^{P_2}) for i = 0, ..., n−1. The flags of the mix are the orbits of the base flag pair (Φ_1, Φ_2) under this group, with i-adjacency given by the diagonal generators. The mix is always a rooted maniplex, but it need not be the flag graph of an abstract polytope.

Problem:

Give a complete characterization of those pairs of rooted polytopes (P_1, Φ_1), (P_2, Φ_2) for which the mix (P_1 ◇ P_2, (Φ_1, Φ_2)) is itself (the flag graph of) an abstract polytope, rather than merely a rooted maniplex.

An (abstract) polytope of rank n is a ranked partially ordered set satisfying the usual axioms (existence of least and greatest faces, the diamond condition, strong flag connectivity). A flag of such a polytope is a maximal chain. The automorphism group acts on the set of flags, and a polytope is called a two-orbit polytope if this action has exactly two orbits.

The symmetry type graph of a polytope is the quotient multigraph whose vertices are the flag orbits of the automorphism group and whose i-colored edges record i-adjacency between flags modulo the group action (for i = 0, 1, ..., n−1).

A geometric polytope P realized in some Euclidean space E is said to be of full rank (relative to its symmetry type graph) if there is no polytope of rank one higher than P, realized in the same Euclidean space E, that has the same symmetry type graph as P.

Problem. Classify, up to similarity, all two-orbit polytopes of full rank in this sense; that is, determine all Euclidean realizations of abstract two-orbit polytopes P such that no polytope of strictly higher rank in the same Euclidean space possesses the same symmetry type graph as P.

Consider the following zero-sum pursuit-evasion game (the "princess and monster" game) played on a connected graph G = (V, E) whose edges are isometric to closed intervals of given positive lengths, equipped with the induced shortest-path metric. Two players, a Searcher S (the monster) and a Hider H (the princess), each move continuously along G with speed at most 1. The game takes place in continuous time t ≥ 0. At t = 0 each player independently chooses a (possibly randomized) starting point in G, and thereafter each player chooses a (measurable) trajectory of speed at most 1; the Searcher does not see the Hider's position and the Hider does not see the Searcher's position. The capture time T is the first time t ≥ 0 at which the two players occupy the same point of G. The Searcher seeks to minimize, and the Hider to maximize, the expected capture time E[T]. Let V(G) denote the value of this game.

(a) For graphs G other than a single circle (a graph isometric to a circle of given total length L, for which the value is known to equal L/2 times an established constant), determine V(G) and optimal strategies for both players.

(b) In particular, solve the case in which G is a closed interval [0, 1] of length 1: determine the exact value V([0,1]) and exhibit optimal (or ε-optimal) mixed strategies for both the Searcher and the Hider.

The princess-and-monster game on a graph has been solved only for the circle. For the interval, Alpern, Fokkink, Lindelauf, and Olsder (SIAM J. Consider a bounded region R in the Euclidean plane whose complement (within some bounding box) consists of finitely many "lakes," each lake being an open set whose boundary is a rectifiable Jordan curve. Three players — two "lions" L_1, L_2 and one "man" M — are modeled as points moving inside the closure of R. All three move along continuous trajectories and have the same maximum speed (normalized to 1); that is, each trajectory is 1-Lipschitz with respect to time. The lions choose their strategy knowing the position of the man at every time, and the man likewise knows the positions of the lions. The lions "capture" the man if at some finite time t ≥ 0 the position of at least one lion coincides with the position of the man.

Question: Do the two lions always have a strategy that guarantees capture of the man in finite time, regardless of the shape of R (subject to the rectifiable-lakes condition) and regardless of the man's strategy?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question (originally posed by Littlewood) has been resolved in the negative: there exists a bounded planar region with finitely many rectifiable lakes in which the man has a strategy to evade two lions forever. The same line of work shows that three lions always suffice to capture the man under these conditions, so two lions are not enough in general.

Consider the Princess-and-Monster pursuit-evasion game played on the closed interval [-1,1]. The Monster moves continuously along the interval with speed at most 1; the Princess may relocate instantaneously to any point (her position is hidden). Neither player observes the other. The payoff to the Monster is the (first) capture time, defined as the first time t ≥ 0 at which the two players occupy the same point; the Monster minimizes and the Princess maximizes the expected capture time.

Define the following pure Monster strategies, parameterized by an initial point x₀ ∈ [-1,1] and a direction d ∈ {-1,+1}:
• M1(x₀,d): start at x₀, move at speed 1 in direction d until reaching the corresponding endpoint, then reverse and traverse to the opposite endpoint.
• M2(x₀,d): start at x₀, move at speed 1 in direction d until meeting the "sweeper" coming from that direction (i.e., a Monster trajectory of type M1 traveling toward the same endpoint), then turn around and join that sweeper to the endpoint in direction d, then reverse and traverse to the opposite endpoint.

Fix an infinitesimal ε > 0 and define the following pure Princess strategies, forming a class P:
• Stay forever at an endpoint -1 or +1.
• Choose an initial point y₀ ∈ [-1+ε, -ε] ∪ [ε, 1-ε], remain stationary until the M1-type sweeper that starts at the endpoint nearest to y₀ is within distance ε of y₀, then run at unbounded speed to the midpoint 0, and finally run back to the endpoint on the same side as y₀.

The princess-and-monster game on an interval remains unsolved: while the value on a circle is known, on the interval only bounds (e.g., 15/11 ≤ V ≤ 13/9) are established, and the conjecture that optimal strategies are supported on the described classes M1 ∪ M2 and P (which would reduce the game to a finite linear program) is reported as unproven in subsequent literature including a numerical-approach paper and a 2023 thesis.

Consider the princess-and-monster search game played on a finite tree $T$ (a connected graph without cycles, viewed as a metric space with unit-length edges). Two players, the princess (hider) and the monster (searcher), move continuously along $T$ with speeds bounded by $1$. Neither player can see the other; capture occurs at the first time $t \ge 0$ at which the two players occupy the same point of $T$. The princess wishes to maximize, and the monster wishes to minimize, the expected capture time.

A (mixed) strategy for the princess is a probability distribution over Lipschitz trajectories $p:[0,\infty) \to T$ with $|p'| \le 1$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the support of such a strategy. The strategy is said to have the confluency property if for every pair of trajectories $p_1, p_2 \in \mathcal{P}$ and every time $t_0 \ge 0$ such that $p_1(t_0) = p_2(t_0)$, one has $p_1(t) = p_2(t)$ for all $t \in [0, t_0]$ (i.e., trajectories that meet at some time must have coincided at every earlier time).

Question: For the princess-and-monster game on an arbitrary finite tree, does there exist an optimal strategy for the princess that satisfies the confluency property?

Consider the following two-player zero-sum search game with parameter $n \geq 1$. Blue secretly maintains a number $h \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. In each round, Red announces a guess $g \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, and Blue must truthfully answer "too high", "too low", or "correct" relative to some value $h$, but Blue is allowed to change $h$ between rounds as long as every answer given so far remains consistent with at least one fixed sequence of valid choices (equivalently, Blue maintains the set $S$ of remaining candidates; on a guess $g$, Blue chooses one of the responses "high", "low", or "correct" and updates $S$ to $\{x \in S : x < g\}$, $\{x \in S : x > g\}$, or $\{g\}$ respectively). The game ends when Red identifies the unique remaining value; the payoff to Blue (and the loss to Red) is the number of guesses Red used. Both players play optimally. Let $V(n)$ denote the value of this game starting from $S = \{1,\ldots,n\}$.

Determine whether
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(V(n) - \log_2 n\bigr) = c$$
exists, and whether $c \approx 0.487$.

Consider the following two-player zero-sum continuous high–low guessing game. Player Blue (the hider) chooses a number h ∈ [0,1]. Player Red (the searcher) makes an infinite sequence of guesses g_1, g_2, … ∈ [0,1]. After each guess g_n, Red is told whether g_n > h or g_n < h (the event g_n = h has probability zero and is ignored). Red's strategy may be adaptive: each g_n may depend on the responses to g_1,…,g_{n-1}. Blue's payoff (which Red wishes to minimize and Blue wishes to maximize) is
   P(h, (g_n)) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ |g_n − h|.
A pure searcher strategy is a deterministic rule producing g_n from the history of responses; a mixed searcher strategy is a probability distribution over pure searcher strategies, with payoff taken in expectation. It is known that there exists a pure searcher strategy achieving the minimax value V* = sup_h P(h, ·) among pure strategies.

Question: Does there exist a mixed searcher strategy σ such that
   sup_{h ∈ [0,1]} E_{σ}[ Σ_n |g_n − h| ] < V* ?
That is, can randomization strictly improve the searcher's worst-case expected total error below the best pure-strategy guarantee?

Two players, a Hider and a Guesser, play the following infinite-horizon game. The Hider secretly chooses a number $h \in [0,1]$ (possibly according to a randomized strategy, i.e., a probability distribution on $[0,1]$). The Guesser then makes a sequence of guesses $g_1, g_2, g_3, \ldots \in [0,1]$; after each guess $g_n$, the Guesser is told only whether $g_n > h$ ("too high") or $g_n < h$ ("too low"). (The event $g_n = h$ occurs with probability zero under any nonatomic distribution and is ignored.) The Guesser uses this high/low feedback to choose subsequent guesses, and aims to minimize the total payoff
$$P = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |g_n - h|,$$
which is paid to the Hider; the Hider aims to maximize the expected value of $P$.

Determine an optimal (in general, randomized) strategy for the Hider in this zero-sum game, i.e., a probability distribution on $[0,1]$ that attains
$$\sup_{\mu} \inf_{\text{Guesser strategies}} \mathbb{E}_{h \sim \mu}\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |g_n - h|\right].$$

Consider the following two-player zero-sum continuous guessing game between a Hider and a Guesser. At each step n = 1, 2, 3, ..., the Hider selects a real number h_n ∈ ℝ (which may differ from h_{n-1}), and the Guesser, without observing h_n, announces a guess g_n ∈ ℝ. After each guess, the Hider truthfully reveals whether g_n < h_n, g_n = h_n, or g_n > h_n. The sequence (h_n) is assumed to converge to a limit h_∞ ∈ ℝ. The Hider's strategy space therefore allows the secret to move between consecutive guesses, subject only to the comparison responses already given and to the existence of the limit h_∞. The payoff (paid by the Guesser to the Hider) is
    P = Σ_{n=1}^{∞} |g_n - h_∞|.
The Guesser seeks to minimize P and the Hider seeks to maximize it.

In the classical static version of this game (where h_n = h is fixed), Alpern's pure minimax strategy for the Guesser is known to be optimal. The same pure minimax strategy is still well-defined when the Hider is allowed to move, and it yields a finite value against any admissible Hider strategy with payoff Σ |g_n - h_∞|.

Prove that Alpern's pure minimax Guesser strategy is optimal (i.e. achieves the value of the game) in this moving-hider variant with payoff Σ |g_n - h_∞|.

Prove or disprove the following conjecture (Johnson): for every integer n > 4, every optimal Blue strategy p* satisfies
   p*_1 = p*_2 + p*_3.

Let $(M^{2n}, \omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold and let $F = (F_1, \dots, F_n) : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a completely integrable system, i.e., the functions $F_1, \dots, F_n$ are smooth, functionally independent on an open dense set, and pairwise Poisson-commute: $\{F_i, F_j\} = 0$. Near a regular fiber, Arnold–Liouville coordinates yield action variables $I_1(c), \dots, I_n(c)$, where $c = (c_1, \dots, c_n)$ ranges over values of $F$ in a punctured neighbourhood of a critical value corresponding to a singular fiber $F^{-1}(c_0)$.

Assume explicit formulas for the action variables $I_k(c)$ are available, so that their asymptotic expansion as $c \to c_0$ can be analysed. Decompose $I_k$ as $I_k = I_k^{reg} + I_k^{sing}$, where $I_k^{reg}$ is real-analytic at $c_0$ and $I_k^{sing}$ carries the non-smooth part.

(a) Determine to what extent the topology of the singular fiber and of its tubular neighbourhood (the local and semi-local topological type of the singularity, in the sense of the Eliasson–Williamson classification and its degenerate generalizations) is reconstructible from the asymptotic behaviour of $I_k^{sing}(c)$ as $c \to c_0$. In particular, can different topological types of singularities always be distinguished by these asymptotics?

(b) It is known that, for one degree of freedom, a non-degenerate hyperbolic singularity produces a singular part of the form $I^{sing}(h) = h \ln h + \dots$ near the critical value $h = 0$. Prove or disprove: in arbitrary dimension $n$, the appearance of an $h \ln h$-type term in $I_k^{sing}$ is a characteristic property of non-degenerate hyperbolic singularities (and singularities containing a hyperbolic block).

(c) Investigate the analogous question for degenerate singularities: classify the possible asymptotic forms of action variables near degenerate singular fibers and relate them to the topology of the singularity.

(d) Describe which local and semi-local singularities can occur in algebraically integrable systems, in the following sense: $F_1, \dots, F_n$ are polynomials on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, the system admits a complexification to a complex integrable system whose generic complex fibers are isomorphic to affine parts of abelian varieties. (For one degree of freedom this restricts the Milnor number of a singular point to be at most $2$.) Provide a classification of admissible singularity types in this algebraic setting.

Let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a symplectic manifold equipped with a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, i.e. a smooth map $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ whose components Poisson-commute and are functionally independent on a dense open subset. A fiber $F^{-1}(c)$ is called singular if some $df_i$ fail to be linearly independent on it; a singular fiber is called degenerate when it is not modelled on the standard non-degenerate (elliptic, hyperbolic, focus-focus) building blocks of Williamson type.

(a) Investigate the topology and local geometry of degenerate singular fibers of completely integrable Hamiltonian systems and of small saturated neighbourhoods of such fibers. In particular, prove or disprove the following conjecture: for a generic / "most" completely integrable systems arising in the literature (such as bending flows on moduli spaces of $3$-dimensional polygons, the integrable system on the Grassmannian of $2$-planes, and the Gelfand–Cetlin system on coadjoint orbits of $U(n)$), every degenerate singular fiber is a smooth manifold or orbifold and is, moreover, an isotropic submanifold of $(M,\omega)$ — possibly even a Lagrangian submanifold when its dimension equals $n$. Develop the corresponding theory of symplectic invariants, symplectic normal forms, and stability under perturbation for these new classes of degenerate singularities.

(b) In the SYZ setting of mirror symmetry, let $\pi:X^{6}\to B^{3}$ be a Lagrangian torus fibration of a Calabi–Yau $3$-fold. Generic singularities of $\pi$ form $1$-dimensional strata of focus-focus type, but at finitely many isolated points of $B$ several such strata meet, producing special "intersection" singular fibers. Describe the topology, symplectic local model, and invariants of these special degenerate singular fibers occurring at intersections of focus-focus strata.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture has been confirmed in several specific examples since being posed: Bouloc handled the bending flows on 3D polygon spaces and the Grassmannian Gr(2,n) system; Bouloc–Miranda–Zung and Cho–Kim–Oh studied the Gelfand–Cetlin system on u(n)*, showing the singular fibers are smooth isotropic submanifolds (with Lagrangian "diamond" fibers); Cho–Kim handled the SO(n)-type Gelfand–Cetlin systems. The general conjecture for arbitrary integrable systems, the symplectic invariants/normal forms/stability theory of these degenerate fibers, and the description of the special intersection fibers in SYZ Calabi–Yau 3-fold fibrations remain open.

Setup. Let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold and let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a smooth integrable system, i.e. the functions $f_1,\dots,f_n$ are Poisson-commuting with respect to $\omega$ and are functionally independent on an open dense subset of $M$. The fibers of $F$ that contain critical points are called singular fibers; nondegenerate singular points are locally of elliptic, hyperbolic, or focus-focus type in the sense of Eliasson and Vey.

In the geometric context motivated by special Lagrangian fibrations on Calabi--Yau manifolds (in particular in real dimension $2n\ge 6$), there typically appear codimension-two strata of focus-focus type singularities forming one-parameter families, together with a finite collection of additional singular fibers that lie at the intersections/limits of these focus-focus families. Call these latter fibers the special singular fibers.

Problem. Give a clear topological and symplectic description of these special singular fibers: describe
(i) the local structure of the integrable system near such a fiber (a normal form, including the types of degeneracies of the critical points that occur on it),
(ii) the topology of the fiber itself and of a saturated neighborhood, including the monodromy of $F$ around it, and
(iii) classifying invariants (analogous to the Vũ Ngọc invariants for focus-focus fibers) that determine such a fiber up to a suitable notion of symplectic equivalence.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth connected Riemannian manifold. Call $(M,g)$ locally homogeneous if for every pair of points $p,q\in M$ there exist open neighborhoods $U\ni p$, $V\ni q$ and an isometry $\varphi:(U,g|_U)\to(V,g|_V)$ with $\varphi(p)=q$. Call $(M,g)$ $1$-homogeneous if for every pair of points $p,q\in M$ there exists a local isometry between neighborhoods of $p$ and $q$ matching the metric and its first covariant derivatives at the basepoints; equivalently (in terms of geodesic flow), there exist linear-in-momenta first integrals of the geodesic flow whose values at each point of $M$ span the tangent space.

Question: Must every $1$-homogeneous Riemannian manifold be locally homogeneous?

It is known that the answer is affirmative in dimensions $3$ and $4$, while the analogous statement fails for indefinite (pseudo-Riemannian) metrics. Determine whether the implication "$1$-homogeneous $\Rightarrow$ locally homogeneous" holds for Riemannian manifolds of all dimensions.

Let Ω ⊂ ℝ² be a strictly convex planar domain with smooth boundary γ. The (Birkhoff) billiard in Ω is the dynamical system describing the free motion of a point particle inside Ω that reflects off γ according to the law "angle of incidence equals angle of reflection." A smooth closed curve Γ ⊂ Ω is called a caustic of the billiard if every billiard trajectory tangent to Γ remains tangent to Γ after each reflection off γ.

Conjecture (Birkhoff): If there exists an open neighbourhood U of γ inside Ω such that U \ γ is foliated by caustics of the billiard in Ω, then γ is an ellipse.

Prove or disprove this conjecture. Also consider the generalized form: if some open subset of Ω is foliated by caustics of the billiard, must γ be an ellipse?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The smooth Birkhoff conjecture remains open in full generality. Major partial progress includes Bialy's theorem (boundary foliated except possibly one point), the local version proved by Avila–De Simoi–Kaloshin and Kaloshin–Sorrentino (small perturbations of ellipses must be ellipses), and complete proofs of the polynomial version by Bialy–Mironov and Glutsyuk. New integrable examples (e.g., billiards inside cones, 2025) suggest the landscape is still being mapped, but the original conjecture for general smooth convex tables is unresolved.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real (or complex) vector space equipped with a polynomial Poisson bracket $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$, that is, a Poisson bracket on $C^\infty(V)$ (or on the polynomial algebra $\mathbb{R}[V]$) such that the bracket of any two linear coordinate functions is a polynomial on $V$. Recall:

1. A "linear" Poisson bracket on $V$ corresponds to a Lie algebra structure on $V^*$: it is the canonical Lie–Poisson bracket on $\mathfrak{g}^* \cong V$. For such linear brackets, the Mischenko–Fomenko conjecture (proved by Sadetov) asserts that there always exists a complete family of polynomials on $V$ in involution, i.e. a polynomial integrable system.

2. A Poisson pencil is a one-parameter family $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_\lambda = \{\cdot,\cdot\}_1 + \lambda \{\cdot,\cdot\}_2$ of compatible Poisson brackets (any linear combination is again Poisson). A "quadratic + linear" pencil consists of a quadratic Poisson bracket $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_2$ (bracket of linear coordinates is homogeneous of degree $2$) compatible with a linear Poisson bracket $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_1$.

3. A family $\mathcal{F} \subset \mathbb{R}[V]$ of polynomials is said to be in bi-involution with respect to a Poisson pencil if $\{f,g\}_\lambda = 0$ for every $\lambda$ and every $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$. The family is complete (defines an integrable system) if at a generic point $x \in V$, $\dim\, d\mathcal{F}(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}(\dim V + \mathrm{corank}\,\{\cdot,\cdot\}_\lambda$ at $x)$ for generic $\lambda$.

Problem. (a) Investigate concrete examples of "quadratic + linear" Poisson pencils on vector spaces $V$, determine their algebraic types (i.e. the structure of the associated linear pencil of bivectors and the singular set), and for each such pencil construct an explicit complete family of polynomials in bi-involution.

(b) More generally, given a vector space $V$ equipped with a polynomial Poisson bracket of degree $\geq 2$, does there always exist a complete family of Poisson-commuting polynomials on $V$? In other words, does the analogue of the Mischenko–Fomenko theorem hold for polynomial Poisson brackets of higher degree?

The Mischenko–Fomenko conjecture for linear Poisson brackets was proved by Sadetov (2003/2004). The analogous question for polynomial Poisson brackets of higher degree, and the systematic study of "quadratic + linear" Poisson pencils with construction of complete bi-involutive families, remains an active research direction with only partial results (e.g., families of quadratic Poisson structures on gl(3)* compatible with the Lie–Poisson bracket due to Sokolov and others). No general result establishing existence of complete polynomial integrable systems for arbitrary higher-degree polynomial Poisson brackets has been reported.

The problem belongs to the program of describing singular points of two- and three-dimensional Nijenhuis operators. Let $M$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional manifold endowed with two compatible Poisson brackets $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_0$ and $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_1$ (i.e., every linear combination $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_0+\lambda\{\cdot,\cdot\}_1$ is again a Poisson bracket) such that $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_0$ is non-degenerate. The corresponding recursion operator $R:TM\to TM$, defined by $\{f,g\}_1=\{f,R\,dg\}_0$ (equivalently $R=P_1 P_0^{-1}$ where $P_i$ are the Poisson tensors), is then a Nijenhuis operator. Let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ denote the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of $R$ (so $\det(tI-R)=(t^n-\sigma_1 t^{n-1}+\sigma_2 t^{n-2}-\dots)^2$ after taking the square root in the symplectic case, with $\sigma_k$ a smooth function on $M$). Assume these functions are functionally independent almost everywhere and pairwise Poisson-commute, so that $\Phi=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ serves as the momentum map of the resulting bi-Hamiltonian integrable system.

Consider the linearization of this setup at a singular point: at such a point one obtains, after a suitable choice of coordinates $x_1,\dots,x_n$, a collection of algebraically independent homogeneous polynomials $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $\deg\sigma_k=k$ that pairwise commute with respect to a constant Poisson structure and arise as the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of a linear Nijenhuis operator.

Problem. Describe and classify all such collections $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ of algebraically independent homogeneous polynomials with $\deg\sigma_k=k$ in $n$ variables having this property, and use the classification to describe the singular points of the momentum map $\Phi=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ of a bi-Hamiltonian system of symplectic (i.e., non-degenerate) type in terms of the singularities of the underlying Poisson pencil / Nijenhuis operator.

Let $(M,\pi)$ be a Poisson manifold of dimension $n$ and let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_s):M\to\mathbb{R}^s$ be an integrable system on $(M,\pi)$ in the sense that the components $f_i$ pairwise Poisson-commute and define, on the regular part, a foliation by isotropic tori of maximal dimension. Assume the system is "splittable" at a point $p\in M$: in a neighbourhood of $p$ the Poisson structure $\pi$ admits a Weinstein-type splitting into a symplectic factor and a transverse Poisson factor that is compatible with the integrable system $F$, and assume that $p$ lies on a compact regular fibre (Liouville torus) of $F$ but is a singular point of the Poisson structure $\pi$ (i.e., the rank of $\pi$ drops at $p$).

(a) (Local problem.) Establish an action–angle theorem in a neighbourhood of the Liouville torus through $p$: find coordinates $(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_r, p_1,\dots,p_r, z_1,\dots,z_{n-2r})$ in a tubular neighbourhood of the torus, where $\theta_i$ are angle coordinates on the torus, $p_i$ are action coordinates conjugate to the $\theta_i$, and the $z_j$ are transverse coordinates, in which $\pi$ takes a normal form and $F$ depends only on $(p_1,\dots,p_r,z_1,\dots,z_{n-2r})$. Identify the precise hypotheses (for example, stability of the transverse Poisson structure, or the existence of an associated effective torus action preserving $F$) under which such coordinates exist for natural classes of Poisson manifolds.

(b) (Global problem.) On a regular Poisson manifold $(M,\pi)$ carrying an integrable system $F$, the image of the moment-type map $F$ is foliated by affine manifolds carrying integral affine structures coming from action variables on each symplectic leaf. Determine the obstructions (cohomological/monodromy/Chern-class-type invariants associated with this affine foliation) to the existence of global action–angle coordinates, in analogy with Duistermaat's symplectic obstruction theory.

Problem. Characterize the closed $n$-manifolds $B^n$ that arise in this way: give necessary and sufficient conditions on a closed smooth manifold $B^n$ for the existence of a symplectic manifold $(M^{2n}, \omega)$ and a locally trivial Lagrangian $T^n$-fibration $\pi: M^{2n} \to B^n$.

Let $M$ be a $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and let $P_1(\hbar), \dots, P_n(\hbar)$ be a family of self-adjoint semiclassical $\hbar$-pseudodifferential operators on $M$ (or on a quantizable Kähler manifold via Berezin–Toeplitz quantization) depending on a small parameter $\hbar \in (0,\hbar_0]$. Assume that:

1. The operators pairwise commute: $[P_i(\hbar), P_j(\hbar)] = 0$ for all $i,j$.
2. Each $P_i$ admits a principal symbol $p_i \in C^\infty(M;\mathbb{R})$, and the joint principal symbol map $F = (p_1, \dots, p_n) : M 	o \mathbb{R}^n$ is proper on each level (so the joint spectrum is discrete).

A classical integrability condition further requires:

3. The functions $p_1, \dots, p_n$ are almost everywhere independent, i.e.\ $dp_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge dp_n 
eq 0$ on a dense open subset of $M$.

The joint spectrum $\mathrm{JointSpec}(P_1(\hbar), \dots, P_n(\hbar))$ is the set of $E = (E_1,\dots,E_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that there exists a nonzero common eigenvector $\psi$ with $P_i(\hbar)\psi = E_i \psi$ for all $i$.

Question: Suppose only conditions (1) and (2) are known. Is there a purely spectral criterion — formulated through the asymptotic behavior, as $\hbar 	o 0^+$, of the joint eigenvalues $E(\hbar)$ and/or the joint eigenfunctions of $(P_1(\hbar),\dots,P_n(\hbar))$ — that is equivalent to condition (3) (almost-everywhere independence of the principal symbols)?

For a fibration $f\colon X \to B$ from a smooth complex projective surface $X$ onto a smooth projective curve $B$, the relative irregularity is classically defined as $q_f := h^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X) - g(B)$, where $g(B)$ is the genus of $B$. This invariant plays a central role in the geometry of surface fibrations (e.g., in Xiao's conjecture and the Severi inequality).

Investigate analogous notions of relative irregularity for families $f\colon X \to B$ of higher-dimensional smooth projective varieties (i.e., where the general fibre $F$ has $\dim F \geq 2$), under suitable hypotheses on the fibres (for instance, fibres of general type, fibres of maximal Albanese dimension, or fibres with prescribed Hodge-theoretic properties). Formulate the possible definitions of relative irregularity in this higher-dimensional setting, compare them, establish their basic properties, and determine the inequalities or geometric constraints (analogous to those known in the surface case) that they must satisfy.

Let $f\colon S\to B$ be a non-isotrivial fibration from a smooth complex projective surface $S$ onto a smooth complex projective curve $B$, with connected fibers of genus $g\ge 2$, and assume $f$ is relatively minimal. Let $\omega_f=\omega_S\otimes f^*\omega_B^{-1}$ be the relative canonical bundle, and define
$$\chi_f=\deg f_*\omega_f,\qquad K_f^2=c_1(\omega_f)^2.$$
By the Fujita decomposition, $f_*\omega_f=\mathcal{U}\oplus\mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{U}$ is a unitary flat bundle and $\mathcal{A}$ is an ample vector bundle; let $q_f$ denote the relative irregularity of $f$ (equivalently, $q(S)-g(B)$, with $\mathcal{U}$ contributing the unitary rank). The slope of $f$ is
$$\lambda(f)=\frac{K_f^2}{\chi_f}.$$
The classical Cornalba–Harris–Xiao bound asserts $\lambda(f)\ge 4(g-1)/g$.

Problem: Establish sharper lower bounds for $\lambda(f)$ that improve the classical bound as the relative irregularity $q_f$ grows. In particular, decide whether one can prove
$$\lambda(f)\ge \frac{4(g-1)}{g-q_f}$$
for relatively minimal non-isotrivial fibrations under appropriate hypotheses, and identify the largest range of $q_f$ (relative to $g$) for which such a bound holds.

The Barja–Stoppino slope conjecture $\lambda(f)\ge 4(g-1)/(g-q_f)$ has been partially resolved: Lu and Zuo (Ann. Sc. Norm. Super. Pisa, 2019) proved it when $q_f$ is small compared to $g$, and constructed counterexamples when $g$ is odd and $q_f=(g+1)/2$, showing the bound cannot hold in full generality. Sharper slope inequalities involving the unitary rank and Clifford index were obtained by Riva (Proc. LMS, 2022) and further refined in subsequent work (Sci. China Math., 2024). So the broad program of sharpening slope bounds in terms of $q_f$ is actively progressing but not fully closed.

Let $f: S \to B$ be a fibred surface, that is, a surjective morphism with connected fibres from a smooth complex projective surface $S$ onto a smooth complex projective curve $B$, whose general fibre is a smooth curve of genus $g \geq 2$. Let $\omega_f$ denote the relative dualizing sheaf and consider the Hodge bundle $f_*\omega_f$, a vector bundle of rank $g$ on $B$. By the second Fujita decomposition, $f_*\omega_f$ admits a splitting $f_*\omega_f = A \oplus U$, where $A$ is a locally free sheaf with ample Hodge-theoretic part and $U$ is the maximal unitary flat summand (i.e., the maximal subbundle coming from a unitary representation of $\pi_1(B)$). Let $u_f := \mathrm{rk}(U)$.

(a) Determine the general relation between the unitary rank $u_f$ and the genus $g$ of the fibration. In particular, decide whether there exists a Xiao-type lower bound for $u_f$ in terms of $g$ and the invariants of $f$.

(b) Answer the same question in the isotrivial case, namely when all smooth fibres of $f$ are mutually isomorphic.

Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective surface and let $L$ be an ample line bundle on $X$. For a point $x \in X$, the Seshadri constant of $L$ at $x$ is defined by
$$\varepsilon(X,L;x) \;=\; \inf_{C \ni x} \frac{L \cdot C}{\mathrm{mult}_x C},$$
where the infimum runs over all irreducible curves $C \subset X$ passing through $x$. The Seshadri constant of $L$ at a very general point is the value $\varepsilon(X,L) := \varepsilon(X,L;x)$ for $x$ in the complement of a countable union of proper Zariski-closed subsets of $X$ (this common value exists).

Either:
(a) exhibit an explicit polarised smooth complex projective surface $(X,L)$ with $L$ ample such that $\varepsilon(X,L)$ at a very general point is an irrational real number; or
(b) prove that for every polarised smooth complex projective surface $(X,L)$, the Seshadri constant $\varepsilon(X,L)$ at a very general point is a rational number.

The rationality of Seshadri constants on surfaces at a very general point is a well-known long-standing open problem. All explicitly computed Seshadri constants to date are rational, but no unconditional example of irrationality is known. Recent works (e.g., on blow-ups of ruled surfaces and of P^2) establish rationality in special cases or produce irrational examples only conditionally on conjectures such as a strengthened SHGH conjecture. No unconditional resolution has been published as of 2026.

$$\mathrm{Aut}(X_3, S_3) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}(V_3)$$
yield an equality $\mathrm{Aut}(V_3) = \mathrm{Aut}(X_3, S_3)$? In particular, is $\mathrm{Aut}(V_3)$ a finite group?

Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve over the complex numbers of genus $g$ and gonality $k$, i.e., $k$ is the minimal degree of a non-constant morphism $C \to \mathbb{P}^1$. For an integer $d \geq 0$, let
$$W^1_d(C) = \{\, L \in \mathrm{Pic}^d(C) : h^0(C,L) \geq 2 \,\}$$
denote the Brill–Noether locus parametrizing line bundles of degree $d$ on $C$ admitting at least a pencil of sections.

Say that $C$ satisfies the linear growth condition if
$$\dim W^1_{k+n}(C) \leq n \quad \text{for every integer } n \text{ with } 0 \leq n \leq g - 2k + 2.$$

Prove or disprove: every smooth projective curve $C$ of gonality $k$ and genus $g$ such that $\dim W^1_k(C) = 0$ satisfies the linear growth condition.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The linear growth condition was introduced by Aprodu in connection with Green's conjecture, and the implication "dim W^1_k(C) = 0 ⇒ linear growth" is a conjectural strengthening used to deduce Green's conjecture in several settings (e.g., curves on K3 surfaces, general k-gonal curves). Available literature continues to refer to it as a conjecture and uses it as a hypothesis rather than a theorem in general; no general proof was located.

Let $\mathbb{X}$ be an exceptional curve in the sense of Lenzing–Kussin, i.e. a noncommutative smooth projective curve of genus zero over a field $k$: a small connected hereditary $k$-linear abelian category $\mathcal{H} = \mathrm{coh}(\mathbb{X})$ that contains a tilting object, that has Serre duality, and whose objects decompose into a "line bundle" part and a torsion part formed of tubes. Equivalently, $\mathbb{X}$ is a weighted noncommutative regular projective curve over $k$, obtained from a noncommutative regular projective curve of genus zero by attaching positive integer weights at finitely many closed points.

The "ELMS conjecture" on exceptional curves asserts a precise structural prediction about $\mathbb{X}$ (for instance, on the classification, function field invariants, or representation-theoretic invariants of exceptional curves of a given type). Resolve this conjecture: either prove that the predicted statement holds for every exceptional curve $\mathbb{X}$ over an arbitrary base field $k$, or exhibit an exceptional curve violating it.

(a) Determine the possible birational types of the image $X$. In particular, must $X$ be a rational surface?

(b) As partial information, verify that any such $X$ satisfies $p_g(X) = q(X) = 0$ and $\pi_1(X) = 1$, and decide whether these constraints force $X$ to be rational.

Let $\mathcal{M}_g$ denote the (coarse) moduli space of smooth complex projective curves of genus $g\ge 2$. A theorem of Diaz states that every complete subvariety $Y\subset \mathcal{M}_g$ satisfies $\dim Y \le g-2$.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, let $S\mathbb{P}_d$ denote the moduli space of smooth surfaces of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{P}^3$, that is, the geometric quotient of the open locus $U_d\subset \mathbb{P}(H^0(\mathbb{P}^3,\mathcal{O}(d)))$ parametrizing smooth surfaces by the natural action of $\mathrm{PGL}(4,\mathbb{C})$. Similarly, for integers $a,b\ge 1$, let $S\mathbb{P}_{a,b}$ denote the moduli space of smooth complete intersections in $\mathbb{P}^4$ of bidegree $(a,b)$, obtained as the geometric quotient by $\mathrm{PGL}(5,\mathbb{C})$ of the open locus in the appropriate Grassmannian-bundle parametrizing such smooth intersections.

Problem. Under appropriate non-degeneracy hypotheses (for instance, restricting to a very general surface or complete intersection of general type), establish a Diaz-type upper bound on the dimension of any complete subvariety $Y\subset S\mathbb{P}_d$, and likewise on the dimension of any complete subvariety $Y\subset S\mathbb{P}_{a,b}$. Specifically: find an explicit function $\phi(d)$ (resp. $\phi(a,b)$), depending only on the numerical invariants, such that every complete subvariety $Y$ satisfies $\dim Y\le \phi(d)$ (resp. $\dim Y\le \phi(a,b)$), in analogy with Diaz's bound $g-2$ for $\mathcal{M}_g$.

Let $d \geq 3$ be an integer. A finite set $Z \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ (over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero) is called $(d,d)$-geproci if for a general point $x \in \mathbb{P}^3$ the image of $Z$ under linear projection $\pi_x : \mathbb{P}^3 \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^2$ from $x$ is the complete intersection of two plane curves of degree $d$. A trivial example is given by an $(d,d)$-grid: a set of $d^2$ points obtained as the pairwise intersections of two families of $d$ pairwise skew lines (a "ruling-like" configuration) such that every line of one family meets every line of the other.

Classify all configurations $Z \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ of $|Z| = d^2$ points such that for every general linear projection from a point $x \in \mathbb{P}^3$, the resulting configuration of $d^2$ points in $\mathbb{P}^2$ is the complete intersection of two plane curves of degree $d$. Equivalently, describe all $(d,d)$-geproci sets of $d^2$ points in $\mathbb{P}^3$ for $d \geq 3$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem is the well-known geproci classification problem. The case $d=3$ is solved: any non-degenerate set of 9 points with the property is a $(3,3)$-grid. For general $d$, classification remains open; new non-grid examples (e.g. from the $D_4$, $F_4$, and $H_4$ root systems, and a 120-point configuration) have been discovered, and partial classification results exist (e.g., under assumptions of being supported on skew lines with transversals). Active research as of 2023–2025 continues to investigate the full classification.

Let $q \ge 2$ be a prime power and let $\mathbb{F}_q$ denote the finite field with $q$ elements. For vectors $x,y \in \mathbb{F}_q^n$, define the Hamming distance $d_H(x,y) := |\{i \in \{1,\dots,n\} : x_i \ne y_i\}|$. A $q$-ary code of length $n$ and minimum distance $d$ is a subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ such that $d_H(x,y) \ge d$ for every pair of distinct $x,y \in C$. Define
$$A_q(n,d) := \max\{\,|C| : C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n \text{ is a code with minimum distance at least } d\,\}.$$
Problem: For fixed integers $n \ge 1$, $1 \le d \le n$, and a fixed prime power $q$, determine the exact value of $A_q(n,d)$.

Let $q \ge 2$ be a prime power and let $\mathbb{F}_q$ denote the finite field with $q$ elements. For vectors $x,y \in \mathbb{F}_q^n$, define the Hamming distance $d_H(x,y) := |\{i \in \{1,\dots,n\} : x_i \ne y_i\}|$. A $q$-ary code of length $n$ and minimum distance $d$ is a subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ such that $d_H(x,y) \ge d$ for every pair of distinct $x,y \in C$. Define
$$A_q(n,d) := \max\{\,|C| : C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n \text{ is a code with minimum distance at least } d\,\}.$$
Problem: For fixed integers $n \ge 1$, $1 \le d \le n$, and a fixed prime power $q$, determine the exact value of $A_q(n,d)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Determining $A_q(n,d)$ exactly is a long-standing central open problem in coding theory. Exact values are known only in restricted cases (e.g., MDS codes meeting the Singleton bound, perfect codes, small parameters); tables of best known upper and lower bounds are maintained (e.g., Brouwer's and Grassl's tables), but no general formula is known and the problem remains open.

Let $G$ be a finite group and let $n \geq 1$. A (group) code of length $n$ over $G$ is a subgroup $C \leq G^n$. When $G$ is abelian, the classical MacWilliams identity relates the complete weight enumerator of $C$ to that of its dual code $C^\perp \leq \widehat{G}^n$ (where $\widehat{G}$ is the Pontryagin dual), via the character table of $G$.

Question: Does there exist a notion of duality $C \mapsto C^\perp$ for codes $C \leq G^n$ over non-abelian finite groups $G$ that produces a MacWilliams-type identity, i.e., a linear transformation expressing a suitable weight enumerator of $C^\perp$ in terms of that of $C$ (and vice versa) so that the enumerators of $C$ and $C^\perp$ determine each other? If no such duality exists for all non-abelian finite groups, identify a non-trivial subclass of non-abelian finite groups for which such a duality together with a MacWilliams identity can be defined.

Let A denote a finite algebraic structure (for example, a finite group, ring, module, or more general finite algebraic object) and, for each positive integer n, equip A^n with a notion of "code" (a distinguished family of substructures C ⊆ A^n) and a notion of "dual code" C^⊥ ⊆ A^n. Assume each code C carries a Hamming weight enumerator W_C(x,y) = Σ_{c∈C} x^{n−wt(c)} y^{wt(c)}, where wt(c) is the number of nonzero coordinates of c. One says that a "duality theory with MacWilliams relations" exists for A if there is an involutive duality operation C ↦ C^⊥ on codes in A^n (for every n) together with an identity of the form
   W_{C^⊥}(x,y) = (1/|C|) · W_C(x + (q−1)y, x − y)
or, more generally, W_{C^⊥}(x,y) = (1/|C|) · W_C(T(x,y)) for some fixed linear transformation T depending only on A, that holds for every code C ⊆ A^n and every n ≥ 1.

It is classically known that such a duality theory with MacWilliams relations exists when A is a finite field, a finite abelian group (with additive codes), or a finite Frobenius ring (with left/right linear codes).

Problem. Determine the largest class of finite algebraic structures A for which a duality theory together with MacWilliams relations (in the sense above) can be defined.

Background. A linear $[n,k,d]$ code $C$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, where $d$ denotes its minimum Hamming distance. Its dual code $C^\perp$ is defined with respect to the standard inner product and has minimum distance denoted $d^\perp$. For a codeword $c\in C$, its support is $\mathrm{supp}(c)=\{i:c_i\neq 0\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$. For each integer $w$, let $\mathcal{B}_w(C)$ denote the multiset of supports of codewords of $C$ of Hamming weight $w$ (taken up to scalar multiplication). A $t$-$(n,w,\lambda)$ design is a collection of $w$-element blocks from an $n$-element point set such that every $t$-element subset of points lies in exactly $\lambda$ blocks.

The Assmus–Mattson theorem asserts: let $C$ be an $[n,k,d]$ linear code over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with dual code $C^\perp$ of minimum distance $d^\perp$. Fix a positive integer $t<d$. If the number of nonzero weights in $C^\perp$ that are at most $n-t$ is at most $d-t$, then for every $w$ with $d\le w\le n$, the supports $\mathcal{B}_w(C)$ form (the blocks of) a $t$-design (and similarly for $C^\perp$).

Problem. Either:
(a) prove that there exists an absolute upper bound $T<\infty$ such that, for every prime power $q$, every length $n$, and every linear code $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, the largest value of $t$ for which the Assmus–Mattson theorem applied to $C$ produces a nontrivial $t$-design is at most $T$; or
(b) prove no such bound exists, by exhibiting, for every positive integer $t$, a linear code $C$ over some finite field for which the Assmus–Mattson theorem yields a $t$-design.

Let A be an alphabet, which is either a finite set of size |A| ≥ 2 or a finite (commutative) principal ideal ring R. A code of length n over A is a subset C ⊆ A^n; when A = R is a ring, a linear code C is an R-submodule of R^n, and its rank is the smallest cardinality of a generating set of C as an R-module. The Hamming distance between x, y ∈ A^n is d(x, y) = |{i : x_i ≠ y_i}|, and the minimum distance of C is d(C) = min{d(x, y) : x, y ∈ C, x ≠ y}.

Set k = log_{|A|}|C| when A is a finite alphabet, and let k be the rank of C when C is a linear code over a finite principal ideal ring. Then in both settings one has the Singleton-type bound d(C) ≤ n − k + 1. Codes attaining this bound are called Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) in the alphabet case, and Maximum Distance with respect to Rank (MDR) in the linear-over-PIR case.

Problem. Classify (give existence parameters and, up to suitable equivalence, an enumeration of) all MDS codes over finite alphabets and all MDR linear codes over finite principal ideal rings. Concretely, determine the complete set of admissible parameters (n, k, d = n − k + 1) and, for each admissible parameter triple, describe all such codes up to monomial/module-equivalence, across the classes of alphabets and principal ideal rings under consideration (in particular finite fields, Galois rings, finite chain rings, and general finite principal ideal rings).

Codes attaining this bound are called Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) in the alphabet case, and Maximum Distance with respect to Rank (MDR) in the linear-over-PIR case.

Problem. Classify (give existence parameters and, up to suitable equivalence, an enumeration of) all MDS codes over finite alphabets and all MDR linear codes over finite principal ideal rings. Concretely, determine the complete set of admissible parameters (n, k, d = n − k + 1) and, for each admissible parameter triple, describe all such codes up to monomial/module-equivalence, across the classes of alphabets and principal ideal rings under consideration (in particular finite fields, Galois rings, finite chain rings, and general finite principal ideal rings).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

A full classification remains open. Even over finite fields, the MDS conjecture (the main classification question for MDS codes) is unresolved in general, despite Ball's proof for prime fields. Let R be a finite ring of order 4 (for instance Z/4Z or F_2[u]/(u^2) or F_4). Consider linear codes C ⊆ R^n. Three weight functions are considered on R:

(i) the Lee weight w_L,
(ii) the Euclidean weight w_E,
(iii) the Bachoc weight w_B.

For a codeword x ∈ R^n, define the corresponding distance d_•(x) as the sum of the per-coordinate weights, and for a code C set d_•(C) = min{d_•(x) : x ∈ C, x ≠ 0}. Each codeword x ∈ R^n also has a rank rk(x), defined (as in the rank-metric setting for codes over rings of order 4) via the matrix associated to x over the underlying prime field; the rank distance of a code is rk(C) = min{rk(x) : x ∈ C, x ≠ 0}.

Known bounds relate the Lee, Euclidean, and Bachoc distances of a linear code to its rank K and length n:
  (1)  d_L(C) ≤ Φ_L(n,K),
  (2)  d_E(C) ≤ Φ_E(n,K),
  (3)  d_B(C) ≤ Φ_B(n,K),
for explicit functions Φ_L, Φ_E, Φ_B (the rank-metric Singleton-type bounds for these weights).

A code attaining bound (1) is called a Maximum Lee Distance with respect to Rank (MLDR) code; attaining (2) gives a Maximum Euclidean Distance with respect to Rank (MEDR) code; attaining (3) gives a Maximum Bachoc Distance with respect to Rank (MBDR) code.

A binary linear code of length n is a linear subspace C ⊆ F_2^n. The Hamming weight of a codeword is the number of its nonzero coordinates, and the minimum distance d(C) is the minimum Hamming weight among nonzero codewords. The dual code is C^⊥ = { x ∈ F_2^n : x·c = 0 for all c ∈ C }, where x·c is the standard inner product modulo 2. A code C is self-dual if C = C^⊥, which forces dim C = n/2. A binary self-dual code is called Type II (doubly even) if the Hamming weight of every codeword is divisible by 4; this requires n ≡ 0 (mod 8). For a Type II code of length n, the minimum distance satisfies d ≤ 4⌊n/24⌋ + 4, and a code attaining this bound is called extremal.

Question: Does there exist a binary Type II self-dual code with parameters [72, 36, 16] (i.e., length 72, dimension 36, and minimum distance 16, with all codeword weights divisible by 4)?

Let $G$ be a right-orderable group, i.e., there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ such that $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a,b,c \in G$. A subgroup $H \le G$ is called right relatively convex in $G$ if there exists a total order $\preceq$ on the set of right cosets $H\backslash G$ which is invariant under the right action of $G$ (i.e., $Hx \preceq Hy$ implies $Hxg \preceq Hyg$ for all $x,y,g \in G$). The collection of all right relatively convex subgroups of $G$, ordered by inclusion, forms a lattice $\mathrm{RC}(G)$.

Prove or disprove: For every right-orderable group $G$, the lattice $\mathrm{RC}(G)$ is distributive if and only if it is a chain (i.e., totally ordered by inclusion).

A sequence of works has progressively restricted the automorphism group of a putative extremal Type II [72,36,16] binary code. It has been shown that the group cannot contain various subgroups (S_3, A_4, D_8, Z_2×Z_4, Q_8, Z_10) and is not elementary abelian of order 8. Combining these results, Aut(C) has order at most 5; it is now known to be cyclic of order 1, 2, 3, or 5. The full conjecture that the automorphism group is trivial has not been established.

A counterexample has been provided: take $A$ to be the additive group of $\mathbb{F}_3[x,y]/I^3$ where $I=(x,y)$, let $B$ be the group of automorphisms of $A$ generated by multiplication by $1+x$ and $1+y$, and form $G = A \rtimes B$. Let $k\ge 1$ and consider the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}=\mathbb{Z}/2k\mathbb{Z}$. For a vector $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{2k}^n$, define its Euclidean weight by
$$\mathrm{wt}_E(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n \min\{x_i^2,(2k-x_i)^2\},$$
where $x_i$ is identified with its representative in $\{0,1,\dots,2k-1\}$. A linear code $C\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{2k}^n$ is self-dual if $C=C^\perp$ with respect to the standard inner product modulo $2k$. The code $C$ is called Type II if it is self-dual and every codeword has Euclidean weight divisible by $4k$. Let $d_E(C)$ denote the minimum nonzero Euclidean weight of $C$.

Construction A assigns to such a code $C$ the lattice
$$\Lambda(C)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2k}}\bigl\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n : x \bmod 2k \in C\bigr\}.$$
If $C$ is Type II, then $\Lambda(C)$ is an even unimodular lattice of minimum norm $\min\{2k,\,d_E(C)/(2k)\}$. An even unimodular lattice in dimension $n$ (a multiple of $8$) is called extremal if its minimum norm equals $2\lfloor n/24\rfloor+2$.

Problem: Let $n$ be a positive multiple of $8$, and write $s=\lfloor n/24\rfloor$. Construct a Type II self-dual code $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$ of length $n$ with $2k\ge 2s+2$ such that
$$\frac{d_E(C)}{2k}=2s+2,$$
so that $\Lambda(C)$ is an extremal even unimodular lattice. Determine, for each such $n$ and each admissible $k$, whether such an extremal Type II $\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$-code exists.

For a full-rank lattice $L\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, define its theta series by
\[ \theta_L(y) \;=\; \sum_{x\in L} q^{\,x\cdot x}, \qquad q = e^{-\pi y}, \quad y>0, \]
where $x\cdot x$ denotes the standard Euclidean inner product. For the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^n$, set $\theta_{\mathbb{Z}^n}(y)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n} q^{x\cdot x}$. A lattice $L\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is called unimodular if it equals its dual $L^*=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n : v\cdot x\in\mathbb{Z}\ \forall x\in L\}$. For a unimodular lattice $L$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, define the secrecy ratio
\[ r_L(y) \;=\; \frac{\theta_{\mathbb{Z}^n}(y)}{\theta_L(y)}, \qquad y\geq 0. \]
Prove that for every unimodular lattice $L$, the function $y\mapsto r_L(y)$ is unimodal on $[0,\infty)$ and attains its maximum at $y=1$.

This is the Belfiore–Solé secrecy-function conjecture. It has been verified for many specific families (e.g., all known extremal even unimodular lattices in dimensions less than 80, and unimodular lattices from Type II codes of length up to 40), but it remains open in general for unimodular lattices. Let p be a prime and let L be a finite extension of the prime field F_p such that the degree [L : F_p] is a power of 2. Let μ : L → C be the canonical additive character of L, defined by μ(x) = exp(2πi · Tr_{L/F_p}(x) / p), where Tr_{L/F_p} denotes the absolute trace. For an integer s with gcd(s, |L^×|) = 1 (an "invertible exponent"), define the Weil sum

   W_{L,s}(a) = ∑_{x ∈ L} μ(x^s − a x),   for a ∈ L.

The reduced spectrum of s over L is the set of distinct values taken by W_{L,s}(a) as a ranges over L^× = L \ {0}.

Question: Does there exist any such prime p, field L with [L : F_p] a power of 2, and invertible exponent s for which this reduced spectrum has exactly three distinct values? Equivalently, prove or disprove that for every prime p, every finite extension L/F_p of 2-power degree, and every invertible exponent s, the reduced spectrum of x ↦ x^s on L is never three-valued.

A binary linear code $C$ of length $n$ is self-dual if $C = C^\perp$ with respect to the standard inner product on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$. It is singly-even (Type I) if all codeword weights are even but not all are divisible by 4. The shadow of a singly-even self-dual code $C$ is $S = C_0^\perp \setminus C$, where $C_0$ is the subcode of codewords of weight divisible by 4. A self-dual code of length $n$ and minimum distance $d$ is called extremal if $d$ attains the maximal value allowed by the Mallows–Sloane bound; for Type I codes of length $48$ this maximum is $10$.

It is known that there are exactly two possible weight enumerators for extremal singly-even self-dual $[48,24,10]$ codes. Consider the second one, namely
$$W(y) \;=\; 1 + 768\,y^{10} + 8592\,y^{12} + 57600\,y^{14} + \cdots,$$
together with the corresponding shadow weight enumerator
$$S(y) \;=\; 54\,y^{8} + 16976\,y^{12} + \cdots .$$

Classify, up to equivalence, all extremal singly-even self-dual binary $[48,24,10]$ codes whose Hamming weight enumerator equals $W(y)$ (equivalently, whose shadow enumerator equals $S(y)$).

Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and let $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ be a linear code of length $n$ and dimension $k$. The dual code is $C^\perp = \{ x \in \mathbb{F}_q^n : \langle x, c \rangle = 0 \text{ for all } c \in C \}$, where $\langle x, c \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i c_i$. The code $C$ is called self-dual if $C = C^\perp$ (which forces $n = 2k$). Given a received word $y = c + e \in \mathbb{F}_q^n$, where $c \in C$ and $e$ is an error vector of Hamming weight at most $\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor$ (with $d$ the minimum distance of $C$), the decoding problem asks to recover $c$ from $y$.

Exhibit an infinite family $\{C_n\}$ of self-dual codes (with $n \to \infty$) together with a decoding algorithm running in time polynomial in $n$ that corrects up to $\lfloor (d_n-1)/2 \rfloor$ errors for every $C_n$ in the family. More ambitiously, produce such a polynomial-time decoding algorithm that works for all self-dual codes (given a generator matrix as input).

No general efficient decoding algorithm for self-dual codes is known. For positive integers $n$ and $d$ with $1 \le d \le n$, let $A_2(n,d)$ denote the maximum number of codewords in a binary code $C \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ such that any two distinct codewords differ in at least $d$ coordinates. Define the asymptotic rate function
$$R(\delta) \;=\; \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log_2 A_2(n, \lfloor \delta n \rfloor)}{n}, \qquad \delta \in (0, 1/2).$$
Two classical bounds on $R(\delta)$ are:

1. The Gilbert–Varshamov (existence) lower bound:
$$R(\delta) \;\ge\; 1 - H_2(\delta), \qquad H_2(x) = -x \log_2 x - (1-x)\log_2(1-x).$$

2. The linear programming (LP) upper bound: any function $\beta : \{0,1,\dots,n\} \to \mathbb{R}$ that arises as the Hamming-weight enumerator of a code of minimum distance $d$ must satisfy the MacWilliams inequalities, and optimizing over all such functions yields an upper bound $R_{\mathrm{LP}}(\delta)$ on $R(\delta)$. Explicit asymptotic forms (e.g. the McEliece–Rodemich–Rumsey–Welch bound) give
$$R(\delta) \;\le\; H_2\!\left( \tfrac{1}{2} - \sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)} \right).$$

For every $\delta \in (0, 1/2)$, there is a strict gap between the GV lower bound and the LP upper bound. Determine $R(\delta)$ for $\delta \in (0,1/2)$, or more generally close the gap between the Gilbert–Varshamov lower bound and the linear-programming upper bound on $R(\delta)$.

Determining the true asymptotic rate function $R(\delta)$ for binary codes — equivalently closing the gap between the Gilbert–Varshamov lower bound and the linear-programming (MRRW) upper bound — is widely recognized as a longstanding central open problem in coding theory. The tightness of the binary Gilbert–Varshamov bound is a long-standing open problem in coding theory. For alphabets of size q ≥ 49, the Tsfasman–Vlăduț–Zink bound from algebraic-geometry codes improves on Gilbert–Varshamov, but no asymptotic improvement is known for binary codes, and it remains a conjecture (often attributed to Goppa) that the bound is asymptotically tight in the binary case. Let $\mathbb{Z}_4 = \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ denote the ring of integers modulo $4$. A cyclic code of length $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}_4$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_4$-submodule $C \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_4^n$ closed under the cyclic shift $(c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n-1}) \mapsto (c_{n-1}, c_0, \dots, c_{n-2})$. Equivalently, $C$ corresponds to an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}_4[x]/(x^n-1)$. The Lee weight on $\mathbb{Z}_4$ is defined by $w_L(0)=0,\, w_L(1)=w_L(3)=1,\, w_L(2)=2$, extended additively to $\mathbb{Z}_4^n$, and the Lee (or Hamming) distance of $C$ is the minimum Lee (or Hamming) weight of a nonzero codeword.

Recall the classical BCH bound for cyclic codes over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ (with $\gcd(n,q)=1$): if the defining set of $C$ contains $\delta-1$ consecutive powers of a primitive $n$-th root of unity, then the minimum Hamming distance of $C$ is at least $\delta$.

Problem: Establish a BCH-type lower bound on the minimum (Hamming or Lee) distance of an arbitrary cyclic code over $\mathbb{Z}_4$, expressed in terms of structural data (such as a defining set with respect to Galois extensions of $\mathbb{Z}_4$, or zeros of the generator polynomial) analogous to the classical BCH bound over finite fields.

Let q ≥ 2 be an integer (the alphabet size) and let A be a set with |A| = q. For words x, y ∈ A^n, let d(x,y) denote the Hamming distance, i.e. the number of coordinates in which x and y differ. A code C ⊆ A^n is called a perfect e-error-correcting code (or perfect code of radius e) if the Hamming balls of radius e centered at the codewords of C partition A^n; equivalently, every word in A^n lies in exactly one ball B(c, e) = { y ∈ A^n : d(y, c) ≤ e } with c ∈ C. Trivial perfect codes (the whole space A^n, single-codeword codes, and repetition codes of odd length over a binary alphabet, together with their natural generalizations) are excluded.

Question: Does there exist a nontrivial perfect code of length n ≥ 2 and radius e ≥ 1 over an alphabet of size q, where q is not a prime power?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is widely cited as folklore-open. For e ≥ 3 the parameters of perfect codes are fully classified, and for e = 2 nonexistence is known for q a prime power, for q = 2^r 3^s, and for a small finite list of additional q. Recent work (2024) using Diophantine techniques (e.g. generalized Ramanujan–Nagell equations) ruled out 172 further non-prime-power values of q, but a complete answer for arbitrary non-prime-power q remains unresolved.

A binary code of length $n$ is a subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$. The Hamming distance $d(x,y)$ between two vectors is the number of coordinates in which they differ. A code $C$ is called a perfect single-error-correcting code (a perfect 1-error-correcting code) if the closed Hamming balls of radius $1$ centered at the codewords partition $\mathbb{F}_2^n$; equivalently, $|C| = 2^n/(n+1)$ (so $n = 2^m - 1$ for some integer $m \ge 2$) and every vector of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ lies within Hamming distance $1$ of exactly one codeword. The code $C$ is called linear if it is an $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, and nonlinear otherwise. Two codes are considered equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a permutation of coordinates together with a translation by a fixed vector.

Problem: Provide a complete classification, up to equivalence, of all perfect nonlinear single-error-correcting binary codes (of every admissible length $n = 2^m - 1$).

For a positive integer $m$, the first-order Reed–Muller code $R(1,m)$ is the binary linear code of length $2^m$ whose codewords are the truth tables (evaluations on $\mathbb{F}_2^m$) of all affine Boolean functions $f(x_1,\dots,x_m)=a_0+a_1x_1+\cdots+a_mx_m$ with $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_m\in\mathbb{F}_2$. The covering radius of a binary code $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is
$$\rho(C)=\max_{v\in\mathbb{F}_2^n}\min_{c\in C} d_H(v,c),$$
where $d_H$ denotes Hamming distance. Equivalently, $\rho(R(1,m))$ is the maximum, over all Boolean functions $f:\mathbb{F}_2^m\to\mathbb{F}_2$, of the Hamming distance from $f$ to the set of affine functions (the nonlinearity of $f$).

For even $m$, it is known that $\rho(R(1,m))=2^{m-1}-2^{m/2-1}$, the value being attained by bent functions.

Determine the exact value of $\rho(R(1,m))$ for all odd $m\ge 1$.

where $d_H$ denotes Hamming distance. Equivalently, $\rho(R(1,m))$ is the maximum, over all Boolean functions $f:\mathbb{F}_2^m\to\mathbb{F}_2$, of the Hamming distance from $f$ to the set of affine functions (the nonlinearity of $f$).

For even $m$, it is known that $\rho(R(1,m))=2^{m-1}-2^{m/2-1}$, the value being attained by bent functions.

Determine the exact value of $\rho(R(1,m))$ for all odd $m\ge 1$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The exact value of the covering radius of $R(1,m)$ for odd $m$ (equivalently, the maximum nonlinearity of Boolean functions on an odd number of variables) is a long-standing open problem. Only small cases are settled; for general odd $m$ only bounds are known, with the classical lower bound $2^{m-1}-2^{(m-1)/2}$ and improved upper bounds such as $\rho(1,2k+1)\le 2\lfloor 2^{2k-1}-2^{2k-3/2}\rfloor$. The problem remains open as of recent surveys.

A binary linear code of length $n$, dimension $k$, and minimum Hamming distance $d$ is denoted $[n,k,d]$. Such a code $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$ is called cyclic if $(c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n-1}) \in C$ implies $(c_{n-1}, c_0, \dots, c_{n-2}) \in C$. A sequence of binary linear codes $C_i$ with parameters $[n_i, k_i, d_i]$ (with $n_i \to \infty$) is called asymptotically good if
$$\liminf_{i \to \infty} \frac{k_i}{n_i} > 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \liminf_{i \to \infty} \frac{d_i}{n_i} > 0.$$
Question: Does there exist an asymptotically good sequence of binary cyclic linear codes?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether binary cyclic codes are asymptotically good is a well-known long-standing open problem (over 50 years old). Partial and related results exist: quasi-cyclic codes (index >1) are known to be asymptotically good, certain additive cyclic codes and $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4$-additive cyclic codes have been shown asymptotically good, and long BCH codes are known asymptotically bad. The original problem for (ordinary) binary cyclic codes remains unresolved.

A linear code of length $n$, dimension $k$, and minimum distance $d$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ such that every nonzero codeword $c \in C$ has Hamming weight $\mathrm{wt}(c) \geq d$, where $\mathrm{wt}(c)$ is the number of nonzero coordinates of $c$. Such a code is called an $[n,k,d]_q$ code, and it can correct any pattern of up to $\lfloor (d-1)/2 floor$ errors; a 2-error-correcting linear code is one with $d \geq 5$.

Let q be a prime power and let F(x,y) be a homogeneous polynomial of degree n in two variables with non-negative integer coefficients, written
  F(x,y) = sum_{i=0}^{n} A_i x^{n-i} y^i,
with A_0 = 1. Call F a virtual weight enumerator over GF(q) if its coefficients are non-negative integers and A_0 = 1. Call F a virtually self-dual weight enumerator over GF(q) if, in addition, F is invariant under the MacWilliams transform at q, i.e.
  F(x,y) = q^{-n/2} F(x + (q-1) y,\ x - y).
A linear code C ⊆ GF(q)^n is self-dual if C = C^⊥ with respect to the standard inner product, and its Hamming weight enumerator is W_C(x,y) = sum_{c∈C} x^{n - wt(c)} y^{wt(c)}.

Problem: Find necessary and sufficient conditions, not requiring exhaustive enumeration over codes of length n, that determine whether a given virtually self-dual weight enumerator F(x,y) over GF(q) is realized as the Hamming weight enumerator W_C(x,y) of some self-dual linear code C ⊆ GF(q)^n.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

This is a form of the Katok–Spatzier local rigidity conjecture for higher-rank abelian (split Cartan) actions on homogeneous spaces. The full conjecture remains open in general. Significant partial results are known: local (and global) rigidity has been established for the full split Cartan action (Katok–Spatzier; Goetze–Spatzier; Damjanović–Katok and subsequent work), for various Anosov/genuinely higher-rank cases, and for actions not contained in a Weyl chamber wall. No source verifies a complete proof of the conjecture as stated.

Let $M$ be a closed smooth manifold and $f: M \to M$ a diffeomorphism. Recall that $f$ is called Anosov if there exists a continuous $Df$-invariant splitting of the tangent bundle $TM = E^s \oplus E^u$ and constants $C > 0$, $0 < \lambda < 1$ such that for all $n \geq 0$,
$$\|Df^n v\| \leq C\lambda^n \|v\| \text{ for } v \in E^s, \qquad \|Df^{-n} v\| \leq C\lambda^n \|v\| \text{ for } v \in E^u.$$

An infranilmanifold is a manifold of the form $N/\Gamma$, where $N$ is a simply connected nilpotent Lie group and $\Gamma$ is a torsion-free discrete subgroup of $N \rtimes K$ (with $K$ a compact subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$) acting freely and cocompactly on $N$, such that $\Gamma \cap N$ has finite index in $\Gamma$. An automorphism of an infranilmanifold is the diffeomorphism induced by an automorphism of $N$ that normalizes $\Gamma$; such an automorphism is called hyperbolic if its differential at the identity has no eigenvalues of modulus $1$.

Question: Is every Anosov diffeomorphism of a closed manifold topologically conjugate to a hyperbolic automorphism of an infranilmanifold? That is, does there always exist an infranilmanifold $N/\Gamma$, a hyperbolic infranilmanifold automorphism $A: N/\Gamma \to N/\Gamma$, and a homeomorphism $h: M \to N/\Gamma$ such that $h \circ f = A \circ h$?

Let $k \geq 2$ and let $G$ be either $\mathbb{Z}^k$ or $\mathbb{R}^k$. A smooth action $\alpha : G \times M \to M$ on a closed smooth manifold $M$ is called Anosov if there exists an element $g_0 \in G$ such that the diffeomorphism $\alpha(g_0, \cdot)$ is Anosov (i.e., the tangent bundle $TM$ admits a continuous $D\alpha(g_0,\cdot)$-invariant splitting $TM = E^s \oplus E^u$ on which $D\alpha(g_0,\cdot)$ is uniformly contracting and expanding, respectively).

An algebraic action is one of the following: $M = K \backslash H / \Gamma$ where $H$ is a connected Lie group, $\Gamma \subset H$ is a cocompact lattice, $K$ is a compact subgroup of $H$ commuting with the action, and $G$ acts via a homomorphism into $H$ acting by left translations; or more generally an action on an infranilmanifold by affine automorphisms.

The action $\alpha$ is called irreducible if it does not have non-trivial rank-one factors (equivalently, no finite cover of the action splits as a product in which one factor is an action of a rank-one subgroup of $G$), and every finite-index subaction is topologically transitive.

Question: Is every irreducible Anosov action of $\mathbb{Z}^k$ or $\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k \geq 2$ on a closed manifold $C^\infty$-conjugate to an algebraic action?

The global smooth rigidity conjecture for higher-rank semisimple Lie group and lattice actions with a uniformly partially hyperbolic element is a central open problem in the Katok–Spatzier rigidity program. Let $A$ be a higher-rank abelian group (for instance $\mathbb{Z}^k$ or $\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k \ge 2$), and let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold. Call an action of $A$ on $M$ irreducible if it does not factor (in an appropriate sense) through an action of a rank-one subgroup or split nontrivially as a product of lower-dimensional actions. Recent measure-rigidity theorems classify the invariant probability measures for various classes of higher-rank abelian actions (e.g., positive-entropy invariant measures for $\mathbb{Z}^k$-actions by toral automorphisms, and related results in homogeneous and hyperbolic settings).

Question: Do these measure-rigidity results for higher-rank abelian group actions yield obstructions to the existence of smooth, or merely continuous, irreducible actions of a higher-rank abelian group on a compact manifold? More precisely, can one use such measure-rigidity theorems to rule out the existence of irreducible smooth (respectively continuous) $A$-actions on certain compact manifolds $M$, or to constrain the topology/geometry of $M$ when such an action exists?

Let $m, n \geq 2$ be multiplicatively independent positive integers (i.e., there are no positive integers $a, b$ with $m^a = n^b$, equivalently $\log m / \log n \notin \mathbb{Q}$). Consider the semigroup $S$ of continuous self-maps of the circle $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ generated by the maps $T_m: x \mapsto mx \pmod 1$ and $T_n: x \mapsto nx \pmod 1$. A Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ is called $S$-invariant if it is invariant under both $T_m$ and $T_n$, and $S$-ergodic if every Borel set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with $T_m^{-1}(A) = A$ and $T_n^{-1}(A) = A$ satisfies $\mu(A) \in \{0, 1\}$.

Prove or disprove: the only $S$-ergodic Borel probability measures on $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ are the Lebesgue measure and the measures supported on a finite set (necessarily a finite union of periodic orbits of the semigroup).

This is Furstenberg's classical ×2, ×3 measure rigidity conjecture, which has remained open for over 50 years. The principal partial result is Rudolph's theorem (extended by Johnson): any jointly ergodic invariant measure of positive entropy must be Lebesgue. The zero-entropy case remains unresolved, and recent surveys (2021, 2024) confirm the conjecture is still open.

Let $G$ be a connected Lie group and let $M$ be a biquotient of $G$, i.e. $M = A\backslash G / B$ where $A,B$ are closed subgroups of $G$ acting freely and properly on $G$ by left and right translations respectively. An action of $\mathbb{R}^k$ or $\mathbb{Z}^k$ on $M$ is called algebraic if it is induced (via the biquotient construction) by translations of $G$ coming from a homomorphism into $G$. Such an action is called Anosov if some element of $\mathbb{R}^k$ (resp. $\mathbb{Z}^k$) acts as an Anosov diffeomorphism/flow on $M$. Assume $k \ge 2$, and let $\mu$ be an ergodic invariant Borel probability measure on $M$ for the action.

Prove or disprove: at least one of the following must hold.
(i) $\mu$ is a finite sum (convex combination) of measures each of which is constructed from a Haar measure supported on a closed subgroup of $G$ (i.e., $\mu$ is "algebraic").
(ii) The support of $\mu$ fibers equivariantly over a manifold $N$ in such a way that the induced action on $N$ reduces to a rank-one action (i.e., factors through a homomorphism $\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{Z}^k\to\mathbb{Z}$).

For a word $w\in L$, the subtree generated by $w$ is the induced subtree of $T_L$ consisting of $w$ together with all its descendants (i.e., all words in $L$ that have $w$ as a prefix).

Provide an algorithm (or prove that none exists) that, given as input a word $w\in L$, decides whether the subtree of $T_L$ generated by $w$ is finite or infinite. Equivalently, decide whether $w$ can be extended on the right to arbitrarily long words in $L$.

For each place $v$ of $K$, let $U_v \subset \mathbf{G}(K_v)$ be a subgroup generated by one-parameter unipotent subgroups, and let $U$ be a subgroup of $\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{A})$ that is a product (restricted with respect to compact open unipotent subgroups at non-archimedean places) of such groups $U_v$.

Establish an adelic analogue of Ratner's measure-classification theorem in this setting: prove that every $U$-invariant ergodic probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{A})/\mathbf{G}(K)$ is the homogeneous (algebraic) measure supported on a closed orbit $H x$, where $H$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{A})$ containing $U$ such that $Hx$ carries an $H$-invariant probability measure. Equivalently, extend the orbit-closure and equidistribution conclusions for unipotent flows from the real Lie group setting to the adelic homogeneous space $\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{A})/\mathbf{G}(K)$.

The measure classification for unipotent flows was extended to the S-arithmetic (and hence essentially adelic) setting by Ratner and independently by Margulis–Tomanov in the 1990s, treating products of unipotent groups over local fields acting on S-arithmetic quotients. The linearization technique was likewise adapted to this context by Tomanov and by Gorodnik–Oh. These S-arithmetic/adelic measure-rigidity results are now standard tools in the area, so the problem as posed is regarded as solved.

Let $G$ be a Lie group (or, more generally, an algebraic group over a local field) acting on a space $X$ that carries a $G$-invariant geometric structure, and let $P \le G$ be a parabolic subgroup. Let $H \le G$ be a subgroup that preserves the geometric structure on $X$. A finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $X$ is said to be $P$-invariant if $p_*\mu = \mu$ for every $p \in P$, and $H$-invariant if $h_*\mu = \mu$ for every $h \in H$. The action of $H$ on $X$ is called stiff if every finite $P$-invariant Borel measure on $X$ is automatically $H$-invariant.

Problem: Determine general conditions on the space $X$ (together with its geometric structure and the embeddings $H, P \le G$) under which the $H$-action on $X$ is stiff, i.e., every finite $P$-invariant Borel measure on $X$ is $H$-invariant. Equivalently, characterize the class of $H$-actions of this form that are stiff.
