representations.normalized:
An Earth–Moon map consists of a finite collection of countries, where each country comprises exactly two regions: one region drawn on a sphere representing the Earth and one region drawn on a separate sphere representing the Moon. Each individual region (on either sphere) is a connected, simply connected closed subset, and on each sphere the regions form a planar map (their interiors are pairwise disjoint and any two regions meet, if at all, along boundary arcs). Two countries are said to be adjacent if some region of one shares a boundary arc with some region of the other (on either the Earth or the Moon). A proper colouring of an Earth–Moon map is an assignment of a colour to each country (so that the Earth region and Moon region of the same country receive the same colour) such that any two adjacent countries receive different colours.

Equivalently, in graph-theoretic terms, associate to each Earth–Moon map the graph G whose vertices are the countries and whose edges correspond to adjacencies; such a graph G is precisely a biplanar graph, i.e., a graph that can be written as the edge-union of two planar graphs on the same vertex set.

Determine the smallest integer k such that every Earth–Moon map admits a proper colouring using at most k colours; equivalently, determine
   max { χ(G) : G is biplanar }.

The Earth–Moon (biplanar) chromatic number is known to lie between 9 and 12: Heawood-style arguments give the upper bound 12, and a 9-chromatic biplanar graph (e.g., the join of C5 and K6) is known. No biplanar graph requiring 10, 11, or 12 colours has been exhibited, and the exact value remains unknown. Gethner (2018) conjectured the answer is 11. The problem is listed as open in standard references including the Open Problem Garden and Wikipedia.

The thickness of a graph $G$, denoted $\theta(G)$, is the minimum number of planar subgraphs into which the edge set of $G$ can be partitioned. The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the minimum number of colors needed to properly color the vertices of $G$ so that adjacent vertices receive different colors.

For each positive integer $t$, define
$$f(t) = \sup\{\chi(G) : G \text{ is a finite simple graph with } \theta(G) \le t\}.$$

Determine $f(t)$ for every $t \ge 1$. In particular, find the exact value (or improve the known bounds) of the maximum chromatic number attainable by a graph of thickness $t$. (Known elementary bounds give $f(t) \le 6t$ via degeneracy, and one has $f(1)=4$ by the Four Color Theorem; for $t=2$ it is known that $9 \le f(2) \le 12$.)

Let $K_{r,s}$ denote the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $r$ and $s$. Determine $\mathrm{pn}(K_{r,s})$ as an exact function of $r$ and $s$ for all positive integers $r, s$.

The exact page number of $K_{r,s}$ remains unknown in general. Partial results are known: Muder, Weaver, and West (1988) and subsequent work give upper bounds such as $\mathrm{pn}(K_{m,n}) \le \lceil (m+2n)/4 \rceil$ (conjectured optimal), $\mathrm{pn}(K_{n,n}) \le \lfloor 2n/3 \rfloor + 1$, and the asymptotic identity $\min\{m : \mathrm{pn}(K_{m,n}) = n\} = n^2/4 + O(n^{7/4})$ due to Enomoto, Nakamigawa, and Ota. Exact values are known only for small or special cases (e.g., $\mathrm{pn}(K_{4,4}) = 3$).

Let $G$ and $H$ be finite simple graphs. A graph homomorphism $p: H \to G$ is called a covering projection (and $H$ is called a cover of $G$) if $p$ is surjective and, for every vertex $v \in V(H)$, the restriction of $p$ to the neighborhood of $v$ in $H$ is a bijection onto the neighborhood of $p(v)$ in $G$. A finite planar cover of $G$ is a cover $H$ of $G$ such that $H$ is finite and embeds in the plane.

A graph $G$ is said to embed in the projective plane if it has a topological embedding into the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$. Let $K_{1,2,2,2}$ denote the complete multipartite graph on parts of sizes $1, 2, 2, 2$ (equivalently, the graph on $7$ vertices obtained from $K_7$ by removing a perfect matching on $6$ of its vertices).

Prove or disprove: a connected graph $G$ admits a finite planar cover if and only if $G$ embeds in the projective plane. Equivalently, show that $K_{1,2,2,2}$ has no finite planar cover.

The slope of a non-degenerate segment is the (unoriented) direction of the line containing it. Given a finite set $D$ of slopes, $G$ is said to be representable by segments with slopes in $D$ if there is a segment intersection representation of $G$ in which every segment has slope belonging to $D$. A graph is planar if it admits an embedding in the plane with no edge crossings.

Question: Is it true that for every planar graph $G$ there exists a set $D$ of four slopes such that $G$ admits a segment intersection representation with all segments having slopes in $D$?

Every planar graph is known to be an intersection graph of segments in the plane (Chalopin–Gonçalves, 2009), confirming Scheinerman's conjecture. For the four-slope refinement (West's 1991 conjecture), the PURE-4-DIR version—where parallel segments are forbidden to intersect—has been refuted: there exist planar graphs that are not in PURE-4-DIR (JGAA paper "Not all planar graphs are in PURE-4-DIR"). The unrestricted four-slope version, allowing collinear/parallel segments to intersect, does not appear to be settled in the literature found.

A graph $G$ is $3$-colourable if its vertices can be partitioned into three independent sets, and it is planar if it admits an embedding in $\mathbb{R}^2$ without edge crossings.

Question: Does every $3$-colourable planar graph admit a segment representation (with no restriction on the set of slopes used)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The stronger form of this question — that every 3-colourable planar graph has a segment intersection representation using only 3 slopes — was proved by Castro, Gonçalves and Ochem (WG 2019, with extended version on arXiv:2511.20368 and HAL). This in particular answers the unrestricted-slope version affirmatively. The fully general Scheinerman conjecture (all planar graphs are segment intersection graphs) was earlier established by Chalopin and Gonçalves (2009), which also implies the result for the 3-colourable case.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

While the analogous 2-dimensional problem is settled by the Koebe–Andreev–Thurston circle packing theorem (planar graphs), the characterization of graphs representable as tangency graphs of interior-disjoint balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is widely regarded as an open problem. Sphere contact/tangency configurations in 3-space remain an active area of investigation, with partial results on edge counts and special families but no known full combinatorial characterization.

A graph $G=(V,E)$ is said to be representable by spheres in three-dimensional space if there exists an assignment $v\mapsto S_v$ of a closed ball (or sphere) $S_v\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ to each vertex $v\in V$ such that the interiors of the balls are pairwise disjoint and two balls $S_u$ and $S_v$ are tangent (touch in exactly one point) if and only if $uv\in E$.

Kuratowski's classical theorem states that a finite graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$, giving a finite list of forbidden topological subgraphs characterizing planarity.

Question: Does the class of finite graphs representable by spheres in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (in the above sense) admit a "Kuratowski-type" characterization, i.e. a characterization by a finite list of forbidden subgraphs (or subdivisions thereof)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The asymptotic part (b) is settled: Pach, Rubin, and Tardos (SODA 2015 / CPC) proved the Richter–Thomassen conjecture, showing that any n pairwise intersecting simple closed curves in the plane, no three concurrent, determine at least (1 − o(1))n² intersection points, which together with the obvious upper bound 2·C(n,2) gives lim f(n)/C(n,2) = 2. The exact determination of f(n) for all n remains open.

representations.normalized:
The orientable genus of a graph G, denoted g(G), is the smallest nonnegative integer g such that G admits a cellular embedding in the orientable closed surface of genus g (the sphere with g handles attached). The non-orientable genus of G, denoted \tilde g(G), is the smallest positive integer k such that G admits a cellular embedding in the non-orientable closed surface N_k (the sphere with k crosscaps); by convention, planar graphs are also allowed. Computing either genus is known to be NP-hard in general, but for each fixed surface there is a linear-time algorithm that decides embeddability.

Question: Does there exist, for each fixed positive integer k, an algorithm with running time polynomial in |V(G)|+|E(G)| that, given as input a graph G with \tilde g(G) = k, outputs the orientable genus g(G)?

Equivalently, prove or disprove that the orientable-genus computation problem, restricted to inputs whose non-orientable genus equals a fixed value k, is solvable in polynomial time.

Computing either genus is known to be NP-hard in general, but for each fixed surface there is a linear-time algorithm that decides embeddability.

Question: Does there exist, for each fixed positive integer k, an algorithm with running time polynomial in |V(G)|+|E(G)| that, given as input a graph G with \tilde g(G) = k, outputs the orientable genus g(G)?

Searches surface no result resolving this conjecture. While Mohar's linear-time algorithm decides embeddability in any fixed surface, and recent works give EPTAS for dense graphs and approximation algorithms for general graphs, no polynomial-time exact algorithm restricted to graphs of fixed non-orientable genus k for computing the orientable genus appears in the literature. The problem appears to remain open.

A class $\mathcal{F}$ of finite simple graphs is called minor-closed if, whenever $G \in \mathcal{F}$ and $H$ is obtained from $G$ by a sequence of vertex deletions, edge deletions, and edge contractions, then $H \in \mathcal{F}$. The (orientable) genus $\gamma(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the minimum integer $g \geq 0$ such that $G$ admits a cellular embedding into the orientable surface $S_g$ of genus $g$. Computing $\gamma(G)$ for an arbitrary input graph $G$ is NP-hard.

Characterize the minor-closed families $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs for which there exists an algorithm that, given $G \in \mathcal{F}$, computes $\gamma(G)$ in time polynomial in $|V(G)|$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Computing the genus of a graph is NP-hard in general, and only fixed-parameter or approximation results are known (e.g., linear-time embeddability into a fixed surface, EPTAS for dense graphs). No general characterization of polynomial-time-tractable minor-closed families for genus computation appears in the literature, and the question remains open.

Let G be a finite graph cellularly embedded in a (possibly non-orientable) closed surface Σ, with positive edge weights. A cycle in G is a closed walk visiting each vertex at most once; viewed as a closed curve on Σ, it is called:
(a) contractible, if it is null-homotopic in Σ;
(b) surface-separating, if removing its image disconnects Σ;
(c) orientation-preserving (two-sided), if a small tubular neighborhood of it in Σ is an annulus (rather than a Möbius band).
Determine whether each of the following three problems admits a polynomial-time algorithm in the size of G:
1. Compute a shortest contractible cycle in G.
2. Compute a shortest surface-separating cycle in G.
3. Compute a shortest orientation-preserving cycle in G.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

All three subquestions appear to be resolved. Cabello (SODA 2008 / "Finding shortest contractible and shortest separating cycles in embedded graphs") gave a polynomial-time algorithm for a shortest contractible cycle and proved that finding a shortest surface-separating cycle is NP-hard. For shortest orientation-preserving (Π-two-sided) cycles, a polynomial-time algorithm is known (e.g., the work on "Finding short cycles in an embedded graph in polynomial time", arXiv:0807.1620, which resolved the corresponding open problem of Mohar–Thomassen).

Let G be a finite graph 2-cell embedded in a closed surface. A weight function on G is an assignment w: E(G) → ℝ_{>0} of positive real numbers to edges. For a closed walk C in G, let w(C) denote the sum of the weights of the edges traversed by C (with multiplicity). The weight function w is called a large-edge-width (LEW) weight function if, for every non-contractible closed walk C in the embedded graph G and every facial walk F, one has w(C) > w(F).

Decide the following:

(a) Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm which, given an embedded graph G, determines whether G admits an LEW-weight function?

(b) Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm which, given an abstract graph G, determines whether G has some 2-cell embedding (in some closed surface) that admits an LEW-weight function?

In classical general relativity, consider one-parameter families of smooth, asymptotically flat initial data for the Einstein equations coupled to some matter model (for instance, a massless scalar field, a perfect fluid, electromagnetism, or vacuum gravitational waves). Let p denote the parameter, and assume that for p > p* the evolution produces a black hole while for p < p* the matter disperses, so that p = p* is the black-hole threshold. Numerical evidence (originally for spherically symmetric massless scalar collapse) shows three universal "critical phenomena" near p = p*: (i) the threshold solution is a discretely or continuously self-similar attractor of codimension one in phase space; (ii) the universality of this critical solution within a given matter model; and (iii) a power-law scaling M_BH ∝ (p − p*)^γ for the mass of the black hole formed for p slightly greater than p*, with a critical exponent γ depending only on the matter model.

Provide a complete theoretical understanding of these critical phenomena in gravitational collapse. In particular:

1. Rigorously establish the existence, uniqueness, and codimension-one stability of the self-similar critical attractor solutions for the various matter models (scalar field, perfect fluid with equation of state p = kρ, Yang–Mills, etc.).
2. Derive the universality and the values of the critical exponents γ and (for discretely self-similar cases) the echoing period Δ from first principles.
3. Determine to what extent these phenomena persist without the assumption of spherical symmetry, including the case of vacuum gravitational collapse where the threshold is approached by purely gravitational degrees of freedom.
4. Clarify the relationship of critical collapse to weak cosmic censorship, given that arbitrarily large curvature is visible from infinity in the threshold limit.

Let G = (V, E) be an infinite, locally finite, one-ended, vertex-transitive simple graph. Equip G with the graph metric, and call a doubly-infinite path D = (..., v_{-1}, v_0, v_1, ...) a geodesic if for all integers i < j the subpath from v_i to v_j is a shortest path in G. For such a geodesic D, let G − V(D) denote the subgraph of G induced by V(G) ∖ V(D).

Prove or disprove: G is planar (i.e., can be embedded in the plane without edge crossings) if and only if, for every doubly-infinite geodesic D in G, the graph G − V(D) has exactly two connected components, both of which are infinite.

Recent work (2025) on uniformly bisecting quasi-geodesics in vertex-transitive graphs resolves a related Kourovka Notebook problem for quasi-geodesics, showing that the uniform bisection property characterizes graphs quasi-isometric to the Euclidean or hyperbolic plane. However, the authors explicitly leave open the corresponding statement for geodesics only, which matches the conjecture in question. No proof or disproof of the geodesic-only planarity characterization for one-ended locally-finite vertex-transitive graphs has been found.

Consider an operational forest harvesting area of roughly 400 hectares partitioned into a finite set C of timber cells, each with a known harvestable volume. Available extraction resources consist of:
(i) a set S of candidate skidder locations (each with a setup/fixed cost, a reachable subset of cells, and per-unit-volume operating cost),
(ii) a set T of candidate cable-tower locations (each with a fixed installation cost, a cable-reach subset of cells subject to slope/length constraints, and per-unit-volume operating cost),
(iii) a directed road network graph G = (N, A), where N includes all candidate landings (skidder/tower positions) and exit nodes, A is a set of potential road segments each having a fixed construction cost and a per-unit-volume haul cost, and where existing roads are modeled as arcs with zero construction cost.

Decisions to be made:
• For each candidate skidder s ∈ S and tower t ∈ T, a binary opening decision.
• For each cell c ∈ C, an assignment to exactly one opened skidder or tower whose reachable subset contains c.
• For each arc a ∈ A, a binary build decision plus a continuous flow variable carrying timber volume from active landings to exit nodes; flow conservation must hold at every node, and arcs can carry positive flow only if built (fixed-charge network flow).

The objective is to minimize the total cost (fixed equipment-opening costs + fixed road-building costs + variable operating/haul costs) subject to all cells being assigned and all assigned volume being routed to exit nodes through built arcs.

Problem: Provide an exact mixed-integer programming formulation, together with an exact solution algorithm (e.g., based on decomposition, valid inequalities, or branch-and-cut/price), that is provably capable of solving large-scale instances of this combined plant-location and fixed-charge network-flow road-building problem to optimality within practical computing time.

Consider an operational forest-management setting over a short planning horizon discretized into days (or weeks) t = 1, ..., T. The following data are given:

- A set H of harvest units (stands), each with available standing volume by product/assortment a ∈ A, and access constraints (e.g., road availability, seasonal restrictions).
- A set M of harvesting machines (felling, processing, forwarding) with daily productivities, mobilization/relocation costs, and minimum dwell times on a stand.
- A set R of roadside storage points and a road network linking stands to a set D of demand points (mills, terminals).
- A fleet K of trucks, each with capacity, daily availability windows, driver shift rules, loading/unloading times, and travel times along the network.
- Daily demands d_{j,a,t} at each mill j ∈ D for each assortment a, with possible inventory bounds at roadside and at mills.

Decision variables jointly model, for every day t:
(i) which stands are harvested, by which machines, and how much volume of each assortment is produced and placed at roadside;
(ii) machine relocations between stands;
(iii) truck dispatch decisions: routes, loads, sequence of pickups and deliveries, and resulting inventories at roadside and at mills.

Formulate a single mixed-integer optimization model that simultaneously decides the short-term harvesting schedule and the detailed transportation schedule over the horizon, with an objective combining harvesting cost, machine relocation cost, transportation cost, inventory cost, and penalties for unmet demand, subject to flow conservation of timber from stumps to mills, machine and truck capacity/time constraints, and roadside inventory balance.

Problem: Construct such an integrated model in sufficient detail to be operationally meaningful, and design an exact or heuristic solution method that can solve instances of realistic industrial size (hundreds of stands, tens of machines and trucks, several mills, horizons of one to several weeks) within computation times acceptable for daily operational planning.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Several integrated MILP models for jointly scheduling short-term harvesting and transportation of forest products at daily/weekly granularity have been proposed since the question was posed (e.g., Bordón et al., Forests 2019; metaheuristic approaches in Operational Research 2021; simulation-based multi-objective studies in 2025; and a "Forestry 4.0" integrated framework in 2024). These works provide formulations and solution heuristics, but no single fully scalable exact method is universally accepted for industrial instances, so the problem is best characterized as partially solved with active ongoing research.

Consider a forest management area modeled as a spatial network of harvest units (stands), road segments, and hydrological features (streams, riparian zones, slopes characterized by gradient, soil type, and erodibility). A harvest plan specifies, for each stand, a harvesting practice chosen from a finite set of alternatives (for example: ground-based skidding, cable logging, helicopter yarding), together with the width of riparian buffers retained along watercourses and the placement and construction standard of forest roads used to access the stands. Each combination of practice, buffer choice, and road placement induces measurable environmental impacts, in particular: (i) soil erosion rate, (ii) sediment delivery to streams, and (iii) residual soil damage (compaction and disturbance area) on the harvested unit.

Classical harvest scheduling minimizes a cost functional combining timber value losses and operational/transport cost, subject to wood-flow and accessibility constraints, without explicit environmental terms.

Problem. Develop quantitative models that
(a) for each candidate operational harvesting practice, predict the induced erosion, sedimentation, and soil-damage impacts as functions of the stand, road, and buffer attributes; and
(b) embed these impact functions as constraints (or as additional objectives) in a tractable optimization model whose decision variables are the choice of harvesting practice per stand, riparian buffer widths, and road network design, in such a way that an optimal plan can be computed which avoids violating prescribed environmental thresholds on erosion, sedimentation, and soil damage, rather than merely minimizing timber losses and operating cost.

Provide either (1) a model formulation together with a solution method whose output is provably feasible with respect to the environmental thresholds and optimal (or with a bounded optimality gap) with respect to the economic objective, or (2) a proof that no such tractable formulation exists under stated assumptions.

Consider a forest supply chain in which standing timber must be (i) harvested at a set of cut blocks over a discrete operational planning horizon, (ii) sorted in the field or at landings into a finite set of assortments distinguished by species, dimension, and fiber characteristics, and (iii) transported by trucks (and possibly other modes) to a set of downstream customers consisting of sawmills, pulp mills, and heating plants, each with time-varying demands for specific assortments and with process-efficiency parameters that depend on the fiber characteristics of the delivered material.

Formally, let H be a set of harvest units, A a set of assortments, M a set of mills, and T a discrete time horizon. Decision variables include, for each (h,t), the harvest intensity and crew/machine allocation; for each (h,a,t), the volume of timber sorted into assortment a at unit h in period t, with associated sorting cost c^S(h,a,t) that depends on the fiber-to-assortment yield relationships; for each (h,m,a,t), the volume transported from h to mill m of assortment a in period t with transport cost c^T(h,m,a,t); and for each (m,a,t), the volume processed at mill m with process-efficiency function e(m,a) mapping fiber characteristics to product yield and revenue. Constraints include harvesting capacity, sorting capacity, truck/route capacity, inventory dynamics at landings and mills, and demand satisfaction (or penalized shortfall) at each (m,a,t).

The objective is to maximize total net value (revenue from delivered products, weighted by process efficiencies, minus harvesting, sorting, transportation, and inventory costs) over the horizon.

Problem: Develop a mathematical optimization model and a solution methodology that jointly synchronizes the harvesting, sorting, and transportation decisions above at operational scale (forest instances with hundreds of harvest units, tens of mills, dozens of assortments, and weekly or daily periods over a multi-month horizon), including a principled calibration of the sorting cost functions c^S, the mill process-efficiency functions e, and the fiber-to-product yield relationships, and provide computational evidence that the method produces near-optimal synchronized plans within operational time limits.

representations.normalized:
In mechanized timber harvesting, a harvester equipped with an on-board bucking computer cross-cuts each felled stem into logs assigned to diameter–length classes. The bucking decision at each stem is driven by an internal price list that assigns a value to every (diameter class, length class) combination; the on-board optimizer selects the cutting pattern that maximizes the total internal value of the logs produced from the stem. When several harvest areas operate in parallel and feed multiple downstream demand points (mills, terminals, customer orders) with possibly differing product mixes, capacities, and time windows, the choice of internal price lists across stands becomes a coordination instrument: it determines, indirectly, the realized product assortment, inventories, and transport flows.

Formulate a general framework for using such internal prices as an explicit coordination mechanism for operational forest decisions. Concretely:

1. Define a model in which a central planner (or a market-style mechanism) chooses, for each harvest area $h$ in a set $H$ and each time period $t$, a price list $p_{h,t}:D\times L\to\mathbb{R}$, where $D$ is the set of diameter classes and $L$ the set of length classes. Each stem $s$ harvested in area $h$ at time $t$ is bucked according to $\arg\max$ of $\sum p_{h,t}(d,\ell)\cdot x_{s}(d,\ell)$ subject to the geometric/taper feasibility constraints on the cutting pattern $x_s$.

2. Identify conditions on $\{p_{h,t}\}$ under which the resulting aggregate supply of log classes solves (or approximately solves) a global operational optimization problem that maximizes total value (revenue minus harvesting, storage, and transportation cost) subject to mill demands, capacity, and inventory constraints, in the spirit of duality / Lagrangian decomposition for the global problem.

3. Determine whether prices can be updated dynamically (e.g., by subgradient or auction-type procedures) using only locally observable harvest information so as to converge to a coordinated optimum, and characterize the loss of optimality compared to a fully centralized bucking-and-distribution model.

Provide such a pricing-based coordination scheme together with a theoretical or computational analysis of its optimality, convergence, and information requirements.

Consider a finite set N = {1, 2, ..., n} of organizations (for instance, forestry companies), each of which has its own transportation demand consisting of a set of orders to be moved between supply and demand locations under capacity, time-window, fleet, and routing constraints. For every coalition S ⊆ N let c(S) denote the minimum total transportation cost obtainable when the members of S pool their orders and jointly plan vehicle routes and schedules; assume c(∅) = 0 and that c is subadditive, so that joint planning may reduce cost compared with stand-alone operation.

When the grand coalition N collaborates, the realized total benefit is v(N) = Σ_{i∈N} c({i}) − c(N) ≥ 0. Each participant must, however, keep certain information private (its customer identities, contractual agreements, and individual order details) and will only join a collaboration whose cost/benefit allocation it considers acceptable.

The problem is the following:

(a) Propose a mathematical model of practical collaborative transportation among the organizations in N that captures the joint routing/scheduling optimization producing c(S) under realistic operational constraints, while respecting the privacy of each participant's sensitive data.

(b) Within this model, design an allocation rule φ : 2^N → R^n assigning to every coalition S a vector (φ_i(S))_{i∈S} of cost shares (or, equivalently, benefit shares) such that the rule is
  (i) efficient: Σ_{i∈S} φ_i(S) = c(S);
  (ii) individually rational: φ_i(S) ≤ c({i}) for every i ∈ S;
  (iii) stable in a cooperative-game-theoretic sense (e.g. lies in the core of (N, c) whenever the core is nonempty, or otherwise satisfies an explicit acceptability criterion);
  (iv) computable using only information that respects each participant's privacy constraints; and
  (v) acceptable to the participants in practice.

Provide such a model and sharing principle, or prove that no rule can simultaneously satisfy the listed requirements.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded, simply connected domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. Consider the Dirichlet eigenvalue problem
$$-\Delta u = \lambda u \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
and let $u$ be any eigenfunction associated with the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2(\Omega)$. The nodal set of $u$ is defined as $N(u) = \{x \in \overline{\Omega} : u(x) = 0\}$, and the nodal line is $N(u) \cap \Omega$.

Prove or disprove: the nodal line of $u$ is a simple open arc (i.e., the homeomorphic image of an open interval, with no self-intersections) whose two endpoints lie on $\partial\Omega$ and are distinct.

$$-\Delta u = \lambda u \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
and let $u$ be any eigenfunction associated with the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2(\Omega)$. The nodal set of $u$ is defined as $N(u) = \{x \in \overline{\Omega} : u(x) = 0\}$, and the nodal line is $N(u) \cap \Omega$.

Prove or disprove: the nodal line of $u$ is a simple open arc (i.e., the homeomorphic image of an open interval, with no self-intersections) whose two endpoints lie on $\partial\Omega$ and are distinct.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is the classical Payne nodal line conjecture (1967), strengthened to the statement that the nodal line is a simple arc connecting two distinct boundary points. Hoffmann-Ostenhof, Hoffmann-Ostenhof and Nadirashvili (1997) disproved the conjecture for multiply connected planar domains; subsequent works produced counterexamples with as few as one hole, and recently even on doubly-connected domains. For simply connected planar domains with smooth boundary the problem remains open as of 2026.

[{"title": "A counterexample to Payne's nodal line conjecture with few holes", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02276", "snippet": "Counterexample to Payne's nodal line conjecture in multiply connected planar domains; the simply connected case remains open.", "claim": "Payne's conjecture is false for multiply connected domains, but the simply connected case is still open."}, {"title": "Payne's nodal line conjecture fails on doubly-connected planar domains", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24436", "snippet": "Shows failure of Payne's conjecture even on doubly-connected planar domains.", "claim": "The conjecture fails for doubly-connected domains; the simply connected case is the remaining open question."}, {"title": "On the nodal line of the second eigenfunction of the Laplacian in R^2", "url": "https://projecteuclid.org/journals/journal-of-differential-geometry/volume-35/issue-1/On-the-nodal-line-of-the-second-eigenfunction-of-the/10.4310/jdg/1214447811.pdf", "snippet": "Classical work on Payne's nodal line conjecture for planar domains.", "claim": "Payne's conjecture is a longstanding open problem for simply connected planar domains."}]

Consider the following forestry truck-routing problem. Over a planning horizon of T consecutive days, a fleet of heterogeneous trucks must transport timber from a set S of supply locations (harvest sites) to a set D of demand locations (mills). The problem has the following features that distinguish it from the classical capacitated vehicle routing problem:

(i) Pickup and delivery: every truck trip consists of loading at some supply location s in S and unloading at some demand location d in D; trucks may perform multiple loaded trips per day.

(ii) Multi-period structure: the routing decisions span T days, and supply and demand quantities are defined per day.

(iii) Repeated visits: the same supply location may be visited many times within a single day and across days, by the same or different trucks.

(iv) Daily demand windows: for each demand location d and each day t, the total quantity delivered must lie in a prescribed interval [L_{d,t}, U_{d,t}] (lower and upper daily demand limits), rather than meeting an exact quantity.

(v) Driver change-overs: each truck is operated by drivers whose shifts are bounded by legal driving and working-time limits; drivers may be exchanged at designated change-over points, so a single truck route during one day may be served by a sequence of drivers subject to scheduling constraints.

(vi) Loading constraints: loading at a supply location requires a loader (machine or crew) with limited capacity per time unit, so simultaneous loadings at the same site are restricted, inducing time-coupling among trucks.

Design a mixed-integer programming formulation (e.g., arc-flow, commodity-flow, or set-partitioning/route-based) that exactly represents all of (i)–(vi), and develop an exact solution algorithm (such as branch-and-cut, branch-and-price, or branch-and-cut-and-price) capable of solving industrial-scale instances of this problem to proven optimality (or with a guaranteed optimality gap), rather than relying solely on heuristic or metaheuristic methods.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Literature on forestry/timber transportation routing (e.g., the Timber Transport VRP) presents heuristic and metaheuristic methods, and exact methods exist for various multi-period pickup-and-delivery VRP variants, but no published exact formulation and algorithm is reported that simultaneously handles all of the forestry-specific features (multi-period, repeated supply visits, daily demand intervals, driver change-overs, loader/loading constraints) at industrial scale. The problem therefore appears still open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work has addressed parts of the problem—e.g., Amrouss et al. (2017) developed real-time methods for managing transportation disruptions in forestry, and several recent papers model simultaneous routing and scheduling of logging trucks with synchronization at loaders to reduce waiting times. However, a comprehensive forestry VRP framework that jointly handles real-time re-planning, queueing at loading/unloading points, and dynamic events such as weather and breakdowns remains an active research area without a definitive solution.

$$u_t - \mathrm{div}(a\nabla u) = f \quad \text{in } \Omega\times(0,T),$$
$$u = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial\Omega\times(0,T),\qquad u(\cdot,0)=0 \quad \text{in }\Omega,$$
where $a:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is a time-independent scalar coefficient satisfying the uniform ellipticity bound $K^{-1}\le a(x)\le K$ for some constant $K>1$. Suppose that the source $f$ is known throughout $\Omega\times(0,T)$, and that the solution $u(x,t)$ is known for every $x\in\Omega$ at one or finitely many fixed positive times $t_1,\dots,t_N\in(0,T)$.

Question: is the coefficient $a$ uniquely determined by this data? Equivalently, if $a_1,a_2$ are two such coefficients producing solutions $u_1,u_2$ to the above problem with the same $f$ and with $u_1(x,t_j)=u_2(x,t_j)$ for all $x\in\Omega$ and $j=1,\dots,N$, must $a_1\equiv a_2$ in $\Omega$?

Consider the forestry vehicle routing problem (forestry VRP) defined as follows. A fleet of heterogeneous log trucks must transport timber from a set of forest harvest sites (stands) to a set of demand points (mills or terminals) over a planning horizon. At each harvest site and at each mill there is a limited set of shared service resources—self-loaders (cranes) for loading at stands and unloading equipment at mills—whose availability is constrained in time and which can serve only one truck at a time. Each truck has a capacity and may or may not carry its own loader; trucks without onboard loaders must rely on a stationary or mobile loader being present and idle at the moment of (un)loading. A feasible plan assigns to each truck a sequence of trips (each trip consisting of an origin stand, a destination mill, a load type, and timing) such that:

(i) supply at stands and demand at mills are met within prescribed time windows;
(ii) for every loading or unloading event, the truck and the required loader (or unloading resource) are simultaneously present at the same location, i.e. their schedules are synchronized;
(iii) no two activities requiring the same resource overlap in time; and
(iv) standard routing constraints (capacity, working hours, compatibility of trucks with load types) hold.

The objective is to minimize total operating cost (e.g., a weighted sum of travel time, waiting time at stands and mills, and number of trucks used).

Develop mathematical optimization models and exact or heuristic solution methods for this synchronized forestry VRP that explicitly enforce the synchronization of trucks with loaders and other shared (un)loading resources, and that scale to instance sizes encountered in industrial practice.

where $a:\overline{\Omega} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a scalar coefficient satisfying $0 < \lambda \le a(x) \le \Lambda < \infty$, and where the trace $a|_{\partial\Omega}$ is assumed known.

Setting. Consider a forest landscape partitioned into a finite set $V$ of management cells, with a planar adjacency graph $G=(V,E)$ in which two cells are adjacent if and only if they share a boundary of positive length. A planning horizon is divided into time periods $T=\{1,\dots,P\}$. Each cell $i\in V$ has area $a_i>0$ and, for each period $t\in T$, an economic value $v_{i,t}$ that is collected if cell $i$ is harvested in period $t$. A cell may be harvested at most once over the horizon. After harvest, a cell remains "disturbed" (open/recently cut) for a fixed green-up duration of $g$ periods before being considered recovered.

Area Restriction Model (ARM). The ARM imposes that in every period $t\in T$, any connected component (in the subgraph of $G$ induced by currently disturbed cells) of contiguous disturbed cells has total area at most a prescribed maximum opening size $A_{\max}$. Note that this is genuinely combinatorial: contiguous clusters of harvested cells are allowed up to $A_{\max}$, but their composition is not fixed a priori (in contrast with the Unit Restriction Model).

Roads. Superimposed on $V$ is a road network represented by a graph $H=(N,R)$ whose nodes $N\supseteq V$ include cell access points and existing/potential road junctions, with arcs $R$ representing potential road segments. Each segment $r\in R$ has a construction cost $c_r$ and a per-period maintenance cost $m_{r,t}$. In order to harvest cell $i$ in period $t$, there must exist in period $t$ a path of built and maintained road segments in $H$ from a designated mill/exit node to the access point of $i$. Once built, a segment may be maintained or temporarily closed in subsequent periods; the cost structure $(c_r,m_{r,t})$ is given.

Objective. Maximize the discounted net revenue
$$\sum_{i\in V}\sum_{t\in T} v_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \;-\;\sum_{r\in R}\Bigl( c_r\, y_r + \sum_{t\in T} m_{r,t}\, z_{r,t}\Bigr),$$
where $x_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}$ indicates harvesting cell $i$ in period $t$, $y_r\in\{0,1\}$ indicates building segment $r$ at some time, and $z_{r,t}\in\{0,1\}$ indicates that segment $r$ is active in period $t$, subject to the ARM contiguity/area constraints, the green-up constraints, the road-access constraints, and standard logical linking constraints between $x$, $y$, $z$.

Problem. Develop an exact mixed-integer programming formulation, together with an exact solution method (e.g., branch-and-bound, branch-and-cut, branch-and-price, or decomposition), that is provably correct for the above ARM-with-roads problem and is able to solve to proven optimality (or with a certified optimality gap) instances with thousands of cells ($|V|\ge 10^3$) and many time periods (e.g., $P\ge 10$), with simultaneous road-building and road-maintenance decisions, at realistic forestry scales.

Exact branch-and-price methods exist for ARM harvest scheduling (e.g., cluster/path/bucket formulations) and have been tested on instances up to roughly 2,900 stands and 12 periods without roads, while separate models address integrated harvest-and-road planning, often via heuristics/metaheuristics or only on small/medium instances. Consider the forest-products supply chain, modeled as a directed network whose nodes represent (i) forest resources (stands available for harvest over a long planning horizon), (ii) processing plants (sawmills, pulp mills, bioenergy facilities, etc.), (iii) distribution systems (transportation, storage, intermediate logistics), and (iv) final product markets. Suppose the chain is partitioned among a finite set of independent stakeholders S = {s_1, …, s_n}, each of whom controls a subset of nodes/arcs and chooses strategic, long-horizon decisions (e.g., harvest schedules, mill capacities, transportation contracts, market allocations) to optimize an individual objective (e.g., discounted profit, sustained yield, market share) subject to ecological, capacity, and policy constraints.

Develop a rigorous mathematical framework that:

(a) Provides a visualization and a formal model of strategic planning for the entire supply chain when stakeholders are independent decision-makers with private objectives and constraints, capturing the long planning horizon, biological growth dynamics of the forest resource, and the flow of products through plants, distribution, and markets.

(b) Defines an appropriate equilibrium concept (for instance, a Nash, generalized Nash, Stackelberg, or variational equilibrium) for the resulting multi-stakeholder strategic game, and gives conditions guaranteeing the existence, uniqueness, and computability of such an equilibrium.

(c) Provides tools to analyze and evaluate the equilibrium that emerges, including efficiency (price of anarchy / stability with respect to a centralized social optimum), stability under perturbations of demands or resource availability, and sensitivity to policy interventions.

Consider a wildlife reserve planning setting in which a conservation agency selects parcels of land to acquire and protect over a finite sequence of decision epochs t = 1, 2, ..., T. At each epoch the planner observes a state describing: (i) the set of parcels currently available for purchase, (ii) the habitat quality of each parcel (which may evolve stochastically), (iii) the remaining capital budget (which may itself be random across epochs), (iv) the state of land development on non-reserved parcels, and (v) prevailing parcel prices, which respond endogenously to the planner's prior acquisition decisions (a land-price feedback in which earlier protections raise or lower prices of remaining parcels through amenity premia and equilibrium adjustments). The planner chooses, at each epoch, a subset of currently available parcels to acquire, subject to the current budget, in order to maximize an objective measuring the long-run ecological value of the assembled reserve system (for example, expected total habitat or species representation, possibly with spatial contiguity or compactness requirements).

Develop a mathematical formulation of this sequential stochastic reserve selection and reserve design problem that simultaneously incorporates:
(a) uncertainty about future site availability,
(b) uncertainty about habitat quality,
(c) uncertainty about future budgets,
(d) endogenous land development on unprotected parcels, and
(e) feedback of past reserve decisions on future parcel prices,
together with solution methods (exact or approximate, with provable guarantees or empirically validated performance) capable of handling instances of realistic size, i.e. thousands of candidate parcels and multiple planning periods.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Several components of this problem have been addressed in the literature. Tóth, Haight, and Rogers (Operations Research, 2011) introduced a dynamic reserve selection model with land-price feedbacks, solved via stochastic dynamic programming and capable of accounting for budget, development, and price uncertainty. Scenario optimization models (e.g., Snyder et al.) and heuristics for large dynamic minimum-set reserve design problems have also appeared. However, no single formulation/solution method has been demonstrated to simultaneously handle all listed uncertainties (availability, quality, budget) together with land-price feedbacks at the realistic scales targeted by the open problem, so the full question remains only partially resolved.

Consider a predictive or decision-making system modeled as a function f : X_1 × ... × X_d → Y together with an underlying structural causal model M = (V, U, F, P) over the input features (X_1, ..., X_d), where V are endogenous variables, U exogenous variables with distribution P, and F a set of structural assignments. For an instance x ∈ X_1 × ... × X_d and prediction y = f(x), two families of causal explanations are of interest:

1. Causal attribution: assign to each feature i ∈ {1,...,d} a score φ_i(x) measuring its causal contribution to y, defined via interventional or counterfactual quantities under M (for example, Shapley-style averages of causal effects E[f(X) | do(X_S = x_S)] over subsets S ⊆ {1,...,d}, or path-specific effects in the causal graph of M).

2. Contrastive (counterfactual) explanations: given x with prediction y, find an alternative input x' minimizing a cost c(x, x') such that f(x') = y' for some target y' ≠ y, subject to (a) a plausibility constraint requiring x' to lie in the support of the observational or interventional distribution induced by M, and (b) an actionability constraint requiring that x' be reachable from x by interventions only on a designated subset A ⊆ {1,...,d} of actionable features, with downstream effects propagated through F.

Exact computation of causal Shapley-type attributions requires evaluation over 2^d subsets, and exact counterfactual search under plausibility and actionability constraints is generally NP-hard.

Problem. Design algorithms that, for arbitrary M and f drawn from broad and explicitly specified classes, produce:
(i) approximate causal attribution scores φ̂_i(x) with provable approximation guarantees (e.g., additive ε-error with high probability) in time polynomial in d and in the number n of users/instances to be explained, and
(ii) approximate contrastive explanations x̂' satisfying the plausibility and actionability constraints up to controlled slack, with cost c(x, x̂') within a guaranteed factor of the optimal feasible counterfactual, again computable in time polynomial in d and n.

Characterize the largest classes of structural causal models M, prediction functions f, cost functions c, and constraint sets for which such scalable approximation algorithms with non-trivial guarantees exist, and prove matching computational lower bounds where they do not.

Consider the reserve selection problem in conservation planning: given a landscape partitioned into a finite set of candidate parcels $S = \{1, \dots, n\}$, each with an associated acquisition/management cost $c_i \ge 0$ and ecological attributes (habitat suitability, connectivity, etc.) for a set of target species $K$, one wishes to select a subset $R \subseteq S$ (subject to a budget $\sum_{i \in R} c_i \le B$ or other resource constraints) that maximizes a conservation objective for those species.

Classical formulations maximize deterministic surrogates such as the number of species represented, total covered habitat area, or weighted habitat amounts. However, the long-term persistence of a species on a reserve $R$ is more accurately described by a stochastic demographic model: for each species $k \in K$, given the selected reserve $R$, there is a stochastic population process $\{N^k_t(R)\}_{t \ge 0}$ (e.g.\ a stage-structured matrix model with environmentally and demographically stochastic vital rates, a metapopulation incidence-function model, or an individual-based simulation) whose extinction time $\tau_k(R) = \inf\{t : N^k_t(R) = 0\}$ defines a population viability measure
$$ V_k(R) \;=\; \Pr\!\big[\tau_k(R) > T\big], $$
for some planning horizon $T$. The viability-maximizing reserve selection problem is then
$$ \max_{R \subseteq S} \; \Phi\big(V_1(R), \dots, V_{|K|}(R)\big) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i \in R} c_i \le B, $$
where $\Phi$ aggregates per-species viabilities (e.g.\ weighted sum, minimum, or product). The maps $R \mapsto V_k(R)$ are typically available only through Monte Carlo simulation of the demographic model and are neither linear nor submodular in general.

Problem. Develop a mathematically principled methodology to solve, or approximately solve, the above viability-maximizing reserve selection problem. Specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Identify tractable closed-form or convex surrogates $\widetilde V_k(R)$ (e.g.\ derived from diffusion approximations, mean-field limits, or analytic extinction-probability bounds for stochastic matrix or metapopulation models) that provably approximate $V_k(R)$ within controllable error, and that yield mixed-integer linear, conic, or submodular optimization formulations amenable to off-the-shelf solvers with provable optimality gaps.
\item[(b)] Alternatively, design simulation-based optimization algorithms (e.g.\ sample average approximation, stochastic gradient on a relaxation, simulation-optimization with ranking and selection, or learning-augmented heuristics) that directly optimize the simulation model $V_k(\cdot)$ over $R \subseteq S$ with finite-sample performance guarantees on the achieved objective $\Phi$.
\item[(c)] Characterize structural properties (monotonicity, submodularity, supermodularity, concavity along chains) of $R \mapsto V_k(R)$ under standard demographic-stochastic models that justify greedy or local-search guarantees.
\end{enumerate}

The integration of stochastic demographic population viability models into reserve selection optimization is broadly recognized as a long-standing open challenge bridging conservation biology and operations research. While there are works on probabilistic/chance-constrained and stochastic site-selection models and on connectivity-based reserve design, no general method is established for embedding full stochastic demographic viability models into tractable optimization. The problem remains open.

Consider a metropolitan landscape modeled as a finite set of parcels $P=\{1,\dots,n\}$ over a discrete planning horizon $t=1,\dots,T$. Each parcel $i$ at time $t$ can be in one of three states: undeveloped, residentially developed, or designated as a wildlife reserve. Let $x_{it}\in\{0,1\}$ denote whether parcel $i$ is in the reserve at time $t$ (with an irreversibility constraint $x_{it}\le x_{i,t+1}$ if reserves are permanent), and let $y_{it}\in\{0,1\}$ indicate residential development.

Biodiversity is measured by a function $B(x_1,\dots,x_T)$ that depends on the spatial-temporal configuration of reserves (for example, expected species persistence under a metapopulation or species-distribution model with connectivity considerations).

Household location choice is modeled by a social/economic model: there is a population of households $H$, and each household $h\in H$ choosing to locate at parcel $i$ at time $t$ derives utility $U_{hit}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p})$, where $\mathbf{p}$ are endogenous land prices/rents determined by a market-clearing or equilibrium condition (e.g., a discrete-choice/logit residential sorting model, a bid-rent equilibrium, or a dynamic Tiebout-type model). Aggregate household welfare is $W(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{h,i,t} \pi_{hit} U_{hit}$, where $\pi_{hit}$ are equilibrium choice probabilities.

The development pattern $\mathbf{y}$ is jointly determined with $\mathbf{p}$ by the residential choice equilibrium, and is influenced by the reserve decisions $\mathbf{x}$ (which remove parcels from the developable pool and alter location amenities and prices).

Problem. Formulate and solve a planner's dynamic reserve-selection problem of the form
$$\max_{\mathbf{x}} \; \alpha\, B(\mathbf{x}) + (1-\alpha)\, W(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^*(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{p}^*(\mathbf{x}))$$
subject to budget, area, and connectivity constraints on $\mathbf{x}$, where $(\mathbf{y}^*(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{p}^*(\mathbf{x}))$ is the residential-choice equilibrium induced by $\mathbf{x}$, and $\alpha\in[0,1]$ trades off biodiversity against household welfare. Provide an integrated mathematical framework combining social/economic residential-location-choice models with dynamic reserve-selection optimization, together with algorithms that compute optimal or provably good reserve policies under the induced bilevel/equilibrium structure.

Consider an airtanker deployment system modeled as a spatial, time-dependent queueing system in which fire incidents arrive stochastically according to rates that vary in both space and time, and a finite fleet of airtankers act as mobile servers that travel from bases to fires and may serve multiple incidents per day, with service (travel plus suppression) rates depending on the spatial configuration. Let a day be partitioned into time periods, and let the system state include the locations of airtankers, ongoing fires, and the realized history of arrivals.

Develop a spatial, time-dependent queueing model of this system together with an optimization framework, coupled to the queueing model, that is computationally tractable and produces:
(i) an initial daily deployment of the airtanker fleet to a set of candidate bases at the start of each day, minimizing an appropriate operational performance measure (e.g., expected response time, expected number of fires escaping initial attack, or expected damage); and
(ii) a dynamic redeployment policy that updates the locations of airtankers during the day as new fire activity is observed, again optimizing the same performance measure.

The problem is to construct such a coupled queueing–optimization methodology and to establish its tractability and performance guarantees.

The problem is to construct such a coupled queueing–optimization methodology and to establish its tractability and performance guarantees.

Consider a large wildfire that has escaped initial attack and continues to spread across a heterogeneous landscape. Let the landscape be partitioned into a finite set of spatial cells, each characterized by fuel type, topography, ecological value, and the presence or absence of people, structures, and other assets to be protected. Time evolves over a finite horizon partitioned into discrete decision epochs. At each epoch, a decision maker chooses, for each cell, one of several management actions: (i) aggressive suppression, (ii) preemptive burnout of fuels, (iii) point protection of structures, or (iv) no intervention (allowing fire to play its natural ecological role). The evolution of the fire is governed by a stochastic process whose transition law depends on uncertain weather (wind, temperature, humidity), uncertain fire-behavior parameters (rate of spread, intensity, spotting), and uncertain availability of suppression resources (crews, engines, aircraft). Associated with each trajectory of fire and management actions are: a loss functional accounting for damage to people, property, and forest resources; a benefit functional reflecting ecological gains from fire on the landscape; and a cost functional for deployed resources.

Formulate and analyze a decision-support framework that produces management policies optimizing an aggregate objective that weighs expected ecological benefit against expected losses and costs under the stochastic dynamics described, subject to operational constraints on resources and to spatial coupling between cells induced by fire spread. Specifically: (a) propose a mathematical model (e.g., a multi-stage stochastic program, partially observable Markov decision process, or robust optimization formulation) that captures the dynamics, uncertainties, and trade-offs above; (b) establish existence and structural properties of optimal policies; and (c) develop tractable algorithms that scale to landscape-sized instances and provide provable guarantees on solution quality.

Let a population of individuals be modeled by a structural causal model M = (U, V, F, P(U)), where V = {X, A, Y} with A a protected attribute partitioning the population into groups G_a = {i : A_i = a}, X a vector of features (some of which may be actionable), and Y a binary decision output of a predictor h: X -> {0,1}. A (causal) algorithmic recourse system is a mapping that, for each individual i with h(X_i) = 0, returns a set of interventions Θ_i ⊆ A_int (a fixed space of admissible interventions on subsets of V) together with a recommended policy π_i ∈ Θ_i such that, under the post-intervention distribution induced by do(π_i) in M, the predicted outcome becomes 1 with probability at least some threshold τ, while the cost c(π_i; U_i) of the intervention (defined on the structural counterfactual for individual i) is minimized.

Develop a formal definition of fairness for such recourse systems that goes beyond fairness of the predictor h itself. Concretely:

(a) Propose mathematical fairness criteria for recourse that quantify whether the set of available recourse opportunities Θ_i and the minimal recourse cost c*(i) := min_{π ∈ Θ_i} E[c(π; U_i) | X_i, A_i] are distributed equitably across the groups G_a; for example, criteria of the form
   ρ_a := E[c*(i) | A_i = a, h(X_i)=0],
and conditions such as ρ_a = ρ_{a'} for all a, a', or analogous counterfactual-recourse criteria comparing c*(i) for an individual to the cost that would have been incurred had A_i taken a different value under M.

(b) Provide a corresponding evaluation procedure (estimator and identifiability conditions in terms of M and observational/interventional data) that allows these criteria to be tested.

(c) Address whether, and under which structural assumptions on M, it is normatively and causally appropriate to perform a societal-level intervention (i.e., a policy applied uniformly to every member of a subgroup G_a) as a means of equalizing recourse, and characterize the trade-offs between such group-level interventions and individual-level recourse recommendations.

The task is to give precise definitions, prove basic properties (existence, identifiability, compatibility/incompatibility results between different fairness-of-recourse criteria), and to formulate the conditions under which causal algorithmic recourse can be certified as fair across protected and unprotected groups.

Consider a multi-stage value chain in which raw material (e.g., standing trees or logs) is transformed through a sequence of divergent processes. A process is called divergent when a single input stream is partitioned into several co-products and by-products whose relative yields are determined by the input characteristics and the chosen process settings (typical examples include bucking trees into logs, sawing logs into lumber of various dimensions, cutting boards, and converting residues into chips, pulp, or energy). At each stage, the realized output proportions cannot be chosen independently for each product; they are coupled through the divergent yield structure of the process. Downstream, each final product faces an exogenous (possibly stochastic) demand process, and safety-stock requirements must be maintained at intermediate and final inventory points to hedge against demand and yield uncertainty.

Formulate and analyze an integrated, demand-driven planning framework that simultaneously decides, over a finite planning horizon:
(a) harvesting and procurement volumes of the raw input,
(b) the assignment of input batches and process settings at each divergent stage,
(c) inventory and safety-stock levels at all stages, and
(d) flows to downstream customers,
in such a way that downstream demand is met (or backorder/lost-sales costs are minimized), capacity and yield-coupling constraints of every divergent process are respected, and total expected cost is minimized.

Specifically, provide:
1. A mathematical model (e.g., a multi-stage stochastic program, MDP, or equivalent) that explicitly captures divergent yields, safety stocks, and downstream demand propagation across the chain.
2. Solution methods with provable performance guarantees, or computational schemes that scale to industrially realistic instances.
3. Structural results characterizing optimal policies, in particular how safety-stock placement and process-setting decisions interact with divergent yields under demand uncertainty.

Consider a forest value chain modeled as a set of decision-making units U = {1, 2, ..., n} (e.g., forest owners, harvesters, transporters, sawmills, pulp and paper plants, distributors, retailers). Each unit i has:

- a private feasible decision set X_i (its local plans, e.g., harvest schedules, production schedules, transport plans, inventory policies),
- a private objective function f_i : X_i -> R that unit i seeks to optimize,
- possibly private information (costs, capacities, demands, forecasts) not shared with other units,
- linking constraints g(x_1, ..., x_n) <= 0 representing material flows, timing, and capacity couplings between units.

Because the units have different owners, objectives, and strategies, a centralized planner cannot be assumed; each unit will only adopt a plan that is individually rational given its own objective and information.

Design a coordination mechanism M — chosen from instruments such as information-sharing protocols, bilateral or multilateral contracts, auctions, collaboration schemes, transfer-pricing schemes, or regulatory/legislative rules — that selects a tuple (x_1*, ..., x_n*) of plans with the following properties:

1. Feasibility: x_i* in X_i for every i and g(x_1*, ..., x_n*) <= 0.
2. Individual rationality and incentive compatibility: under M, each unit i finds it optimal (with respect to f_i) to participate and to truthfully follow the mechanism.
3. System-level efficiency: the resulting plan approximates, in a quantifiable sense, the centralized optimum max sum_i w_i f_i(x_i) subject to the linking constraints, for appropriate weights w_i >= 0.
4. Synchronization: the plans of all units are temporally and logistically consistent across the value chain.

Provide a constructive design of such a mechanism M for the forest value chain, together with a proof (or quantitative bound) of properties (1)–(4), or establish impossibility results delineating which combinations of these properties can be simultaneously achieved.

Consider a forest value-chain planning model formulated as a large-scale network optimization problem with the following ingredients:

- A set of spatial units (e.g., harvest blocks, mills, storage yards, markets) connected by transportation arcs forming a directed network.
- A set of products and a set of processes (harvesting, transportation, transformation, storage) that transform inputs into outputs along the network.
- A finite planning horizon partitioned into multiple discrete periods t = 1, ..., T (multi-stage).
- A vector of K conflicting objective functions f_1, ..., f_K (e.g., economic return, environmental impact, social criteria) that must be optimized simultaneously, yielding a multi-objective program.
- A probability space (Omega, F, P) and a filtration {F_t} modelling uncertainty in parameters such as demand, prices, yields, and disturbances; decisions at stage t must be F_t-measurable (non-anticipativity).
- Risk constraints expressed via coherent or convex risk measures (e.g., CVaR) bounding the tail of cost or impact distributions.

The problem is: design and analyze tractable solution methods (exact or approximate, with provable performance or convergence guarantees) capable of computing an efficient (Pareto) frontier, or a decision-maker-preferred efficient solution, for instances of this multi-objective, multi-stage stochastic program whose deterministic equivalent has on the order of millions of variables and constraints. In particular, develop algorithms that simultaneously handle (i) scenario-tree size growth across T stages, (ii) Pareto-set approximation with quality guarantees over K objectives, and (iii) risk constraints, with empirical or theoretical evidence of scalability to realistic forestry value-chain instances.

Consider a multistage stochastic optimization problem arising in forest management at one of three planning levels: strategic (long-horizon decisions such as land use, road network design, and sustainable harvest levels), tactical (medium-horizon decisions such as annual harvest scheduling and transportation planning), or operational (short-horizon decisions such as daily crew assignment, bucking, and routing). The uncertainty in such a problem may involve any combination of: timber and product prices, product demand, biological growth and yield, natural disasters (fire, wind, pests, disease), and operational factors (machine availability, weather, productivity).

Formally, let the underlying uncertainty be modeled by a stochastic process ξ = (ξ_1, …, ξ_T) on a probability space (Ω, F, P), and let the optimization problem be of the form

   min_{x ∈ X} E_ξ[ f(x, ξ) ],

subject to nonanticipativity and possibly multistage recourse constraints, where X encodes feasibility (resource, ecological, logistical) and f is a forestry-specific cost or negative-value functional.

A scenario representation replaces ξ by a finite tree {ξ^s, p_s}_{s=1}^S with S scenarios and probabilities p_s, giving the deterministic equivalent

   min_{x ∈ X} Σ_{s=1}^S p_s f(x, ξ^s).

Develop a methodology for constructing such a scenario set {(ξ^s, p_s)} for strategic, tactical, and operational forestry problems that simultaneously:

  (a) captures the essential features of the joint distribution of prices, demand, growth, disasters, and operational uncertainty (e.g., in terms of moments, tail behavior, temporal/spatial dependence, or a probability metric such as Wasserstein or nested distance from the true process),

  (b) yields a deterministic equivalent that is computationally tractable on instances of realistic size, and

  (c) admits quantitative guarantees relating the optimal value and optimal first-stage decisions of the scenario-based problem to those of the true stochastic problem.

The problem is to give a constructive procedure—together with conditions under which the above three requirements can be met—for representing uncertainty by scenarios in strategic, tactical, and operational forestry optimization.

Consider a multistage mixed-integer optimization problem of the form

  minimize  E[ sum_{t=1}^{T} c_t(x_t, y_t, xi_t) ]
  subject to  (x_t, y_t) in X_t(x_{1:t-1}, y_{1:t-1}, xi_{1:t}),  x_t in R^{n_t}, y_t in Z^{m_t},

where T is a long planning horizon, the decision variables include both continuous variables x_t and integer variables y_t at every stage, and xi_t is a vector-valued random process that jointly captures several heterogeneous sources of uncertainty acting simultaneously, including but not limited to:
 (i) commodity/output prices,
 (ii) discrete catastrophic events such as fires (losses of stock, disjunctive in nature),
 (iii) environmental and biological conditions (growth rates, weather, yields).

Each of these sources may have a different statistical nature (continuous distributions, jump processes, spatially correlated random fields), and they may be statistically dependent on one another.

Problem. Devise a representation of the joint multi-source uncertainty process {xi_t}_{t=1}^{T} (for example, by means of a scenario tree, a Markov chain, a stochastic dual dynamic representation, a robust/ambiguity set, or any other formalism) together with a corresponding reformulation of the above multistage mixed-integer stochastic optimization problem, such that:

 (a) the representation is faithful, in the sense that the marginal and joint statistical behavior of all considered uncertainty sources, including their interdependencies and the discrete/jump character of events like fires, are accurately preserved;

 (b) the resulting optimization model is solvable in practice, i.e., admits an algorithm that returns a provably good (optimal, epsilon-optimal, or with quantifiable optimality gap) solution within tractable computational resources for instance sizes typical of large-scale long-horizon planning;

 (c) the approach scales with the number of stages T, the number of independent uncertainty sources, and the dimension of the integer decision space.

Either exhibit such a representation and solution methodology together with a proof of its faithfulness and tractability guarantees, or prove an impossibility/hardness result delineating the achievable trade-offs between faithfulness of representation and solvability.

Consider a forest-management optimization problem of the generic form

  minimize_{x ∈ X}  c(x)
  subject to  g(x, ξ) ≤ 0   for every realization ξ of an uncertain parameter,

where x ∈ X ⊂ ℝⁿ is the decision vector (e.g., harvest schedules, transportation flows, road-building decisions), c : ℝⁿ → ℝ is a cost or revenue functional, g : ℝⁿ × ℝᵐ → ℝᵏ encodes operational constraints, and ξ ∈ ℝᵐ represents uncertain quantities (such as future timber yields, demands, prices, growth rates, or weather-driven productivity losses).

In robust optimization one does not specify a probability distribution for ξ; instead one fixes an uncertainty set U ⊂ ℝᵐ and requires the constraints to hold for every ξ ∈ U. The choice of U is critical: if U is too small, the solution fails to be robust; if U is too large or badly shaped (e.g., a loose hyper-rectangle ignoring correlations), the resulting decisions are excessively conservative and economically inefficient.

Problem. Develop a principled methodology for constructing an uncertainty set U ⊂ ℝᵐ for robust optimization models arising in forestry planning such that:

(i) U faithfully reflects the practical variability and dependence structure of the uncertain parameters ξ observed in forestry operations (yields, demands, prices, growth and disturbance processes);

(ii) the resulting robust optimal solution x*(U) is not unnecessarily pessimistic, in a quantifiable sense (for example, with respect to expected cost under a plausible underlying distribution, or relative to a deterministic benchmark);

(iii) the robust counterpart remains computationally tractable for problem sizes typical of operational and tactical forestry planning.

Provide either a constructive procedure for U with theoretical guarantees relating (i)–(iii), or prove fundamental limitations on what such guarantees can achieve.

Consider a forestry planning problem formulated as a large-scale mixed-integer linear program of the following general form. Let T be a finite planning horizon, let S be a finite set of forest stands (management units), and for each stand s in S let P_s be a finite set of admissible silvicultural prescriptions (each specifying a schedule of harvest, thinning, regeneration, and other treatments over the horizon). Introduce binary variables x_{s,p} in {0,1} indicating whether prescription p in P_s is assigned to stand s, together with continuous variables y representing flows such as harvested volumes, transported quantities, inventories, and revenues per period. The deterministic model has the form

   minimize   c^T x + d^T y
   subject to A x + B y <= b,
              sum_{p in P_s} x_{s,p} = 1   for all s in S,
              x in {0,1}^n,  y >= 0,

with side constraints that may include adjacency / green-up restrictions on simultaneous harvesting of neighboring stands, even-flow or volume bounds across periods, road-building decisions, and demand satisfaction at mills.

Assume that some of the data (A, B, b, c, d), in particular timber yields, growth rates, prices, demands, and costs, are uncertain and known only to lie in a prescribed uncertainty set U (for example a box, budgeted, polyhedral, or ellipsoidal set, or a data-driven set constructed from historical observations). The robust counterpart requires feasibility (or, in adjustable/two-stage variants, recourse feasibility) for every realization of the uncertain parameters in U and optimizes a worst-case objective.

Problem. Develop a methodology — including modeling choices for U, reformulation or decomposition techniques, and algorithms — that makes such robust mixed-integer forestry planning models solvable to provable near-optimality on industrial-scale instances (with tens of thousands of stands and multi-decade horizons) within computation times acceptable for operational use, and that produces solutions whose robustness, cost, and implementability are demonstrably superior to those obtained by deterministic or simple stochastic alternatives on realistic forest data.

Consider a hierarchical forest management planning framework with three nested decision levels:

- A strategic level L1 with long planning horizon T1, coarse spatial aggregation S1, and decision variables x1 chosen to optimize an objective f1(x1) subject to constraints g1(x1) ≤ 0 (covering sustainability, yield, and budget).
- A tactical level L2 with medium horizon T2 ⊂ T1, finer spatial units S2 that refine S1, decision variables x2, objective f2(x2), and constraints g2(x2) ≤ 0.
- An operational level L3 with short horizon T3 ⊂ T2, finest spatial resolution S3 refining S2, decision variables x3, objective f3(x3), and constraints g3(x3) ≤ 0.

Aggregation operators A21 and A32 map the lower-level decisions to the corresponding higher-level resolution (e.g., temporal and spatial summation). A solution (x1*, x2*, x3*) is called consistent if:
(i) A21(x2*) = x1* and A32(x3*) = x2*;
(ii) for each level k the restricted lower-level problem remains feasible, i.e., the sets {x2 : g2(x2) ≤ 0, A21(x2) = x1*} and {x3 : g3(x3) ≤ 0, A32(x3) = x2*} are nonempty;
(iii) the lower-level optimal objective values are economically meaningful with respect to the higher level, in the sense that the value f1(A21(x2*)) (resp. f2(A32(x3*))) is within a prescribed tolerance of the standalone optimum of level 1 (resp. level 2).

Open problem: Design a systematic modeling and algorithmic framework (e.g., a coupled optimization model, a decomposition scheme, or a set of structural constraints linking the three levels) that, for any instance of the above hierarchy, produces solutions guaranteed to satisfy properties (i)–(iii), without relying on ad hoc post-hoc adjustments. Equivalently, characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on f_k, g_k, and the aggregation operators A21, A32 under which such consistency can be enforced, and provide an effective method to compute consistent solutions.

Consider a forest resource planning problem formulated as a multicriteria optimization model with a feasible set X (encoding silvicultural, ecological, logistic, and budgetary constraints) and a vector-valued objective F(x) = (f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_k(x)) whose components represent economic, environmental, and social criteria (e.g., net present value, harvested volume, carbon storage, biodiversity indices, recreation value, employment). A decision maker has preferences over the criteria that may include relative importance, trade-off rates, aspiration and reservation levels, lexicographic priorities, indifference and preference thresholds, and possibly non-compensatory or interactive preference structures that are not fully captured by a fixed weight vector in weighted goal programming.

Devise a methodology that rigorously incorporates the decision maker's preferences directly into the multicriteria optimization model for forest planning. Specifically:

(a) Propose a formal mathematical representation of the decision maker's preferences (for example, via utility/value functions, outranking relations, reference points, fuzzy preference relations, or interactive elicitation protocols) that can be embedded into the optimization problem over X.

(b) Define a corresponding solution concept (e.g., most-preferred Pareto-optimal solution) and produce an algorithm that computes such a solution while remaining tractable for realistic forest planning instances.

(c) Establish properties of the resulting method, including consistency with the elicited preferences, Pareto-optimality of returned solutions, robustness to imprecise or evolving preference information, and a justification that the encoded preferences faithfully reflect those of the decision maker.

Consider a forest planning problem in which a decision maker (or a group of stakeholders) must choose among management alternatives evaluated on multiple, possibly conflicting criteria (e.g., timber yield, biodiversity, carbon sequestration, recreation, economic return). A multicriteria decision method consists of (i) a procedure for eliciting the decision maker's preferences over criteria and outcomes, and (ii) an aggregation rule that combines criterion-level evaluations into an overall ranking or recommendation of alternatives. Call such a method rigorous if it provides axiomatically justified, internally consistent preference elicitation and aggregation (e.g., guaranteeing transitivity, independence properties, and faithful representation of trade-offs), and call it user-friendly if a non-expert practitioner can apply it with a reasonable cognitive and time burden, providing only information that the practitioner can reliably supply.

Design a multicriteria decision-making framework for forest planning that simultaneously:
(a) is rigorous in the above sense in its preference elicitation and aggregation;
(b) is user-friendly for practitioners;
(c) supports combining several multicriteria methods within a single planning process; and
(d) accommodates multiple stakeholders with differing preference structures.

Provide formal definitions of rigor and user-friendliness suitable for this context, propose such a framework, and establish its theoretical properties (e.g., consistency, convergence of group preferences, complexity of elicitation).
