Let $\Phi$ be a finite irreducible crystallographic root system spanning a Euclidean space $V$, with Weyl group $W$, set of positive roots $\Phi^+$ (with respect to a fixed choice of simple roots), rank $r$, Coxeter number $h$, fundamental degrees $d_1,\dots,d_r$, and index of connection $f = [P^\vee : Q^\vee]$ (the index of the coroot lattice in the coweight lattice).

A subspace $U \subseteq V$ is called a $\Phi$-subspace if it is spanned by some subset of $\Phi$ (equivalently, $\Phi \cap U$ is a root subsystem of $\Phi$ whose span is $U$). For such a $U$, let $\pi_U : V \to U$ denote the orthogonal projection.

Define the projection-dilation invariant
$$\kappa(\Phi, U) \;=\; \min\bigl\{\, c \in \mathbb{R}_{>0} \;:\; c\cdot \pi_U(\alpha) \in \mathbb{Z}\text{-span of } \Phi \cap U \text{ for every } \alpha \in \Phi \,\bigr\},$$
i.e., the smallest positive real $c$ such that scaling the orthogonal projection of every root of $\Phi$ onto $U$ by $c$ yields a vector in the root lattice of the subsystem $\Phi \cap U$. Then set
$$\kappa(\Phi) \;=\; \max_{U}\; \kappa(\Phi, U),$$
the maximum taken over all $\Phi$-subspaces $U$.

Problem. Give a root-system-theoretic interpretation of the invariants $\kappa(\Phi, U)$ and $\kappa(\Phi)$ in terms of standard invariants of $\Phi$ such as the rank $r$, the Coxeter number $h$, the fundamental degrees $d_i$, and the index of connection $f$ (or other natural invariants of $\Phi$ and of the embedded subsystem $\Phi \cap U$).

For a function s: ℕ → ℕ with s(n) ≥ log n, let SPACE(s(n)) denote the class of languages decided by a deterministic Turing machine using O(s(n)) work-tape cells, and let NSPACE(s(n)) denote the class of languages decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine using O(s(n)) work-tape cells. Savitch's theorem asserts the inclusion NSPACE(s(n)) ⊆ SPACE(s(n)²).

Prove or disprove the following strengthening of Savitch's theorem: every language in NSPACE(s(n)) can be decided by a deterministic Turing machine using o(s(n)²) space; that is,
    NSPACE(s(n)) ⊆ SPACE(o(s(n)²)).
Equivalently, exhibit a deterministic simulation of nondeterministic s-space computations whose space usage is asymptotically strictly smaller than s² (for instance, s² / ω(1), or s^{2−ε} for some ε > 0), or rule out the existence of such a simulation.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $\lambda$ be a partition with at most $n$ parts. Denote by $W_\lambda$ the irreducible polynomial representation of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ indexed by $\lambda$ (so that $W_\lambda$ has highest weight $\lambda$ in the standard ordering). The symmetric group $S_n$ embeds in $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ as the subgroup of permutation matrices. Restricting $W_\lambda$ along this embedding yields a finite-dimensional representation of $S_n$, which decomposes as
$$ \mathrm{Res}^{\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})}_{S_n} W_\lambda \;\cong\; \bigoplus_{\mu \vdash n} r^\lambda_\mu \, S^\mu, $$
where $S^\mu$ denotes the Specht (irreducible) module of $S_n$ associated with the partition $\mu$ of $n$, and the nonnegative integers $r^\lambda_\mu$ are called restriction coefficients.

Problem: Give a combinatorial description (an explicit manifestly nonnegative formula in terms of a set of combinatorial objects to be enumerated) of the multiplicities $r^\lambda_\mu$ for arbitrary partitions $\lambda$ (with at most $n$ parts) and $\mu \vdash n$.

The problem of finding a combinatorial rule for the restriction coefficients from polynomial GL_n(C) representations to S_n is a well-known longstanding open problem in algebraic combinatorics. Partial progress exists (e.g., bases related to these coefficients by Assaf–Speyer and Orellana–Zabrocki, and a combinatorial interpretation in the hook-shape case by recent work in 2024), but no general combinatorial formula is known.

For a space-constructible function $s: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $s(n) \geq \log n$, let $\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s)$ denote the class of languages decided by randomized Turing machines that, on inputs of length $n$, use $O(s(n))$ workspace, halt in finite time on every random-string branch, and err with probability at most $1/3$. Let $\mathrm{DSPACE}(t)$ denote the class of languages decided by deterministic Turing machines using $O(t(n))$ workspace.

The Saks–Zhou theorem gives the inclusion $\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(s^{3/2})$, and subsequent work has obtained the slightly stronger inclusion $\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(s^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log s})$.

Problem: Improve the deterministic space complexity of $\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s)$. That is, exhibit a function $t(s) = o(s^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log s})$ such that
$$\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(t(s)),$$
or, ideally, prove that $\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(s^{1+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ (or even $\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(s)$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Saks–Zhou bound $\mathrm{BPSPACE}(s) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(s^{3/2})$ from 1999 remained the best known for over two decades. A recent improvement by Hoza (APPROX/RANDOM 2021) achieves $\mathrm{DSPACE}(s^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log s})$ using weighted pseudorandom generators, but this is only a sub-polynomial improvement. Reducing the exponent below $3/2$ (and, in particular, proving $\mathrm{BPL} \subseteq \mathrm{L}$) remains a major open problem in complexity theory.

Let $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n$ be a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$. For a (possibly empty) word $u$, let $\mathrm{asc}(u)$ denote the number of indices $i$ with $u_i < u_{i+1}$ (ascents), and define $\mathrm{asc}^*(u) = 0$ if $u$ is empty and $\mathrm{asc}^*(u) = 1 + \mathrm{asc}(u)$ otherwise. For a word $u$, let $d(u)$ denote the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $u$ (with $d(\emptyset)=0$).

For each integer $k \geq 0$, define two "localized Greene" statistics:
$$A'_k(w) := \max_{(u_1,\ldots,u_k)} \bigl( \mathrm{asc}^*(u_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{asc}^*(u_k) \bigr),$$
where the maximum is over all choices of $k$ pairwise disjoint subsequences $u_1,\ldots,u_k$ of $w$; and
$$D'_k(w) := \max_{w = u_1 | u_2 | \cdots | u_k} \bigl( d(u_1) + \cdots + d(u_k) \bigr),$$
where the maximum is over all ways of cutting $w$ into $k$ consecutive (possibly empty) blocks $u_1,\ldots,u_k$.

Set $A'_0 = D'_0 = 0$, and for $k \geq 1$ define
$$\lambda'_k := A'_k - A'_{k-1}, \qquad \mu'_k := D'_k - D'_{k-1}.$$

It is known that $\lambda' = (\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\ldots)$ and $\mu' = (\mu'_1,\mu'_2,\ldots)$ are weakly decreasing sequences of nonnegative integers summing to $n$ (so they are integer partitions of $n$), and that they are conjugate partitions of each other. Currently, the only known proof of this fact passes through the dynamics of the (multicolor) box-ball system.

Problem: Give a direct proof of this theorem—that $\lambda'$ and $\mu'$ are conjugate partitions of $n$—using only permutation combinatorics, without invoking the machinery of box-ball systems.

Determine the exact space complexity of this problem as a function of the input size n (equivalently, of h and k). Specifically, decide whether the Tree Evaluation Problem belongs to deterministic logarithmic space L, and more generally pin down tight upper and lower bounds on the deterministic space required to solve it.

Let $P$ be a finite poset. Recall the classical Greene–Kleitman invariants: for each positive integer $k$, let
$$a_k(P) = \max\{|A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_k| : A_i \text{ antichains of } P\},\qquad d_k(P) = \max\{|C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_k| : C_i \text{ chains of } P\},$$
and recall that the sequences $(a_k(P)-a_{k-1}(P))_k$ and $(d_k(P)-d_{k-1}(P))_k$ are conjugate partitions of $|P|$.

Now, for a permutation $w = w_1w_2\cdots w_n \in S_n$, define the following "localized" quantities for each $k\ge 1$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $A'_k(w)$ is the maximum, over choices of $k$ pairwise disjoint subsequences $u^{(1)},\ldots,u^{(k)}$ of $w$, of $\sum_{i=1}^k \mathrm{asc}^*(u^{(i)})$, where $\mathrm{asc}^*(u)$ denotes the number of ascents of $u$ plus $1$ if $u$ is nonempty (and $0$ otherwise).
\item $D'_k(w)$ is the maximum, over choices of $k$ pairwise disjoint subsequences $u^{(1)},\ldots,u^{(k)}$ that together exhaust $w$ in a way respecting some "localized" structure (e.g.\ each $u^{(i)}$ is a maximal decreasing run inside one of $k$ consecutive blocks partitioning the one-line notation of $w$), of $\sum_{i=1}^k \ell(u^{(i)})$, where $\ell$ denotes length.
\end{itemize}

Construct, for an arbitrary finite poset $P$, "localized" versions $\widetilde{a}_k(P)$ and $\widetilde{d}_k(P)$ of the Greene–Kleitman invariants — refining the classical $a_k(P)$ and $d_k(P)$ and satisfying an analogous conjugate-partition duality — such that, in the case where $P$ is the natural poset associated to a permutation $w$ (for instance, the inversion poset or an analogous combinatorial structure on the cells of $w$), one recovers $\widetilde{a}_k(P) = A'_k(w)$ and $\widetilde{d}_k(P) = D'_k(w)$ for all $k\ge 1$.

A register program $P$ with space $s = s(n)$ over a ring $R$ is a finite sequence of instructions operating on $s$ registers $R_1, \ldots, R_s$, each storing an element of $R$. Each instruction has the form
$$R_i \;\leftarrow\; R_i + f(R_1, \ldots, R_{i-1}, R_{i+1}, \ldots, R_s),$$
where $f$ is a polynomial in the other registers (or, more generally, the instruction may be a recursive call to a subprogram). The program may make calls to subprograms; in particular let $P_x$ denote the subprogram whose effect is to add the values $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ to the registers $R_1, \ldots, R_n$ respectively, leaving all other registers unchanged.

Question: Does there exist a register program that, on input access provided only through the oracle subprogram $P_x$, computes an arbitrary polynomial $p(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ (in the sense of adding $p(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ to a designated output register and leaving all other registers in their initial state), while using
\begin{itemize}
  \item only $O(n)$ registers, each over a fixed ring $R$ of constant size, and
  \item only $O(1)$ recursive calls to $P_x$?
\end{itemize}

Let $G$ be a reductive algebraic group (or Lie algebra) and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional representation of $G$. For each integer $n \geq 1$, the symmetric group $S_n$ acts on the tensor power $V^{\otimes n}$ by permuting tensor factors, and this action commutes with the diagonal $G$-action. For each dominant weight $\lambda$ of $G$, let $W_\lambda \subseteq V^{\otimes n}$ denote the space of highest-weight vectors of weight $\lambda$; then $W_\lambda$ carries an $S_n$-representation whose Frobenius characteristic is a symmetric function $\mathrm{ch}(n,\lambda)$.

A "highest-weight word" of length $n$ and weight $\lambda$ is a combinatorial object indexing a basis of $W_\lambda$ (for example, for $V$ the defining representation of $GL_k$, these are column-strict tableaux or lattice words of content $\lambda$; for other $V$ they are oscillating tableaux, King tableaux, Kashiwara–Nakashima tableaux, etc., depending on $V$).

Gessel's fundamental quasisymmetric functions are defined for a subset $D \subseteq \{1,\dots,n-1\}$ by
$$F_{n,D}(x) = \sum_{\substack{i_1 \leq i_2 \leq \cdots \leq i_n \\ i_j < i_{j+1} \text{ if } j \in D}} x_{i_1} x_{i_2} \cdots x_{i_n}.$$
For any $S_n$-representation, its Frobenius characteristic admits a unique expansion as a nonnegative integer combination of $F_{n,D}$'s, indexed by a set whose cardinality equals the dimension; equivalently, one seeks a statistic $\mathrm{Des}$ on a combinatorial set $\mathcal{H}_{n,\lambda}$ of highest-weight words such that
$$\mathrm{ch}(n,\lambda) = \sum_{w \in \mathcal{H}_{n,\lambda}} F_{n,\mathrm{Des}(w)}.$$

Problem: For representations $V$ of reductive groups or Lie algebras beyond the cases where it is already known (for instance, beyond the defining representation of $GL_k$, where the standard descent set on semistandard tableaux works), give an explicit combinatorial construction of a descent set $\mathrm{Des}(w) \subseteq \{1,\dots,n-1\}$ on highest-weight words $w$ of length $n$ and weight $\lambda$ that realizes the above quasisymmetric expansion of $\mathrm{ch}(n,\lambda)$.

A (deterministic) branching program of width $w$ and length $\ell$ over input variables $x_1,\dots,x_n \in \{0,1\}$ is a layered directed graph with $\ell+1$ layers, each layer containing at most $w$ vertices. Each non-final vertex is labeled by an input variable $x_i$ and has two outgoing edges, labeled $0$ and $1$, going to vertices in the next layer; vertices in the final layer are labeled by output values (accept/reject, or more generally by elements of some output alphabet). On input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, computation starts at a designated source in the first layer and, at each vertex labeled $x_i$, follows the edge labeled by the current value of $x_i$; the program outputs the label of the final vertex reached. Two branching programs are equivalent if they compute the same function $\{0,1\}^n \to \{\text{outputs}\}$.

Prove or disprove: there exists a constant $w_0$ such that for every branching program $B$ of width $w \ge w_0$ and length $\ell$, there exists an equivalent branching program $B'$ of width $\lfloor w/2 \rfloor$ and length $O(\ell)$ (with the implicit constant independent of $w$ and $\ell$) computing the same function as $B$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer, let $G$ be a subgroup of the symmetric group $S_n$ acting on $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$. Write $\chi^\lambda$ for the irreducible character of $S_n$ indexed by $\lambda$, and define
$$K_{\lambda,G} \;=\; \langle \mathrm{Ind}_G^{S_n} \mathbf{1}_G,\; \chi^\lambda\rangle_{S_n} \;=\; \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi^\lambda(g),$$
the multiplicity of the irreducible $S_n$-representation $S^\lambda$ in the permutation representation $\mathbb{C}[S_n/G]$. Equivalently, via Pólya theory, $K_{\lambda,G}$ is the coefficient of the Schur function $s_\lambda$ in the cycle-index-derived symmetric function $Z_G(p_1,p_2,\dots)$, where $p_i$ denotes the power-sum symmetric function. The number $K_{\lambda,G}$ is a non-negative integer, and when $G$ is trivial it equals the number $f^\lambda$ of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$.

Let $\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)$ denote the set of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$. Construct, for every finite permutation group $G\le S_n$ and every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, an explicitly defined subset
$$\mathcal{T}_{\lambda,G}\;\subseteq\;\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)$$
(specified by a combinatorial rule depending only on $G$ and $\lambda$) such that
$$|\mathcal{T}_{\lambda,G}|\;=\;K_{\lambda,G}.$$
In other words, give a combinatorial interpretation of $K_{\lambda,G}$ as the cardinality of a naturally defined subset of $\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)$.

Let $G \le S_n$ be a finite permutation group acting on $[n] = \{1,2,\ldots,n\}$, and let $\mu = (\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots)$ be a composition (or partition) of $n$. A $\mu$-coloring of $[n]$ is a function $c \colon [n] \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that $|c^{-1}(i)| = \mu_i$ for every $i$. The group $G$ acts on $\mu$-colorings by $(g \cdot c)(x) = c(g^{-1} x)$; let $\Delta_\mu$ denote the set of $G$-orbits of $\mu$-colorings of $[n]$.

For a partition $\lambda \vdash n$, let $S^\lambda$ denote the irreducible representation of $S_n$ indexed by $\lambda$. Define:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $K_{\lambda,\mu}$ = the Kostka number, i.e. the number of semistandard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$ (equivalently, the multiplicity of $S^\lambda$ in the induced representation $\mathrm{Ind}_{S_\mu}^{S_n} \mathbf{1}$);
  \item $K_{\lambda,G} = \dim (S^\lambda)^G$, the dimension of the $G$-fixed subspace of $S^\lambda$.
\end{itemize}

A classical orbit-counting argument (Pólya enumeration combined with Frobenius reciprocity) yields the identity
$$
|\Delta_\mu| \;=\; \sum_{\lambda \vdash n} K_{\lambda,\mu} \, K_{\lambda,G}. \qquad (*)
$$

Problem: Construct an explicit Robinson–Schensted-type bijection that proves identity $(*)$ combinatorially. That is, exhibit a bijection between the set of $G$-orbits of $\mu$-colorings of $[n]$ and the disjoint union, over partitions $\lambda \vdash n$, of pairs $(T, v)$ where $T$ is a semistandard Young tableau of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$ and $v$ is an element of a chosen basis for $(S^\lambda)^G$ (or any combinatorial set of cardinality $K_{\lambda,G}$), valid uniformly for arbitrary finite permutation groups $G \le S_n$.

A classical orbit-counting argument (Pólya enumeration combined with Frobenius reciprocity) yields the identity
$$
|\Delta_\mu| \;=\; \sum_{\lambda \vdash n} K_{\lambda,\mu} \, K_{\lambda,G}. \qquad (*)
$$

Problem: Construct an explicit Robinson–Schensted-type bijection that proves identity $(*)$ combinatorially. That is, exhibit a bijection between the set of $G$-orbits of $\mu$-colorings of $[n]$ and the disjoint union, over partitions $\lambda \vdash n$, of pairs $(T, v)$ where $T$ is a semistandard Young tableau of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$ and $v$ is an element of a chosen basis for $(S^\lambda)^G$ (or any combinatorial set of cardinality $K_{\lambda,G}$), valid uniformly for arbitrary finite permutation groups $G \le S_n$.

Setup. A catalytic Turing machine has, in addition to its input tape and an ordinary work tape of size s, a separate "catalytic" work tape of size c that is initialized with an arbitrary string τ ∈ {0,1}^c. The machine may read and write on the catalytic tape during computation, but at the end of computation the catalytic tape must be returned to its initial content τ, for every choice of τ. The class CSPACE(s, c) is defined as the set of all functions f computable in this model with ordinary work space at most s and catalytic space at most c. Let SPACE(s) denote the usual deterministic space-s class.

Problem. Exhibit any function f together with a parameter s = s(n) such that:
(i) the best known (or known optimal) algorithm for f in the ordinary model uses work space Θ(s); and
(ii) f ∈ CSPACE(s', c) where s' = o(s) (i.e., s' ≪ s, the ordinary work tape is asymptotically much smaller than s) and c = Θ(s) (i.e., the catalytic tape size is comparable to the original space bound).

In words: find any computational task whose ordinary-space algorithm can be converted into one in which almost all of the memory used is restorable catalytic memory, with only a much smaller residual ordinary work tape. Alternatively, prove no such function exists.

Let $M$ be a deterministic Turing machine equipped with three tapes: a read-only input tape, a read-write work tape, and a read-write auxiliary tape called the catalytic tape. The catalytic tape is initialized with an arbitrary string $\tau \in \{0,1\}^{s_c(n)}$ (the "catalyst"), and $M$ may read and write its cells freely during the computation, but is required to restore the catalytic tape to its initial content $\tau$ upon halting, for every input $x$ of length $n$ and every choice of $\tau$. We say $M$ uses work space $s_w(n)$ and catalytic space $s_c(n)$ if on every input of length $n$ and every initial catalyst, $M$ uses at most $s_w(n)$ cells of the work tape and the catalytic tape has length $s_c(n)$. The class $\mathrm{CSPACE}(s_w(n), s_c(n))$ consists of all languages decided by such machines with work space $O(s_w(n))$ and catalytic space $O(s_c(n))$, with the correctness and restoration conditions holding for every catalyst $\tau$. Define
$$\mathrm{CL} \;=\; \mathrm{CSPACE}\bigl(O(\log n),\; n^{O(1)}\bigr).$$
Let $\mathrm{P}$ denote the class of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in time $n^{O(1)}$.

Question: Is $\mathrm{CL} \subseteq \mathrm{P}$? Equivalently, can every catalytic logspace computation (using polynomial-length catalytic tape) be simulated by some deterministic algorithm running in polynomial time?

Let L denote the class of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using O(log n) work space, and let P denote the class of languages decidable in deterministic polynomial time. Catalytic logspace, denoted CL, is the class of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing machine equipped with: (i) a read-only input tape, (ii) a standard work tape of size O(log n), and (iii) an auxiliary "catalytic" tape of size 2^{O(log n)} = poly(n) that is initialized with an arbitrary string and must be restored to its exact initial contents by the end of the computation; the machine must accept/reject correctly for every initial content of the catalytic tape.

Prove the following conditional containment: if L ⊊ P (i.e., logspace is a strict subclass of polynomial time), then CL ⊆ P.

Recall the following complexity classes.

- P is the class of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing machine running in time polynomial in the input length.
- ZPP (zero-error probabilistic polynomial time) is the class of languages decided by a probabilistic Turing machine that always outputs the correct answer and whose expected running time is polynomial in the input length.
- CL (catalytic logspace) is the class of languages decided by deterministic Turing machines equipped with: (i) a read-only input tape, (ii) a work tape of size O(log n), and (iii) an auxiliary "catalytic" tape of size 2^{O(log n)} = poly(n) that is initialized with an arbitrary string and must be restored to its original content at the end of every computation, with the machine required to halt and output the correct answer on every input regardless of the initial content of the catalytic tape.

Establish a formal connection of the following form: prove that the containment CL ⊆ P would imply strong evidence that ZPP ⊆ P. More precisely, exhibit a theorem showing that if CL ⊆ P holds, then either ZPP = P, or ZPP ⊆ P follows under widely believed hypotheses, or some standard derandomization-style consequence (such as the existence of pseudorandom generators sufficient to derandomize ZPP) follows from CL ⊆ P.

A word parking function of length $n$ is a sequence $(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n)$ of positive integers together with a labelling of an underlying Dyck path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$, defined as follows. Let $D$ be a Dyck path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ consisting of $n$ north steps $N_1,\dots,N_n$ (read from bottom to top) and $n$ east steps, staying weakly above the diagonal $y=x$. A word parking function $P=(D,w)$ assigns to each north step $N_i$ a positive-integer label $w_i$ such that, if two north steps $N_i$ and $N_{i+1}$ lie in the same column, then $w_i<w_{i+1}$.

Define two statistics on word parking functions:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathrm{area}(P)$ is the number of complete lattice squares strictly between the path $D$ and the diagonal $y=x$.
\item $\mathrm{dinv}(P)$ is the number of pairs $(i,j)$ with $i<j$ such that either
\begin{itemize}
\item $a_i=a_j$ and $w_i<w_j$, or
\item $a_i=a_j+1$ and $w_i>w_j$,
\end{itemize}
where $a_i$ denotes the number of complete squares in row $i$ between $D$ and the diagonal.
\end{itemize}

For a fixed composition (or weight) of the labels, the Shuffle Theorem expresses a certain symmetric-function evaluation as
$$\sum_{P} q^{\mathrm{dinv}(P)}\, t^{\mathrm{area}(P)}\, x^{w(P)},$$
where the sum ranges over all word parking functions of length $n$. This expression is known to be symmetric in $q$ and $t$.

Problem. Construct an explicit bijection $\varphi$ on the set of word parking functions of length $n$ (preserving the multiset of labels $w$) such that
$$\mathrm{area}(\varphi(P)) = \mathrm{dinv}(P) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{dinv}(\varphi(P)) = \mathrm{area}(P).$$
Equivalently, give a combinatorial proof, via such a bijection, of the $(q,t)$-symmetry of the above summation.

A word parking function of length $n$ is a sequence $(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n)$ of positive integers together with a labelling of an underlying Dyck path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$, defined as follows. Let $D$ be a Dyck path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ consisting of $n$ north steps $N_1,\dots,N_n$ (read from bottom to top) and $n$ east steps, staying weakly above the diagonal $y=x$. A word parking function $P=(D,w)$ assigns to each north step $N_i$ a positive-integer label $w_i$ such that, if two north steps $N_i$ and $N_{i+1}$ lie in the same column, then $w_i<w_{i+1}$.

Define two statistics on word parking functions:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathrm{area}(P)$ is the number of complete lattice squares strictly between the path $D$ and the diagonal $y=x$.
\item $\mathrm{dinv}(P)$ is the number of pairs $(i,j)$ with $i<j$ such that either
\begin{itemize}
\item $a_i=a_j$ and $w_i<w_j$, or
\item $a_i=a_j+1$ and $w_i>w_j$,
\end{itemize}
where $a_i$ denotes the number of complete squares in row $i$ between $D$ and the diagonal.
\end{itemize}

For a fixed composition (or weight) of the labels, the Shuffle Theorem expresses a certain symmetric-function evaluation as
$$\sum_{P} q^{\mathrm{dinv}(P)}\, t^{\mathrm{area}(P)}\, x^{w(P)},$$
where the sum ranges over all word parking functions of length $n$. This expression is known to be symmetric in $q$ and $t$.

Problem. Construct an explicit bijection $\varphi$ on the set of word parking functions of length $n$ (preserving the multiset of labels $w$) such that
$$\mathrm{area}(\varphi(P)) = \mathrm{dinv}(P) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{dinv}(\varphi(P)) = \mathrm{area}(P).$$
Equivalently, give a combinatorial proof, via such a bijection, of the $(q,t)$-symmetry of the above summation.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of finding a bijection on (word) parking functions that swaps area and dinv, thereby giving a combinatorial proof of the q,t-symmetry in the Shuffle Theorem, is widely regarded as a long-standing open problem. Partial results exist, including the zeta map for the t=1 case (equidistribution of area and dinv) and bijections proving q,t-symmetry for the q,t-Catalan numbers in restricted cases (Lee-Li-Loehr for k≤9), as well as recent area-depth symmetric variants, but no full bijective proof of q,t-symmetry for word parking functions is known.

Define catalytic logspace, denoted CL, as the class of languages decided by deterministic Turing machines equipped with: (i) a read-only input tape, (ii) a work tape of size O(log n), and (iii) an auxiliary "catalytic" tape of size polynomial in n that may be initialized with an arbitrary string and may be modified during the computation, provided that at the end of the computation its contents are restored to the original initialization (the machine must operate correctly for every initialization of the catalytic tape). Define NC^2 as the class of languages decided by uniform families of Boolean circuits over fan-in 2 AND/OR/NOT gates having polynomial size and O(log^2 n) depth.

Question: Show that NC^2 ⊆ CL. More generally, show that every language decided by a uniform family of polynomial-size Boolean circuits of depth ω(log n) is contained in CL.

Let $\mu$ be a partition of $n$, and let $\mu^{*}$ denote its conjugate (transpose) partition. For a filling $\sigma : \mu \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ of the cells of the Young diagram of $\mu$ with positive integers, define the statistics $\mathrm{inv}(\sigma)$ and $\mathrm{maj}(\sigma)$ as in Haglund–Haiman–Loehr's combinatorial formula for the modified Macdonald polynomials, so that
$$\widetilde{H}_{\mu}(X; q, t) \;=\; \sum_{\sigma : \mu \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}} q^{\mathrm{inv}(\sigma)}\, t^{\mathrm{maj}(\sigma)}\, x^{\sigma} \qquad (**)$$
where $x^{\sigma} = \prod_{c \in \mu} x_{\sigma(c)}$. It is known (via symmetric function identities for $\widetilde{H}_{\mu}$) that
$$\widetilde{H}_{\mu}(X; q, t) \;=\; \widetilde{H}_{\mu^{*}}(X; t, q).$$
Provide a combinatorial proof of this conjugate $(q,t)$-symmetry directly from the right-hand side of $(**)$: exhibit an explicit bijection (or equivalent combinatorial mechanism) between fillings of $\mu$ and fillings of $\mu^{*}$ that preserves the content (multiset of entries) and interchanges the statistics $\mathrm{inv}$ and $\mathrm{maj}$, thereby explaining why conjugating the partition swaps these two statistics.

A register program is a straight-line/recursive program that manipulates values stored in a fixed collection of registers, where each register holds an element of some (possibly noncommutative) algebraic structure (e.g., elements of an associative ring or monoid, or matrices). The program may perform multiplications and assignments between registers and may recursively invoke itself on inputs. The "space" used by a computation is the total number of registers (counted with the depth of recursion) needed during execution, and a "recursive call to x" is an invocation of the program on the input x.

Problem. Working in the noncommutative setting (so the input x belongs to a noncommutative monoid/ring, and at no point may one assume xy = yx), design a register program that on input x and a positive integer k computes the power x^k, subject to the following two requirements simultaneously:
(1) the program uses only linear space in k (i.e., O(k) registers / O(k) total working space), and
(2) the program makes only a constant number (independent of k) of recursive calls on the argument x.

Either exhibit such a register program or prove that no such program exists.

The problem is a broad structural question that subsumes many specific conjectures (e.g., diagonal coinvariants for $k=2, l=0$, the Delta Conjecture, the fermionic/theta coinvariant conjectures, and superspace coinvariants for $k=l=1$). However, a complete structural description for general $W$, $k$, $l$ remains open.

Define the following complexity classes.

(1) NC^1 is the class of languages decidable by a uniform family of Boolean circuits of fan-in 2, polynomial size, and depth O(log n).

(2) BPNC^1 is the randomized version of NC^1 with two-sided bounded error and read-multiple randomness: a language L is in BPNC^1 if there is a uniform family of polynomial-size, O(log n)-depth fan-in 2 Boolean circuits {C_n(x, r)} such that the random bits r (of length poly(n)) can be read multiple times by the circuit gates, and for every input x of length n,
 - if x ∈ L, then Pr_r[C_n(x, r) = 1] ≥ 2/3,
 - if x ∉ L, then Pr_r[C_n(x, r) = 1] ≤ 1/3.

(3) Catalytic logspace CL is the class of languages decided by Turing machines equipped with an O(log n)-size read/write work tape and an additional poly(n)-size catalytic tape that is initialized with an arbitrary (adversarial) string w; the machine may read and write the catalytic tape during computation, but must restore it exactly to w upon halting. The machine must decide the language correctly for every initial content w of the catalytic tape.

Question: Prove or disprove that BPNC^1 ⊆ CL.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected graph with $V=\{1,\dots,n+1\}$ and edges $E=\{e_1,\dots,e_m\}$. For each subset $I\subseteq V$, let $d_I$ denote the number of edges of $G$ with exactly one endpoint in $I$ (the size of the cut determined by $I$). Working over a field of characteristic $0$, consider the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb{R}[x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}]$ and define the linear forms $\ell_I=\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ for $I\subseteq V$.

Define two graded quotient algebras:
- The central zonotopal algebra $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G):=R/J^{(0)}_G$, where $J^{(0)}_G$ is the ideal generated by $\ell_I^{d_I}$ for all $\emptyset\neq I\subsetneq V$ (equivalently, defined via the standard kernel/Macaulay-inverse-system construction associated with the graphical matroid).
- The internal zonotopal algebra $\mathcal{C}^{(-1)}(G):=R/J^{(-1)}_G$, where $J^{(-1)}_G$ is generated by $\ell_I^{d_I-1}$ for all $\emptyset\neq I\subsetneq V$.

A bridge of $G$ is an edge whose removal disconnects $G$. The bridge-free matroid of $G$ is the matroid on the non-bridge edges obtained from the graphical matroid $M(G)$ by deleting all bridges.

Problem. Classify, up to graded $\mathbb{R}$-algebra isomorphism, the central zonotopal algebras $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G)$ and the internal zonotopal algebras $\mathcal{C}^{(-1)}(G)$ as $G$ ranges over connected graphs. In particular, prove or disprove the following conjecture: for connected graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$, the central zonotopal algebras $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G_1)$ and $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}(G_2)$ are isomorphic as graded algebras if and only if the bridge-free matroids of $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic.

A catalytic branching program on $n$ Boolean input variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is a finite directed acyclic multigraph in which:
- each non-sink node is labeled by an input variable $x_i$ and has exactly two outgoing edges, labeled $0$ and $1$;
- there is a distinguished set $S$ of start nodes;
- each sink (end node) carries a label of the form $(b,\tau)$ with $b\in\{0,1\}$ and $\tau\in S$.

On input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, starting from a node $v$ the program follows, at each non-sink node labeled $x_i$, the outgoing edge labeled $x_i$ until a sink is reached; denote this sink by $\mathrm{end}(v,x)$.

The program is said to compute a Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ catalytically if for every start node $\tau\in S$ and every input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$,
$$\mathrm{end}(\tau,x) = (f(x),\tau).$$
The size of the program is its total number of nodes.

Question: Does every Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ admit a catalytic branching program computing it with $|S|=2^{O(n)}$ start nodes and total size $2^{O(n)}\cdot O(n)$?

representations.normalized:
A catalytic Turing machine is a deterministic Turing machine equipped with three tapes: a read-only input tape, a read/write work tape, and a read/write auxiliary "catalytic" tape. The catalytic tape is initialized with an arbitrary string τ (the catalyst); the machine may freely read and overwrite the catalytic tape during its computation, but at the end of every computation, on every input and for every initial catalyst τ, the catalytic tape must be restored to exactly its initial content τ. The machine's output on input x must be the same for every initial catalyst τ.

Define catalytic logspace CL as the class of languages decidable by a catalytic Turing machine that uses O(log n) cells on the work tape and at most n^c cells on the catalytic tape, for some constant c, on inputs of length n, in time polynomial in n.

For a complexity class C, the advice class C/poly is the class of languages L such that there exists a sequence of advice strings {α_n}_{n≥0} with |α_n| ≤ p(n) for some polynomial p, and a language L' ∈ C, with x ∈ L if and only if ⟨x, α_{|x|}⟩ ∈ L'.

Problem:
(a) Determine the computational power of CL/poly, i.e., characterize which languages lie in CL/poly, and locate this class relative to standard complexity classes (such as L/poly, NL/poly, P/poly, ZPP, etc.).
(b) Give a natural syntactic characterization of CL/poly (for example, in terms of a uniform machine model, circuit family, or algebraic computation model) that does not refer explicitly to non-uniform advice strings.

representations.normalized:
A quiver is a finite directed multigraph with no loops and no 2-cycles. Given a quiver $Q$, a covering pair is a pair of vertices $(u,v)$ such that there is at least one arrow from $u$ to $v$, the neighborhoods around $u$ and $v$ satisfy certain combinatorial conditions making $\{u,v\}$ "isolating," and removing $u$ and $v$ (together with any arrows incident to them) produces a quiver that, in turn, has its own covering pair or is empty. The class $\mathcal{B}$ of Banff quivers is the smallest class of quivers containing the empty quiver and closed under the following operation: a quiver $Q$ belongs to $\mathcal{B}$ if it has a covering pair $(u,v)$ such that the quiver obtained from $Q$ by deleting $u$ and $v$ belongs to $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $\mathcal{B}'$ denote the subclass of $\mathcal{B}$ defined analogously, but where at each step the covering pair $(u,v)$ used to certify membership is required to have at least one of $u,v$ being a source (a vertex with no incoming arrows) or a sink (a vertex with no outgoing arrows) of the current quiver.

Either exhibit a quiver belonging to $\mathcal{B} \setminus \mathcal{B}'$, or prove that no such quiver exists, i.e., $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}'$.

Background and definitions.

A catalytic Turing machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine equipped with three tapes: a read-only input tape, a work tape, and an additional catalytic tape. On input x of length n, the work tape has O(log n) cells and the catalytic tape has poly(n) cells. The catalytic tape is initialized with an arbitrary string w of length poly(n), and the machine must produce the correct output for every choice of initial content w, with the additional requirement that, upon halting, the catalytic tape contents are exactly equal to the initial w. The class CL (catalytic logspace) consists of all languages decided by such machines.

A randomized catalytic logspace machine is defined analogously but is additionally given access to a one-way random tape. The class CBPL consists of all languages L for which there exists a randomized catalytic logspace machine M such that for every input x and every initialization w of the catalytic tape:
 (i) Pr[M(x,w) accepts] ≥ 2/3 if x ∈ L, and Pr[M(x,w) accepts] ≤ 1/3 if x ∉ L,
 (ii) with probability 1 the catalytic tape is restored to its initial content w upon halting.

The class BPL is the standard bounded-error randomized logspace class (no catalytic tape), and the inclusion BPL ⊆ CL is known.

Problem. Prove that CBPL ⊆ CL. That is, show that every language decided by a bounded-error randomized catalytic logspace machine can also be decided by a deterministic catalytic logspace machine.

representations.normalized:
Let $B_n$ denote the hyperoctahedral group (the Weyl group of type $B_n$), realized as the group of signed permutations on $\{\pm 1, \pm 2, \dots, \pm n\}$, equipped with its Bruhat order. Embed $B_n$ into the symmetric group $S_{2n}$ by sending a signed permutation to the unique permutation matrix of size $2n \times 2n$ that is invariant under the half-turn (i.e., invariant under $180^\circ$ rotation: $M_{i,j} = M_{2n+1-i,\, 2n+1-j}$). This gives an order-preserving embedding of $B_n$ into $(S_{2n}, \leq_{\mathrm{Bruhat}})$, and hence into the lattice $\mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$ of $2n \times 2n$ alternating sign matrices ordered by entry-wise comparison of their corner-sum (rank) matrices.

An alternating sign matrix (ASM) is a square matrix with entries in $\{0, 1, -1\}$ such that, in every row and every column, the nonzero entries alternate in sign and sum to $1$. The lattice $\mathrm{ASM}_N$ is the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of $(S_N, \leq_{\mathrm{Bruhat}})$, and is a distributive lattice under the order induced by corner sums. A matrix $M \in \mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$ is called half-turn symmetric (HTSASM) if $M_{i,j} = M_{2n+1-i,\, 2n+1-j}$ for all $i, j$.

Recall that the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of a poset $P$ is the smallest complete lattice containing $P$ as a sub-order; concretely it is realized as the set of "cuts" of $P$.

Problem. Describe the Dedekind–MacNeille completion of the Bruhat order on $B_n$ as an explicit subset of $\mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$. Equivalently, give an exact combinatorial characterization of which half-turn-symmetric alternating sign matrices in $\mathrm{ASM}_{2n}$ arise as elements of this completion. (Note: not every HTSASM arises; for $n=3$ the completion has cardinality $140$ while the number of HTSASMs is $132$, so a strictly intermediate subclass of HTSASMs must be identified.)

Let a catalytic Turing machine be a deterministic machine with three tapes: a read-only input tape, a read/write work tape of length O(log n), and a read/write catalytic tape of length s(n) = n^{O(1)}. The catalytic tape is initialized with an arbitrary string τ ∈ {0,1}^{s(n)} (the "auxiliary content"), and the machine is required, on every input x and every initial catalytic content τ, to halt with the catalytic tape restored exactly to τ. The class CL (catalytic logspace) consists of all languages decided by such machines.

For a function e: ℕ → ℕ, define the lossy variant LCL[e] in the same way except that, upon halting, the catalytic tape is required to agree with τ in all but at most e(n) positions (for every input x and every τ). Define the expected-lossy variant E-LCL[e] by requiring instead that, when τ is drawn uniformly at random from {0,1}^{s(n)} (and x is arbitrary), the expected number of positions in which the final catalytic tape differs from τ is at most e(n).

Prove or disprove each of the following:

(a) For every function e(n) = ω(1), LCL[e] = CL.

(b) There exists a constant C such that E-LCL[C] = CL, i.e., allowing an expected O(1) number of restoration errors (over a uniformly random initial catalytic tape) does not increase the class beyond CL.

Background and definitions. A catalytic Turing machine is a space-bounded Turing machine equipped with three tapes: a read-only input tape, a work tape of size s(n) which is initially blank, and a catalytic (auxiliary) tape of size c(n) which is initialized with an arbitrary string τ. The machine may read and write freely on the catalytic tape during the computation, but is required to restore the catalytic tape to its original content τ by the end of every computation, for every initial τ. The class CSPACE[s(n), c(n)] consists of languages decided by such deterministic machines; the catalytic logspace class CL is defined by s(n) = O(log n) and c(n) = poly(n). A nondeterministic catalytic Turing machine is defined analogously, but the transition relation is nondeterministic; the restoration condition requires that on every computation path (or, in the standard definition, on every accepting path) the catalytic tape is returned to its initial content τ. The corresponding nondeterministic class is denoted NCL.

Problem. Exhibit a "genuinely nontrivial" use of nondeterminism in conjunction with catalytic computation. More precisely, one of the following:

(a) Give a computational task, a complexity-theoretic separation, or a structural result whose proof uses a nondeterministic catalytic algorithm in an essential way — i.e., a way that does not reduce immediately to either a standard deterministic catalytic simulation or to ordinary nondeterministic space, and that goes beyond the use of nondeterminism implicit in the definition of NCL.

(b) Equivalently, design a nondeterministic catalytic logspace algorithm for some language L such that the algorithm crucially exploits both the catalytic tape and the nondeterministic branching (for instance, by solving a problem not known to lie in CL via a guessing-and-verification strategy that maintains the catalyst), and prove its correctness and the catalyst-restoration property.

The task is to produce such an application, or to prove that no such nontrivial combination is possible (e.g., by showing NCL = CL via a simulation that renders nondeterminism inessential in this setting).

Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Its complex irreducible representations are indexed by partitions $\lambda \vdash n$, and its conjugacy classes are indexed by partitions $\mu \vdash n$ (cycle types). The character table of $S_n$ is the square matrix whose entry in row $\lambda$ and column $\mu$ is the value $\chi^\lambda(\mu)$ of the irreducible character $\chi^\lambda$ on the conjugacy class of cycle type $\mu$. The row indexed by the partition $(1^n)$ corresponds to the sign representation, whose character value on a permutation of cycle type $\mu$ equals $(-1)^{n - \ell(\mu)}$, where $\ell(\mu)$ is the number of parts of $\mu$.

For each partition $\lambda \vdash n$, let $N(\lambda) = \#\{\mu \vdash n : \chi^\lambda(\mu) < 0\}$ denote the number of conjugacy classes on which the irreducible character $\chi^\lambda$ takes a strictly negative value.

Prove that for all sufficiently large $n$, the maximum of $N(\lambda)$ over all partitions $\lambda \vdash n$ is attained by, and only by, the partition $(1^n)$ corresponding to the sign representation.

representations.normalized:
A catalytic Turing machine is a multitape Turing machine equipped with three tapes: a read-only input tape, a read/write work tape, and a read/write catalytic (auxiliary) tape. At the start of the computation, the catalytic tape is initialized with an arbitrary string w ∈ {0,1}^c (the "catalytic content"). During the computation the machine may freely modify both the work tape and the catalytic tape, but it is required that, on every accepting and rejecting computation path and for every initial content w of the catalytic tape, the catalytic tape returns to its original content w at the end of the computation. The work tape uses space at most s = s(n) and the catalytic tape uses space at most c = c(n), where n is the length of the input.

A deterministic catalytic computation must satisfy the above restoration condition on its unique computation path. A nondeterministic catalytic computation is allowed to have a nondeterministic transition function; it accepts an input x if there exists at least one computation path that accepts, and the catalytic-tape restoration condition must hold along every computation path (accepting or rejecting) and for every initial catalytic content.

Define:
- CSPACE(s, c) = the class of languages decided by deterministic catalytic Turing machines using O(s) work space and O(c) catalytic space.
- CNSPACE(s, c) = the class of languages decided by nondeterministic catalytic Turing machines using O(s) work space and O(c) catalytic space.

Problem. Prove or disprove that for all space bounds s = s(n) ≥ log n and c = c(n) ≥ s(n),
    CNSPACE(s, c) ⊆ CSPACE(s^2, c^2).
That is, establish a catalytic analogue of Savitch's theorem showing that every nondeterministic catalytic computation using work space s and catalytic space c can be simulated by a deterministic catalytic computation using work space O(s^2) and catalytic space O(c^2).

\[ T(n) = \begin{cases} 3n+1 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd},\\ n/2 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}. \end{cases} \]

Prove or disprove the following: for every positive integer $a_0$, there exists a finite $n \ge 0$ such that $a_n = 1$. Equivalently, show that no positive integer starting value $a_0$ produces a trajectory $\{a_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ that never attains the value $1$.

The Collatz (3n+1) conjecture is a famous, long-standing open problem. Let $\Delta_{k}$ denote the standard $k$-dimensional simplex (the convex hull of $k+1$ affinely independent points). For positive integers $m,n$, consider the product polytope $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{m}$, and let $\mathcal{T}(n,m)$ denote the set of all triangulations of this polytope (i.e., subdivisions into simplices whose vertices are vertices of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{m}$, fitting together face-to-face and covering the polytope).

A flip is a minimal local modification that transforms one triangulation of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{m}$ into another: it corresponds to a circuit of the point configuration, replacing one of its two triangulations by the other while leaving the rest of the triangulation unchanged. The flip graph $F(n,m)$ has $\mathcal{T}(n,m)$ as its vertex set, with an edge joining two triangulations whenever they differ by a single flip.

Question: For every $n\ge 1$, are the flip graphs $F(n,2)$ (triangulations of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{2}$) and $F(n,3)$ (triangulations of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{3}$) Hamiltonian, i.e., do they admit a Hamiltonian cycle visiting every triangulation exactly once?

The flip graph $F(n,m)$ has $\mathcal{T}(n,m)$ as its vertex set, with an edge joining two triangulations whenever they differ by a single flip.

Question: For every $n\ge 1$, are the flip graphs $F(n,2)$ (triangulations of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{2}$) and $F(n,3)$ (triangulations of $\Delta_{n-1}\times\Delta_{3}$) Hamiltonian, i.e., do they admit a Hamiltonian cycle visiting every triangulation exactly once?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Related work establishes flip-connectivity for triangulations of Δ_{n-1} × Δ_3 (and disconnectedness for Δ_{n-1} × Δ_k with large k), but no result establishing or refuting Hamiltonicity of the flip graphs of Δ_{n-1} × Δ_2 or Δ_{n-1} × Δ_3 was found. The question appears to remain open.

Let n ≥ 4 and consider a convex n-gon whose vertices are labeled 1, 2, …, n around the boundary. A triangulation of the n-gon is a maximal set of non-crossing diagonals, which partitions the polygon into triangles. The associahedron graph G_n has as its vertex set all triangulations of the n-gon; two triangulations are adjacent in G_n if and only if they differ by a single flip, i.e. removing one diagonal shared by two triangles and replacing it by the other diagonal of the resulting quadrilateral.

Now suppose n is odd, n ≥ 7, and color the vertices of the n-gon alternately red and blue around the boundary (so that exactly one pair of adjacent vertices receives the same color). Call a triangulation colorful if no triangle of the triangulation is monochromatic, i.e. every triangle has vertices of both colors. Let H_n be the subgraph of G_n induced by the set of colorful triangulations.

Question: For every odd n ≥ 7, does H_n contain a Hamilton path, or a Hamilton cycle? If such paths/cycles exist, can they be generated by an algorithm whose amortized running time per produced triangulation is bounded by a small (e.g. constant or polylogarithmic) function of n?

Background. In catalytic computation one considers a Turing machine equipped with two work tapes: a small "clean" work tape of size s(n), initially blank, and an additional "auxiliary" (catalytic) tape of size c(n), initialized with an arbitrary (worst-case) string τ. The machine may freely read and write the catalytic tape during its computation, but at the end of the computation the catalytic tape must again contain exactly the initial string τ, for every choice of τ. The class CSPACE(s(n), c(n)) consists of languages decided by such machines, and CL = CSPACE(O(log n), 2^{O(log n)}). It is known that uniform TC^1 ⊆ CL, even though no direct simulation of CL by small uniform circuits is known.

Problem. Exhibit an explicit family of Boolean circuits C = {C_n} computing some specific function f : {0,1}^* → {0,1} such that:
(a) the construction of C_n is obtained by translating a catalytic-computation or space-reuse algorithm (i.e., one that crucially exploits being able to reuse cells that hold arbitrary "junk" data and to restore them) into the circuit model; and
(b) the resulting circuit family achieves a size bound s(n) or depth bound d(n) for f that is strictly better than any known bound for f obtained by direct circuit-model techniques (without going through space reuse or catalytic computing).

In other words, produce a concrete example where catalytic / space-reuse ideas yield a new upper bound on circuit size or depth that is not currently achievable by purely circuit-based methods.

Define the following complexity classes.

(1) TC^1: the class of Boolean languages decided by a non-uniform family of Boolean circuits {C_n} of polynomial size and O(log n) depth, with gates of unbounded fan-in computing AND, OR, NOT, and MAJORITY (threshold) functions.

(2) VP (Valiant's class P): the class of families of multivariate polynomials (f_n) over a field (say ℚ, or any fixed field) such that f_n has polynomially bounded degree in n and is computed by an arithmetic circuit of polynomial size in n using +, ×, and field constants, with inputs being variables or constants.

A Boolean class C is said to be contained in VP if there is a polynomial-size projection / appropriate reduction sending each language L ∈ C to a polynomial family in VP whose coefficients encode membership in L (formally: for every language L ∈ TC^1 there exists a polynomial family (f_n) ∈ VP and a polynomial-time–computable projection from inputs x of length n to monomials/variable settings such that f_n evaluated at this setting equals 1 if x ∈ L and 0 otherwise).

Problem: Prove or disprove that TC^1 ⊆ VP.

Definitions and setup.

(a) Let P be a finite point set in general position in the plane. A triangulation of P is a maximal planar straight-line graph on P. The flip graph F(P) has the triangulations of P as vertices, with two triangulations joined by an edge whenever they differ in exactly one diagonal (i.e., one is obtained from the other by replacing a diagonal e shared by two triangles forming a convex quadrilateral with the other diagonal of that quadrilateral).

(b) Let P be a simple polygon. A triangulation of P is a maximal set of non-crossing diagonals of P together with the boundary edges. The flip graph F(P) is defined analogously, with edges given by flips of a single diagonal between two triangulations.

(c) Let G = (V,E) be a connected graph on n vertices. An elimination tree of G is a rooted tree T on V defined recursively: choose a root r ∈ V; then for each connected component C of G − r, recursively form an elimination tree of G[C] and attach its root as a child of r. Two elimination trees of G are related by a rotation (tree rotation) if one is obtained from the other by a single local "edge rotation" operation on adjacent vertices, generalizing the rotation operation on binary search trees (the case G = Pn). The rotation graph R(G) has elimination trees of G as vertices and rotation moves as edges.

Problem. Determine, as a function of natural parameters of the underlying object (e.g., the number of points |P|, the size and structure of the polygon P, or the size and structural type of the graph G, including special structured families such as grids and trees), how large the chromatic number χ can be for:

1. the flip graph F(P) of triangulations of a finite planar point set P;
2. the flip graph F(P) of triangulations of a simple polygon P;
3. the rotation graph R(G) of elimination trees of a graph G.

Provide upper and lower bounds, in particular for the cases when G is a path Pn (recovering rotations of binary search trees), a grid graph, or a tree.

The chromatic number of flip graphs is an active research topic. Fabila-Monroy et al. obtained bounds for several flip graphs (matchings, triangulations of convex polygons, non-crossing Hamiltonian paths, triangles of convex point sets), but the general questions for arbitrary point sets, simple polygons, and rotation graphs of elimination trees (beyond binary search trees / G = Pn, and structured families like grids and trees) remain open with no tight answers in the literature.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be an undirected graph with edge capacities $c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, together with a set of $k$ source–sink pairs $(s_1,t_1),\dots,(s_k,t_k)\in V\times V$. For a rate vector $(r_1,\dots,r_k)\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^k$, say that the rate vector is achievable by multicommodity flow if there exist flows $f_i$ from $s_i$ to $t_i$ of value $r_i$ such that for every edge $e\in E$, $\sum_{i=1}^k |f_i(e)|\le c(e)$ (where each undirected edge of capacity $c(e)$ may carry flow in either direction with total absolute flow at most $c(e)$). Say that the rate vector is achievable by network coding if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a (block) coding scheme that uses each edge $e$ at average rate at most $c(e)$ (with edges usable in either direction subject to a total capacity constraint) and allows each sink $t_i$ to recover the message of source $s_i$ at rate at least $r_i-\varepsilon$ with vanishing error probability.

The undirected multiple-unicast network coding conjecture asserts that for every such instance, every rate vector achievable by network coding is also achievable by multicommodity flow; equivalently, network coding offers no throughput advantage over multicommodity flow in undirected networks.

Question: Is this conjecture true or false?

The undirected multiple-unicast network coding conjecture of Li and Li (2004) remains an open problem. Partial progress includes results showing that even an arbitrarily small coding advantage in any undirected instance can be amplified to a near-maximal gap (Braverman–Garg–Schvartzman 2016/17), and that multicommodity flow achieves capacity in certain infinite families of graphs. As of 2025, including recent work on undirected multicast network coding gaps via locally decodable codes, the general conjecture is still unresolved.

A cycle-plus-triangles graph is a 4-regular graph on 3n vertices obtained as the edge-disjoint union of a Hamiltonian cycle C of length 3n and a set of n pairwise vertex-disjoint triangles whose vertex set is the same 3n vertices. It is known (non-constructively, via the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz) that every such graph has an independent set of size n, and in fact is n-colorable. A simple greedy/algorithmic argument shows that one can efficiently (in polynomial time) find an independent set of size at least 3n/5 in every cycle-plus-triangles graph.

Determine the largest constant α ∈ [3/5, 1] for which there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any cycle-plus-triangles graph on 3n vertices (with its Hamiltonian cycle and triangle decomposition as input), outputs an independent set of size at least αn. In particular, design an efficient algorithm achieving α strictly larger than 3/5, and ideally as close to 1 as possible.

Let $G = (V, E)$ be a finite directed acyclic graph with edge capacities, together with a set of $k$ source–sink pairs $(s_1, t_1), \ldots, (s_k, t_k)$. Each source $s_i$ holds an independent message $X_i$ taking values in a finite alphabet (identified with a vector space over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$), and the goal is for sink $t_i$ to recover $X_i$ exactly. A network code assigns to every edge $e = (u,v)$ a function whose output (sent along $e$) is computed from the symbols received by $u$ on its incoming edges (and, if $u = s_i$, from $X_i$); each sink $t_j$ applies a decoding function to its incoming symbols. The routing rate of an instance is the maximum throughput achievable when every internal node may only forward (copy) symbols received on incoming edges, while the network coding rate is the maximum throughput achievable when arbitrary functions are allowed at internal nodes.

The network coding conjecture asserts that for every multiple-unicast instance on a directed acyclic graph, the network coding rate equals the routing rate (equivalently, coding offers no throughput advantage over routing for multiple unicast).

A network code is called linear if for every edge $e = (u,v)$, the symbol transmitted on $e$ is an $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear transformation of the vector of symbols available at $u$ (its incoming symbols, together with its source message if $u$ is a source), and every sink's decoder is also $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear.

Problem: Either prove or disprove the network coding conjecture under the restriction that every node is allowed to send only linear transformations of its incoming messages. That is, decide whether, for every multiple-unicast instance, the maximum rate achievable by a linear network code equals the routing rate.

Consider the following two-party communication model for the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP). An instance consists of n cities together with a distance function d : [n] × [n] → ℝ≥0 (not necessarily symmetric, not necessarily satisfying the triangle inequality). Alice receives the full instance and is computationally unbounded: in particular she can compute an optimal Hamiltonian tour. She then sends a single message (the "advice") to Bob, who also receives the same instance but is restricted to polynomial-time computation. Upon reading Alice's message together with the instance, Bob must output an optimal TSP tour (a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum total length).

It is known that an advice length of n·log₂ n bits suffices (Alice can perturb distances so that an optimal tour becomes recoverable by Bob via a polynomial-time minimum-weight matching computation, encoding the perturbation in n·log₂ n bits).

(a) Does there exist a protocol in which Alice's advice uses at most 0.4999·n·log₂ n bits while Bob still recovers an optimal tour in polynomial time?

(b) More ambitiously, does there exist such a protocol with advice length o(n log n) bits?

(c) Do stronger upper bounds on the required advice length hold when the distance function d is restricted to be metric (symmetric and satisfying the triangle inequality), or Euclidean (cities are points in ℝ² with Euclidean distances)?

Background. In the model of catalytic computation, a Turing machine is equipped with two work tapes: a clean work tape of small size s(n), and a much larger auxiliary tape of size c(n) (the catalytic tape) which is initialized with an arbitrary string τ ∈ {0,1}^{c(n)}. The machine may read and write the catalytic tape freely during its computation, but on every input x and every initial content τ, when the computation halts the catalytic tape must be restored to its original content τ. The class CSPACE(s,c) consists of languages decidable in this model, and catalytic logspace CL = CSPACE(O(log n), 2^{O(log n)}). The catalytic-memory model is known to allow surprising algorithmic gains over ordinary space-bounded computation when computing functions.

A data structure in this context would be a representation D(S) of a set or object S, stored on the catalytic tape, that supports a collection of query operations (and possibly updates), where each operation is carried out by a catalytic procedure: it reads from D(S), uses a small clean workspace, may temporarily modify the catalytic tape (including the region holding D(S)), but at the end of the operation must leave the catalytic tape exactly as it was at the start. Standard data-structure parameters (space, query time, update time, preprocessing) are measured with respect to this restoration requirement.

Problem. Formulate a meaningful and non-trivial notion of a "catalytic data structure" in the sense above, and determine whether there exists any data-structuring task — for example dictionary lookup, predecessor search, dynamic connectivity, range queries, or any other natural problem — for which storing the data structure in catalytic memory (subject to the restoration constraint) yields a genuine quantitative advantage in space and/or operation time compared to what is achievable by ordinary (non-catalytic) data structures of comparable resources. Either exhibit such a problem together with a catalytic data structure achieving a provable improvement, or prove that no such advantage is possible under a suitable model.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a complete graph on $n$ vertices equipped with edge weights $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. A tour is a Hamiltonian cycle in $G$, and its cost is the sum of the weights of its edges. For an integer $k\ge 2$, the k-Opt neighborhood of a tour $\tau$ consists of all tours $\tau'$ that can be obtained from $\tau$ by removing some $k$ edges of $\tau$ and reconnecting the resulting fragments into a single Hamiltonian cycle by adding $k$ new edges (so $\tau'$ differs from $\tau$ in at most $k$ edges). The k-Opt local-search algorithm starts from an initial tour and, at each step, replaces the current tour by a strictly cheaper tour in its k-Opt neighborhood, terminating at a k-Opt local optimum. A pivot rule is a (deterministic) procedure that, given the current tour, selects which improving k-Opt move to perform whenever such a move exists.

Question: For each $k\in\{2,3,4\}$, does there exist a pivot rule for the k-Opt algorithm such that, for every edge-weighted complete graph $G$ and every initial tour $\tau$, the number of improving k-Opt steps performed before termination is bounded by a polynomial in $n$? The case $k=2$ is of particular interest when the edge weights come from Euclidean distances between points in the plane.

Background. Define catalytic logspace, denoted CL, as the class of decision problems decidable by a deterministic Turing machine that has (i) a read-only input tape of length n, (ii) a read/write work tape of length O(log n), and (iii) a read/write auxiliary "catalytic" tape of length 2^{O(log n)} = poly(n) which is initialized to an arbitrary string and is required to be restored to its exact initial contents at the end of every computation, regardless of the input. The machine must accept or reject correctly for every input on every possible initial contents of the catalytic tape.

Let P denote deterministic polynomial time, and let NC denote the class of problems solvable by uniform Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth (with fan-in 2 gates). It is known that L ⊆ CL ⊆ ZPP, and CL contains uniform TC^1, but no nontrivial upper bound of CL inside P is known.

Problem. Assuming some believable cryptographic hardness assumption (for example, the existence of one-way functions, hardness of factoring, or hardness of discrete logarithm), prove that CL ⊆ C for some plausible proper subclass C of P. In particular, determine whether one can establish CL ⊆ NC under such a cryptographic assumption.

Background. The class PLS (Polynomial Local Search) consists of local search problems whose instances specify a finite set of feasible solutions, a polynomial-time-computable cost function, and a polynomial-time-computable neighborhood, such that for each solution one can in polynomial time either output a strictly better neighbor or certify that the current solution is locally optimal. A problem is PLS-complete if every problem in PLS reduces to it under PLS-reductions.

For an integer k ≥ 2, the k-Opt neighborhood for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is defined on the set of Hamiltonian tours of a complete weighted graph: two tours are neighbors if one can be obtained from the other by removing k edges and adding k other edges (so as to again form a Hamiltonian tour). The local search problem TSP/k-Opt asks, given an instance, to find a tour that is locally optimal with respect to this neighborhood (no k-Opt move strictly decreases the total length).

In the Euclidean version, the input consists of n points in the plane R^2 (or more generally R^d), and the cost of an edge between two points is their Euclidean (ℓ^2) distance; the tour length is the sum of edge costs along the cycle.

It is known that, for general (metric) TSP, the problem TSP/k-Opt is PLS-complete for sufficiently large k.

Question. Does there exist an integer k ≥ 2 for which the local search problem Euclidean TSP/k-Opt (points in the Euclidean plane, ℓ^2 distances, k-Opt neighborhood) is PLS-complete?

A cryptographic primitive (for example, a one-way function, pseudorandom generator, pseudorandom function, collision-resistant hash function, or public-key encryption scheme) is said to be "broken" by an algorithm A if A computes the corresponding inverse/distinguishing/collision task with non-negligible advantage in resources substantially smaller than those guaranteed by the security assumption.

For a positive integer $n$, let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. For an $n\times n$ matrix $A=(A_{i,j})$ with entries in a commutative ring (e.g., $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$) and a subset $C\subseteq S_n$, define the restricted determinant and restricted permanent
$$\det\nolimits_C(A) \;:=\; \sum_{\pi\in C}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}, \qquad \operatorname{per}\nolimits_C(A) \;:=\; \sum_{\pi\in C}\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}.$$
More generally, for an irreducible character $\chi^\lambda$ of $S_n$ associated with a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, define the restricted immanant
$$\operatorname{imm}\nolimits_C^{\lambda}(A) \;:=\; \sum_{\pi\in C}\chi^\lambda(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}.$$
A family $\mathcal C = (C_n)_{n\ge 1}$ with $C_n\subseteq S_n$ is called a permutation class. It is "trivial" in cases such as $C_n = S_n$ (giving the usual determinant, permanent, or immanant) or $C_n = \emptyset$.

Problem. Exhibit nontrivial permutation classes $\mathcal{C}=(C_n)_{n\ge 1}$ (for instance, classes defined by avoidance of fixed permutation patterns, or by other combinatorial restrictions) for which the maps $A\mapsto \det_{C_n}(A)$, $A\mapsto \operatorname{per}_{C_n}(A)$, and, more generally, $A\mapsto \operatorname{imm}_{C_n}^{\lambda}(A)$ can be evaluated in time polynomial in $n$ on arbitrary $n\times n$ input matrices. Furthermore, classify all permutation classes for which such polynomial-time algorithms exist.

Call a deterministic algorithm computing a function f : {0,1}* → {0,1}* a "clean computation" if, at every single time step of its execution, the entire contents of its memory (work tape, registers, and any other internal state) can be simulated efficiently from public information alone, so that the instantaneous memory state at any single time step reveals no secret information about f or its inputs/outputs beyond what is publicly known. (Intuitively, no individual snapshot of the evolving memory leaks any secret, even though the computation as a whole produces a meaningful output.)

Problem: Exhibit a natural class of cryptographic objects — for instance, one-way functions, pseudorandom generators, public-key encryption, digital signatures, or similar primitives — whose existence can be established, either unconditionally or under standard cryptographic assumptions, by means of a clean computation in the above sense. Equivalently, demonstrate that the paradigm of clean computation is powerful enough to yield a natural cryptographic primitive.

Let $G$ be a tree on $n$ vertices. An elimination tree of $G$ is a rooted tree $T$ on the same vertex set defined recursively: pick any vertex $r$ of $G$ as the root, and then for each connected component $C$ of $G - r$, recursively form an elimination tree of $G[C]$ and attach its root as a child of $r$. For a vertex $v$ in an elimination tree $T$, let $T_v$ denote the rooted subtree of $T$ at $v$, and define its boundary in $G$ as the set of vertices in $V(G)\setminus V(T_v)$ that are adjacent in $G$ to some vertex of $V(T_v)$. An elimination tree $T$ of $G$ is called a 2-cut elimination tree if for every vertex $v$ of $T$ the boundary of $T_v$ in $G$ has size at most $2$. A rotation on an elimination tree of $G$ is the elementary move corresponding to an edge of the associated graph associahedron (equivalently, swapping the order of two consecutive vertices in a generating elimination ordering). The rotation distance between two elimination trees is the minimum number of such rotations needed to transform one into the other.

It is known that for any two 2-cut elimination trees of a tree $G$ on $n$ vertices, their rotation distance is at most $5n$. (For comparison, when $G$ is a path, the 2-cut elimination trees are exactly binary search trees on $n$ nodes, and the tight rotation distance bound is $2n-6$ for $n \ge 11$.)

Question: Can the upper bound of $5n$ on the rotation distance between two 2-cut elimination trees of an $n$-vertex tree $G$ be improved to a smaller function of $n$?

Background and definitions.

(1) A function f : {0,1}* -> {0,1}* is called a one-way function if it is computable in polynomial time and, for every probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm A, every polynomial p, and all sufficiently large n,
    Pr_{x ~ {0,1}^n}[ A(1^n, f(x)) ∈ f^{-1}(f(x)) ] < 1/p(n).

(2) NC^0 denotes the class of functions f : {0,1}* -> {0,1}* computable by a uniform family of constant-depth, bounded-fan-in Boolean circuits; equivalently, each output bit of f depends on only O(1) input bits.

(3) Catalytic logspace, denoted CL, is the class of languages (or functions) decidable (computable) by a Turing machine equipped with a read-only input tape, an O(log n)-size read/write clean work tape, and an additional polynomially long "catalytic" auxiliary tape that may be initialized with arbitrary content, may be read and written during the computation, but must be restored to its initial contents at the end of the computation, for every input and every initial content of the auxiliary tape.

(4) A register program of length L over R registers, each holding an element of a finite group (or ring) of size 2^O(1), is a sequence of L instructions of the form r_i <- r_i · g(x), r_i <- r_i + g(x_{j_1}, ..., x_{j_k}), or similar bounded local updates depending on a constant number of input bits, where the output is read off from designated registers at the end. The program has poly-size if R is polynomial in n, and poly-length if L is polynomial in n.

Problem. Prove or disprove the following implication: if there exists a one-way function computable in catalytic logspace CL — or, more generally, if there exists a one-way function computable by a polynomial-size, polynomial-length register program in the sense above — then there exists a one-way function in NC^0.

Assume that $f$ is differentiable at $x(t)$ for every $t > 0$, so that the gradient $\nabla f(x(t)) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ exists for all $t > 0$.

Question: Must the one-sided limit
$$\lim_{t \downarrow 0} \nabla f(x(t))$$
exist in $\mathbb{R}^n$? Equivalently, does there exist a convex function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ (with $n \geq 2$) such that $\nabla f(x(t))$ exists for every $t > 0$ but the limit above fails to exist?

Let $G$ be a connected graph on $n$ vertices. A $k$-cut elimination tree of $G$ is a rooted tree $T$ whose vertex set is $V(G)$, defined recursively as follows: pick a set $S \subseteq V(G)$ with $|S| \le k$ such that removing $S$ disconnects $G$ (or $V(G) = S$); make $S$ the root (a path of $|S|$ nodes from the parent), and recursively build $k$-cut elimination trees for each connected component of $G - S$, attaching them as subtrees of the root. It is known that $G$ admits a $k$-cut elimination tree if and only if $G$ has treewidth at most $k$.

A rotation on a $k$-cut elimination tree is a local restructuring operation that produces another valid $k$-cut elimination tree of the same graph $G$ (the natural generalization of tree rotations on binary search trees / elimination trees). The rotation distance between two $k$-cut elimination trees of $G$ is the minimum number of rotations needed to transform one into the other.

For a graph $G$ of treewidth at most $t$ on $n$ vertices, the rotation distance between any two $k$-cut elimination trees of $G$ is known to be $O(t \cdot n \log n)$. When $G$ is a tree, the bound $O(k \cdot n)$ is known.

Question: For $k$-cut elimination trees of graphs $G$ with treewidth at most $t$ on $n$ vertices, can the upper bound $O(t \cdot n \log n)$ on rotation distance be improved to $O(t \cdot k \cdot n)$?

representations.normalized:
Let M be a matroid on a ground set of m elements, given via an independence oracle (a subroutine that, for any subset S of the ground set, reports whether S is independent in M). The base polytope of M is the convex hull in R^m of the indicator vectors of the bases of M. Its 1-skeleton (the graph whose vertices are the bases and whose edges connect pairs of bases that differ by a single element exchange) has a well-defined graph-theoretic diameter δ(M).

(a) In the independence-oracle model, design an algorithm that computes δ(M) strictly faster than the current best approach, which proceeds by a polynomial-time reduction to matroid intersection; alternatively, establish a superlinear (possibly conditional) lower bound on the number of oracle queries required to compute δ(M).

(b) Design improved algorithms for computing δ(M) when M is given in one of the following more structured representations:
   (i) graphic matroids (specified by a graph),
   (ii) realizable matroids (specified by a matrix over some field),
   (iii) lattice path matroids,
   (iv) transversal matroids (specified by a bipartite incidence structure).

A polytope P ⊂ ℝ^n is given in "implicit" or "partially implicit" form when it is not specified directly by an explicit list of all vertices or facets, but rather succinctly via some combinatorial or algebraic data (for example, by an oracle, by a small set of generators, or as the convex hull of objects parametrized by a graph, matroid, or other combinatorial structure). The graph (or 1-skeleton) of P has the vertices of P as nodes, with two vertices joined by an edge whenever they are connected by an edge of P; the diameter of P is the diameter of this graph.

A polymatroid is a polytope of the form
  P(f) = { x ∈ ℝ^E_{≥0} : x(S) ≤ f(S) for all S ⊆ E },
where E is a finite ground set and f : 2^E → ℝ_{≥0} is a nonnegative, nondecreasing, submodular set function with f(∅) = 0. Its diameter is defined as the diameter of its 1-skeleton.

Problems:

(a) Identify classes of polytopes presented in implicit or partially implicit form (other than already-known cases) for which the diameter of the polytope graph can be computed in time polynomial in the size of the implicit description.

(b) Identify nontrivial classes of polymatroids P(f) (specified, for instance, by an evaluation oracle for f, or by a succinct description of f) for which the diameter of P(f) can be computed efficiently, i.e., in polynomial time.

The question is posed as a vague open research direction. Known complexity results show that computing the combinatorial diameter of a polytope given by linear inequalities is hard (e.g., NP-/DP-hard in general), and only limited classes (such as 0/1 polytopes via specific combinatorial structure, or certain matroid polytopes) have efficient diameter algorithms. No source found that resolves the general question of identifying further implicit polytope classes or polymatroid classes with polynomial-time diameter computation; the problem appears open.

Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a real normed space and let $f:X	o\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ be a convex function. Fix a point $x\in X$ and a nonzero direction $w\in X$, and assume that there exists an open convex set $U\subseteq X$ with $x\in U$ such that the restriction $f|_U$ is continuous. For each $y\in U$, denote by $\partial f(y)\subseteq X^*$ the convex-analytic subdifferential, namely
$$\partial f(y) = \{\, x^*\in X^* : f(z) \ge f(y) + \langle x^*, z-yangle\ 	ext{for all } z\in X\,\}.$$
For sufficiently small $t>0$, the point $x+tw$ lies in $U$ and $\partial f(x+tw)$ is a nonempty, weak-$*$ compact, convex subset of $X^*$. Consider the set-valued one-sided limit
$$\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\, \partial f(x+tw)\subseteq X^*$$
(taken, for example, in the sense of Painlevé–Kuratowski with respect to a specified topology on $X^*$, such as the norm topology or the weak-$*$ topology).

Problem: Characterize, in terms of $X$, $f$, $x$, and $w$, precisely when this directional set-valued limit of subdifferentials exists. In particular, give necessary and sufficient conditions on the data $(X,f,x,w)$ ensuring the existence of $\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\partial f(x+tw)$, and identify the resulting limit set when it exists.

representations.normalized: Let $G = (U \cup V, E)$ be a balanced bipartite graph with $|U| = |V| = n$. A perfect matching of $G$ is a subset $M \subseteq E$ such that every vertex of $G$ is incident to exactly one edge of $M$. The bipartite perfect matching polytope $P(G)$ is the convex hull in $\mathbb{R}^E$ of the characteristic vectors of all perfect matchings of $G$. Two perfect matchings $M, M'$ correspond to adjacent vertices of $P(G)$ if and only if the symmetric difference $M \triangle M'$ is a single alternating cycle (equivalently, $M$ and $M'$ differ by a single cycle flip). The diameter of $P(G)$ is the maximum, over all pairs of perfect matchings $M, M'$ of $G$, of the minimum number of such cycle flips needed to transform $M$ into $M'$.\n\nDetermine the computational complexity of the following problem: given a balanced bipartite graph $G$ (and an integer $k$), compute (resp. decide whether the diameter of $P(G)$ is at most $k$).
