The general one-sided-ties MAX-SMTI approximation ratio has been progressively improved (3/2, then 25/17 ≈ 1.4706 by Iwama–Miyazaki–Yanagisawa, then 22/15 ≈ 1.4667 by Huang–Kavitha, then 13/9 ≈ 1.444 by Bauckholt–Pashkovich–Sanità in 2018), but none reach 5/4. An instance I of the Stable Marriage problem with ties (SMT) consists of a set of n men and n women, together with, for each person, a preference list ranking some subset of the members of the opposite sex, where ties are allowed (i.e., a person may rank several alternatives as equally preferred). A matching M is a set of disjoint man–woman pairs. A pair (m,w) not in M is a (weakly) blocking pair for M if m and w each strictly prefer each other to their current partner under M (with unmatched persons treated as worst). A matching M is weakly stable if it admits no blocking pair. Let S_I denote the set of all weakly stable matchings of I, and let n denote the size of I.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given any instance I of SMT, outputs every matching in S_I (each exactly once) within total running time
  O(p(n) + |S_I| · q(n)),
where p and q are fixed polynomials? Equivalently, is there an output-sensitive polynomial-delay algorithm for enumerating all weakly stable matchings of an SMT instance?

Consider the Stable Roommates problem on an even number n of agents. An instance consists of n agents, each of whom provides a strict total ordering (preference list) of the remaining n-1 agents. A matching is a partition of the n agents into n/2 unordered pairs. A pair {a,b} of agents who are not matched to each other blocks a matching M if a prefers b to its partner in M and b prefers a to its partner in M. A matching is stable if no blocking pair exists.

Equip the set of all instances of size n with the uniform probability measure (equivalently, each agent's preference list is chosen independently and uniformly at random from the (n-1)! possible orderings). Let p_n denote the probability that a uniformly random instance admits at least one stable matching.

Determine p_n exactly, and determine the asymptotic behavior of p_n as n → ∞.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Historically posed as Problem 8 of Gusfield–Irving. Pittel and Irving (1994) gave an upper bound (≈ e^{1/2}/2 ≈ 0.8244) and a lower bound for p_n. Mertens' numerical simulations conjectured p_n = Θ(n^{-1/4}). A 2026 preprint by Chin and Michelen ("The random stable roommates problem typically has no solution") proves p_n → 0 as n → ∞, confirming the Gusfield–Irving conjecture that stable matchings are atypical. The precise asymptotic rate (e.g., the conjectured Θ(n^{-1/4})) does not appear to be fully established, so the problem is partially solved.

Setup. Consider a Stable Marriage with Incomplete lists (SMI) instance, or more generally a Stable Roommates with Incomplete lists (SRI) instance: there is a finite set of agents, each of whom ranks a subset of the other agents in strict order of preference. A matching M is a set of acceptable pairs such that each agent appears in at most one pair. A pair (x,y) not in M blocks M if x and y find each other acceptable and each of x,y is either unmatched in M or strictly prefers the other to their current partner. M is stable if it has no blocking pair.

Given two nonnegative integers a and b, a stable matching M is called an (a,b)-supermatch if, for every subset S of at most a pairs in M, removing these pairs (so that the 2|S| agents involved become single) can be "repaired" by producing a new stable matching M' such that:
 (i) every agent in S is matched in M' (possibly to a different partner), and
 (ii) M' differs from M\S in at most b additional pairs (i.e., apart from the pairs in S being replaced, at most b other pairs of M are modified).

Question. Determine whether the following decision problem belongs to the complexity class NP: given an SMI (or SRI) instance and integers a, b, does there exist an (a,b)-supermatch?

Equivalently: is there a polynomial-size certificate, verifiable in polynomial time, witnessing the existence of an (a,b)-supermatch for arbitrary a (in particular a > 1)?

Consider the Stable Roommates problem with incomplete preference lists (SRI), defined as follows. Let A be a set of agents. Each agent a ∈ A has a strict preference list ranking a subset of A \ {a} (the agents it finds acceptable); acceptability is symmetric. A matching M is a set of disjoint acceptable pairs. A pair {x, y} with x, y unmatched-to-each-other in M blocks M if x and y find each other acceptable and each of x, y is either unmatched in M or strictly prefers the other to its partner in M. A matching is stable if it admits no blocking pair.

Given a stable matching M and an integer b ≥ 0, M is called a (1, b)-supermatch if, for every agent a that is matched in M, after removing the pair containing a from M one can repair the matching by altering the assignments of at most b other matched agents so as to obtain another stable matching of the remaining instance in which a remains unmatched only if necessary (equivalently, after any single forced break-up, stability can be restored by modifying at most b additional pairs). More generally, define a robust stable matching to be one that can be repaired under any single perturbation by changing at most b pairs.

Problem: Determine the approximation complexity of the following optimization problem. Given an SRI instance that admits at least one stable matching, find a stable matching M and the smallest integer b such that M is a (1, b)-supermatch (or more generally, a robust stable matching with repair parameter b). Specifically, establish the best possible polynomial-time approximation ratio for minimizing b, and prove matching hardness-of-approximation lower bounds (assuming P ≠ NP or standard complexity hypotheses).

Stable Roommates setting. Let $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ be a finite set of agents with $n$ even. A preference profile $P$ assigns to each agent $a\in A$ a strict total order $\succ_a$ over $A\setminus\{a\}$ (the complete-list case), or a strict total order over some subset of $A\setminus\{a\}$ representing acceptable partners (the incomplete-list case). A matching is a partition $M$ of $A$ into pairs (and, in the incomplete-list case, possibly singletons). A pair $\{a,b\}\notin M$ is blocking if $a$ and $b$ each prefer the other to their partner in $M$ (with being unmatched ranked below every acceptable partner). $M$ is stable if it admits no blocking pair.

Two notions of robust stability have been studied for the Stable Marriage problem:

(i) Robustness to errors / swaps in preferences (Mai–Vazirani style). Given a preference profile $P$ and an integer $d\geq 0$, define the $d$-neighbourhood $N_d(P)$ to consist of all profiles $P'$ obtainable from $P$ by performing at most $d$ adjacent swaps in the preference lists (over all agents in total, or per agent, depending on the variant). A stable matching $M$ for $P$ is called $d$-robust if $M$ is stable in every $P'\in N_d(P)$, or, in a weaker variant, if for every $P'\in N_d(P)$ there exists a stable matching $M'$ for $P'$ that is "close" to $M$ in a prescribed sense (e.g. small symmetric difference).

(ii) Robustness to changes in preferences (Chen et al. style). Here one studies how stable matchings adapt to bounded modifications of the profile, parameterized by combinatorial measures of change, and asks for matchings simultaneously stable, or simultaneously "almost stable", across a set of profiles.

Task. Develop an analogous theory of robust stable matchings for the Stable Roommates problem, both with complete and with incomplete preference lists. In particular:

(a) Formulate precise definitions of $d$-robust stable matchings for Stable Roommates in the senses of (i) and (ii), accounting for the fact that some Stable Roommates instances admit no stable matching at all.

(b) Determine the computational complexity of deciding, given an instance $(A,P)$ of Stable Roommates and an integer $d$, whether a $d$-robust stable matching exists, and of finding one if it does.

(c) Establish structural results (existence guarantees, lattice or poset structure of robust stable matchings, characterizations of instances admitting robust stable matchings, bounds on the size of $d$ for which they exist) parallel to those known in the Stable Marriage case.

Provide such definitions, algorithms, hardness results, and structural theorems for Stable Roommates and its incomplete-list variants.

Let P be a simple polygon in the plane with N vertices, where each edge e of P is assigned a positive real weight w(e). The weighted straight skeleton of P is defined by the following continuous wavefront propagation: each edge translates inward (into the interior of P) in the direction of its inward normal at speed w(e); adjacent moving edges remain incident at their shared moving vertex, while topological events (edge events, in which a wavefront edge collapses, and split events, in which a reflex wavefront vertex hits a wavefront edge) modify the wavefront combinatorially. The traces of the wavefront vertices over time form a planar straight-line graph inside P called the weighted straight skeleton of (P, w).

There is a known algorithm that computes the weighted straight skeleton of (P, w) in worst-case time O(N^5), where the bottleneck is a reduction to a Stable Roommates instance (in which the candidate pairings of wavefront elements are encoded as preference lists, and selecting the next event corresponds to finding a stable matching).

Problem. Design an algorithm that computes the weighted straight skeleton of an arbitrary simple polygon with weighted edges in worst-case time strictly better than O(N^5), ideally by exploiting structural properties of the associated Stable Roommates instance arising from the geometric reduction.

Consider the Stable Marriage problem with n men and n women. In the classical setting, each agent has a strict linear preference order over the agents of the opposite sex, and a perfect matching M is called stable if there is no man–woman pair (m, w) such that m prefers w to his partner in M and w prefers m to her partner in M.

In the lottery model of uncertain preferences, the input is a probability distribution P_a over strict linear orders over the opposite sex for each agent a, and these distributions are mutually independent. A preference profile is sampled by drawing each agent's preference order independently from its distribution. The stability probability of a perfect matching M is the probability, taken over a random preference profile sampled from these independent distributions, that M is stable.

Problem. Determine the computational complexity of the following decision/search problem: given such a lottery-model instance (the n × n probability distributions, encoded as explicit lists of (linear order, probability) pairs with rational probabilities), compute a perfect matching M* whose stability probability is maximum among all perfect matchings (equivalently, decide, given a rational threshold q, whether some perfect matching has stability probability at least q). In particular, is this problem NP-hard, and does it belong to NP, to PP, or to some other natural complexity class?

representations.normalized:
An instance of the Stable Marriage problem with Ties and Incomplete lists (SMTI) consists of a set U of men and a set W of women. Each person p has a preference list that ranks an acceptable subset of the opposite side; the ranking is a weak order, i.e., it may contain ties (groups of equally preferred partners). Acceptability is symmetric: w appears on m's list if and only if m appears on w's list.

A matching M is a set of mutually acceptable pairs in which each person appears in at most one pair. A pair (m,w) not in M is a blocking pair (in the weak stability sense) if m and w find each other acceptable, and each of m,w is either unmatched in M or strictly prefers the other to their current partner in M. A matching is weakly stable if it admits no blocking pair. The MAX-SMTI problem asks for a weakly stable matching of maximum cardinality.

A master list for one side is a single weak order over all members of that side such that every preference list on the other side is the restriction of this master list to the acceptable partners. The instance is said to be derived from master lists on one (resp. both) sides if such a master list exists on that side (resp. on both sides).

It is known that MAX-SMTI is NP-hard and admits a polynomial-time 3/2-approximation algorithm in the general case, while no approximation ratio below 4/3 (and not below some smaller explicit constant such as roughly 21/19) is achievable under standard complexity assumptions.

Question: When the preferences on one side, or on both sides, are derived from a master list, does there exist a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for MAX-SMTI with approximation ratio strictly better than 3/2? More generally, determine the best possible polynomial-time approximation ratio for MAX-SMTI restricted to instances with a master list on one side, and restricted to instances with master lists on both sides.

Consider the positive sentential logic L defined as follows. The language has propositional variables and the connectives →, ∧, ∨. The pure implicational fragment L→ is the Hilbert-style system with the following axiom schemas and rule:

• (AxB)  (B → C) → ((A → B) → (A → C))
• (AxI)  A → A
• (AxB0) (A → B) → ((C → A) → (C → B))
• (Ax L) ((A → B) ∧ (B → C)) → (A → C)    (here, when stated for the implicational fragment, taken in its appropriate purely implicational form; the conjunction is added with its axioms below)
• (AxTO) A → ((A → B) → B)
• (Det)  from A and A → B infer B (modus ponens).

The full positive logic L = TW+[Ax L, AxTO] is obtained by adding to this implicational base the standard axioms and rule for conjunction and disjunction:

• (Ax∧E1) (A ∧ B) → A
• (Ax∧E2) (A ∧ B) → B
• (Ax∧I) ((A → B) ∧ (A → C)) → (A → (B ∧ C))
• (Ax∨I1) A → (A ∨ B)
• (Ax∨I2) B → (A ∨ B)
• (Ax∨E) ((A → C) ∧ (B → C)) → ((A ∨ B) → C)
• (Adj) from A and B infer A ∧ B.

Question: Is the distributivity schema
    (Dist)  (A ∧ (B ∨ C)) → ((A ∧ B) ∨ (A ∧ C))
derivable in L?

Consider the positive (negation-free) sentential relevance logic TW₊, whose language is built from propositional variables using the binary connectives → (implication), ∧ (conjunction), and ∨ (disjunction). The axioms and rules of TW₊ are:

Axioms:
 (A1) A → A
 (A2) (A → B) → ((C → A) → (C → B))
 (A3) (A → B) → ((B → C) → (A → C))
 (A4) (A ∧ B) → A,  (A ∧ B) → B
 (A5) ((A → B) ∧ (A → C)) → (A → (B ∧ C))
 (A6) A → (A ∨ B),  B → (A ∨ B)
 (A7) ((A → C) ∧ (B → C)) → ((A ∨ B) → C)
 (A8) (A ∧ (B ∨ C)) → ((A ∧ B) ∨ C)

Rules: modus ponens (from A and A → B infer B) and adjunction (from A and B infer A ∧ B).

Extend TW₊ by adding the following two axiom schemes:
 (Ax L) ((A → B) ∧ (C → D)) → ((A ∨ C) → (B ∨ D))
 (Ax TO) (A → B) ∨ (B → C)

Call the resulting system TW₊ + [Ax L, Ax TO].

The "right-top-or" schema (RTO) is the schema
 (RTO)  (A → B) ∨ (B → A).

Question: Is every instance of (RTO) derivable in TW₊ + [Ax L, Ax TO]?

derivable in BCK→[Ax L] + (Resid)? Equivalently, does adjoining fusion together with the residuation rule (Resid) to BCK→[Ax L] suffice to obtain a negation-free proof of (AxTO)?

Consider the purely implicational propositional language with a binary connective →, and the following axiom schemes and rule:

- (AxB)  (B → C) → ((A → B) → (A → C))
- (AxI)  A → A
- (AxB0)  (A → B) → ((B → C) → (A → C))
- (Ax L)  ((A → B) → C) → ((C → A) → (B → A))
- (Det) From A and A → B infer B (modus ponens / detachment).

Let TW→[Ax L] denote the implicational logic whose theorems are generated from (AxB), (AxI), (AxB0), and (Ax L) by the rule (Det).

Now extend the language by a binary connective ∘ (fusion) and add the residuation rule

(Resid)   (A ∘ B) → C   is a theorem   iff   A → (B → C)   is a theorem.

Question: In the system TW→[Ax L] + (Resid), is every instance of the axiom scheme

(AxK)  A → (B → A)

a theorem?

Let $\Omega = B^3 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : |x| < 1\}$ be the open unit ball with boundary $\partial\Omega = S^2$. Let $g : S^2 \to S^2$ be a smooth map of topological degree $\deg g = 0$. Define the Sobolev space
$$H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) = \{ u \in H^1(\Omega; \mathbb{R}^3) : |u(x)| = 1 \text{ a.e. in } \Omega,\ u = g \text{ on } \partial\Omega\}.$$
A map $u \in H^1_g(\Omega; S^2)$ is called a weak harmonic map (into $S^2$) if it satisfies, in the sense of distributions, the system
$$\Delta u_i = u_i\, |\nabla u|^2 \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad i = 1,2,3,$$
together with the boundary condition $u = g$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Question: For every smooth $g : S^2 \to S^2$ with $\deg g = 0$, does there exist at least one weak harmonic map $u \in H^1_g(\Omega; S^2)$ that is continuous on the closed ball $\overline{\Omega}$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is listed as an open problem in Brezis's collection of favorite open problems. Even when the boundary degree vanishes (removing the obvious topological obstruction), energy-minimizing harmonic maps from B^3 to S^2 are known to develop singularities in general (Hardt–Lin gap phenomenon), and no general construction of a continuous harmonic extension is known. Recent literature (e.g., on the Lavrentiev gap for harmonic maps into spheres) continues to treat this as open.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a bounded smooth domain and let $g : \partial\Omega \to S^2$ be a smooth boundary datum, where $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denotes the unit sphere. Define the constrained Sobolev space
$$H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) = \{ u \in H^1(\Omega; \mathbb{R}^3) : u(x) \in S^2 \text{ for a.e. } x \in \Omega,\ u|_{\partial\Omega} = g \},$$
and the Dirichlet energy
$$E(u) = \int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\, dx.$$
Let $C(\overline\Omega)$ denote the space of continuous maps on $\overline\Omega$. Assume that $H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) \cap C(\overline\Omega)$ is nonempty, and consider the variational problem
$$\inf\{ E(u) : u \in H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) \cap C(\overline\Omega) \}.$$
Is this infimum attained by some map $u \in H^1_g(\Omega; S^2) \cap C(\overline\Omega)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether the Dirichlet energy infimum, taken over continuous $H^1$ maps from a 3D domain into $S^2$ with prescribed boundary data, is attained is a long-standing open problem connected to work of Hardt–Lin and Bethuel–Brezis–Coron. Related results address the Lavrentiev gap phenomenon and relaxed energies, but no source found establishes attainment or non-attainment in this continuous class.

For real numbers 1 < p < ∞ and integers d, consider the fractional Sobolev space W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1) of measurable maps f : S^1 → S^1 ⊂ ℂ (where S^1 denotes the unit circle) with finite Gagliardo seminorm

  [f]_{W^{1/p,p}}^p := ∫_{S^1} ∫_{S^1} |f(x) − f(y)|^p / |x − y|^2  dx dy,

equipped with the norm ‖f‖_{W^{1/p,p}}^p := ‖f‖_{L^p}^p + [f]_{W^{1/p,p}}^p. For any f ∈ W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1), the topological degree deg f ∈ ℤ is well-defined (via, e.g., a VMO/density argument: every such f can be approximated in W^{1/p,p} by smooth maps to S^1, and the degree of those smooth approximants stabilizes).

Define
  m_{p,d} := inf { ‖f‖_{W^{1/p,p}}^p : f ∈ W^{1/p,p}(S^1; S^1),  deg f = d }.

Answer the following questions:
(a) Does the equality m_{p,d} = |d| · m_{p,1} hold for every integer d and every 1 < p < ∞?
(b) Is the infimum defining m_{p,d} achieved (for d ≠ 0)?
(c) If the linearity in (a) fails, give an explicit formula for the limit
  lim_{d → +∞} m_{p,d} / d  =  inf_{d > 0} m_{p,d} / d.

Consider the following two-player game on a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$. The players, called Algy (the Strategist) and Strategist's adversary Mindy (the Adversary), proceed in rounds. In each round, the Adversary selects an edge $e\in E$ whose orientation has not yet been decided and queries it; the Strategist must then immediately assign a direction to $e$, subject to the constraint that the set of oriented edges chosen so far does not contain a directed cycle. The game ends when the partial orientation produced so far extends to a unique acyclic orientation of $G$, at which point every remaining edge is considered oriented in the forced way. Let $c(G)$ denote the value of the game, i.e. the minimum over Adversary strategies of the maximum over Strategist strategies (or vice versa) of the number of edges that the Adversary actually queries before the game ends, when both players play optimally.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision/search problems:

(a) Given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, decide whether $c(G)\le k$.
(b) Given $G$ and the current state of the game (i.e. the partial acyclic orientation), compute an optimal next move for the Adversary, and likewise compute an optimal next move for the Strategist.

In particular, are these problems solvable in polynomial time, or are they NP-hard / PSPACE-hard?

Let $N \ge 2$ and let $\mathbb{T}^N = (\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^N$ denote the $N$-dimensional torus. For a scalar function $\varphi : \mathbb{T}^N \to \mathbb{R}$, denote by $\fint \varphi = \int_{\mathbb{T}^N} \varphi$ its mean value.

Recall the sum-space norms: for two Banach spaces $X$ and $Y$ of distributions on $\mathbb{T}^N$, the space $X+Y$ is equipped with the norm
$$\|u\|_{X+Y} = \inf\{\|u_1\|_X + \|u_2\|_Y : u = u_1 + u_2,\ u_1 \in X,\ u_2 \in Y\}.$$
Here $H^{1/2}(\mathbb{T}^N)$ is the Sobolev space of order $1/2$, $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{T}^N)$ is the Sobolev space of $L^1$ functions whose distributional gradient is in $L^1$, and $\|\nabla \varphi\|_{H^{1/2}+L^1}$ denotes the sum-space norm of the gradient considered componentwise (i.e.\ $\nabla \varphi = F + G$ with $F \in H^{1/2}$, $G \in L^1$, and one takes the infimum of $\|F\|_{H^{1/2}} + \|G\|_{L^1}$).

Does there exist a constant $C = C(N) > 0$ such that for every scalar function $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{T}^N$ one has
$$\Big\| \varphi - \fint \varphi \Big\|_{H^{1/2}+W^{1,1}} \le C\, \|\nabla \varphi\|_{H^{1/2}+L^1}\,?$$

Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex manifold of complex dimension $n$. For each integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le n$, the singular cohomology group $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$ admits, after tensoring with $\mathbb{C}$, the Hodge decomposition
$$H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{C}) = \bigoplus_{p+q=2k} H^{p,q}(X),$$
where $H^{p,q}(X)$ denotes the space of cohomology classes representable by closed forms of type $(p,q)$. Define the space of rational Hodge classes of degree $2k$ to be
$$\mathrm{Hdg}^{k}(X) := H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q}) \cap H^{k,k}(X).$$
An algebraic class on $X$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination of cohomology classes of the form $[Z]$, where $Z \subset X$ is a closed irreducible algebraic subvariety of complex codimension $k$ and $[Z] \in H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$ is its fundamental cohomology class.

Prove or disprove: for every smooth projective complex manifold $X$ and every integer $k \ge 0$, every element of $\mathrm{Hdg}^{k}(X)$ is an algebraic class, i.e. lies in the $\mathbb{Q}$-span of the classes $[Z]$ of codimension-$k$ algebraic subvarieties of $X$.

The Hodge conjecture is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open in general. It is known in special cases (e.g., divisor classes by the Lefschetz (1,1)-theorem, and certain classes of varieties), but counterexamples are known for the integral version (Atiyah–Hirzebruch, Kollár), while the rational statement above is still unresolved.

Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in three spatial dimensions:
\[\partial_t v + (v\cdot\nabla)v = -\nabla p + \nu\,\Delta v, \qquad \nabla\cdot v = 0,\]
where $v(x,t)=(v_1,v_2,v_3)(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field, $p(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}$ is the pressure, and $\nu>0$ is a fixed kinematic viscosity. Consider two settings for the spatial domain:

(a) The whole space $\mathbb{R}^3$. Let $v_0:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ be a divergence-free $C^\infty$ vector field satisfying, for every multi-index $\alpha$ and every $K\ge 0$, a decay bound of the form
\[|\partial^\alpha v_0(x)| \le C_{\alpha,K}(1+|x|)^{-K} \quad \text{for all } x\in\mathbb{R}^3.\]

(b) The periodic torus $\mathbb{T}^3 = \mathbb{R}^3/\mathbb{Z}^3$. Let $v_0:\mathbb{T}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ be a divergence-free $C^\infty$ vector field.

Prove or disprove: For every such initial datum $v_0$, there exist functions $v\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^3)$ (respectively $C^\infty(\mathbb{T}^3\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^3)$) and $p\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R})$ (respectively on $\mathbb{T}^3\times[0,\infty)$) satisfying the Navier-Stokes equations for all $t\ge 0$ with $v(x,0)=v_0(x)$, and, in the non-periodic case, with bounded kinetic energy $\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|v(x,t)|^2\,dx < C$ for all $t\ge 0$.

By the Mordell–Weil theorem, the abelian group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points is finitely generated, so $E(\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}^n \oplus T$ for some non-negative integer $n$ (the algebraic rank of $E$) and a finite torsion group $T$. Attached to $E$ is its Hasse–Weil $L$-function $L(E,s)$, defined for $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 3/2$ by the Euler product
$$L(E,s) = \prod_{p 
mid N} \left(1 - a_p p^{-s} + p^{1-2s}ight)^{-1} \cdot \prod_{p \mid N} \left(1 - a_p p^{-s}ight)^{-1},$$
where $N$ is the conductor of $E$ and $a_p = p + 1 - \#E(\mathbb{F}_p)$ for primes $p$ of good reduction. By the modularity theorem, $L(E,s)$ admits an analytic continuation to all of $\mathbb{C}$. The analytic rank $r_{\mathrm{an}}(E)$ is defined as the order of vanishing of $L(E,s)$ at $s = 1$.

(a) Prove or disprove: for every elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, the algebraic rank $n$ equals the analytic rank $r_{\mathrm{an}}(E)$.

(b) Letting $r = r_{\mathrm{an}}(E)$, prove the refined formula for the leading Taylor coefficient of $L(E,s)$ at $s=1$:
$$\lim_{s 	o 1}  rac{L(E,s)}{(s-1)^r} \;=\;  rac{\#\Sha(E/\mathbb{Q}) \cdot \Omega_E \cdot \mathrm{Reg}(E/\mathbb{Q}) \cdot \prod_p c_p}{(\#E(\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{tors}})^2},$$
where $\Sha(E/\mathbb{Q})$ is the Tate–Shafarevich group, $\Omega_E$ is the real period, $\mathrm{Reg}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ is the regulator computed from the Néron–Tate height pairing on a basis of the free part of $E(\mathbb{Q})$, and $c_p$ are the Tamagawa numbers at primes $p$ of bad reduction.

The Birch–Swinnerton–Dyer conjecture remains one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems and is open in general. Partial results are known: Coates–Wiles (1977), Gross–Zagier (1986), and Kolyvagin (1989) established BSD for analytic rank 0 and 1 over $\mathbb{Q}$ (for modular elliptic curves, now all elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ by the modularity theorem). The conjecture remains unresolved for rank $\geq 2$ and the full refined formula is also not proved in general.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a symmetrizable Kac–Moody algebra with Weyl group $W$, and let $B_\lambda$ and $B_\mu$ denote the highest weight crystals associated to dominant integral weights $\lambda$ and $\mu$, with highest weight elements $b_\lambda \in B_\lambda$ and $b_\mu \in B_\mu$, respectively. Let $\sigma_{B_\lambda, B_\mu}: B_\lambda \otimes B_\mu \to B_\mu \otimes B_\lambda$ be the crystal commutor (the Henriques–Kamnitzer commutor, equivalently realized by Kashiwara's involution combined with the natural identification), characterized on tensor products with a highest weight element by the rule: for every $b \in B_\lambda$ there is a unique $c \in B_\mu$ with
$$\sigma_{B_\lambda, B_\mu}(b \otimes b_\mu) = c \otimes b_\lambda.$$
For an element $x$ of a highest weight crystal, let $\kappa(x) \in W$ denote the key of $x$ (the Weyl group element associated to $x$ via the standard key/Demazure construction).

Prove or disprove: for all dominant integral weights $\lambda, \mu$ and all $b \in B_\lambda$, the corresponding element $c \in B_\mu$ defined above satisfies
$$\kappa(c) = \kappa(b)^{-1} \quad \text{in } W.$$

Let $(N,h)$ be a Riemannian manifold and let $\phi:(M,g)\to(N,h)$ be an isometric immersion of a Riemannian manifold $M$ into $N$. The tension field of $\phi$ is $\tau(\phi)=\operatorname{tr}_g\nabla d\phi$, and the bitension field is $\tau_2(\phi)=-\Delta\tau(\phi)-\operatorname{tr}_g R^N(d\phi,\tau(\phi))d\phi$, where $\Delta$ is the rough Laplacian on sections of $\phi^{-1}TN$ and $R^N$ is the Riemann curvature tensor of $(N,h)$. The immersion $\phi$ (or the submanifold $M\subset N$) is called biharmonic if $\tau_2(\phi)\equiv 0$, and minimal if $\tau(\phi)\equiv 0$.

Question (Generalized Chen Conjecture): Is it true that every biharmonic submanifold of a Riemannian manifold with non-positive sectional curvature is minimal?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The generalized Chen conjecture has been disproved in general. Ou and Tang constructed proper biharmonic hyperplanes in certain conformally flat 5-manifolds of negative sectional curvature, giving explicit counterexamples; further counterexamples have appeared subsequently. The original Chen conjecture (ambient Euclidean space) and various restricted versions remain open, but the generalized version with non-positive sectional curvature is known to be false.

Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the unit sphere centered at the origin $O$, i.e., $S = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : \|x\| = 1\}$. For each point $p \in S$, let $T_p$ denote the tangent plane to $S$ at $p$, that is, the affine plane $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : \langle x, p\rangle = 1\}$. Consider rectifiable curves $\gamma:[0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\gamma(0) = O$ such that for every $p \in S$ the image of $\gamma$ meets $T_p$ (equivalently, every closed half-space at distance $1$ from $O$ contains at least one point of $\gamma$).

Determine the infimum
$$L^* = \inf\{ \operatorname{length}(\gamma) : \gamma(0) = O,\ \gamma \cap T_p \neq \emptyset\ \forall p \in S\},$$
and describe the geometric structure of an optimal (or minimizing) curve $\gamma^*$ achieving (or approaching) this infimum.

The problem is a 3D analogue of the "opaque set/escape from sphere" family of geometric optimization problems, known in the literature as the "asteroid surveying problem" (Timothy M. Chan). The exact minimal length and the geometric structure of an optimal curve appear unknown: only upper bounds (e.g., curves of length below roughly 12.08) have been exhibited, and no matching lower bound or characterization of the optimum is established.

A diffeomorphism $f : \mathbb{T}^2 \to \mathbb{T}^2$ is called expansive if there exists a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ (an expansivity constant) such that, for any two points $x, y \in \mathbb{T}^2$ with $x \neq y$, there is some integer $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d(f^n(x), f^n(y)) > \varepsilon$. A diffeomorphism $f$ is called Anosov if there exists a continuous $Df$-invariant splitting $T\mathbb{T}^2 = E^s \oplus E^u$ of the tangent bundle, together with constants $C > 0$ and $0 < \lambda < 1$, such that for all $n \geq 0$, $\|Df^n|_{E^s}\| \leq C \lambda^n$ and $\|Df^{-n}|_{E^u}\| \leq C \lambda^n$. Let $\mathrm{Diff}^1(\mathbb{T}^2)$ denote the space of $C^1$ diffeomorphisms of $\mathbb{T}^2$ with the $C^1$ topology, and let $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathrm{Diff}^1(\mathbb{T}^2)$ be the subset of Anosov diffeomorphisms. Determine whether every expansive diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{T}^2$ belongs to the $C^1$-closure $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ of $\mathcal{A}$; equivalently, decide whether every expansive diffeomorphism of the two-torus can be approximated in the $C^1$ topology by Anosov diffeomorphisms.

A web search did not produce a definitive resolution. While it is classically known (Hiraide, Lewowicz) that expansive homeomorphisms of closed surfaces of genus one are conjugate to Anosov diffeomorphisms, the differentiable question of whether every $C^1$ expansive diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{T}^2$ lies in the $C^1$-closure of the Anosov diffeomorphisms is not clearly resolved in the available literature, and related recent works ($C^1$-generic continuum-wise expansive surface diffeomorphisms) treat genericity rather than full closure. The problem appears to remain open, but verification is inconclusive.

Let $(M,d)$ be a compact metric space and let $f\colon M\to M$ be a homeomorphism. We say $f$ is expansive if there exists a constant $c>0$ (an expansivity constant) such that for any $x,y\in M$ with $x\neq y$ there is some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $d(f^n(x),f^n(y))>c$. Endow the space $H(M)$ of homeomorphisms of $M$ with the $C^0$ (uniform) topology, where a basic neighborhood of $f$ consists of all $g$ with $\sup_{x\in M}d(f(x),g(x))<\delta$ and $\sup_{x\in M}d(f^{-1}(x),g^{-1}(x))<\delta$.

For $x\in M$, the forward semi-trajectory of $x$ is the sequence $\{f^n(x)\}_{n\geq 0}$, and the backward semi-trajectory is $\{f^n(x)\}_{n\leq 0}$. Say that the forward semi-trajectory of $x$ is persistent in the future if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a $C^0$-neighborhood $\mathcal{N}_x$ of $f$ in $H(M)$ such that for every $g\in\mathcal{N}_x$ there exists $y\in M$ with
$$d(f^n(x),g^n(y))\leq\varepsilon\quad\text{for all }n\geq 0.$$
Persistence in the past for the backward semi-trajectory of $x$ is defined analogously, requiring the inequality to hold for all $n\leq 0$.

Question: Is it true that for every expansive homeomorphism $f$ of every compact metric space $M$, every point $x\in M$ has its forward semi-trajectory persistent in the future and its backward semi-trajectory persistent in the past?

$$f_c(x,y) = \left(2x + y - \tfrac{c}{2\pi}\sin(2\pi x),\; x + y - \tfrac{c}{2\pi}\sin(2\pi x)\right) \pmod{1}.$$
For $c = 0$, $f_0$ is the linear Anosov (cat) map $(x,y)\mapsto(2x+y,\,x+y)$, which is area-preserving and uniformly hyperbolic. One verifies that $f_c$ is area-preserving for all $c$. For a point $p\in\mathbb{T}^2$ and a nonzero vector $v\in T_p\mathbb{T}^2$, the Lyapunov exponent of $f_c$ at $p$ in direction $v$ is
$$\lambda(p,v) = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{n}\log\|Df_c^n(p)\,v\|,$$
and one says $f_c$ has a positive Lyapunov exponent at $p$ if $\lambda(p,v) > 0$ for some $v\neq 0$.

Question: For every $c > 1$, does the set
$$\{p \in \mathbb{T}^2 : f_c \text{ has a positive Lyapunov exponent at } p\}$$
have positive Lebesgue measure?

Let $X$ be a separable infinite-dimensional Banach space. A biorthogonal system in $X$ is a sequence $\{(e_n, e_n^*)\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset X \times X^*$ satisfying $e_j^*(e_k) = \delta_{jk}$ for all $j, k \in \mathbb{N}$. For each $n$, define the partial sum operator $S_n : X \to X$ by
\[ S_n(x) = \sum_{k=1}^n e_k^*(x)\, e_k. \]
The biorthogonal system $\{(e_n, e_n^*)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is called an almost basis for $X$ if the identity operator $I_X$ is a limit point of the sequence $\{S_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ in the topology of pointwise convergence on $X$; that is, for every finite set $\{x_1, \dots, x_m\} \subset X$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist infinitely many indices $n$ such that $\|S_n(x_i) - x_i\| < \varepsilon$ for $i = 1, \dots, m$.

Question: Does every separable infinite-dimensional Banach space admit an almost basis?

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces. For constants $K>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1]$, a map $f:S\to Y$ defined on a subset $S\subseteq X$ is called $(K,\alpha)$-Hölder if
$$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le K\,d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}\quad\text{for all }x,x'\in S.$$
For $C\ge 1$, let $B_C(X,Y)$ denote the set of those $\alpha\in(0,1]$ such that every $(K,\alpha)$-Hölder map $f:S\to Y$, defined on any subset $S\subseteq X$, admits an extension $\tilde f:X\to Y$ which is $(CK,\alpha)$-Hölder. Define
$$A(X,Y)=B_1(X,Y),\qquad A_e(X,Y)=\bigcap_{C>1}B_C(X,Y).$$
Thus $\alpha\in A_e(X,Y)$ means every $(K,\alpha)$-Hölder map from a subset of $X$ into $Y$ admits, for every $C>1$, a $(CK,\alpha)$-Hölder extension to all of $X$ (an "almost isometric" extension), while $\alpha\in A(X,Y)$ means an isometric ($C=1$) extension always exists.

(a) Is the set $A_e(X,Y)$ always closed in $(0,1]$?

(b) Whenever $A_e(X,Y)$ is closed, must one have $A_e(X,Y)=A(X,Y)$?

Say that $X$ has the metric $\mathcal{A}$-approximation property (M-$\mathcal{A}$-AP) if for every compact subset $K \subset X$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $T \in B_{\mathcal{A}(X,X)}$ such that $\|Tx - x\| \leq \varepsilon$ for all $x \in K$.

Let $X^* \mathbin{\hat{\otimes}_\pi} X$ denote the projective tensor product of $X^*$ and $X$, and let
$$ V : X^* \mathbin{\hat{\otimes}_\pi} X \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}(X,X)^* $$
be the trace mapping defined on elementary tensors by $V(x^* \otimes x)(T) = x^*(Tx)$ for $x \in X$, $x^* \in X^*$, $T \in \mathcal{A}(X,X)$, and extended by linearity and continuity.

Question: If $X$ has the metric $\mathcal{A}$-approximation property, must $V$ be an isometry onto its image?

Let $(A, \to)$ be an abstract reduction system, i.e. a set $A$ together with a binary relation $\to \subseteq A \times A$; write $\to^*$ for its reflexive–transitive closure. For a term (element) $t \in A$, define the reduction graph of $t$ to be the directed graph $G(t) = (V_t, E_t)$ whose vertex set is the set of reducts $V_t = \{ s \in A : t \to^* s \}$ and whose edge set is $E_t = \{ (s, s') : s, s' \in V_t,\ s \to s' \}$. Call the isomorphism class of $G(t)$ the spectrum of $t$, and call the collection of spectra of all terms the spectrum of the rewrite system.

Reduction graphs can in general have very complicated structure. For specific, well-behaved classes of rewrite systems (for example: orthogonal first-order term rewriting systems, left-linear systems, the untyped $\lambda$-calculus and its sub-calculi, combinatory logic, string rewriting systems, ground rewrite systems, and confluent or terminating systems), determine the structural properties of the spectrum. Specifically, give a characterization of which directed graphs (up to isomorphism) can arise as reduction graphs $G(t)$ of terms $t$ in such a class, and identify invariants (such as cardinality, branching structure, presence of cycles, lattice/order-theoretic properties of the induced reduction order, or forbidden subgraph patterns) that distinguish the spectra of these classes from arbitrary directed graphs.

Let all topological spaces be Hausdorff. For a function f: X × Y → ℝ, let C(f) denote the set of points of joint continuity of f. A function f: X × Y → ℝ is called separately continuous if for every fixed x ∈ X the map y ↦ f(x,y) is continuous on Y and for every fixed y ∈ Y the map x ↦ f(x,y) is continuous on X. A function f: X × Y → ℝ is called horizontally almost separately continuous if for every y ∈ Y the map x ↦ f(x,y) is continuous on X, and for every x ∈ X the map y ↦ f(x,y) is continuous on Y at all but possibly countably many points (more generally, on a residual set).

A compact space Y is called co-Namioka if for every Baire space X and every separately continuous function f: X × Y → ℝ there exists a dense G_δ subset A ⊆ X such that A × Y ⊆ C(f).

A topological space Y is called a Hahn space with respect to ℝ if for every topological space X and every horizontally almost separately continuous function f: X × Y → ℝ, the set
   C_Y(f) := { x ∈ X : {x} × Y ⊆ C(f) }
is residual in X.

Problem: Characterize those compact spaces Y which are co-Namioka and which are also Hahn spaces with respect to ℝ. Equivalently, give an internal topological characterization of the class of compact Hausdorff spaces lying in the intersection of these two classes.

Let F be a finite ranked signature and let T(F) denote the set of ground (variable-free) terms over F, assumed nonempty. A term rewrite system R over F is a finite set of rewrite rules l → r with l, r terms over F and variables. A term t (possibly with variables) is called ground-reducible with respect to R if for every ground substitution σ assigning terms in T(F) to the variables of t, the ground instance tσ contains a redex with respect to R (i.e., some subterm of tσ is an instance of the left-hand side of some rule in R).

Determine the exact computational complexity of the following decision problem: given a finite signature F, a finite term rewrite system R over F, and a term t over F, decide whether t is ground-reducible with respect to R. In particular, identify a complexity class C such that this problem is C-complete under standard reductions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem was solved by Hubert Comon-Lundh and Florent Jacquemard, who proved that ground reducibility is EXPTIME-complete (LICS 1997; Information and Computation 187(1):123–153, 2003). EXPTIME-hardness was shown by encoding emptiness of the intersection of tree automata, and a matching upper bound is achieved via deterministic tree automata with disequality constraints of size O(2^(|R|·|t|)).

Consider the second-order (polymorphic) λ-calculus, also known as System F (Curry style), whose types are generated by the grammar τ ::= α | τ → τ | ∀α. τ, where α ranges over a countable set of type variables. A term M of the untyped λ-calculus (built from variables, application, and abstraction) is said to be typable in System F if there exist a type τ and a type assignment Γ (a finite map from term variables to types) such that Γ ⊢ M : τ is derivable using the standard Curry-style typing rules for System F (variable, application, abstraction, ∀-introduction with the usual eigenvariable condition, and ∀-elimination by instantiation).

Decide whether the following problem is algorithmically decidable: given an arbitrary term M of the untyped λ-calculus, determine whether M is typable in System F.

J. B. Wells (LICS 1994; journal version in Annals of Pure and Applied Logic, 1999) proved that typability in the Curry-style second-order λ-calculus (System F) is undecidable, and equivalent to type checking, by reduction from semi-unification. The problem is thus resolved (undecidable).

For two isomorphic Banach spaces $X$ and $Y$, the Banach–Mazur distance is defined by
$$d(X,Y)\;=\;\inf\bigl\{\|T\|\cdot\|T^{-1}\|\;:\;T:X\to Y\text{ is a linear isomorphism}\bigr\}.$$
It is well known that $d(X,Y)\ge 1$, with $d(X,Y)=1$ whenever $X$ and $Y$ are isometrically isomorphic; however, in general the converse fails, i.e. there exist non-isometric Banach spaces $X,Y$ with $d(X,Y)=1$.

Give an intrinsic characterization of the separable infinite-dimensional (real) Banach spaces $X$ with the following rigidity property: for every Banach space $Y$,
$$d(X,Y)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y\text{ is isometrically isomorphic to }X.$$

Let $X$ be a (real or complex) Banach space, let $L(X)$ denote the Banach space of all bounded linear operators on $X$, and let $K(X) \subseteq L(X)$ denote the closed subspace of all compact operators on $X$.

Recall the following definitions for a closed subspace $Y$ of a Banach space $Z$:

(i) $Y$ has property U in $Z$ if every continuous linear functional $g \in Y^{*}$ admits exactly one Hahn–Banach extension to $Z$, i.e., there is a unique $f \in Z^{*}$ with $f|_{Y} = g$ and $\|f\| = \|g\|$.

(ii) $Y$ is an ideal in $Z$ if there exists a bounded linear projection $P: Z^{*} \to Z^{*}$ with $\|P\| = 1$ and $\ker P = Y^{\perp} = \{f \in Z^{*} : f|_{Y} = 0\}$.

It is known that being an ideal implies property U is not automatic, and conversely. The question is:

Does there exist a Banach space $X$ such that $K(X)$ has property U in $L(X)$ but $K(X)$ is not an ideal in $L(X)$?

Setting. A term rewriting system (TRS) consists of a set of rewrite rules l → r over terms built from a signature of function symbols and a countable set of variables, where l is not a variable and every variable in r occurs in l. A TRS is called left-linear if, in every rule l → r, no variable occurs more than once in l. The one-step rewrite relation → is generated by replacing an instance lσ (a redex) appearing as a subterm of a term by rσ. The relation →* denotes its reflexive-transitive closure. A TRS is confluent (Church–Rosser) if whenever s →* t1 and s →* t2 there exists u with t1 →* u and t2 →* u.

A critical pair of a TRS is a pair (t, s) obtained as follows: choose two (renamed-apart) rules l1 → r1 and l2 → r2, a non-variable position p in l1, and a most general unifier σ of l2 and the subterm of l1 at p; then t = l1[r2]p σ and s = r1 σ. Huet proved that a left-linear TRS is confluent provided that for every critical pair (t, s) one has t → || s, where → || denotes parallel reduction (simultaneous contraction of pairwise-disjoint redex occurrences).

Problem. Give a decidable criterion characterizing (a useful sufficient and, ideally, both necessary and sufficient class of) left-linear term rewriting systems for which the Church–Rosser (confluence) property holds. In particular, exhibit a decidable condition on the critical pairs of an arbitrary finite left-linear TRS that implies, and as broadly as possible captures, confluence — strictly extending Huet's parallel-closed criterion.

  Ix → x
  Kxy → x
  Sxyz → (xz)(yz)
  CTxy → x
  CFxy → y

together with the conditional rule

  if x ↔* y then Czxy → x,

where ↔* denotes the reflexive–symmetric–transitive closure of →. (That is, the conditional rule allows Czxy to reduce to x whenever the two branches x and y are convertible.)

Consider the following semi-equational conditional term rewriting system R over a signature containing the constants I, K, S, D₁, D₂, P and a binary application operator (written by juxtaposition, left-associative). The unconditional rules are the usual Combinatory Logic rules together with projection rules for surjective pairing:

  I x → x
  K x y → x
  S x y z → x z (y z)
  D₁ (P x y) → x
  D₂ (P x y) → y

Surjective pairing is then added in a "linearized" conditional form by the semi-equational conditional rule

  P (D₁ z) (D₂ z) → z   ⇐   D₁ z ↓ D₁ z,  D₂ z ↓ D₂ z

(or, equivalently, by replacing the non-left-linear axiom P(D₁ x)(D₂ x) → x with a linear rule whose firing is conditioned on the semi-equational joinability of its two left-hand-side instances of the same variable). Here "semi-equational" means a conditional rule l → r ⇐ s₁ ↓ t₁, …, sₙ ↓ tₙ is applicable to a term when the corresponding instances of sᵢ and tᵢ are convertible (joinable by the underlying conversion) for each i.

Question: Is this conditional term rewriting system confluent?

Setting. Let R = (Σ, R) be an orthogonal term-rewriting system over a (possibly infinite) signature Σ. Terms are formed from Σ and a countable set of variables, and may be finite or infinite (i.e., elements of the metric completion of finite terms under the usual distance d(s, t) = 2^{-n}, where n is the minimum depth of a position at which s and t differ). A transfinite reduction sequence is a sequence (t_α)_{α ≤ λ} of terms, indexed by an ordinal λ, together with rewrite steps t_α → t_{α+1} contracting redexes in the orthogonal system, such that at every limit ordinal β ≤ λ the sequence (t_α)_{α<β} converges to t_β in the above metric. Such a sequence is called strongly convergent (or "convergent") if, in addition, the depth of the contracted redex tends to infinity along every limit approach.

Two terms s and t are said to be reducible to a common reduct (Church–Rosser) if there exist convergent transfinite reductions s ↠ u and t ↠ u for some term u. The system is "almost-confluent" if for every term s and any two convergent transfinite reductions s ↠ t_1 and s ↠ t_2, the terms t_1 and t_2 can be brought to a common reduct by convergent transfinite reductions, modulo identification of certain "meaningless" subterms (e.g., replacing root-active or hypercollapsing subterms by a fresh constant ⊥).

Problem. Characterize precisely those orthogonal term-rewriting systems for which the infinitary Church–Rosser property (almost-confluence) holds for all strongly convergent transfinite reduction sequences. In particular, determine whether almost-confluence holds in general for orthogonal systems, and if not, identify the obstruction in terms of the collapsing rules of the system.

Setting. Let R = (Σ, R) be an orthogonal term-rewriting system over a (possibly infinite) signature Σ. Terms are formed from Σ and a countable set of variables, and may be finite or infinite (i.e., elements of the metric completion of finite terms under the usual distance d(s, t) = 2^{-n}, where n is the minimum depth of a position at which s and t differ). A transfinite reduction sequence is a sequence (t_α)_{α ≤ λ} of terms, indexed by an ordinal λ, together with rewrite steps t_α → t_{α+1} contracting redexes in the orthogonal system, such that at every limit ordinal β ≤ λ the sequence (t_α)_{α<β} converges to t_β in the above metric. Such a sequence is called strongly convergent (or "convergent") if, in addition, the depth of the contracted redex tends to infinity along every limit approach.

The system is "almost-confluent" if for every term s and any two convergent transfinite reductions s ↠ t_1 and s ↠ t_2, the terms t_1 and t_2 can be brought to a common reduct by convergent transfinite reductions, modulo identification of certain "meaningless" subterms (e.g., replacing root-active or hypercollapsing subterms by a fresh constant ⊥).

Problem. Characterize precisely those orthogonal term-rewriting systems for which the infinitary Church–Rosser property (almost-confluence) holds for all strongly convergent transfinite reduction sequences. In particular, determine whether almost-confluence holds in general for orthogonal systems, and if not, identify the obstruction in terms of the collapsing rules of the system.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem has been resolved by Kennaway, Klop, Sleep, and de Vries (Information and Computation, 1995, and earlier RTA 1991): strongly convergent reduction in an orthogonal term-rewriting system is confluent if and only if the system contains at most one collapsing rule whose left-hand side has only one variable. In general, the infinitary Church–Rosser property fails for strongly converging reductions, but it does hold once meaningless terms are identified (e.g., for Böhm reduction with ⊥-replacement of root-active/hypercollapsing subterms). Thus "almost-confluence" in the appropriate sense holds, and a precise characterization is known.

Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a non-atomic $\sigma$-finite measure space (for instance $[0,1]$ or $[0,\infty)$ with Lebesgue measure). For a measurable function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}$, let $f^{*}:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ denote its non-increasing rearrangement, defined by $f^{*}(t)=\inf\{s\ge 0:\mu(\{|f|>s\})\le t\}$. For $1<p<\infty$ and $1\le q<\infty$, the Lorentz space $L_{p,q}(\Omega)$ consists of all measurable $f$ such that
$$\|f\|_{p,q}:=\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}\bigl(t^{1/p}f^{*}(t)\bigr)^{q}\,\frac{dt}{t}\right)^{1/q}<\infty,$$
with the obvious modification $\|f\|_{p,\infty}=\sup_{t>0}t^{1/p}f^{*}(t)$ when $q=\infty$.

A Schauder basis $(e_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of a Banach space $X$ is called \emph{greedy} if there exists a constant $C\ge 1$ such that for every $x\in X$ and every $m\in\mathbb{N}$,
$$\|x-G_m(x)\|\le C\,\inf\Bigl\{\bigl\|x-\sum_{n\in A}a_n e_n\bigr\|:|A|=m,\ a_n\in\mathbb{C}\Bigr\},$$
where $G_m(x)$ is any $m$-term greedy approximation obtained by keeping $m$ of the largest (in modulus) coefficients in the expansion $x=\sum_n e_n^{*}(x)e_n$. Equivalently (Konyagin–Temlyakov), a basis is greedy if and only if it is unconditional and democratic.

\textbf{Problem.} Suppose $1<p<\infty$, $1\le q\le\infty$, and $p\neq q$. Does the Lorentz space $L_{p,q}(\Omega)$ admit a greedy basis?

Consider the simply typed λ-calculus, with terms built from variables, applications, and λ-abstractions, equipped with the standard typing rules assigning simple types over a set of base types, and with β-reduction (λx.M)N → M[N/x]. A term is strongly normalizing if every reduction sequence starting from it is finite; it is a classical theorem that every typable term is strongly normalizing.

Existing proofs of this fact (e.g., via Tait–Girard reducibility candidates) are widely regarded as non-elementary, since they interpret types as sets of terms closed under saturation/reducibility conditions rather than directly assigning an ordinal-like measure to each term.

Problem: Does there exist a "reasonably straightforward" mapping
  μ : { typable simply typed λ-terms } → (W, <)
into some well-founded ordering (W, <) such that whenever M β-reduces to M′, one has μ(M′) < μ(M)? In other words, can strong normalization of the simply typed λ-calculus be proved by exhibiting an explicit, elementary, syntax-directed decreasing measure into a well-founded order, rather than via reducibility/candidate techniques?

Several decreasing-measure proofs of strong normalization for the simply typed λ-calculus into well-founded orderings (e.g., hereditarily finite multisets, ordinals below ε₀, and recently the W-measure and Tm-measure of van Daalen / Joachimski–Matthes / De Vrijer style) are known. Whether any such measure is considered "reasonably straightforward" enough to fully settle the informal question posed in the RTA problem list is subjective; the underlying mathematical question of finding elementary well-founded measures has been substantially addressed but no canonical answer is universally accepted.

Question: Does there exist a homeomorphic embedding $h : S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ of the 2-sphere into $\mathbb{R}^4$ whose image $h(S^2)$ is 2-convex in the above sense? Consider the term rewrite system H over a signature containing constants and the unary symbol e, the binary symbols c, h, and the ternary symbol d, g, defined (in the style of Dershowitz–Jouannaud) by the rewrite rules encoding the Battle of Hydra and Hercules:

  h(z, e(x)) → h(c(z), d(z, x))
  d(z, g(0, 0)) → e(z)
  d(c(z), g(x, y)) → g(x, d(z, g(x, y)))
  d(c(z), g(x, y)) → d(z, g(x, g(x, y)))
  (together with the remaining standard rules of the Hydra encoding).

It is known that H is terminating, but its termination is not provable in Peano Arithmetic (PA), since termination of H is equivalent to the Kirby–Paris hydra theorem.

A reduction order on terms is a well-founded strict order on ground terms that is closed under contexts and substitutions; its order type is the ordinal length of the induced well-ordering on ground terms. A reduction order ≻ proves termination of a rewrite system R if ℓ ≻ r for every rule ℓ → r of R (after suitable closure).

Question: Must every reduction order that proves termination of the Hydra rewrite system H have order type strictly greater than ε₀ (equivalently, must any such termination ordering exceed the proof-theoretic strength of Peano Arithmetic)? In other words, does there exist a reduction order compatible with H whose order type is at most ε₀?

Let F be a finite set of function symbols containing at least one binary symbol declared to be associative and commutative (AC). Let T(F) denote the set of ground terms built from F, taken modulo the congruence generated by the AC axioms f(x,y)=f(y,x) and f(f(x,y),z)=f(x,f(y,z)) for every AC symbol f. Consider the first-order language with equality whose intended structure has universe T(F)/=_AC and where each function symbol is interpreted as the corresponding term constructor (modulo AC). The Σ2 fragment consists of all closed formulas of the form ∃x_1…∃x_m ∀y_1…∀y_n φ(x_1,…,x_m,y_1,…,y_n), where φ is a quantifier-free formula built from equations between terms over F and the variables shown, using Boolean connectives.

Question: Is the Σ2 fragment of this first-order theory of ground terms modulo AC decidable?

Let R be a term-rewriting system (or, more generally, a combinatory reduction system) over a set of terms, with a set of redexes (instances of left-hand sides of rewrite rules). Say that R has the property of decreasing redexes (DR) if there exists a labeling map # from the redexes of R to some well-founded partial order (W, <) such that for every rewrite step that contracts a redex u, every redex v that is a residual of, or is created by, the contraction of u has label #(v) strictly less than #(u) (with the usual convention that residuals of v that are not u itself satisfy the appropriate decreasing condition with respect to the well-founded order).

It is known that for orthogonal systems, DR implies strong normalization (every reduction sequence terminates).

Question: Does the property of decreasing redexes (DR) imply termination (strong normalization) for non-orthogonal term-rewriting systems and combinatory reduction systems as well?

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite signature and let $T(\Sigma, X)$ denote the set of terms over $\Sigma$ and a countably infinite set of variables $X$. A *simplification ordering* on $T(\Sigma, X)$ is a strict partial order $>$ that is stable under contexts, stable under substitutions, and satisfies the subterm property $f(\dots, t, \dots) > t$. A *well-rewrite ordering* is an extension of the homeomorphic term-embedding quasi-ordering that strictly generalizes the notion of simplification ordering, in the sense that every simplification ordering is a well-rewrite ordering but not conversely; informally, it is a well-quasi-order on terms compatible with rewriting that need not satisfy the full subterm property.

Problem: Using well-rewrite orderings as the foundational notion in place of simplification orderings, define a new family of syntactic path orderings on $T(\Sigma, X)$ (generalizing the classical recursive path ordering of Dershowitz built from a precedence on $\Sigma$) with the following properties:

(a) The new ordering is a well-rewrite ordering on $T(\Sigma, X)$.
(b) It strictly contains the standard recursive path ordering for every precedence.
(c) It is defined syntactically by recursion on term structure, in the style of the recursive path ordering.
(d) It can be used to prove termination of term rewriting systems $R$ over $\Sigma$ by checking $\ell > r$ for every rule $\ell \to r \in R$.

Construct such a "recursive path ordering" based on well-rewrite orderings and prove that properties (a)–(d) hold.

A term rewriting system (TRS) is a finite set R of rewrite rules l → r over terms built from a signature of function symbols and a set of variables. The TRS R is terminating if there is no infinite rewrite sequence t₁ → t₂ → t₃ → ⋯ generated by R.

A standard method for proving termination is via monotone interpretations: assign to each n-ary function symbol f a strictly monotone function [f]: A^n → A on a well-founded ordered domain (A, >), and verify that for every rule l → r and every assignment of values to variables, [l] > [r]. Two well-known classes of such interpretations are:

(i) Polynomial interpretations, where A = ℕ (or a well-founded subset of ℝ⁺) and each [f] is a polynomial with non-negative integer (or real) coefficients that is strictly monotone in each argument.

(ii) Exponential interpretations, where each [f] is built from constants, variables, addition, multiplication, and exponentiation x ↦ c^x (c ≥ 2), again required to be strictly monotone in each argument and to take values in a well-founded ordered set.

Problem. Develop effective (algorithmic) methods to decide, given a finite TRS R, whether there exists an exponential interpretation of the function symbols in R such that, under the resulting interpretation, every rewrite rule of R is strictly decreasing (i.e., [l] > [r] holds for all variable assignments, for every l → r ∈ R). In particular, identify a natural restricted class of exponential interpretations for which this existence problem is decidable, and provide a corresponding decision procedure.

A Banach space $X$ is said to have the approximation property if for every compact subset $K \subset X$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a bounded finite-rank linear operator $T : X \to X$ such that $\|Tx - x\| < \varepsilon$ for all $x \in K$.

Consider the following two Banach spaces:

(a) $B(\ell_2)$, the space of all bounded linear operators from $\ell_2$ into itself, equipped with the operator norm $\|T\| = \sup_{\|x\|_{\ell_2} \le 1} \|Tx\|_{\ell_2}$.

(b) $H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$, the space of all bounded analytic functions $f$ on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$, equipped with the supremum norm $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{z \in \mathbb{D}} |f(z)|$.

Determine whether each of these Banach spaces has the approximation property.

Work in the setting of abstract/term rewriting. A rewrite relation on a set of terms is a binary relation closed under contexts and substitutions. A binary relation → is called terminating if there is no infinite sequence t_1 → t_2 → t_3 → … . The strict-subterm relation ▷ is the binary relation defined by s ▷ t iff t is a proper subterm of s. It is known that ▷ commutes with every rewrite relation, and consequently, for every terminating rewrite relation →, the union → ∪ ▷ is again terminating (in fact, the union remains terminating even when ▷ is closed under contexts and substitutions).

Determine the coarsest binary relation R (on terms) with the following property: for every terminating rewrite relation →, the union → ∪ R is terminating. Equivalently, characterize the largest such relation R, and decide whether ▷ (or its closure under contexts and substitutions) is optimal, or whether a strictly larger relation enjoys the same universal preservation-of-termination property.

This is a long-standing open problem in Banach space theory. By a theorem of James, a Banach space with an unconditional basis is reflexive if and only if it contains neither c₀ nor ℓ₁, so the question is closely tied to the existence of unconditional basic sequences. Gowers–Maurey showed that not every infinite-dimensional Banach space contains a subspace with an unconditional basis (hereditarily indecomposable spaces exist), but this does not refute the trichotomy reflexive / c₀ / ℓ₁ at the subspace level. The problem continues to be cited as open in surveys of Banach space theory.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has a negative answer. Ribe (1984) constructed two separable Banach spaces that are uniformly homeomorphic but not linearly isomorphic; in particular, a reflexive Banach space can be uniformly homeomorphic to a non-reflexive one. Subsequent work by Aharoni–Lindenstrauss and others (including more recent examples involving subspaces and quotients of $\ell_p$ and $c_0$) provides further counterexamples.

Background. Hsiang's approach to first-order theorem proving translates clauses into polynomials over the Boolean ring B = GF(2)[X_1, X_2, ...]/(X_i^2 - X_i), where logical "and" corresponds to ring multiplication, "exclusive or" corresponds to addition, and the constants true and false correspond to 1 and 0 respectively. A first-order formula φ is unsatisfiable if and only if its Boolean-ring translation, together with the equations expressing idempotence of atoms, can be reduced to the polynomial 1 by a complete set of inference rules (typically a superposition/N-rule plus simplification by an AC-rewrite system implementing the Boolean-ring axioms).

In this framework an inference strategy is a restriction on which pairs of polynomials may be combined and on which atoms (monomials) of a polynomial may be used as the "key" atom for superposition. A strategy is called complete if, whenever the input set of polynomials is unsatisfiable, the strategy still derives 1.

Examples of known strategies include:
 • Hsiang's unrestricted N-strategy,
 • Kapur–Narendran superposition (every pair of polynomials and every atom can be used),
 • restrictions to pairs in which at least one polynomial has an odd number of monomials,
 • restrictions to maximal atoms under a given ordering on atoms,
 • linear, O-linear, and pseudo O-linear strategies.

Problem. Design new inference strategies for Boolean-ring based methods of resolution-like first-order theorem proving that are strictly more restrictive (i.e. prune more inferences) than the currently known complete strategies listed above, while remaining refutationally complete for first-order logic. Prove the completeness of the proposed strategies and, where possible, establish that they properly refine the existing ones.

Background. Hsiang's approach to first-order theorem proving translates clauses into polynomials over the Boolean ring B = GF(2)[X_1, X_2, ...]/(X_i^2 - X_i), where logical "and" corresponds to ring multiplication, "exclusive or" corresponds to addition, and the constants true and false correspond to 1 and 0 respectively. A first-order formula φ is unsatisfiable if and only if its Boolean-ring translation, together with the equations expressing idempotence of atoms, can be reduced to the polynomial 1 by a complete set of inference rules (typically a superposition/N-rule plus simplification by an AC-rewrite system implementing the Boolean-ring axioms).

In this framework an inference strategy is a restriction on which pairs of polynomials may be combined and on which atoms (monomials) of a polynomial may be used as the "key" atom for superposition. A strategy is called complete if, whenever the input set of polynomials is unsatisfiable, the strategy still derives 1.

Examples of known strategies include:
 • Hsiang's unrestricted N-strategy,
 • Kapur–Narendran superposition (every pair of polynomials and every atom can be used),
 • restrictions to pairs in which at least one polynomial has an odd number of monomials,
 • restrictions to maximal atoms under a given ordering on atoms,
 • linear, O-linear, and pseudo O-linear strategies.

Problem. Design new inference strategies for Boolean-ring based methods of resolution-like first-order theorem proving that are strictly more restrictive (i.e. prune more inferences) than the currently known complete strategies listed above, while remaining refutationally complete for first-order logic. Prove the completeness of the proposed strategies and, where possible, establish that they properly refine the existing ones.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Several partial refinements of Hsiang's N-strategy have been proposed (restrictions to maximal atoms, to pairs with an odd number of monomials, linear and O-linear strategies, intersection-based methods, etc.), each shown complete in its own setting. However, the problem of identifying the most restrictive complete strategy for Boolean-ring based first-order theorem proving is open-ended and no definitive solution is reported; the question continues to be investigated.

Consider the rule-based framework for solving unification problems in an arbitrary equational theory E, in which a unification problem is represented as a set of multi-equations and is transformed by a fixed system of inference rules toward a so-called "dag-solved form" (a directed-acyclic-graph form in which each multi-equation contains at most one non-variable term and from which a most general E-unifier can be read off directly). Among these inference rules is the Merge rule, which combines two multi-equations sharing a common variable. As stated, the Merge rule carries an application condition restricting when two multi-equations may be merged (this condition is needed in the proof that the rule system is sound, complete and terminating on dag-solved forms).

Question: Can the application condition imposed on the Merge rule in the computation of dag-solved forms of unification problems in equational theories be removed (or essentially weakened) while preserving soundness, completeness, and termination of the overall transformation system?

representations.normalized:
Consider the framework of equational problems represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) for solving systems of equations modulo a theory. A problem is said to be in dag-solved form when its equations are arranged in a triangular DAG structure x_1 = t_1, x_2 = t_2, …, x_n = t_n in which each variable x_i does not occur in t_j for j ≤ i and the dependency relation is acyclic. To complete a system into dag-solved form one uses transformation rules including a Merge rule, which combines two equations x = s and x = t having the same left-hand variable into x = s together with s = t, provided a syntactic side-condition C(s,t) holds (for instance, a condition restricting the relative sizes or shapes of s and t so as to preserve termination of the completion procedure).

A stronger variant of the Merge rule and an extended Check rule (which detects occur-check failures across the DAG) are known to yield a complete decision procedure when the side-condition C is weakened to a more permissive condition C'.

Question: Working only with the original Merge rule (not its stronger variant) and the original Check rule (not its extended form), can the side-condition C in the Merge rule be weakened to a strictly more permissive condition while still preserving soundness, termination, and completeness of the transformation into dag-solved form?

Fix a finite first-order signature Σ consisting of finitely many function symbols (each with a fixed arity, including constants of arity 0). Let T(Σ) denote the term algebra of all finite ground terms built from Σ, viewed as a first-order structure whose domain is the set of finite Σ-terms and whose function symbols are interpreted as the term constructors. The first-order theory of finite trees over Σ is the set Th(T(Σ)) of all first-order sentences over Σ (with equality) that are true in T(Σ).

It is known that Th(T(Σ)) is decidable and that the decision problem is PSPACE-hard. Determine whether the decision problem for Th(T(Σ)) lies in PSPACE; that is, does there exist an algorithm deciding, given a first-order sentence φ over Σ, whether φ ∈ Th(T(Σ)), using only space polynomial in the length of φ?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Vorobyov (CADE 1996, "An Improved Lower Bound for the Elementary Theories of Trees") proved that the first-order theory of finite trees (over a finite constructor signature) is non-elementary in the sense of Kalmar: its decision problem cannot be decided within k-fold exponential time for any fixed k, and in fact requires nondeterministic time exceeding any tower-of-exponentials infinitely often. Since PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME is elementary, this rules out a PSPACE algorithm, answering the question in the negative.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite signature of function symbols, and consider first-order formulas built from atomic equations $s = t$ between terms over $\Sigma$ (with variables), using the connectives $\wedge$, $\vee$, $\neg$ and the quantifiers $\forall$, $\exists$. Interpret such formulas in the algebra $T(\Sigma)$ of finite ground terms (equivalently, finite trees) over $\Sigma$, where equality is the only predicate symbol and the only nonlogical symbols are the constructors in $\Sigma$.

Call a formula positive if it is built from atomic equations using only $\wedge$, $\vee$, $\forall$ and $\exists$ (no occurrence of $\neg$). Two formulas $\varphi(\overline{x})$ and $\psi(\overline{x})$ are equivalent if they define the same relation on $T(\Sigma)$.

Problem. Is there an algorithm that, given an arbitrary first-order formula $\varphi$ over this language, decides whether $\varphi$ is equivalent (over $T(\Sigma)$) to some positive formula, and, whenever this is the case, effectively constructs such an equivalent positive formula $\psi$?

Let $\mathrm{DC} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ denote the set of Diophantine vectors: those $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that there exist constants $\gamma, \tau > 0$ with $|\langle k, \alpha\rangle - m| \geq \gamma |k|^{-\tau}$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}^n \setminus \{0\}$ and every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$.

For each $\alpha \in \mathrm{DC}$, let $\mathcal{U}_\alpha$ denote the set of perturbation potentials $V$ for which the associated exact symplectic map $F_V$ admits a smooth invariant Lagrangian torus on which the dynamics is conjugate to the rigid translation $\theta \mapsto \theta + \alpha$. Define
$$\mathcal{U} = \bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathrm{DC}} \mathcal{U}_\alpha.$$

Determine the smallest real number $k \geq 0$ such that $\mathcal{U}$ is a neighborhood of $0$ in the $C^k$ topology on the space of perturbation potentials.

Background. Fix a first-order signature Σ and a set X of variables. An equational theory E is a set of universally quantified equations between Σ-terms; let =_E denote the congruence on Σ-terms generated by E. A substitution σ is an E-unifier of two terms s and t if σ(s) =_E σ(t). A set U of E-unifiers of (s,t) is called complete if for every E-unifier τ there exists σ ∈ U and a substitution ρ with τ =_E ρ ∘ σ (restricted to the variables of s,t). The theory E is called finitary (for unification) if every solvable E-unification problem admits a finite complete set of E-unifiers.

A presentation E of an equational theory is called syntactic (also called "resolvent") if it admits a finite set of equational axioms such that every equational proof s =_E t can be transformed into one in which the topmost equational step uses an axiom whose head symbol matches the head of s or t (in the standard precise sense of resolvent/syntactic presentations of equational theories).

Problem. Provide a general algorithm that, given any syntactic presentation E of an equational theory which is finitary for unification, and given any E-unification problem, computes a finite and complete set of E-unifiers. Equivalently, derive a uniform unification (and semi-unification) procedure from the axioms of an arbitrary syntactic theory that is guaranteed to terminate with a finite complete set of unifiers whenever the theory is finitary.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite signature and let $E$ be an equational theory on $\Sigma$-terms (for example, the theory $\mathrm{AC}$ asserting associativity and commutativity of one or more binary symbols). A rewrite system modulo $E$ is a finite set $R$ of rewrite rules $\ell 	o r$; a term $t$ rewrites modulo $E$ to $t'$ if there exist $u \equiv_E t$ and $u' \equiv_E t'$ such that $u$ rewrites to $u'$ by one application of a rule in $R$. A term $t$ is said to be ground reducible modulo $E$ by $R$ if every ground (variable-free) instance $t\sigma$ of $t$ is reducible modulo $E$ by some rule of $R$.

The ground reducibility problem modulo $E$ asks: given a finite rewrite system $R$ and a term $t$, decide whether $t$ is ground reducible modulo $E$ by $R$.

For empty $E$ this problem is known to be decidable (in fact EXPTIME-complete), while for $E = \mathrm{AC}$ it is known to be undecidable.

Problem: Characterize precisely those equational theories $E$ for which the ground reducibility problem modulo $E$ is decidable.

Setting. Let $\Sigma$ be a signature and let $\mathrm{Ter}^\infty(\Sigma)$ denote the metric completion of the set of finite first-order terms over $\Sigma$ (equipped with the usual depth-based metric), so that $\mathrm{Ter}^\infty(\Sigma)$ contains both finite and infinite terms. Let $R$ be an orthogonal term rewriting system over $\Sigma$ (left-linear and without critical pairs).

A transfinite reduction of length an ordinal $\alpha$ is a sequence $(t_\beta)_{\beta\le\alpha}$ of terms in $\mathrm{Ter}^\infty(\Sigma)$ together with redex occurrences and rewrite steps $t_\beta \to_{u_\beta} t_{\beta+1}$ for each $\beta<\alpha$, such that for every limit ordinal $\lambda\le\alpha$ the sequence $(t_\beta)_{\beta<\lambda}$ converges to $t_\lambda$ in the metric topology. Such a reduction is called strongly converging if, additionally, at every limit ordinal $\lambda\le\alpha$ the depth of the contracted redex $u_\beta$ tends to infinity as $\beta\uparrow\lambda$.

Given a strongly converging reduction $D: t \twoheadrightarrow t'$ and a set $U$ of redex occurrences in $t$, one can define the residuals $U/D$ of $U$ after $D$ via the standard descendant relation extended continuously to transfinite reductions. A development of $U$ is a (possibly transfinite) reduction that contracts only residuals of redexes in $U$; it is complete if it terminates in a term in which no residual of $U$ remains.

Problem (Transfinite Parallel Moves Lemma). Prove that for every orthogonal term rewriting system $R$, every term $t\in\mathrm{Ter}^\infty(\Sigma)$, every set $U$ of redex occurrences in $t$, and every strongly converging reduction $D: t \twoheadrightarrow t'$:

(i) every complete development of $U$ is strongly converging and all complete developments of $U$ end in the same term $t_U$;

(ii) there exist strongly converging reductions $D': t_U \twoheadrightarrow s$ and a complete development $E: t' \twoheadrightarrow s$ of $U/D$ such that the diagram
$$ t \xrightarrow{D} t',\qquad t \xrightarrow{\text{dev. of }U} t_U \xrightarrow{D'} s,\qquad t' \xrightarrow{E} s $$
commutes, i.e. projecting $D$ over a complete development of $U$ and projecting a complete development of $U$ over $D$ yield reductions that meet in a common term $s$.

Background. Consider an abstract rewriting setting (for example, an orthogonal term rewriting system or the infinitary lambda calculus) in which terms may be infinite and reduction sequences may have transfinite length. A reduction sequence is called Cauchy-convergent if, with respect to the usual metric on (possibly infinite) terms, the sequence of intermediate terms converges at every limit ordinal to the corresponding term in the sequence (no requirement on the depth of contracted redexes is imposed, in contrast to strongly convergent reductions).

Given a set R of redexes in a term t, a development of R is a (possibly transfinite) reduction that contracts only residuals of redexes in R. The classical (finite) Parallel Moves Lemma states: for any two coinitial reductions, one can complete the resulting diagram by contracting the residuals, yielding a common reduct; equivalently, all developments of a set of redexes terminate at the same term.

Problem. Characterize the restricted classes of infinitary rewriting systems and/or restricted classes of Cauchy-convergent (possibly transfinite) reduction sequences for which an infinitary analogue of the Parallel Moves Lemma holds: namely, that for any two coinitial Cauchy-convergent reductions in the class, the residuals can be contracted to produce a common Cauchy-convergent reduct, so that the projection diagram closes. In particular, identify natural syntactic or convergence-theoretic restrictions on the rewrite system, on the form of admissible redex sets, or on the convergence mode, under which such a transfinite Parallel Moves Lemma is provable, given that no such lemma holds for general Cauchy-convergent infinitary reductions.

Let $X$ be an infinite set of variables, and consider the set $X^*$ of finite strings over $X$. Define a binary relation $\hookrightarrow$ on $X^*$ as follows: given two strings $u = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_m$ and $v = y_1 y_2 \cdots y_n$ in $X^*$, write $u \hookrightarrow v$ if and only if there exist a function $\rho : X \to X$ (a renaming) and indices $1 \le j_1 < j_2 < \cdots < j_m \le n$ such that $\rho(x_i) = y_{j_i}$ for every $1 \le i \le m$.

Question: Is the relation $\hookrightarrow$ a well-quasi-ordering on $X^*$? That is, is $\hookrightarrow$ reflexive and transitive, and does every infinite sequence $u_1, u_2, u_3, \ldots$ of elements of $X^*$ contain indices $i < j$ with $u_i \hookrightarrow u_j$?
