Consider the Knuth–Bendix style equational completion procedure: given a finite set E of equations over a term algebra, a reduction ordering >, and a fair completion strategy, completion repeatedly orients equations into rewrite rules, computes critical pairs between rules, and adds normalized critical pairs back as equations. It is known that for some inputs (E, strategy, >) ordinary completion does not terminate.

Define the depth of a position in a term as its distance from the root, and define a depth-bounded variant of completion as follows: fix a natural number d, and during completion only consider critical pairs arising from overlaps at positions of depth at most d (all other critical pairs are ignored), while otherwise running an ordinary fair completion procedure.

Question: Is it true that for every finite set of equations E, every reduction ordering >, and every fair completion strategy, there exists a depth bound d ∈ ℕ such that the depth-bounded completion procedure with bound d terminates? Equivalently, can ordinary completion always be made terminating by restricting attention to critical pairs whose overlap positions have bounded depth?

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a typed $\lambda$-calculus (for instance, the simply typed $\lambda$-calculus, System F, or $\lambda\omega$) over a signature of base types, equipped with the usual rules of $\beta$- (and possibly $\eta$-) reduction. Let $\mathcal{R}$ be a (first-order or higher-order) term rewriting system over an algebraic signature whose function symbols may be typed with the base types of $\mathcal{L}$. The combined system $\mathcal{L} \oplus \mathcal{R}$ is the rewrite relation on well-typed terms built from both the $\lambda$-calculus constructors and the algebraic function symbols, in which a term may be reduced either by a $\beta$-step of $\mathcal{L}$ or by an application of a rewrite rule of $\mathcal{R}$ (with matching performed modulo the typing discipline).

Investigate, in this general setting, sufficient and (where possible) necessary conditions on $\mathcal{L}$ and on $\mathcal{R}$ under which the combined reduction relation of $\mathcal{L} \oplus \mathcal{R}$ enjoys:

(1) confluence (the Church–Rosser property: whenever $t \twoheadrightarrow u$ and $t \twoheadrightarrow v$, there exists $w$ with $u \twoheadrightarrow w$ and $v \twoheadrightarrow w$); and

(2) strong normalization (termination: every reduction sequence starting from a well-typed term is finite).

In particular, determine under what assumptions these two properties are modular, i.e. transfer from $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{R}$ taken separately to their combination $\mathcal{L} \oplus \mathcal{R}$.

The general program is the subject of an extensive literature. Substantial partial results are known: modularity of confluence and termination has been established for combinations of $\lambda\omega$ with first-order (and certain higher-order) rewrite systems under conservativity/non-duplication hypotheses; general frameworks (higher-order rewrite systems, layered rewrite systems, algebraic-functional systems) provide further sufficient conditions. status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem is solved: Ralf Treinen (1996) proved that the first-order theory of one-step rewriting is undecidable in general; subsequent results strengthened this to show undecidability even for linear and/or terminating term rewriting systems (Treinen 1998, and Marcinkowski et al.). representations.normalized:
Let $M$ be a closed symplectic manifold of dimension $2d \ge 2$ with symplectic form $\omega$. Fix a smooth Hamiltonian-type function (or, more generally, a cohomology class) $\psi$, and consider the space $G^1_\psi(M)$ of $C^1$ symplectomorphisms of $M$ preserving $\psi$ (equivalently, the $C^1$ closure of an appropriate class of $\psi$-preserving symplectic diffeomorphisms), endowed with the $C^1$ topology. Inside $G^1_\psi(M)$ let $SE^1_\psi$ denote the (open) subset of stably ergodic, or more precisely, stably-nonzero-exponent diffeomorphisms — those $f$ admitting a $C^1$ neighborhood on which every element has all Lyapunov exponents (with respect to the invariant volume) bounded away from zero almost everywhere.

For $f \in G^1_\psi(M)$ let $\lambda^+_{\max}(f,x)$ denote the largest Lyapunov exponent at a point $x$, and let $\Lambda^+_{\max}(f) = \int \lambda^+_{\max}(f,x)\,d\mathrm{vol}(x)$.

Consider the complement $G^1_\psi(M) \setminus SE^1_\psi$. Decide which of the following alternatives holds:

(a) There is a $C^1$-residual subset $\mathcal{R} \subset G^1_\psi(M) \setminus SE^1_\psi$ on which the maximal Lyapunov exponent vanishes almost everywhere, i.e. $\lambda^+_{\max}(f,x) = 0$ for vol-a.e. $x$ and every $f \in \mathcal{R}$ (equivalently, the metric entropy of $f$ with respect to volume is zero);

(b) There exists a nonempty $C^1$-open set $\mathcal{U} \subset G^1_\psi(M) \setminus SE^1_\psi$ and a constant $c > 0$ such that the topological entropy (or the volume-metric entropy) of every $f \in \mathcal{U}$ is at least $c$.

Determine which of (a) or (b) is true.

Work in untyped combinatory logic (CL) or the untyped λ-calculus. Write →* for the reflexive–transitive closure of (one-step) reduction (β-reduction in λ-calculus, or weak reduction generated by the usual S, K axioms in CL), and ↔* for the symmetric reflexive–transitive closure of reduction (i.e., convertibility).

A term M is called recurrent if for every term N with N ↔* M one has N →* M; equivalently, every term convertible with M reduces to M.

A term M is called hyper-recurrent if every term N with N ↔* M is itself recurrent (so that the entire convertibility class of M consists of recurrent terms, each of which reduces to M).

Question: Does there exist a hyper-recurrent combinator (i.e., a closed term that is hyper-recurrent) in combinatory logic, or in the λ-calculus?

Let →* denote the reflexive–transitive closure of β-reduction (resp. weak reduction in Combinatory Logic), and let ↔* denote β-convertibility. A "ground term" means a closed λ-term, and a set S of closed terms is said to be closed under conversion if M ∈ S and M ↔* N imply N ∈ S.

   { M : Q →* P M }
for some closed terms P and Q. That is, give a necessary and sufficient condition (e.g., in recursion-theoretic or syntactic terms) for a set S of closed λ-terms to be representable in this form.

Let $(A,\to)$ be an abstract reduction system, that is, a set $A$ equipped with a binary relation ${\to}\subseteq A\times A$. Write $\twoheadrightarrow$ for the reflexive–transitive closure of $\to$. The system is Church–Rosser (confluent) if for every $a,b,c\in A$ with $a\twoheadrightarrow b$ and $a\twoheadrightarrow c$ there exists $d\in A$ with $b\twoheadrightarrow d$ and $c\twoheadrightarrow d$.

A labelling of $\to$ is a function $\ell$ assigning to each step in $\to$ an element of a well-founded partially ordered set $(L,\prec)$. For $\alpha\in L$ write $\to_\alpha$ for the steps with label $\alpha$, $\twoheadrightarrow_{\prec\alpha}$ for the reflexive–transitive closure of $\bigcup_{\beta\prec\alpha}\to_\beta$, and $\twoheadrightarrow_{\preceq\alpha} = \twoheadrightarrow_{\prec\alpha}\cup\to_\alpha\cdot\twoheadrightarrow_{\prec\alpha}$ (allowing one step labelled $\alpha$ followed by smaller ones). The system $(A,\to)$ together with the labelling $\ell$ is decreasing if for every local peak $b\,{}_\alpha{\leftarrow}\,a\to_\beta c$ there exists $d\in A$ such that
$$b\;\twoheadrightarrow_{\prec\alpha}\;\cdot\;\to_\beta^{=}\;\cdot\;\twoheadrightarrow_{\prec\alpha\beta}\;d\quad\text{and}\quad c\;\twoheadrightarrow_{\prec\beta}\;\cdot\;\to_\alpha^{=}\;\cdot\;\twoheadrightarrow_{\prec\alpha\beta}\;d,$$
where $\prec\alpha\beta$ means strictly below $\{\alpha,\beta\}$ and $\to^{=}$ denotes at most one step. The system $(A,\to)$ is decreasing Church–Rosser if there exists a well-founded labelled set $(L,\prec)$ and a labelling $\ell$ of $\to$ making it decreasing.

Question: Does every Church–Rosser abstract reduction system $(A,\to)$ admit some well-founded labelling making it decreasing? Equivalently, is the decreasing diagrams method complete for Church–Rosser of abstract reduction systems of arbitrary cardinality?

The problem has been partially resolved. Completeness of the decreasing diagrams method for confluence of countable abstract reduction systems was established (with two labels sufficing whenever the system has the cofinality property), and a 2025 FSCD paper by Ivanov extends completeness to systems of the least uncountable cardinality. Completeness for abstract reduction systems of arbitrary (higher) cardinality appears to remain open, and the analogous completeness question for commutation has a negative answer.

Let an equational theory of semigroups be given by a set $E$ of equations between terms built from a binary associative operation and a (possibly infinite) set of variables, with no constants appearing in $E$. A term-rewriting system $R$ is a set of rewrite rules $\ell \to r$ such that every variable of $r$ occurs in $\ell$. The system $R$ is called canonical (i.e. convergent) if it is terminating and confluent, and it is called reduced if for every rule $\ell \to r \in R$ the right-hand side $r$ is irreducible by $R$ and every proper subterm of $\ell$ is irreducible by $R$. Two rewriting systems are considered equivalent if they generate the same equational theory.

Question: Does there exist an equational theory of semigroups (with no constants appearing in the equations) that admits a finite reduced canonical term-rewriting system which is not equivalent to any finite canonical string-rewriting system (i.e., no presentation by a finite canonical rewriting system on words alone exists), so that the use of genuine term structure is essential? Let an equational theory of semigroups be given by a set $E$ of equations between terms built from a binary associative operation and a (possibly infinite) set of variables, with no constants appearing in $E$. A term-rewriting system $R$ is a set of rewrite rules $\ell \to r$ such that every variable of $r$ occurs in $\ell$. The system $R$ is called canonical (i.e. convergent) if it is terminating and confluent, and it is called reduced if for every rule $\ell \to r \in R$ the right-hand side $r$ is irreducible by $R$ and every proper subterm of $\ell$ is irreducible by $R$. Two rewriting systems are considered equivalent if they generate the same equational theory.

Question: Does there exist an equational theory of semigroups (with no constants appearing in the equations) that admits a finite reduced canonical term-rewriting system which is not equivalent to any finite canonical string-rewriting system (i.e., no presentation by a finite canonical rewriting system on words alone exists), so that the use of genuine term structure is essential? Equivalently: does there exist a semigroup theory possessing a finite reduced canonical term-rewriting system but no finite canonical word-rewriting system?

Let a term rewriting system (TRS) be a finite set R of rewrite rules l → r over a signature Σ and a set of variables V, where l is not a variable and every variable in r occurs in l. A rule l → r is right-linear if every variable occurs at most once in r; the TRS R is right-linear if all its rules are right-linear. For two rules l1 → r1 and l2 → r2 (with disjoint variable renaming) and a non-variable position p of l1, an overlap is a most general unifier of l1|_p and l2 (excluding the trivial overlap of a rule with itself at the root). A TRS is non-overlapping if it has no overlaps. Strengthen this notion as follows: call a TRS strongly non-overlapping if, after renaming the left-hand sides of any two (not necessarily distinct) rules to use pairwise disjoint variables and replacing each variable occurrence in those left-hand sides by a fresh constant (so that variables in different positions become distinct constants), the resulting ground terms have no overlaps; equivalently, no two left-hand sides can be made to unify at a non-variable position even after arbitrarily instantiating their variables independently. The TRS R is confluent if for every term t and every pair of reductions t →* u and t →* v, there exists w with u →* w and v →* w.

Question: Is every strongly non-overlapping right-linear term rewriting system confluent?

representations.normalized:
A term rewriting system (TRS) over a signature $\Sigma$ is a set $R$ of rewrite rules $\ell \to r$ where $\ell, r$ are terms over $\Sigma$ and variables, with $\ell$ not a variable and $\mathrm{Var}(r)\subseteq \mathrm{Var}(\ell)$. The induced one-step rewrite relation $\to_R$ on terms is obtained by closing $R$ under substitutions and contexts. A TRS $(\Sigma,R)$ is confluent if for all terms $s,t_1,t_2$ with $s \to_R^* t_1$ and $s \to_R^* t_2$, there exists a term $u$ such that $t_1 \to_R^* u$ and $t_2 \to_R^* u$.

A property $P$ of TRSs is called modular for a class $\mathcal{C}$ of pairs of TRSs $(R_1,R_2)$ over signatures $\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2$ if: whenever both $R_1$ and $R_2$ satisfy $P$, their combined system $R_1 \cup R_2$ over $\Sigma_1 \cup \Sigma_2$ also satisfies $P$.

It is known (Toyama's theorem) that confluence is modular for disjoint unions, i.e., when $\Sigma_1 \cap \Sigma_2 = \emptyset$. Modularity, however, can fail for non-disjoint combinations such as constructor-sharing systems (where $\Sigma_1 \cap \Sigma_2$ consists only of constructors, i.e., symbols not appearing as the root of any left-hand side) or composable systems.

Problem: Identify general, mathematically interesting sufficient conditions on two TRSs $R_1$ and $R_2$ (possibly sharing function symbols, constructors, or rules) under which the confluence of $R_1$ and the confluence of $R_2$ imply the confluence of the combined system $R_1 \cup R_2$. In particular, give such sufficient conditions that are independent of termination assumptions on $R_1$ and $R_2$.

A many-sorted term-rewriting system consists of a many-sorted signature (each function symbol has a fixed arity together with sort information specifying the sort of each argument and of the result), a set of sorted variables, and a set of rewrite rules l → r in which both l and r are well-sorted terms of the same sort and every variable occurring in r also occurs in l. Such a system R is terminating if there is no infinite rewrite sequence t1 → t2 → t3 → ... .

Given a many-sorted term-rewriting system R, let R' denote the one-sorted term-rewriting system obtained from R by collapsing all sorts into a single sort: the function symbols and rules of R' are exactly those of R, but every function symbol is now regarded as taking arguments of a single common sort, and every variable is of that single sort.

Question: Does termination of R always imply termination of R'? Equivalently, is the property "terminating" persistent under removal of sort information for many-sorted term-rewriting systems?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question of persistence of termination under removal of sort information has been settled. In general, termination of a many-sorted TRS does not imply termination of its one-sorted collapse: counterexamples are known, and positive results are available under additional restrictions (e.g., Zantema's persistence theorem for non-collapsing or non-duplicating systems, with later refinements by Ohlebusch, Aoto–Toyama, and others). Thus the general reduction fails, while restricted cases are well understood.

representations.normalized:
A higher-order rewrite system (in the sense of Nipkow or Klop's combinatory reduction systems) is a rewrite system whose terms are simply-typed lambda-terms (or terms over a signature with binding) and whose rewrite rules l → r are pairs of patterns rewriting modulo α, β, η (with the appropriate pattern restriction on left-hand sides). Two rules overlap when there is a (non-trivial) unifier of a non-variable subterm of one left-hand side with the left-hand side of another rule, after suitable renaming; such an overlap gives rise to a critical pair. A rewrite system is orthogonal if it is left-linear and has no critical pairs. It is weakly orthogonal (or weakly non-overlapping) if it is left-linear and all of its critical pairs are trivial, i.e. of the form ⟨t, t⟩. A rewrite system is confluent if, whenever s →* t₁ and s →* t₂, there exists a term u with t₁ →* u and t₂ →* u.

Problem: Prove or disprove that every weakly orthogonal higher-order rewrite system (in either of the above formalisms) is confluent.

A combinatory reduction system (CRS) is a higher-order rewriting formalism (in the sense of Klop) consisting of an alphabet of function symbols and meta-variables together with a set of rewrite rules of the form l → r, where l and r are meta-terms. A rule is left-linear if every meta-variable occurs at most once in its left-hand side. A CRS is confluent (Church–Rosser) if whenever t →* u and t →* v, there exists w with u →* w and v →* w. Given two CRSs R and S over the same alphabet, we say that the rules of R do not overlap the rules of S if no left-hand side of a rule of R unifies (modulo the usual notion of CRS overlap, excluding overlaps at variable positions) with a non-variable subterm of a left-hand side of a rule of S, and vice versa (so only overlaps within R itself or within S itself are permitted).

Question: Suppose R and S are two left-linear, confluent combinatory reduction systems over the same alphabet such that the rules of R do not overlap the rules of S. Must the union R ∪ S be confluent?

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite signature and let $E$ be a finite set of equations between terms over $\Sigma$ (and a set of variables). Let $>$ be a reduction ordering on terms that is total on ground terms (i.e., a well-founded ordering, stable under contexts and substitutions, such that for any two distinct ground terms $s, t$ either $s > t$ or $t > s$).

Define the ordered rewriting relation $\to_{E,>}$ by: $s \to_{E,>} t$ iff there exist a position $p$ in $s$, an equation $\ell \approx r$ (or $r \approx \ell$) in $E$, and a substitution $\sigma$ such that $s|_p = \ell\sigma$, $t = s[r\sigma]_p$, and $\ell\sigma > r\sigma$. Thus $\to_{E,>}$ is the intersection of one-step replacement of equals (using $E$) with the orientation imposed by $>$.

The relation $\to_{E,>}$ is said to be confluent if for all terms $s, t_1, t_2$ with $s \to_{E,>}^{*} t_1$ and $s \to_{E,>}^{*} t_2$, there exists $u$ with $t_1 \to_{E,>}^{*} u$ and $t_2 \to_{E,>}^{*} u$.

Assume that the existential fragment of the first-order theory of $>$ (the satisfiability problem for conjunctions of ordering constraints $s > t$ over $\Sigma$-terms with variables, interpreted in the ground-term ordering) is decidable.

Question: Under this hypothesis, is the confluence of $\to_{E,>}$ decidable for arbitrary finite $E$?

Consider the following term rewriting system for integer arithmetic, intended to compute sums and products of integers represented in a positional (decimal-like) notation. Integers are built from digit constants together with a successor-like constructor encoding place value, and the system contains rewrite rules implementing addition and multiplication (including handling of carries and of signed integers) of the form proposed by Cohen and Watson for efficient arithmetic by rewriting. The system is known to be locally confluent, but standard termination methods such as the Knuth–Bendix ordering and the recursive path ordering are known not to orient all of its rules.

Problem: Prove or disprove that this rewrite system is terminating, i.e. that there is no infinite sequence of rewrite steps starting from any term.

Let $\Sigma$ be a signature of function symbols (each with a fixed arity), and let $E$ be an equational theory over $\Sigma$, i.e. a set of equations $s = t$ between $\Sigma$-terms, together with its smallest congruence closure $=_E$ under the usual rules of equational logic. Given finite sets of variables $V$ and terms, an $E$-unification problem is a finite set of equations $\Gamma = \{s_1 \stackrel{?}{=} t_1, \dots, s_n \stackrel{?}{=} t_n\}$, and a solution (unifier) is a substitution $\sigma$ such that $s_i\sigma =_E t_i\sigma$ for all $i$. Two variants are distinguished:

(i) $E$-unification with constants: the terms in $\Gamma$ are built from $\Sigma$, variables, and finitely many additional free constants (i.e.\ symbols of arity $0$ not appearing in $E$).

(ii) General $E$-unification: the terms in $\Gamma$ may additionally contain free function symbols of arbitrary arities not appearing in $E$.

Question: Does there exist an equational theory $E$ such that $E$-unification with constants is decidable, while general $E$-unification is undecidable?

Let E be an equational theory over a signature Σ. An E-unification problem with constant restrictions is a finite system of equations Γ = { s_1 =? t_1, …, s_n =? t_n } together with a finite set C of free constants (symbols not occurring in Σ but available for use in s_i, t_i) and a restriction relation R ⊆ V × C, where V is the set of variables occurring in Γ. A substitution σ is a solution of (Γ, R) if σ(s_i) =_E σ(t_i) for every i, and, for every (x, c) ∈ R, the constant c does not occur in σ(x).

The restriction R is called a linear constant restriction if there exists a linear ordering < on V ∪ C such that R = { (x, c) ∈ V × C : c < x }; otherwise R is called an arbitrary constant restriction.

Define:
 • LCR(E) = the class of E-unification problems with linear constant restrictions, together with the decision problem of whether a solution exists;
 • ACR(E) = the analogous class and decision problem for arbitrary constant restrictions.

It is known that decidability of LCR(E) for the component theories is the property that ensures decidability of unification in the union of disjoint equational theories E_1 ∪ E_2.

Problem. Characterize precisely the difference between LCR and ACR. In particular:
 (a) Exhibit, if possible, an equational theory E for which LCR(E) is decidable but ACR(E) is undecidable, or prove that no such theory exists.
 (b) Determine whether decidability (respectively, the unification type) of LCR(E) and of ACR(E) coincide for every equational theory E.
 (c) Give a structural/algorithmic reduction between the two problems whenever such a reduction exists, and identify natural classes of theories E for which LCR(E) and ACR(E) are equivalent.

Web searches confirm that linear constant restrictions are the standard tool for combining unification algorithms over disjoint equational theories (Baader–Schulz), and that algorithms for arbitrary constant restrictions are a stronger requirement. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

Background. In equational logic, given an equational theory E (a set of axioms closed under congruence, symmetry, transitivity, and substitution), a proof of an equation s = t is a finite sequence s = t_0, t_1, …, t_n = t such that each step t_i → t_{i+1} is obtained by replacing a subterm of t_i that is an instance of one side of an axiom in E by the corresponding instance of the other side. Following the framework of n-syntactic equational theories, one assigns to each equation a "syntactic type", defined as the smallest integer n such that every provable equation s = t admits a proof in which at most n of the rewrite steps occur at the top (root) position of the term, where the supremum is taken over all valid proofs minimised in this sense. An equational theory E is said to be n-syntactic when n is finite and equals this maximum number of top-level steps required.

Problem. Determine the syntactic type of the (two-sided) distributivity axiom
  x · (y + z) = (x · y) + (x · z),  (x + y) · z = (x · z) + (y · z),
and, more generally, of the mid-distributivity axiom
  (x + y) · (z + w) = (x · z) + (y · w)
and the three-way distributivity axiom
  (x + y + z) · (u + v + w) = (x · u) + (y · v) + (z · w).
That is, for each of these axioms, find the least n (if any) such that the equational theory generated by the axiom is n-syntactic, or show that no such finite n exists.

There exist well-developed notions of finite automata that recognize formal languages of finite words, of finite (ranked) trees, and of finite directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with robust closure, decidability, and logical-correspondence properties (e.g., closure under Boolean operations, decidable emptiness, and Büchi/Doner/Thatcher–style equivalences with monadic second-order logic on the corresponding structures).

Design an analogous notion of "finite automaton" that operates on arbitrary finite graphs (for instance, finite directed or undirected labelled graphs, possibly with unbounded vertex degree and cycles) and that recognizes classes of finite graphs. The notion should:

1. Coincide with, or naturally specialize to, the classical notions of finite automata on words, trees, and DAGs when the input graph is a word, a tree, or a DAG respectively.
2. Define a class of "regular" graph languages that enjoys good closure properties (closure under union, intersection, and complement) and decidable basic problems (in particular, decidable membership and emptiness).
3. Admit a Myhill–Nerode-style algebraic characterization and/or a logical characterization comparable to the equivalence between regular word/tree languages and monadic second-order definable languages.

Formulate such a notion of graph automaton and prove that it satisfies the above properties, or show that no notion satisfying these requirements can exist.

representations.normalized:
Efficient pattern-matching algorithms are well known in two structural settings:

1. Strings: given a pattern string $p$ of length $m$ and a text string $t$ of length $n$ over a finite alphabet, one can decide whether $p$ occurs as a (contiguous) substring of $t$ in time $O(n+m)$ (e.g., by the Knuth–Morris–Pratt algorithm).

2. Trees: given a labeled, ordered (or unordered) pattern tree $P$ and a labeled host tree $T$, one can decide in polynomial time whether $P$ occurs as a subtree (or as a homomorphic image / rooted subterm) of $T$.

The problem is to develop analogous efficient pattern-matching algorithms in the setting of graphs. Concretely:

Let $G = (V_G, E_G, \ell_G)$ be a finite labeled graph (directed or undirected, with vertex and/or edge labels from a finite alphabet $\Sigma$), called the host, and let $H = (V_H, E_H, \ell_H)$ be another finite labeled graph, called the pattern. Design an algorithm that, given $H$ and $G$ as input, decides whether $H$ occurs in $G$ under a specified notion of occurrence (such as subgraph isomorphism, induced subgraph isomorphism, or graph homomorphism), and that runs as efficiently as possible.

The challenge is to identify natural classes of graphs $G$ and $H$, and natural notions of "occurrence," for which one can design pattern-matching algorithms whose efficiency is comparable to the known linear/polynomial-time algorithms for words and trees, going beyond the general subgraph isomorphism problem which is NP-complete.

The challenge is to identify natural classes of graphs $G$ and $H$, and natural notions of "occurrence," for which one can design pattern-matching algorithms whose efficiency is comparable to the known linear/polynomial-time algorithms for words and trees, going beyond the general subgraph isomorphism problem which is NP-complete.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

This is a broad design challenge rather than a precise conjecture. General subgraph isomorphism is known to be NP-complete, but efficient algorithms exist for restricted graph classes (planar graphs, bounded-treewidth graphs, etc.). Substantial work has been done (e.g., Eppstein's planar subgraph isomorphism, color-coding, graph databases, term graph rewriting), so it is partially addressed in many special cases, but the open-ended task of designing "good" graph pattern-matching algorithms in full generality remains active. Status of the problem as stated is best classified as unknown/ongoing.

A rational word transduction is a (partial multi-valued) relation from finite words over an alphabet $\Sigma$ to finite words over an alphabet $\Gamma$ that is realized by a finite-state one-way transducer; equivalently, it is a relation definable by a rational expression over the product monoid $\Sigma^* \times \Gamma^*$ (with componentwise concatenation, union, and Kleene star). Such a transduction is in general finitely branching: each input word is mapped to finitely or infinitely many output words, but realized by a finite mechanism that produces outputs incrementally.

A graph rewriting system operates on (directed, labeled) finite graphs by replacing occurrences of left-hand-side patterns with right-hand-side patterns according to local rewrite rules. Graph rewriting, like term rewriting and word rewriting, is typically finitely branching.

Problem. Provide a definition of a "graph transduction", i.e. a relation between finite (directed, labeled) graphs, that properly extends the notion of rational word transduction in the following sense: when the input and output graphs are restricted to linear path graphs encoding words over $\Sigma$ and $\Gamma$ respectively, the graph transductions definable in the proposed framework should coincide exactly with the rational word transductions from $\Sigma^*$ to $\Gamma^*$. The definition should be natural with respect to graph rewriting (in particular respecting finite branching) and should support closure properties analogous to those of rational transductions (such as composition and a Kleene-style characterization).

Background. Kruskal's tree theorem states that the class of finite trees labeled from a well-quasi-ordered set, equipped with the homeomorphic embedding relation, is well-quasi-ordered: in any infinite sequence T_1, T_2, T_3, ... of such labeled finite trees, there exist indices i < j such that T_i homeomorphically embeds into T_j. This well-quasi-ordering is a fundamental tool for proving termination of term rewriting systems, since it underlies simplification orderings and the homeomorphic-embedding (Higman/Kruskal) termination arguments.

Problem. Formulate and prove an analogous embedding (well-quasi-ordering) theorem for finite directed graphs whose vertices and/or edges are labeled from a well-quasi-ordered set. Specifically:

(a) Define a notion of "embedding" of one finite (labeled) directed graph into another that
    (i) reduces, in the case where the graphs are trees, to the usual homeomorphic tree embedding,
    (ii) is preserved by the natural operations used in graph rewriting (such as contraction, sharing of subgraphs, and edge subdivision), and
    (iii) has the subgraph property, in the sense that any directed subgraph embeds into the whole graph.

(b) Prove that, under this notion of embedding, the class of finite directed graphs labeled by a well-quasi-ordered alphabet is itself well-quasi-ordered; equivalently, every infinite sequence G_1, G_2, G_3, ... of such directed graphs contains indices i < j with G_i embedding into G_j.

(c) Use this result to derive a termination criterion for graph rewriting systems that strictly generalizes Kruskal-style termination criteria for term rewriting.

The task is to give such a definition of embedding, establish the well-quasi-ordering theorem, and exhibit its application to termination of graph rewriting.

representations.normalized:
Background. A term rewriting system (TRS) over a signature $\Sigma$ consists of a set of rewrite rules $\ell \to r$ between $\Sigma$-terms, with $\ell$ not a variable and $\mathrm{Var}(r) \subseteq \mathrm{Var}(\ell)$. The TRS is terminating if no infinite rewrite sequence $t_0 \to t_1 \to \cdots$ exists. Termination is typically established by exhibiting a well-founded reduction ordering $>$ on terms such that $\ell\sigma > r\sigma$ for every rule and substitution $\sigma$ (e.g. recursive path orderings, Knuth–Bendix orderings, polynomial interpretations, semantic path orderings).

A graph rewriting system that implements a TRS represents terms as directed acyclic graphs (with shared subterms) and replaces redexes by performing in-place rewriting without duplicating shared subgraphs. It is known that whenever the underlying TRS is terminating, the corresponding graph rewriting system is terminating. The converse fails: there exist TRSs whose term-level rewriting is non-terminating but whose graph-rewriting implementation (which avoids duplication of shared subgraphs) is terminating.

Problem. Develop a general method for adapting termination orderings designed for term rewriting so that they apply to graph rewriting systems implementing TRSs. Specifically, devise a class of well-founded orderings on term graphs (or an analogous proof technique) that can prove termination of graph rewriting in those cases where the corresponding term rewriting system is not terminating, while remaining systematic and applicable to standard families of term-rewriting termination orderings.

representations.normalized:
In the so-called "Berlin approach" to (hyper-)graph rewriting (the double-pushout DPO framework over the category of hypergraphs with total morphisms), a hypergraph rewriting system R consists of a finite set of rules L ← K → R, where L, K, R are hypergraphs and the arrows are injective hypergraph morphisms. Rewriting of a hypergraph G to a hypergraph H, written G ⇒_R H, is defined by the standard DPO construction. The system R is confluent if for every hypergraph G and every pair of derivations G ⇒*_R H_1 and G ⇒*_R H_2 there is a hypergraph H' with H_1 ⇒*_R H' and H_2 ⇒*_R H'. It is known that confluence of such systems is undecidable in general, even when the system is terminating (every derivation sequence has finite length).

Problem: Identify nontrivial, broadly applicable structural or syntactic sufficient conditions on a (terminating) hypergraph rewriting system R in the Berlin approach under which confluence of R becomes decidable.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem is open-ended (asking for sufficient conditions), and several partial answers exist. Plump's Critical Pair Lemma gives a sufficient condition for local confluence via joinability of critical pairs with compatibility of node maps. Later work has identified additional decidable subclasses, e.g., terminating systems whose critical pairs satisfy a coverability condition, and decidability has been obtained for DPO hypergraph rewriting with interfaces and for PROP/string-diagram rewriting modulo Frobenius structure. No complete characterization of decidable confluence for general terminating hypergraph rewriting is known.

Let a binary Horn clause be a clause of the form L ← R, where L and R are first-order atoms built from a fixed signature of function symbols and a countable set of variables. Such a clause defines a "cycle" when the atoms L and R are weakly unifiable (i.e. unifiable after renaming variables apart). For two atoms G and F, the cycle unification problem modulo L ← R asks whether there exists a finite number n ≥ 0 and a substitution θ such that θ unifies G with the atom obtained by n successive resolution steps starting from F using only the clause L ← R; equivalently, whether the goal ←G has an SLD-refutation using only the single binary clause L ← R from an initial goal involving F.

Question: Is the cycle unification problem decidable? That is, does there exist an algorithm that, given a binary Horn clause L ← R and two atoms G and F, decides whether G and F are cycle-unifiable modulo L ← R?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Cycle unification is equivalent to the derivation/halting problem for a single binary Horn clause, which was shown to be undecidable by Devienne, Lebègue and Routier (1993) ("Halting problem of one binary Horn clause is undecidable", STACS 1993). Hence the general cycle unification problem is undecidable; only restricted subclasses (e.g. matching cycles studied by Hsiang, Bol and others, and infinite-term methods of Salzer) are known to be decidable.

A calculus of explicit substitutions extends the ordinary λ-calculus by adding a new syntactic constructor for substitutions, together with rewrite rules that compute substitutions step by step (rather than performing meta-level substitution atomically as in β-reduction). Call such a rewrite system:

- confluent (on the chosen class of terms, e.g. on open terms with substitution variables) if whenever a term t reduces to t₁ and to t₂, there exists a common term s with t₁ ↠ s and t₂ ↠ s;
- preserving strong normalization (PSN) with respect to the λ-calculus if every λ-term that is strongly normalizing under β-reduction is also strongly normalizing under the rewrite rules of the calculus of explicit substitutions.

Question: Does there exist a calculus of explicit substitutions that simulates β-reduction and is simultaneously confluent (on open terms) and preserves strong normalization?

The problem has been solved affirmatively. Several calculi of explicit substitutions have been designed that are both confluent (on open terms) and preserve strong normalization, including λυ (Lescanne), λse extended by Kamareddine–Ríos to be confluent on open terms, λζ (Muñoz), and the λd / λdn calculi with weak composition. Consider first-order term rewriting systems over a signature $\Sigma$ and a countable set of variables. Unification with infinite terms (unification without the occur-check, sometimes denoted $\mathrm{Unif}^{\infty}$) is the unification procedure obtained from the standard syntactic unification algorithm by omitting the occur-check step; it may succeed and return a (possibly infinite, rational) unifier in cases where ordinary syntactic unification fails. A rewrite system $R$ is called nonoverlapping under unification with infinite terms if no two left-hand sides of rules of $R$ (taken with disjoint variables, and including the case of a rule with itself at a nonroot position) have overlapping redexes when unification is performed in this extended sense — that is, every potential critical pair is excluded already at the level of $\mathrm{Unif}^{\infty}$.

A rewrite system is said to have unique normal forms if whenever two normal forms $s$ and $t$ are convertible via the symmetric–transitive closure of the one-step rewrite relation, then $s = t$.

Question: Does every term rewriting system that is nonoverlapping under unification with infinite terms have unique normal forms?

Searches surface related work on uniqueness of normal forms for nonoverlapping systems (Chew's theorem and its refinements), and on distinguishing occur-check nonoverlaps (O-nonoverlap) from inhomogeneity nonoverlaps (I-nonoverlap). A term rewriting system (TRS) is a pair $(\Sigma, R)$ where $\Sigma$ is a signature of function symbols (each with an arity) and $R$ is a set of rewrite rules $\ell \to r$ where $\ell, r$ are terms over $\Sigma$ and a set of variables, with every variable in $r$ occurring in $\ell$. The rewrite relation $\to_R$ on terms is the closure of $R$ under substitution and context. A term is a normal form if no rule applies to it or any of its subterms.

For a term $t$ with a designated redex occurrence (or, more generally, an unevaluated position), the position is called needed if every reduction sequence from $t$ to a normal form must, at some point, reduce a residual of that position. A rewriting strategy is normalizing if, applied to any term having a normal form, it eventually reaches one.

Huet and Lévy introduced the notion of strong sequentiality: roughly, a TRS is strongly sequential if, for every term not in normal form, one can identify (using only the left-hand sides of the rules, viewed via the "$\omega$-reduction" approximation that replaces variables and subterms not matching any pattern by a constant $\omega$) an index, i.e., a position whose reduction is necessary in every normalizing reduction. Strong sequentiality guarantees the existence of an effectively computable, optimal (call-by-need) reduction strategy.

Problem. Is strong sequentiality a decidable property of arbitrary term rewriting systems? That is, does there exist an algorithm which, given as input a finite term rewriting system $(\Sigma, R)$ (without any restriction such as left-linearity, orthogonality, or non-overlapping), decides whether $(\Sigma, R)$ is strongly sequential?

Let R be a finite term rewrite system over a finite signature Σ whose termination can be established by some simplification ordering (i.e., R is simply terminating). For a term t, let dl_R(t) denote the maximal length of any rewrite derivation t = t_0 →_R t_1 →_R … →_R t_n, and define the derivation-length function

  Dl_R(n) = max { dl_R(t) : t ∈ T(Σ), |t| ≤ n },

where |t| is the size (number of symbols) of t.

The Hardy hierarchy (H_α)_{α an ordinal} is defined by H_0(n) = n, H_{α+1}(n) = H_α(n+1), and H_λ(n) = H_{λ[n]}(n) for limit ordinals λ with a fixed fundamental sequence (λ[n])_{n<ω}. A function f : ℕ → ℕ is called multiply recursive iff it is primitive recursive in the Ackermann function, equivalently iff it is eventually dominated by H_α for some α < ω^ω.

Question: For every finite, simply terminating rewrite system R over a finite signature, is the derivation-length function Dl_R bounded above by a Hardy function H_α with α below some fixed recursive ordinal (in particular, can Dl_R always be bounded by a multiply recursive function)? Equivalently, determine the optimal ordinal bound α such that every simply terminating finite rewrite system has Dl_R eventually dominated by H_α.

A ternary Boolean algebra is an algebraic structure (A, f, ¬) where f: A³ → A is a ternary operation and ¬: A → A is a unary operation satisfying the equations:
  (1) f(x, y, y) = y,
  (2) f(x, y, ¬x) = y,
  (3) f(f(v, w, x), y, f(v, w, z)) = f(v, w, f(x, y, z)),
together with the permutative (symmetry) equations
  f(x, y, z) = f(x, z, y) = f(y, x, z) = f(y, z, x) = f(z, x, y) = f(z, y, x).

An extended rewrite system modulo a set E of equations is a pair (R, E) consisting of a term rewriting system R together with the equations E, where rewriting is performed on E-equivalence classes (i.e., the relation →_{R/E} or →_{R,E}). The system is convergent if it is terminating and confluent modulo E (so every term has a unique normal form up to E-equivalence).

Question: Does there exist a convergent extended term rewriting system (R, E) that decides the equational theory of ternary Boolean algebra, in which E contains the permutative equations of f listed above (so that f is treated as fully symmetric in its three arguments)?

Work in the simply typed λ-calculus modulo αβη-conversion. A *higher-order pattern* (in the sense of Miller) is a simply typed λ-term in βη-normal form such that every free (existential) variable F occurs only in subterms of the form F(x₁,…,xₙ) where x₁,…,xₙ are pairwise distinct bound variables.

An equational theory E is given by a finite set of equations s ≈ t between simply typed λ-terms. E is called *variable-preserving* if for every equation s ≈ t in E, the set of free variables occurring in s equals the set of free variables occurring in t (and, in the usual formulation, each free variable occurs the same number of times on both sides — i.e., the equations are linearity- and variable-preserving). Let =_E denote the smallest congruence (closed under αβη) containing E.

The *pattern E-unification problem* takes as input two higher-order patterns s and t (over a common signature and typing context) and asks whether there exists a substitution σ (mapping free variables to simply typed λ-terms of matching type) such that σ(s) =_E σ(t).

Question: Is pattern E-unification decidable for every variable-preserving equational theory E? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform decision procedure that, given any finite variable-preserving equational presentation E and any two higher-order patterns s, t, decides whether s and t are E-unifiable?

Background. In equational and first-order theorem proving with equality, ordered paramodulation is an inference rule that restricts paramodulation steps using a reduction ordering ≻ on terms. Classical completeness results (e.g., for refutational theorem proving on clauses with equality) require ≻ to be a simplification ordering (a well-founded, monotonic rewrite ordering having the subterm property) that is total on ground terms, or at least totalizable. Several related saturation-based strategies (superposition, basic paramodulation, Knuth–Bendix completion, etc.) impose analogous restrictions on the ordering used to orient equations and prune inferences.

Problem. Determine whether the standard restrictions imposed on the term ordering ≻ in ordered paramodulation and in related ordered theorem-proving strategies can be relaxed while preserving refutational completeness. Specifically:

(a) Can the requirement that ≻ be total (or totalizable) on ground terms be dropped, so that ordered paramodulation remains refutationally complete for arbitrary sets of equational (or first-order with equality) clauses when ≻ is only required to be, say, a well-founded rewrite ordering, or merely a well-founded ordering?

(b) Can monotonicity of ≻ also be dropped, yielding completeness of ordered paramodulation for non-monotonic well-founded orderings?

(c) Can such relaxations be made compatible with the standard redundancy and simplification techniques (demodulation, subsumption, tautology deletion) used in practical saturation-based provers, and analogously extended to other ordered strategies such as superposition and Knuth–Bendix completion?

Provide either completeness proofs under the weakest possible hypotheses on ≻ or counterexamples showing that the corresponding hypotheses cannot be removed.

A TRS (Σ, R) is called totally terminating if there exists a total monotonic well-ordering > on the set of ground terms over Σ (extended, if needed, by sufficiently many constants) such that ℓσ > rσ for every rule ℓ → r in R and every ground substitution σ; equivalently, termination of R can be shown by interpreting terms in a totally ordered well-founded monotone algebra.

Given two totally terminating TRSs (Σ₁, R₁) and (Σ₂, R₂) with Σ₁ ∩ Σ₂ = ∅, is their disjoint union (Σ₁ ∪ Σ₂, R₁ ∪ R₂) necessarily totally terminating?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

General termination is known to be non-modular under disjoint unions of TRSs, but the specific question of whether total termination (existence of a monotonic well-ordering of ground terms) is preserved under disjoint unions does not appear to have a clearly documented resolution in available sources. No definitive solution was located via web search.

Consider the explicit substitution calculus λυ, a first-order rewriting system implementing β-reduction via explicit substitution operators on de Bruijn-indexed λ-terms. The calculus λυ is known to preserve strong β-normalisation (PSN) and to be confluent on closed (ground) terms, but it is not confluent on open terms (terms with meta-variables).

Allow the signature of λυ to be infinite and allow the rewrite rules to be replaced by rule schemes (i.e. infinite families of rules parametrised in a uniform way). Under these relaxations, does there exist an extension of λυ which simultaneously:

(1) is confluent on open terms (terms containing meta-variables),
(2) simulates one-step β-reduction of the λ-calculus,
(3) preserves strong β-normalisation, and
(4) implements the substitution operation of the λ-calculus?

Determine whether such an extension exists.

Let Σ be a finite signature and let T(Σ, X) denote the set of first-order terms over Σ with variables in X. Fix a total precedence > on Σ, and let >_lpo denote the induced lexicographic path ordering on T(Σ, X): namely, s >_lpo t iff (i) t is a variable occurring strictly in s, or (ii) s = f(s_1,...,s_n), t = g(t_1,...,t_m), and either some s_i ≥_lpo t, or f > g and s >_lpo t_j for every j, or f = g and (s_1,...,s_n) >_lpo^lex (t_1,...,t_m) with s >_lpo t_j for every j.

It is known that satisfiability of conjunctions of ordering atoms s >_lpo t and s = t (where s, t ∈ T(Σ, X)) over total precedences is decidable.

Now let R be a fixed finite term rewrite system over Σ. Call a term s irreducible by R if no subterm of s is an instance of any left-hand side of R. Consider formulas built from atoms of the form
  s >_lpo t,    s = t,    IRR_R(s),
where IRR_R(s) is the predicate "s is irreducible by R", combined by conjunction (and possibly negation/disjunction).

Problem: Is the satisfiability of such ordering constraints over the lexicographic path ordering, taken in conjunction with irreducibility predicates IRR_R for a given rewrite system R, decidable?

Background. Fix a ranked signature Σ of function symbols, each with a fixed arity. A term over Σ (and a set X of first-order variables) is built as usual from variables and function symbols respecting arities. A context is a term containing exactly one occurrence of a distinguished "hole" symbol □ (of arity 0); applying a context C to a term t, written C[t], denotes the term obtained by replacing □ in C by t.

Context unification. Introduce a separate set of context variables, each of which ranges over contexts. A context unification problem is a finite system of equations s_1 = t_1, …, s_n = t_n where each s_i, t_i is a term built from Σ, first-order variables, and applications F(u) of context variables F to terms u. A solution assigns a ground context to each context variable and a ground term to each first-order variable so that, after substitution, every equation s_i = t_i becomes a syntactic identity of ground terms.

Linear second-order unification. Consider simply-typed lambda-terms in β-normal η-long form whose free higher-order variables have order at most 2. A linear second-order unification problem is a finite system of equations between such terms in which every bound variable of every λ-abstraction occurs exactly once in the body of that abstraction. Solutions are substitutions of linear second-order λ-terms making each equation βη-equal.

Question. Is the satisfiability problem decidable
 (a) for context unification, and
 (b) for linear second-order unification?

Let $M$ be a finitely generated monoid with a finite generating set $\Sigma$, and let $\pi:\Sigma^*\to M$ be the canonical surjection. An automatic structure for $(M,\Sigma)$ consists of a regular language $L\subseteq \Sigma^*$ such that $\pi(L)=M$, together with the requirement that for each $a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}$ the relation $\{(u,v)\in L\times L : \pi(ua)=\pi(v)\}$ is recognised by a synchronous two-tape finite automaton over $\Sigma$. The monoid $M$ is called automatic if such a regular language $L$ exists. A subset $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ is called a cross-section (with respect to $\pi$) if $\pi$ restricts to a bijection $L\to M$; it is called prefix-closed if every prefix of every word in $L$ also lies in $L$.

Question: Does every automatic monoid admit an automatic structure $L$ such that $L$ is a prefix-closed cross-section?

Consider the free monoid generated by an alphabet consisting of finitely many constants together with countably many variables. A word equation is a pair (U, V) of finite strings over constants and variables, usually written U = V. A solution to a word equation is an assignment of finite strings of constants to the variables such that, after substitution, the two sides U and V become identical strings in the free monoid. The word equation satisfiability (word unification) problem asks, given a word equation, whether it admits a solution.

It is known that this problem is decidable, NP-hard, and contained in PSPACE (in fact in nondeterministic linear space). Determine the exact computational complexity of the word equation satisfiability problem. In particular, decide whether the problem belongs to NP, or is PSPACE-complete, or lies strictly between these classes.

Fix a finite first-order signature Σ and a term rewrite system R over Σ, i.e. a finite set of rewrite rules ℓ → r with ℓ, r ∈ T(Σ, V), where V is a countable set of variables. Let T(Σ) denote the set of ground (variable-free) terms over Σ. The theory of one-step rewriting by R is the first-order theory of the structure whose domain is T(Σ) and which is equipped with a single binary predicate →_R defined by

  s →_R t  iff  there exist a position p in s, a rule ℓ → r in R, and a substitution σ such that s|_p = ℓσ and t = s[rσ]_p.

The existential fragment of this theory consists of all true first-order sentences of the form ∃x_1 … ∃x_n φ(x_1, …, x_n) where φ is quantifier-free. The positive fragment consists of all true sentences built from atomic formulas using only ∧, ∨, ∃, and ∀ (i.e., without negation).

Question: Is the existential fragment of the theory of one-step rewriting decidable, uniformly in R? Is the positive fragment of the theory of one-step rewriting decidable, uniformly in R?

(Equivalently: is there an algorithm that, given a finite signature Σ, a finite rewrite system R over Σ, and an existential — respectively positive — first-order sentence in the language with equality and the binary predicate →_R, decides whether the sentence holds in the structure (T(Σ), →_R)?)

For the closely related parallel one-step rewriting predicate, the existential fragment was shown undecidable. However, for the standard one-step rewriting predicate the decidability of the existential fragment, and of the positive fragment, does not appear to have been settled in the literature; it is still listed as an open question.

Work in the simply typed lambda-calculus with βη-equality. A higher-order matching problem is a finite set of equations {s_i = t_i : i = 1,...,n}, where each s_i and t_i is a simply typed lambda-term, the right-hand sides t_i are ground (i.e., contain no free variables), and both sides of each equation have the same type. A solution is a substitution σ, mapping the free variables of the s_i to typed lambda-terms, such that σ(s_i) =_{βη} t_i for every i.

Question: Is it decidable, given an arbitrary such higher-order matching problem (with no restriction on the order of the types involved), whether a solution σ exists?

The result appeared as "Decidability of higher-order matching" in Logical Methods in Computer Science, vol. 5(3), 2009 (arXiv:0907.3804), using a game-theoretic characterisation.

Question: Is higher-order matching, in this generalized setting where types are built from several base types and several type variables, decidable?

representations.normalized:
A string rewriting system over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is a finite set $R$ of rules $\ell \to r$ with $\ell, r \in \Sigma^*$. The induced one-step rewrite relation $\to_R$ on $\Sigma^*$ is defined by $u \ell w \to_R u r w$ for all $u, w \in \Sigma^*$ and all $(\ell \to r) \in R$; let $\to_R^*$ denote its reflexive-transitive closure. The system $R$ is called terminating if there is no infinite chain $x_0 \to_R x_1 \to_R x_2 \to_R \cdots$, and looping if there exist $x \in \Sigma^*$ and $u, v \in \Sigma^*$ with $x \to_R^+ u x v$ (where $\to_R^+$ is the transitive closure of $\to_R$).

Question: Does there exist a one-rule string rewriting system $R = \{\ell \to r\}$ over some finite alphabet that is non-terminating but non-looping (i.e., admits an infinite rewrite sequence but no rewrite sequence of the form $x \to_R^+ u x v$)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether a non-terminating, non-looping one-rule string rewriting system exists is widely cited as an open problem. McNaughton conjectured the answer is negative (in the one-rule case, non-termination should imply looping). Related work has constructed loops of superexponential length and analyzed restricted classes (e.g., systems with one pair of overlaps, normalizing cases), but no resolution of the general one-rule problem has been published as of recent surveys.

representations.normalized:
A proper combinator is defined by an equation of the form C x_1 x_2 ... x_n = t, where t is an applicative term built from the variables x_1, ..., x_n using only application (no abstraction), and every variable occurring in t is among x_1, ..., x_n. The natural number n is called the order of the combinator. For example, the combinator K defined by K x y = x has order 2.

Given a finite set S of proper combinators, the word problem for S is the problem of deciding, for two closed applicative terms built from the symbols in S, whether they are equal in the equational theory generated by the defining equations of the members of S (equivalently, whether they have a common reduct under the induced rewriting system).

Question: Is the word problem decidable for every finite set S consisting of proper combinators each of order strictly less than 3?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is listed as RTA open problem #96, originally posed by Statman (1989). The word problem for order-1 combinators is easy, and partial results exist (Statman 1989, 2000) for specific combinators such as the Lark and for co-compositors, but the general decidability for all proper combinators of order less than 3 taken together remains unresolved as of the most recent listings.

Consider combinatory logic over a single constant S. Terms are built from S using a binary application operation, written by juxtaposition and associated to the left, so that t₁ t₂ ⋯ tₙ abbreviates (⋯((t₁ t₂) t₃) ⋯ tₙ). The reduction rule for S is

    S x y z  →  x z (y z),

applied to any subterm matching the left-hand side, where x, y, z range over arbitrary terms. Let → denote one-step reduction and let =_S denote the equivalence relation generated by →, i.e. the smallest equivalence relation on terms containing →.

A ground S-term is a term built only from the constant S (no variables). The word problem for the S-combinator asks:

    Is there an algorithm which, given two ground S-terms t and u, decides whether t =_S u?

Determine whether this word problem is decidable.

representations.normalized:
Let Σ be a finite first-order signature consisting of function symbols (each with a fixed arity) and let T(Σ) denote the set of ground terms over Σ. A Knuth–Bendix ordering on T(Σ) is determined by:
(i) a weight function w that assigns a non-negative real weight to each symbol of Σ, such that all constants have weight at least some fixed positive constant w₀ > 0, and at most one unary function symbol may have weight 0 (and if such a unary symbol f exists, it must be maximal in the precedence);
(ii) a strict total order ≫ ("precedence") on Σ.
The weight of a ground term t, denoted W(t), is defined by W(f(t₁,…,tₙ)) = w(f) + Σᵢ W(tᵢ). The Knuth–Bendix ordering >_{KBO} on T(Σ) is the strict order defined recursively by s >_{KBO} t iff either
 (a) W(s) > W(t), or
 (b) W(s) = W(t) and one of the following holds:
   – s = f^k(t) for the maximal unary symbol f of weight 0, with k ≥ 1;
   – s = f(s₁,…,sₘ), t = g(t₁,…,tₙ), and f ≫ g;
   – s = f(s₁,…,sₙ), t = f(t₁,…,tₙ), and there exists i with s₁=t₁,…,s_{i−1}=t_{i−1} and sᵢ >_{KBO} tᵢ.

Consider the structure (T(Σ); =, >_{KBO}, {f}_{f∈Σ}) — the ground-term algebra of Σ equipped with the relation >_{KBO}. Decide:

Is there an algorithm which, given as input a finite signature Σ, a weight function w, and a precedence ≫, decides whether an arbitrary first-order sentence φ (in the language of this structure) is true in (T(Σ); =, >_{KBO})?

Background. Kruskal's Tree Theorem states that the set of finite trees with labels from a well-quasi-ordered set is itself well-quasi-ordered under the homeomorphic embedding relation that respects labels. Harvey Friedman strengthened this by imposing a gap condition: for an embedding f from a labeled tree s into a labeled tree t (where labels lie in a quasi-ordered set with a distinguished partition or ordering), one requires that for every node x of s and every node y of t lying strictly on the path between f(x) and f(parent of x) (the "gap"), the label of y is constrained (typically, no smaller than the label of f(x), or restricted to a given subset of labels). Friedman proved, and I. Kříž extended, well-quasi-ordering theorems for finite trees under such gap-embedding relations.

A term rewriting system R over a signature Σ is a finite set of rewrite rules l → r on terms. R is terminating if there is no infinite rewrite sequence t₁ → t₂ → t₃ → ⋯. A termination method is a syntactic/semantic criterion that proves termination of classes of term rewriting systems, typically by exhibiting a well-founded order on terms compatible with rewriting and closed under contexts and substitutions.

Problem. Design new termination methods for term rewriting systems whose well-foundedness arguments are based on the gap-embedding well-quasi-ordering theorems of Friedman and Kříž (and their extensions). Specifically, produce term orderings on terms (or labeled trees representing terms) that:
  (i) are well-founded, with well-foundedness justified via the Friedman–Kříž gap-embedding theorems;
  (ii) are stable under substitutions and closed under contexts (i.e., are rewrite orders);
  (iii) properly extend the termination power of orderings based on the standard Kruskal Tree Theorem (such as the recursive path ordering and simplification orderings); and
  (iv) admit effective procedures for proving termination of concrete rewrite systems.

Let Σ be a finite ranked signature, and let AC ⊆ Σ be a distinguished subset of binary function symbols, each declared to be associative and commutative. Terms over Σ are considered modulo the congruence ≡_AC generated by the axioms f(x,y) ≡ f(y,x) and f(f(x,y),z) ≡ f(x,f(y,z)) for every f ∈ AC.

An AC-tree automaton is a tuple A = (Σ, AC, Q, Q_f, Δ), where Q is a finite set of states, Q_f ⊆ Q is a set of final states, and Δ is a finite set of transition rules of the form f(q_1, …, q_n) → q, where f ∈ Σ has arity n and q_1, …, q_n, q ∈ Q. The move relation →_A is defined on terms over Σ ∪ Q by rewriting with Δ, taken modulo ≡_AC (so that the transitions for AC-symbols apply up to associativity and commutativity of their arguments). A ground term t over Σ is accepted by A if t →_A* q for some q ∈ Q_f. The language L(A) is the set of ≡_AC-equivalence classes of accepted ground terms; such a language is called AC-recognizable.

Decide the following two problems:

(1) Universality. Given an AC-tree automaton A over (Σ, AC), is L(A) equal to the set of all ≡_AC-equivalence classes of ground terms over Σ?

(2) Inclusion. Given two AC-tree automata A_1 and A_2 over the same (Σ, AC), is L(A_1) ⊆ L(A_2)?

Determine, for the class of AC-recognizable tree languages (defined by general, not necessarily monotone, AC-tree automata as above), whether universality and inclusion are decidable.

Define a polyomino to be a subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ formed by a strongly connected (edge-connected) union of axis-aligned closed unit squares centered at points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$. A tiling of the plane by congruent copies $\{T_i\}$ of such a polyomino $P$ is called isohedral if for every pair of tiles $T_i, T_j$ there is a symmetry of the tiling (an isometry of $\mathbb{R}^2$ preserving the entire tiling) that maps $T_i$ to $T_j$. Let $n$ denote the number of unit-length edges on the boundary of $P$.

Is there an algorithm that, given $P$ specified by its boundary word of length $n$, decides in $O(n)$ time whether $P$ admits an isohedral tiling of the plane?

representations.normalized:
Consider trees built from a finite ranked alphabet in which some binary function symbols are declared associative and commutative (AC). Two terms are considered equal modulo AC if one can be transformed into the other by repeatedly applying the associativity and commutativity axioms for the AC symbols. A tree language L (a set of equivalence classes of ground terms modulo AC) is said to be AC-recognizable if there exists a finite tree automaton that accepts a set of representatives of L closed under the AC axioms, in the standard sense of tree automata modulo associativity and commutativity.

It is known that the inclusion problem "Given two AC-recognizable tree languages L₁ and L₂, is L₁ ⊆ L₂?" is undecidable.

Question: Is the universality problem decidable for AC-recognizable tree languages? That is, given a finite description (e.g., an AC tree automaton) of an AC-recognizable tree language L over a ranked alphabet Σ, can one algorithmically decide whether L equals the set of all ground terms over Σ modulo AC?

Let $F$ be a finite ranked alphabet and consider possibly infinite terms over $F$. A first-order substitution of arity $n$ is an operation that takes a term $t$ together with $n$ argument terms $u_1,\dots,u_n$ and returns the term obtained from $t$ by simultaneously replacing all occurrences of the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ in $t$ by $u_1,\dots,u_n$ respectively. Extend $F$ by symbols for first-order substitutions, indexed by the tuples of variables to which substitutions are made, and consider the evaluation mapping $\mathrm{ev}$ that sends a (possibly infinite) term over this extended alphabet to the (possibly infinite) term over $F$ obtained by performing all substitutions.

Regard $\mathrm{ev}$ as being implemented by a canonical term rewrite system $R$ whose rules express how a substitution symbol is pushed through a constructor in $F$; the normal forms of $R$ are exactly the terms over $F$.

Problem: Investigate the normalization behaviour of $R$ in the setting of monadic second-order (MSO) logic on terms. Concretely, determine whether the evaluation mapping $\mathrm{ev}$ defined by $R$ is MSO-compatible in the following sense: for every MSO formula $\varphi(\bar X)$ interpreted on terms over $F$, there exists an MSO formula $\psi(\bar X)$ interpreted on terms over the extended alphabet such that for every input term $t$ (finite or infinite) and every tuple $\bar S$ of sets of positions of $t$, one has
$$\mathrm{ev}(t) \models \varphi(\bar S') \iff t \models \psi(\bar S),$$
under a fixed MSO-definable correspondence between positions of $t$ and positions of $\mathrm{ev}(t)$. Characterise the classes of input terms (for example, regular terms, or terms generated by safe higher-order recursion schemes of a given level) for which this MSO-compatibility holds, and use it to identify classes of infinite terms whose monadic second-order theory is decidable.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Courcelle and Knapik (2002) proved that the evaluation of first-order substitution on infinite terms is monadic second-order compatible, yielding decidability of the MSO theory of the resulting hierarchy of terms (which coincides with level-2 safe recursion schemes of Knapik–Niwiński–Urzyczyn). Subsequent work by Ong, and by Salvati–Walukiewicz, extended such MSO-compatibility / decidability results to higher levels of recursion schemes. The general programme of investigating normalization by canonical term rewriting in the MSO setting therefore has substantial positive results, but it is not closed as a single problem.

A polycube is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ formed by a strongly connected union of finitely many axis-aligned closed unit cubes centered at points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ (strong connectivity meaning that the union remains connected after removing all cubes' shared edges and vertices, i.e., adjacent cubes share a full 2-dimensional face). A tiling of $\mathbb{R}^3$ by congruent copies of a polycube $P$ is a covering of $\mathbb{R}^3$ by isometric copies of $P$ with pairwise disjoint interiors. Such a tiling is called isohedral if its symmetry group acts transitively on the tiles; equivalently, for any two tiles there is an isometry of $\mathbb{R}^3$ that preserves the tiling globally and maps one tile to the other.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a polycube $P$ (described, say, by the list of lattice positions of its constituent unit cubes), decides in time polynomial in the number of unit cubes of $P$ whether $P$ admits an isohedral tiling of $\mathbb{R}^3$?

Let $\mathcal{G}$ denote a class of finite graphs (possibly with labeled or distinguished "source" vertices) endowed with a fixed finite set $\Omega$ of natural operations such as disjoint union, parallel composition, source renaming, source fusion, and addition of edges between sources. Viewing $(\mathcal{G},\Omega)$ as an algebra, terms built from variables and operations in $\Omega$ are called graph expressions, and two graph expressions are equivalent if they evaluate to isomorphic graphs for every assignment of graphs to the variables.

Problem: Provide an equational axiomatization of this equivalence. More precisely, exhibit a (preferably finite, or at least recursive) set $E$ of equations between graph expressions such that two graph expressions $t_1$ and $t_2$ define isomorphic graphs (for every assignment) if and only if the equation $t_1 = t_2$ is derivable from $E$ by the usual rules of equational logic. Settle whether such an axiomatization exists for the chosen signature $\Omega$, and if so describe it explicitly; in particular determine whether the equational theory of $(\mathcal{G},\Omega)$ is finitely based.

  aa → bc,  bb → ac,  cc → ab.

A rewrite step transforms a finite string s ∈ Σ* into a string t ∈ Σ* if t is obtained from s by replacing one occurrence of a left-hand side of a rule (a substring of the form aa, bb, or cc) by the corresponding right-hand side (bc, ac, or ab respectively). Starting from an arbitrary finite string over Σ and applying rewrite steps repeatedly (choosing at each step which redex to rewrite), does there exist an infinite rewrite sequence, or does every such sequence terminate after finitely many steps? Equivalently, prove or disprove that the string rewriting system R is terminating.

Let R and S be term rewrite systems (TRSs) over a common signature. The relation →_{R/S} is defined as →_S* ∘ →_R ∘ →_S*, and R is said to be relatively terminating with respect to S (written SN(R/S)) if there is no infinite →_{R/S}-derivation, equivalently, no infinite →_{R∪S}-derivation containing infinitely many →_R-steps.

The dependency pair (DP) method of Arts and Giesl provides a powerful technique for proving termination of an ordinary TRS R: from R one constructs the set DP(R) of dependency pairs (pairs ⟨l#, t#⟩ where l → C[t] ∈ R, t is a subterm of the right-hand side whose root is a defined symbol of R, and # marks the root), and SN(→_R) holds iff there is no infinite minimal chain of dependency pairs. This reduces termination of R to the absence of infinite chains, enabling modular reasoning via the DP framework (dependency graphs, reduction pairs, subterm criterion, etc.).

Problem: Develop a genuine dependency pair method tailored to relative termination. Concretely, given TRSs R and S, define a notion of "relative dependency pairs" DP_rel(R, S) (and an associated notion of relative chains) such that:

(1) SN(R/S) holds if and only if there is no infinite relative chain over DP_rel(R, S);
(2) the resulting framework admits the usual DP processors (dependency graph decomposition, reduction pair processor, subterm criterion, etc.) adapted soundly to the relative setting; and
(3) the method strictly extends both the classical DP method for ordinary termination (recovering it when S = ∅) and currently known sufficient criteria that reduce relative termination to ordinary DP problems.

Provide such a framework, or prove that no such characterization with the analogous modular properties exists.

A polyomino is a finite, edge-connected union of unit squares in the integer lattice. A tiling of the plane is a covering of the Euclidean plane by isometric copies of a prototile (in this case, a polyomino) such that the interiors of distinct copies are disjoint. Given a tiling T, two tiles are said to be in the same transitivity class if there is a symmetry of T (i.e., an isometry of the plane that maps T to itself) carrying one tile to the other. A tiling T is called k-isohedral if k is the smallest number of transitivity classes of T under its symmetry group; equivalently, k is the smallest integer such that the tiles of T can be partitioned into k parts where for any two tiles in the same part there is a symmetry of T mapping one to the other.

Consider the decision problem: given a polyomino P (encoded, e.g., by its boundary word or the list of its cells) and a positive integer k, determine whether there exists a k-isohedral tiling of the plane by isometric copies of P.

Question: Is this decision problem, parameterized by k, fixed-parameter tractable? That is, does there exist a computable function f and a constant c such that the problem can be solved in time f(k) · |P|^c, where |P| is the size of the input polyomino?

A term rewriting system (TRS) is a finite set R of rewrite rules ℓ → r over terms built from a signature Σ and variables. For a terminating TRS R, the derivation height of a term t is dh_R(t) = max{n : there exists a rewrite sequence t →_R t_1 →_R ⋯ →_R t_n}, and the derivational complexity function is

  dc_R(n) = max{dh_R(t) : t a term with |t| ≤ n},

where |t| denotes the size of t. The TRS R is said to have polynomial derivational complexity if there exists a polynomial p ∈ ℕ[x] such that dc_R(n) ≤ p(n) for all n ∈ ℕ.

It is known that well-founded monotone algebras provide a sound and complete characterisation of termination: a TRS R is terminating if and only if it is compatible with some well-founded monotone algebra. The problem is the following analogue for polynomial derivational complexity:

Give a complete, resource-free (i.e. not phrased in terms of a particular proof method such as matrix or polynomial interpretations) characterisation of the class of term rewriting systems whose derivational complexity is bounded by a polynomial. Concretely, exhibit a class C of algebraic/semantic structures such that a TRS R has polynomial derivational complexity if and only if R is compatible with some structure in C.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Existing methods (triangular matrix interpretations, weighted automata, joint spectral radius techniques, polynomial interpretations) yield sufficient conditions for polynomial derivational complexity, but each is known to be incomplete: there exist TRSs with polynomial derivational complexity not captured by them. A polyomino is a finite, edge-connected union of unit squares of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$. A finite set $S = \{P_1, \dots, P_k\}$ of polyominoes is said to tile the plane if there exists a covering of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by interior-disjoint copies of the $P_i$, where each copy is obtained from some $P_i$ by a translation, rotation, and/or reflection (and every $P_i$ may be used arbitrarily many times). The polyomino tiling problem with $k$ tiles asks: given as input a finite set $S$ of $k$ polyominoes (specified by their unit-square coordinates), decide whether $S$ tiles the plane.

It is known that this decision problem is undecidable for $k = 5$. Determine whether the polyomino tiling problem is undecidable when $k = 3$, and whether it is undecidable when $k = 4$.

Recent progress has tightened the undecidability bound for polyomino tilings: Yang–Zhang proved undecidability for translational tiling with 8 polyominoes (2024), and a 2025 preprint establishes undecidability for sets of 5 polyominoes. Let $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ be a real normed linear space. For a nonempty subset $G \subseteq X$ and a point $x \in X$, a best approximation to $x$ from $G$ is an element $g_0 \in G$ such that $\|x - g_0\| = \inf_{g \in G} \|x - g\|$. The set $G$ is called a Chebyshev subspace if $G$ is a linear subspace of $X$ and every point $x \in X$ has exactly one best approximation in $G$.

Question: Does there exist a separable (infinite-dimensional) Banach space $X$ which has no Chebyshev subspace whatsoever — i.e., such that for every linear subspace $G \subseteq X$ there exists some $x \in X$ that fails to have a unique best approximation in $G$?

Let $X$ be a real normed linear space. A nonempty subset $G \subseteq X$ is called a Chebyshev set if for every $x \in X$ there exists a unique element $\pi_G(x) \in G$ with $\|x - \pi_G(x)\| = \inf_{g \in G} \|x - g\|$. The map $\pi_G : X \to G$ is called the metric projection onto $G$.

The map $\pi_G$ is said to be weakly continuous at $x \in X$ if, whenever $(x_n)_{n \ge 1} \subset X$ converges in norm to $x$, the sequence $(\pi_G(x_n))$ converges weakly to $\pi_G(x)$. It is said to be strongly continuous at $x$ if $(\pi_G(x_n))$ converges in norm to $\pi_G(x)$ whenever $x_n \to x$ in norm.

Question: If $G$ is a Chebyshev set in a normed linear space $X$ such that the metric projection $\pi_G$ is weakly continuous (at every point of $X$), must $\pi_G$ also be strongly continuous?

Let $n\ge 3$ and let $W_n$ denote the wheel graph on $n+1$ vertices, obtained by joining a single hub vertex to every vertex of a cycle of length $n$. To each connected Feynman graph $G$ one associates a (convergent, scheme-independent) period; more generally, by varying the kinematic/regulator setup one obtains a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $P_c(G)$ of convergent generalized Feynman periods attached to $G$, spanned by all convergent projective integrals
$$\int_{\sigma}\frac{N(\alpha)\,\Omega}{\Psi_G(\alpha)^{D/2}}$$
arising from $G$ (where $\Psi_G$ is the first Symanzik polynomial of $G$, $\Omega$ is the canonical projective volume form on $\mathbb{P}^{|E(G)|-1}$, $\sigma$ is the positive coordinate simplex, and $N$ ranges over admissible numerators making the integral convergent).

Prove or disprove the following: for every $n\ge 3$,
$$P_c(W_n) \;=\; \mathbb{Q} + \mathbb{Q}\,\zeta(3) + \mathbb{Q}\,\zeta(5) + \cdots + \mathbb{Q}\,\zeta(2n-3),$$
where $\zeta(s)=\sum_{k\ge 1}k^{-s}$ is the Riemann zeta function. Equivalently, show that no even Riemann zeta value $\zeta(2k)$, no product of Riemann zeta values, and no irreducible multiple zeta value of depth $\ge 2$ appears in the period space of any wheel graph $W_n$.

Background and definitions. Consider scalar massless φ⁴ theory in four dimensions. To each connected 4-regular graph G obtained as a Feynman graph in this theory (equivalently, after taking a vertex at infinity, a 4-regular graph with one vertex removed) one associates its period P(G), defined as the convergent projective integral
   P(G) = ∫_{x_i ≥ 0} (1/Ψ_G(x)^2) Ω,
where Ψ_G is the (first) Symanzik/Kirchhoff polynomial of G and Ω = Σ_i (−1)^i x_i dx_1 ∧ … ∧ d̂x_i ∧ … ∧ dx_n is the standard projective volume form on the simplex {x_i ≥ 0}/ℝ_{>0}. The "loop number" (first Betti number) of G is denoted ℓ(G).

A multiple zeta value (MZV) is a real number of the form
   ζ(s_1, s_2, …, s_k) = Σ_{n_1 > n_2 > … > n_k ≥ 1} 1/(n_1^{s_1} n_2^{s_2} ⋯ n_k^{s_k}),
where s_i are positive integers and s_1 ≥ 2. Let MZV ⊂ ℝ denote the ℚ-vector space spanned by all multiple zeta values. (Equivalently, MZV is the ℚ-span of iterated integrals of dt/t and dt/(1−t) from 0 to 1.)

Question. Is it true that for every connected Feynman graph G arising in massless φ⁴ theory with loop number ℓ(G) ≤ 5, the period P(G) lies in MZV?

(In particular, for those graphs at ℓ(G) ≤ 5 whose periods are presently known only to be ℚ-linear combinations of alternating Euler sums or values of multiple polylogarithms at −1, do these combinations always reduce to multiple zeta values?)
