representations.normalized:
Consider the computational problem FACTOR: given a composite positive integer $N$ (encoded in binary, so the input size is $n = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$), output a nontrivial divisor $d$ of $N$ with $1 < d < N$.

A naive deterministic algorithm trial-divides $N$ by $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, \dots$ until a divisor is found; this runs in time $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ in the worst case, which is exponential in $n$. More refined algorithms (such as the general number field sieve) achieve sub-exponential but still super-polynomial expected running time, e.g.\ $\exp\!\big(O(n^{1/3} (\log n)^{2/3})\big)$.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic (or, more generally, classical randomized) algorithm running in time polynomial in $n = \log N$ that, on input a composite integer $N$, outputs a nontrivial factor of $N$? Equivalently, is integer factorization in the complexity class $\mathrm{P}$ (or $\mathrm{BPP}$)? Phrased informally: when factoring a large composite integer on a classical computer, is some form of search through candidate divisors fundamentally required, or can it be avoided entirely?

Whether integer factorization admits a classical polynomial-time algorithm is a long-standing open problem in computational number theory and complexity theory. The best known classical algorithm, the general number field sieve, runs in heuristic sub-exponential time. Shor's algorithm gives a polynomial-time quantum algorithm, but no analogous classical result is known, and as of 2026 the problem remains open.

representations.normalized:
A clique of size k in a simple undirected graph G = (V, E) is a subset S ⊆ V of cardinality k such that every two distinct vertices in S are joined by an edge. The k-Clique decision problem asks, given as input a finite simple graph G and a positive integer k, to determine whether G contains a clique of size k. The brute-force search algorithm enumerates all subsets of V of size k and checks whether each is a clique; for n = |V| = 100 and k = 10 this requires examining on the order of C(100,10) ≈ 1.7 × 10^13 subsets, which is infeasible in a reasonable time.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, on every input graph G with n vertices and every input integer k, decides whether G contains a clique of size k in time bounded by a polynomial in n (in particular, an algorithm that fundamentally avoids exhaustive search)? Equivalently, is the k-Clique decision problem solvable in deterministic polynomial time?

No such algorithm is known, and the P vs NP question is listed as an unresolved Clay Millennium Prize Problem.

A coloring of the plane with $c$ colors is a function $\chi:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \{1,2,\dots,c\}$ such that for every pair of points $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\|x-y\|=1$ one has $\chi(x)\neq \chi(y)$. The chromatic number of the plane $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$ is the smallest positive integer $c$ for which such a coloring exists. Equivalently, a unit-distance graph is a graph $G=(V,E)$ admitting an injection $f:V\to\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $\{u,v\}\in E$ if and only if $\|f(u)-f(v)\|=1$, and $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$ equals the supremum of the chromatic numbers of all finite unit-distance graphs. It is classically known that $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)\in\{4,5,6,7\}$ via a 7-coloring of the plane by a hexagonal tiling (upper bound) and a finite unit-distance graph with chromatic number 4 such as the Moser spindle (lower bound). Determine the exact value of $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)$. As an explicit subtask, construct a coloring of the plane with $7$ colors witnessing the upper bound $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2)\le 7$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The Hadwiger–Nelson problem remains open. In 2018, de Grey raised the lower bound to 5 by exhibiting a non-4-colorable unit-distance graph, so it is now known that the chromatic number of the plane lies in {5, 6, 7}. The upper bound of 7 (via a hexagonal tiling) and the new lower bound of 5 have not been improved as of 2025; the exact value is still undetermined.

A unit-distance graph is a graph G=(V,E) admitting an embedding f:V→ℝ² such that {u,v}∈E if and only if ‖f(u)−f(v)‖=1 (some authors require only the "only if" direction; here we adopt the same convention as in the source tradition: edges correspond exactly to pairs at Euclidean distance 1). The chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colors needed to properly color the vertices of G, and the girth g(G) is the length of a shortest cycle of G (∞ if G is a forest).

Currently known constructions include 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs of girth 4 on 23 vertices and of girth 5 on 45 vertices, and a unit-distance graph of girth 12 with chromatic number at least 4 having an extremely large number of vertices.

(a) For each integer k≥4, determine the minimum number of vertices in a 4-chromatic unit-distance graph in the plane of girth at least k. In particular, improve the bounds 23 (for girth 4) and 45 (for girth 5).

(b) Decide whether, for every integer k, there exists a 4-chromatic unit-distance graph in the plane of girth at least k. Equivalently, do there exist 4-chromatic planar unit-distance graphs of arbitrarily large girth?

A drawing of a graph in the plane assigns each vertex a distinct point and each edge a continuous simple curve joining its two endpoints, subject to the conditions that (i) the interior of any edge curve contains no vertex, (ii) any two edge curves meet in finitely many points, each of which is either a common endpoint or a transverse crossing, and (iii) no three edge curves pass through a common interior point. The crossing number cr(G) of a graph G is the minimum, over all such drawings of G in the plane, of the number of pairs of edges whose curves cross.

Let K_{9,9} denote the complete bipartite graph with parts of size 9 (so 18 vertices and 81 edges, each vertex of one part joined to every vertex of the other part). Determine cr(K_{9,9}).

(It is conjectured, in line with Zarankiewicz's general formula cr(K_{m,n}) = ⌊m/2⌋⌊(m-1)/2⌋⌊n/2⌋⌊(n-1)/2⌋, that cr(K_{9,9}) = 256; prove or disprove this value.)

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Zarankiewicz crossing number conjecture has been verified for K_{m,n} when min(m,n) ≤ 6 and for several additional cases up through K_{7,10} and K_{8,10}, but K_{9,9} remains among the smallest unresolved cases. Surveys (e.g., Székely's "Turán's Brick Factory Problem: The Status of the Conjectures of Zarankiewicz and Hill", 2016) and the Wikipedia article on Turán's brick factory problem list K_{9,9} as still open. The conjectured value is 256.

Let $k \geq 2$ be an integer. A graph $G$ is $k$-connected if it has more than $k$ vertices and remains connected after the removal of any set of fewer than $k$ vertices. A Hamiltonian cycle in $G$ is a cycle that passes through every vertex of $G$. A set of vertices is independent if no two of its members are adjacent. For a vertex $v$, let $N(v)$ denote the set of neighbors of $v$ in $G$.

Question: Is it true that every $k$-connected graph $G$ that does not contain a Hamiltonian cycle must contain a cycle $C$ and a set $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ of $k$ pairwise independent vertices such that $\{v_1, \ldots, v_k\} \cup N(v_1) \cup N(v_2) \cup \cdots \cup N(v_k) \subseteq V(C)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Web search did not return a definitive resolution of this conjecture for general k. The cases k = 2 and k = 3 are known to hold (the k = 2 case being a classical result attributed to Chvátal–Erdős–style arguments and the k = 3 case established later), but no source confirming or refuting it for all k ≥ 4 was located. Current status appears to remain open, but this could not be verified with certainty from the available search results.

An oriented graph is a simple directed graph $D=(V,A)$ obtained from a simple undirected graph by assigning to each edge exactly one of the two possible orientations; equivalently, for every pair of distinct vertices $u,v$ at most one of the arcs $(u,v),(v,u)$ belongs to $A$. For a vertex $v\in V$, the out-degree $d^+_D(v)$ is the number of arcs of $D$ of the form $(v,w)$. Define the square $D^2$ of $D$ to be the directed graph on the same vertex set $V$ whose arc set consists of all arcs of $D$ together with every ordered pair $(u,w)$ with $u\neq w$ such that there exists a vertex $v$ with $(u,v),(v,w)\in A$ and $(u,w)\notin A$ (arcs are not repeated).

Prove or disprove: for every oriented graph $D$ there exists a vertex $v\in V$ such that
$$d^+_{D^2}(v)\;\ge\;2\,d^+_D(v).$$

Equivalently, every oriented graph contains a vertex whose second out-neighbourhood (the set of vertices at directed distance exactly two from $v$ in $D$) has cardinality at least that of its first out-neighbourhood.

This is Seymour's Second Neighbourhood Conjecture. It is established for tournaments (Fisher, and later Havet–Thomassé) and various special classes, but the general case remains open as of 2025. Recent work (2024–2025) has improved the constant factor (e.g., 0.715538 times the out-neighbourhood) and explored random and reduction-based approaches, but no accepted proof of the full conjecture exists.

Let N be a positive integer and let P be a set of N points in the plane in general position (no three collinear). Consider all closed line segments whose endpoints lie in P. Call a collection of such segments a crossing family if every two segments in the collection cross, i.e., share exactly one point lying in the relative interior of both. Let T(N) denote the maximum integer k such that every N-point set P in general position contains a crossing family of size at least k.

Determine the supremum of all real numbers t for which there exists a constant c=c(t)>0 with T(N) ≥ c N^t for all N. In particular, decide whether t can be taken strictly greater than 1/2, and identify the correct growth exponent of T(N).

Call a collection of such segments a crossing family if every two segments in the collection cross, i.e., share exactly one point lying in the relative interior of both. Let T(N) denote the maximum integer k such that every N-point set P in general position contains a crossing family of size at least k.

Determine the supremum of all real numbers t for which there exists a constant c=c(t)>0 with T(N) ≥ c N^t for all N. In particular, decide whether t can be taken strictly greater than 1/2, and identify the correct growth exponent of T(N).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The classical lower bound T(N) ≥ √(N/12) from 1994 stood for decades. In 2021, Pach, Rubin, and Tardos achieved a major breakthrough, proving T(N) ≥ N^{1−o(1)}, so the exponent t can be taken arbitrarily close to 1. The best known upper bound is T(N) ≤ ⌈8N/41⌉ (Aichholzer, Kynčl, Scheucher, Valtr, Vogtenhuber). Thus while the exponent question (whether t can exceed 1/2) is settled affirmatively, the exact asymptotic value of T(N) remains open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is the empty hexagon problem of Erdős. It was resolved in the affirmative by Tobias Gerken (2008, "Empty convex hexagons in planar point sets", Discrete & Computational Geometry) and independently by Carlos M. Nicolás (2007, "The empty hexagon theorem"). Subsequent work by Valtr gave a simpler proof and better bounds. Hence such an N exists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The general empty-hexagon problem (whether every sufficiently large planar point set in general position contains an empty convex hexagon) was settled affirmatively by Gerken and, independently, Nicolás (published 2008). Since the restricted variant assumes the points lie in a bounded square with a minimum pairwise distance—still requiring an empty hexagon among the configuration—the affirmative answer to the general problem implies the affirmative answer to this restricted version once $K$ is large enough to guarantee the cardinality threshold (now known to be 30, proved by Heule and Scheucher, 2024). Hence the problem is solved.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Let $C$ be a circle of length $N$ bounding a disk $D$. Let $S \subset D$ be a set of $N^2$ points such that any two distinct points of $S$ are at Euclidean distance at least $1/100$. A Venn diagram of n curves is a collection of n simple closed curves in the plane such that, for every subset S of the n curves, the region consisting of points lying inside every curve in S and outside every curve not in S is nonempty and connected. Such a Venn diagram is called simple if (i) whenever two curves meet, they cross transversally (no tangencies), and (ii) no three curves meet at a common point. A simple Venn diagram naturally gives rise to a planar graph whose vertices are the intersection points of the curves and whose edges are the arcs of curves between consecutive intersection points; the dual graph of the diagram is the dual of this plane graph.

Question: Is it true that every simple Venn diagram on n curves can be extended to a simple Venn diagram on n+1 curves by adding one additional simple closed curve? Equivalently, is the dual graph of every simple Venn diagram Hamiltonian?

Let R be a commutative ring with identity. An element of R is called regular if it is not a zero-divisor, and an ideal of R is called regular if it contains a regular element. The ring R is called a Prüfer ring if every finitely generated regular ideal of R is invertible (equivalently, projective as an R-module). The (small) finitistic projective dimension of R is defined by
  fp.dim R = sup{ pd_R(M) : M is an R-module admitting a finite projective resolution by finitely generated projective modules, with pd_R(M) < ∞ }.

Question: Is it true that for every Prüfer ring R one has fp.dim R ≤ 1?

The question was answered negatively. Wang et al. Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity, and let $R[x]$ denote the polynomial ring in one indeterminate over $R$. For a polynomial $f = \sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^i \in R[x]$, let $c(f)$ denote its content, namely the ideal of $R$ generated by the coefficients $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n$. The ring $R$ is called Gaussian if for every pair of polynomials $f, g \in R[x]$ one has $c(fg) = c(f)\,c(g)$. The weak global dimension $\mathrm{w.dim}\,R$ is defined as the supremum of the flat dimensions of all $R$-modules (equivalently, the supremum of $n$ such that $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(M,N) \neq 0$ for some $R$-modules $M,N$), with value $\infty$ if no finite supremum exists.

Question: Must the weak global dimension of every Gaussian ring $R$ lie in the set $\{0, 1, \infty\}$?

This is the Bazzoni–Glaz conjecture (2007). It has been verified in many cases: for coherent Gaussian rings (Bazzoni–Glaz 2007), for fqp-rings (Abuhlail–Jarrar–Kabbaj 2011), and reduced/Prüfer-like cases. Donadze–Thomas (2011, arXiv:1107.0440) claimed a full proof, and a 2014 J. Algebra paper by Bazzoni–Glaz/related authors addresses the conjecture, but the literature (e.g., Adarbeh's survey and the 2016 paper on weak global dimension of Prüfer-like rings) indicates the conjecture is still considered open in full generality, with significant partial progress.

The weak (global) dimension of $R$, denoted $\mathrm{w.dim}\,R$, is defined as
$$\mathrm{w.dim}\,R = \sup\{\mathrm{fd}_R(M) : M \text{ is an } R\text{-module}\},$$
where $\mathrm{fd}_R(M)$ denotes the flat dimension of $M$ (the smallest non-negative integer $n$, or $\infty$, such that $M$ admits a flat resolution of length $n$).

Question: If $R$ is a total ring of quotients, must $\mathrm{w.dim}\,R \in \{0,\,1,\,\infty\}$? That is, prove that no total ring of quotients has finite weak global dimension strictly greater than $1$, or else exhibit a total ring of quotients $R$ with $2 \le \mathrm{w.dim}\,R < \infty$.

This problem is closely tied to the Bazzoni–Glaz conjecture asserting that a Gaussian ring has weak global dimension 0, 1, or ∞. Let $D$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$. Recall that $D$ is called coherent if every finitely generated ideal of $D$ is finitely presented (equivalently, the intersection of any two finitely generated ideals is finitely generated, and the annihilator of every element is finitely generated). The (Krull) dimension of $D$ is the supremum of the lengths of chains of prime ideals. The integral closure $\overline{D}$ of $D$ in $K$ is the set of all elements of $K$ that satisfy a monic polynomial with coefficients in $D$. A domain $R$ is a Prüfer domain if every nonzero finitely generated ideal of $R$ is invertible.

Question: Suppose $D$ is a one-dimensional coherent domain. Must the integral closure $\overline{D}$ of $D$ in its field of fractions $K$ be a Prüfer domain?

Let R be a commutative ring with identity. Recall the following definitions:

- R is called a finite conductor ring if for every pair of elements a, b ∈ R, the ideal aR ∩ bR is finitely generated.
- R is called a quasi coherent ring if for every finite set of elements a_1, …, a_n ∈ R, the intersection a_1 R ∩ … ∩ a_n R is finitely generated.
- R is called a G-GCD ring if every principal ideal of R is projective and the intersection of any two finitely generated flat ideals of R is again a finitely generated flat ideal.

Let G be a finitely generated abelian group, and let RG denote the group ring of G over R.

Question: If R is a G-GCD ring, do the finite conductor property and the quasi coherent property necessarily ascend from R to RG? That is, must RG be a finite conductor ring, and must RG be a quasi coherent ring?

Let R be a commutative ring with identity and let G be an abelian group such that the order of every torsion element of G is invertible in R. The group ring RG is the free R-module with basis G, endowed with the multiplication induced by the group operation. The (left) global dimension gl.dim S of a ring S is the supremum of the projective dimensions of all left S-modules; the weak (flat) global dimension w.dim S is the supremum of the flat dimensions of all left S-modules. The torsion-free rank of an abelian group G is the cardinality of a maximal Z-linearly independent subset of G, equivalently dim_Q(G ⊗_Z Q).

Under the above hypotheses it is known that
   w.dim(RG) = w.dim(R) + rank(G).

Question: Does there exist an analogous formula expressing gl.dim(RG) in terms of gl.dim(R) together with some invariant of the abelian group G? Either exhibit such a formula and prove it, or show that no such formula can exist.

Let R be a commutative ring (with identity) and let G be an abelian group. Consider the group ring R[G]. Recall that a ring is semisimple if it is isomorphic to a finite direct product of matrix rings over division rings (equivalently, has global dimension 0), and is hereditary if every submodule of a projective module is projective (equivalently, has global dimension at most 1).

Provide a complete characterization, in terms of ring-theoretic properties of R and group-theoretic properties of G, of:
(a) all pairs (R, G) such that the group ring R[G] is semisimple;
(b) all pairs (R, G) such that the group ring R[G] is hereditary.

Equivalently, describe exactly when R[G] has global dimension 0, and when R[G] has global dimension at most 1.

Background. Several extensions of the Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein properties to non-Noetherian commutative rings have been developed. For a commutative ring A, one such notion (Hamilton–Marley) declares A to be Cohen–Macaulay if every strong parameter sequence of A is a regular sequence, where a sequence x_1,…,x_n in A is a strong parameter sequence if (x_1,…,x_n) has height n and, for each i, the Čech cohomology H^i_{(x_1,…,x_i)}(A) vanishes below degree i in an appropriate sense. Analogously, one has a non-Noetherian notion of Gorenstein ring (e.g., via finite self–FP-injective dimension or via Hummel–Marley's coherent Gorenstein definition) that agrees with the classical one when A is Noetherian and that implies the Cohen–Macaulay property in the coherent case.

Problem. Let R be a commutative ring and let G be an abelian group, and form the group ring RG. Give necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair (R, G) for RG to be:
(a) Cohen–Macaulay in the non-Noetherian sense above;
(b) Gorenstein in the non-Noetherian sense above.

In particular, characterize these properties when R is a (coherent) Cohen–Macaulay or Gorenstein ring and G is a torsion-free abelian group, and determine how the structure of G (rank, torsion, cyclically Noetherian property, etc.) interacts with the corresponding property of R.

regular $\Rightarrow$ complete intersection $\Rightarrow$ Gorenstein $\Rightarrow$ Cohen–Macaulay,

and notions of coherent (non-Noetherian) local Gorenstein rings and coherent (non-Noetherian) local Cohen–Macaulay rings have been formulated that extend the classical Noetherian notions and preserve the implication "coherent local Gorenstein $\Rightarrow$ coherent local Cohen–Macaulay."

(a) When $R$ is Noetherian, the definition is equivalent to the classical notion of a local complete intersection ring.

(b) Every coherent local complete intersection ring (in the sense of the new definition) is a coherent local Cohen–Macaulay ring.

(c) Every coherent local Gorenstein ring is a coherent local complete intersection ring (in the sense of the new definition), or more generally the definition is compatible with the existing coherent theories so that the hierarchy regular $\Rightarrow$ complete intersection $\Rightarrow$ Gorenstein $\Rightarrow$ Cohen–Macaulay extends to the coherent non-Noetherian setting.

Does such a non-Noetherian characterization of local complete intersection rings exist, and if so, give one explicitly.

Let $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ be a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated $R$-module. Call $M$ quasi-complete if, for every descending chain $N_1 \supseteq N_2 \supseteq \cdots$ of $R$-submodules of $M$ and every integer $k \geq 1$, there exists an index $s_k$ such that $N_{s_k} \subseteq \bigcap_{n\geq 1} N_n + \mathfrak{m}^k M$. Call $M$ weakly quasi-complete if the same property holds for every descending chain of cyclic $R$-submodules of $M$. The ring $R$ is called (weakly) quasi-complete if $R$ itself, viewed as an $R$-module, is (weakly) quasi-complete.

Question: If a Noetherian local ring $R$ is weakly quasi-complete, must $R$ be quasi-complete?

Call R weakly quasi-complete if for every descending chain of ideals I_1 ⊇ I_2 ⊇ ... of R, and for every choice of element in the intersection-completion sense, the following holds: for each sequence (a_k) with a_k ∈ I_k there exists an element a ∈ R such that a - a_k ∈ I_k + J^k for all k (equivalently, R is quasi-complete if this property holds in the strong form characterizing Chevalley-style completeness for descending chains).

A commutative ring R with identity is called a McCoy ring if for every finitely generated ideal I of R whose elements are all zero-divisors, there exists a nonzero element r in R such that rI = 0 (equivalently, the annihilator of I is nonzero). The ring R is said to be locally a domain if for every prime (equivalently, maximal) ideal P of R, the localization R_P is an integral domain. A ring R is integrally closed if R equals its integral closure in its total ring of quotients, and R is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotent elements.

Question: Does there exist a commutative ring R that is integrally closed and reduced, such that for every maximal ideal M of R the localization R_M is an integrally closed McCoy ring, while R itself is not a McCoy ring and is not locally a domain?

representations.normalized:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Recall the following definitions.

(i) An element of $R$ is a zero-divisor if it annihilates some nonzero element of $R$; write $Z(R)$ for the set of zero-divisors.

(ii) $R$ is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotent elements.

(iii) For an integer $n \geq 1$, $R$ is said to satisfy property $(A_n)$ if every ideal of $R$ generated by at most $n$ elements and contained in $Z(R)$ has nonzero annihilator in $R$. (Property $(A)$ is the case where the bound on the number of generators is removed.)

(iv) $R$ satisfies the annihilator condition $(a.c.)$ if for every pair $a,b \in R$ there exists $c \in R$ such that $\operatorname{Ann}_R(a,b) = \operatorname{Ann}_R(c)$.

(v) $R$ is a McCoy ring if whenever a polynomial $f(x) \in R[x]$ is a zero-divisor in $R[x]$, there exists a nonzero $r \in R$ with $rf(x) = 0$. Equivalently, $R$ has property $(A)$ together with the requirement that finite annihilators behave compatibly so that every zero-divisor polynomial has a nonzero constant annihilator.

Question: Does there exist a reduced commutative ring $R$ that satisfies both the annihilator condition $(a.c.)$ and the property $(A_n)$ for some integer $n \geq 2$, yet is not a McCoy ring?

Let $A$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$. A prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $A$ is said to be divided if $\mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}} = \mathfrak{p}$, equivalently if $\mathfrak{p}$ is comparable (with respect to inclusion) to every principal ideal of $A$. The domain $A$ is called divided if every prime ideal of $A$ is divided, and $A$ is called locally divided if the localization $A_{\mathfrak{m}}$ is a divided domain for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ of $A$.

For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $A$, the CPI-extension of $A$ along $\mathfrak{p}$ is the subring $A + \mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ of $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$. The domain $A$ is called straight if for every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $A$ and every overring $B$ of $A$ contained in $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$, the extension $A + \mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}} \subseteq B + \mathfrak{p} A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ has the going-down property (equivalently, the natural ring-theoretic condition characterizing straightness as introduced by Dobbs–Picavet).

Question: Does there exist a straight domain that is not locally divided?

Let $D$ be a one-dimensional local Noetherian integral domain with finite residue field, and let
$$\mathrm{Int}(D) = \{ f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D \},$$
where $K$ denotes the field of fractions of $D$, be the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $D$.

For a nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$, define
$$\mathrm{Int}(I,D) = \{ f \in \mathrm{Int}(D) : f(D) \subseteq I \}.$$

The ring $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is said to satisfy the almost strong Skolem property if, for every pair of finitely generated ideals $\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}$ of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ such that $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ contain a nonzero constant from $D$, the equality $\mathfrak{A}(\alpha) = \mathfrak{B}(\alpha)$ for every $\alpha \in D$ (where $\mathfrak{A}(\alpha) = \{ f(\alpha) : f \in \mathfrak{A}\}$) implies $\mathfrak{A} = \mathfrak{B}$.

Determine a necessary and sufficient condition on $D$ for $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ to satisfy the almost strong Skolem property.

representations.normalized:
Let $E$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{Z}$. For each prime $p$, a $p$-ordering of $E$ is a sequence $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ of elements of $E$ defined recursively by choosing $a_0 \in E$ arbitrarily and, for $k \ge 1$, choosing $a_k \in E$ so as to minimize the $p$-adic valuation $v_p\!\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(a_k - a_i)\right)$. The associated $p$-sequence of $E$ is $v_k(E,p) = v_p\!\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(a_k - a_i)\right)$, which is independent of the choice of $p$-ordering. The Bhargava factorial of $E$ of order $n$ is defined by
$$ n!_E \; := \; \prod_{p \text{ prime}} p^{\,v_n(E,p)}. $$
(When $E = \mathbb{Z}$ one recovers the ordinary factorial $n!$.)

Question: Does there exist a subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ such that the sequence $\{n!_E\}_{n \ge 0}$ fails to be ultimately strictly increasing, i.e., such that for every integer $N$ there exist integers $n \ge N$ with $n!_E \ge (n+1)!_E$?

$$d(Y,X) = \inf\{\|T\|\cdot\|T^{-1}\| : T : Y \to X \text{ is a linear isomorphism}\}.$$
A closed subspace $Z \subseteq L^1$ is called complemented if there exists a bounded linear projection $P : L^1 \to L^1$ with range $Z$; the projection constant of $Z$ is $\lambda(Z) = \inf\{\|P\| : P \text{ is a bounded linear projection of } L^1 \text{ onto } Z\}$.

Decide the following:

(a) Does there exist a universal constant $\varepsilon_1 > 0$ such that whenever $X$ is a complemented subspace of $L^1$ and $Y$ is a closed subspace of $L^1$ with $d(Y,X) < 1+\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon \le \varepsilon_1$, the subspace $Y$ must also be complemented in $L^1$?

(b) If the answer is affirmative, possibly with $\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_1(K)$ allowed to depend on the projection constant $K = \lambda(X)$, give a quantitative bound on the projection constant $\lambda(Y)$ in terms of $K$ and $\varepsilon$.

representations.normalized:
For a nonempty subset E of the integers Z and a prime p, a p-ordering of E is a sequence {a_0, a_1, a_2, ...} of elements of E defined recursively as follows: a_0 is chosen arbitrarily in E, and for k ≥ 1, a_k is chosen in E so as to minimize the p-adic valuation v_p( (a_k - a_0)(a_k - a_1) ⋯ (a_k - a_{k-1}) ). The associated p-sequence of E is v_k(E,p) = v_p( (a_k - a_0) ⋯ (a_k - a_{k-1}) ); this sequence depends only on E and p, not on the choice of p-ordering. The Bhargava factorial of order k of E is then defined by

  k!_E  =  ∏_{p prime} p^{v_k(E,p)}  ∈  Z_{>0},

and it agrees with the usual k! when E = Z. Associated to any infinite subset E ⊆ Z one defines the generalized constant

  e_E  =  ∑_{k=0}^{∞} 1 / k!_E.

Problem: Characterize the infinite subsets E ⊆ Z for which the real number e_E is transcendental. In particular, determine sufficient conditions on E (and, where possible, necessary conditions) that guarantee the transcendence of e_E.

For a Banach space $Y$, define the density character $\operatorname{dens}(Y)$ to be the smallest cardinality of a norm-dense subset of $Y$. A (possibly transfinite) family $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$ of nonzero vectors in $Y$ is called an unconditional basic sequence of cardinality $\kappa$ if there exists a constant $C\ge 1$ such that, for every finite set $F\subset\kappa$, every choice of scalars $(a_\alpha)_{\alpha\in F}$, and every choice of signs $(\varepsilon_\alpha)_{\alpha\in F}\in\{-1,+1\}^F$, one has
$$\Big\|\sum_{\alpha\in F}\varepsilon_\alpha a_\alpha x_\alpha\Big\|\le C\Big\|\sum_{\alpha\in F}a_\alpha x_\alpha\Big\|.$$
Question: Must every closed infinite-dimensional subspace $X\subseteq L^1(\mu)$ contain an unconditional basic sequence of cardinality equal to $\operatorname{dens}(X)$?

Let $D$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$. Define the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $D$ by
$$\mathrm{Int}(D) := \{\, f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D \,\}.$$
Then $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is naturally a $D$-module (in fact a $D$-algebra). 

Question: Is it true that for every integral domain $D$, the $D$-module $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is free?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether Int(D) is a free D-module for every integral domain D is a well-known open problem in commutative ring theory. Recent surveys and papers on integer-valued polynomials (e.g., work on the module structure of Int(D), the probability that Int_n(D) is free, and related conjectures involving the Pólya group PO(D)) treat the freeness of Int(D) as still unresolved, with conjectures that counterexamples should exist (possibly even integrally closed), but no proof has been published.

Recall that a $D$-$D$-biring is a commutative $D$-algebra $B$ equipped with a lift of the covariant representable functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{D\text{-alg}}(B,-)$ from the category of commutative $D$-algebras to itself (equivalently, $B$ carries a cocommutative $D$-coalgebra structure in the category of commutative $D$-algebras, with comultiplication, counit, and co-inverse making $\mathrm{Hom}_{D\text{-alg}}(B,A)$ into a commutative $D$-algebra functorially in the $D$-algebra $A$). The polynomial ring $D[X]$ carries a canonical $D$-$D$-biring structure in which $\mathrm{Hom}_{D\text{-alg}}(D[X],A) \cong A$ as $D$-algebras. A homomorphism of $D$-$D$-birings is a $D$-algebra homomorphism that is compatible with the cobring structures.

Question: Does $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ always admit a (necessarily unique) structure of a $D$-$D$-biring such that the natural inclusion $D[X] \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Int}(D)$ is a homomorphism of $D$-$D$-birings?

Let $D \subseteq A$ be an extension of integral domains sharing the same field of fractions (or more generally, with $A$ contained in the field of fractions of $D$ extended appropriately). For a subset $S$ of a domain $R$ with field of fractions $K$, recall that the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $S$ is
$$\mathrm{Int}(S, R) = \{ f \in K[X] : f(S) \subseteq R \},$$
and we write $\mathrm{Int}(R) = \mathrm{Int}(R, R)$. For a positive integer $n$, $\mathrm{Int}(R^n)$ denotes the ring of polynomials $f \in K[X_1, \dots, X_n]$ such that $f(R^n) \subseteq R$.

The extension $D \subseteq A$ is called polynomially complete if $\mathrm{Int}(D^n, A) = \mathrm{Int}(A^n)$ for every positive integer $n$, and is called almost polynomially complete if $\mathrm{Int}(D^n) \subseteq \mathrm{Int}(A^n)$ for every positive integer $n$.

Question: If $\mathrm{Int}(D) \subseteq \mathrm{Int}(A)$, does it follow that the extension $D \subseteq A$ is almost polynomially complete, i.e., that $\mathrm{Int}(D^n) \subseteq \mathrm{Int}(A^n)$ holds for all positive integers $n \geq 1$?

  Int_n(O_K) := { f ∈ K[X] : deg(f) ≤ n and f(O_K) ⊆ O_K },
which is an O_K-module. Recall that the Pólya–Ostrowski group PO(O_K) is the subgroup of the ideal class group of O_K generated by the classes of the ideals Π_q(O_K) = ∏_{𝔭, N(𝔭)=q} 𝔭, where q ranges over prime powers and the product is over prime ideals of O_K of norm q. Let
  S(O_K) := { n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} : Int_n(O_K) is a free O_K-module },
and define the natural density
  δ(Int(O_K)) := lim_{N→∞} |S(O_K) ∩ [0, N]| / (N+1),
when this limit exists.

Prove or disprove the following statements:
(a) The density δ(Int(O_K)) exists for every number field K.
(b) When it exists, δ(Int(O_K)) is a rational number.
(c) δ(Int(O_K)) ≥ 1 / |PO(O_K)|.
Furthermore, give an explicit formula for δ(Int(O_K)) in terms of arithmetic invariants of K.

$$\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z}) = \{\, f\in\mathbb{Q}[X] : f(E)\subseteq \mathbb{Z}\,\}.$$

$$\alpha_p(n) = -v_p\bigl(I_n^{(p)}(E)\bigr),$$
where $v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation.

(b) For every prime $p$, compute the characteristic sequence $(\alpha_p(n))_{n\ge 0}$ of $\operatorname{Int}(E,\mathbb{Z})$ at $p$.

(c) Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\alpha_p(n)$ as $n\to\infty$.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. Consider the ring of $n \times n$ matrices with integer entries, $M_n(\mathbb{Z})$, viewed as a subset of $M_n(\mathbb{Q})$. Define
$$\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z})) := \{\, f(X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X] : f(A) \in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) \text{ for every } A \in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) \,\},$$
i.e., the ring of polynomials with rational coefficients that take integer-matrix values on every integer matrix of size $n \times n$. This is a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module graded by degree; a *regular basis* is a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis $\{f_k\}_{k \geq 0}$ with $\deg f_k = k$ for every $k$. For each prime $p$ and each integer $k \geq 0$, let $\alpha_p(k)$ denote the $p$-adic valuation of the denominator of the leading coefficient of $f_k$ (equivalently, $-v_p$ of the generator of the fractional ideal of leading coefficients of degree-$k$ elements). The sequence $(\alpha_p(k))_{k \geq 0}$ is called the *characteristic sequence* of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$ at $p$.

(a) Construct an explicit regular basis of $\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb{Q}}(M_n(\mathbb{Z}))$.

(b) For every prime $p$, compute the characteristic sequence $(\alpha_p(k))_{k \geq 0}$.

(c) Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\alpha_p(k)$ as $k \to \infty$.

Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $A$ be a torsion-free $D$-algebra that is finitely generated as a $D$-module. For each element $a \in A$, let $\mu_a(X) \in D[X]$ denote the minimal monic polynomial of $a$ over $D$ (equivalently, the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $a$ on $A \otimes_D K$, taken in a fixed normalization so that $\mu_a(a) = 0$). Define the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $A$ by
$$\mathrm{Int}_K(A) = \{\, f(X) \in K[X] : f(a) \in A \text{ for every } a \in A \,\}.$$
It is known that one always has the containment
$$\bigcap_{a \in A}\bigl(D[X] + \mu_a(X)\,K[X]\bigr) \;\subseteq\; \mathrm{Int}_K(A).$$
Characterize the $D$-algebras $A$ (within the class above) for which this containment is an equality, i.e.
$$\bigcap_{a \in A}\bigl(D[X] + \mu_a(X)\,K[X]\bigr) \;=\; \mathrm{Int}_K(A).$$

For a Banach space $X$, a bounded linear operator $T: L_1 \to X$ is called narrow if for every measurable set $A \subseteq [0,1]$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a function $x \in L_1$ of the form $x = \mathbf{1}_B - \mathbf{1}_{A\setminus B}$ (a sign on $A$, i.e. $|x| = \mathbf{1}_A$ and $\int_A x\,d\mu = 0$) such that $\|T x\| < \varepsilon$.

Question: Is it true that for every Banach space $X$ and every pair of narrow operators $T_1, T_2: L_1[0,1] \to X$, the sum $T_1 + T_2$ is again a narrow operator?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered in the negative. A theorem of V. Mykhaylyuk and M. Popov (J. Math. Anal. Appl. 404 (2013), 554–561, "On sums of narrow operators on Köthe function spaces") shows that for every Köthe Banach space E on [0,1] — in particular for E = L_1[0,1] — there exist a Banach space X and two narrow operators from E to X whose sum is not narrow. Thus the sum-of-two-narrow-operators property of L_1 does not extend to arbitrary Banach-space-valued operators.

For each complex parameter $\lambda$ in the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, consider the quadratic polynomial
$$P_\lambda(z)=\lambda(z-z^2),$$
which fixes $0$ with multiplier $\lambda$. When $\lambda=e^{2\pi i\alpha}$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, the map $P_\lambda$ is said to be linearizable at $0$ if there exists a holomorphic injection $\phi:\mathbb{D}_r\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\phi(0)=0$, $\phi'(0)=1$, defined on a disk of some positive radius $r>0$, such that $P_\lambda\circ\phi(z)=\phi(\lambda z)$; the supremum of such $r$ is called the linearization radius $r_\lambda$ (the conformal radius of the Siegel disk at $0$). For $|\lambda|<1$, $P_\lambda$ has an attracting fixed point at $0$ and one defines $r_\lambda$ as the conformal radius of the immediate basin.

A theorem of Yoccoz asserts that there exists a bounded holomorphic function $U:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $|U(\lambda)|=r_\lambda$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{D}$, and that for $\lambda=e^{2\pi i\alpha}$ with $\alpha$ irrational, $P_\lambda$ is linearizable if and only if $\alpha$ is a Brjuno number. Recall that an irrational $\alpha$ is a Brjuno number if
$$B(\alpha):=\sum_{n\geq 0} \beta_{n-1}(\alpha)\,\log\frac{1}{\alpha_n}<\infty,$$
where $\alpha_0=\{\alpha\}$, $\alpha_{n+1}=\{1/\alpha_n\}$, $\beta_{-1}=1$, and $\beta_n=\alpha_0\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_n$; the function $B$ is the Brjuno function.

By Fatou's theorem the radial boundary values $U(e^{2\pi i\alpha}):=\lim_{r\to 1^-}U(re^{2\pi i\alpha})$ exist for almost every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$.

Question: Does the function
$$\alpha\;\longmapsto\;B(\alpha)+\log\bigl|U(e^{2\pi i\alpha})\bigr|,$$
defined on the set of Brjuno numbers, belong to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Yoccoz established that the restriction of $\alpha\mapsto B(\alpha)+\log r(\alpha)$ to Brjuno numbers is bounded above and below by universal constants, answering the boundedness question affirmatively. X. Buff and A. Chéritat (Annals of Mathematics, 2006) strengthened this by showing the function extends continuously to all of $\mathbb{R}$. Let D be an integral domain with quotient field K. For a nonzero fractional ideal I of D, set I^{-1} = (D : I) = { x in K : xI ⊆ D } and I_v = (I^{-1})^{-1}. An ideal I is called divisorial (or a v-ideal) if I = I_v. The endomorphism ring of I is E(I) = (I : I) = { x in K : xI ⊆ I }. A nonzero ideal I of D is said to be stable if I is invertible in E(I), i.e. I·(I^{-1}·I)·... — equivalently, I·(E(I) : I) = E(I). The domain D is called stable if every nonzero ideal of D is stable, and v-stable if every divisorial ideal of D is stable (i.e. invertible in its endomorphism ring).

The domain D is Archimedean if for every nonzero, noninvertible element a of D, ⋂_{n≥1} a^n D = 0. The domain D is a Mori domain if it satisfies the ascending chain condition on divisorial ideals. A divisorial ideal I is said to be 2-v-generated if there exist a, b ∈ I such that I = (a, b)_v.

Answer the following three questions:

(a) Must every stable Archimedean domain be one-dimensional (i.e. have Krull dimension one)?

(b) Let D be a one-dimensional Mori domain such that every divisorial ideal of D is 2-v-generated. Must every divisorial ideal of D be stable?

(c) Let D be a Mori domain such that every divisorial ideal of D is 2-v-generated. Must D be v-stable?

Consider the family of degree-4 Blaschke products
$$Q_{a,\alpha}(z) = P_a\, z^2 \cdot \frac{z+a}{1+az},$$
where $a \in (3,+\infty)$ is a real parameter and $P_a \in \mathbb{S}^1$ is the unique unimodular constant chosen so that the rotation number of the restriction $Q_{a,\alpha}\!\restriction_{\mathbb{S}^1}$ to the unit circle is equal to a prescribed irrational number $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$. Assume that $\alpha$ is a Brjuno number, i.e. $\sum_{n\ge 0} \frac{\log q_{n+1}}{q_n} < \infty$, where $(p_n/q_n)$ are the convergents of the continued-fraction expansion of $\alpha$.

For each such $\alpha$, suppose that there exists a maximal open interval $(a_0(\alpha), +\infty)$ with $a_0(\alpha) \ge 3$ such that for every $a \in (a_0(\alpha), +\infty)$ the restriction $Q_{a,\alpha}\!\restriction_{\mathbb{S}^1}$ is analytically conjugate to the rigid rotation $R_\alpha(z) = e^{2\pi i \alpha} z$, while $Q_{a_0(\alpha),\alpha}\!\restriction_{\mathbb{S}^1}$ is not analytically conjugate to $R_\alpha$.

Determine the regularity (e.g. $C^k$, $C^\infty$, quasisymmetric, Hölder, etc.) of the conjugacy between $Q_{a_0(\alpha),\alpha}\!\restriction_{\mathbb{S}^1}$ and $R_\alpha$ at the endpoint $a = a_0(\alpha)$, and describe how this regularity depends on the arithmetic properties of $\alpha$.

Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ is called stable if $I$ is invertible in its endomorphism ring $(I:I) = \{x \in K : xI \subseteq I\}$, where $K$ is the quotient field of $D$. The domain $D$ is called finitely stable if every nonzero finitely generated ideal of $D$ is stable. A nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ is locally principal if, for every maximal ideal $M$ of $D$, the localization $I_M$ is a principal ideal of $D_M$. The domain $D$ is called an LPI-domain (locally principal ideal domain) if every nonzero locally principal ideal of $D$ is invertible. The domain $D$ is said to have finite character if every nonzero element of $D$ belongs to only finitely many maximal ideals of $D$.

Question: If $D$ is a finitely stable LPI-domain, must $D$ have finite character?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Related results are known: Bazzoni (2011) proved that a finitely stable domain has finite character if and only if it has the local stability property, and the Bazzoni conjecture for Prüfer domains (Prüfer LPI ⟹ finite character) was proved by Holland–Martinez–McGovern–Tesemma and independently by Halter-Koch. Subsequent work by Gabelli–Roitman ("On finitely stable domains, I, II") and others on LPI domains continues to address related characterizations, but I did not find a published resolution of the question of whether every finitely stable LPI-domain must have finite character. The problem appears to remain open.

For a real number s>0, let $G_s$ denote the Gevrey-$s$ class of formal power series $F(z)=\sum_{n\ge 1} a_n z^n \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ with $F'(0)\ne 0$, namely those formal germs satisfying a bound of the form $|a_n|\le C\,K^n (n!)^s$ for some constants $C,K>0$. For an irrational number $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, write $R_\alpha(z)=e^{2\pi i\alpha}z$ for the corresponding rotation, and say a germ $F\in G_s$ with multiplier $F'(0)=e^{2\pi i\alpha}$ is conjugate to $R_\alpha$ in $G_r$ if there exists a tangent-to-identity formal germ $H\in G_r$ with $H(0)=0$, $H'(0)=1$, such that $H^{-1}\circ F\circ H = R_\alpha$ as formal series.

For real numbers $r>s>0$, define
$$g_{r,s}\;=\;\bigl\{\,\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}\;:\;\text{every }F\in G_s\text{ with }F'(0)=e^{2\pi i\alpha}\text{ is conjugate to }R_\alpha\text{ via some }H\in G_r\,\bigr\}.$$

Determine the set $g_{r,s}$ explicitly as an arithmetic subset of $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$; that is, characterize precisely which irrational numbers $\alpha$ belong to $g_{r,s}$ in terms of the Diophantine properties of $\alpha$ (e.g. continued fraction expansion, Brjuno-type sums).

The problem of fully characterizing the sets $g_{r,s}$ for $r>s>0$ appears to remain open. It is classically known that every Brjuno number lies in $g_{s,s}$ (Carletti–Marmi), and recent work (e.g. Bounemoura and collaborators on optimal linearization in non-analytic Gevrey classes for circle diffeomorphisms and vector fields on the torus) has identified weaker-than-Brjuno arithmetic conditions when one allows the conjugacy to be less regular than the germ. However, a complete description of $g_{r,s}$ for arbitrary $r>s>0$ in the germ setting has not been established.

Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$. For a nonzero fractional ideal $I$ of $D$, set $I^{-1}=\{x\in K : xI\subseteq D\}$, $I_v=(I^{-1})^{-1}$, and $I_t=\bigcup\{J_v : J\subseteq I \text{ is a nonzero finitely generated subideal}\}$. The ideal $I$ is called a $t$-ideal if $I=I_t$, and $I$ is $t$-invertible if $(II^{-1})_t=D$. A maximal $t$-ideal is an ideal maximal among proper integral $t$-ideals; every such ideal is prime. The domain $D$ is said to be of finite $t$-character if every nonzero nonunit of $D$ is contained in only finitely many maximal $t$-ideals. A nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ is $t$-locally principal if, for every maximal $t$-ideal $M$ of $D$, the extension $ID_M$ is a principal ideal of $D_M$.

The domain $D$ is called an almost GCD domain (AGCD domain) if for every pair $x,y\in D\setminus\{0\}$ there exists a positive integer $n=n(x,y)$ such that $x^nD\cap y^nD$ is principal.

Question: Suppose $D$ is an almost GCD domain in which every nonzero $t$-locally principal ideal is $t$-invertible. Must $D$ be of finite $t$-character?

Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$ denote the set of all nonzero $D$-submodules of $K$. A semistar operation on $D$ is a map $\star:\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)\to\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$, $E\mapsto E^\star$, such that for all $E,F\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$ and all $0\ne x\in K$:
(i) $(xE)^\star=xE^\star$;
(ii) $E\subseteq E^\star$;
(iii) $E\subseteq F\Rightarrow E^\star\subseteq F^\star$;
(iv) $(E^\star)^\star=E^\star$.

A semistar operation $\star$ is said to be of finite type if for every $E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$, $E^\star=\bigcup\{F^\star:F\subseteq E,\ F\text{ a finitely generated }D\text{-submodule of }K\}$.

Two constructions are considered:

(a) Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a family of overrings of $D$ (i.e.\ rings with $D\subseteq T\subseteq K$), and for each $T\in\mathcal{T}$ let $\star_T$ be a semistar operation on $T$. Define a semistar operation $\star_\mathcal{T}$ on $D$ by
$$E^{\star_\mathcal{T}}:=\bigcap_{T\in\mathcal{T}}(ET)^{\star_T}\qquad(E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)).$$

(b) Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of semistar operations on $D$. Define the intersection semistar operation $\wedge_\mathcal{S}$ on $D$ by
$$E^{\wedge_\mathcal{S}}:=\bigcap_{\star\in\mathcal{S}}E^\star\qquad(E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)).$$

Problem: Determine necessary and sufficient conditions
(a) on the family $\mathcal{T}$ and the operations $\{\star_T\}_{T\in\mathcal{T}}$ under which $\star_\mathcal{T}$ is of finite type;
(b) on the family $\mathcal{S}$ under which $\wedge_\mathcal{S}$ is of finite type.

A semistar operation $\star$ is said to be of finite type if for every $E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)$, $E^\star=\bigcup\{F^\star:F\subseteq E,\ F\text{ a finitely generated }D\text{-submodule of }K\}$.

Two constructions are considered:

(a) Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a family of overrings of $D$ (i.e.\ rings with $D\subseteq T\subseteq K$), and for each $T\in\mathcal{T}$ let $\star_T$ be a semistar operation on $T$. Define a semistar operation $\star_\mathcal{T}$ on $D$ by
$$E^{\star_\mathcal{T}}:=\bigcap_{T\in\mathcal{T}}(ET)^{\star_T}\qquad(E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)).$$

(b) Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of semistar operations on $D$. Define the intersection semistar operation $\wedge_\mathcal{S}$ on $D$ by
$$E^{\wedge_\mathcal{S}}:=\bigcap_{\star\in\mathcal{S}}E^\star\qquad(E\in\overline{\mathbf{F}}(D)).$$

Problem: Determine necessary and sufficient conditions
(a) on the family $\mathcal{T}$ and the operations $\{\star_T\}_{T\in\mathcal{T}}$ under which $\star_\mathcal{T}$ is of finite type;
(b) on the family $\mathcal{S}$ under which $\wedge_\mathcal{S}$ is of finite type.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem has been partially addressed via topological/spectral methods on the space of semistar operations of finite type. It is known that the infimum of a quasi-compact family of finite-type semistar operations is of finite type, and a converse holds when each operation is induced by a localization or a valuation overring; the general converse for arbitrary families of overrings remains conjectural. No complete characterization in the generality posed appears to have been established.

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions. Let D be an integral domain with field of fractions K. The Krull dimension dim(D) is the supremum of lengths of chains of prime ideals of D. The valuative dimension dim_v(D) is the supremum of the Krull dimensions of all valuation overrings of D (valuation rings V with D ⊆ V ⊆ K). For every integral domain D one has the inequalities

  dim(D) + 1 ≤ dim(D[X]) ≤ 2·dim(D) + 1, and dim(D[X]) ≤ dim(D) + dim_v(D) + 1.

D is called a Jaffard domain if dim(D) is finite and dim(D) = dim_v(D). D is locally Jaffard if D_P is a Jaffard domain for every prime ideal P of D (equivalently, every localization of D at a prime is Jaffard). Noetherian domains, Prüfer domains of finite dimension, and finite-dimensional universally catenary domains are all locally Jaffard. A Krull domain is an integral domain that is the intersection of a family of discrete valuation overrings with the finite-character property; a factorial (UFD) domain is in particular a Krull domain.

There is a known construction (referred to as "David's domain") of a three-dimensional non-Noetherian Krull domain J obtained by a pullback / D + M-type construction that exhibits anomalous polynomial-dimension behavior; let J denote such a domain.

Problems.

(a) Does there exist a Krull domain D — or, more strongly, a factorial domain D — such that
  dim(D) + 1 < dim(D[X])?

(b) Is the domain J described above a locally Jaffard domain?

(c) Let A ⊆ D be an extension of integral domains in which A is Noetherian and D is an A-subalgebra of some affine A-domain T (i.e., T is a finitely generated A-algebra that is a domain, and D is a sub-A-algebra of T). Must D necessarily be a locally Jaffard domain?

An integral domain $R$ is called a Mori domain if it satisfies the ascending chain condition on divisorial (i.e., $v$-) ideals. An atomic domain $R$ (every nonzero non-unit factors as a product of atoms/irreducibles) is said to be locally tame if for every atom $u \in R$ there exists a constant $\omega(R,u) \in \mathbb{N}_0 \cup \{\infty\}$, finite, such that whenever $u$ divides a product $a_1 \cdots a_n$ of atoms of $R$, there is a subproduct of length at most $\omega(R,u)$ which is divisible by $u$ (equivalently, the local tame degree at every atom is finite).

Let $R$ be a one-dimensional local Mori domain (i.e., a Mori domain with Krull dimension one and a unique maximal ideal). Must $R$ be locally tame?

Let $n \geq 1$ and $k > n$ be integers, and let $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be vectors that generate $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a real vector space. For each $i$, let $R_{\alpha_i}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ denote the translation $x \mapsto x + \alpha_i$. These translations commute and define a $\mathbb{Z}^k$-action on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by translations.

Consider real-analytic diffeomorphisms $f_1, \dots, f_k \in \mathrm{Diff}^{\omega}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ that pairwise commute, are sufficiently close to $R_{\alpha_1}, \dots, R_{\alpha_k}$ in the real-analytic topology, and thus define a $\mathbb{Z}^k$-action on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Assume there exists a homeomorphism $h: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ such that
$$ h \circ f_i \circ h^{-1} = R_{\alpha_i} \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, k, $$
i.e., the action is $C^0$-conjugate to the translation action.

Determine, in terms of arithmetic (Diophantine-type) conditions on the rotation vectors $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k$, for which choices of $(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k)$ the conjugating homeomorphism $h$ must be real-analytic.

The question is posed as an open problem on rigidity of higher-rank abelian translation actions under small-divisor (Diophantine) conditions. Let $D$ be a discrete valuation ring with finite residue field, and let $K$ be its field of fractions. Consider the ring of integer-valued polynomials
$$\mathrm{Int}(D) = \{f \in K[X] : f(D) \subseteq D\}.$$
It is known that $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ is an atomic domain that is not a unique factorization domain: there exist nonzero non-unit elements admitting essentially distinct factorizations into irreducibles, and even into irreducibles of different lengths. Call an irreducible $f \in \mathrm{Int}(D)$ absolutely irreducible if every power $f^n$ factors uniquely (up to units and order) into irreducibles; otherwise call $f$ non-absolutely irreducible.

Provide a complete analysis and description of non-unique factorization in $\mathrm{Int}(D)$. In particular:
(a) Characterize, in terms of arithmetic data of $D$, the irreducible elements of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$ and distinguish the absolutely irreducible ones from the non-absolutely irreducible ones.
(b) Determine, for each nonzero non-unit $f \in \mathrm{Int}(D)$, the set of factorization lengths $\mathcal{L}(f) = \{n : f = a_1 \cdots a_n \text{ with each } a_i \text{ irreducible}\}$, and describe which finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ arise as length sets of elements of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$.
(c) Describe the structure of the system of sets of lengths and other standard arithmetic invariants (elasticity, sets of distances, catenary and tame degrees) of $\mathrm{Int}(D)$.

For a commutative ring R, let Spec(R) denote its prime spectrum, viewed as a partially ordered set under inclusion of prime ideals. Consider the following questions about order-types of spectra of two-dimensional polynomial rings.

(a) Find a list of axioms (in the language of partially ordered sets) that characterizes Spec(ℚ[x,y]) up to order-isomorphism, analogously to the known axiomatic characterization of Spec(ℤ[x]).

(b) Decide whether the posets Spec(ℚ[x,y]) and Spec(ℚ(√2)[x,y]) are order-isomorphic.

(c) More generally, let F and K be algebraic number fields (finite extensions of ℚ) and let A be a two-dimensional affine F-domain (i.e., an integral domain that is finitely generated as an F-algebra and has Krull dimension 2). Decide whether Spec(A) must be order-isomorphic, as a partially ordered set, to Spec(K[x,y]).

(d) Suppose F and K are fields, each of which is not algebraic over a finite field, and suppose Spec(F[x,y]) and Spec(K[x,y]) are order-isomorphic as partially ordered sets. Must F and K be isomorphic as fields?

Let $V$ be a compact smooth (i.e. $C^\infty$) manifold without boundary, and let $f\colon V\to V$ be a $C^\infty$-diffeomorphism. Assume that $f$ is cohomologically rigid in the following sense: for every smooth function $\varphi\in C^\infty(V)$, there exist a smooth function $\psi\in C^\infty(V)$ and a real constant $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$\psi\circ f-\psi=\varphi+\lambda.$$
A translation $T_\alpha\colon x\mapsto x+\alpha$ on the torus $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ is called Diophantine if there exist constants $C>0$ and $\tau>0$ such that for every $k\in\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}$ one has $|\langle k,\alpha\rangle-n|\geq C|k|^{-\tau}$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z$.

Prove or disprove: under the above hypothesis, $V$ must be diffeomorphic to a torus $\mathbb T^d$ and $f$ must be $C^\infty$-conjugate to a Diophantine translation of $\mathbb T^d$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classification of triples $(a,b,c)$ for which the integral closure of $(x^a,y^b,z^c)$ in $k[x,y,z]$ is normal is a well-known open problem in commutative algebra. Partial results exist (e.g., a recent result that every integrally closed monomial ideal in $k[x,y,z]$ with at most seven minimal monomial generators is normal, while $(x^7,y^3,z^2)$ produces a counterexample with eight generators), but no complete classification of the triples appears in the literature.

Let $\mathbb{A} = \mathbb{T} \times \mathbb{R}$ denote the closed (or open) annulus with coordinates $(\theta, r)$, equipped with the standard area form $d\theta \wedge dr$. A diffeomorphism $f: \mathbb{A} \to \mathbb{A}$ of class $C^r$ is called an area-preserving twist map if it preserves $d\theta \wedge dr$, preserves orientation and the two ends of the annulus, and satisfies the twist condition $\partial \theta_1 / \partial r > 0$, where $(\theta_1, r_1) = f(\theta, r)$ (with $\theta_1$ taken as a lift to $\mathbb{R}$). A rotational (essential) invariant curve for $f$ is a homotopically nontrivial simple closed curve $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{A}$ with $f(\Gamma) = \Gamma$; by Birkhoff's theorem, every such curve is the graph of a Lipschitz function $\psi: \mathbb{T} \to \mathbb{R}$.

For each fixed regularity class $r \in [1, \infty] \cup \{\omega\}$ (where $\omega$ denotes real-analytic), does there exist an area-preserving twist map $f$ of class $C^r$ on $\mathbb{A}$ that admits a rotational invariant curve $\Gamma$ which is not of class $C^1$ (equivalently, whose graphing function $\psi$ is not continuously differentiable)?

The question is resolved affirmatively in low regularity: M.-C. Arnaud constructed a $C^1$ symplectic twist map with a non-differentiable essential invariant curve (2011), and Avila–Fayad (2019) extended this to a $C^1$ example with minimal dynamics on the curve. Background. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and $I \subseteq R$ an ideal. The integral closure of $I$ is the ideal $\overline{I} = \{x \in R : x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n = 0 \text{ for some } n \geq 1 \text{ and } a_i \in I^i\}$. Two known algorithms for computing the integral closure of a reduced ring $R$ finitely generated over a finite field of characteristic $p>0$ are:

(i) The Leonard–Pellikaan algorithm, which applies to suitably weighted affine domains over finite fields and proceeds by iteratively constructing modules $V_{e+1} = \{f \in V_e : f^{p} \in V_e\}$ from an initial finite module $V_0$ containing the integral closure.

(ii) The Singh–Swanson algorithm, which is a generalization of (i) computing the integral closure of any reduced ring finitely generated over a finite field, also using the Frobenius/$p$-th power map.

Both algorithms compute the integral closure of the ambient ring rather than of an ideal.

Problem.
(a) Construct a direct algorithm for computing the integral closure $\overline{I}$ of a general ideal $I$ in a Noetherian commutative ring, more efficient or more direct than reducing to the integral closure of the Rees ring $R[It] = \bigoplus_{n \geq 0} I^n t^n$.

(b) In particular, modify the Leonard–Pellikaan algorithm and/or the Singh–Swanson algorithm so that, given an ideal $I$ in an affine domain (or a reduced affine ring) over a finite field of characteristic $p > 0$, the algorithm directly outputs a presentation of the integral closure $\overline{I}$ (rather than the integral closure of a ring).

Setup. Let $R$ be a Noetherian domain with field of fractions $K$, and let $S$ be a Noetherian extension domain of $R$ with field of fractions $L$, where $L/K$ is a finite separable field extension. Assume that:

(a) $R$ is universally catenary;
(b) for every prime ideal $Q$ of $S$ lying over a prime $P$ of $R$, the local ring $R_P$ is Cohen–Macaulay and $\mathrm{ht}(Q)=\mathrm{ht}(P)$;
(c) $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra, generically étale over $R$, and the integral closure $\overline{S}$ of $S$ in $L$ is module-finite over $R$.

Let $J_{S/R}$ denote the Jacobian ideal of $S$ over $R$ (the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a Jacobian matrix coming from a presentation of $S$ as an $R$-algebra). The general Lipman–Sathaye theorem in this setting asserts the containment
$$ J_{S/R}\cdot \overline{S} \;\subseteq\; (R : _{L}\, \overline{S})\, , $$
where $(R:_L \overline{S}) = \{x\in L : x\overline{S}\subseteq R\}$ is the conductor-type module, equivalently $J_{S/R}$ multiplies $\overline{S}$ into $R$ relative to the standard trace pairing.

Problem. Determine how sharp the hypotheses (a)–(c) are. Specifically, choose a proper relaxation of one of the assumptions — for example, dropping the Cohen–Macaulay hypothesis on $R_P$, weakening the equidimensionality condition $\mathrm{ht}(Q)=\mathrm{ht}(P)$, removing universal catenarity, weakening separability of $L/K$, or replacing module-finiteness of $\overline{S}$ over $R$ by a weaker finiteness condition — and either:

(i) prove that the conclusion $J_{S/R}\cdot \overline{S}\subseteq (R:_L \overline{S})$ continues to hold under the relaxed hypotheses, or
(ii) construct an explicit example of $R\subseteq S$ satisfying the relaxed hypotheses for which the conclusion fails.

The problem, posed as a meta-question about relaxing the hypotheses of the general Lipman–Sathaye Jacobian theorem, is not a single precise statement with a recorded resolution. Refinements and reformulations exist (e.g., presentation-depth versions and Mather–Jacobian variants), but no comprehensive result determining the exact sharpness of the assumptions appears in the literature. The status is therefore taken to be open.

Let $A = \mathbb{T} \times \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{T} \times [0,1]$) be the annulus, and let $f : A \to A$ be a $C^r$ area-preserving diffeomorphism with $r \ge 3$ satisfying the twist condition (in suitable coordinates $(x,y)$, lifting $f$ to $\tilde f(x,y) = (X(x,y), Y(x,y))$ on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$, one has $\partial X/\partial y > 0$). An $f$-invariant set $K \subset A$ is called action-minimizing (Aubry–Mather) if it is the support of an invariant Borel probability measure that minimizes the average of a generating-function action among all $f$-invariant probability measures with the same rotation number; equivalently, every orbit in $K$ is globally action-minimizing with respect to a generating function for $f$. Define
$$ \mathcal{M}(f) = \bigcup \bigl\{ K : K \text{ is an action-minimizing invariant set of } f,\ K \text{ is not a closed (rotational) invariant curve, and } K \text{ contains no periodic orbit}\bigr\}. $$
Is it true that $\dim_H \mathcal{M}(f) = 0$, where $\dim_H$ denotes Hausdorff dimension?

Consider the Newtonian n+1-body problem in $\mathbb{R}^d$: point masses $m_0, m_1, \dots, m_n > 0$ with positions $q_0(t), \dots, q_n(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ evolving according to
$$ m_i \ddot q_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{m_i m_j (q_j - q_i)}{\|q_j - q_i\|^3}, \qquad i = 0, 1, \dots, n. $$
The total energy is $H = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_i m_i \|\dot q_i\|^2 - \sum_{i<j} \frac{m_i m_j}{\|q_i - q_j\|}$, and the moment of inertia about the center of mass is
$$ I(t) = \sum_{i=0}^n m_i \|q_i(t) - q_{\mathrm{cm}}\|^2, \qquad q_{\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{\sum_i m_i q_i}{\sum_i m_i}. $$
Restrict to initial conditions with $H < 0$ (negative total energy), so that the system is bounded in mean (and one may further restrict to planar motion, $d = 2$).

(a) For $n = 2$ (the three-body problem in the plane with negative total energy), is it true that the set of initial conditions for which $I(t) \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$ contains a dense open subset of the phase space of bounded-energy initial data?

(b) Answer the analogous question for general $n \geq 3$.

Let $\omega \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be a fixed Diophantine frequency vector, and consider one-parameter families $\{A_\lambda\}_{\lambda \in I}$ (with $I \subset \mathbb{R}$ a parameter interval) of analytic maps $A_\lambda : \mathbb{T}^d \to G$, where $G$ is a (semisimple) matrix Lie group such as $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, $SU(2)$, or more generally a compact or noncompact reductive group. To each $A_\lambda$ one associates the linear quasiperiodic skew-product (cocycle) on $\mathbb{T}^d \times \mathbb{C}^n$ defined by
$$ (\theta, v) \longmapsto (\theta + \omega, \; A_\lambda(\theta) v). $$
Such a cocycle is called reducible if there exists an analytic map $B : \mathbb{T}^d \to G$ (possibly on a double cover) and a constant matrix $C \in G$ such that
$$ B(\theta + \omega)^{-1} A_\lambda(\theta) B(\theta) = C \quad \text{for all } \theta \in \mathbb{T}^d. $$
Assume the family $\lambda \mapsto A_\lambda$ is analytic and sufficiently close to a constant family (i.e., $A_\lambda(\theta)$ is uniformly close to a $\theta$-independent matrix on a complex neighborhood of $\mathbb{T}^d$).

Prove that for a generic such analytic one-parameter family that is sufficiently close to constant coefficients, the cocycle defined by $A_\lambda$ is reducible for Lebesgue-almost every parameter $\lambda \in I$.

The full statement, asking for almost-everywhere reducibility along generic analytic one-parameter families near constant coefficients in arbitrary Lie groups, remains a guiding conjecture in the area. Substantial partial results are known: Eliasson proved reducibility for a positive-measure set of parameters for Diophantine frequencies and cocycles close to constant; Avila established the Almost Reducibility Conjecture for one-frequency analytic SL(2,R) cocycles, and various extensions (Gevrey classes, finitely differentiable cocycles, nonperturbative versions by Hou–You and others) have been obtained. However, the general genericity and a.e.-reducibility statement in the form posed has not been fully resolved.

Consider the discrete quasiperiodic Schrödinger equation on $\mathbb{Z}$,
$$(H_{\theta,\omega}\psi)_n = \psi_{n+1} + \psi_{n-1} + V(\theta + n\omega)\,\psi_n = E\,\psi_n,$$
where $V \in C^0(\mathbb{T}^d,\mathbb{R})$ is a real-valued function on the torus $\mathbb{T}^d = \mathbb{R}^d/\mathbb{Z}^d$, $\omega \in \mathbb{T}^d$ is a fixed rationally independent frequency vector, and $\theta \in \mathbb{T}^d$ is a phase. Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{T}$ be a spectral parameter (rotation number / quasi-momentum), and equip $\mathbb{T}$ with its Haar measure.

Assume there exist:
(i) a measurable function $E_\infty : \mathbb{T} \to \mathbb{R}$, and
(ii) for almost every $\alpha \in \mathbb{T}$, a measurable map $\theta \mapsto u(\theta;\alpha) \in L^2(\mathbb{T}^d)$ (also measurable in $\alpha$) such that the sequence
$$\psi_n(\theta;\alpha) = e^{i n \alpha} u(\theta + n\omega;\alpha), \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z},$$
solves the equation above with $E = E_\infty(\alpha)$ for almost every $\theta$.

Assume further the non-degeneracy condition: for every measurable set $Y \subset \mathbb{T}$, if the Lebesgue measure of $E_\infty(Y)$ is zero, then the Haar measure of $Y$ is also zero.

Question: Under these hypotheses, is the spectrum of $H_{\theta,\omega}$ (for a.e. $\theta$) purely absolutely continuous?

Develop a non-perturbative method for constructing time-periodic solutions of a Hamiltonian partial differential equation. More precisely, consider a Hamiltonian PDE of the form
   u_t = J ∇H(u),
where u(t,x) belongs to a suitable function space over a spatial domain (e.g. the torus T^d or an interval with appropriate boundary conditions), J is a symplectic structure, and H is a Hamiltonian functional. Produce a method—not relying on a small-parameter (perturbative) expansion around an integrable or linear equation, and not relying on KAM/Nash–Moser-type perturbation theory near such an unperturbed system—that establishes the existence of genuine time-periodic solutions u(t+T,x) = u(t,x) for some period T > 0. The required solutions must not be traveling waves; that is, they should not be obtainable from a stationary profile via the ansatz u(t,x) = v(x - ct) for some constant velocity c.

No general non-perturbative construction (excluding traveling waves) appears to be available, and the problem is still cited as a guiding open question in surveys on Hamiltonian PDEs.

Consider the massless φ⁴ nonlinear wave equation
   u_tt = u_xx − u³,   x ∈ T¹ = R/2πZ,   t ∈ R,
posed on the one-dimensional torus with periodic boundary conditions. Note that this equation is completely resonant: the linearized equation u_tt = u_xx has the integer spectrum of frequencies {|k| : k ∈ Z}, so there is no parameter (such as a mass term m²u or a potential V(x)u) to tune frequencies away from resonances.

Problem. For any integer d ≥ 2, construct small-amplitude time-quasiperiodic solutions of this equation with d rationally independent frequencies. More precisely, exhibit a positive-measure (in the sense of Lebesgue or Whitney-smooth Cantor-like) family of frequency vectors ω = (ω₁,…,ω_d) ∈ R^d and corresponding classical (or analytic) solutions
   u(t,x) = U(ω₁ t, …, ω_d t, x),
where U : T^d × T¹ → R is continuous (and as smooth as possible), such that ‖u‖ → 0 as the family parameter tends to zero, and such that the closure of the orbit {(ω₁ t, …, ω_d t) : t ∈ R} is dense in T^d.

Partial results exist: quasi-periodic solutions with two frequencies for completely resonant nonlinear wave equations u_tt − u_xx ± u³ = 0 on T¹ have been constructed (Berti–Bolle, Gentile–Procesi, and related works), typically via Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction combined with resummation/Nash–Moser techniques. For a finite point set P in the Euclidean plane, a triangulation of P is a maximal plane straight-line graph whose vertex set is P. For a plane straight-line graph G with vertex set P, the spanning ratio (stretch factor, or dilation) of G is

  sr(G) = max_{u,v ∈ P, u ≠ v} d_G(u,v) / |uv|,

where d_G(u,v) is the length of a shortest path from u to v in G (edges weighted by Euclidean length) and |uv| is the Euclidean distance. For a finite point set P, let

  τ(P) = inf { sr(T) : T is a triangulation of P },

and define the universal lower bound

  t* = sup_P τ(P),

where the supremum is taken over all finite planar point sets P.

  τ(P) = inf { sr(T) : T is a triangulation of P },

and define the universal lower bound

  t* = sup_P τ(P),

where the supremum is taken over all finite planar point sets P.

It is known that t* ≥ √2.005367532. Determine the exact value of t*. In particular, decide whether there exists a real number t > √2.005367532 and a finite planar point set P such that every triangulation of P has spanning ratio at least t.

Let $P$ be a finite set of points in the plane, and let $G=(P,E)$ be a plane straight-line graph on $P$ (i.e., a planar graph whose edges are non-crossing straight-line segments between points of $P$). For a parameter $0<\alpha<\pi/2$, say that $G$ has the $\alpha$-diamond property if, for every edge $e=uv\in E$, at least one of the two isosceles triangles having $e$ as base and base angle $\alpha$ (one on each side of $e$) contains no point of $P\setminus\{u,v\}$ in its interior. For a parameter $d\ge 1$, say that $G$ has the $d$-good polygon property if, for every face $F$ of $G$ and every pair of vertices $u,v$ on the boundary of $F$ such that the open segment $uv$ lies in the interior of $F$, the shorter of the two boundary paths from $u$ to $v$ along $\partial F$ has Euclidean length at most $d\cdot\|u-v\|$.

The spanning ratio of $G$ is $\sup_{u\ne v\in P} \frac{d_G(u,v)}{\|u-v\|}$, where $d_G$ denotes shortest-path distance in $G$ using Euclidean edge lengths.

It is known that any such $G$ satisfying both properties has spanning ratio at most
$$\frac{8d(\pi-\alpha)^2}{\alpha^2\sin^2(\alpha/4)}.$$

Question: Can this upper bound be replaced by a strictly smaller function of $\alpha$ and $d$ that still holds for every finite point set $P$ and every plane straight-line graph $G$ on $P$ with the $\alpha$-diamond property and the $d$-good polygon property?

Let P be a finite set of points in general position in the Euclidean plane, and let DT(P) denote its (standard) Euclidean Delaunay triangulation: the straight-line plane graph in which two points p, q ∈ P are joined by an edge if and only if there exists a closed disk that has p and q on its boundary and contains no other point of P in its interior.

For a real number t ≥ 1, a geometric graph G on the vertex set P (with straight-line edges weighted by Euclidean distance) is called a t-spanner of P if for every pair of points p, q ∈ P, the length of a shortest path from p to q in G is at most t · |pq|, where |pq| denotes the Euclidean distance. The graph G is called plane if its edges do not cross.

Define
   d* := inf { Δ : there exists a constant t ≥ 1 such that, for every finite point set P in general position in the plane, there is a plane t-spanner of P that is a subgraph of DT(P) and has maximum vertex degree at most Δ }.

Determine the exact value of d*.

The best known upper bound is maximum degree 7, achieved by Bonichon, Gavoille, Hanusse and Ilcinkas (2010), giving a plane constant-spanner that is a subgraph of the Delaunay triangulation with max degree 7. Let P be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane. A geometric graph on P is a graph whose vertex set is P and whose edges are straight line segments between pairs of points of P, with the weight of each edge equal to the Euclidean distance between its endpoints. Such a graph is called plane if no two of its edges cross. For t ≥ 1, a geometric graph G on P is a t-spanner of P if for every pair of points p, q ∈ P the length of a shortest path between p and q in G is at most t · |pq|; the spanning ratio of G is the infimum of such t. The maximum degree of G is the largest number of edges of G incident to a single vertex.

Determine whether the planarity constraint forces a worst-case lower bound on the maximum degree that is strictly larger than 3. Equivalently, prove or disprove the following statement:

For every real number t > 1, there exists a finite point set P ⊂ ℝ² (in general position) such that every plane spanning subgraph of the complete geometric graph on P with maximum degree at most 3 has spanning ratio greater than t.

(In other words: is there a constant t > 1 and a construction that produces, for every finite point set P in general position in the plane, a plane t-spanner of P with maximum degree at most 3?)

Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a finite set of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane, and let $\varepsilon > 0$. A plane Steiner $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner for $P$ is a planar straight-line graph $G = (V, E)$ in the plane with $P \subseteq V$ (vertices in $V \setminus P$ are called Steiner points) such that for every pair $p, q \in P$ the shortest-path distance from $p$ to $q$ in $G$ (where each edge has Euclidean length) is at most $(1+\varepsilon)\,\|p-q\|_2$. A classical construction yields such a spanner whose total number of vertices (equivalently, number of Steiner points) is $O(n/\varepsilon^{4})$.

Determine the optimal dependence on $\varepsilon$ in the size of plane Steiner $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanners. In particular, prove or disprove: for every finite planar point set of size $n$ and every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, there exists a plane Steiner $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner with $o(n/\varepsilon^{4})$ vertices (and provide matching upper and lower bounds on the worst-case size as a function of $n$ and $\varepsilon$).

A construction giving Euclidean noncrossing Steiner (1+ε)-spanners with O(n/ε^{3/2}) edges has been established for n points in the plane, together with an almost matching lower bound of Ω(n/ε^{3/2-μ}) for any μ>0. Let P be a finite set of points in the plane and let L be a finite set of line segments with endpoints in P such that no two segments of L cross in their interiors (a noncrossing constraint set). The visibility graph VIS(P, L) has vertex set P, and an edge uv whenever the open segment uv is not properly intersected by any segment of L (segments of L are themselves considered visible). A plane constrained spanner of VIS(P, L) is a planar subgraph G of VIS(P, L), containing L, whose Euclidean stretch factor relative to VIS(P, L) is bounded by a constant t; that is, for every edge uv of VIS(P, L), the shortest-path distance in G between u and v (using Euclidean edge weights) is at most t times the length |uv|.

Determine, in this constrained setting, the analogues of the principal open quantitative questions known for unconstrained plane spanners. Concretely:

(a) What is the smallest constant t for which, for every finite point set P and every noncrossing constraint set L, there exists a plane constrained t-spanner of VIS(P, L)?

(b) What is the smallest constant t for which, for every such (P, L), there exists a plane constrained t-spanner of VIS(P, L) of bounded maximum degree, and what is the minimum degree bound achievable simultaneously with a given t?

(c) Establish matching lower bounds (impossibility results) on t in (a) and (b).

The task is to settle these constants and tradeoffs, or to obtain improved upper and lower bounds beyond the currently known ones.

Consider a single-server queue with a finite buffer of size $K$ (a GI/G/1/K queue): customers arrive according to a renewal process with i.i.d. inter-arrival times having distribution $A$ (mean $1/\lambda$, squared coefficient of variation $c_a^2$), are served by a single server with i.i.d. service times having distribution $S$ (mean $1/\mu$, squared coefficient of variation $c_s^2$), and any customer arriving to a full buffer is lost. Operate the queue in the critically loaded regime $\lambda=\mu$, and let $D(t)$ denote the number of customer departures in $[0,t]$ in steady state. Define the asymptotic variance rate
$$ V_K := \lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{\operatorname{Var}(D(t))}{t}, $$
and the BRAVO factor
$$ B_K := \frac{V_K}{\lambda\,(c_a^2+c_s^2)}. $$
It is conjectured that for "nice" inter-arrival and service distributions, $B_K \to 1/3$ as $K\to\infty$ (the GI/G/1/K BRAVO conjecture).

Numerical experiments suggest the following dichotomy when $A$ and $S$ are chosen from heavy-tailed families with matched first two moments:
(i) If $A$ and $S$ are heavy-tailed Weibull distributions (shape parameter $<1$), then $B_K$ appears to converge to $1/3$, behaving like light-tailed distributions.

$$ V_K := \lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{\operatorname{Var}(D(t))}{t}, $$
and the BRAVO factor
$$ B_K := \frac{V_K}{\lambda\,(c_a^2+c_s^2)}. $$

(i) If $A$ and $S$ are heavy-tailed Weibull distributions (shape parameter $<1$), then $B_K$ appears to converge to $1/3$, behaving like light-tailed distributions.
